boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis, וְאִם כֶּבֶשׂ יָבִיא קָרְבָּנוֹ לְחַטָּאת, opens the lamb alternative within the commoner offender class, structurally identical in evidence class (fresh casuistic protasis) to the signal that earned 4:22 (M8-Lev-013) 'high' and 4:27 (M8-Lev-014) 'medium.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: Could be merged with 4:27-31 as one 'commoner case' since the procedure duplicates it almost verbatim except for the named animal, but the fresh protasis opening is the same tier-1 marker honored throughout ch.4's offender-class structure.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.4.32 וְאִם כֶּבֶשׂ יָבִיא קָרְבָּנוֹ לְחַטָּאת (single-witness)
oshb:Lev.4.35 וְנִסְלַח לוֹ (single-witness, matching 4:31's closing atonement formula)

boundary_rationale: Chapter 5 opens without a fresh 'Yahweh spoke' formula, continuing ch.4's sin-offering discourse but introducing a new list-register of four distinct guilt-triggers (withheld testimony, unclean-carcass contact, human-uncleanness contact, rash oath) stacked as parallel 'or if' clauses before the shared confession-and-offering apodosis in vv.5-6, marking this as its own case type structurally distinct from ch.4's offender-class organization.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because ch.5 has no new messenger formula, a reader could treat all of 4:1-5:13 as one undivided sin-offering discourse; but ch.5's organizing principle visibly shifts from 'who sinned' to 'what triggered the guilt,' a genuine register change even without a fresh superscription.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.5.1 "If anyone sins, in that he hears a public adjuration to testify"
oshb:Lev.5.4 אוֹ נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תִשָּׁבַע לְבַטֵּא בִשְׂפָתַיִם

boundary_rationale: A means-tested protasis, 'if he can't afford a lamb,' opens the first of two graduated alternatives for the poor, matching the same provision-scaling pattern used later for the leper's offering in ch.14, and specifies a wholly different bird-based procedure (wringing the neck without severing it) absent from the base case.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be treated as a mere footnote to vv.1-6 rather than an independent chunk, since it addresses the same underlying sin; but the text opens it with its own conditional and its own complete offering procedure, the same formal marker used to split offender classes in ch.4.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.5.7 "If he can't afford a lamb...two turtledoves, or two young pigeons"
oshb:Lev.5.7 וְאִם לֹא תַגִּיעַ יָדוֹ דֵּי שֶׂה

boundary_rationale: A second means-tested protasis, 'if he can't afford two turtledoves,' opens the poorest tier of provision, distinguished procedurally by the total absence of oil and frankincense and by the priest's handful substituting for slaughter entirely -- the clearest functional break in the whole graduated sequence.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might fold this into the bird case as 'the poor-provision unit' generally, but this flour case uniquely omits blood ritual altogether, which is too large a procedural difference to bury inside a chunk built around bird sacrifice.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.5.11 "if he can't afford two turtledoves...one tenth of an ephah of fine flour"
web:Lev.5.11 "He shall put no oil on it, and he shall not put any frankincense on it"

boundary_rationale: A fresh full messenger formula, 'Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,' opens a new asham (guilt-offering) case entirely -- unwitting misuse of holy things -- introducing for the first time in the book a monetary restitution-plus-a-fifth mechanism alongside the ram offering.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because it is still a guilt/trespass offering like vv.1-13, a reader might merge it into the same undivided 'guilt offering' span; but the fresh messenger formula is exactly the kind of tier-1 boundary marker that opened every offender-class case in ch.4, and the restitution-plus-fifth mechanism is functionally new.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.5.16 וְאֶת חֲמִישִׁתוֹ יוֹסֵף עָלָיו ("and shall add a fifth part to it")

boundary_rationale: A new protasis without a fresh messenger formula, 'if anyone sins, doing any of the things which Yahweh has commanded not to be done, though he didn't know it,' addresses a distinct evidentiary situation -- sin never made known to the offender at all -- closing the chapter with the summary formula 'he is certainly guilty before Yahweh.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might merge this with the sacrilege case in vv.14-16 as 'guilt offerings generally,' but the two cases address different epistemic situations (misuse of a specific holy thing versus never learning what was done wrong at all), and this case has its own closing formula distinct from v.16's.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.5.17 "though he didn't know it, he is still guilty"
web:Lev.5.19 "It is a trespass offering. He is certainly guilty before Yahweh"

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens this case (WEB 6:1 = MT 5:20, oshb Lev.5.20), continuing the guilt-offering topic from ch.5 but addressing an entirely different trigger class -- deposit fraud, robbery, oppression, and false denial against a fellow Israelite -- unified by its own restitution-plus-a-fifth apodosis at v.5.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Since the topic (guilt offerings) is continuous with ch.5's close, a reader might treat 5:14-6:7 as one long undivided guilt-offering unit; but each of the three sub-cases (5:14-16, 5:17-19, 6:1-7) opens with its own protasis addressing a distinct kind of wrong, which is the book's consistent principle for splitting torot.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.6.1 "Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying" (MT Lev.5.20)
oshb:Lev.5.21 וּמָעֲלָה מַעַל בַּיהוָה וְכִחֵשׁ בַּעֲמִיתוֹ (MT numbering; "deals falsely with his neighbor")

boundary_rationale: A command formula addressed to Aaron rather than the usual 'speak to the children of Israel' -- 'Command Aaron and his sons' (MT 6:2, oshb Lev.6.2) -- opens the first of the book's five explicit zot torat ('this is the law of...') superscriptions, זֹאת תּוֹרַת הָעֹלָה, beginning a priest-facing companion series to chs.1-5's lay-facing offering instructions.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might see this as merely repeating ch.1's burnt-offering material and fold it in there; but the addressee changes from the general offerer to Aaron and his sons specifically, and the content is new (overnight altar-tending, ash removal, perpetual fire), so this is a distinct priestly-procedure torah, not a doublet.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.6.9 "This is the law of the burnt offering" (MT Lev.6.2)
oshb:Lev.6.2 צַו אֶת אַהֲרֹן וְאֶת בָּנָיו לֵאמֹר זֹאת תּוֹרַת הָעֹלָה (MT numbering)

boundary_rationale: A second zot torat superscription, 'this is the law of the meal offering' (MT 6:7, oshb Lev.6.7), opens a fresh priest-facing procedural unit covering the priestly handful, the unleavened eating requirement, and the who-may-eat restriction, distinct in both addressee and content from ch.2's lay-facing meal-offering instructions.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because the underlying offering type (meal offering) is the same as ch.2, a minimal reading might treat this as a mere appendix to ch.2 rather than its own chunk; but the zot torat formula is the book's own marker for opening a new priestly-procedure unit, matching the burnt-offering torah immediately before it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.6.14 "This is the law of the meal offering" (MT Lev.6.7)

boundary_rationale: A fresh 'Yahweh spoke to Moses' formula (MT 6:12, oshb Lev.6.12) opens a one-off ordinance rather than a general zot torat torah -- the high priest's own perpetual twice-daily grain offering, first presented on his anointing day -- distinguished from the surrounding torot by its unique occasion and its rule that it is wholly burned and never eaten.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged into the meal-offering torah immediately before it since both concern grain offerings; but this unit is introduced by its own messenger formula and governs a specific, non-repeatable class of offering (the priest's own perpetual minchah) rather than restating the general meal-offering procedure.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.6.19 "Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying" (MT Lev.6.12)
web:Lev.6.23 "Every meal offering of a priest shall be wholly burned. It shall not be eaten" (MT Lev.6.16)

boundary_rationale: A third full messenger-plus-command formula, 'Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, Speak to Aaron...this is the law of the sin offering' (MT 6:17-18, oshb Lev.6.17-18), opens the priestly-procedure sin-offering torah, closing the chapter on the disposition rule that blood-bearing sin offerings must be burned rather than eaten.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might see this and the guilt-offering torah that opens ch.7 as one continuous priestly-torot list without a real break at the chapter line; I kept them separate because this unit closes on its own complete disposition rule (v.30) before ch.7 opens with yet another independent zot torat formula for a different offering.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.6.25 "This is the law of the sin offering" (MT Lev.6.18)

boundary_rationale: A fourth zot torat superscription opens the chapter with no intervening messenger formula, 'this is the law of the trespass offering,' picking up the priestly-procedure series exactly where ch.6 left off and closing on the same most-holy disposition formula used for the sin offering.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because there is no fresh 'Yahweh spoke' formula here (only the zot torat tag), a reader might read 6:24-7:6 as one continuous unit spanning the chapter break; I kept them separate because each zot torat opening functions as its own superscription throughout this series regardless of whether a messenger formula precedes it, exactly as with the meal- and sin-offering torot in ch.6.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.7.1 "This is the law of the trespass offering: It is most holy"

boundary_rationale: The discourse shifts from the trespass-offering procedure itself to a generalizing principle spanning multiple offering types at once -- 'as is the sin offering, so is the trespass offering; there is one law for them' -- and then further generalizes to meal-offering portions, marking a coda that widens beyond any single torah just introduced.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as the closing clause of the trespass-offering torah in vv.1-6; but its opening 'as is the sin offering, so is the trespass offering' explicitly compares two DIFFERENT offering types, which is a broader claim than a single torah's own closing formula would make.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.7.7 "As is the sin offering, so is the trespass offering; there is one law for them"
oshb:Lev.7.7 כַּחַטָּאת כָּאָשָׁם תּוֹרָה אַחַת לָהֶם

boundary_rationale: A fifth zot torat superscription, 'this is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings,' opens the last of the book's five priestly torot and is immediately narrowed by its own sub-protasis, 'if he offers it for a thanksgiving,' specifying accompanying bread types and a same-day eating deadline unique to this sub-case.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might merge the superscription with the thanksgiving sub-case that immediately follows without distinguishing them, since there is no separating formula between v.11 and v.12; but the superscription itself covers ALL peace offerings while v.12 narrows to one occasion, so I judged them close enough in function to keep together as the chapter's opening torah unit rather than split a one-verse superscription off on its own.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.7.11 "This is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings"
web:Lev.7.15 "shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning"

boundary_rationale: A contrasting protasis, 'but if the sacrifice of his offering is a vow, or a free will offering,' opens a second peace-offering occasion with a relaxed two-day eating window (against the thanksgiving case's same-day rule) and its own third-day abomination penalty clause.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Since both this and the preceding case are peace offerings differing only in occasion and eating deadline, a reader might merge them into one 'peace offering eating rules' chunk; but the deadlines and penalty consequences genuinely differ (same-day-only versus two-day-with-abomination-penalty), a functional split the text marks with its own contrasting protasis.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.7.16 "if the sacrifice of his offering is a vow, or a free will offering"
oshb:Lev.7.16 וְאִם נֶדֶר אוֹ נְדָבָה זֶבַח קָרְבָּנוֹ

boundary_rationale: The topic shifts from time-limits on eating to contamination conditions -- meat touching anything unclean, or an unclean person eating it -- introduced by its own 'the meat that touches' and 'the soul who eats' clauses, and closing on the cut-off penalty rather than the burn-it disposition of the preceding cases.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as continuing the vow-offering eating-deadline rules in vv.16-18 as one long 'disposition of leftover meat' unit; but the concern genuinely shifts from time (how many days) to purity (contact with uncleanness), a different axis of regulation entirely.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.7.19 "The meat that touches any unclean thing shall not be eaten"
web:Lev.7.20 "the soul who eats of the meat...having his uncleanness on him, that soul shall be cut off"

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger-plus-address formula, 'Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, Speak to the children of Israel,' reopens direct address to the laity (after the priestly torot of 6:8-7:21) and introduces a general prohibition on eating fat and blood, applicable across all offering types rather than to peace offerings specifically.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Since fat-eating was already forbidden as part of the peace-offering procedure in ch.3, one could fold this into the peace-offering material as a reminder clause; but the fresh full messenger formula and the address to 'the children of Israel' generally (not offerers of a specific sacrifice) mark this as a new, freestanding prohibition.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.7.23 "You shall eat no fat, of bull, or sheep, or goat"

boundary_rationale: A third fresh messenger-plus-address formula opens a new topic, the wave-breast and heave-thigh allocated to the priesthood from every peace offering, distinguished from the immediately preceding fat/blood prohibition by both its formula and its entirely different subject (priestly income rather than lay prohibition).
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the fat/blood prohibition as 'more peace-offering rules,' since both concern disposal of parts of the same sacrifice; but the fresh 'Yahweh spoke...speak to the children of Israel' formula at v.28 is the same kind of marker that opened every other sub-unit in this chapter, and the content (who gets which cut) is a distinct concern from what may not be eaten.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.7.34 "the waved breast and the heaved thigh I have taken from the children of Israel...and have given them to Aaron"

boundary_rationale: A summary colophon closes the entire offering-law section (chs.1-7) by naming all six offering types together and dating the whole complex to Sinai -- 'this is the law of the burnt offering...which Yahweh commanded Moses in Mount Sinai' -- a backward-looking retrospective formula distinct in kind from every forward-looking zot torat superscription that preceded it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might tack this onto the wave-breast/heave-thigh unit as its closing verse; but a colophon that names all six offering types and dates the whole corpus to Sinai is closing the entire section (chs.1-7), not just the immediately preceding paragraph, matching the colophon function seen later at 11:46-47, 13:59, 14:54-57, and 26:46.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.7.37 "This is the law of the burnt offering, the meal offering, the sin offering, the trespass offering, the consecration, and the sacrifice of peace offerings"
oshb:Lev.7.38 בְּיוֹם צַוֹּתוֹ אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל...בְּמִדְבַּר סִינָי

boundary_rationale: The book's second major narrative section opens with a messenger formula, 'Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying,' followed by a list of items and persons to assemble, functioning as a discrete command-scene that stands apart from the legal torot of chs.1-7 by its narrative frame (Moses is instructed to perform an action, not to relay legislation to Israel).
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could run this straight into Moses's compliance in v.4 as a single 'command and compliance' unit; but the command itself (assemble persons and materials) is complete and self-contained before any action is narrated, matching the book's pattern of separating divine instruction from its narrated fulfillment (as in the tabernacle-execution parallel structure).
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.8.3 "assemble all the congregation at the door of the Tent of Meeting"

boundary_rationale: A compliance notice, 'Moses did as Yahweh commanded him,' opens the narrated fulfillment of the preceding command, and Moses's address to the assembled congregation -- 'this is the thing which Yahweh has commanded to be done' -- functions as a scene-opening announcement before the actual ordination actions begin in v.6.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the washing/vesting sequence beginning at v.6 as its introduction; but the compliance formula and congregational announcement are a distinct narrative beat (assembly achieved, purpose stated) before any ritual action is performed on Aaron's person.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.8.4 "Moses did as Yahweh commanded him"
web:Lev.8.5 "This is the thing which Yahweh has commanded to be done"

boundary_rationale: The narrative shifts to concrete ritual action on Aaron's person -- washing, then a sequential vesting in tunic, sash, robe, ephod, breastplate, turban, and golden plate -- forming one continuous investiture sequence closed by the compliance tag 'as Yahweh commanded Moses.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the washing (v.6) from the vesting proper (7-9), but the two are bound by a single unbroken narrative action with no participant or object change between them, unlike the shift to the anointing oil that follows in v.10.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.8.6 "Moses brought Aaron and his sons, and washed them with water"

boundary_rationale: The anointing-oil sequence (tabernacle, altar, Aaron, then the sons' vesting) is bounded on both ends by the כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה refrain: it opens immediately after the refrain closes 8:9, and closes on the refrain's own recurrence at v.13, the same delimiting device honored throughout ch.8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Could be folded into M8-Lev-036 as one continuous 'Aaron's ordination' unit, but the object of the ritual action genuinely shifts from vestments to the anointing oil itself, and the span is refrain-delimited at both ends independent of that broader-merge question.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.8.9 (refrain closing the preceding unit, single-witness)
oshb:Lev.8.13 כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (single-witness)

boundary_rationale: The narrative moves from vesting/anointing preparation to the first sacrificial act of the ordination, the bull of the sin offering, opened by the new object 'he brought the bull' and following the same blood-application and outside-camp-burning procedure used for the priest's own sin offering in ch.4.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader could treat this as simply the next beat in one long ordination-day narrative running continuously from v.1 to v.36; but the shift to a distinct sacrificial animal with its own complete kill-blood-burn sequence is the same kind of functional unit that structures every other offering torah in the book.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.8.14 "He brought the bull of the sin offering"

boundary_rationale: A new offering object, 'the ram of the burnt offering,' opens the second sacrifice of the ordination day, following the same hand-laying, killing, and burning sequence as ch.1's burnt-offering torah and closing on the same compliance formula used throughout this chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the sin offering immediately before it as 'the first two ordination sacrifices,' since both close identically with 'as Yahweh commanded Moses'; but each opens with a fresh presentation of a new animal ('he presented the ram'), matching the animal-by-animal division used consistently elsewhere in the offering torot.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.8.18 "He presented the ram of the burnt offering"

boundary_rationale: The ram-of-consecration rite -- blood on ear/thumb/toe, the wave offering combining fat, bread, and thigh -- now closes precisely on the כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה refrain at v.29, the identical closing device that already brackets M8-Lev-036 through M8-Lev-039 (8:9, 8:13, 8:17, 8:21). The original 8:22-30 span crossed this refrain into un-refrained territory at v.30 without the rationale ever confronting the discrepancy, even though the refrain is the only internal structural signal available anywhere in ch.8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Could retain the original 8:22-30 span on the ground that v.30 is thematically continuous with the same sacrifice (it reuses 'blood...on the altar'), but that reading requires treating the refrain as selectively non-delimiting here while it delimits identically at four other sites in the same chapter, with no stated textual ground for the difference.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.8.29 כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (single-witness)
oshb:Lev.8.9, 8.13, 8.17, 8.21 (same refrain closing each preceding sub-unit, single-witness)

boundary_rationale: V.30 (anointing oil and altar-blood sprinkled on Aaron, his garments, his sons, and their garments) carries no closing refrain of its own and reads as the final sanctifying act completing the ordination rite, immediately followed by Moses's direct-speech instruction to eat the ordination meat and remain at the Tent door seven days (vv.31-36); grouping the unrefrained coda with the following speech-act, rather than leaving it stranded inside the refrain-bounded ram-of-consecration unit, respects the refrain's own delimiting function established across the rest of the chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Could keep v.30 attached to 8:22-29 as originally drafted, but that requires the refrain at v.29 to not actually close its unit, which is the very inconsistency this revision resolves.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.8.30 וַיִּקַּח מֹשֶׁה מִשֶּׁמֶן הַמִּשְׁחָה וּמִן הַדָּם...וַיְקַדֵּשׁ (no refrain, single-witness)
oshb:Lev.8.31 וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל אַהֲרֹן וְאֶל בָּנָיו (single-witness)

boundary_rationale: A new time notice, 'on the eighth day,' opens a fresh narrative unit following the seven-day seclusion mandated at the close of ch.8, and Moses's instructions to Aaron and to Israel to prepare specific animals form a self-contained command scene before any action is narrated.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Since ch.9 continues the same ordination process begun in ch.8, one could treat the chapter break as artificial and merge 8:31-9:4 into one 'completion of ordination' unit; but the eighth-day notice marks a genuine narrative time-jump past the seven-day interval, and the participants (Aaron, sons, and now the elders of Israel) expand beyond ch.8's cast.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.9.1 "On the eighth day, Moses called Aaron and his sons, and the elders of Israel"

boundary_rationale: The scene shifts from Moses's private instructions to a public assembly scene -- 'all the congregation came near and stood before Yahweh' -- followed by Moses's direct charge to Aaron to begin the ritual, marking the transition from preparation to performance.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with vv.1-4 as one continuous instruction-and-gathering unit; but the assembly's arrival and standing 'before Yahweh' is itself a new narrative beat marking the moment the public ceremony formally begins, distinct from Moses's private instructions to Aaron and the elders.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.9.5 "All the congregation came near and stood before Yahweh"
web:Lev.9.7 "Draw near to the altar, and offer your sin offering"

boundary_rationale: Aaron's compliance begins with his own sin offering (self-referential, 'the calf of the sin offering, which was for himself') followed immediately by his own burnt offering, both performed for Aaron's personal atonement before he moves to the people's offerings, a distinction the text draws explicitly at v.7's 'offer your sin offering...and offer the offering of the people.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the sin offering (8-11) from the burnt offering (12-14) as distinct sacrifices, matching the book's usual per-offering-type division; I merged them because both are explicitly 'for himself' as opposed to the people's offerings that follow, and the text does not reintroduce Aaron as subject between them.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.9.8 "Aaron came near to the altar, and killed the calf of the sin offering, which was for himself"

boundary_rationale: A new object, 'the people's offering,' opens Aaron's second round of sacrifices -- sin, burnt, grain, and peace offerings performed on behalf of the congregation rather than himself -- matching the explicit self/people distinction Moses drew in his charge at v.7.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could treat all of Aaron's sacrificial actions (8-21) as one undivided 'Aaron offers' sequence; but the text itself frames the offerings as two distinct movements (for himself, then for the people), and this second movement covers four offering types rather than two, a substantially larger unit with its own internal completeness.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.9.15 "He presented the people's offering, and took the goat of the sin offering which was for the people"
web:Lev.9.21 "Aaron waved the breasts and the right thigh for a wave offering"

boundary_rationale: The scene culminates in Aaron's blessing gesture and the appearance of Yahweh's glory to the entire people, followed by fire consuming the offerings and the people's collective shout and prostration -- a theophanic climax distinct in kind from the preceding sacrificial procedure, closing the eighth-day inauguration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as the natural closing clause of the people's-offering unit in vv.15-21; but the blessing and theophany are addressed to the whole congregation rather than being part of any single offering's procedure, and the fire-from-Yahweh motif recurs as its own scene-type in the very next chapter's tragedy, marking this as a structurally significant close rather than a mere coda.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.9.23 "Yahweh's glory appeared to all the people"
web:Lev.9.24 "Fire came out from before Yahweh, and consumed the burnt offering...they shouted, and fell on their faces"

boundary_rationale: A new pair of participants, 'Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron,' enters the narrative performing an unauthorized act, and the unit closes on Moses's quotation of a divine saying -- marked in the WEB substrate by q1/q2 poetic-line tags -- 'I will show myself holy to those who come near me,' followed by the narrative notice 'Aaron held his peace.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might read this as continuing straight from ch.9's theophany as one long 'fire from Yahweh' narrative, since both chapters share the fire motif; but ch.10 opens with new participants performing a new and contrary action (strange fire rather than commanded fire), marking a genuine scene break despite the thematic echo.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.10.1 "Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, each took his censer"
web:Lev.10.3 "I will show myself holy to those who come near me...Aaron held his peace"

boundary_rationale: New participants, Mishael and Elzaphan, are summoned by name for a specific task -- carrying the bodies out of the camp -- forming a discrete action beat distinct from the confrontation and silence of vv.1-3.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged into vv.1-3 as the immediate aftermath of the deaths; but the introduction of two new named participants receiving a direct command is the same kind of participant-change marker that opens scenes throughout the book's narrative portions.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.10.4 "Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel"
web:Lev.10.5 "they came near, and carried them in their tunics out of the camp"

boundary_rationale: Moses addresses a new set of participants -- Aaron, Eleazar, and Ithamar together -- with mourning restrictions (no loosened hair, no torn clothes) distinct from the removal-of-bodies task just completed, closing on a compliance notice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader could fold this into the body-removal scene as one continuous aftermath sequence; but the address shifts from the two body-bearers to Aaron and his surviving sons specifically, and the content shifts from action to prohibition, marking a genuine addressee and topic change.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.10.6 "Don't let the hair of your heads go loose, and don't tear your clothes"
web:Lev.10.7 "They did according to the word of Moses"

boundary_rationale: A fresh formula, 'Then Yahweh said to Aaron,' shifts the speaker from Moses to Yahweh directly and the addressee to Aaron alone, opening a freestanding statute (no wine before entering the Tent, and the priestly mandate to distinguish holy from common) unrelated in form to the surrounding narrative.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might read this as Moses continuing to relay instruction as part of the same crisis-aftermath scene; but the formula explicitly names Yahweh, not Moses, as speaker for the first and only time in this chapter, which is itself a strong discourse-frame marker for a new unit.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.10.10 "You are to make a distinction between the holy and the common, and between the unclean and the clean"

boundary_rationale: The speaker reverts to Moses ('Moses spoke to Aaron, and to Eleazar and to Ithamar'), addressing the practical matter of eating the remaining ordination offerings, a distinct topic and discourse frame from Yahweh's wine/discernment statute immediately before it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the wine-prohibition unit as 'more priestly regulations,' since both concern proper priestly conduct; but the speaker changes back to Moses and the content returns to the concrete ordination-offering leftovers, resuming the narrative's practical thread rather than continuing Yahweh's general statute.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.10.12 "Moses spoke to Aaron, and to Eleazar and to Ithamar, his sons who were left"

boundary_rationale: A new investigative action, 'Moses diligently inquired about the goat of the sin offering,' opens the chapter's final scene -- Moses's anger, his charge against Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's defense, and Moses's acceptance of it -- forming a self-contained dispute-and-resolution unit closing on 'it was pleasing in his sight.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might see this as continuing the eating-instructions unit as one long discourse on what may be eaten; but the shift from general instruction to a specific investigated failure, Moses's emotional response, and a resolved dispute constitutes its own narrative scene rather than a continuation of legal instruction.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.10.16 "Moses diligently inquired about the goat of the sin offering, and, behold, it was burned"
web:Lev.10.20 "When Moses heard that, it was pleasing in his sight"

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula addressed jointly to Moses and Aaron opens the book's third major legal section, and the land-animal criterion (split hoof plus cud-chewing) together with its four named exceptions (camel, hyrax, hare, pig) forms one complete register before the substrate changes to water creatures.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the general criterion (2-3) from the four named exceptions (4-8), since each exception has its own clause; I kept them together because all four exceptions share one identical explanatory formula ('because it...but doesn't have a parted hoof, is unclean to you') applied to a single criterion just stated, functioning as one register rather than four independent cases.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.11.1 "Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying to them"
web:Lev.11.3 "Whatever parts the hoof, and is cloven-footed, and chews the cud among the animals, that you may eat"

boundary_rationale: The substrate shifts from land animals to 'all these that are in the waters,' introducing a new criterion (fins and scales) that structures the whole sub-unit, closing on the summary statement that whatever lacks fins and scales is an abomination.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the land-animal unit as 'permitted foods generally,' but the criterion itself changes entirely (hoof/cud versus fins/scales), and the book consistently treats each animal domain as its own register throughout this chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.11.9 "You may eat of all these that are in the waters: whatever has fins and scales"
oshb:Lev.11.9 אֶת זֶה תֹּאכְלוּ מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בַּמָּיִם

boundary_rationale: The substrate shifts again to birds, and unlike the land and water categories, this unit is a bare list of named species with no stated criterion, functioning as a distinct list/register form -- an enumeration rather than a rule-plus-application.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could try to merge this with the flying-insect unit that follows since both concern winged creatures; but the birds are handled as an unexplained list while the insects that follow are handled by an explicit locomotion criterion (walking on all fours versus jointed hopping legs), a genuine form difference.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.11.13 "You shall detest these among the birds; they shall not be eaten"
web:Lev.11.19 "the stork, any kind of heron, the hoopoe, and the bat"

boundary_rationale: A new criterion opens this unit, 'all flying insects that walk on all fours,' distinguished by jointed hopping legs into a permitted sub-list (locust, katydid, cricket, grasshopper types), matching the rule-plus-exception form of the land-animal unit rather than the bare-list form of the bird unit just before it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the bird list as 'more forbidden flying things'; but the criterion-based form (walking on all fours versus jointed legs for hopping) and the permitted sub-list mark this as functionally closer to the land-animal register than to the unexplained bird enumeration.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.11.20 "All flying insects that walk on all fours are an abomination to you"
web:Lev.11.22 "any kind of locust...you may eat"

boundary_rationale: The register shifts from what may be eaten to what causes uncleanness by contact -- 'by these you will become unclean' -- covering carcasses of the animal categories just listed and a further general four-footed-animal contamination rule, a functionally distinct concern (contact defilement rather than consumption prohibition).
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might keep this attached to the flying-insect unit as its closing clause; but the topic genuinely shifts from eating to touching, and the contamination rule applies retroactively to categories already covered (land animals, insects), functioning as a new cross-cutting register rather than a continuation of any one category.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.11.24 "By these you will become unclean: whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening"
web:Lev.11.27 "Whoever touches their carcass shall be unclean until the evening"

boundary_rationale: A new named list opens, 'these are they which are unclean to you among the creeping things that creep on the earth,' followed immediately by an extensive vessel- and food-contamination register (earthen vessels, wood, water, ovens, seed) triggered specifically by these swarming creatures, kept together because the contamination rules in vv.32-38 all hang directly off the list just given rather than generalizing to every category in the chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split would separate the bare species list (29-30) from the vessel-contamination rules (31-38), matching how the bird list and its criterion-based neighbor were kept separate earlier; I merged them here because the contamination rules explicitly say 'anything they fall on when they are dead,' tying the two spans together with an explicit pronoun reference rather than a fresh independent topic.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.11.29 "These are they which are unclean to you among the creeping things that creep on the earth"
web:Lev.11.33 "Every earthen vessel into which any of them falls...You shall break it"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if any animal of which you may eat dies,' addresses a case not covered by the preceding categories -- a permitted animal that dies of itself rather than by slaughter -- a short but functionally distinct case marked by its own conditional.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be absorbed into the swarming-creature contamination rules as 'more carcass contact rules'; but the subject is explicitly a permitted, edible animal that died naturally, a different situation from the unclean swarming creatures just discussed, and the text opens it with its own fresh protasis.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.11.39 "If any animal of which you may eat dies, he who touches its carcass shall be unclean"
oshb:Lev.11.39 וְכִי יָמוּת מִן הַבְּהֵמָה אֲשֶׁר הִיא לָכֶם לְאָכְלָה

boundary_rationale: A summary prohibition, 'every creeping thing that creeps on the earth is an abomination,' generalizes beyond any single category just discussed and pivots into the chapter's theological rationale -- 'for I am Yahweh your God...be holy for I am holy' -- the first appearance in the book of the holiness refrain that will structure chs.18-26.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might keep this attached to the swarming-creature unit as its closing exhortation; but the language generalizes to 'every creeping thing' rather than continuing the specific list-and-contamination register of vv.29-38, and the holiness rationale is a distinct rhetorical move (motive clause) rather than a further case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.11.44 "For I am Yahweh your God...be holy; for I am holy"
oshb:Lev.11.44 כִּי אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם וְהִתְקַדִּשְׁתֶּם וִהְיִיתֶם קְדֹשִׁים

boundary_rationale: A zot torat colophon closes the chapter, 'this is the law of the animal, and of the bird, and of every living creature,' summarizing the entire dietary-law chapter's scope and restating its purpose (to distinguish clean from unclean) -- the same backward-looking closing-formula device used at 7:37-38.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the holiness-rationale unit immediately before it as one closing section; but the zot torat formula is a distinct and recognizable colophon type throughout the book (also closing chs.12, 13, 14, and 15), warranting its own chunk consistent with how those later colophons are treated.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.11.46 "This is the law of the animal, and of the bird, and of every living creature"

boundary_rationale: MT 12:7's colophon, זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַיֹּלֶדֶת לַזָּכָר אוֹ לַנְּקֵבָה, explicitly brackets both the sex-differentiated uncleanness timeline (12:2-5) and the offering procedure that follows (12:6-7) as one torah; the internal seam previously relied on (a temporal-transition clause, ובמלאת ימי טהרה, not a fresh casuistic protasis) is weaker than that closing bracket. The colophon's explicit dual-gender bracketing carries the merge on its own.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The 7:11-36 precedent (one zot-torat superscription split into five occasion-based chunks) might seem to argue for splitting ch.12 too, but that precedent is distinguishable: 7:11ff is followed by multiple fresh protases marking genuinely distinct occasions, while ch.12 contains only one internal transition within a single, tightly unified case, closed by a colophon that explicitly names both halves as one torah.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.12.7 זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַיֹּלֶדֶת לַזָּכָר אוֹ לַנְּקֵבָה (single-witness, carries the merge alone)
oshb:Lev.12.6 וּבִמְלֹאת יְמֵי טָהֳרָהּ (temporal transition, not a protasis, single-witness)

boundary_rationale: A means-tested protasis, 'if she cannot afford a lamb,' opens a poor-alternative provision matching the graduated-offering pattern already established in 5:7-13, substituting two birds for the lamb-plus-bird combination just prescribed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could fold this one-verse alternative back into the preceding offering-and-colophon unit rather than isolating it; I kept it separate for consistency with how ch.5's and ch.14's poor-provision alternatives are each given their own chunk on the strength of their own conditional opening, even though this is among the thinnest units in the book.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.12.8 "If she cannot afford a lamb, then she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons"
oshb:Lev.12.8 וְאִם לֹא תִמְצָא יָדָהּ דֵּי שֶׂה

boundary_rationale: A fresh joint messenger formula to Moses and Aaron opens the diagnostic case-series torah, and the first case, marked by its own protasis 'when a man shall have a swelling in his body's skin,' establishes the chapter's basic examine-isolate-reexamine procedure before any of the specialized sub-cases that follow.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could treat the whole of vv.1-46 as a single undifferentiated 'skin disease' unit, since the examine/isolate/pronounce procedure repeats throughout; I split at each new casuistic protasis instead, since each names a distinct triggering condition (swelling, chronic disease, boils, burns, scalp/beard, bright spots, baldness) and the owner addendum treats a syntactic protasis/apodosis as tier-1 boundary-driving evidence.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.13.1 "Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying"
oshb:Lev.13.2 אָדָם כִּי יִהְיֶה בְעוֹר בְּשָׂרוֹ שְׂאֵת אוֹ סַפַּחַת אוֹ בַהֶרֶת

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'when the plague of leprosy is in a man,' opens the case of an already-advanced condition (raw flesh visible, no isolation required since uncleanness is certain), which the text itself extends without a further protasis break into the further extreme case of leprosy covering the entire body turning wholly white.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the chronic case (9-11) from the all-over-white case (12-17) at v.12's 'if the leprosy breaks out all over the skin'; I kept them merged since v.12 continues describing the same referent (a man already diagnosed with the disease of vv.9-11) rather than opening a fresh, independent triggering condition.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.13.9 "When the plague of leprosy is in a man, then he shall be brought to the priest"
web:Lev.13.13 "if the leprosy has covered all his flesh, he shall pronounce him clean of the plague"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'when the body has a boil on its skin, and it has healed,' opens a distinct diagnostic case addressing scar tissue from a specific prior wound-type, closed on its own clean-verdict formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the burn-scar case immediately following it, since both address disease breaking out in a healed wound; but each opens with its own triggering wound-type (boil versus fire-burn) and the book consistently marks each new protasis as a fresh case throughout this chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.13.18 "When the body has a boil on its skin, and it has healed"
oshb:Lev.13.18 וּבָשָׂר כִּי יִהְיֶה בְעֹרוֹ שְׁחִין

boundary_rationale: A parallel protasis, 'or when the body has a burn from fire on its skin,' opens the burn-scar case, matching the boil-scar case's structure (raw flesh in the wound becomes a bright spot, examine, isolate if uncertain, pronounce) but triggered by a different wound-type.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A minimal reading could merge this with the boil-scar case as 'wound-scar diseases generally,' since the procedure is nearly identical; I kept them separate because the text's own connective, 'or when,' explicitly marks this as a distinct triggering condition rather than a continuation.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.13.24 "when the body has a burn from fire on its skin"
oshb:Lev.13.24 אוֹ בָשָׂר כִּי יִהְיֶה בְעֹרוֹ מִכְוַת אֵשׁ

boundary_rationale: A new protasis addressing a new class of participant, 'when a man or woman has a plague on the head or on the beard,' opens the scalp/beard case (netek), distinguished procedurally by yellow rather than white hair as the diagnostic marker and by shaving as part of the isolation procedure.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could fold this into the preceding burn-scar case as a further sub-variety of skin disease; but this case explicitly introduces the first mention of women as potential subjects and a body location (head/beard) never addressed before, together with a diagnostic marker (yellow hair) unique to this case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.13.29 "When a man or woman has a plague on the head or on the beard"

boundary_rationale: A brief protasis, 'when a man or a woman has bright spots in the skin of the body,' opens a case whose entire content is a clean verdict for a harmless rash (bohaq), the shortest and simplest of the chapter's diagnostic cases.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the baldness case that follows, since both are brief benign-condition verdicts without an isolation procedure; but each opens with its own protasis addressing a distinct bodily phenomenon (skin bright spots versus hair loss), and I judged the formula break, though short, worth preserving rather than collapsing two textually distinct conditions into one chunk.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.13.38 "When a man or a woman has bright spots in the skin of the body"
web:Lev.13.39 "it is a harmless rash...He is clean"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if a man's hair has fallen from his head, he is bald,' opens the baldness case, immediately distinguishing ordinary natural baldness (clean) from disease breaking out within a bald area (unclean), a two-part case with its own internal contrast.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader could treat ordinary baldness (40-41) and diseased baldness (42-44) as two separate chunks, matching the fine granularity used for scalp/beard sub-cases elsewhere; I kept them merged since v.42's 'but if' is a direct contrastive continuation of the same bodily condition just introduced, not an independent new triggering event.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.13.40 "If a man's hair has fallen from his head, he is bald. He is clean"
web:Lev.13.44 "He is a leprous man. He is unclean"

boundary_rationale: The discourse shifts from diagnostic casuistry to an apodictic behavioral mandate for anyone diagnosed a leper -- torn clothes, loose hair, the covered lip, the 'unclean, unclean' cry, and dwelling alone outside the camp -- functioning as a coda that closes the human skin-disease portion of the chapter before the register shifts entirely to fabric and leather.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be tacked onto the baldness case immediately before it as its closing application; but its content applies to every diagnosed leper regardless of which specific case produced the diagnosis, making it a generalizing coda for vv.1-44 as a whole rather than a continuation of the baldness case specifically.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.13.45 "The leper in whom the plague is shall wear torn clothes...and shall cry, Unclean! Unclean!"
web:Lev.13.46 "He shall dwell alone. His dwelling shall be outside of the camp"

boundary_rationale: A new substrate opens the chapter's final case, 'the garment also that the plague of leprosy is in,' shifting from human skin to woolen, linen, or leather material entirely, and running through its own examine-isolate-burn-or-wash procedure to the chapter's own zot torat colophon at v.59.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the initial diagnosis (47-52) from the wash-and-reexamine procedure (53-58) and the colophon (59), matching the granularity used for human skin cases earlier; I kept the whole garment case together because, unlike the human cases, there is no fresh casuistic protasis reopening the topic partway through -- the whole span describes one continuous examination-and-disposition procedure for a single kind of object.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.13.47 "The garment also that the plague of leprosy is in"
web:Lev.13.59 "This is the law of the plague of mildew in a garment of wool or linen"

boundary_rationale: WLC 14:3-7 is a single unbroken הכהן-subject chain (וְצִוָּה הַכֹּהֵן repeats at v.4 and v.5) with no tier-1 signal -- no fresh protasis, no addressee shift, no new participant -- falling at 14:4. V.6 varies this chain stylistically with a fronted-object construction, אֶת הַצִּפֹּר הַֽחַיָּה יִקַּח אֹתָהּ ('the living bird -- he shall take it'), a yiqtol rather than a strict verb-initial weqatal; the fronting foregrounds the ritual object for emphasis and does not introduce a new subject, protasis, or participant, so it does not constitute a tier-1 boundary signal and the chain's functional continuity from v.3 through v.7 is unaffected.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The introduction of new ritual objects at v.4 (two birds, cedar wood, scarlet, hyssop) might look like grounds for a fresh unit, but that warrant is applied nowhere else in this cluster and was explicitly disavowed for comparable object-introductions elsewhere in ch.13-14's own case material.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.14.6 אֶת הַצִּפֹּר הַֽחַיָּה יִקַּח אֹתָהּ (fronted-object yiqtol, not verb-initial weqatal -- a stylistic variation within the chain, not a boundary signal, single-witness)

boundary_rationale: The subject shifts from the priest's actions to the cleansed person's own required actions -- washing clothes, shaving all hair, bathing -- performed first on day one and repeated on day seven, forming a distinct two-stage personal-purification interval before the offerings of the eighth day.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the two-bird rite as its immediate aftermath; but the two-bird rite is performed entirely by the priest upon the person, while this unit shifts to actions the person performs upon himself across a seven-day interval, a genuine change in agency and timeframe.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.14.8 "he who is to be cleansed shall wash his clothes, and shave off all his hair"
web:Lev.14.9 "he shall shave all his hair off his head and his beard and his eyebrows"

boundary_rationale: A new time notice, 'on the eighth day,' opens the full-price offering procedure -- two male lambs, a ewe lamb, grain, and oil, with blood and oil applied to ear, thumb, and toe exactly as in the priestly ordination rite of ch.8 -- one continuous ceremonial sequence ending in the completed atonement formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the trespass-offering blood/oil application (12-18) from the sin- and burnt-offering conclusion (19-20); I kept them merged since no new object or participant is introduced between them, and the entire sequence is bound together as the one ceremony performed 'before Yahweh' on this single eighth day.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.14.10 "On the eighth day he shall take two male lambs without defect"
web:Lev.14.20 "The priest shall make atonement for him, and he shall be clean"

boundary_rationale: A means-tested protasis, 'if he is poor, and can't afford so much,' opens the graduated alternative to the full-price offering just given, mirroring 5:7-13's poor-provision pattern, and closes on its own sub-colophon, 'this is the law for him in whom is the plague of leprosy, who is not able to afford the sacrifice.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be treated as a mere footnote appended to the full-offering unit; but it is a complete, independently structured procedure (its own lamb, its own oil measure, its own bird-substitution) sealed by its own colophon, exactly the kind of self-contained unit the book elsewhere gives its own chunk.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.14.21 "If he is poor, and can't afford so much"
web:Lev.14.32 "This is the law for him in whom is the plague of leprosy, who is not able to afford the sacrifice for his cleansing"

boundary_rationale: A fresh joint messenger formula to Moses and Aaron, together with a new land-entry temporal clause, 'when you have come into the land of Canaan,' opens an entirely new substrate (houses) and its own examine-quarantine-reexamine procedure, structurally parallel to but independent of the garment-mildew case in ch.13.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might see this as a straightforward continuation of the leper-cleansing torah just concluded, since both concern purity diagnosis; but the fresh messenger formula and the shift to an entirely new substrate (dwelling structures) mark this as its own torah, matching how garment mildew was separated from human skin disease in ch.13.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.14.34 "When you have come into the land of Canaan...I put a spreading mildew in a house"
oshb:Lev.14.33 וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְאֶל אַהֲרֹן לֵאמֹר

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if the plague comes again, and breaks out in the house after he has taken out the stones,' opens the recurrence sub-case, escalating from quarantine and stone-replacement to complete demolition, a distinct outcome from the initial-diagnosis procedure just given.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the initial diagnosis as one long house-mildew procedure; but the recurrence case is explicitly conditioned on the prior remedial steps having already failed, and its outcome (tearing down the house) is categorically different from anything in the initial procedure, marking a real escalation-triggered boundary.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.14.43 "If the plague comes again, and breaks out in the house after he has taken out the stones"
web:Lev.14.45 "He shall break down the house"

boundary_rationale: The topic shifts from the house's own diagnosis and disposition to a cross-cutting contamination rule for anyone who enters or eats in the quarantined house during its shut-up period, a distinct concern (third-party defilement) from either the diagnosis or demolition procedures.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might fold this into the recurrence/demolition unit as incidental detail; but this rule applies during the shut-up interval regardless of whether the house is ultimately cleared or demolished, functioning as a freestanding cross-cutting rule rather than the conclusion of either preceding case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.14.46 "he who goes into the house while it is shut up shall be unclean until the evening"
web:Lev.14.47 "he who eats in the house shall wash his clothes"

boundary_rationale: A contrasting protasis, 'if the priest shall come in, and examine it, and behold, the plague hasn't spread,' opens the positive outcome case, in which the house is pronounced clean and undergoes its own two-bird cleansing rite paralleling the leper's cleansing rite in vv.4-7 but applied to a structure.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the contamination-rule unit immediately before it as 'more house-mildew procedure'; but it opens with its own contrastive protasis marking the favorable outcome, and performs a complete ritual (materials, dipping, sevenfold sprinkling, release) rather than stating a cross-cutting rule.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.14.48 "if the priest...examine it, and behold, the plague hasn't spread in the house...he shall pronounce the house clean"
web:Lev.14.53 "he shall let the living bird go out of the city into the open field"

boundary_rationale: A summary colophon closes the entire skin/garment/house-plague complex spanning chs.13-14, 'this is the law for any plague of leprosy...to teach when it is unclean, and when it is clean,' explicitly naming every condition-type covered across both chapters.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could attach this to the house-clearance rite immediately before it as its closing verse; but its scope explicitly reaches back across all of chs.13-14 rather than just the house case, matching the retrospective, whole-section-closing function of the colophons at 7:37-38 and 11:46-47.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.14.54 "This is the law for any plague of leprosy, and for an itch"
web:Lev.14.57 "This is the law of leprosy"

boundary_rationale: A fresh joint messenger formula to Moses and Aaron opens the book's fourth purity torah, and its general definition -- 'this shall be his uncleanness in his discharge' -- states the underlying principle (running or stopped discharge both count) that every following contamination case will presuppose.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could run the superscription straight into the bed/seat contamination rules that follow as one unit; but v.3's definitional clause is a distinct discourse move (defining the condition itself) from v.4's shift to concrete contamination consequences, and it closes with its own summary 'it is his uncleanness.'
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.15.1 "Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying"
web:Lev.15.3 "This shall be his uncleanness in his discharge"

boundary_rationale: A list-register of contamination consequences opens with 'every bed on which he who has the discharge lies shall be unclean,' running through bed, seat, touch, spittle, saddle, and vessel contact -- eight short parallel contamination cases sharing one wash-bathe-unclean-until-evening formula, kept together as a single register because none is separated by an independent protasis introducing a new legal principle rather than a new contact-object.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A stricter per-object reading could split this into as many as six or seven one- or two-verse chunks (bed, seat, touch, spittle, saddle, sitting-object, hand-contact, vessel); I judged that degree of fragmentation would over-split a single repetitive register whose only variable is the object touched, not the underlying legal principle -- the same restraint the book shows elsewhere toward repetitive list material.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.15.4 "Every bed on which he who has the discharge lies shall be unclean"
web:Lev.15.12 "every vessel of wood shall be rinsed in water"

boundary_rationale: A temporal-transition protasis, 'when he who has a discharge is cleansed of his discharge,' shifts from the contamination-consequences register to the purification procedure itself (seven-day count, washing, eighth-day bird offering), matching the pattern of similarly structured purity chapters.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as the final item in the contamination-rules list; but its content (count seven days, then a dated offering procedure) is structurally a purification ritual, not a further contamination case, the same functional distinction drawn elsewhere between diagnosis and cleansing.

boundary_rationale: WLC 15:16 opens with the top-level protasis וְאִישׁ כִּי תֵצֵא מִמֶּנּוּ שִׁכְבַת זָרַע; vv.17-18 continue with asher-fronted relative clauses (וְכָל בֶּגֶד...אֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה עָלָיו שִׁכְבַת זָרַע; וְאִשָּׁה אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁכַּב אִישׁ אֹתָהּ שִׁכְבַת זָרַע) listing further consequences of the identical trigger, שִׁכְבַת זָרַע -- the same asher-fronted list-item pattern that keeps 15:4-12's eight-item contamination register merged as one case. 15:19 and 15:25, by contrast, both reopen with their own independent כִּי.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The recurrence of אִשָּׁה across 15:18/19/25 and the petuchah after 15:17 both look like grounds to move the boundary to 15:18, but the lexical repetition is the wrong signal to key on given the asher-vs-ki discriminator this book applies consistently elsewhere, and the petuchah is corroboration only, not a sole driver, under the evidence rules.

oshb:Lev.15.18 וְאִשָּׁה אֲשֶׁר יִשְׁכַּב אִישׁ אֹתָהּ שִׁכְבַת זָרַע (asher-fronted, single-witness)

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if a woman has a discharge, and her discharge in her flesh is blood,' opens the menstrual-impurity case, restating the bed/seat contamination register from vv.4-12 in a female-specific form and extending it to the case of a man having intercourse with a menstruating woman.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the baseline menstrual rules (19-23) from the intercourse case (24), matching how ch.20 later splits menstrual intercourse into its own listed offense; I kept them merged here because v.24 functions as a direct consequence clause continuing the same referent (contact with a menstruating woman) without a fresh independent protasis structure.

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if a woman has a discharge of her blood many days not in the time of her period,' opens the female parallel to the chronic male discharge case (zov) of vv.4-12, extending the same bed/seat contamination consequences to abnormal or prolonged bleeding.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the menstrual-impurity unit as 'more female bleeding rules'; but the text explicitly distinguishes normal-period bleeding from abnormal, prolonged bleeding as two separate conditions with two separate protases, mirroring the male chronic-discharge/emission distinction earlier in the chapter.

boundary_rationale: The temporal-transition protasis at v.28 opens the female purification procedure (count seven days, eighth-day bird offering), closing on its own complete atonement formula at v.30, וְכִפֶּר עָלֶיהָ הַכֹּהֵן לִפְנֵי יְהוָה מִזּוֹב טֻמְאָתָהּ, exactly matching the male case's own close at 15:15.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Could extend through v.31 as originally drafted, but v.30 already supplies this case's own atonement close, making a v.31 extension redundant with, rather than part of, this case's conclusion.
