boundary_rationale: V.31 shifts to 2mp (וְהִזַּרְתֶּם) with nation-wide scope (בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, מִשְׁכָּנִי), a person-and-scope shift of the identical class treated as a splitter elsewhere in this book at 16:29, 18:24, 20:7, and 20:22, and is not scoped to the female-discharge case specifically -- it is a motive clause for the whole discharge-purity chapter, distinct from both the female case's own already-supplied atonement close (v.30) and from M8-Lev-091's chapter-wide zot-torat colophon (15:32-33), which needs no span change to absorb it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Could merge forward into the 15:32-33 colophon as LF-M8-Lev-090-1 originally proposed, but M8-Lev-091's colophon is scoped correctly as-is under the scope-based criterion both challenges independently supply, and a forward merge would misstate that decision's own scope; standing alone as a one-verse rationale coda between the two is the better fit.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.15.31 וְהִזַּרְתֶּם אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מִטֻּמְאָתָם (2mp, single-witness)
oshb:Lev.16.29, 18.24, 20.7, 20.22 (same person/scope-shift splitting device elsewhere, single-witness)

boundary_rationale: A zot-torat colophon closes the chapter, זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַזָּב, retrospectively summarizing every case-class covered across the chapter's now four preceding units (base discharge, purification rite, seminal emission, and the two female cases) in one chapter-wide, non-case-specific formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The original precedent list cited '11:46-47, 12:7, 13:59, 14:54-57' as parallel standalone-colophon chunks, but checked directly: 12:7 is merged into M8-Lev-062 and 13:59 is merged into M8-Lev-073, neither standalone. The actual governing criterion is colophon scope (chapter-wide retrospective vs. narrow single-case), which correctly still yields this decision as its own chunk; only 11:46-47 and 14:54-57 should be cited as standalone-colophon precedents.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.11.46-11.47 and Lev.14.54-14.57 (single-witness, the corrected standalone-colophon precedent set)

boundary_rationale: The chapter opens by explicitly dating itself to 'after the death of the two sons of Aaron,' tying the Day of Atonement procedure directly back to ch.10's crisis, then states the warning against casual entry into the Most Holy Place and the required animals and garments before any ritual action begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the warning (1-2) from the required-elements list (3-5), since v.3's 'with this Aaron shall come into the sanctuary' opens a fresh statement; I merged them because v.3 functions as the positive counterpart to v.2's negative warning ('not at just any time...but with this'), a single contrastive unit rather than two independent topics.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.16.1 "Yahweh spoke to Moses after the death of the two sons of Aaron"
web:Lev.16.3 "Aaron shall come into the sanctuary with a young bull for a sin offering, and a ram for a burnt offering"

boundary_rationale: 16:11's near-verbatim repetition of 16:6 (וְהִקְרִיב אַהֲרֹן אֶת פַּר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לוֹ וְכִפֶּר בַּעֲדוֹ וּבְעַד בֵּיתוֹ) is classical resumptive repetition (Wiederaufnahme): a proleptic summary at v.6, an inserted digression required by the larger procedure (vv.7-10, the goat-lot casting, structurally necessary before v.15 can name 'the goat of the sin offering for the people'), and a verbatim-repetition resumption at v.11 that continues the interrupted action -- וְשָׁחַט אֶת פַּר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לוֹ, the concrete slaughter the v.6 summary had only announced -- through the coals, incense, and sevenfold blood-sprinkling of vv.12-14. This device marks continuation of one interrupted unit across the digression, not the opening of a second independent one.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The near-verbatim repetition at 16:11 could be read as a fresh unit-opening signal in its own right (a plausible surface reading of 'resumptive repetition' as a boundary marker), but that inverts the device's actual function: Wiederaufnahme brackets an interrupting digression to signal that the bracketed material completes the same statement, not that it restarts a new one. The real, stronger seam is v.15's new sacrificial object (שְׂעִיר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לָעָם, explicitly contrasted with the אֲשֶׁר לוֹ of vv.6/11) and new beneficiary, where the atonement's scope visibly widens from the mercy seat alone to the Holy Place, Tent, and altar.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.16.6 וְהִקְרִיב אַהֲרֹן אֶת פַּר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לוֹ וְכִפֶּר בַּעֲדוֹ וּבְעַד בֵּיתוֹ (single-witness)
oshb:Lev.16.11 (near-verbatim repetition then וְשָׁחַט, the resumption's new content, single-witness)
oshb:Lev.16.15 שְׂעִיר הַחַטָּאת אֲשֶׁר לָעָם (contrastive אֲשֶׁר לָעָם vs. אֲשֶׁר לוֹ, single-witness, marking the real seam)

boundary_rationale: A new action object, 'the goat of the sin offering that is for the people,' opens the second blood application, extending the atonement from the mercy seat itself outward to the Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, and finally the altar -- a widening-scope sequence distinct from the bull's application to the mercy seat alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the bull's blood rite as 'one continuous atonement action'; but a new sacrificial animal (the people's goat, not Aaron's bull) is introduced and the scope of atonement visibly widens from the innermost mercy seat outward to the altar, marking a real procedural escalation.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.16.15 "he shall kill the goat of the sin offering that is for the people"
web:Lev.16.18 "He shall go out to the altar that is before Yahweh and make atonement for it"

boundary_rationale: A transition marker, 'when he has finished atoning for the Holy Place, the Tent of Meeting, and the altar,' opens the chapter's most distinctive rite -- confession of Israel's sins over the live goat's head and its release into the wilderness -- a ritual gesture (transfer by confession rather than blood) found nowhere else in the book.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might fold this into the preceding sanctuary-atonement unit as its natural sequel; but the scapegoat rite is explicitly marked as beginning only 'when he has finished' the prior atonement, and its mechanism (verbal confession and transfer, not blood application) is categorically different from every rite that precedes it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.16.21 "Aaron shall lay both his hands on the head of the live goat, and confess over him all the iniquities"
web:Lev.16.22 "he shall release the goat in the wilderness"

boundary_rationale: Aaron re-enters the Tent of Meeting to remove his linen garments and change into his regular vestments before offering the burnt offerings for himself and the people, a distinct sequence (return, change, offer) marking the transition out of the innermost rites toward the ceremony's conclusion.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as continuing the scapegoat unit, since Aaron's return follows immediately upon sending the goat away; but the vestment change is a self-contained action with its own location (the Tent of Meeting, not the wilderness) and its own new sacrificial acts (burnt offerings) not part of the scapegoat rite itself.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.16.23 "Aaron shall come into the Tent of Meeting, and shall take off the linen garments"
web:Lev.16.24 "he shall bathe himself in water...and offer his burnt offering"

boundary_rationale: The topic shifts to the two subordinate participants who handled unclean material during the ceremony -- the man who released the scapegoat and the one who burned the sin-offering carcasses outside the camp -- each requiring his own washing before re-entering the camp, a distinct cleanup-and-reintegration concern from the central atonement rites just completed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might attach this to the vestment-change unit as further closing procedure; but the participants here are different persons (the scapegoat-handler and the carcass-burner, not Aaron), and their concern is their own reentry into the camp rather than the completion of Aaron's atonement duties.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.16.26 "He who lets the goat go as the scapegoat shall wash his clothes"
web:Lev.16.28 "He who burns them shall wash his clothes, and bathe his flesh in water"

boundary_rationale: The discourse shifts from narrated procedure to direct legislative address, 'it shall be a statute to you forever: in the seventh month, on the tenth day,' establishing the rite as an annual perpetual observance, and the chapter closes with the compliance notice 'it was done as Yahweh commanded Moses.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split further at v.32's shift to describing the future officiating priest ('the priest, who is anointed'), since it briefly generalizes beyond Aaron specifically; I kept the whole closing statute together since vv.29-34 share one unbroken 'statute forever' framing without any new ritual action being introduced.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.16.29 "It shall be a statute to you forever: in the seventh month, on the tenth day"
web:Lev.16.34 "It was done as Yahweh commanded Moses"

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula addressed to Aaron, his sons, and all Israel together opens a new legal section (chs.17-26, sometimes called the Holiness collection) with the requirement that every slaughtered animal be brought to the Tent of Meeting, closing on the goat-idol prohibition and its 'statute forever' formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could read this as a continuation of the sacrificial-procedure material in chs.1-9, since it still concerns proper slaughter; but the addressee widens for the first time to 'all the children of Israel' alongside the priests, and the topic shifts from how to perform a sacrifice to where it may lawfully occur at all, a legal question chs.1-9 never raised.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.17.2 "Speak to Aaron, and to his sons, and to all the children of Israel"
web:Lev.17.4 "blood shall be imputed to that man...That man shall be cut off from among his people"

boundary_rationale: A resumptive address formula, 'you shall say to them,' reopens the centralized-worship requirement in more compact form, explicitly extending it for the first time to resident foreigners alongside native Israelites.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into vv.1-7 as a restatement of the same rule; but the explicit 'you shall say to them' reopening formula and the newly widened addressee (foreigners included) mark it as the chapter's own second, distinct legal statement rather than a mere repetition.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.17.8 "You shall say to them, Any man there is of the house of Israel, or of the strangers"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'any man...who eats any kind of blood,' opens the blood-eating prohibition proper, distinguished from the centralized-slaughter rules by its own theological rationale clause, 'for the life of the flesh is in the blood...it is the blood that makes atonement.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might see this as continuing the same 'proper handling of sacrificial blood' topic as vv.1-9; but the concern shifts from where an animal may be slaughtered to whether its blood may be consumed at all, a distinct legal question with its own rationale, not a restatement of the centralization rule.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.17.10 "who eats any kind of blood, I will set my face against that soul"
web:Lev.17.11 "the life of the flesh is in the blood"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'whatever man...who takes in hunting any animal or bird,' addresses game animals never brought to an altar at all, requiring the blood to be covered with dust rather than offered, extending the blood-sanctity principle into a case the centralized-offering rules do not reach.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the blood-eating prohibition immediately before it as one continuous 'blood is sacred' unit; but hunted game presents a genuinely distinct situation (no altar is involved at all) requiring its own disposal procedure (covering with dust) not found in the eating-prohibition case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.17.13 "who takes in hunting any animal or bird that may be eaten, he shall pour out its blood, and cover it with dust"
oshb:Lev.17.13 וְשָׁפַךְ אֶת דָּמוֹ וְכִסָּהוּ בֶּעָפָר

boundary_rationale: A final protasis, 'every person that eats what dies of itself, or that which is torn by animals,' closes the chapter with a purification remedy (washing, bathing, evening uncleanness) rather than a cut-off penalty, marking a distinct, lesser class of violation from the deliberate blood-eating and improper-slaughter offenses addressed earlier.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might expect this to be merged with the blood-prohibition unit as a related dietary restriction; but its remedy structure (purification rather than being cut off) and its address to 'whether he is native-born or a foreigner' as an inadvertent-contact case mark it as functionally closer to the purity-law chapters than to the deliberate-violation cases in the rest of this chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.17.15 "Every person that eats what dies of itself...shall wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water"
web:Lev.17.16 "if he doesn't wash them...then he shall bear his iniquity"

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the chapter with a distinctive preamble frame -- 'I am Yahweh your God' repeated three times, contrasting Israel's coming conduct with both Egypt's and Canaan's practices -- establishing the inclusio that will close the chapter at v.30 before any specific prohibition is named.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might run the preamble directly into the first prohibition at v.6 as one continuous unit; but the preamble names no specific act at all, functioning purely as a framing exhortation ('you shall keep my statutes...he shall live in them'), a distinct rhetorical unit from the list of concrete prohibitions that follows.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.18.5 "which if a man does, he shall live in them"

boundary_rationale: 18:7-16 uniformly open עֶרְוַת-X...לֹא תְגַלֶּה; 18:17's SECOND clause already carries the transitional construction 18:18 continues -- אֶת בַּת בְּנָהּ וְאֶת בַּת בִּתָּהּ לֹא תִקַּח לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ -- so 18:18 (וְאִשָּׁה אֶל אֲחֹתָהּ לֹא תִקָּח לִצְרֹר לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ) is verbally bonded to 18:17's own closing clause, not to 18:19's ve'el-ishshah...lo tiqrav construction family. Content confirms the grouping: 18:18 (a wife's sister) remains a she'er-class kinship prohibition under 18:6's own heading, while 18:19-23 turn to non-kinship matters.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The claim that the ervat-X formula is exceptionless through v.17 and breaks cleanly at v.18 looks decisive in isolation, but the laqach-plus-legallot-ervatah construction that supposedly marks the break is already present within 18:17b itself, so the formula transition straddles v.17 rather than falling cleanly at the 17/18 boundary as claimed.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.18.17 אֶת בַּת בְּנָהּ וְאֶת בַּת בִּתָּהּ לֹא תִקַּח לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ (single-witness, the straddling construction)
oshb:Lev.18.18 וְאִשָּׁה אֶל אֲחֹתָהּ לֹא תִקָּח לִצְרֹר לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָתָהּ (single-witness)
oshb:Lev.18.6 כָּל שְׁאֵר בְּשָׂרוֹ (single-witness, the kinship heading 18:18 still falls under)

boundary_rationale: The register genuinely shifts away from the ervat-X formula at v.19 to a series of differently-worded prohibitions (menstrual intercourse, adultery, Molech, male homosexual intercourse, bestiality) sharing no she'er-class kinship logic; 18:18 stays with the preceding kinship list per M8-Lev-106's revised rationale, so this span's start at v.19 is unaffected by that correction.
strongest_rejected_alternative: OLC-Lev-107-01 (the mirror challenge) proposed starting this span at 18:18 instead of 18:19 on the ground that 18:18's laqach-verb marks a clean break from the ervat-X list; that claim fails for the same reason recorded at M8-Lev-106: the laqach-plus-legallot-ervatah construction 18:18 uses is already present in 18:17b, so the transition straddles v.17, not v.18, and 18:18 remains content-bonded to the kinship list.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.18.19 "You shall not approach a woman to uncover her nakedness, as long as she is impure"
web:Lev.18.21 "You shall not give any of your children as a sacrifice to Molech" (non-sexual content within the span)

boundary_rationale: The discourse shifts from prohibition to motive clause, 'don't defile yourselves in any of these things; for in all these the nations...were defiled,' introducing the land-vomiting warning and closing the chapter's inclusio with a final 'I am Yahweh your God,' matching the preamble's opening frame.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be attached to the non-kinship prohibition list as its closing verses; but the land-vomiting rationale and the closing inclusio formula are addressed to the whole chapter's prohibitions collectively, not to the immediately preceding cluster alone, functioning as the chapter's own coda.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.18.25 "the land vomited out her inhabitants"
web:Lev.18.30 "you do not defile yourselves with them. I am Yahweh your God"

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula addressed to 'all the congregation of the children of Israel' opens the chapter with the book's central holiness declaration, 'you shall be holy; for I, Yahweh your God, am holy,' functioning as the superscription and thematic key for the miscellaneous law-list that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could run the superscription directly into the first commandment cluster at v.3 as a single opening unit; but the qedoshim tihyu declaration is a distinct, self-contained thesis statement addressed to the whole nation, structurally set apart from the specific commands that begin immediately after it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.19.2 "Speak to all the congregation of the children of Israel...You shall be holy"
oshb:Lev.19.2 קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם

boundary_rationale: The first concrete commandment cluster opens, echoing the Decalogue's parent-honor and Sabbath commands before pivoting to idol prohibition, each item closed by its own 'I am Yahweh your God' refrain, a recurring closing tag that will structure the whole chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer reading could split parent/Sabbath reverence (v.3) from idol prohibition (v.4) into two chunks, since each closes with its own refrain; I merged them because both are short, thematically adjacent 'first-table' commands opening the list without any topic drift of the kind that separates later clusters in this chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.19.3 "Each one of you shall respect his mother and his father. You shall keep my Sabbaths"
web:Lev.19.4 "Don't turn to idols, nor make molten gods for yourselves"

boundary_rationale: The ki-protasis at v.5 (וְכִי תִזְבְּחוּ) opens the peace-offering eating-deadline rule, closing on its own karet-adjacent penalty formula at v.8, distinct from the gleaning law's own be-plus-infinitive-construct temporal-clause opener at v.9.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Could stay merged with the gleaning law as one 'practical provisions' block as originally drafted, but each opens with its own casuistic marker and closes with its own formula, and Leviticus's own precedent at 23:22 (where the identical gleaning phrase functions as its own independently-recognized appended law) confirms v.9 opens a self-contained provision rather than continuing v.5-8.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.19.5 "When you offer a sacrifice of peace offerings to Yahweh, you shall offer it so that you may be accepted"
web:Lev.19.8 "that soul shall be cut off from his people"

boundary_rationale: V.9's וּבְקֻצְרְכֶם opens the gleaning provision with a be-plus-infinitive-construct temporal clause; this exact phrase recurs near-verbatim at 23:22 (differing only by an added בְּקֻצְרֶךָ) where it already functions as its own independently-recognized appended law, both closing on the identical לֶעָנִי וְלַגֵּר תַּעֲזֹב אֹתָם אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם formula -- Leviticus's own internal precedent that this formula opens a self-contained provision rather than continuing an adjacent one. A setumah falls immediately after 23:22 itself, corroborating (weakly, as required) that MT independently paragraphs that parallel law as freestanding, strengthening the family-precedent argument this decision's rationale already makes.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Could remain a continuation clause of the offering-timing rule as originally drafted, but the 23:22 parallel -- now further corroborated by its own setumah -- shows this book itself treats this exact phrase as a freestanding law-opener, not a subordinate clause of whatever precedes it.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A stricter per-command reading could split theft/lying/deceit (11-12) from wage-withholding and cursing-the-vulnerable (13-14) into two chunks; I merged them as one honesty-and-fair-dealing register since both clusters share the same rapid-fire single-clause apodictic form without any casuistic or list-register shift between them.

strongest_rejected_alternative: One might merge this into the honesty cluster immediately before it as 'more interpersonal ethics'; but this cluster is organized around a single escalating theme (fair treatment of the vulnerable and the neighbor) culminating in one climactic command, a rhetorical shape distinct from the flatter list-of-prohibitions form in vv.11-14.

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the justice/neighbor-love cluster as its closing item; but the three-part parallel-mixture list is a self-contained list/register form on its own topic (forbidden mixing) unrelated to the interpersonal-justice theme of vv.15-18.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader could fold this into the mixture-law unit as 'more miscellaneous rules'; but this is the chapter's only genuinely casuistic case complete with a trespass offering and atonement formula, a functionally distinct legal form from every apodictic 'you shall not' command elsewhere in ch.19.

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the chapter's penalty series, and the Molech child-sacrifice case (1-5) is grouped with the mediums/wizards case (6) because both close on the identical divine-first-person refrain, 'I will set my face against that person...and cut him off,' a shared formula marking both as the same penalty-class (divine curse) distinct from the human-administered death sentences that dominate the rest of the chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer reading could split Molech (1-5) from mediums (6) since they are substantively different offenses; I merged them on the strength of the repeated 've'natati/ve'natti et panai' ('I will set my face') refrain that brackets both, a stronger unifying signal than the topic difference is a separating one.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might see vv.9-21 as one undivided 'sexual offense list,' since the offenses are thematically continuous with vv.10-16; but the penalty formula itself changes categorically at v.17 (no longer 'put to death' but 'cut off' or 'childless'), which is a genuine functional break in the list's own apparatus, not merely a topic drift.

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be attached to the cut-off penalty list as its closing verse; but its content shifts entirely away from any specific offense to a generalized rationale spanning the whole chapter, matching the coda function seen at the close of ch.18 rather than continuing the casuistic list form.

boundary_rationale: 21:1-4 is uniformly 3ms (לְנֶפֶשׁ לֹא יִטַּמָּא, לָהּ יִטַּמָּא, לֹא יִטַּמָּא בַּעַל בְּעַמָּיו): corpse-contact defilement and its permitted close-relative exceptions, addressed in the third person throughout, not the second-person-plural sweep the original rationale claimed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The original merge (21:1-6) rested on a stated 'unbroken second-person plural sweep' that a direct check falsifies on both counts -- the material is third person, not second, and the register is not unbroken, since it shifts in number exactly at v.5. Narrowing to 21:1-4 corrects both defects at once.

boundary_rationale: 21:5-7 is uniformly 3mp throughout (לֹא יְגַלֵּחוּ, לֹא יִשְׂרְטוּ; קְדֹשִׁים יִהְיוּ לֵאלֹהֵיהֶם וְלֹא יְחַלְּלוּ; אִשָּׁה זֹנָה וַחֲלָלָה לֹא יִקָּחוּ...לֹא יִקָּחוּ), covering the mourning self-disfigurement prohibitions and the marriage restrictions on ordinary priests as one register, absorbing 21:5-6 from the neighboring decision's narrowed tail (v.7 continues the identical register with no addressee change or protasis at the 6/7 seam) and closing on its own formula at v.7, כי קדש הוא לאלהיו.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A merged 21:5-8 span remains the strongest rejected alternative, and I held it in the prior round on the theory that v.8's second-person material functions as this block's own closing motive clause rather than a severable unit -- in effect, a sanction-clause differentiator, since v.9's fresh case carries a stated penalty (באש תשרף) and v.8 does not. That differentiator was overruled on the grammar: v.8 is second person in every clause, built from two independent כי clauses forming its own complete rationale rather than a subordinate aside, addressed to a different party than vv.5-7, and penalty-language presence was never the book's actual splitting criterion. The 24:15 addressee-redirect and 15:31 person-shift precedents apply with equal force here.

boundary_rationale: V.8 is second person in every clause from its first word -- וְקִדַּשְׁתּוֹ (2ms, 'and you shall sanctify him'), כִּי אֶת לֶחֶם אֱלֹהֶיךָ הוּא מַקְרִיב (2ms suffix), קָדֹשׁ יִהְיֶה לָּךְ (2ms dative) -- closing on a second independent כי clause, כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אֲנִי יְהוָה מְקַדִּשְׁכֶם (2mp suffix), a divine self-predication grounding the command. This addresses a different party (the lay Israelite instructed to treat the priest as holy) than the priests addressed in third person throughout 21:1-7, matching the person-shift class treated as decisive elsewhere in this book at the addressee redirect of 24:15 and the standalone one-verse coda at 15:31.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Could stay merged with 21:5-7 as this block's own closing motive verse, the reading I held in the prior round; but that requires treating an addressee change and two independent, self-standing כי clauses as non-delimiting here while an addressee change is decisive at 24:15 and a bare person/scope shift alone earns 15:31 its own standalone row -- an inconsistency in how the same signal class is weighted, not a genuine textual distinction. No penalty/sanction language differentiates v.9 from v.8 in a way that would justify treating presence-or-absence of a penalty clause, rather than person and clause structure, as the operative criterion.

boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.25.35 "If your brother has become poor, and his hand can't support himself among you, then you shall uphold him"
web:Lev.25.37 "You shall not lend him your money at interest, nor give him your food for profit"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you,' opens the chapter's most extensive case, prohibiting Israelite slavery in favor of hired-servant status until Jubilee release, then explicitly contrasting this with the different rule permitting the acquisition of foreign slaves as permanent property.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the Israelite bondservant rule (39-43) from the foreign-slave permission (44-46), since the two address different classes of unfree labor; I merged them because the text explicitly frames the foreign-slave rule as a direct contrast to the Israelite rule just given ('as for your male and your female slaves, whom you may have from the nations'), making the pairing itself the point being made.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.25.39 "you shall not make him to serve as a slave"
web:Lev.25.44 "As for your male and your female slaves, whom you may have from the nations that are around you"

boundary_rationale: A final protasis, 'if an alien or temporary resident with you becomes rich, and your brother beside him has grown poor, and sells himself to the stranger,' opens the chapter's last and most elaborate redemption case -- an Israelite who has fallen into servitude to a resident foreigner -- closing the chapter on the theological ground, 'the children of Israel are servants...whom I brought out of the land of Egypt.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might merge this with the Israelite-bondservant unit as 'more slavery provisions'; but this case addresses a structurally distinct situation (an Israelite indentured not to a fellow Israelite but to a resident alien), requiring its own extensive kinsman-redemption mechanism not needed in the simpler case of Israelite-to-Israelite servitude.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.25.47 "an alien or temporary resident with you becomes rich, and your brother beside him has grown poor"
web:Lev.25.55 "the children of Israel are servants; they are my servants whom I brought out of the land of Egypt"

boundary_rationale: A brief preamble opens without a fresh messenger formula, restating the idol prohibition and sanctuary-reverence command already given at 19:4 and 19:30, functioning as a bridge from ch.25's economic laws into the covenant-conclusion material that follows, before the blessings proper begin at v.3.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as the closing verses of ch.25's slavery material, given the absence of a new speech formula; but its content (idols, Sabbaths, sanctuary) is entirely unrelated to ch.25's economic topic, and it functions as the standard covenant-preamble device (renewed basic loyalty commands) preceding the blessing/curse structure that follows in every ancient Near Eastern treaty-like document, including this one.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.26.1 "You shall make for yourselves no idols"
web:Lev.26.2 "You shall keep my Sabbaths, and have reverence for my sanctuary"

boundary_rationale: A protasis-apodosis pair opens the covenant conclusion proper, 'if you walk in my statutes and keep my commandments...then I will give you your rains in their season,' listing an extensive, escalating series of blessings (rain, harvest, peace, victory, fertility, divine presence) contingent on obedience.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the agricultural blessings (4-5) from the peace/military blessings (6-8) and the divine-presence blessings (9-13); I kept the whole span together since all three sub-lists hang off the single 'if you walk in my statutes' protasis at v.3 with no fresh conditional reopening the topic until the curse section begins at v.14.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.26.3 "If you walk in my statutes and keep my commandments, and do them"
web:Lev.26.12 "I will walk among you, and will be your God, and you will be my people"

boundary_rationale: A sharply contrastive protasis opens the curse section, 'but if you will not listen to me, and will not do all these commandments,' listing the first tier of consequences (terror, disease, crop failure, military defeat), the first of five escalating 'if you still do not listen' cycles that structure the rest of the chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might treat all the curses (14-39) as one undivided list given their shared theme; I split by tier instead because each new tier is introduced by its own repeated 'and if...still' (ve'im...od) protasis with an explicit sevenfold-intensification apodosis, a recurring formulaic structure the text itself uses to escalate, making each tier its own marked unit.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.26.14 "if you will not listen to me, and will not do all these commandments"
web:Lev.26.17 "you will flee when no one pursues you"

boundary_rationale: The second escalation cycle opens with the chapter's recurring formula, 'if you in spite of these things will not listen to me, then I will chastise you seven times more for your sins,' narrowing this tier's consequence to agricultural failure (iron sky, bronze soil) distinct from tier one's disease-and-defeat consequences.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with tier one as 'more of the same curse list'; but the 'seven times more' escalation formula explicitly marks this as a new, intensified stage rather than a continuation, and this is the pattern that structures the whole passage into five recognizable movements.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.26.18 "I will chastise you seven times more for your sins"
web:Lev.26.19 "I will make your sky like iron, and your soil like bronze"

boundary_rationale: The third escalation cycle opens with the same recurring formula, 'if you walk contrary to me, and won't listen to me, then I will bring seven times more plagues,' this time specifying wild animals as the consequence, the shortest of the five tiers.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might collapse this brief two-verse tier into the surrounding tiers rather than giving it its own chunk; but the formulaic escalation marker recurs here exactly as it does at every other tier boundary in this passage, and brevity alone is not grounds to erase a formula-marked seam the owner addendum treats as tier-1 evidence.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.26.21 "if you walk contrary to me...I will bring seven times more plagues on you"
web:Lev.26.22 "I will send the wild animals among you"

boundary_rationale: The fourth escalation cycle opens with the recurring formula, 'if by these things you won't be turned back to me...then I will also walk contrary to you,' specifying sword, pestilence, and famine (siege conditions) as this tier's distinct consequence.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the wild-animals tier as 'more plague escalation'; but the recurring protasis marks a fresh tier exactly as at every other boundary in this sequence, and the siege-and-famine imagery here is materially distinct from the wild-animal consequence of the tier before it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.26.23 "if by these things you won't be turned back to me, but will walk contrary to me"
web:Lev.26.26 "When I break your staff of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven"

boundary_rationale: The fifth escalation cycle's weqatal threat chain (וְהִשְׁמַדְתִּי...וְאֶתְכֶם אֱזָרֶה בַגּוֹיִם) runs unbroken in 2mp address through v.33; v.34 shifts the grammatical subject to הָאָרֶץ (3fs) with the discourse particle אָז firing twice (אָז תִּרְצֶה הָאָרֶץ אֶת שַׁבְּתֹתֶיהָ), a genuine text signal marking a new proposition rather than a mere causal continuation of the 2mp threat.
strongest_rejected_alternative: V.34-35 remains addressed to the same audience causally ('you are in your enemies' land') and a real WEB paragraph break falls before v.36 rather than v.34, which could support extending this unit through v.35; but the subject-shift-plus-doubled-אָז marker is a genuine Hebrew signal the evidence rules privilege, while the paragraph-break evidence is metadata-only and cannot override it. The v.36 reading is preserved on record as a live alternative, not adopted.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.26.33 וְאֶתְכֶם אֱזָרֶה בַגּוֹיִם...אַרְצְכֶם שְׁמָמָה (2mp throughout, single-witness)
oshb:Lev.26.34 אָז תִּרְצֶה הָאָרֶץ אֶת שַׁבְּתֹתֶיהָ (3fs subject shift, אָז doubled, single-witness)

boundary_rationale: This unit opens on the same אָז-plus-land-subject-shift signal that closes M8-Lev-168 (see that decision), the genuine Hebrew marker of a new descriptive proposition; an internal sub-seam recurs at v.36/v.39 (וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים בָּכֶם, repeated), correctly treated as internal structure within this one unit rather than grounds to shrink its outer boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Rescoping this unit to begin at v.36 (matching its 'survivors' terror' content and a real WEB paragraph break there) was proposed, with 26:34-35 folded into M8-Lev-168 instead as that tier's causal outworking; but the paragraph-break evidence is metadata-only, and the אָז-plus-land-subject signal at v.34 is the stronger, evidence-rule-privileged marker for this unit's actual start. Preserved on record as a considered alternative, not adopted.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.26.34 אָז תִּרְצֶה הָאָרֶץ אֶת שַׁבְּתֹתֶיהָ (single-witness)
oshb:Lev.26.36 וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים בָּכֶם and Lev.26.39 וְהַנִּשְׁאָרִים בָּכֶם (internal envelope, not an outer-boundary signal, single-witness)

boundary_rationale: V.40, וְהִתְוַדּוּ אֶת עֲוֺנָם וְאֶת עֲוֺן אֲבֹתָם, is a waw-consecutive perfect continuing v.39's 3mp chain (יִמַּקּוּ), not a marked conditional; the original 'if they confess' framing was a WEB interpretive rendering with no oshb ref actually tested against it. The seam at 26:39/40 is retained but re-grounded on the real Hebrew markers instead: the אוֹ אָז discourse pivot at v.41 (אוֹ אָז יִכָּנַע לְבָבָם הֶעָרֵל) and the וְזָכַרְתִּי covenant-remembrance chain recurring at vv.42 and 45.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The seam itself could be abandoned along with the mistaken 'protasis' framing, folding vv.40-45 back into the preceding tier-five/exile material as one continuous 3mp chain; but the אוֹ אָז pivot and the repeated covenant-remembrance formula are real, checkable turns in the discourse that justify keeping this as its own restoration unit, just not on the conditional-clause ground originally claimed.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Lev.26.40 וְהִתְוַדּוּ אֶת עֲוֺנָם (veqatal, no אִם/כִּי, single-witness)
oshb:Lev.26.41 אוֹ אָז יִכָּנַע לְבָבָם הֶעָרֵל (discourse pivot, single-witness)
oshb:Lev.26.42 וְזָכַרְתִּי אֶת בְּרִיתִי יַעֲקוֹב (covenant-remembrance chain, echoed v.45, single-witness)
cf. oshb:Lev.26.3, 26.14, 26.18, 26.21, 26.23, 26.27 (this chapter's genuinely אִם/וְאִם-marked seams, all properly rated high, single-witness)

boundary_rationale: A summary colophon closes the entire legislative corpus reaching back to the beginning of the book, 'these are the statutes, ordinances, and laws, which Yahweh made between him and the children of Israel in Mount Sinai by Moses,' the most comprehensive of the book's colophons in scope.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be attached to the restoration unit as its closing verse; but its retrospective, whole-corpus-summarizing language (naming three distinct categories of law and dating them all to Sinai) matches the colophon function seen at 7:37-38 and 11:46-47 exactly, marking it as its own closing unit for the whole Sinai legislation rather than a continuation of ch.26's blessing/curse material specifically.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.26.46 "These are the statutes, ordinances, and laws, which Yahweh made between him and the children of Israel in Mount Sinai by Moses"

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the book's final appendix, explicitly outside the Sinai-corpus colophon just given at 26:46, addressing vows to dedicate a person's value to Yahweh, with a graduated fee schedule by age and sex closing on a means-tested provision for the poor matching the pattern of similar provisions in chs.5, 12, and 14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could read the whole chapter as continuing the legal material of chs.1-26 without a real break; but the closing colophon at 26:46 explicitly marks the end of 'the statutes...which Yahweh made...in Mount Sinai,' and ch.27's fresh messenger formula opens genuinely new subject matter (personal and property vows) not covered by anything preceding it, functioning as a recognized appendix.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.2 "When a man consecrates a person to Yahweh in a vow, according to your valuation"
web:Lev.27.8 "if he is poorer than your valuation...The priest shall assign a value according to his ability to pay"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if it is an animal of which men offer an offering to Yahweh,' shifts the vow object from a person to an animal, introducing a distinct substitution rule (any exchange, good for bad, renders both animals holy) not applicable to the person-valuation case.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the person-valuation unit as 'vows generally'; but the valuation mechanism itself changes entirely -- persons are priced by a fixed age/sex schedule, while animals are subject to a substitution-penalty rule with no fixed schedule at all -- marking a genuine functional break.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.9 "If it is an animal of which men offer an offering to Yahweh"
web:Lev.27.10 "if he shall at all exchange animal for animal, then both it and that for which it is exchanged shall be holy"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'when a man dedicates his house to be holy to Yahweh,' opens a third vow-object category, houses, with its own priestly-evaluation-plus-redemption mechanism distinct from both the person and animal cases.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might fold this into the animal-substitution unit as 'more property vows'; but a house is evaluated and redeemed by an entirely different procedure (priestly appraisal plus a fifth added for redemption, with no substitution concept at all), matching the book's pattern of treating each new vow-object as its own case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.14 "When a man dedicates his house to be holy to Yahweh, then the priest shall evaluate it"
web:Lev.27.15 "he shall add the fifth part of the money of your valuation to it, and it shall be his"

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'if a man dedicates to Yahweh part of the field of his possession,' opens the fourth vow-object category, ancestral land, with a valuation mechanism explicitly tied to the Jubilee cycle (seed-yield pricing, redemption windows scaled to years remaining) not present in any of the preceding cases.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the house-dedication unit as 'more real-property vows'; but the field's valuation is explicitly anchored to the Jubilee calendar established in ch.25, an entirely different pricing logic from the flat priestly appraisal used for houses, and the field case is substantially longer and more elaborate.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.16 "If a man dedicates to Yahweh part of the field of his possession"
web:Lev.27.17 "If he dedicates his field from the Year of Jubilee, according to your valuation it shall stand"

boundary_rationale: A contrasting protasis, 'if he dedicates a field to Yahweh which he has bought, which is not of the field of his possession,' opens a distinct sub-case for purchased (rather than ancestral) land, whose Jubilee-year disposition differs sharply -- it reverts to the original owner rather than becoming the dedicator's own permanent holding.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might treat this as a mere footnote to the ancestral-field unit rather than its own chunk; but the outcome at Jubilee is categorically different between the two field types (permanent priestly holding for ancestral land devoted outright, versus reversion to the original owner for purchased land), a distinction significant enough that the text opens this case with its own explicit contrast.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.22 "if he dedicates a field to Yahweh which he has bought"
web:Lev.27.24 "In the Year of Jubilee the field shall return to him from whom it was bought"

boundary_rationale: A restrictive clause, 'however the firstborn among animals, which belongs to Yahweh as a firstborn, no man may dedicate,' opens a brief exclusion rule -- firstborn animals already belong to Yahweh by an earlier claim and so cannot be freshly vowed -- a distinct legal point from the field-valuation cases just concluded.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the purchased-field case as 'more valuation exceptions'; but its logic is different in kind (a prior claim precluding a fresh vow, not a valuation-and-redemption schedule), and its opening adversative 'however' (akh) explicitly marks it as a new restriction rather than a continuation.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.26 "the firstborn among animals, which belongs to Yahweh as a firstborn, no man may dedicate"
oshb:Lev.27.26 אַךְ בְּכוֹר אֲשֶׁר יְבֻכַּר לַיהוָה בִּבְהֵמָה לֹא יַקְדִּישׁ אִישׁ אֹתוֹ

boundary_rationale: A new protasis, 'no devoted thing that a man devotes to Yahweh...shall be sold or redeemed,' introduces cherem (irrevocable devotion), the vow appendix's most absolute category, explicitly contrasted with every preceding case by its total exclusion of redemption -- extending in v.29 to the case of a person devoted to destruction, who cannot be ransomed at all.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split could separate the general devoted-things rule (28) from the human-cherem case (29); I merged them because both share the same absolute no-redemption logic and the human case reads as the most extreme instance of the general principle just stated rather than an independently triggered new topic.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.28 "Everything that is permanently devoted is most holy to Yahweh"
web:Lev.27.29 "No one devoted to destruction...shall be ransomed. He shall surely be put to death"

boundary_rationale: A new topic opens, 'all the tithe of the land...is Yahweh's,' shifting from vow-and-dedication law (a voluntary act) to the tithe (a standing obligation), covering both agricultural produce and livestock passing under the shepherd's rod, with its own redemption-plus-a-fifth mechanism for produce but an explicit no-substitution rule for livestock.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the devoted-things unit as 'more holy-property rules'; but the tithe is conceptually distinct from a vow or cherem -- it is a regular, obligatory portion rather than a special dedication -- and the chapter itself signals the shift with a fresh topic-opening clause rather than continuing the cherem logic.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.30 "All the tithe of the land, whether of the seed of the land or of the fruit of the trees, is Yahweh's"
web:Lev.27.32 "All the tithe of the herds or the flocks, whatever passes under the rod, the tenth shall be holy to Yahweh"

boundary_rationale: A final colophon closes both the vow appendix and the whole book, 'these are the commandments which Yahweh commanded Moses for the children of Israel on Mount Sinai,' explicitly echoing the 'Mount Sinai' bookend of 7:38, 25:1, and 26:46 one last time to frame the entirety of Leviticus as Sinai-given legislation.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be attached to the tithe-law unit as its closing verse; but its retrospective, whole-book-summarizing language and its explicit dating formula match the function of every other colophon in the book rather than the specific content of the tithe law just given, marking it as the book's own final closing frame.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Lev.27.34 "These are the commandments which Yahweh commanded Moses for the children of Israel on Mount Sinai"
oshb:Lev.27.34 אֵלֶּה הַמִּצְוֹת אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּהַר סִינָי

boundary_rationale: The book opens on its own dated superscription, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה ("Yahweh spoke to Moses") anchored to the wilderness of Sinai and the first day of the second month, which opens the census command; the roster of twelve tribal representatives that follows (vv.5-15) is bound to that command by its own introducing clause, "these are the names of the men who shall stand with you," and the whole span closes on its own colophon in v.16 naming them קְרוּאֵי הָעֵדָה ("those called of the congregation").
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could split the twelve-name roster (vv.5-15) away from the census command as its own register, but the roster has no independent opening formula of its own -- it is syntactically the direct object of v.5's "these are the names" -- so severing it would cut a single command-plus-witness-list unit in half.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.1.1 “Yahweh spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai…on the first day of the second month…saying”

oshb:Num.1.16 אֵ֚לֶּה קריאי קְרוּאֵ֣י הָעֵדָ֔ה נְשִׂיאֵ֖י מַטּ֣וֹת אֲבוֹתָ֑ם רָאשֵׁ֛י אַלְפֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל הֵֽם (“these were the called of the congregation, the princes of the tribes of their fathers; they were the heads of the thousands of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: Narration pivots from Yahweh's command to Moses and Aaron's compliance -- וַיִּקַּח מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן ("Moses and Aaron took") -- an execution notice distinct in grammatical subject and mood from the imperative-laden command it fulfills, closed by the recurring compliance tag כַּאֲשֶׁר צִּוָּה יְהוָה ("as Yahweh commanded").
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep vv.17-19 fused with the register above on the theory that assembling the named men and counting the people are one continuous administrative act; but the shift from Yahweh's second-person instruction to third-person narrated fulfillment is the same command/execution seam this book marks repeatedly elsewhere, and treating it as scenery rather than boundary would blur that recurring device.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.1.17 “Moses and Aaron took these men who are mentioned by name”
oshb:Num.1.19 כַּאֲשֶׁר צִּוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (“as Yahweh commanded Moses”)

boundary_rationale: Each of the twelve tribal entries repeats one identical template -- lineage clause, family/fathers'-house phrase, age threshold, then the tally verb -- with only the tribe name and the resulting number changing; because no entry introduces a new legal or procedural element, this reads as one register closed by its own grand-total colophon in vv.44-46, and extended through v.47's Levite-exclusion clause, which functions as the census total's own qualifying exception rather than the opening of the next unit. On revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-003-1), the twelve per-tribe petuchot standing after each tribe's own tally (approximately 1:21, 23, 25, 27, 29, 31, 33, 35, 37, 39, 41, 43 -- "(two-witness)") are recorded here as preserved, addressed counterevidence: a mark this strong and this regular is real corroboration for reading each tribe as its own sub-unit, but per the owner addendum petuchah alone cannot drive a boundary, and it does not outweigh the register's own content-identity test (no entry introduces a new legal or procedural element), the same test M8-Num-176 applies openly to a comparable case rather than passing over in silence.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer reading would give each tribe its own decision the way the camp order in ch.2 gets one per standard, and the twelve petuchot recorded above are real, marked support for that finer reading -- but ch.2's four camps differ materially in composition and each closes on a distinguishing march-order clause, whereas here all twelve entries are the same sentence with two variables swapped, so the marks corroborate a boundary the content itself does not independently support. Separately, v.47 could stay with the following Levite instruction (its original placement) rather than this register, but v.48's own fresh וַיְדַבֵּר formula marks the true onset of that instruction, and the divine-speech formula opens a decision at twenty-two of twenty-four comparable sites across Num.1-10.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.1.20 “The children of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn, their generations…all who were able to go out to war:”
web:Num.1.21 “those who were counted of them, of the tribe of Reuben, were forty-six thousand five hundred”
oshb:Num.1.44 אֵ֣לֶּה הַפְּקֻדִ֡ים אֲשֶׁר֩ פָּקַ֨ד מֹשֶׁ֤ה וְאַהֲרֹן֙ (“these are they who were counted, whom Moses and Aaron counted”)
oshb:Num.1.47 וְהַלְוִיִּם לְמַטֵּה אֲבֹתָם לֹא הָתְפָּקְדוּ בְּתוֹכָם (“but the Levites after the tribe of their fathers were not counted among them”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh speech formula, כִּי דִבֶּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה (v.48), pivots the chapter's topic from counting fighting men to appointing tabernacle-carriers, matching the corpus-wide pattern in which a divine-speech formula opens a decision at twenty-two of twenty-four comparable sites in Num.1-10; the Levite-exclusion note that previously opened this span (v.47) now closes the census register instead (M8-Num-003), leaving this decision's own onset at the genuine formula boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: v.47 could remain this decision's own opening exception clause, since it names the very group v.48-53 goes on to instruct; but v.47 is a vav-disjunctive note attachable either direction, and the corpus-pattern of divine-speech-formula onsets is too regular across this stretch of the book to treat this one site as the exception without a stated reason.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.1.48 “For Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying, ‘Only the tribe of Levi you shall not count’”
oshb:Num.1.54 וַיַּעֲשׂוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (“thus the children of Israel did…so they did”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh double-addressee formula, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְאֶל אַהֲרֹן ("Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron"), opens the chapter and states the governing principle for everything that follows -- each man by his own standard, at a set distance around the Tent of Meeting -- before any specific camp is named, functioning as the superscription for the whole four-camp system rather than part of any single camp's entry.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the Judah-camp entry that immediately follows it, since nothing else intervenes; but v.2's instruction is stated in general terms that apply equally to all four standards, not specifically to Judah's position, so treating it as Judah's opening would misassign a rule that governs the system as a whole to one camp within it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.1 “Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying”

oshb:Num.2.2 אִ֣ישׁ עַל דִּגְל֤וֹ בְאֹתֹת֙ לְבֵ֣ית אֲבֹתָ֔ם יַחֲנ֖וּ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל מִנֶּ֕גֶד סָבִ֥יב לְאֹֽהֶל מוֹעֵ֖ד יַחֲנֽוּ (“every man by his own standard, with the banners of their fathers’ houses; they shall encamp around the Tent of Meeting at a distance from it”)

boundary_rationale: The east-side camp entry is marked off by its own orientation clause, וְהַחֹנִים קְֳֵמָה מִזְרָחָה ("those who encamp on the east, toward the sunrise"), names Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun under one standard, and closes on the sequence-marking clause רִאשֹׁנָה יִסָּעוּ ("they shall set out first").
strongest_rejected_alternative: The four camps could be treated as one undivided register the way ch.1's census tally is, since each entry shares a broadly similar shape; but unlike ch.1's twelve identical tribe-formulas, each camp here names a different trio of tribes and closes on its own distinct march-position clause (first/second/third/last), a functional distinction the pure census tally never carries.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.3 “Those who encamp on the east side toward the sunrise shall be of the standard of the camp of Judah”
oshb:Num.2.9 רִאשֹׁנָה יִסָּעוּ (“they shall set out first”)

boundary_rationale: A parallel orientation clause, עַל הַצּ֣ד נֶגֶמלע קֶ ("on the south side"), reopens the register for a different trio of tribes -- Reuben, Simeon, Gad -- and closes on its own ordinal marker, וְשְׁנִּיִם יִסָּעוּ ("they shall set out second"), matching the east camp's form while naming distinct people.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Since the internal formula (prince name, division count, cumulative total) is identical to the Judah camp's, a reader could argue this is mere repetition undeserving of a fresh boundary; but the orientation clause and the ordinal close are themselves the text's own device for segmenting the four camps, and ignoring them to save a decision would understate a marker the chapter itself uses four times over.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.10 “On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben”
oshb:Num.2.16 וְשְׁנִּיִם יִסָּעוּ (“they shall set out second”)

boundary_rationale: This single verse interrupts the four-camp sequence to place the Tent of Meeting and the Levite camp in the middle of the march, marking a different participant class (Levites, not a tribal standard) and a different kind of statement (a structural rule about march order rather than a roster entry), sitting precisely at the chapter's midpoint between the second and third camps.
strongest_rejected_alternative: It would be simpler to append this verse to the Reuben-camp entry that precedes it, since nothing marks a new speech formula here; but its subject is the Levites' Tent-of-Meeting position, not Reuben's division, and folding it into either neighboring camp would misattribute a rule about the whole march's structure to one tribe's register entry.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.17 “Then the Tent of Meeting shall set out, with the camp of the Levites in the middle of the camps”
oshb:Num.2.17 וְנָסַע אֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵד מַחֲנֵה הַלְוִּיִם בְּתוּךְ הַמַּחֲנֹת (“the Tent of Meeting shall set out, the camp of the Levites, in the midst of the camps”)

boundary_rationale: The register resumes with a third orientation clause, דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה אֶפְרַיִם…יָמָּה ("the standard of the camp of Ephraim…on the west"), naming Ephraim, Manasseh, and Benjamin, and closes on the third ordinal, וּשְׁלִשִׁים יִסָּעוּ ("they shall set out third").
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might merge this with the preceding Levite-hinge verse into one "west side" unit, but the hinge concerns march order for the whole camp while this span is a self-contained tribal register with its own prince names and totals; conflating them would erase the participant-class distinction the hinge verse exists to mark.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.18 “On the west side shall be the standard of the camp of Ephraim”
oshb:Num.2.24 כָּל הַפְּקֻדִים לְמַחֲנֵה אֶפְרַיִם...וּשְׁלִשִׁים יִסָּעוּ (“all who were counted of the camp of Ephraim…they shall set out third”)

boundary_rationale: The fourth and final orientation clause, דֶּּגֶל מַחֲנֵה דָן צָפֹנָה ("the standard of the camp of Dan, on the north"), completes the fourfold structure, naming Dan, Asher, and Naphtali, and closes on the distinguishing rear-guard clause לָאַחֲרֹנָה יִסְעוּ ("they shall set out last"), a different ordinal marker from the other three camps'.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Given that all four camps share the same three-tribe-plus-total shape, a minimal-split reading would treat vv.3-31 as one continuous four-part list needing no internal decisions at all; but each camp's own orientation-and-ordinal frame is a real, repeated structural device the text uses to segment the march, and collapsing all four into one span would erase that device entirely.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.25 “On the north side shall be the standard of the camp of Dan”
oshb:Num.2.31 לָאַחֲרֹנָה יִסְעוּ לְדִגְלֵיהֶם (“they shall set out last by their standards”)

boundary_rationale: After the fourth camp, the text steps back from the tribe-by-tribe register to a whole-book grand total (matching ch.1's), a repeated note that the Levites were excluded, and the closing fulfillment tag, וַיַּעֲשׂוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִּוָּה יְהוָה ("the children of Israel did according to all that Yahweh commanded"), a summary register-close distinct in function from any single camp's entry.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This closing note could be attached to the Dan-camp entry as its final clause, since nothing separates them typographically; but v.32's total covers all four camps together, not Dan's alone, and the compliance formula in v.34 answers the whole chapter's opening command in v.1-2, so it functions as the chapter's close rather than the fourth camp's.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.2.34 “Thus the children of Israel did…so they encamped by their standards, and so they set out”
oshb:Num.2.32 אֵ֚לֶּה פְּקוּדֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (“these are the numbered ones of the children of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: A genealogical superscription, וְאֵּלֶּה תוֹלְדֹת אַהֲרֹן ומֹשֶׁה ("now these are the generations of Aaron and Moses"), opens a new topic (the priestly line, not the tribal census) and this unit is closed by the Nadab/Abihu death notice, which explains why only Eleazar and Ithamar remain active in the priesthood -- a self-contained genealogical unit before the Levites are ever mentioned.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because "generations" formulas elsewhere in the Torah often open much larger units, one could extend this span through the whole Levite material in ch.3-4; but v.5's fresh וַיְדַבֵּר formula immediately begins a new topic (the Levites given to Aaron) with its own imperative, so the toledot notice reads as a self-contained priestly-lineage preface rather than the header for everything that follows.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.1 “Now this is the history of the generations of Aaron and Moses”
oshb:Num.3.4 וַיְכַהֵן אֶלְעָזָר וְאִיתָמָר עַל פְּנֵי אַהֲרֹן אֲבִיהֶם (“Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests in the presence of Aaron their father”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר, opens the imperative to bring the tribe of Levi near and set it before Aaron, closed on the same capital-crime refrain used for the sanctuary throughout this book, וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת ("the stranger who comes near shall be put to death").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the next speech formula's firstborn-substitution rationale (vv.11-13) as one continuous "Levites for Aaron" instruction, since both concern the same broad arrangement; v.11 reopens on its own fresh וַיְדַבֵּר formula and shifts from procedural assignment (Levites serve Aaron) to theological rationale (Levites replace firstborns), a real change of register the formula break marks.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.6 “Bring the tribe of Levi near, and set them before Aaron the priest, that they may minister to him”
oshb:Num.3.10 וְהַזָּר הַקָּרֵב יוּמָת (“and the stranger who comes near shall be put to death”)

boundary_rationale: A second fresh וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר formula shifts the topic from procedural assignment to theological grounding -- the Levites stand in place of every Israelite firstborn spared in Egypt -- closed by the self-identifying refrain אֲנִי יְהוָה ("I am Yahweh").
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader might fold this rationale into the census command that follows (vv.14-16), since both address the Levites' special status; v.14, though, carries a fresh formula of its own and a wholly different action verb (count, not take), so keeping the rationale statement distinct from the counting instruction it grounds better reflects two speech acts rather than one continuous command.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.12 “I have taken the Levites…instead of all the firstborn”
oshb:Num.3.13 לִי יִהְיוּ אֲנִי יְהוָה (“they shall be mine; I am Yahweh”)

boundary_rationale: A third fresh messenger formula opens a distinct imperative -- פְּקֹד אֶת בְּנֵי לֵוִי ("count the children of Levi") -- setting a month-old-and-upward threshold that contrasts sharply with the twenty-year war-census age in ch.1, and closes on Moses' compliance notice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Since both this span and the census-execution register that follows concern counting the Levites, one could merge them into a single command-plus-results unit; but the register (vv.17ff) opens with its own distinct genealogical formula naming Gershon, Kohath, and Merari rather than continuing the command's second-person imperative, so I keep the command separate from the roster it authorizes.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.15 “Count the children of Levi by their fathers’ houses…every male from a month old and upward”
oshb:Num.3.16 וַיִּפְקֹד אֹתָם מֹשֶׁה עַל פִּּי יְהוָה (“Moses counted them according to Yahweh’s word”)

boundary_rationale: The three-clan skeleton -- Gershon, Kohath, Merari, each immediately followed by its own sub-family names -- opens the detailed Levite register proper, closed by its own summary clause, אֵּלֶּה הֵּם מִשְׁפְּחֹת הַלֵּוִי לְבֵית אֲבֹתָם ("these are the families of the Levites according to their fathers' houses").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This bare name list could be treated as an inseparable heading fused to the Gershonite entry that immediately follows, since it has no count or duty of its own; but its own closing colophon (v.20b) marks it as a complete three-clan skeleton in its own right, structurally parallel to how the twelve-prince roster in ch.1 closes before the tribal counts proper begin.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.17 “These were the sons of Levi by their names: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari”

oshb:Num.3.20 וּבְנֵ֧י מְרָרִ֛י לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֖ם מַחְלִ֣י וּמוּשִׁ֑י אֵ֥לֶּה הֵ֛ם מִשְׁפְּחֹ֥ת הַלֵּוִ֖י לְבֵ֥ית אֲבֹתָֽם (“the sons of Merari by their families: Mahli and Mushi; these are the families of the Levites according to their fathers’ houses”)

boundary_rationale: The Gershonite entry has the same five-part shape that recurs for Kohath and Merari -- sub-family names, count, camp position, prince, and itemized duty -- opened by its own clause לְגֵּרְשׁוֹן מִשְׂפַּחת ("of Gershon was the family of") and closed on its own itemized-duty list, distinguishing it structurally from the Kohathite and Merarite entries that share its form but not its content.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The three clan entries could be merged into one register the way I merged the twelve tribes of ch.1, since all three share one five-part template; but unlike ch.1's tribes, each clan here carries a materially different duty list (curtains and coverings for Gershon; ark and furniture for Kohath; frames and pillars for Merari), so the template's content, not just its names and numbers, changes clan to clan.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.21 “Of Gershon was the family of the Libnites, and the family of the Shimeites”

oshb:Num.3.25 וּמִשְׁמֶ֤רֶת בְּנֵֽי גֵרְשׁוֹן֙ בְּאֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֔ד הַמִּשְׁכָּ֖ן וְהָאֹ֑הֶל מִכְסֵ֕הוּ וּמָסַ֕ךְ פֶּ֖תַח אֹ֥הֶל מוֹעֵֽד (“the duty of the sons of Gershon in the Tent of Meeting shall be the tabernacle, the tent, its covering, the screen for the door of the Tent of Meeting”)

boundary_rationale: וְלִקְהָת ("and of Kohath") reopens the register for the second clan, whose duty list -- ark, table, lampstand, altars, sanctuary vessels -- is distinct enough in content and gravity that a special chief-of-princes, Eleazar himself, is named to oversee it, a detail none of the other two clans receives.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep Kohath fused to Gershon under a single "Levite duties" span, treating the whole three-clan run as one topic; but the fresh וְלִקְהָת opening and the unique addition of a supervising prince over Kohath alone mark this as a structurally and functionally separate entry, not a continuation of Gershon's.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.31 “Their duty shall be the ark, the table, the lamp stand, the altars, the vessels of the sanctuary”

oshb:Num.3.27 וְלִקְהָ֗ת מִשְׁפַּ֤חַת הַֽעַמְרָמִי֙ וּמִשְׁפַּ֣חַת הַיִּצְהָרִ֔י וּמִשְׁפַּ֨חַת֙ הַֽחֶבְרֹנִ֔י וּמִשְׁפַּ֖חַת הָֽעָזִּיאֵלִ֑י אֵ֥לֶּה הֵ֖ם מִשְׁפְּחֹ֥ת הַקְּהָתִֽי (“of Kohath was the family of the Amramites, the family of the Izharites, the family of the Hebronites, and the family of the Uzzielites; these are the families of the Kohathites”)

boundary_rationale: לְמְרָרִי ("of Merari") opens the third and last clan entry, whose duty list -- the tabernacle's frames, bars, pillars, and sockets -- is the structural rather than sacred-furniture portion of the tabernacle, completing the three-clan set begun at v.21.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because Merari's entry closely mirrors Kohath's in grammatical shape, a reader could treat vv.27-37 as one undifferentiated "remaining two clans" span; but Merari's own opening formula and wholly distinct duty content (structural framework rather than sacred vessels) mark it as the register's third discrete entry, consistent with how Gershon and Kohath were each given their own span above.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.36 “The appointed duty of the sons of Merari shall be the tabernacle’s boards, its bars, its pillars”

oshb:Num.3.33 לִמְרָרִ֕י מִשְׁפַּ֨חַת֙ הַמַּחְלִ֔י וּמִשְׁפַּ֖חַת הַמּוּשִׁ֑י אֵ֥לֶּה הֵ֖ם מִשְׁפְּחֹ֥ת מְרָרִֽי (“of Merari was the family of the Mahlites and the family of the Mushites; these are the families of Merari”)

boundary_rationale: The register shifts from clan-by-clan entries to Moses and Aaron's own eastward camp position -- a distinct participant class from the three named clans -- and closes the whole Levite census with its grand total, כָּל פְּקוּדֵי הַלְויִּם ("all who were counted of the Levites"), a summary-total function distinct from any single clan's entry.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be attached to the Merarite entry as its closing clause, since nothing else intervenes structurally; but Moses and Aaron's priestly-family camp position is not a fourth Levite clan, and v.39's total sums across all three clans just named, functioning as this register's colophon rather than Merari's.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.39 “All who were counted of the Levites…were twenty-two thousand”

oshb:Num.3.38 וְהַחֹנִ֣ים לִפְנֵ֣י הַמִּשְׁכָּ֡ן קֵ֣דְמָה לִפְנֵי֩ אֹֽהֶל מוֹעֵ֨ד מִזְרָ֜חָה מֹשֶׁ֣ה וְאַהֲרֹ֣ן וּבָנָ֗יו שֹֽׁמְרִים֙ מִשְׁמֶ֣רֶת הַמִּקְדָּ֔שׁ לְמִשְׁמֶ֖רֶת בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וְהַזָּ֥ר הַקָּרֵ֖ב יוּמָֽת (“those who encamp before the tabernacle eastward, in front of the Tent of Meeting toward the sunrise, shall be Moses, with Aaron and his sons, keeping the requirements of the sanctuary”)

boundary_rationale: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה ("Yahweh said to Moses") opens a fresh command to count Israel's own firstborn males, distinct in both addressee logic and purpose from the Levite census just concluded, and the span closes with Moses' execution and the resulting count.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could merge this firstborn census with the redemption-money command that follows (vv.44-51) as one continuous firstborn-related topic; v.44 instead reopens on a fresh messenger formula and shifts from counting people to prescribing a monetary transaction, a real change in the kind of instruction given.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.40 “Count all the firstborn males of the children of Israel…and take the number of their names”

oshb:Num.3.43 וַיְהִי֩ כָל בְּכ֨וֹר זָכָ֜ר בְּמִסְפַּ֥ר שֵׁמ֛וֹת מִבֶּן חֹ֥דֶשׁ וָמַ֖עְלָה לִפְקֻדֵיהֶ֑ם שְׁנַ֤יִם וְעֶשְׂרִים֙ אֶ֔לֶף שְׁלֹשָׁ֥ה וְשִׁבְעִ֖ים וּמָאתָֽיִם (“all the firstborn males according to the number of names from a month old and upward, of those who were counted of them, were twenty-two thousand two hundred seventy-three”)

boundary_rationale: A final fresh וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר formula introduces the five-shekel redemption for the two hundred seventy-three firstborn who exceed the Levite count, and the chapter closes on Moses' payment of that money to Aaron -- an execution notice ending the whole Levite/firstborn census complex begun in v.5.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split further into the redemption command (vv.44-48) and its execution (vv.49-51) as two separate command/execution decisions, matching how I split ch.1's census command from its own execution; but the command and its fulfillment here share the same specific numbers (273 souls, five shekels each) with no intervening narrative gap, reading as one tightly bound transaction rather than two discrete acts.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.3.47 “You shall take five shekels apiece for each one…twenty gerahs”

oshb:Num.3.51 וַיִּתֵּ֨ן מֹשֶׁ֜ה אֶת כֶּ֧סֶף הַפְּדֻיִ֛ם לְאַהֲרֹ֥ן וּלְבָנָ֖יו עַל פִּ֣י יְהוָ֑ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה אֶת מֹשֶֽׁה (“Moses gave the redemption money to Aaron and to his sons, according to Yahweh’s word, as Yahweh commanded Moses”)

boundary_rationale: Merged on review (OL-M8-Num-028-1, merge-direction resolution): a fresh double-addressee formula opens the Kohathite census threshold (thirty to fifty years) and its own זֹאת עֲבֹדַת בְּנֵי קְהָת colophon immediately introduces the wrapping procedure for the most holy things, applied identically across each sacred object -- ark, table, lampstand, golden altar, other vessels, bronze altar -- with the recurring pole-insertion refrain. Command and duty-rubric now read as one block, matching how Gershon's (4:21-28) and Merari's (4:29-33) parallel census-plus-duty blocks were already kept whole.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The census threshold (4:1-3) could stay separate from the wrapping rubric (4:4-14) on the theory that one states who counts as a worker and the other what the worker does; but treating that internal seam as a decision boundary here while leaving the identical seam unmarked in Gershon's and Merari's blocks was the very asymmetry the challenge correctly identified, and resolving it by splitting those two blocks further would fragment material this book elsewhere treats as one register (see M8-Num-030's own merge of the three execution reports on the same principle).
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.4.2 “Take a census of the sons of Kohath…by their families, by their fathers’ houses”
oshb:Num.4.4 זֹ֛את עֲבֹדַ֥ת בְּנֵי קְהָ֖ת בְּאֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֑ד קֹ֖דֶשׁ הַקֳּדָשִֽׁים (“this is the service of the sons of Kohath in the Tent of Meeting, regarding the most holy things”)
oshb:Num.4.14 וְשָׂמ֥וּ בַדָּֽיו (“and put in its poles”)

boundary_rationale: The action shifts from the priests' wrapping work to the Kohathites' carrying duty, opened by the temporal clause וְכִלָּה אַהֲרֹן וָבָנָיו לְכַסֹּת ("when Aaron and his sons have finished covering"), and carries its own capital-danger warning, וְלֹא יִגְּעוּ אֶל הַקֹּדֶשׁ וָמֵתוּ ("and shall not touch the sanctuary, lest they die"), distinct from the priests' own wrapping instructions.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This verse could close out the wrapping-procedure span above as its final clause; but it changes both subject (Kohathites, not Aaron and sons) and action (carrying under prohibition, not covering), and it introduces the death-penalty warning that the wrapping instructions themselves never carry.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.4.15 “they shall not touch the sanctuary, lest they die”
oshb:Num.4.15 אֵּלֶּה מַשְׂא בְּנֵי קְהָת בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד (“this is the burden of the sons of Kohath in the Tent of Meeting”)

boundary_rationale: A single verse assigns lamp oil, incense, the continual meal offering, and anointing oil specifically to Eleazar, an individual office-holder rather than the Kohathite clan as a whole, marking a distinct administrative tier within the same sanctuary-object material.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as simply the last item in the Kohathite carrying-duty list; but its subject is Eleazar's personal oversight, not the clan's collective carrying, and its object list (oil, incense, meal offering) differs entirely from the ark-through-altar items just wrapped, marking a change of both responsible party and content.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.4.16 “The duty of Eleazar the son of Aaron the priest shall be the oil for the light…”

strongest_rejected_alternative: One might read this as a coda to the wrapping-procedure span, repeating its "lest they die" warning; but the fresh messenger formula and the shift from describing what is wrapped to prescribing how Aaron must manage Kohathite exposure risk mark a distinct instruction, not a repetition of the earlier one.

boundary_rationale: A fresh single-addressee formula, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה, opens the second clan's census instruction (v.22, "take a census of the sons of Gershon also") and its own duty summary (v.24, זֹאת עֲבֹדַת), the whole span closing on Ithamar's supervisory hand. On review (OL-M8-Num-028-1), this block's own internal census-command-then-duty-rubric shape (with no cut inserted at the internal זֹאת עֲבֹדַת seam) is now the model resolving the asymmetry the challenge identified: Kohath's parallel block (originally split into two decisions at the corresponding seam) has been merged to match this one, rather than splitting this block to match Kohath -- see M8-Num-023's revised span, Num.4.1-14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because this census-plus-duty span so closely parallels the Merari span that follows, a minimal-split reading might merge the two clans into one 'remaining Levite service' chunk; but each opens on its own fresh messenger formula and each names materially different burden items, exactly the distinction that kept the three clan entries of ch.3 separate. Splitting THIS block further at its own internal זֹאת עֲבֹדַת seam, to match how Kohath's block was originally cut, was the alternative direction the challenge raised; resolved instead by merging Kohath to match Gershon and Merari, since collapsing further would fragment material this book elsewhere treats as one register.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.4.22 “Take a census of the sons of Gershon also, by their fathers’ houses”

oshb:Num.4.28 זֹ֣את עֲבֹדַ֗ת מִשְׁפְּחֹ֛ת בְּנֵ֥י הַגֵּרְשֻׁנִּ֖י בְּאֹ֣הֶל מוֹעֵ֑ד וּמִ֨שְׁמַרְתָּ֔ם בְּיַד֙ אִֽיתָמָ֔ר בֶּֽן אַהֲרֹ֖ן הַכֹּהֵֽן (“this is the service of the families of the sons of the Gershonites in the Tent of Meeting; their duty shall be under the hand of Ithamar the son of Aaron the priest”)

strongest_rejected_alternative: One could argue the Ithamar-oversight refrain shared with Gershon's entry means the two clans should be read as one register; but Merari's own opening clause and wholly distinct structural-component duty list mark it as a discrete instruction, matching the same logic that separated Gershon's entry from Kohath's.

boundary_rationale: Merged on review (LF-M8-Num-030-1/031-1/032-1, verified): the three clan-execution reports -- Kohath (4:34-37), Gershon (4:38-41), Merari (4:42-45) -- share a word-for-word identical age-bracket clause (מִבֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה וָמַעְלָה וְעַד בֶּן חֲמִשִּׁים שָׁנָה) at every occurrence, more uniform than ch.1's own tribal formulas that were merged under this exact criterion; no clan's report introduces a legal or procedural element the others lack, only a changing name and a changing total.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Each clan's execution report could stay its own decision on the theory that each supplies its own distinct final count, matching the reasoning that keeps ch.26's genuinely varying tribal entries separate; but here every entry is the identical sentence with one number swapped, precisely the 'no new procedural or narrative element' test M8-Num-003 already applied to merge ch.1's twelve tribes, and applying a different standard to a structurally identical case would be the inconsistency the challenge correctly named.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.4.36 “Those who were counted of them by their families were two thousand seven hundred fifty”
