oshb:Num.4.45 אֵלֶּה פְקוּדֵי מִשְׁפְּחֹת בְּנֵי מְרָרִי אֲשֶׁר פָּקַד מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן עַל פִּי יְהוָה בְּיַד מֹשֶׁה (“these are those who were counted of the families of the sons of Merari…as Yahweh commanded Moses”)

boundary_rationale: כָּל הַפְּקוּדִים ("all who were counted") sums the three clan totals into one book-total figure, eight thousand five hundred eighty, and closes both the chapter and the whole census-and-duty complex on the recurring כַּאֲשֶׁר צִּוָּה יְהוָה compliance formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This grand total could be treated as simply the final clause of Merari's execution report; but its opening כָּל explicitly aggregates across all three clans named separately above, a distinct level of summary the text itself signals is not Merari's alone.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.4.48 “Those who were counted of them…eight thousand five hundred eighty”
oshb:Num.4.49 עַל פִּּי יְהוָה פָּקַד אוֹתָם בְּיַד מֹשֶׁה (“according to the commandment of Yahweh they were counted by Moses”)

boundary_rationale: The book's topic changes abruptly from tabernacle logistics to camp purity, opened by וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר and the command to expel three unclean classes, closed by the recurring compliance tag כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּּבֶּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה כֵּּן עָשׂוּ.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through v.10's restitution law as one general "purity of the camp" unit; v.5, though, carries a fresh messenger formula of its own and a different topic (guilt restitution, not physical expulsion), a real shift the formula break marks even though both concern camp holiness broadly.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.5.2 “Command the children of Israel that they put out of the camp every leper…”

oshb:Num.5.4 וַיַּֽעֲשׂוּ֙ כֵן֙ בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וַיְשַׁלְּח֣וּ אוֹתָ֔ם אֶל מִח֖וּץ לַֽמַּחֲנֶ֑ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֨ר דִּבֶּ֤ר יְהוָה֙ אֶל מֹשֶׁ֔ה כֵּ֥ן עָשׂ֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (“the children of Israel did so, and put them outside of the camp; as Yahweh spoke to Moses, so the children of Israel did”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh speech formula opens a law of confession and financial restitution for trespass against Yahweh, a topic distinct from physical camp expulsion, closed by the general heave-offering principle that whatever any man gives the priest belongs to the priest.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep this fused with the following sotah law as one "interpersonal wrongs" unit, since both concern guilt and a wronged party; v.11 instead reopens on its own fresh וַיְדַבֵּר formula and shifts from general restitution law to a specific, elaborately staged ordeal procedure, a real change in both scope and form.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.5.7 “he shall confess his sin…and make restitution…add to it the fifth part”
oshb:Num.5.10 וְאִישׁ אֶת קָדָשָׁיו לוֹ יִהְיוּ (“every man’s holy things shall be his”)

boundary_rationale: A third fresh messenger formula opens the jealousy-ordeal law with its own double protasis (אִישִּי אִישִּישׁ וַתַשֶּׂה אִשְׂתּוֹ, "if any man’s wife goes astray") and its own distinct offering prescription -- barley meal with no oil or frankincense, marking this offering as unlike any other in the book -- ending where the priest brings the woman near for the ritual proper to begin.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The whole sotah law (vv.11-31) could be treated as one 21-verse unit given it is a single continuous ritual; but distinct ritual stages -- protasis and offering, the ordeal procedure itself, the written-curse and drinking, and the closing colophon -- each mark their own progression of action, and collapsing all four into one span would obscure the ritual's own staged structure.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.5.15 “he shall pour no oil on it, nor put frankincense on it, for it is a meal offering of jealousy”
oshb:Num.5.12 אִישׁ אִישׁ כִּּי תִשְׂטֶה אִשְׁתּוֹ (“if any man’s wife goes astray”)

boundary_rationale: The priest's own choreographed actions -- setting her before Yahweh, loosening her hair, mixing dust into holy water, and swearing her -- form the ritual's central procedural stage, closed by the woman's own double response, אָמֵן אָמֵן ("Amen, amen"), a formal ritual-response marker distinct from any narrative or legal formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This procedural stage could be merged with the writing-and-drinking stage that follows into one "the ordeal itself" span; but the woman's spoken "Amen, amen" response functions as a real closing punctuation for the oath-taking stage specifically, distinct from the physical drinking that only begins in v.23.
boundary_evidence_refs: oshb:Num.5.22 וְאָמְרָה הָאִשָּׁה אָמֵן אָמֵן (“and the woman shall say, Amen, Amen”)

boundary_rationale: The priest now writes the curses in a book and washes them into the water, then administers the drink, with the span closing on the two-branched contrastive outcome -- guilty (v.27) versus clean (v.28) -- a distinct narrative movement from the oath-swearing stage that precedes it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep the guilty/clean outcome pair fused with the closing colophon (v.29-31) as one "result and law" unit; but vv.29-31 shift from narrating this specific woman's possible outcomes to stating the general זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַקְּנָאֹת colophon that governs any future case, a real change from case-specific narration to timeless statute.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.5.27 “her body will swell, and her thigh will fall away; and the woman will be a curse among her people”
oshb:Num.5.23 וְכָתַב אֶת הָאָלֹת הָאֵלֶּּה הַכֹּהֵן בַּסֵּפֶר (“the priest shall write these curses in a book”)

boundary_rationale: זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַקְּנָאֹת ("this is the law of jealousy") is a genuine closing colophon, restating the general case in timeless terms and adding the final innocence-of-the-husband/bearing-of-iniquity principle, functioning exactly like the זֹאת/אֵּלֶּה colophons that close legal units elsewhere in the Torah's priestly material.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This colophon could be read as merely restating the preceding narrative and thus folded into it; but its own זֹאת תּוֹרַת opening formula is a recognized closing-superscription device functioning to generalize the specific case just narrated into a standing statute, a distinct rhetorical move from case narration.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.5.29 “This is the law of jealousy, when a wife…goes astray, and is defiled”
oshb:Num.5.29 זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַקְּנָאֹת (“this is the law of jealousy”)

boundary_rationale: Merged on review (LF-M8-Num-041-1/042-1, verified): no fresh messenger formula separates the wine, hair, and corpse-avoidance prohibitions -- all three sit inside the single speech opened once at 6:1-2 -- and the recurring כָּל יְמֵי refrain that reopens each prohibition is a formulaic constant (present identically across all twelve tribal entries of ch.1) rather than a discourse-level open/close signal. v.8's holiness declaration, 'all the days of his separation he is holy to Yahweh,' generalizes across the whole triad as a single set-closing colophon, not a corpse-specific close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The three prohibitions could stay split on the strength of their own recurring כָּל יְמֵי refrain, the reading originally adopted; but the same refrain recurs as pure formula in a context (ch.1's tribal tallies) this book already reads as non-boundary-driving, and no fresh speech act, addressee, or officiant separates wine from hair from corpse-avoidance the way it separates, say, the wrapped sacred objects that M8-Num-023 keeps merged under one governing clause -- this is the closer analogy.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.6.2 “When either man or woman shall make a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to Yahweh”
oshb:Num.6.3 מִיַּיִן וְשֵׁכָר יַזִּיר (“he shall separate himself from wine and strong drink”)
oshb:Num.6.8 כֹּל יְמֵי נִזְרוֹ קָדֹשׁ הוּא לַיהוָה (“all the days of his separation he is holy to Yahweh”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis, וְכִּי יָמוּת מֵת עָלָיו בְּפֶתַע פִּּתְאֹם ("if any man dies very suddenly beside him"), opens an exception-case remedy for the vow interrupted by unavoidable corpse contact, prescribing shaving and a fresh start, closed by the ruling that the earlier days become void.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could treat this as continuous with the corpse-prohibition span above, since both concern the same underlying restriction; but this span is casuistic (protasis-apodosis) rather than a blanket rule, and it prescribes an entirely different remedy -- shaving and restarting the count -- not found in the prohibition itself.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.6.9 “If any man dies very suddenly beside him…he shall shave his head”
oshb:Num.6.12 וְהַיָּמִים הַרִאשֹׁנִים יִפְּלוּ (“the former days shall be void”)

boundary_rationale: וְזֹאת תּוֹרַת הַּנָזִיר ("this is the law of the Nazirite") opens the completion ritual as one continuous procedure -- offerings brought, hair shaved and burned under the peace-offering fire, priest's portions given -- unified under a single introducing colophon and closed once the Nazirite may drink wine again, the vow's defining prohibition finally lifted.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This eight-verse ritual could be split further by action (offering-bringing, hair-shaving, portion-giving) the way Leviticus split the Day of Atonement by ritual object; but every action here serves the single unbroken purpose of releasing one vow with no change of officiant, location, or governing formula between them, so I read it as one procedure rather than three.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.6.13 “This is the law of the Nazirite: when the days of his separation are fulfilled”
oshb:Num.6.20 וְאַחַר יִשְׁתֶּה הַּנָזִיר יָיִן (“after that the Nazirite may drink wine”)

boundary_rationale: A one-verse closing colophon restates זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַּנָזִיר in general, timeless terms and adds a beyond-the-minimum allowance clause ("in addition to that which he is able to afford"), the same generalize-the-case move that closed the sotah law at 5:29-31.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This verse could be read as merely the completion ritual's last clause; but its own זֹאת תּוֹרַת reopening -- restating the whole law rather than continuing the specific ritual just narrated -- is the same colophon-closing device the book uses elsewhere, marking a genre shift from procedure to statute.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.6.21 “This is the law of the Nazirite who vows…in addition to that which he is able to afford”
oshb:Num.6.21 זֹאת תּוֹרַת הַּנָזִיר אֲשֶּׁר יִדֹּר (“this is the law of the Nazirite who vows”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula addresses Aaron and his sons specifically -- דַּבֵּר אֶל אַהֲרֹן וְאֶל בָּנָיו -- commissioning the blessing that follows, closed at the very edge of the poem's own opening line so that the command frame stays distinct from the blessing's own poetic register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The command and the blessing text could be read as one unbroken unit, since v.23 grammatically introduces v.24 with no narrative gap; but the has_poetry_or_liturgy_marker flag on this chapter and the poem's tightly patterned tricolon form (q1/q2 lineation) mark vv.24-26 as formally distinct verse, worth separating from its prose commissioning frame.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.6.23 “Speak to Aaron and to his sons, saying, ‘This is how you shall bless the children of Israel.’”
oshb:Num.6.23 כֹּה תְבָרֲכוּ אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (“thus you shall bless the children of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: This three-line poetic benediction (q1/q2 lineation in chapter_profile.json's own markers) forms a tight inclusio of parallel jussive verbs -- יְבָרֶכְךָ, יָאֵר, יִשָּא ("bless," "shine," "lift up") -- the only sustained liturgical verse in the book's first ten chapters, formally distinct from the prose commissioning that frames it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reader could keep the poem fused with its rationale clause in v.27 as one "blessing and its effect" unit; but v.27 returns to prose narration in Yahweh's own first-person voice explaining the blessing's mechanism, a register shift away from the poem's own second-person benedictions.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.6.24 “Yahweh bless you, and keep you”
oshb:Num.6.26 יִשָּׂ֨א יְהוָ֤ה פָּנָיו֙ אֵלֶ֔יךָ וְיָשֵׂ֥ם לְךָ֖ שָׁלֽוֹם (“Yahweh lift up his face toward you, and give you peace”)

boundary_rationale: Yahweh speaks in his own first-person voice, וְשָׂמוּ אֶת שְׁמִי עַל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ("so they shall put my name on the children of Israel"), explaining why the priests' spoken blessing is efficacious -- a closing theological rationale in narrative prose, distinct from both the commissioning frame and the poem itself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could close out the poem span as its final line, since no new speech formula intervenes; but the poem's own tricolon structure is complete at v.26, and v.27 shifts voice from the priests' spoken blessing to Yahweh's own explanatory aside, a real change of speaker and register.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.6.27 “So they shall put my name on the children of Israel; and I will bless them”
oshb:Num.6.27 וְשָׂמוּ אֶת שְׁמִי עַל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וַאֲנִי אֲבָרֲכֵם (“they shall put my name on the children of Israel, and I will bless them”)

boundary_rationale: A dated narrative notice, וַיְהִי בְּיוֹם כַּלּוֹת מֹשֶׁה לְהָקִים אֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן ("on the day that Moses had finished setting up the tabernacle"), opens the whole dedication-offering complex, introducing the twelve princes and their wagon-and-oxen gift before any divine instruction about it is given.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could fold this narrative opening into Yahweh's wagon-distribution instruction that follows (vv.4-9), since the gift and its use are causally linked; but v.4's fresh וַיֹּאמֶר formula marks a distinct speech act responding to the princes' initiative narrated here, so the gift and the instruction about it remain two beats, not one.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.7.1 “On the day that Moses had finished setting up the tabernacle…”
oshb:Num.7.3 וַיָּבִיאוּ אֶת קָרְבָּנָם לִפְנֵי יְהוָה (“they brought their offering before Yahweh”)

boundary_rationale: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר opens Yahweh's instruction to distribute the wagons and oxen according to each Levite clan's carrying burden, and Moses' execution follows immediately in the same span (Gershon two wagons and four oxen; Merari four and eight; Kohath none, since their burden is borne on the shoulder), a tightly bound instruction-and-fulfillment pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split into the instruction (vv.4-5) and its execution (vv.6-9) as two decisions, matching how I split ch.1's census command from its own execution; but here the specific numbers assigned in execution directly answer v.5's "each according to his service" principle with no narrative gap, reading as one continuous transaction rather than command followed by a later, separately narrated compliance.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.7.5 “Accept these from them…you shall give them to the Levites, to every man according to his service”

oshb:Num.7.9 וְלִבְנֵ֥י קְהָ֖ת לֹ֣א נָתָ֑ן כִּֽי עֲבֹדַ֤ת הַקֹּ֨דֶשׁ֙ עֲלֵהֶ֔ם בַּכָּתֵ֖ף יִשָּֽׂאוּ (“but to the sons of Kohath he gave none, because the service of the sanctuary belonged to them; they carried it on their shoulders”)

boundary_rationale: The topic shifts from wagon logistics to the altar's own dedication offering, opened by a fresh notice that the princes gave offerings לַחֲנֻכַּת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ ("for the dedication of the altar"), a single-verse narrative notice standing before the register-opening rubric that now heads the following decision (respanned per OL-M8-Num-051-1: v.11 moves forward to open M8-Num-052).
strongest_rejected_alternative: v.11 could stay attached here as this notice's own continuation, since nothing narrative separates them; but v.11 carries its own complete divine-speech formula and states the literal one-prince-per-day rubric that the twelve-day register enacts, so it functions as that register's own heading rather than as commentary closing the wagon episode.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.7.10 “The princes gave offerings for the dedication of the altar in the day that it was anointed”
oshb:Num.7.10 וַיַּקְרִיבוּ הַנְּשִׂאִים אֵת חֲנֻכַּת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ בְּיוֹם הִמָּשַׁח אֹתוֹ (“the princes gave offerings for the dedication of the altar in the day that it was anointed”)

boundary_rationale: וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה (v.11) opens the register with its own governing rubric, נָשִׂיא אֶחָד לַיּוֹם ("one prince a day"), read as this register's own heading rather than the wagon episode's close. On revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-052-1), a setumah stands after 7:11 itself -- the very verse this respan moved the onset onto -- and is disclosed here as weak-class corroboration against the respan; it does not outweigh v.11's own complete divine-speech formula under this campaign's evidence weighting, so the onset stands. Within the register, the introducing clauses fall into four groups, not the three originally claimed and not one uniform template (corrected per RVOL-M8-Num-052-2): day 1 (v.12) opens וַיְהִי הַמַּקְרִיב...לְמַטֵּה יְהוּדָה; day 2 (v.18) opens with a different verb form, הִקְרִיב, and no לְמַטֵּה clause; days 3-10 (vv.24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60, 66) share בַּיּוֹם plus a definite ordinal (הַשְּׁלִישִׁי through הָעֲשִׂירִי); and days 11-12 (vv.72, 78) switch to an indefinite cardinal construction, בְּיוֹם עַשְׁתֵּי עָשָׂר יוֹם and בְּיוֹם שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר יוֹם, dropping both the definite article and the ordinal form. What remains uniform across every day, without exception, is the item list itself, beginning קַעֲרַת כֶּסֶף אַחַת...: word-for-word identical at every one of the twelve occurrences checked (7:13, 19, 25, 31, 37, 43, 49, 55, 61, 67, 73, 79).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Given the confirmed four-way progression in the introducing clauses, the setumah after v.11, and the twelve petuchot marking each day's entry, a reviewer could reasonably split this into twelve per-day decisions, or at minimum into the four sub-groups the introducing clauses actually fall into, to match the fine granularity used for ch.2's camps and ch.3's clans. I hold the register whole because the offering content -- not the introducing clause -- is what those two comparison cases actually vary: ch.2's camps differ in tribes and march role, ch.3's clans differ in duty inventory, but every one of these twelve entries offers the identical items in the identical amounts, verified word for word. The four-way introducing-clause progression, the setumah at v.11, and the twelve closing petuchot are all real counterevidence, recorded rather than omitted; they corroborate a finer split without, on their own, outweighing the register's uniform substance.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.7.11 “They shall offer their offering, each prince on his day, for the dedication of the altar”

oshb:Num.7.12 וַיְהִי הַמַּקְרִיב בַּיּוֹם הָרִאשׁוֹן אֶת קָרְבָּנוֹ נַחְשׁוֹן בֶּן עַמִּינָדָב לְמַטֵּה יְהוּדָה (“he who offered his offering the first day was Nahshon the son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah”)

boundary_rationale: זֹאת חֲנֻכַּת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ ("this was the dedication offering of the altar") opens and closes a summary colophon that sums every item across all twelve days into single totals -- twelve platters, twelve bowls, twelve ladles, and the aggregated animal counts -- a distinct aggregation function from the day-by-day register it summarizes.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This total could be treated as simply the twelfth day's closing clause; but its own opening זֹאת explicitly reframes everything as one collective dedication offering "by the princes of Israel" rather than Ahira's individual gift, the same colophon-generalizing move seen at the sotah and Nazirite law closes.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.7.84 “This was the dedication offering of the altar…by the princes of Israel”
oshb:Num.7.88 זֹאת חֲנֻכַּת הַמִּזְבֵּחַ אַחֲרֵי הִמָּשַׁח אֹתוּ (“this was the dedication offering of the altar, after it was anointed”)

boundary_rationale: The chapter closes on a wholly different subject -- Moses hearing the divine voice from between the cherubim when he enters the Tent to speak -- a scene-level shift from the offering register's tally language to first-person theophany description, bridging into the lamp instructions that open ch.8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This verse could be read as the dedication colophon's final flourish, since it immediately follows the total; but its subject (Moses' private audience at the mercy seat) has nothing to do with the princes' gifts just tallied, marking a genuine scene change rather than a continuation of the summary.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.7.89 “he heard his voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat…from between the two cherubim”
oshb:Num.7.89 וַיִּשְׁמַע אֶת הַקּוֹל מִּדַּבֵּר אֵלָיו מֵעַל הַכַּפֹּרֶת (“he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh speech formula addressed to Aaron opens the lamp-lighting instruction, and Aaron's compliance follows in the same span with a descriptive aside on the lampstand's beaten-gold construction, closed by the recurring compliance tag כַּאֲשֶׁר צִּוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The instruction (vv.1-2) and its fulfillment (vv.3-4) could be split into two decisions on the ch.1 census model; but here the fulfillment notice is only two verses, immediately follows with no narrative gap, and adds only a descriptive aside about the lampstand's manufacture rather than a separately reported action, so I keep the short instruction-execution pair together.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.8.2 “When you light the lamps, the seven lamps shall give light in front of the lamp stand”

oshb:Num.8.3 וַיַּ֤עַשׂ כֵּן֙ אַהֲרֹ֔ן אֶל מוּל֙ פְּנֵ֣י הַמְּנוֹרָ֔ה הֶעֱלָ֖ה נֵרֹתֶ֑יהָ כַּֽאֲשֶׁ֛ר צִוָּ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה אֶת מֹשֶֽׁה (“Aaron did so. He lit its lamps to light the area in front of the lamp stand, as Yahweh commanded Moses”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the elaborate Levite cleansing procedure -- sprinkling, shaving, clothes-washing, hand-laying, and paired bull offerings -- unified under the imperative קַח אֶת הַלְוִיִּם ("take the Levites") and closed on the separation rationale, וְהָיוּ לִי הַלְוִּיִם ("the Levites shall be mine").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the hand-laying pivot (v.10) into a cleansing stage and an offering stage; but every action from sprinkling through the sin-and-burnt-offering pair serves the single unbroken purpose of consecrating the Levites for service, with no fresh speech formula or addressee change marking an internal seam.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.8.6 “Take the Levites from among the children of Israel, and cleanse them”
oshb:Num.8.14 וְהִבְדַּלְתָ אֶת הַלְויִּם מִתּוֹךְ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהָיוּ לִי הַלְוִּיִם (“you shall separate the Levites…and the Levites shall be mine”)

boundary_rationale: The instruction pivots from procedure to rationale, וְאַחֲרֵי כֵן יָבֹאוּ הַלְויִּם ("after that, the Levites shall go in"), explaining that the Levites substitute for Israel's firstborn -- the same substitution logic already given in ch.3 -- restated here as the theological ground for their commission to serve, closed on the atonement-purpose clause of v.19.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because this rationale largely repeats ch.3's firstborn-substitution logic, one could treat it as redundant scenery folded into the purification procedure above; but it is introduced by its own temporal pivot clause and functions here specifically as the ground for commissioning the Levites to their assigned tabernacle service, not merely as background on why they exist.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.8.16 “For they are wholly given to me from among the children of Israel…”
oshb:Num.8.19 וְלְכַפֵּר עַל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (“to make atonement for the children of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: Narration shifts to third-person fulfillment, וַיַּעַשְׂ מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן וְכָל עֲדַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, reporting that the whole procedure just commanded was in fact carried out, closed by the Levites' entry into actual service before Aaron and his sons.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This execution notice could be folded into the age-limit instruction that follows (vv.23-26), since both concern Levite service; v.23, however, reopens on a fresh messenger formula introducing an entirely new topic (retirement age), distinct from this span's report that the consecration already commanded was performed.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.8.20 “Moses, and Aaron, and all the congregation of the children of Israel did so to the Levites”
oshb:Num.8.22 וְאַחֲרֵי כֵן בָּאוּ הַלְויִּם לַעֲבֹד אֶת עֲבֹדָתָם (“after that, the Levites went in to do their service”)

boundary_rationale: A final fresh messenger formula opens an entirely new topic within this chapter -- the age bracket (twenty-five to fifty) for active Levite service, and the lighter assisting duty owed after retirement -- distinct from both the consecration ritual and its execution notice above.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could read this as simply restating the thirty-to-fifty bracket already given for Kohath, Gershon, and Merari in ch.4, making it redundant scenery; but the age here (twenty-five, not thirty) genuinely differs, and the fresh messenger formula marks it as its own distinct instruction rather than a repeated clause.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.8.24 “from twenty-five years old and upward they shall go in to wait on the service”

oshb:Num.8.26 וְשֵׁרֵ֨ת אֶת אֶחָ֜יו בְּאֹ֤הֶל מוֹעֵד֙ לִשְׁמֹ֣ר מִשְׁמֶ֔רֶת וַעֲבֹדָ֖ה לֹ֣א יַעֲבֹ֑ד (“he shall assist his brothers in the Tent of Meeting, to perform the duty, and shall perform no service”)

boundary_rationale: A dated speech formula, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה…בַּחֹדֶשׁ הָרִאשֹון ("Yahweh spoke…in the first month"), opens the command to keep Passover in its appointed season, and Moses' proclamation plus the people's compliance follow immediately, closed by the fulfillment tag כֵּּן עָשׂוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split into command (vv.1-3) and execution (vv.4-5) as two decisions, matching the pattern used in ch.1; but here both stages are compressed into five verses with no complicating detail between them, forming one tight command-fulfillment unit that the complaint of the unclean men (v.6) then interrupts.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.9.3 “On the fourteenth day of this month, at evening, you shall keep it”
oshb:Num.9.5 כְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר צִּוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה כֵּּן עָשׂוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (“according to all that Yahweh commanded Moses, so the children of Israel did”)

boundary_rationale: A new participant class, men made unclean by a corpse, interrupts the just-completed Passover with a grievance -- לָמָּּה נִגָּרַע ("why are we kept back?") -- and Moses' deferral, עִמְדוּ וְאֶשְׁמְעָה ("wait, that I may hear"), closes this short scene before Yahweh's ruling begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the second-Passover ruling that follows into one continuous episode; v.9, though, carries its own fresh messenger formula marking Yahweh's actual answer, distinct from the men's complaint and Moses' provisional response that precede it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.9.7 “We are unclean because of the dead body of a man. Why are we kept back…?”
oshb:Num.9.8 עִמְדוּ וְאֶשְׁמְעָה מַה יְצַוֶּה יְהוָה לָכֶם (“wait, that I may hear what Yahweh will command concerning you”)

boundary_rationale: וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר opens Yahweh's ruling that the unclean or distant-traveler may keep Passover a month later, closed by the foreigner-inclusion clause that generalizes the ruling, חֻקָּה אַחַת יִהְיֶה לָכֶם וְלַגֵּר ("you shall have one statute, both for the foreigner…").
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could split the exempt-and-alternate-date ruling (vv.9-13) from the foreigner clause (v.14) as two decisions; but v.14 continues the same casuistic register ("if…") applying the identical alternate-date logic to a different class of person, reading as the ruling's own closing extension rather than a fresh topic.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.9.11 “In the second month, on the fourteenth day at evening they shall keep it”
oshb:Num.9.14 חֻקָּה אַחַת יִהְיֶה לָכֶם וּלַגֵּר וּלְאֶזְרַח הָאָרֶץ (“you shall have one statute, both for the foreigner and for him who is born in the land”)

boundary_rationale: The topic shifts entirely from Passover law to the cloud and fire that governed the tabernacle's movement, a descriptive narrative unit unified by its own recurring refrain, עַל פִּּי יְהוָה יִסָּעוּ וְעַל פִּּי יְהוָה יַחֲנו ("at the commandment of Yahweh they traveled, and at the commandment of Yahweh they encamped"), closing the chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This nine-verse description could be split at its own "whenever/whether" case variations (a few days, a year, evening to morning) into several smaller units; but no fresh speech formula or scene change marks any internal seam among these variations -- they are all illustrations of one single principle stated once and restated in the closing refrain, not separately introduced cases.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.9.18 “At the commandment of Yahweh, the children of Israel traveled, and at the commandment of Yahweh they encamped”

oshb:Num.9.23 עַל פִּ֤י יְהוָה֙ יַחֲנ֔וּ וְעַל פִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה יִסָּ֑עוּ אֶת מִשְׁמֶ֤רֶת יְהוָה֙ שָׁמָ֔רוּ עַל פִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַד מֹשֶֽׁה (“at the commandment of Yahweh they encamped, and at the commandment of Yahweh they traveled; they kept Yahweh’s command, at the commandment of Yahweh by Moses”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the trumpet law's mechanical half -- how the two silver trumpets are made and how a single blast versus an alarm signals assembly, war-camp departure, or a gathering without alarm -- closed by the contrastive rule וְלֹא תָרִיעוּ ("but you shall not sound an alarm").
strongest_rejected_alternative: The whole trumpet law (vv.1-10) could be read as one unified command since it shares a single opening formula; but v.8 shifts from describing what the blasts mean to specifying who may blow them (the sons of Aaron specifically), a real change from signal-mechanics to priestly-agency that I read as marking a fresh sub-unit within the one speech.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.2 “Make two trumpets of silver…for the calling of the congregation and for the journeying of the camps”
oshb:Num.10.7 וּבְהַקְהִיל אֶת הַקָּהָל תִּתְקְעוּ וְלֹא תָרִיעוּ (“when the assembly is to be gathered…you shall blow, but not sound an alarm”)

boundary_rationale: The topic narrows from signal mechanics to who blows the trumpets -- וּבְנֵי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֲנִים ("the sons of Aaron, the priests") -- and to their war and festal use, closed on the recurring divine self-identification, אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם ("I am Yahweh your God").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be fused with the mechanics span above as one undivided trumpet law; but the agency shift (priestly blowers specifically) and the closing divine self-identification refrain -- absent from vv.1-7 -- mark this as the speech's own distinct closing movement.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.8 “The sons of Aaron, the priests, shall blow the trumpets”
oshb:Num.10.10 אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם (“I am Yahweh your God”)

boundary_rationale: A precisely dated notice -- second year, second month, twentieth day -- marks the cloud's lifting from the tabernacle and Israel's actual departure from Sinai, a narrative datestamp distinct from the trumpet law it follows and the camp-order register it introduces.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the Judah-camp march notice that immediately follows (v.14ff), since both narrate the same departure; but this span gives the governing date and cloud-movement notice that applies to the whole march, while v.14 begins the tribe-by-tribe register proper, a distinct level of detail.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.11 “the cloud was taken up from over the tabernacle of the covenant”
oshb:Num.10.13 וַיִּסְע֖וּ בָּרִאשֹׁנָ֑ה עַל פִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַד מֹשֶֽׁה (“they first went forward according to the commandment of Yahweh by Moses”)

boundary_rationale: וַיִּסַּע דֶּּגֶל מַחֲנֵה בְנֵי יְהוּדָה בָּרִאשֹנָה ("the standard of the camp of Judah's children set out first") reapplies ch.2's camp order to actual march execution, and the note that the tabernacle was taken down and carried by Gershon and Merari (v.17) belongs with it as the structural hinge between the first and second camps to depart.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The tabernacle-takedown note could stand as its own one-verse hinge, matching how I treated the parallel verse in ch.2; but here it is bound tightly to the Judah camp's departure with no orientation-clause reset of its own, reading as that camp's immediate sequel rather than an independent structural marker.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.14 “First, the standard of the camp of the children of Judah went forward”

oshb:Num.10.17 וְהוּרַ֖ד הַמִּשְׁכָּ֑ן וְנָסְע֤וּ בְנֵֽי גֵרְשׁוֹן֙ וּבְנֵ֣י מְרָרִ֔י נֹשְׂאֵ֖י הַמִּשְׁכָּֽן (“the tabernacle was taken down; and the sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari, who bore the tabernacle, went forward”)

boundary_rationale: וְנָסַע דֶּּגֶל מַחֲנֵה רְאובֵן ("the standard of the camp of Reuben set out") reopens for the second camp, and the Kohathites' bearing of the sanctuary (v.21) belongs with it as the parallel hinge explaining why the Kohathites travel between the second and third camps -- so the tabernacle is already standing when the holy vessels arrive.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep the Kohathite hinge (v.21) as its own decision, mirroring the Gershon/Merari hinge treated with Judah's camp; I instead bound it to Reuben's departure both times for consistency, since in each case the carrying-clan note is grammatically continuous with the preceding camp's departure notice rather than opened by its own orientation clause.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.18 “The standard of the camp of Reuben went forward…Elizur…was over his army”
oshb:Num.10.21 וְנָסְעוּ הַקְּהָתִים נֹשְׂאִי הַמִּקְדָּשׁ (“the Kohathites set forward, bearing the sanctuary”)

boundary_rationale: וְנָסַע דֶּּגֶל מַחֲנֵה בְּנֵי אֶפְרָיִם reopens the register for the third camp's actual departure, naming the same princes as ch.2's Ephraim standard, with no interrupting hinge verse since the Kohathites already travel ahead of it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the Dan-camp departure that follows into one "remaining two camps" span, since no hinge verse separates them; but each camp's own opening וְנָסַע דֶּּגֶל clause is the same recurring device that segmented all four camps in ch.2, and consistency favors applying it here too.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.22 “The standard of the camp of the children of Ephraim set forward”
oshb:Num.10.22 וְנָסַע דֶּּגֶל מַחֲנֵה בְּנֵי אֶפְרָיִם לְצִבְאֹתָם (“the standard of the camp of the children of Ephraim set forward according to their armies”)

boundary_rationale: The fourth and final camp departs under its own distinguishing description, מְאַסֵּף לְכָל הַמַּחֲנֹת ("the rear guard of all the camps"), naming Dan, Asher, and Naphtali; v.28's whole-Israel summary colophon no longer closes this entry (respanned per LF-M8-Num-070-1: it is now its own decision, M8-Num-261, structurally parallel to how 2:32-34/M8-Num-011 stands independent of the Dan-camp entry in ch.2).
strongest_rejected_alternative: v.28 could remain this camp's own closing colophon, since nothing typographically separates them; but v.28's אֵלֶּה-colophon names no camp at all, only 'the children of Israel,' the identical scope as 2:32's colophon, which this book's own ch.2 treatment already reads as covering all four camps together rather than the fourth camp alone.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.25 “The standard of the camp of the children of Dan…was the rear guard of all the camps”
oshb:Num.10.27 וְעַל צְבָא מַטֵּה בְּנֵי נַפְתָּלִי אֲחִירַע בֶּן עֵינָן (“and over the army of the tribe of the children of Naphtali was Ahira the son of Enan”)

boundary_rationale: אֵלֶּה מַסְעֵי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לְצִבְאֹתָם וַיִּסָּעוּ is an אֵלֶּה-colophon covering 'the children of Israel' as a whole, naming no single camp, structurally identical in form and scope to 2:32's colophon (M8-Num-011), which this book already keeps independent of the fourth camp's own entry on exactly that ground -- the total covers all four standards together, not one alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This verse could remain Dan's own closing colophon, the reading originally adopted, since it immediately follows Dan's departure notice with no typographical break; but its own scope ('the children of Israel,' not 'the camp of Dan') matches 2:32's whole-march summary rather than any single camp's ordinal-position close, and treating the two structurally identical texts differently would be the asymmetry the challenge correctly named.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.28 “Thus were the travels of the children of Israel according to their armies; and they went forward”
oshb:Num.10.28 אֵלֶּה מַסְעֵי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לְצִבְאֹתָם וַיִּסָּעוּ (“these are the travels of the children of Israel according to their armies, and they went forward”)

boundary_rationale: A named individual, Hobab son of Reuel the Midianite, enters as a wholly new participant in direct dialogue with Moses, a scene-level shift from the impersonal march register to personal persuasion, closed on Moses' reciprocal-benefit promise.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This dialogue could be read as continuous with the departure narrative overall and left unsplit from the surrounding march notices; but its direct-discourse frame ("Moses said to Hobab…he said to him") and its focus on a single named non-Israelite mark a genuinely distinct scene type from the tribal march register.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.29 “Moses said to Hobab, the son of Reuel the Midianite, Moses’ father-in-law…”
oshb:Num.10.32 וְהָיָה הַטּוֹב הַהוּא אֲשֶׁר יֵיטִיב יְהוָה עִמָּנוּ וְהֵטִבנוּ לָךְ (“whatever good Yahweh does to us, we will do the same to you”)

boundary_rationale: The narrative returns to march description, now specifically focused on the ark going ahead of the camp "three days' journey" and the cloud resting over them by day, setting the immediate stage for the ark song that follows -- distinct from Hobab's personal dialogue and from the poem itself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded directly into the ark song as its narrative introduction; but it describes three days of ordinary travel before the poem's own precisely marked occasion ("when the ark went forward…when it rested"), functioning as scene-setting distinct from the poem's own inclusio structure.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.33 “The ark of Yahweh’s covenant went before them three days’ journey…”
oshb:Num.10.34 וַעֲנַן יְהוָה עֲלֵיהֶם יומָם בְּנָסְעָם מִן הַמַּחֲנֶה (“the cloud of Yahweh was over them by day, when they set forward”)

boundary_rationale: This two-line invocation, spoken וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה ("and Moses said") at the ark's setting-out and its resting, forms a self-contained bracketing couplet -- קוּמָה יְהוָה ("rise up, Yahweh") answered by שׁוּבָה יְהוָה ("return, Yahweh") -- a formally marked poetic inset distinct from the surrounding prose march narrative.
strongest_rejected_alternative: These two verses could be folded into the ark-departure notice above as its concluding flourish; but the song's own tight departure/rest inclusio and its shift into Moses' own quoted invocation mark it as a self-standing poetic unit, the book's shortest liturgical inset, comparable in kind (if not scale) to the priestly blessing of ch.6.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.10.35 “Rise up, Yahweh, and let your enemies be scattered!”
oshb:Num.10.36 שׁוּבָה יְהוָה רִבְבוֹת אַלְפֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (“return, Yahweh, to the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: A new narrative unit opens with an unmotivated complaint, כְּמִתְאֹנְנִים רַע בְּאָזְנֵי יְהוָה ("complaining, evil in the ears of Yahweh"), distinct from every preceding tabernacle-and-camp chapter in both genre (rebellion narrative, not instruction) and location (no named topic beyond generic complaint), and it closes on its own place-naming etiology, תַּבְעֵרָה ("Taberah"), a device this book uses repeatedly to seal a completed episode.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as the opening beat of one long complaint narrative running through v.35, since the craving for meat that follows is causally continuous; but the Taberah episode has its own complete burn/cry/intercede/subside/name arc with no participant carried forward (the mixed multitude of v.4 is a new subject), so I treat it as a self-contained first episode rather than an unresolved opening.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.11.1 “The people were complaining in the ears of Yahweh”
oshb:Num.11.3 וַיִּקְרָא שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא תַּבְעֵרָה (“the name of that place was called Taberah”)

boundary_rationale: A new participant class, הָאסַפְסֻף ("the mixed multitude"), opens a second complaint with its own quoted grievance about lost Egyptian food, and the narrator's own descriptive aside on the manna's appearance and preparation closes this unit before Moses' personal distress is narrated.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep this fused with Moses' own complaint that follows (vv.10-15), since both concern the same underlying craving; but v.10 shifts the acting subject from the people's grumbling to Moses' own private distress before Yahweh, a change of speaker and scene the text itself marks.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.11.4 “The mixed multitude that was among them lusted exceedingly”
oshb:Num.11.9 וּבְרֶדֶת הַטַּל עַל הַמַּחֲנֶה לָיְלָה יֵרֵד הַמָּן עָלָיו (“when the dew fell on the camp in the night, the manna fell on it”)

boundary_rationale: Moses becomes the acting subject for the first time in this chapter, וַיִּשְׁמַע מֹשֶׁה אֶת הָעָם בֹּכֶה ("Moses heard the people weeping"), opening his own direct-address complaint to Yahweh about the burden of leadership, closed on his despairing request, הָרְגֵנִי נָא ("please kill me now").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with Yahweh's answering instruction (vv.16-17) as one continuous complaint-and-response dialogue; but v.16 opens with its own fresh וַיֹּאמֶר marking Yahweh's turn to speak, a real speaker-change boundary distinct from Moses' own complaint.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.11.11 “Why have you treated your servant so badly?”
oshb:Num.11.15 הָרְגֵנִי נָא הָרֹג אִם מָצָאתִי חֵן בְּעֵינֶיךָ (“please kill me right now, if I have found favor in your sight”)

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's answer opens with its own imperative, אֶסְפָה לִּי שִׁבְעִים אִישׁ ("gather to me seventy men"), addressing Moses' burden complaint with an administrative remedy (shared prophetic spirit), closed on the rationale that they will bear the burden with him.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep this fused with the meat-provision instruction that follows (vv.18-20) as one undivided answer to Moses' twin complaints (burden and food); but the two instructions address entirely separate problems -- leadership capacity versus the people's hunger -- and v.18 pivots the addressee from Moses personally to the people at large.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.11.16 “Gather to me seventy men of the elders of Israel”
oshb:Num.11.17 וְנָשְׂאוּ אִתְּךָ בְּמַשָּׂא הָעָם וְלֹא תִשָּׂא אַתָּה לְבַדֶּךָ (“they shall bear the burden of the people with you, that you don’t bear it yourself alone”)

boundary_rationale: The addressee shifts from Moses personally to וְאֶל הָעָם תֹּאמַר ("and to the people you shall say"), opening the meat-provision instruction with its own harsh over-abundance warning -- a month of meat until it comes out their nostrils -- distinct in both audience and content from the elders' commissioning.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as continuous with the elders instruction as one single divine speech; but the explicit addressee shift ("and to the people you shall say," as opposed to the elders instruction's second-person-to-Moses form) marks a distinct pronouncement within the one scene.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.11.19 “You will not eat just one day, or two days, or five days…”
oshb:Num.11.20 יַעַן כִּי מְאַסְתֶּם אֶת יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר בְּקִרְבְּכֶם (“because you have rejected Yahweh who is among you”)

boundary_rationale: Moses speaks again in direct objection to the scale of the promise -- six hundred thousand men on foot, no flock or sea could suffice -- closed on his own rhetorical doubt before Yahweh's answering rebuke opens the next decision (respanned per OL-M8-Num-079-1: 11:23 now splits into its own decision, M8-Num-262, on the strength of its own fresh, complete quotative frame).
strongest_rejected_alternative: 11:23 could stay merged here as Yahweh's terse answer completing the exchange, the original reading; but 11:23 carries a fresh וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה frame of the identical class already treated as boundary-bearing at 11:11, 11:16, and the opening of this very decision at 11:21, and its content -- the 'is Yahweh's hand too short' idiom plus an independent forward-looking promise -- is a complete theological assertion, not a bare interjection comparable to 12:13's two-word cry.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.11.21 “The people, among whom I am, are six hundred thousand men on foot”
web:Num.11.22 “Shall flocks and herds be slaughtered for them, to be sufficient for them?”

boundary_rationale: A fresh, complete quotative frame, וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה, opens Yahweh's rebuttal to Moses' objection, of the identical formula-class already treated as boundary-bearing at 11:11, 11:16, and 11:21 in this same chapter; its content -- the 'is Yahweh's hand too short' idiom plus an independent forward-looking promise -- carries as much stand-alone theological weight as several other single-verse decisions elsewhere in this book.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This verse could stay merged with Moses' preceding objection as one exchange, the reading originally adopted, on the theory that a terse divine reply has no independent content apart from the doubt it answers; but that characterization does not survive comparison with the verse's actual content, which is a complete assertion and promise, not a bare interjection comparable to 12:13's two-word cry.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.11.23 “Has Yahweh’s hand grown short? Now you will see whether my word will happen to you or not”
oshb:Num.11.23 וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה הֲיַד יְהוָה תִּקְצָר (“Yahweh said to Moses, ‘Has Yahweh’s hand grown short?’”)

boundary_rationale: Narration returns to execution -- Moses gathers the seventy, the Spirit rests on them and they prophesy -- and the two named exceptions, Eldad and Medad, prophesying in the camp itself, form the episode's own complication, closed by Moses' own wish that all Yahweh's people were prophets.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The Eldad/Medad complication (vv.26-29) could be split off as its own decision from the elders' commissioning execution (vv.24-25); but the two remain in continuous narrative sequence with no fresh formula or scene reset between them, forming one unbroken commissioning-and-complication episode.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.11.25 “Yahweh came down in the cloud…the Spirit rested on them, they prophesied”
oshb:Num.11.29 וּמִי יִתֵּן כָּל עַם יְהוָה נְבִיאִים (“I wish that all Yahweh’s people were prophets”)

boundary_rationale: A wind from Yahweh brings the promised quail, the people's gluttony triggers the plague Yahweh's anger produces, and the episode closes on its own naming etiology, קִבְרוֹת הַתַּאֲוָה ("graves of craving"), followed by the travel notice to Hazeroth that bridges into ch.12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The travel notice (v.35) could be split off as its own one-verse hinge, matching how I treated similar notices elsewhere; but here it is only three words and directly completes the naming etiology's own closing function (this is where they buried the craving-dead, and this is where they moved on from), so I keep it bound to the episode it concludes.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.11.33 “Yahweh’s anger burned against the people, and Yahweh struck the people with a very great plague”
oshb:Num.11.34 וַיִּקְרָא אֶת שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם הַהוּא קִבְרוֹת הַתַּאֲוָה (“the name of that place was called Kibroth Hattaavah”)

boundary_rationale: A new named-participant scene opens, וַתְּדַבֵּר מִרְיָם וְאַהֲרֹן בְּמֹשֶׁה ("Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses"), over the Cushite wife and their own prophetic-status claim, and the narrator's own aside on Moses' humility closes this exposition before Yahweh's response begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The narrator's humility aside (v.3) could be read as belonging to the following divine-summons unit as its rationale; but grammatically it comments on Moses as a character within the complaint scene just narrated, functioning as the narrator's own closing evaluation of that scene rather than as part of Yahweh's own speech.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.12.2 “Has Yahweh indeed spoken only with Moses? Hasn’t he spoken also with us?”

boundary_rationale: A sudden divine summons, וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה פִּתְאֹם ("Yahweh spoke suddenly"), calls all three siblings to the Tent, and Yahweh's own contrastive speech -- ordinary prophets receive visions and dreams, but Moses is נֶאֱמָן ("faithful") in all his house, spoken to mouth to mouth -- closes on Yahweh's departure in anger.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the summons/speech seam into a scene-arrival unit and a separate rebuke-speech unit; but the summons exists only to stage the rebuke that immediately follows with no intervening action, reading as one continuous theophany-and-speech rather than two discrete beats.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.12.6 “If there is a prophet among you, I, Yahweh, will make myself known to him in a vision”
oshb:Num.12.8 פֶּה אֶל פֶּה אֲדַבֶּר בּוֹ (“with him, I will speak mouth to mouth”)

boundary_rationale: The cloud departs and Miriam is struck leprous, and Aaron's plea to Moses, בִּי אֲדֹנִי, opens the appeal; Moses' own two-word cry to Yahweh, אֵל נָא רְפָא נָא לָהּ (v.13), now closes this decision as his own direct, same-beat response to Aaron's plea rather than opening the ruling that follows (respanned per OL-M8-Num-085-1).
strongest_rejected_alternative: v.13 could open the following ruling decision as its trigger, the original reading; but v.13 carries no independent content of its own -- it is Moses' emotional cry provoked by and continuous with the affliction-and-plea scene just narrated -- while v.14 opens Yahweh's ruling with its own complete quotative frame addressing a distinct question (Miriam's shutout terms), a genuine speaker-and-topic seam that v.13 does not share.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.12.10 “Miriam was leprous, as white as snow”
web:Num.12.13 “Moses cried to Yahweh, saying, ‘Heal her, God, I beg you!’”

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's own ruling now opens this decision directly, וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה (v.14), a complete fresh quotative frame prescribing the seven-day shutout, closed on the people's compliance and travel notice to the wilderness of Paran (respanned per OL-M8-Num-085-1: 12:13 now belongs to the preceding decision, M8-Num-084).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Moses' cry (v.13) could remain this decision's own opening petition, the original reading; but it is addressed to a different question than the one v.14 answers, and it is the same dramatic beat as Aaron's plea in the preceding scene (affliction seen, plea made, cry made) rather than a fresh speech act opening this one.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.12.14 “Let her be shut up outside of the camp seven days”

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the command to spy out Canaan, שְׁלַח לְךָ אֲנָשִׁים ("send men"), one prince per tribe, and Moses' compliance follows immediately, closed by the narrator's note that all were heads of Israel -- a tight command-execution pair before the roster of names begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the twelve-name roster that follows as one continuous "sending the spies" unit; but v.4's own introducing clause, "these were their names," functions as a fresh register opening, distinct from the command-and-compliance narration that authorizes it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.2 “Send men, that they may spy out the land of Canaan…every one a prince among them”

boundary_rationale: וְאֵלֶּה שְׁמוֹתָם ("and these are their names") opens the twelve-tribe roster in the same one-name-per-tribe template used for the census witnesses in ch.1, closed by the register's own colophon and the notable renaming of Hoshea to Joshua.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Following the ch.1 census precedent, one might expect this roster split at every name; but exactly as with ch.1's assistant-princes list, each entry is the identical "of tribe X, name son-of-name" formula with no functional variation, so I keep it as one register rather than twelve near-duplicate decisions.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.4 “Of the tribe of Reuben, Shammua the son of Zaccur”
oshb:Num.13.16 וַיִּקְרָא מֹשֶׁה לְהוֹשֵׁעַ בִּן נוּן יְהוֹשֻׁעַ (“Moses called Hoshea the son of Nun Joshua”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own direct-speech instructions to the twelve -- what to observe about the land's fertility, fortification, and inhabitants -- open with וַיֹּאמֶר אֲלֵהֶם ("and said to them") and close on the narrator's dating aside, the time of first-ripe grapes, before the spies actually depart.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the roster above as Moses' continuing speech to the men just named; but the roster is narration about the spies ("these are their names"), while this span is Moses' own direct quoted instruction to them, a change of both grammatical person and content.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.18 “See the land, what it is; and the people who dwell therein…”
oshb:Num.13.20 וְהַיָּמִים יְמֵי בִּכּוּרֵי עֲנָבִים (“now the time was the time of the first-ripe grapes”)

boundary_rationale: Narration shifts to the spies' own itinerary and the Eshcol grape-cluster episode, closed by the forty-day return notice, מִקֵּץ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם ("at the end of forty days"), a datestamp bridging into the report scene.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep the return-notice (v.25) fused with the report scene that follows, since it directly leads into their arrival; but v.26 opens with its own fresh narration ("they went and came to Moses") describing a distinct action -- reporting, not traveling -- so the journey-and-return notice stays with the journey it summarizes.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.23 “They came to the valley of Eshcol, and cut down from there a branch with one cluster of grapes”
oshb:Num.13.25 וַיָּשֻׁבוּ מִתּוּר הָאָרֶץ מִקֵּץ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם (“they returned from spying out the land at the end of forty days”)

boundary_rationale: The spies arrive and give their joint report -- fertile land, fortified cities, the Anakim, and the surrounding nations' locations -- a single collective speech closed before Caleb's dissenting voice interrupts it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because Caleb's counter-speech and the majority's contrary report both respond to this same report scene, one could treat vv.26-33 as one continuous "the spies speak" unit; but v.30 opens with Caleb specifically silencing the people, a distinct speaker and rhetorical move from the collective report that precedes it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.27 “Surely it flows with milk and honey, and this is its fruit”
