boundary_rationale: Caleb's own dissenting voice, עָלֹה נַעֲלֶה ("let's go up at once"), opens a direct contest against the other spies' fear-driven counter-speech, which escalates into the grasshopper self-comparison that closes the chapter and sets up ch.14's rebellion.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Caleb's speech (v.30) could be split from the majority's rebuttal (vv.31-33) as two decisions, since they are formally two speeches; but they are directly contrastive responses to the very same report with no narrative gap, forming one debate scene rather than two independent speech acts.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.13.30 “Let’s go up at once, and possess it; for we are well able to overcome it!”
oshb:Num.13.33 וַנְּהִי בְעֵינֵינוּ כַּחֲגָבִים (“we were in our own sight as grasshoppers”)

boundary_rationale: The whole congregation's wailing response opens ch.14, וַתִּשָּׂא כָּל הָעֵדָה וַיִּתְּנוּ אֶת קוֹלָם ("all the congregation lifted up their voice"), escalating into an open proposal to appoint a new leader and return to Egypt, a distinct collective-action beat from the report scene it responds to.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as the direct continuation of ch.13's grasshopper report with no fresh boundary; but a genuine shift from the spies' own report speech to the congregation's own collective reaction and proposal marks a new participant class taking the narrative stage -- a change of speaking subject the text itself marks, independent of and not corroborated by the chapter number that happens to fall at the same point (chapter divisions carry no evidentiary weight under the owner addendum).
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.2 “We wish that we had died in the land of Egypt”
oshb:Num.14.4 נִתְּנָה רֹאשׁ וְנָשׁוּבָה מִצְרָיְמָה (“let’s choose a leader, and let’s return into Egypt”)

boundary_rationale: Moses and Aaron fall on their faces before the assembly, and Joshua and Caleb's counter-appeal closes on their own reassurance; the congregation's stoning threat and the glory notice, וּכְבוֹד יְהוָה נִרְאָה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד (v.10), now close this decision as the appeal scene's own resolution rather than opening the judgment speech (respanned per OL-M8-Num-094-1).
strongest_rejected_alternative: v.10 could open the following judgment decision, the original reading, since the stoning threat escalates directly into Yahweh's proposal; but v.10 closes on the same theophany-notice shape already honored as boundary-bearing at 16:19/16:20 elsewhere in this book, and 14:11 opens with its own complete, freshly-addressed quotative frame, the stronger and more consistent seam.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.7 “The land…is an exceedingly good land”
oshb:Num.14.10 וּכְבוֹד יְהוָה נִרְאָה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד אֶל כָּל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (“Yahweh’s glory appeared in the Tent of Meeting to all the children of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's own proposal now opens this decision directly, וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה (v.11), a complete fresh quotative frame matching the identical theophany-then-speech-formula shape already honored at 16:19/16:20, MT 17:8/9, and 20:6/7 in this book (respanned per OL-M8-Num-094-1: 14:10 now belongs to the preceding decision, M8-Num-093).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The theophany notice (v.10) could stay attached here as this decision's own opening, the original reading, on the strength of its direct escalation into Yahweh's speech; but the anaphoric אֹתָם in v.10 has its antecedent (Joshua and Caleb) in the preceding scene, and applying the same theophany-notice-closes-the-scene convention honored at three comparable sites elsewhere in this book argues for the same reading here.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.11 “How long will this people despise me?”
web:Num.14.12 “I will strike them with the pestilence, and disinherit them”

boundary_rationale: Moses' own extended intercessory speech -- appealing to Yahweh's reputation among the nations and quoting the divine attribute formula, יְהוָה אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב חֶסֶד ("Yahweh is slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness") -- forms one continuous petition closed on his final plea for pardon.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the quoted attribute formula (v.18) into two speech-units, since it functions almost as an embedded citation; but Moses introduces it himself with כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבַּרְתָּ ("as you have spoken") as part of his own single continuous argument, not as a separately marked insertion.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.18 “Yahweh is slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness”
oshb:Num.14.19 סְלַח נָא לַעֲוֹן הָעָם הַזֶּה כְּגֹדֶל חַסְדֶּךָ (“please pardon the iniquity of this people according to the greatness of your loving kindness”)

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's own answering speech opens with סָלַחְתִּי כִּדְבָרֶךָ ("I have pardoned according to your word"), pivots into the oath that the generation of complainers will not see the land, carves out the Caleb exception, and closes with the practical instruction to turn back toward the Red Sea.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the pardon/oath seam (vv.20-23 versus 24-25) into a forgiveness unit and a Caleb-exception unit; but both remain part of Yahweh's one uninterrupted reply to Moses' intercession, with no fresh messenger formula marking an internal seam until v.26's turn to the forty-years sentence.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.23 “Surely they shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers”
oshb:Num.14.24 וְעַבְדִּי כָלֵב עֵקֶב הָיְתָה רוּחַ אַחֶרֶת עִמּוֹ (“my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh double-addressee messenger formula, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה וְאֶל אַהֲרֹן, opens the formal sentencing speech proper -- one year for each of the forty days spied -- distinct from the more conversational pardon-and-instruction that preceded it, closed on Yahweh's own self-attesting oath formula, אֲנִי יְהוָה דִּבַּרְתִּי ("I, Yahweh, have spoken").
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could fold this into the pardon-and-turn-back speech above as its continuation, since the topic (consequences for the generation) is the same; but the fresh messenger formula reopens the speech with a wholly new rhetorical register -- day-for-a-year sentencing rather than personal pardon -- marking a distinct pronouncement.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.34 “after the number of the days in which you spied out the land, even forty days, for every day a year”
oshb:Num.14.35 אֲנִי יְהוָה דִּבַּרְתִּי אִם לֹא זֹאת אֶעֱשֶׂה (“I, Yahweh, have spoken; I will surely do this”)

boundary_rationale: Narration reports the immediate fate of the ten spies who brought the evil report -- dead by plague -- against Joshua and Caleb's survival, a short execution-of-judgment notice distinct from Yahweh's own sentencing speech and from the presumptuous-attack narrative that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged into the sentencing speech as its concluding proof; but it is third-person narrated fact (the spies actually died) rather than Yahweh's own first-person pronouncement, marking a shift from speech to narrated consequence.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.37 “those men who brought up an evil report of the land, died by the plague before Yahweh”
oshb:Num.14.38 וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן וְכָלֵב בֶּן יְפֻנֶּה חָיוּ (“Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb the son of Jephunneh remained alive”)

boundary_rationale: Moses reports the sentence to the people, whose mourning turns to a presumptuous attempt to attack the hill country against Moses' explicit warning, closing the chapter on their defeat at Hormah -- a self-contained scene of disobedience distinct from the sentencing and its immediate aftermath.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at Moses' warning (vv.39-43) versus the attack and defeat itself (vv.44-45); but the warning exists only to be immediately and explicitly disregarded ("but they presumed to go up"), forming one tight warn-and-disobey-and-fail sequence rather than two separable beats.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.14.44 “they presumed to go up to the top of the mountain”
oshb:Num.14.45 וַיַּכּוּם וַיַּכְּתוּם עַד הַחָרְמָה (“and struck them and beat them down even to Hormah”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens a law explicitly framed for future settlement, כִּי תָבֹאוּ אֶל אֶרֶץ מוֹשְׁבֹתֵיכֶם ("when you come into the land of your habitations"), tiering the meal-and-drink offering by animal (lamb, ram, bull), closed by the recurring one-law-for-native-and-stranger refrain that seals the whole supplement.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The three animal tiers (lamb, ram, bull) could each get their own decision the way ch.1's offering-torah material is split by animal class elsewhere in the Torah; but here all three tiers share one uninterrupted grammatical structure with no fresh protasis or messenger formula between them, differing only in the measured quantities, so I read the whole graduated scale as one register.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.2 “When you have come into the land of your habitations, which I give to you”
oshb:Num.15.16 תּוֹרָה אַחַת וּמִשְׁפָּט אֶחָד יִהְיֶה לָכֶם וְלַגֵּר (“one law and one ordinance shall be for you and for the stranger”)

boundary_rationale: A second fresh messenger formula opens a distinct topic -- the wave offering of the first dough baked from the land's grain -- unrelated to the animal-offering scale above, closed on its own perpetuity clause, לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם ("throughout your generations").
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could merge this with the animal-offering supplement above as one general "land-entry offerings" unit, since both are triggered by the same "when you come into the land" framing; but this span opens its own fresh messenger formula and addresses a materially different offering (dough, not livestock), marking a distinct instruction.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.20 “Of the first of your dough you shall offer up a cake for a wave offering”
oshb:Num.15.21 מֵרֵאשִׁית עֲרִסֹתֵיכֶם תִּתְּנוּ לַיהוָה תְּרוּמָה לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם (“of the first of your dough, you shall give to Yahweh a wave offering throughout your generations”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis, וְכִי תִשְׁגּוּ ("and when you err"), opens the communal unwitting-sin remedy, specifying the congregation's bull-and-goat offering pair, closed on the blanket forgiveness formula that covers both native and stranger.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the individual unwitting-sin case that follows (vv.27-29) as one "unwitting sin" topic; but v.27 opens its own fresh protasis (וְאִם נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת, "and if a single soul") specifically distinguishing an individual from the collective case just given, a real change of legal subject.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.24 “all the congregation shall offer one young bull for a burnt offering…and one male goat for a sin offering”
oshb:Num.15.26 וְנִסְלַח לְכָל עֲדַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלַגֵּר הַגָּר בְּתוֹכָם (“all the congregation of the children of Israel shall be forgiven, as well as the stranger”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis narrows the case from the whole congregation to a single soul, prescribing a year-old female goat, closed by the same one-law-for-native-and-stranger refrain used to close the land-entry offering scale above, binding the two case-types under a shared closing formula while keeping their distinct protases separate.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep this fused with the high-handed-sin contrast that follows (vv.30-31), since both concern categories of sin; but v.30 opens with a new contrastive subject, וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר תַּעֲשֶׂה בְּיָד רָמָה ("but the soul who does anything with a high hand"), explicitly opposing this unwitting case rather than continuing it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.27 “If a person sins unwittingly, then he shall offer a female goat a year old for a sin offering”
oshb:Num.15.29 תּוֹרָה אַחַת יִהְיֶה לָכֶם לָעֹשֶׂה בִּשְׁגָגָה (“you shall have one law for him who does anything unwittingly”)

boundary_rationale: A sharp contrastive clause, וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר תַּעֲשֶׂה בְּיָד רָמָה ("but the soul who does anything with a high hand"), opens the defiant-sin case as the deliberate foil to the two unwitting cases just given, closed on the emphatic cutting-off penalty, הִכָּרֵת תִּכָּרֵת ("shall surely be cut off").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This two-verse contrast could be folded into the individual unwitting-sin case as its closing exception clause; but its own opening וְ-contrast and total absence of any offering remedy (unlike the two cases before it) mark it as a distinct legal category, not a footnote to the preceding case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.30 “the soul who does anything with a high hand…blasphemes Yahweh”

oshb:Num.15.31 כִּ֤י דְבַר יְהוָה֙ בָּזָ֔ה וְאֶת מִצְוָת֖וֹ הֵפַ֑ר הִכָּרֵ֧ת תִּכָּרֵ֛ת הַנֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַהִ֖וא עֲוֺנָ֥ה בָֽהּ (“because he has despised Yahweh’s word, and has broken his commandment, that soul shall be utterly cut off; his iniquity shall be on him”)

boundary_rationale: A concrete narrative case interrupts the legal material -- וַיִּהְיוּ בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּמִּדְבָּר וַיִּמְצְאוּ ("the children of Israel were in the wilderness, and they found") -- narrating a specific man caught gathering sticks on the Sabbath, distinct in genre (narrative, not casuistic law) from both the high-handed-sin statute before it and the tassels command after it, closed by his execution.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could read this as simply illustrating the high-handed-sin category just legislated, folding it into that span; but this is narrated as a specific historical incident with its own custody-and-ruling procedure (v.34's "it had not been declared what should be done to him"), not a generalized legal case, marking a genre shift from statute to narrative.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.32 “they found a man gathering sticks on the Sabbath day”
oshb:Num.15.36 וַיִּרְגְּמוּ אֹתוֹ בָּאֲבָנִים וַיָּמֹת (“and stoned him to death with stones”)

boundary_rationale: A final fresh messenger formula opens the tassels/fringes command, closed on the double self-identification refrain, אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם ("I am Yahweh your God") repeated at the very close of the chapter, tying the memory-device command back to the Exodus itself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as continuous with the Sabbath-breaker narrative as one "remembering the commandments" unit; but the fresh messenger formula and the wholesale shift from a specific narrated incident to a general, perpetual command mark this as its own distinct legal instruction closing the chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.15.39 “that you may see it, and remember all Yahweh’s commandments, and do them”
oshb:Num.15.41 אֲנִי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם אֲשֶׁר הוֹצֵאתִי אֶתְכֶם מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם (“I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt”)

boundary_rationale: A new named coalition -- Korah, Dathan, Abiram, On, and two hundred fifty princes -- opens the rebellion narrative with their own priesthood-contesting grievance, רַב לָכֶם, addressed jointly to Moses and Aaron, closed before Moses' own reply opens the next decision (re-cut three ways per OL-M8-Num-107-1: the identical 'Moses said to Korah' formula recurs at 16:8 and 16:16, and only the second occurrence was originally treated as boundary-bearing).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The whole of 16:1-11 could stay as one decision reading Moses' response as a single continuous speech-turn narrowing from the coalition-wide censer proposal to the Levite-specific rebuke, the original reading; but the identical formula opening Moses' reply at both 16:8 and 16:16 was treated as a boundary only the second time, an inconsistency of method rather than a defensible literary unity, and the resulting eleven-verse span ran more than double the length of every neighboring decision in this chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.3 “You take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy”
oshb:Num.16.3 רַב לָכֶם כִּי כָל הָעֵדָה כֻּלָּם קְדֹשִׁים וּבְתוֹכָם יְהוָה (“you take too much on yourself, since all the congregation are holy, everyone of them, and Yahweh is among them”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' response to the coalition's grievance opens with narration of his own falling on his face, closed on his censer-test instruction to Korah's whole company, וּתְנוּ בָהֵן אֵשׁ וְשִׂימוּ עֲלֵיהֶן קְטֹרֶת לִפְנֵי יְהוָה מָחָר, before his second, Levite-specific reply opens the next decision at the recurring 'Moses said to Korah' formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This span could stay merged with the coalition's opening grievance (16:1-3) as one continuous scene, since Moses' fall and his censer instruction directly answer that grievance with no intervening scene change; but Moses' own action (falling, then instructing) is a distinct narrative beat from the coalition's own speech, and isolating it lets the recurring 'Moses said to Korah' formula at v.8 do the same boundary-marking work it already does at v.16.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.4 “When Moses heard it, he fell on his face”
oshb:Num.16.7 וְהָיָה הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יִבְחַר יְהוָה הוּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ רַב לָכֶם בְּנֵי לֵוִי (“the man whom Yahweh chooses, he shall be holy. You have gone too far, you sons of Levi!”)

boundary_rationale: וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל קֹרַח (v.8) reopens Moses' speech, narrowing from the coalition-wide censer proposal to a rebuke addressed to the Levites specifically -- 'is it a small thing that the God of Israel has separated you...do you seek the priesthood also?' -- closed on the charge that the whole company has gathered against Yahweh himself. On revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-264-1), this decision's own boundary rests on the verbatim pair וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֶל קֹרַח at v.8 and v.16 alone, letter for letter identical at both occurrences; v.5, Moses' first reply, is not a third instance of that same formula. v.5 reads וַיְדַבֵּר אֶל קֹרַח וְאֶל כָּל עֲדָתוֹ לֵאמֹר -- a different verb (דבר, not אמר), no subject named in the verse at all, and an addressee scope covering the whole company rather than Korah alone. The real case for a boundary at v.8 is that v.5's frame is unmarked in exactly these ways and v.8's is not, a sharper and more accurate ground than the original claim that v.8 'recurs' a formula already used at v.5.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could stay merged with the censer-test instruction (16:4-7) as one continuous speech-turn by Moses with no scene break, the reading originally adopted for the whole 16:1-11 span; but the reopening at v.8 is marked in three independent ways at once -- verb (אמר vs דבר), named subject (מֹשֶׁה vs none), and narrowed addressee (קֹרַח alone vs קֹרַח וְכָל עֲדָתוֹ) -- while v.5 itself carries none of v.8's marking, so treating v.5 as already 'the same formula' (the original rationale's own overstatement) is corrected here rather than repeated.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.8 “Moses said to Korah, ‘Hear now, you sons of Levi!’”
oshb:Num.16.11 לָכֵן אַתָּה וְכָל עֲדָתְךָ הַנֹּעָדִים עַל יְהוָה (“therefore you and all your company have gathered together against Yahweh”)

boundary_rationale: Moses sends specifically to summon Dathan and Abiram, who refuse to come up and voice their own distinct grievance -- failed promises of a land flowing with milk and honey -- closed on Moses' own indignant appeal to Yahweh, אַל תֵּפֶן אֶל מִנְחָתָם ("don't respect their offering").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged into the censer-test instruction that follows as background before the test proceeds; but the fresh summons formula ("Moses sent to call Dathan and Abiram") and their own separately quoted grievance mark this as a discrete confrontation, resolved by Moses' own aside to Yahweh rather than folded into the ritual instructions.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.14 “Will you put out the eyes of these men? We won’t come up”
oshb:Num.16.15 לֹא חֲמוֹר אֶחָד מֵהֶם נָשָׂאתִי (“I have not taken one donkey from them”)

boundary_rationale: Moses reissues the censer-test instruction directly to Korah, and the assembly gathers at the Tent, closed by the theophany notice, וַיֵּרָא כְבוֹד יְהוָה אֶל כָּל הָעֵדָה ("Yahweh's glory appeared to all the congregation"), a scene-capping formula distinct from the instruction that precedes it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the opening rebellion span (vv.1-11) as its continuation, since the censer test was already introduced there; but this span narrates the test's actual staging and assembly -- a distinct action beat -- rather than repeating the earlier instruction, and it closes on the theophany that immediately provokes Yahweh's threat.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.18 “They each took his censer, and put fire in it, and laid incense on it”
oshb:Num.16.19 וַיֵּרָא כְבוֹד יְהוָה אֶל כָּל הָעֵדָה (“Yahweh’s glory appeared to all the congregation”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh double-addressee messenger formula opens Yahweh's threat to consume the whole congregation, closed by Moses and Aaron's own intercessory question, הָאִישׁ אֶחָד יֶחֱטָא וְעַל כָּל הָעֵדָה תִּקְצֹף ("shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the separation command that follows (vv.23-27) as one continuous divine-response sequence; but v.23 opens its own fresh messenger formula narrowing the threat into a specific, actionable instruction, distinct from the general threat and intercession that precede it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.21 “Separate yourselves from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment!”
oshb:Num.16.22 הָאִישׁ אֶחָד יֶחֱטָא וְעַל כָּל הָעֵדָה תִּקְצֹף (“shall one man sin, and will you be angry with all the congregation?”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula narrows the threat into an actionable command -- get away from the tents of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram -- and Moses' and the congregation's compliance follow immediately, closed by Dathan and Abiram standing exposed at their tent doors with their families.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split into command (vv.23-24) and execution (vv.25-27) as two decisions, matching the ch.1 census pattern; but here Moses' physical movement toward Dathan and Abiram, his own repeated warning speech, and the people's compliance form one uninterrupted dramatic sequence building directly toward the judgment scene, without the kind of narrative gap that separated ch.1's command from its later-reported fulfillment.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.24 “Get away from around the tent of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram!”
oshb:Num.16.27 וְדָתָן וַאֲבִירָם יָצְאוּ נִצָּבִים פֶּתַח אָהֳלֵיהֶם (“Dathan and Abiram came out, and stood at the door of their tents”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own sign-speech, בְּזֹאת תֵּדְעוּן ("hereby you shall know"), opens the climactic judgment scene, and the earth's opening and the fire consuming the two hundred fifty censer-bearers close the whole rebellion narrative in one continuous catastrophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The earth-swallowing of Korah's household (vv.31-33) could be split from the fire that consumes the two-hundred-fifty (v.35) as two separate judgments on two separate groups; but both are the direct, immediate fulfillment of the single sign Moses just announced, narrated in one unbroken sequence with no fresh formula between them.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.31 “the ground that was under them split apart”
oshb:Num.16.35 וְאֵשׁ יָצְאָה מֵאֵת יְהוָה וַתֹּאכַל אֵת הַחֲמִשִּׁים וּמָאתַיִם אִישׁ (“fire came out from Yahweh, and devoured the two hundred fifty men”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens a new instruction -- this span is MT 17:1-5, the point at which the Masoretic chapter division happens to fall on this same formula, though the chapter division itself carries no evidentiary weight -- directing Eleazar to hammer the dead men's bronze censers into an altar covering as a warning memorial, closed on the rationale that no unauthorized man should approach to burn incense.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be kept fused with the catastrophe narrative above as its immediate aftermath; but the fresh וַיֹּאמֶר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה formula alone opens a distinct topic (disposal and memorializing of the censers, not further judgment) -- the sole driver of this boundary. That the Masoretic tradition also happens to open a new chapter at this exact formula is a fact worth recording for citation purposes, but per the owner addendum chapter divisions are metadata only and carry no corroborating weight of their own; the boundary rests on the formula alone.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.38 “Let them be beaten into plates for a covering of the altar, for they offered them before Yahweh”
oshb:Num.17.1 וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר (MT 17:1 = WEB 16:36) “Yahweh spoke to Moses, saying”

boundary_rationale: A new complaint cycle opens the very next day (MT 17:6-8) -- אַתֶּם הֲמִתֶּם אֶת עַם יְהוָה -- distinct from the censer-memorial instruction of the preceding decision, closed on the theophany notice as Moses and Aaron approach the Tent (re-cut per OL-M8-Num-114-1: MT 17:9's fresh speech formula now opens the following decision rather than sitting mid-span).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The whole complaint-through-atonement-run sequence (WEB 16:41-50) could stay as one decision reading it as a single unbroken crisis, the original reading; but MT 17:9 (=WEB 16:44) opens with the identical theophany-then-speech-formula shape already honored at 16:19/16:20 in this very chapter, and the frozen span ran straight through that seam without a break.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.41 “On the next day all the congregation of the children of Israel complained against Moses”
web:Num.16.42 “when the congregation was assembled against Moses and against Aaron…the cloud covered it”

boundary_rationale: MT 17:9 (=WEB 16:44) opens with a fresh, complete quotative frame, וַיְדַבֵּר יְהוָה אֶל מֹשֶׁה לֵּאמֹר, the identical theophany-then-speech shape already honored at the 16:19/16:20 seam, ordering Moses and Aaron to get away from the congregation; Aaron's incense-run to halt the plague follows, closed on the final death toll and Aaron's return to Moses.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This span could stay merged with the complaint-and-theophany material (WEB 16:41-43) as one continuous second-crisis narrative, the reading originally adopted for the whole WEB 16:41-50 span; but MT 17:9's fresh formula reopens exactly where the crisis shifts from theophany to explicit divine order, the same seam-marking convention already applied one crisis earlier in this very chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.16.45 “Get away from among this congregation, that I may consume them in a moment!”
web:Num.16.50 “Aaron returned to Moses to the door of the Tent of Meeting, and the plague was stopped”

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula (MT 17:16) opens a wholly new sign-procedure -- one rod per tribal father's house, Aaron's name written on Levi's rod -- distinct from the censer material of the preceding chapter, closed on the rationale that the chosen man's rod will bud.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Because this immediately follows the second plague's resolution, one could read it as continuous aftermath rather than a fresh instruction; but its own fresh messenger formula marks a clean topical restart -- a new sign for a new purpose (ending complaints against the priesthood specifically, not further plague) -- after the prior crisis has already been narrated to its own close. The whole WEB ch.17 sits in a flagged MT offset zone (MT 17:16-28), which is a citation-discipline fact requiring dual reference in the evidence refs below, not itself evidence for where this boundary falls; the boundary rests on the formula alone.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.17.2 “take rods from them, one for each fathers’ house…twelve rods”
oshb:Num.17.20 (MT 17:20 = WEB 17:5) וְהָיָה הָאִישׁ אֲשֶׁר אֶבְחַר בּוֹ מַטֵּהוּ יִפְרָח (“the rod of the man whom I shall choose shall bud”)

boundary_rationale: Narration shifts to execution -- Moses collects the twelve rods and lays them before Yahweh -- and the next-day inspection closes on the sign itself, Aaron's rod having sprouted, budded, blossomed, and borne ripe almonds, a four-stage botanical escalation marking the climax of the sign.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The laying-up (v.7) could be split from the next-day discovery (vv.8-9) as command-execution and result-discovery; but both are narrated in one unbroken sequence with the same subject (Moses) and no fresh formula between placing the rods and returning to inspect them.

boundary_rationale: A fresh instruction, הָשֵׁב אֶת מַטֵּה אַהֲרֹן ("put back the rod of Aaron"), directs the budded rod's permanent preservation as a token against future rebellion, and Moses' compliance closes the sign narrative proper before the people's own response is narrated.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the discovery span above as its immediate sequel; but v.10 opens with a fresh וַיֹּאמֶר instruction shifting from describing the sign to prescribing its permanent memorial function, the same instruction/result-versus-new-command distinction used throughout this book.

boundary_rationale: The chapter -- and the whole rebellion-cycle complex begun at ch.16 -- closes on the people's own despairing cry, הֵן גָּוַעְנוּ ("behold, we perish"), a fresh collective-speech unit distinct from the rod sign's own narration, bridging into ch.18's answer about priestly and Levitical responsibility for sanctuary approach.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the rod-preservation span as the people's immediate reaction; but it is set off as its own fresh collective-speech act ("the children of Israel spoke to Moses, saying") rather than a narrated consequence of the preservation instruction, and its content (fear of approaching the tabernacle at all) directly anticipates ch.18's subject matter rather than commenting on the rod sign itself.

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the priestly-portions material that follows (vv.8-19) as one continuous "priestly privileges and duties" chapter-opening unit; but v.8 opens with its own fresh messenger formula shifting from responsibility-and-danger language to itemized economic entitlements, a real change of topic within the same Aaron-addressed speech.

boundary_rationale: וְזֶה לְּךָ ("and this is yours too") opens the second entitlement category -- wave offerings and firstfruits, open to the whole clean household rather than priestly males alone -- closed on the recurring "everyone clean in your house" eligibility clause repeated at the end of both v.11 and v.13.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split into the wave-offering clause (v.11) and the firstfruits clause (vv.12-13) as two decisions, since they concern different sources of produce; but both share the identical household-wide eligibility formula and no fresh introductory clause separates the oil/vintage/grain firstfruits from the wave offering that precedes them, reading as one continuous entitlement category.

boundary_rationale: The topic shifts to devoted things and firstborn -- כָּל חֵרֶם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל לְךָ יִהְיֶה ("everything devoted in Israel shall be yours") -- opening the redemption-price provision for human and unclean-animal firstborn, closed on the fixed five-shekel redemption sum.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the unredeemable clean-animal firstborn exception that follows (vv.17-19); but v.17 opens with a sharp אַךְ contrast ("but the firstborn of a cow…you shall not redeem"), explicitly excepting clean sacrificial animals from the redemption principle just stated, marking a distinct clause.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.18.15 “you shall surely redeem the firstborn of man, and you shall redeem the firstborn of unclean animals”

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as simply the redemption provision's final clause rather than its own decision; but its own contrastive opening and its closing covenant-of-salt formula -- a recognized covenant-sealing device distinct from any ordinary instruction closing -- mark it as the deliberate capstone of the whole priestly-dues section.

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula pivots from itemized priestly portions to the structural principle of inheritance -- Aaron gets none, אֲנִי חֶלְקְךָ ("I am your portion") -- and the Levites receive the tithe instead, closed on the repeated rationale explaining why Levites hold no tribal land.

boundary_rationale: A final fresh messenger formula, addressed now to the Levites through Moses rather than to Aaron, opens the tithe-of-the-tithe obligation the Levites themselves owe the priests, closed on the chapter's own capital-danger warning against profaning the holy things.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could fold this into the Levite-inheritance span above as its logical continuation (the tithe they receive, then what they owe from it); but the fresh messenger formula and the addressee shift (now the Levites are directly addressed, not just discussed) mark this as its own distinct instruction closing the chapter.

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the following corpse-contact defilement law (vv.11-13) since both concern the ashes' eventual use; but vv.11-13 open a wholly new topic -- who becomes unclean and for how long -- rather than continuing the ash-storage procedure, a shift from ritual mechanics to defilement law.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.19.9 “it shall be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel for use in water for cleansing impurity”

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be kept fused with the general corpse-contact rule above as its continuation; but its own זֹאת הַתּוֹרָה opening functions as a fresh mini-colophon specifically scoping the rule to enclosed spaces and open fields, a distinct rhetorical move from the general timing rule already stated.

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the application-procedure span as its warning coda rather than its own unit; but its contrastive opening and its shift to penalty-and-contagion logic (rather than describing the remedy itself) mark it as the chapter's own distinct closing movement.

boundary_rationale: Merged on review (LF-M8-Num-132-1 and OL-M8-Num-134-1, both verified): unlike the Hazeroth and Paran travel notices at 11:35 and 12:16, the bare arrival-and-death notice at 20:1 follows purely casuistic legislation (ch.19) with no preceding narrative scene to close, so it opens rather than closes a unit; Kadesh remains the fixed setting through the water-shortage complaint and Moses and Aaron's flight to the Tent, closing on the theophany notice, וַיֵּרָא כְבוֹד יְהוָה אֲלֵיהֶם, which matches the same theophany-then-speech-formula seam already honored at 16:19/16:20.
strongest_rejected_alternative: 20:1 could stand alone as its own decision, matching how other short scene-openers in this book are sometimes isolated; but it was in fact the sole one-verse decision across sixty-four consecutive decisions in this stretch of the book, and it supplies no content of its own beyond the datestamp and location the water-shortage complaint immediately depends on -- keeping it as its own unit understated its function as opening material rather than closing material.

web:Num.20.4 “Why have you brought Yahweh’s assembly into this wilderness, that we should die there…?”

strongest_rejected_alternative: v.6 could remain this decision's own opening, the original reading, since WEB itself runs vv.6-8 as one uninterrupted paragraph; but WEB's own paragraphing is metadata, not evidence, and the campaign's own convention applied consistently at 16:19/20 and 14:10/11 treats the fresh divine-speech formula, not translation paragraphing, as the boundary-bearing signal.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.20.8 “speak to the rock before their eyes, that it pour out its water”

boundary_rationale: Moses and Aaron gather the assembly and Moses strikes the rock twice rather than merely speaking to it, and Yahweh's judgment for this deviation -- neither will enter the land -- closes on the naming etiology, מֵי מְרִיבָה ("waters of Meribah").
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the striking/judgment seam (vv.10-11 versus 12-13); but Yahweh's judgment speech responds directly and immediately to the striking just narrated with no scene gap, and both share the same naming-etiology close, reading as one act-and-consequence unit.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.20.11 “Moses lifted up his hand, and struck the rock with his rod twice”

boundary_rationale: Merged on review (OL-M8-Num-137-1, verified): Edom's bare reply-turn at 20:18, וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו אֱדוֹם לֹא תַעֲבֹר בִּי, carries no formula, participant change, or time gap separating it from Israel's petition in the immediately preceding verse, and the campaign's own treatment of the structurally identical Sihon exchange (M8-Num-144, request kept with its flat refusal in one decision) makes a split here the exception rather than the rule. The whole failed negotiation now reads as one unbroken wayyiqtol/direct-speech sequence between the same two parties.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Israel's request (20:14-17) could stay split from Edom's refusal (20:18-21) on the ground that each is its own speaking party's turn; but that is exactly the change-of-speaker-only criterion this book elsewhere declines to treat as decisive on its own (e.g. the Balak/Balaam exchanges of ch.22, where a split is warranted only when an overnight gap or a theophany also changes the answering agent -- neither condition is present at 20:17/18).

boundary_rationale: A dated travel notice opens Aaron's death scene, and a fresh messenger formula announces its cause -- the Meribah rebellion -- and its ritual staging: garments transferred to Eleazar, Aaron gathered to his people, closed on the thirty-day mourning notice for the whole house of Israel.

boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.20.26 “strip Aaron of his garments, and put them on Eleazar his son”

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as continuing straight from Aaron's death and mourning at the end of ch.20 with no fresh boundary, since both are wilderness-journey narrative; but a wholly new participant (the king of Arad) and a wholly new conflict (attack and vow) open independently of the mourning scene, with no causal link stated between them.

oshb:Num.21.3 וַיִּקְרָא שֵׁם הַמָּקוֹם חָרְמָה (“the name of the place was called Hormah”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh travel notice opens a new complaint cycle -- discouragement over the journey, complaint against the manna -- escalating into the venomous-snake plague and its bronze-serpent remedy, closed on the healing formula itself rather than a naming etiology, a distinct closing device from the episode before it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the complaint/remedy seam (vv.4-7 versus 8-9) as two decisions, matching how other complaint cycles in this book split crisis from divine response; but here Moses' intercessory prayer (v.7) and Yahweh's remedy (v.8) are compressed into consecutive verses with no narrative gap or recapitulation, reading as one tight complaint-and-cure unit.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.21.6 “Yahweh sent venomous snakes among the people, and they bit the people”

boundary_rationale: A run of short ויסעו/ויחנו-style travel notices -- Oboth, Iyeabarim, Zered, Arnon -- opens the itinerary register proper, including the poetic citation from the Book of the Wars of Yahweh at vv.14-15, closed on the arrival at Beer, the well that occasions the song that follows.

strongest_rejected_alternative: One could fold this into the Amalek oracle as a paired "minor peoples" unit, since both are short and adjacent; but each carries its own fresh introducing formula naming a distinct people, the consistent marker I use throughout this cycle to separate one oracle from the next regardless of length.

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the Kenite oracle as one continuous closing sequence, since neither has a fully developed narrative frame of its own; but its own fresh citation formula (even without a new וַיַּרְא object clause) still marks a distinct performed unit, consistent with treating every מְשָׁלוֹ-introduced oracle as its own decision throughout chs.23-24.

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the final oracle as its closing narrative tag; but it reports the physical separation of the two principals after every oracle has already concluded, functioning as the whole cycle's own resolution rather than a continuation of the oracle's own poetic close.

boundary_rationale: A wholly new crisis opens the chapter -- intermarriage with Moabite women leading to Baal Peor worship -- closed on Yahweh's own command to hang the chiefs and Moses' relay of that command to the judges, before the Zimri/Cozbi incident narrows to a single named case.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through the Zimri/Cozbi episode (vv.6-9) as one continuous "Baal Peor" crisis; but v.6 opens with a fresh, specific incident -- a named man bringing a named Midianite woman "in the sight of Moses" -- narrowing from the general command just given to a single concrete test case, a real narrative-focus shift.

strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with Phinehas's covenant-of-peace reward that follows (vv.10-13) as one continuous "Phinehas's act and its reward" unit; but v.10 opens with a fresh messenger formula narrating Yahweh's own commendation, distinct from this span's narrated action itself.

boundary_rationale: A final fresh messenger formula opens the command to harass Midian specifically, closed on the rationale referencing Cozbi's own Midianite-prince lineage -- the same detail just supplied in the identification notice -- bridging directly into ch.31's Midianite war.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could read the "after the plague" clause as belonging with ch.25's Baal Peor material rather than ch.26's census, since it refers backward; but WEB's own verse division places it inside 26:1 as this chapter's own opening temporal frame, and per the crosswalk's citation rule this is not treated as evidence for or against a compositional seam, only as a fact requiring dual WEB/MT citation. On review (OL-M8-Num-173-1), an independent content signal reinforces WEB's own placement rather than contradicting it: וַיְהִי אַחֲרֵי [X] is a well-attested pericope-OPENING formula elsewhere in the Torah (Gen.22.1, Gen.40.1, Josh.1.1, Judg.1.1), with no instance functioning as a closing tag, supporting the reading that 'after the plague' opens the census command rather than closing what precedes it. The two-witness petuchah OL cites is real corroboration but, per the addendum, cannot alone drive a sub-verse respan against this independent grammatical pattern.

boundary_rationale: A fresh double-addressee formula, now naming Eleazar rather than Aaron (already dead), opens the second census with the explicit temporal marker אַחֲרֵי הַמַּגֵּפָה ("after the plague") -- WEB's rendering of the clause MT counts as 25:19 -- closed on Moses and Eleazar's relay of the command in nearly identical wording to the instruction itself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could read the "after the plague" clause as belonging with ch.25's Baal Peor material rather than ch.26's census, since it refers backward; but WEB's own verse division places it inside 26:1 as this chapter's own opening temporal frame, and per the crosswalk's citation rule I do not treat this as evidence for or against a compositional seam, only as a fact requiring dual WEB/MT citation. On review (OL-M8-Num-174-1), the independent vayehi-achare pericope-opening argument developed at M8-Num-173 applies equally here: this construction opens rather than closes a unit at every other occurrence checked in the Torah, reinforcing rather than undermining the original placement. The double-addressee onset naming Eleazar (rather than the now-deceased Aaron) remains independent onset evidence regardless of how the temporal-clause question resolves.

boundary_rationale: רְאוּבֵן בְּכוֹר יִשְׂרָאֵל ("Reuben, firstborn of Israel") opens the tribal register with its own sub-clan names and total, and the embedded Dathan/Abiram/Korah retrospective (vv.9-11) stays within this entry because it explains a specific detail of Reuben's own genealogy (why these particular sons of Eliab are remembered) rather than opening an independent topic.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The Korah aside could be split off as its own decision, since it is a narrative retrospective rather than genealogical listing; but it has no independent introducing formula of its own -- it flows directly out of naming Dathan and Abiram as Eliab's sons -- so severing it would cut one continuous Reubenite entry in half over a difference of register within the same tribal unit, not a marked boundary.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.26.5 “Reuben, the firstborn of Israel; the sons of Reuben”
oshb:Num.26.11 וּבְנֵי קֹרַח לֹא מֵתוּ (“notwithstanding, the sons of Korah didn’t die”)

boundary_rationale: Merged on review (LF-M8-Num-176-1/177-1, verified): Simeon's entry (five clans, a total) and Gad's entry (seven clans, a total) each introduce no legal, procedural, or narrative element beyond a changing clan list and a changing number -- the exact bare-tally profile M8-Num-003 used to merge ch.1's twelve tribes into one decision. A longer clan list, as OL's own review conceded, is more data of the same kind, not a new literary form.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Each tribe could keep its own decision on the strength of the register's own recurring 'בני X למשפחתם...אלה משפחת X' introducing formula and its per-entry setumah marking; but ch.1's twelve tribes recur under an equally consistent frame and close on a stronger mark (petuchah) at every boundary, and were still merged, so formula-recurrence alone does not distinguish this case.

boundary_rationale: בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה ("the sons of Judah") opens the fourth entry, embedding its own brief narrative aside -- Er and Onan died in Canaan -- before the surviving line's sub-clans and total close the entry, the tribe with the largest resulting count in the whole register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The Er/Onan death notice could be split off as its own narrative decision, matching how the Reuben entry's Korah aside might tempt a split; but exactly as with Reuben, this notice has no independent introducing formula and exists solely to explain Judah's own sub-clan structure (why Perez and Zerah, not Er and Onan, found the surviving families), so it stays inside the one tribal entry.

boundary_rationale: Merged on review (LF-M8-Num-179-1/180-1, verified): Issachar (four clans, a total) and Zebulun (three clans, a total, the register's shortest entry) are both bare tallies with no distinguishing content, by both primaries' own account the plainest and thinnest entries in the whole register. This entry's own original rationale had already named Zebulun 'the clearest test case for over-atomization' and answered that test only by appeal to the register's own completeness-under-formula, the exact argument M8-Num-003 rejected as sufficient for a structurally identical case in ch.1.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Zebulun's extreme brevity (two verses) could be read as itself distinguishing it from Issachar's four-verse entry, but length alone is not a procedural or narrative element under M8-Num-003's own test, and merging the two shortest, plainest adjacent entries into one decision is the more honest application of that test, not a special exception for brevity.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.26.23 “The sons of Issachar after their families: of Tola, the family of the Tolaites”
web:Num.26.27 “These are the families of the Zebulunites according to those who were counted of them, sixty thousand five hundred”
oshb:Num.26.27 אֵלֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹת הַזְּבוּלֹנִי לִפְקֻדֵיהֶם שִׁשִּׁים אֶלֶף וַחֲמֵשׁ מֵאוֹת (“these are the families of the Zebulunites…sixty thousand five hundred”)

boundary_rationale: Merged on review (LF-M8-Num-182-1, verified directly against oshb): 26:28 opens בְּנֵי יוֹסֵף לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם מְנַשֶּׁה וְאֶפְרָיִם and 26:37 closes אֵלֶּה בְנֵי יוֹסֵף לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם, the identical clause bracketing both Manasseh's and Ephraim's entries as one composed 'Joseph tribes' unit -- a bracketing device operating ACROSS two entries, independent of and stronger than the general bare-tally argument used for the register's other merges.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Manasseh (with its own Gilead genealogy and the Zelophehad's-daughters notice) and Ephraim could stay split on the strength of Manasseh's genuinely richer embedded content, the reasoning that keeps Reuben, Judah, and Naphtali independent elsewhere in this register; but the verbatim inclusio spans and binds both tribes regardless of their unequal internal richness, and severing it would cut a textually self-identified single unit at a point the text itself brackets shut.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.26.28 “The sons of Joseph after their families: Manasseh and Ephraim”
web:Num.26.33 “Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters”
oshb:Num.26.37 אֵלֶּה בְנֵי יוֹסֵף לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם (“these are the sons of Joseph after their families”)

boundary_rationale: Merged on review: Benjamin's extra generational layer (Bela's two named sons) is genealogical depth within one clan's line, the same construction correctly kept internal at Judah's v.20; and Asher's Serah notice was already conceded in this decision's own original rationale to carry no independent legal or narrative weight. Dan's own entry (26:42-43) is recorded here on revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-183-1) with its actual formal profile rather than flattened to plain 'thinness': it is the only tribe in the register that opens and closes within a single verse (26:42, אֵלֶּה בְנֵי דָן לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם...אֵלֶּה מִשְׁפְּחֹת דָּן לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם -- contrast Ephraim's own אֵלֶּה-opening at v.35, which runs three verses to its close at v.37); its tally at 26:43, כָּל מִשְׁפְּחֹת הַשּׁוּחָמִי לִפְקֻדֵיהֶם, is the register's only כָּל-initial tally (every sibling entry at 26:25, 34, 37, 41, 47, 50 opens with אֵלֶּה instead); and two internal setumot stand at 26:41 and 26:43 ("(two-witness)"). None of these three marks rises to a new legal, procedural, or narrative element under the register's own governing test (M8-Num-003), so they corroborate without overturning the merge -- but they are recorded honestly rather than folded into a generic thinness claim.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Dan's self-closure, its unique כָּל-tally, and its two internal setumot, taken together, could be read as distinguishing it enough to stand alone despite the register's general merge criterion; I hold it inside this merge because none of the three is a new legal, procedural, or narrative element, the specific bar M8-Num-003 sets and the one this whole census-tail group is tested against. Separately: Naphtali (26:48-50, M8-Num-186) is an equally bare tally by the same profile that justified this merge and the Simeon+Gad/Issachar+Zebulun merges, and a reviewer could ask why it was not folded in here or elsewhere; the answer is not its content, which is exactly as thin, but its position -- 26:51's אֵלֶּה פְּקוּדֵי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל is the whole-register grand total, scoped to the nation and carrying the nation's own figure (601,730 against Naphtali's own 45,400), not Naphtali's colophon. Naphtali is the only tribe in ch.26 whose neighboring unit is that grand-total colophon rather than another tribe's entry, the same abutment convention that already keeps the Levite-exclusion clause with the census register at 1:47 (M8-Num-003) and the whole-Israel march colophon independent of the Dan-camp entry at 10:28 (M8-Num-261). That positional fact, not Naphtali's own content, is why it stands alone.

boundary_rationale: בְּנֵי נַפְתָּלִי ("the sons of Naphtali") opens the twelfth and final tribal entry, and the register closes on its own book-total colophon, אֵלֶּה פְּקוּדֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ("these are those who were counted of the children of Israel"), summing all twelve entries at once.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The grand-total colophon (v.51) could be split off as its own decision, matching how ch.1's census closed on a separate total; but here it is a single short summary verse immediately following the final tribe's own total with no fresh introductory register-level formula of its own, so I keep it bound to Naphtali's entry as the register's natural close.

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the land-apportionment principle -- larger tribes receive more, smaller less, but the actual assignment falls by lot -- distinct in kind (instruction, not register) from the census entries just concluded, closed on the lot's own between-more-and-fewer clause.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the census register as its practical rationale (why the count matters); but the fresh messenger formula and the shift from enumerating people to prescribing future land distribution mark a distinct instruction, not a continuation of the register's own tallying function.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.26.54 “To the more you shall give the more inheritance, and to the fewer you shall give the less”
oshb:Num.26.56 עַל פִּי הַגּוֹרָל תֵּחָלֵק נַחֲלָתוֹ בֵּין רַב לִמְעָט (“according to the lot shall their inheritance be divided between the more and the fewer”)

boundary_rationale: וְאֵלֶּה פְקוּדֵי הַלֵּוִי ("and these are the numbered ones of Levi") opens a wholly separate register from the war census just completed, using the month-old age threshold distinctive to Levite counts (matching ch.3-4's precedent) rather than the twenty-year war-census threshold, closed on the rationale that Levites hold no inheritance among the tribes.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the twelve-tribe register above as simply its thirteenth entry; but the Levite count uses a fundamentally different eligibility threshold and explicitly excludes itself from the inheritance-by-lot principle just stated, marking it as a structurally separate census with its own logic, not another tribe in the same list.

boundary_rationale: אֵלֶּה פְּקוּדֵי מֹשֶׁה וְאֶלְעָזָר הַכֹּהֵן ("these are they who were counted by Moses and Eleazar the priest") closes the whole census complex with the pointed observation that not one man from the first census (ch.1) remains except Caleb and Joshua, tying the entire generation's death sentence from ch.14 to its narrative fulfillment here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the Levite census as its shared closing note; but its own אֵלֶּה colophon and its explicit comparison to Moses and Aaron's earlier Sinai census (not the Levite count specifically) mark it as the whole chapter's own summary close, not the Levite register's alone.

boundary_rationale: The five named daughters step forward as new participants, opening their direct petition, closed now on Moses' own referral of their case to Yahweh, וַיַּקְרֵב מֹשֶׁה אֶת מִשְׁפָּטָן לִפְנֵי יְהוָה (v.5), the petition scene's own resolution rather than the opening of the ruling (respanned per OL-M8-Num-190-1: v.6's fresh divine-speech formula now opens the following decision).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The petition (vv.1-4) could stay split from Moses' referral (v.5), the original reading; but v.5 has no independent formula of its own and functions as the direct narrative consequence of the petition just made, while v.6 carries the same bare, complete divine-speech formula used as onset evidence five other times in this exact stretch of the book (25:10, 25:16, 26:52, 27:12, 27:18).
