oshb:Num.30.2 (MT 30:3 = WEB 30:2) אִ֚ישׁ כִּֽי יִדֹּ֨ר נֶ֜דֶר לַֽיהוָ֗ה א֣וֹ הִשָּׁ֤בַע שְׁבֻעָה֙ לֶאְסֹ֤ר אִסָּר֙ עַל נַפְשׁ֔וֹ לֹ֥א יַחֵ֖ל דְּבָר֑וֹ כְּכָל הַיֹּצֵ֥א מִפִּ֖יו יַעֲשֶֽׂה (“when a man vows a vow to Yahweh, or swears an oath to bind his soul with a bond, he shall not break his word; he shall do according to all that proceeds out of his mouth”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis narrows the general rule to the first female sub-case, an unmarried daughter still in her father's household, whose vow stands unless her father voids it the very day he hears it, closed on the forgiveness clause specific to a voided vow.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the betrothed/married woman's case that follows (vv.6-8) as one "female vow" topic; but v.6 opens its own fresh protasis specifically distinguishing a woman "who has a husband" from the unmarried daughter just addressed, a materially different life-stage and authority structure.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.5 “if her father forbids her in the day that he hears, none of her vows…shall stand”
oshb:Num.30.6 (MT 30:6 = WEB 30:5) וַיהוָה יִסְלַח לָהּ כִּי הֵנִיא אָבִיהָ אֹתָהּ (“Yahweh will forgive her, because her father has forbidden her”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis, וְאִם הָיוֹ תִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ ("and if she marries a husband"), opens the second female sub-case -- a vow made before marriage now subject to the husband's ratification -- closed on the same day-of-hearing forbid-or-forgive logic applied to the husband's authority instead of the father's.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the unmarried daughter's case above given the shared underlying father-or-husband-authority logic; but its own distinct protasis marking a change of life-stage (from father's household to husband's) is the same kind of casuistic list-item marker that separated every other sub-case in this chapter.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.6 “If she has a husband, while her vows are on her”
oshb:Num.30.7 (MT 30:7 = WEB 30:6) וְאִם הָיוֹ תִהְיֶה לְאִישׁ וּנְדָרֶיהָ עָלֶיהָ (“and if she has a husband, while her vows are on her”)

oshb:Num.30.9 (MT 30:9 = WEB 30:8) וְאִם בְּיוֹם שְׁמֹעַ אִישָׁהּ יָנִיא אוֹתָהּ וְהֵפֵר אֶת נִדְרָהּ...וַיהוָה יִסְלַח לָהּ (“and if her husband disallows her in the day that he hears it, then he makes void her vow…Yahweh will forgive her”)

boundary_rationale: A single-verse case addresses the widow or divorced woman specifically -- וְנֵדֶר אַלְמָנָה וּגְרוּשָׁה ("but the vow of a widow, or of her who is divorced") -- whose vow stands absolutely, with no male authority left to ratify or void it, the shortest and most legally distinct of the four female sub-cases.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Given its brevity, this could be folded into either the preceding married-woman case or the following married-woman-in-her-husband's-house case; but its own protasis names a wholly distinct legal category (a woman under no man's authority at all) whose rule is the simple opposite of every other case in the chapter -- her vow always stands -- meriting its own decision despite its length.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.9 “But the vow of a widow, or of her who is divorced, everything…shall stand against her”
oshb:Num.30.10 (MT 30:10 = WEB 30:9) כֹּל אֲשֶׁר אָסְרָה עַל נַפְשָׁהּ יָקוּם עָלֶיהָ (“everything with which she has bound her soul shall stand against her”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis, וְאִם בֵּית אִישָׁהּ נָדָרָה ("and if she vowed in her husband's house"), opens the fourth and longest sub-case -- a woman already married when she vows -- closed on the delayed-objection ruling that a husband who waits past the day of hearing bears his wife's iniquity himself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the day-of-hearing/delayed-objection seam (vv.10-12 versus 13-15) as two decisions; but both halves address the same married-woman case under one continuous protasis with no fresh introductory formula between them, the delayed-objection ruling functioning as this case's own closing elaboration rather than a fresh sub-case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.13 “Every vow, and every binding oath to afflict the soul, her husband may establish it, or her husband may make it void”
oshb:Num.30.16 (MT 30:16 = WEB 30:15) וְנָשָׂא אֶת עֲוֺנָהּ (“then he shall bear her iniquity”)

boundary_rationale: אֵלֶּה הַחֻקִּים ("these are the statutes") closes the whole vow-law chapter with a generalizing colophon naming its three governing relationships -- husband-wife, father-daughter -- the same colophon-generalizing device used to close the sotah and Nazirite laws in chs.5-6.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the married-woman case above as its closing clause; but its own אֵלֶּה opening explicitly restates the whole chapter's legal scope rather than continuing the specific married-woman case just concluded, the recognized colophon pattern I treat consistently across this book.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.30.16 “These are the statutes which Yahweh commanded Moses, between a man and his wife”
oshb:Num.30.17 (MT 30:17 = WEB 30:16) אֵלֶּה הַחֻקִּים אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (“these are the statutes which Yahweh commanded Moses”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the Midianite war with its own vengeance rationale, נְקֹם נִקְמַת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ("avenge the children of Israel"), explicitly tied back to Balaam's own role in the Peor affair, closed on the levy's own precise count -- twelve thousand, one thousand per tribe -- before battle is joined.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through the battle report (vv.7-12) as one continuous "the war" unit; but the levy's own completed count (v.5-6) is a distinct administrative milestone closed before any fighting is narrated, and v.7's fresh action verb, וַיִּצְבְּאוּ ("they made war"), opens the campaign proper as a separate beat.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.5 “So there were delivered, out of the thousands of Israel, a thousand from every tribe, twelve thousand armed for war”

oshb:Num.31.6 וַיִּשְׁלַח אֹתָם מֹשֶׁה אֶלֶף לַמַּטֶּה לַצָּבָא אֹתָם וְאֶת פִּינְחָס בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר הַכֹּהֵן לַצָּבָא וּכְלֵי הַקֹּדֶשׁ וַחֲצֹצְרוֹת הַתְּרוּעָה בְּיָדוֹ (“Moses sent them, one thousand of every tribe, to the war with Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest…with the vessels of the sanctuary and the trumpets for the alarm in his hand”)

boundary_rationale: וַיִּצְבְּאוּ עַל מִדְיָן ("they made war against Midian") opens the battle report itself -- every male killed, the five kings and Balaam himself among the dead -- closed on the plunder's arrival at the camp before Moses' own reaction is narrated.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with Moses' anger at the surviving women (vv.13-18) as one continuous battle-and-aftermath unit; but v.13 opens with a fresh scene, Moses and Eleazar going out to meet the returning army, a distinct location and action from the battle and plunder-gathering just narrated on the field itself.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.8 “They also killed Balaam the son of Beor with the sword”
oshb:Num.31.12 אֶל הַמַּחֲנֶה אֶל עַרְבֹת מוֹאָב אֲשֶׁר עַל יַרְדֵּן יְרֵחוֹ (“to the camp at the plains of Moab, which are by the Jordan at Jericho”)

boundary_rationale: Moses and Eleazar's meeting of the returning army opens this movement, and Moses' own angry rebuke of the officers -- הַחִיִּיתֶם כָּל נְקֵבָה ("have you saved all the women alive?") -- closes on his explicit kill command for male children and non-virgin women, tying the command directly back to the Peor seduction.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the meeting/rebuke seam (v.13 versus vv.14-18); but the meeting exists only to stage Moses' immediate angry question, with no independent content of its own apart from the rebuke it introduces, so I read it as one continuous confrontation.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.15 “Have you saved all the women alive?”
oshb:Num.31.18 וְכֹל הַטַּף בַּנָּשִׁים אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדְעוּ מִשְׁכַּב זָכָר הַחֲיוּ לָכֶם (“but all the girls, who have not known man by lying with him, keep alive for yourselves”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own instruction shifts from the kill command to procedural purification -- seven days outside the camp, third-and-seventh-day rites for anyone who killed or touched the slain -- closed on the material-purification clause covering garments, skins, and wood.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the kill command above as its continuation; but it addresses a materially different concern (ritual purity of the victorious army, not the treatment of captives) using the same third-and-seventh-day timing already established for corpse contact in ch.19, marking a distinct procedural topic within the same speech.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.19 “Whoever has killed any person, and whoever has touched any slain, purify yourselves”
oshb:Num.31.20 וְכָל מַעֲשֵׂה עִזִּים וְכָל כְּלִי עֵץ תִּתְחַטָּאוּ (“all work of goats’ hair, and all things made of wood”)

boundary_rationale: A new speaker, Eleazar the priest rather than Moses, opens with his own colophon-style introduction, זֹאת חֻקַּת הַתּוֹרָה אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה ("this is the statute of the law which Yahweh has commanded"), addressing the metals and fire-versus-water purification method, a distinct speaker and topic from Moses' own camp-purification instruction above.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the preceding purification span as its continuation, since both concern camp purity after battle; but the change of speaker (Eleazar, not Moses) and the shift from personal/textile purification to metal-object purification by fire mark a distinct instruction with its own colophon opening.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.21 “This is the statute of the law which Yahweh has commanded Moses”
oshb:Num.31.23 אַךְ בְּמֵי נִדָּה יִתְחַטָּא (“nevertheless it shall be purified with the water for impurity”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the plunder-division instruction, splitting spoil between the soldiers and the whole congregation, and prescribing distinct tribute rates for each half -- one in five hundred to Eleazar, one in fifty to the Levites -- closed on the Levites' own tabernacle-duty rationale.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the execution and totals that follow (vv.31-35) as one continuous division-and-accounting unit; but v.31 opens with third-person fulfillment narration, וַיַּעַשׂ מֹשֶׁה וְאֶלְעָזָר ("Moses and Eleazar did"), a distinct shift from the second-person instruction just given.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.28 “Levy a tribute to Yahweh of the men of war…one soul of five hundred”
oshb:Num.31.30 וְנָתַתָּה אֹתָם לַלְוִיִּם שֹׁמְרֵי מִשְׁמֶרֶת מִשְׁכַּן יְהוָה (“give them to the Levites, who perform the duty of Yahweh’s tabernacle”)

boundary_rationale: וַיַּעַשׂ מֹשֶׁה וְאֶלְעָזָר הַכֹּהֵן כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה ("Moses and Eleazar the priest did as Yahweh commanded Moses") opens the fulfillment notice, and the plunder's own grand totals -- sheep, cattle, donkeys, persons -- close this span before the half-by-half accounting begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the half-share accounting that follows (vv.36-47) as one continuous "the numbers" unit; but v.36 opens with its own fresh introducing clause, וַתְּהִי הַמֶּחֱצָה ("and the half was"), narrowing from the grand total just given to the soldiers' specific half-share breakdown, a distinct level of accounting detail.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.32 “the plunder…was six hundred seventy-five thousand sheep”
oshb:Num.31.35 וְנֶפֶשׁ אָדָם מִן הַנָּשִׁים אֲשֶׁר לֹא יָדְעוּ מִשְׁכַּב זָכָר כָּל נֶפֶשׁ שְׁנַיִם וּשְׁלֹשִׁים אָלֶף (“thirty-two thousand persons in all, of the women who had not known man”)

boundary_rationale: וַתְּהִי הַמֶּחֱצָה ("and the half was") opens the detailed parallel accounting -- soldiers' half with its own tribute figures, then the congregation's half with its own tribute figures -- a register of twinned totals closed on the Levites' final receipt of the congregation's tribute.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split into the soldiers'-half accounting (vv.36-41) and the congregation's-half accounting (vv.42-47) as two decisions, since each half is tallied separately; but both halves share one continuous parallel-structure register with no fresh messenger formula between them, and the second half is explicitly introduced as "of the children of Israel's half, which Moses divided" rather than as an independent new topic, reading as one twinned accounting unit.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.37 “Yahweh’s tribute of the sheep was six hundred seventy-five”

oshb:Num.31.47 וַיִּתֵּן אֹתָם לַלְוִיִּם שֹׁמְרֵי מִשְׁמֶרֶת מִשְׁכַּן יְהוָה כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה אֶת מֹשֶׁה (“gave them to the Levites, who performed the duty of Yahweh’s tabernacle, as Yahweh commanded Moses”)

boundary_rationale: A new movement opens as the army's own officers approach Moses voluntarily, distinct from the commanded tribute just accounted for -- their own gift of gold ornaments "to make atonement for our souls" -- closed on the memorial deposit of that gold in the Tent of Meeting, ending the chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the half-shares accounting as its closing addendum; but this gold is explicitly distinguished as a voluntary gift the officers bring on their own initiative ("what every man found"), not the commanded one-in-fifty or one-in-five-hundred tribute just tallied, marking a materially different kind of offering with its own opening scene (the officers' approach) and closing purpose (memorial, not tribute).
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.31.50 “We have brought Yahweh’s offering…to make atonement for our souls before Yahweh”
oshb:Num.31.54 וַיָּבִאוּ אֹתוֹ אֶל אֹהֶל מוֹעֵד זִכָּרוֹן לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לִפְנֵי יְהוָה (“brought it into the Tent of Meeting for a memorial for the children of Israel before Yahweh”)

boundary_rationale: A new topic and new participants open ch.32 -- Reuben and Gad's great livestock holdings and their sight of Jazer and Gilead's grazing land -- closed on their own explicit request not to be brought across the Jordan, before Moses' rebuke begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through Moses' rebuke (vv.6-15) as one continuous request-and-response scene; but v.6 opens with Moses' own fresh speech, הַאַחֵיכֶם יָבֹאוּ לַמִּלְחָמָה וְאַתֶּם תֵּשְׁבוּ פֹה ("shall your brothers go to war while you sit here?"), a distinct speaking turn responding to the request just made. A closer alternative, considered and rejected: v.5 itself sits beside a setumah after v.4, and v.5 opens a second, resumptive וַיֹּאמְרוּ from the same petitioning speakers rather than a genuine addressee change; I judge the speaker change at v.6 (petitioners to Moses) the stronger, text-driven boundary, since it marks an actual change of speaking party rather than a same-party continuation of the request already begun.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.5 “Don’t bring us over the Jordan”
oshb:Num.32.4 אֶרֶץ מִקְנֶה הִוא וְלַעֲבָדֶיךָ מִקְנֶה (“it is a land for livestock, and your servants have livestock”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own extended rebuke opens with a rhetorical accusation, closed on the direct charge that this generation is rising up "in your fathers' place" to repeat the spies' own faithless discouragement of ch.13-14, explicitly recalling that earlier rebellion by name and consequence.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the historical-recollection seam (vv.6-9 versus 10-15), since vv.8-9 retell the spy narrative while vv.10-15 apply it as present warning; but Moses delivers both as one uninterrupted speech with no formula break, the recollection functioning as evidence within his single argument rather than a separate speech act.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.15 “if you turn away from after him, he will yet again leave them in the wilderness”

oshb:Num.32.15 כִּי תְשׁוּבֻן מֵאַחֲרָיו וְיָסַף עוֹד לְהַנִּיחוֹ בַּמִּדְבָּר וְשִׁחַתֶּם לְכָל הָעָם הַזֶּה (“if you turn away from after him, he will yet again leave them in the wilderness, and you will destroy all these people”)

boundary_rationale: Reuben and Gad's own answering proposal, גִּדְרֹת צֹאן נִבְנֶה לְמִקְנֵנוּ ("we will build sheepfolds here for our livestock"), opens their counter-offer -- build first, then fight alongside Israel -- closed on their explicit renunciation of any Cisjordan inheritance.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with Moses' conditional acceptance that follows (vv.20-24) as one continuous negotiation; but v.20 opens with Moses' own fresh reply, אִם תַּעֲשׂוּן אֶת הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה ("if you will do this thing"), a distinct speaking turn responding to the proposal just offered.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.17 “we ourselves will be ready armed to go before the children of Israel”
oshb:Num.32.19 כִּי בָאָה נַחֲלָתֵנוּ אֵלֵינוּ מֵעֵבֶר הַיַּרְדֵּן מִזְרָחָה (“because our inheritance has come to us on this side of the Jordan eastward”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own conditional response, אִם תַּעֲשׂוּן אֶת הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה ("if you will do this thing"), opens the acceptance with its own positive and negative branches -- fulfillment brings the land, failure brings sin -- closed on his instruction to build the promised cities and folds regardless of the outcome.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be split at the positive/negative-consequence seam (vv.20-22 versus 23-24); but both branches are stated as two sides of the same single conditional pronouncement with no fresh formula between them, reading as one continuous if/then-else ruling.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.22 “and the land is subdued before Yahweh; then afterward you shall return”
oshb:Num.32.24 בְּנוּ לָכֶם עָרִים לְטַפְּכֶם וּגְדֵרֹת לְצֹנַאֲכֶם (“build cities for your little ones, and folds for your sheep”)

boundary_rationale: Reuben and Gad's own short confirmation, עֲבָדֶיךָ יַעֲשׂוּ כַּאֲשֶׁר אֲדֹנִי מְצַוֶּה ("your servants will do as my lord commands"), closes the negotiation cycle before Moses' formal commission to the officials begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into Moses' conditional acceptance as its narrated response; but it is the tribes' own distinct speech act, a formal acceptance of terms rather than a continuation of Moses' own pronouncement, and it is followed by an administrative commissioning scene rather than more negotiation.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.25 “Your servants will do as my lord commands”
oshb:Num.32.27 וַעֲבָדֶיךָ יַעַבְרוּ כָּל חֲלוּץ צָבָא לִפְנֵי יְהוָה לַמִּלְחָמָה (“your servants will pass over, every man who is armed for war, before Yahweh”)

boundary_rationale: Moses formally commissions Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal heads, his continuing speech running from the commission itself (v.28) through his two-branch conditional charge (v.29-30) -- v.29 opens וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֲלֵהֶם, the identical 'said to them' construction already used at v.20, unmarked here as a continuation of the same speech act -- closing this decision before the tribes' own answer opens the next. On revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-232-1), the original ground for this split is corrected: it is not bare formula-recurrence across 'every other speaking turn' in the negotiation (32:16 in fact opens on a bare plural verb with no subject named at all, וַיִּגְּשׁוּ אֵלָיו וַיֹּאמְרוּ, and v.29's own formula matches v.20's exactly yet stays unit-internal here), but a change in verb TYPE at 32:31: וַיַּעֲנוּ בְּנֵי גָד וּבְנֵי רְאוּבֵן ('they ANSWERED'), the negotiation's only response-form verb, marking the tribes' formal ratification of terms Moses has just set -- a different legal act in kind, not merely a fresh speaking turn like the ones that precede it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The commissioning and the tribes' answering oath could stay bundled as one legal transaction -- name witnesses, then ratify before them; that witnessed-oath reading has real force, and it is not defeated by treating every speaking turn in this negotiation as equally boundary-bearing, since it is not: 32:29's own 'Moses said to them' formula, identical to 32:20's, remains inside this span without being read as a fresh decision, so bare formula-recurrence cannot be the actual criterion. The split instead rests on 32:31's own וַיַּעֲנוּ marking a distinct act of ratification, unlike ordinary speech turns -- contrast the Edom negotiation (20:18, 20:20), where both of Edom's replies are plain וַיֹּאמֶר repeating the identical flat refusal with nothing new ratified, correctly kept as one continuous exchange (M8-Num-136) rather than split. The same verb-type distinction that merges Edom's exchange is what splits this one.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.28 “Moses commanded concerning them to Eleazar the priest, and to Joshua the son of Nun”
web:Num.32.30 “if they will not pass over with you armed, they shall have possessions among you in the land of Canaan”
oshb:Num.32.29 וַיֹּאמֶר מֹשֶׁה אֲלֵהֶם (“Moses said to them” — identical to 32:20’s formula, unit-internal here)

oshb:Num.32.31 וַיַּעֲנוּ בְנֵי גָד וּבְנֵי רְאוּבֵן לֵאמֹר (“the children of Gad and the children of Reuben answered, saying” — the negotiation’s only response-form verb, opening the following decision)

boundary_rationale: וַיַּעֲנוּ בְנֵי גָד וּבְנֵי רְאוּבֵן לֵאמֹר opens the tribes' own formal, binding answer to Moses' commission, closed on their own restatement of the inheritance terms already agreed. On revision review (RVOL-M8-Num-266-1), the boundary is re-grounded on the verb type of וַיַּעֲנוּ ('answered') itself, the negotiation's only response-form verb, rather than on formula-recurrence generally: every earlier turn in this negotiation (32:6, 32:16, 32:20, 32:25, 32:29) uses ordinary speech-introducing verbs (אמר or a bare verb with no subject at all at 32:16), while 32:31 alone marks a distinct act of ratifying terms just set, not merely speaking.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could stay bundled with Moses' commissioning speech as one 'witnessed-oath' legal transaction -- naming witnesses, then ratifying before them; the original defense of the split (that 'every other turn' in this negotiation is bounded by the same named-speaker formula) overstated the pattern, since 32:16 names no speaker at all and 32:29 repeats 32:20's formula without triggering a boundary. The split holds on sharper ground: contrast the Edom negotiation (20:18, 20:20), where both replies are plain וַיֹּאמֶר repeating the identical flat refusal with nothing new ratified -- correctly merged as one continuous exchange (M8-Num-136) inside one bounded Masoretic paragraph (setumah 20:13, petuchah 20:21). Here, by contrast, ch.32 runs unbroken from the petuchah at 32:19 to 32:42 with no comparable external corroboration, so the split rests entirely on 32:31's own verb, marking the tribes' binding ratification as a different legal act in kind from Edom's repeated refusal-refrain -- a distinction in what is done with speech, not merely that speech occurs.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.31 “As Yahweh has said to your servants, so will we do”

oshb:Num.32.31 וַיַּעֲנוּ בְנֵי גָד וּבְנֵי רְאוּבֵן לֵאמֹר אֵת אֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר יְהוָה אֶל עֲבָדֶיךָ כֵּן נַעֲשֶׂה (“the children of Gad and the children of Reuben answered, saying, ‘As Yahweh has said to your servants, so will we do’”)
oshb:Num.20.18 וַיֹּאמֶר אֵלָיו אֱדוֹם לֹא תַעֲבֹר בִּי (“Edom said to him, ‘you shall not pass through me’” — contrast: repeated plain refusal, no ratification, kept merged at M8-Num-136)

boundary_rationale: וַיִּתֵּן לָהֶם מֹשֶׁה ("Moses gave to them") opens the formal land grant to Gad, Reuben, and half of Manasseh, and the register of cities each tribe built and renamed closes this span before the Machir/Jair/Nobah clan-level notices begin.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through the Machir/Jair/Nobah conquests (vv.39-42) as one continuous "settlement" unit; but those notices concern individual clan leaders acting on their own initiative ("the children of Machir…went to Gilead, took it") rather than Moses' own formal grant and the tribes' own city-building already reported, a shift from official allotment to ad hoc clan conquest.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.33 “Moses gave to them…the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, and the kingdom of Og king of Bashan”
oshb:Num.32.38 וַיִּקְרְאוּ בְשֵׁמֹת אֶת שְׁמוֹת הֶעָרִים אֲשֶׁר בָּנוּ (“they gave other names to the cities which they built”)

boundary_rationale: Machir's own clan-level conquest of Gilead opens this decision, its plural subject and distinct verb sequence (וַיֵּלְכוּ...וַיִּלְכְּדֻהָ וַיּוֹרֶשׁ) unlike the Jair/Nobah naming template; it closes on Moses' own formal grant, וַיִּתֵּן מֹשֶׁה אֶת הַגִּלְעָד לְמָכִיר (v.40), the identical verb-plus-subject construction M8-Num-233 uses to define official Mosaic allotment (split per OL-M8-Num-234-1: the uniformity claim originally used to justify keeping all four verses together is false for 32:39, and v.40's grant language belongs with the official-allotment class, not the two ad hoc naming notices that follow).
strongest_rejected_alternative: All four verses (32:39-42) could stay one decision on the theory that all three notices share one template, the original reading; but only 32:41 and 32:42 actually share the personal-name-plus-הָלַךְ-וַיִּלְכֹּד-plus-naming template, while 32:39 has neither a singular named subject nor a naming clause, and 32:40's grant construction duplicates the criterion that defines the preceding span's own boundary, contradicting the uniformity claim this span was built on.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.39 “The children of Machir the son of Manasseh went to Gilead, took it”
web:Num.32.40 “Moses gave Gilead to Machir the son of Manasseh; and he lived therein”

boundary_rationale: Two matched clan-level notices close the chapter, each sharing the identical personal-name-plus-הָלַךְ-וַיִּלְכֹּד-plus-naming template: Jair's own villages renamed Havvoth Jair, and Nobah's Kenath renamed after his own name, distinct in construction from Machir's own conquest-and-grant notice that precedes them.
strongest_rejected_alternative: These two verses could stay merged with Machir's conquest and Moses' grant (32:39-40) as one undifferentiated closing register, the reading originally adopted for all four verses; but Machir's plural subject and Moses' own grant-verb construction (וַיִּתֵּן מֹשֶׁה, duplicating the criterion that defines the preceding span's own official-allotment boundary) are genuinely distinct from Jair's and Nobah's shared ad hoc naming template, and treating all four as one template was the inaccuracy the challenge identified.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.32.41 “Jair the son of Manasseh went and took its villages, and called them Havvoth Jair”
oshb:Num.32.42 וְנֹבַח הָלַךְ וַיִּלְכֹּד אֶת קְנָת וְאֶת בְּנֹתֶיהָ וַיִּקְרָא לָה נֹבַח בִּשְׁמוֹ (“Nobah went and took Kenath and its villages, and called it Nobah, after his own name”)

boundary_rationale: אֵלֶּה מַסְעֵי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ("these are the journeys of the children of Israel") opens the itinerary catalog with its own explicit authorship note -- Moses wrote the starting points by Yahweh's own command -- a superscription distinct in form from every travel notice that follows it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the departure notice that follows (vv.3-4) as one continuous opening; but its own self-referential authorship claim ("Moses wrote…these are their journeys according to their starting points") functions as a title for the whole register rather than the register's first entry.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.33.2 “Moses wrote the starting points of their journeys by the commandment of Yahweh”
oshb:Num.33.1 אֵלֶּה מַסְעֵי בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר יָצְאוּ מֵאֶרֶץ מִצְרַיִם לְצִבְאֹתָם (“these are the journeys of the children of Israel, when they went out of the land of Egypt”)

boundary_rationale: A dated narrative aside opens the register's first substantive content -- the fifteenth of the first month, the day after Passover, Egypt burying its firstborn while Yahweh executes judgment on its gods -- distinct from the bare ויסעו/ויחנו formula that structures every station notice from v.5 onward.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded directly into the station-by-station register that follows as its first entry; but its content is narrative commentary (Egyptian mourning, divine judgment on Egyptian gods) rather than the bare travel formula every subsequent entry uses, marking it as the register's own narrative frame rather than its first station.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.33.3 “on the next day after the Passover, the children of Israel went out with a high hand”
oshb:Num.33.4 וּבֵאלֹהֵיהֶם עָשָׂה יְהוָה שְׁפָטִים (“Yahweh also executed judgments on their gods”)

boundary_rationale: The register proper opens with the recurring formula וַיִּסְעוּ מִ...וַיַּחֲנוּ בְּ... ("they traveled from…and encamped at…"), repeated for every station from Rameses through Mount Hor with no narrative interruption; I read this whole thirty-three-verse run as one register rather than atomizing it per station, since each entry shares the identical two-verb formula and none introduces a new principle, only a new place name.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The task's own guidance warns against atomizing this catalog per station, but the opposite error -- reading all fifty-two verses of the whole itinerary (5-49) as one undivided register straight through Aaron's death -- would erase a real interruption; I split at v.37/38 specifically because the pure travel formula genuinely breaks there for a dated narrative aside (Aaron's death), then resumes unchanged afterward, so this first run ends where the formula itself stops, not at an arbitrary verse count.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.33.5 “The children of Israel traveled from Rameses, and encamped in Succoth”
oshb:Num.33.37 וַיִּסְעוּ מִקָּדֵשׁ וַיַּחֲנוּ בְּהֹר הָהָר בִּקְצֵה אֶרֶץ אֱדוֹם (“they traveled from Kadesh, and encamped in Mount Hor, in the edge of the land of Edom”)

boundary_rationale: The span 33:38-40 crosses the sole Masoretic paragraph mark reported in this stretch of the itinerary (a setumah after 33:39, per OL-M8-Num-238-1), binding Aaron's death notice to the Arad-king flashback as one interruption of the pure travel-formula register. 33:38 opens with וַיַּעַל אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן, a genuine motion verb ('went up') -- correcting the original claim that these verses 'contain no travel verb at all,' which was inexact -- though it is not the register's own recurring וַיִּסְעוּ/וַיַּחֲנוּ pair. 33:39 is a verbless summary closing the age-and-death notice, and 33:40 opens a fresh wayyiqtol with an entirely unrelated subject (the king of Arad), a real, checkable alternative seam independent of the setumah.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A seam at 33:39/33:40 -- splitting the Aaron notice itself from the Arad flashback -- is a genuine, text-supported alternative I tested and did not adopt: both verses share the same function of interrupting the travel-formula register with non-register content anchored at Mount Hor, and I read them as one coherent interruption unit rather than two further fragments, even though the setumah after 33:39 and the verbless-clause/new-subject shift both count as real, weighable evidence for the finer split. Per the instruction not to atomize this catalog, I hold the three verses together as the honest middle reading between treating the register as unbroken and cutting it at every available seam.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.33.38 “Aaron the priest went up into Mount Hor at the commandment of Yahweh and died there”
oshb:Num.33.40 וַיִּשְׁמַע הַכְּנַעֲנִי מֶלֶךְ עֲרָד…בְּבֹא בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל (“the Canaanite king of Arad…heard of the coming of the children of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: The pure travel formula resumes unchanged, וַיִּסְעוּ מֵהֹר הָהָר ("they traveled from Mount Hor"), continuing the register from where the Aaron interruption paused it, through to the final encampment in the plains of Moab -- the staging ground for the rest of the book -- again kept as one unsplit register consistent with the non-atomization reading applied to the first run.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could split this second run at any of its individual stations, matching a per-station reading someone might apply to the whole chapter; I reject that here for the same reason as the first run -- every entry is the identical two-verb formula with only the place name changing, and the chapter's own explicit instruction is to judge its internal structure honestly rather than atomize by station.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.33.48 “They traveled from the mountains of Abarim, and encamped in the plains of Moab”
oshb:Num.33.49 בְּעַרְבֹת מוֹאָב (“in the plains of Moab”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens a wholly distinct genre -- command, not itinerary -- instructing the conquest of Canaan, destruction of idols, and division of the land by lot, closed on the warning that failure to drive out the inhabitants will leave them as thorns and pricks.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as the itinerary register's own natural conclusion, since it follows immediately upon arrival in the plains of Moab; but the fresh messenger formula and the total shift from travel-notice form to imperative legal command mark a clean genre break, not a continuation of the ויסעו/ויחנו register.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.33.52 “you shall drive out all the inhabitants of the land from before you”
oshb:Num.33.56 כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּמִּיתִי לַעֲשׂוֹת לָהֶם אֶעֱשֶׂה לָכֶם (“as I thought to do to them, so I will do to you”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the land-boundary description with its own southern-quarter clause, וְהָיָה לָכֶם פְּאַת נֶגֶב ("and your south quarter shall be"), tracing the border from the wilderness of Zin to Azmon and the brook of Egypt, closed on that border's own terminus at the sea.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through the western border (v.6) as one continuous circuit; but v.6 opens its own fresh clause, וּגְבוּל יָם ("and for the western border"), a distinct compass-direction heading matching the pattern each subsequent side of the border uses to open its own description.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.34.3 “your south quarter shall be from the wilderness of Zin along by the side of Edom”
oshb:Num.34.5 וְהָיוּ תוֹצְאֹתָיו הַיָּמָּה (“and it shall end at the sea”)

boundary_rationale: וּגְבוּל יָם ("and for the western border") opens the shortest of the four border descriptions -- the Mediterranean coastline itself serves as the boundary, needing no further tracing -- closed within the same verse on its own naming formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Given its extreme brevity, this could be folded into either the southern border above or the northern border that follows; but its own fresh compass-direction opening clause is the same recurring formula marking every side of this border tour, and a one-verse entry is still a complete entry by that formula's own criterion.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.34.6 “you shall have the great sea and its border. This shall be your west border”
oshb:Num.34.6 זֶה יִהְיֶה לָכֶם גְּבוּל יָם (“this shall be your west border”)

boundary_rationale: וְזֶה יִהְיֶה לָכֶם גְּבוּל צָפוֹן ("and this shall be your north border") opens the third leg of the boundary tour, tracing from the great sea through Mount Hor to Hazar Enan, closed on its own naming formula matching the western border's close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the western border into one "west and north" span, since both are relatively short; but each carries its own fresh compass-heading clause and its own distinct list of way-points, the same criterion separating every other side of this border description.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.34.7 “This shall be your north border: from the great sea you shall mark out for yourselves Mount Hor”
oshb:Num.34.9 זֶה יִהְיֶה לָכֶם גְּבוּל צָפוֹן (“this shall be your north border”)

boundary_rationale: וְהִתְאַוִּיתֶם לָכֶם לִגְבוּל קֵדְמָה ("and you shall mark out your east border") opens the fourth and final leg, tracing from Hazar Enan down to the Jordan and the Salt Sea, closed on the whole boundary-tour's own summary colophon, זֹאת תִּהְיֶה לָכֶם הָאָרֶץ ("this shall be your land").
strongest_rejected_alternative: The closing colophon (v.12b) could be split off as its own decision, matching how other זֹאת colophons were treated elsewhere in this book; but here it is a single short clause immediately capping the fourth border's own description with no independent content, so I keep it bound to the eastern border it closes rather than elevating it to its own span.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.34.12 “The border shall go down to the Jordan, and end at the Salt Sea”
oshb:Num.34.12 זֹאת תִּהְיֶה לָכֶם הָאָרֶץ לִגְבֻלֹתֶיהָ סָבִיב (“this shall be your land according to its borders around it”)

boundary_rationale: Moses' own instruction, זֹאת הָאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר תִּתְנַחֲלוּ ("this is the land which you shall inherit"), pivots from Yahweh's border description to Moses' own reminder that nine and a half tribes receive this land while two and a half already hold their portion east of the Jordan.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the eastern-border description as its practical conclusion; but it opens with its own fresh speaker (Moses commanding the people directly, not Yahweh speaking to Moses) and shifts from geographic boundary-tracing to administrative distribution logic, a distinct instruction.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.34.14 “the tribe of the children of Reuben…the tribe of the children of Gad…and the half-tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance”
oshb:Num.34.15 מֵעֵבֶר לְיַרְדֵּן יְרֵחוֹ קֵדְמָה מִזְרָחָה (“beyond the Jordan at Jericho eastward, toward the sunrise”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the naming of the land-division commissioners -- Eleazar, Joshua, and one prince per tribe -- in the same one-name-per-tribe template used for the census witnesses of ch.1 and the spies of ch.13, closed on its own colophon identifying these as the men Yahweh commanded for the task.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Following the census-witness precedent, this twelve-name roster could be split at every entry; but as with those two earlier registers, every entry here shares the identical "of the tribe of X, name son of name" formula with no functional variation, so I keep the whole roster as one register rather than twelve near-duplicate decisions.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.34.18 “You shall take one prince of every tribe, to divide the land for inheritance”
oshb:Num.34.29 אֵלֶּה אֲשֶׁר צִוָּה יְהוָה לְנַחֵל אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּאֶרֶץ כְּנָעַן (“these are they whom Yahweh commanded to divide the inheritance to the children of Israel”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula opens the Levitical-cities instruction, צַו אֶת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְנָתְנוּ לַלְוִיִּם ("command the children of Israel to give to the Levites") -- the Levites' own promised compensation for holding no tribal land, per ch.18 -- closed on the general rule that the cities are for dwelling, the pasture lands for livestock.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be extended through the pasture-land measurements that follow (vv.4-5) as one continuous instruction; but the measurements are introduced by their own fresh clause specifying exact cubit counts, a level of technical detail distinct from this span's general policy statement.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.35.2 “Command the children of Israel to give to the Levites cities to dwell in out of their inheritance”
oshb:Num.35.3 וּמִגְרְשֵׁיהֶם יִהְיוּ לִבְהֶמְתָּם וְלִרְכֻשָׁם וּלְכֹל חַיָּתָם (“their pasture lands shall be for their livestock, and for their possessions, and for all their animals”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh technical clause opens the precise pasture-land measurements -- one thousand cubits from the city wall, then two thousand cubits per side -- a mathematical specification distinct in register from the general policy statement just given.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the general cities-command span as elaborating detail; but its own fresh measurement clause and its shift into precise cubit arithmetic (a genre this book uses sparingly, mostly for offering quantities) mark it as its own distinct technical specification.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.35.5 “you shall measure outside of the city for the east side two thousand cubits”

oshb:Num.35.4 וּמִגְרְשֵׁי הֶעָרִים אֲשֶׁר תִּתְּנוּ לַלְוִיִּם מִקִּיר הָעִיר וָחוּצָה אֶלֶף אַמָּה סָבִיב (“the pasture lands of the cities, which you shall give to the Levites, shall be from the wall of the city and outward one thousand cubits around it”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh clause opens the total accounting -- six refuge cities plus forty-two others, forty-eight in all -- closed on the proportional-contribution principle that larger tribal holdings give more cities, smaller holdings give fewer.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the cities-of-refuge purpose statement that follows (vv.9-15) as one continuous "Levitical and refuge cities" unit; but v.9 opens with its own fresh messenger formula reintroducing the topic specifically for the refuge cities' legal function, distinct from this span's numerical accounting.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.35.7 “All the cities…shall be forty-eight cities together with their pasture lands”
oshb:Num.35.8 אִישׁ כְּפִי נַחֲלָתוֹ אֲשֶׁר יִנְחָלוּ יִתֵּן מֵעָרָיו לַלְוִיִּם (“everyone according to his inheritance which he inherits shall give some of his cities to the Levites”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh messenger formula reopens specifically for the refuge cities' legal purpose, distinguishing them from the forty-eight Levitical cities just totaled -- protection for the unwitting manslayer from the avenger of blood -- closed on the inclusive clause covering native, stranger, and foreigner alike.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be read as simply restating the six-refuge-cities detail already given in v.6, folding it into that span; but the fresh messenger formula and the shift from a bare numerical total to a full statement of legal purpose and eligible fugitive class mark this as a distinct instruction opening the refuge-law material proper.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.35.11 “appoint for yourselves cities to be cities of refuge for you, that the man slayer who kills any person unwittingly may flee there”
oshb:Num.35.15 לָנוּס שָׁמָּה כָּל מַכֵּה נֶפֶשׁ בִּשְׁגָגָה (“that everyone who kills any person unwittingly may flee there”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh series of protases opens the deliberate-murder cases -- struck with iron, stone, or wood -- each closed on the identical מוֹת יוּמַת הָרֹצֵחַ ("the murderer shall surely be put to death") formula; I keep the whole weapon-varied series as one chunk because every case shares one identical apodosis and none introduces a new legal principle, only a new instrument.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Each weapon-type case (iron, stone, wood) could be split into its own decision, mirroring how offering-law material elsewhere in the Torah is sometimes split by object; but here, exactly as with Leviticus's eight-case capital-crime list kept as one chunk, splitting by weapon alone would multiply decisions at a point where the text itself marks no functional difference beyond the means of killing.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.35.16 “if he struck him with an instrument of iron, so that he died, he is a murderer”
oshb:Num.35.21 גֹּאֵל הַדָּם יָמִית אֶת הָרֹצֵחַ בְּפִגְעוֹ בוֹ (“the avenger of blood shall put the murderer to death when he meets him”)

boundary_rationale: A sharply contrastive protasis opens the accidental case, וְאִם בְּפֶתַע בְּלֹא אֵיבָה ("but if he shoved him suddenly without hostility"), the deliberate cases' own foil, closed on the congregation's duty to protect the manslayer in his city of refuge rather than hand him to the avenger.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be merged with the deliberate-murder register above as its concluding exception clause; but its own sharply contrastive וְאִם opening and its entirely opposite legal outcome (protection, not execution) mark a distinct case category, the same casuistic contrast device used to separate the unwitting-versus-high-handed sin cases in ch.15.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.35.22 “if he shoved him suddenly without hostility, or hurled on him anything without lying in wait”
oshb:Num.35.25 עַד מוֹת הַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדֹל אֲשֶׁר מָשַׁח אֹתוֹ בְּשֶׁמֶן הַקֹּדֶשׁ (“until the death of the high priest, who was anointed with the holy oil”)

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis narrows the case further -- what if the protected manslayer leaves his city of refuge's own boundary -- closed on the ruling that the avenger of blood incurs no guilt for killing him outside that boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: This could be folded into the accidental-manslaughter case above as its continuing elaboration; but it opens its own fresh protasis addressing a materially distinct scenario (violation of the refuge boundary, not the original killing itself), narrowing the general protection rule with a specific limiting case.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:Num.35.26 “if the man slayer shall at any time go beyond the border of his city of refuge”
oshb:Num.35.28 אַחֲרֵי מוֹת הַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדֹל יָשׁוּב הָרֹצֵחַ אֶל אֶרֶץ אֲחֻזָּתוֹ (“after the death of the high priest, the man slayer shall return into the land of his possession”)

boundary_rationale: The book opens on its dated, located superscription — 'These are the words which Moses spoke to all Israel' (אֵ֣לֶּה הַדְּבָרִ֗ים אֲשֶׁ֨ר דִּבֶּ֤ר מֹשֶׁה֙ אֶל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל) — but the record now has to reckon with 1:3, which the earlier draft passed over: a dated wayehi-formula (וַיְהִי֙ בְּאַרְבָּעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה) attached to its own clause of the same verb, this time addressed אֶל בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל rather than אֶל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל. I read v.3 as the superscription's own internal date-stamp rather than a second speech-act: v.1 states the general fact and full addressee, v.3 supplies the calendar date on which that speaking occurred, using the identical verb because it is dating the same act. v.4 supplies a second dating clause of the same kind (after striking Sihon and Og), and v.5's הוֹאִ֣יל מֹשֶׁ֔ה בֵּאֵ֛ר אֶת הַתּוֹרָ֥ה הַזֹּ֖את לֵאמֹֽר remains the hinge handing off to the first-person quotation opening v.6. Nothing across vv.1-5 shifts to first person or changes the entity being described; the whole stretch functions as one composite, dated superscription. No petuchah or setumah exists anywhere in ch.1 to arbitrate the question, so this reading rests on text signal alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The stronger competing reading, now stated rather than omitted: split 1:1-2 | 1:3-5, treating v.3's dated דִּבֶּ֤ר מֹשֶׁה֙ אֶל בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל as a second, independent speech-introduction parallel to v.1's, matching the granularity applied to the bare imperative cluster at 2:24 and the addressee-narrowing charge at 3:21. I subordinate it because both clauses remain third-person narration about the same act of Moses speaking to the same people on the same occasion — unlike 2:24 (a fresh imperative addressed to the people themselves) or 3:21 (a charge to a newly named individual) — but the case for treating v.3 as its own unit is real enough that a future pass could reasonably go the other way.

boundary_rationale: The doomed-attack scene at 1:41-46 runs in unbroken second-plural narration -- וַֽתַּעֲנ֣וּ וַתֹּאמְר֣וּ, וַתַּמְרוּ֙, וַתָּזִ֖דוּ, וַתַּעֲל֥וּ, וַתֵּשְׁב֥וּ -- closing with 'you dwelt in Kadesh many days' (וַתֵּשְׁב֥וּ בְקָדֵ֖שׁ יָמִ֣ים רַבִּ֑ים כַּיָּמִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר יְשַׁבְתֶּֽם). 2:1 restates the same duration phrase at its own close -- 'you circled Mount Seir many days' (וַנֵּ֜פֶן וַנִּסַּ֤ע הַמִּדְבָּ֨רָה֙ דֶּ֣רֶךְ יַם ס֔וּף כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר דִּבֶּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֵלָ֑י וַנָּ֥סָב אֶת הַר שֵׂעִ֖יר יָמִ֥ים רַבִּֽים) -- but both instances of יָמִים רַבִּים are verse-final, so the repetition is a catchword linking two successive stage-closes rather than an inclusio, which would require the phrase to frame a unit from one edge to the other; nothing here is bracketed. Crossing the seam this decision draws also crosses a real person shift: 1:41-46 addresses the audience in the second plural throughout, and 2:1 switches without remark to first-plural narration, וַנֵּ֜פֶן וַנִּסַּ֤ע ... וַנָּ֥סָב. That shift is disclosed here as counter-evidence rather than absorbed silently. The span is kept at 1:41-2:1 because the catchword still binds the two verses more tightly to each other than either binds to its own chapter-internal neighbors, and the first paragraph mark in the book -- a samekh -- falls only after 2:1, corroborating (not driving) that the wandering notice belongs together through the end of 2:1. Given a real person-shift running against a catchword repetition that is not the inclusio it was called, confidence is lowered from high to medium.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting at 1:46 and letting 2:1 open the next decision was reconsidered directly because of the 2mp/1cp shift: 1:41-46 never leaves the second plural, so a boundary drawn on person alone would fall exactly at 1:46|2:1. It is not adopted here because the catchword repetition of יָמִים רַבִּים and the samekh after 2:1 still bind 2:1 to 1:46 more strongly than 2:1 binds forward to 2:2's fresh divine-speech formula; but the alternative is close enough, and the person shift real enough, that the merge no longer supports high confidence.

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's self-declaration, 'I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt' (אָֽנֹכִי֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ אֲשֶׁ֧ר הוֹצֵאתִ֛יךָ מֵאֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרַ֖יִם מִבֵּ֥ית עֲבָדִֽים), is grammatically declarative — a predicate-nominal clause identifying the speaker — set against every command from v.7 onward, each an apodictic prohibition built on לֹא plus the imperfect. That mood contrast is a genuine register signal internal to the Hebrew, not the WEB paragraph break the original entry leaned on, which is inadmissible under this campaign's own rule. Disclosed honestly: the Masoretic tradition does not corroborate this cut — no mark falls after 5:6 or after 5:7, and the next samekh is two verses later, after 5:10, so MT positively binds 5:6-10 as one closed section, running against rather than for this isolate. Low confidence reflects that the register signal is real but stands against, not with, the paragraph tradition.
strongest_rejected_alternative: MT's own section division argues for merging v.6 forward into 5:6-10 as one unbroken unit closed by the samekh after v.10, treating the self-declaration as the Decalogue's shared preamble rather than a decision-sized unit of its own. I keep the isolate provisionally because the declarative-versus-apodictic mood shift is a real text-internal signal, admissible on its own terms, independent of any paragraph mark; but the case for merging is the stronger one on Masoretic grounds, and the low confidence rating is meant to say so.

boundary_rationale: 'You shall have no other gods before me' (לֹ֥א יִהְיֶ֥ה לְךָ֛ אֱלֹהִ֥ים אֲחֵרִ֖ים עַל פָּנָֽיַ) is kept as its own decision on the strength of the traditional Decalogue enumeration, not any signal internal to this verse or corroborated by the Masoretic paragraphing. Checked directly against v.8, the two prohibitions share identical syntax (לֹא + imperfect + לְךָ), which argues against, not for, a register break between them; and no pe or samekh falls anywhere between 5:6 and 5:10, so MT does not mark this join either. The isolate survives here only as a record of the reception-tradition convention of ten discrete commandments, disclosed as such rather than dressed up as a textual seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The stronger reading merges v.7 forward with v.8 (or further, to the samekh at 5:10), since both are unelaborated apodictic prohibitions bound by identical syntax and by the absence of any Masoretic mark between them. I keep the traditional one-command isolate only because the campaign's working unit here is tracking the received Decalogue enumeration, and I flag plainly that this is a convention being followed, not a boundary the Hebrew text or its paragraph tradition supplies.

boundary_rationale: Five commands run in series -- murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting -- bound together not by a uniform bare-לֹא register, which the text does not actually exhibit, but by a waw-coordination chain: only 5:17 is asyndetic (לֹ֖א תִּרְצָֽח); every command from 5:18 through 5:21 opens with וְלֹא, syntactically coordinating each new prohibition back to the series 5:17 begins, a feature of this Deuteronomic Decalogue not shared by the asyndetic Exodus recension. That coordination is a genuine text-internal signal for treating the five as one continuous unit rather than an artifact of formatting. Set against it, disclosed rather than suppressed: a samekh follows each of 5:17, 5:18, 5:19, 5:20 and 5:21 individually -- five section marks, one after every command in the series, with no doubled mark at 5:21 recorded in the two-witness file (oshb_count and uxlc_count both 135, no duplicate sites) -- converging with (though not driven by) WEB's own separate editorial paragraphing of the same five commands. This is not the densest cluster of paragraph marks in the book: the twelve-curse liturgy at 27:14-27:25 carries a samekh after every one of its twelve verses in succession, closed by a petuchah at 27:26, a longer and more strongly corroborated run than the five here. The coordination-chain reading is kept, but at low confidence, because the Masoretic tradition's own witness runs the other way at every internal seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A five-way split, one decision per command, is fully defensible and arguably better corroborated: each command carries its own setumah, and each is a distinct legal topic (murder is not theft). I do not adopt it because the waw-chain binding 18-21 back to 17 is a real syntactic feature the split would sever, treating five grammatically coordinated clauses as five independent sentences when the Hebrew does not read that way. Both readings have genuine textual support; this is recorded as the closest call in the block, resolved toward the merge only because the coordination is a positive text signal and not merely the absence of one.

Yahweh is one” (שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד), extending through the love-command and its household-transmission instructions (teaching children, hand, frontlets, doorposts), closing before a fresh warning-conditional opens v.10.

boundary_rationale: A fresh conditional opens on 'It shall be, when Yahweh your God brings you into the land' (וְהָיָ֞ה כִּ֥י יְבִיאֲךָ֣ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֗יךָ אֶל הָאָ֜רֶץ), the book's recurring prosperity-amnesia pattern, following directly on the samekh that closes the Shema unit at 6:9. The span now runs through the beware-lest-you-forget caution (v.12), the fear-and-serve command (v.13), and the jealous-God warning (v.15), closing on the samekh that falls at the end of 6:15 — one of a run of four section marks across this stretch of the chapter (6:9, 6:15, 6:19, 6:25) that the earlier 6:13 cut never engaged. Nothing marks a discourse turn at 6:13 itself: no vocative, no presentative, no fresh imperative-of-remembering, only a continuation of the same second-person warning chain 6:10 already opened. The real internal seam in this stretch sits one verse later, at the Massah prohibition opening 6:16 (see M8-Deut-043).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The original cut placed the boundary at 6:13, on the strength of a fronted-object construction treated as opening a fresh positive command. Checked against the samekh pattern across 6:9-25, that fronting is real but corresponds to no Masoretic division, while the samekh after 6:15 does; the fronted object reads more naturally as continuing the same warning-and-exhortation register that began at 6:10 (fear, serve, swear — all responses to the same forgetting-danger) than as opening independent content.

boundary_rationale: A fresh prohibition opens the unit, 'You shall not test Yahweh your God, as you tested him in Massah' (לֹ֣א תְנַסּ֔וּ אֶת יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵיכֶ֑ם כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר נִסִּיתֶ֖ם בַּמַּסָּֽה), naming a specific past failure by name — a fresh case, not a continuation of the fear-serve-swear exhortation that precedes it — and following directly on the samekh closing 6:15. It runs through the renewed command to keep the commandments diligently (v.17) and the do-what-is-right formula (v.18) to the dispossession promise closing v.19, where a further samekh corroborates the stop before the catechetical unit opens fresh at v.20.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The original span opened at 6:13 on the fear-and-serve command; I decline to keep that edge because nothing there marks a fresh turn, while 6:16's own named prohibition and the samekh at 6:15 both converge on a real seam one full sub-unit later. A full merge of 6:10-19, as one challenge proposed, is also defensible in that 6:13 alone cannot bear the weight of a boundary, but it overlooks the Masoretic section break that does exist at 6:15, one verse earlier than this span's new opening.

boundary_rationale: A scripted father-son catechesis opens on its own question formula, “When your son asks you in time to come, saying, What do the testimonies…mean?” (כִּי יִשְׁאָלְךָ בִנְךָ מָחָר לֵאמֹר), closing ch.6 on the “it shall be righteousness to us” formula before ch.7’s conquest-law address opens fresh.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could split the question (v.20) from the scripted answer (vv.21-25), but the answer is explicitly framed as direct speech Moses supplies for the parent to give (“then you shall tell your son”), one continuous scripted exchange rather than two independent units.

boundary_rationale: Ch.7 opens the conquest-law address proper on its own conditional, “When Yahweh your God brings you into the land…and casts out many nations before you” (כִּי יְבִיאֲךָ יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֶל הָאָרֶץ…וְנָשַׁל גּוֹיִם רַבִּים מִפָּנֶיךָ), naming the seven nations and the herem, no-covenant, no-intermarriage rules, closing on the holy-people rationale before a shift to election theology opens v.7.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could keep vv.1-11 as one election-and-herem unit, but v.7’s “Yahweh didn’t set his love on you…because you were more in number” pivots from concrete prohibitions to abstract theological argument about the ground of election, a real shift in mode.

boundary_rationale: The argument turns explicitly abstract at v.7, 'Yahweh didn't set his love on you nor choose you, because you were more in number...but because Yahweh loves you' (לֹ֣א מֵֽרֻבְּכֶ֞ם...כִּ֚י מֵֽאַהֲבַ֤ת יְהוָה֙ אֶתְכֶ֔ם), grounding obedience in love and oath rather than merit. The verse echoes 7:6's closing verb (בָּחַר, 'chose') but is its own main clause with its own subject and predicate, a rhetorical hinge picking up a word, not a grammatical continuation of the prior sentence. Both edges of this decision carry Masoretic support: a samekh closes 7:6 immediately before this span begins, and a petuchah — the heaviest class of division Torah paragraphing offers — closes 7:11 exactly at the span's end, closing on the 'keep the covenant' formula before the blessing catalog opens v.12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The root repetition invites reading v.7 as a clarification hanging directly off v.6's election claim, in which case 045 and 046 should merge into one span, Deut.7.1-7.11. I decline: v.7 has its own finite verbs and its own subject, launching a fresh not-X-but-Y argument in a different rhetorical register from the concrete herem instructions of vv.1-6, and the petuchah at 7:11 independently confirms that MT itself treats the material ending there as a closed section, distinct from the case-law list before it.

You are to pass over the Jordan today” (שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל אַתָּה עֹבֵר הַיּוֹם אֶת הַיַּרְדֵּן), the Anakim reassurance closing on “as Yahweh has spoken” before the warning against self-righteous interpretation opens v.4.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might keep the whole golden-calf episode (vv.7-21) as one long narrative block, but v.11’s “It came to pass at the end of forty days and forty nights” opens a fresh temporal clause marking the narrative’s next beat (the actual calf report), distinguishing setup from event.

boundary_rationale: A fresh temporal clause opens the unit, “It came to pass at the end of forty days and forty nights” (וַיְהִי מִקֵּץ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם וְאַרְבָּעִים לָיְלָה), reporting Yahweh’s command to descend and his threat to destroy the people, closing before Moses’s own descent narrative opens with “So I turned and came down” in v.15.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could merge this report with Moses’s descent that follows as one continuous calf episode, but v.15’s shift to first-person action (“So I turned and came down from the mountain”) marks Moses resuming his own narrated action after reporting Yahweh’s speech to him.

boundary_rationale: A fresh place-name catalog opens on “At Taberah, at Massah, and at Kibroth Hattaavah you provoked Yahweh to wrath” (וּבְתַבְעֵרָה וּבְמַסָּה וּבְקִבְרֹת הַתַּאֲוָה מַקְצִפִים הֱיִיתֶם אֶת יְהוָה), adding the Kadesh Barnea rebellion, closing on the summary “rebellious…from the day I knew you” before Moses’s own prayer text opens v.25.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could fold this brief catalog into the preceding calf narrative as further evidence of rebellion, but it shifts from narrated event to a bare place-name list with no scene of its own, a distinct rhetorical device (cumulative indictment) from the narrative that precedes it.

boundary_rationale: The unit opens on a resumptive verb, 'So I fell down before Yahweh the forty days and forty nights' (וָֽאֶתְנַפַּ֞ל לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֗ה אֵ֣ת אַרְבָּעִ֥ים הַיּ֛וֹם וְאֶת אַרְבָּעִ֥ים הַלַּ֖יְלָה), explicitly re-narrating the prostration first reported at 9:18 (וָֽאֶתְנַפַּל֩ לִפְנֵ֨י יְהוָ֜ה כָּרִאשֹׁנָ֗ה) with its own matching duration phrase, and closing the cumulative-indictment catalogue of 9:22-24 that immediately precedes it. The quoted prayer text itself does not begin until v.26's own speech-onset clause, וָאֶתְפַּלֵּ֣ל אֶל יְהוָה֮ וָאֹמַר֒; v.25 is still first-person narration of posture, not the prayer, so the span's opening edge is a resumptive re-narration, not a shift out of third-person narrative — there is no third-person narration anywhere in this chapter to shift out of. The unit closes ch.9 on the covenant-inheritance appeal, corroborated by a petuchah landing exactly at the end of v.29.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One might read vv.15-29 as one continuous intercession scene with no internal seam, since the posture-and-prayer material is thematically unbroken; I decline because v.25's resumptive וָאֶתְנַפַּל and its matching forty-day phrase deliberately echo v.18 to mark a fresh telling — the narrative circles back to re-narrate the prostration before quoting the prayer that accompanied it, a real structural restart even without a change in grammatical person.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might treat this as continuous with the surrounding ark narrative since Levi’s ark-bearing role connects them thematically, but the shift to third-person plural subject (“the children of Israel traveled”) breaks the first-person “I” voice used throughout the rest of chs.9-10, a real grammatical seam WEB itself marks with parentheses.

boundary_rationale: The climactic summary exhortation opens on its own rhetorical question, 'Now, Israel, what does Yahweh your God require of you' (וְעַתָּה֙ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל מָ֚ה יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ שֹׁאֵ֖ל מֵעִמָּ֑ךְ כִּ֣י אִם לְ֠יִרְאָה אֶת יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֜יךָ לָלֶ֤כֶת בְּכָל דְּרָכָיו֙ וּלְאַהֲבָ֣ה אֹת֔וֹ וְלַֽעֲבֹד֙ אֶת יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ֖ וּבְכָל נַפְשֶֽׁךָ), following directly on the petuchah at 10:11, and moves through God's supremacy, impartial justice, and love for the foreigner to a closing infinitive series in 10:12-13 (לִשְׁמֹ֞ר אֶת מִצְוֺ֤ת יְהוָה֙ וְאֶת חֻקֹּתָ֔יו אֲשֶׁ֛ר אָנֹכִ֥י מְצַוְּךָ֖ הַיּ֑וֹם לְט֖וֹב לָֽךְ) that 11:1's weqatal pair directly resumes: 'You shall love Yahweh your God, and keep his instructions' (וְאָ֣הַבְתָּ֔ אֵ֖ת יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֑יךָ וְשָׁמַרְתָּ֣ מִשְׁמַרְתּ֗וֹ וְחֻקֹּתָ֧יו וּמִשְׁפָּטָ֛יו וּמִצְוֺתָ֖יו כָּל הַיָּמִֽים) is the finite verb answering the infinitives just given, not a fresh address. The span now closes at 11:1, immediately before 11:2 opens a plural retrospective recital, 'you have known this day... your eyes have seen' (וִֽידַעְתֶּם֮ הַיּוֹם֒ ... ; כִּ֤י עֵֽינֵיכֶם֙ הָֽרֹאֹ֔ת אֶת כָּל מַעֲשֵׂ֥ה יְהוָ֖ה הַגָּדֹ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֖ר עָשָֽׂה) -- a shift in content, from second-singular exhortation to a plural generation-facing recital of the wilderness deeds, not the plural marking by itself. Person and number shift on their own do not discriminate this seam from two others inside the very span this decision draws: 10:15 is singular (רַ֧ק בַּאֲבֹתֶ֛יךָ חָשַׁ֥ק יְהוָ֖ה לְאַהֲבָ֣ה אוֹתָ֑ם וַיִּבְחַ֞ר בְּזַרְעָ֣ם אַחֲרֵיהֶ֗ם בָּכֶ֛ם מִכָּל הָעַמִּ֖ים כַּיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּה) and 10:16 turns plural (וּמַלְתֶּ֕ם אֵ֖ת עָרְלַ֣ת לְבַבְכֶ֑ם וְעָ֨רְפְּכֶ֔ם לֹ֥א תַקְשׁ֖וּ עֽוֹד), and 10:19 is plural (וַאֲהַבְתֶּ֖ם אֶת הַגֵּ֑ר כִּֽי גֵרִ֥ים הֱיִיתֶ֖ם בְּאֶ֥רֶץ מִצְרָֽיִם) while 10:20 returns to singular (אֶת יְהוָ֧ה אֱלֹהֶ֛יךָ תִּירָ֖א אֹת֣וֹ תַעֲבֹ֑ד וּב֣וֹ תִדְבָּ֔ק וּבִשְׁמ֖וֹ תִּשָּׁבֵֽעַ), and neither internal alternation is treated as a seam. What distinguishes 11:1|11:2 from those two is that the shift there coincides with a change of discourse mode -- exhortation giving way to retrospective recital addressed to a new audience horizon ('not your children, who have not known and have not seen') -- while the internal shifts at 10:15|16 and 10:19|20 are register variation within one continuous exhortation, not a change of what is being done with the discourse. No Masoretic mark falls anywhere inside this stretch -- the petuchah at 10:11 and the samekh at 11:9 bracket the whole of 10:12-11:9 without an internal break -- so this internal close rests on the content-and-discourse-mode turn, honestly disclosed as unmarked and as co-occurring with, but not reducible to, a person shift that recurs elsewhere in the span without effect.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The chapter line at 10:22|11:1 offers a tempting stopping point, and the earlier draft asserted a new address opens there; checked against the Hebrew, nothing supports it -- 11:1 is second-singular throughout, continuing 10:12-13's own infinitive series rather than opening independent content, and the real new movement doesn't arrive until 11:2's plural retrospective recital, וִידַעְתֶּם; that number shift co-occurs with the discourse-mode turn to recital rather than causing it, since the same kind of shift recurs unremarked at 10:15|16 and 10:19|20 without marking anything. The chapter number was doing work the grammar does not.

boundary_rationale: The retrospective proper opens on a plural verb marking a real address shift, 'And you shall know today...that it was not your children (who have not known...)' (וִֽידַעְתֶּם֮ הַיּוֹם֒ כִּ֣י לֹ֣א אֶת בְּנֵיכֶ֗ם), switching from 11:1's second-singular continuation of 10:12-13's infinitive series into second-plural address that holds through the Exodus-wonders catalogue and the Dathan-and-Abiram episode, closing on 'your eyes have seen' (v.7) before a fresh imperative to keep the entire commandment opens v.8. No Masoretic mark exists at the 11:1|11:2 join itself; the petuchah after 10:11 and the samekh after 11:9 bracket this whole stretch without an internal break, so the boundary rests on the person-and-number shift alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could keep 11:1 as this unit's opener, reading the whole of 10:12-11:7 as one address; I decline because 11:1's verbs remain second-singular, directly continuing 10:12-13's own infinitive series (an antecedent 11:1's finite verb resumes rather than a fresh command), while the retrospective's own plural marker, וִידַעְתֶּם, does not arrive until v.2 — the true address shift, and the more defensible opening edge.

strongest_rejected_alternative: This land-contrast could be merged with the conditional rain promise that follows as one agricultural argument; instead, v.13’s “It shall happen, if you shall listen diligently” opens a fresh formal conditional (protasis-apodosis) distinct from the descriptive contrast that precedes it.

strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could treat this refrain as inseparable from the surrounding rain conditional as one continuous exhortation, but its close verbal match to the distinct 6:6-9 unit shows it functions as the book’s own recurring formula, deserving the same boundary treatment given there.

boundary_rationale: A fresh diligent-keeping conditional opens on “For if you shall diligently keep all these commandments…then Yahweh will drive out all these nations” (כִּי אִם שָׁמֹר תִּשְׁמְרוּן אֶת כָּל הַמִּצְוָה הַזֹּאת…וְהוֹרִישׁ יְהוָה), promising total dispossession and universal dread, closing before the blessing-and-curse formula opens v.26.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this with the closing blessing-and-curse unit as one continuous promise is defensible on paper, yet v.26’s “Behold, I set before you today a blessing and a curse” opens a fresh, formally distinct declaration (a binary choice formula) rather than continuing the total-dispossession promise’s own logic.

boundary_rationale: The binary-choice formula opens the unit, 'Behold, I set before you today a blessing and a curse' (רְאֵ֗ה אָנֹכִ֛י נֹתֵ֥ן לִפְנֵיכֶ֖ם הַיּ֑וֹם בְּרָכָ֖ה וּקְלָלָֽה), stating the terms of blessing (obedience) and curse (turning aside after other gods) in vv.27-28, and closing on a setumah that falls at the end of 11:28 — corroboration the original span never engaged. Splitting the deposition of that blessing and curse onto specific mountains (vv.29-32) into its own decision honors both the Masoretic section mark and the fresh protasis that opens it (see the new sibling decision).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The whole of 11:26-32 reads smoothly as one instruction — declare the choice, then say where to enact it — and could be kept merged on that thematic continuity alone, which is what the original entry did. I now reject that reading because a setumah, not merely its absence, sits at the exact seam being crossed, and 11:29's opening formula matches a pattern this campaign already credits as unit-opening elsewhere in the same chapter; treating the formula one way at 11:13 and another way here was the inconsistency the challenge correctly named.

boundary_rationale: A fresh protasis opens the unit, 'It shall be, when Yahweh your God brings you into the land that you are going in to possess it' (וְהָיָ֗ה כִּ֤י יְבִֽיאֲךָ֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֶ֔יךָ אֶל הָאָ֕רֶץ), the same וְהָיָה כִּי/אִם formula this campaign already treats as unit-opening at 11:13, here directing where the blessing and curse just declared (11:26-28) are to be deposited — on Gerizim and Ebal — before a closing geographic aside and the charge to observe all the statutes that bridges into the law code's own heading at 12:1. A setumah closes 11:28 immediately before this span begins, corroborating the split from the preceding decision.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One could read this material as inseparable from the blessing-curse declaration it enacts, one continuous instruction from proclamation to deposition; I split it instead because the setumah after 11:28 marks a real Masoretic division at exactly this seam, and the fresh וְהָיָה כִּי protasis matches a construction this campaign elsewhere credits as unit-opening, so treating it as subordinate here alone would be an inconsistent application of the same rule.

boundary_rationale: A fresh warning opens on 'When Yahweh your God cuts off the nations...be careful that you...not inquire after their gods' (כִּֽי יַכְרִית֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֜יךָ אֶת הַגּוֹיִ֗ם...הִשָּׁ֣מֶר לְךָ֔ פֶּן תִּנָּקֵ֖שׁ), closing the centralization laws on the canon formula, WEB 12:32 = MT 13:1: 'this word which I command you, that you shall observe to do — you shall not add to it, nor take away from it' (אֵ֣ת כָּל הַדָּבָ֗ר אֲשֶׁ֤ר אָנֹכִי֙ מְצַוֶּ֣ה אֶתְכֶ֔ם אֹת֥וֹ תִשְׁמְר֖וּ לַעֲשׂ֑וֹת לֹא תֹסֵ֣ף עָלָ֔יו וְלֹ֥א תִגְרַ֖ע מִמֶּֽנּוּ). A petuchah — the strongest class of Masoretic division — sits at the end of this verse (MT 13:1), with nothing marked anywhere between the setumah closing 12:28 and that petuchah, so the manuscript tradition delimits exactly this stretch, MT 12:29-13:1, as one closed section. The שְׁמֹר...אֵת כָּל...אֲשֶׁ֥ר אָנֹכִ֖י מְצַוֶּ֑ךָּ frame that closes 12:28 recurs almost verbatim to close 13:1 — a doubled closing device, not an opening one — and הַדָּבָר's definiteness here is grammatically identical to its use at 4:2 (לֹ֣א תֹסִ֗פוּ עַל הַדָּבָר֙ אֲשֶׁ֤ר אָנֹכִי֙ מְצַוֶּ֣ה אֶתְכֶ֔ם), where the reference is unmistakably forward (cataphoric) rather than backward: the noun is made definite by its own relative clause in both places, not by pointing at what precedes. The one real counter-signal is a Numeruswechsel across the seam — 12:28-31 stays second-singular throughout (הִשָּׁמֶר לְךָ, תִּנָּקֵשׁ, תִּדְרֹשׁ, תַּעֲשֶׂה), MT 13:1 opens plural (אֶתְכֶם, תִשְׁמְרוּ) and closes singular (תֹסֵף, תִגְרַע), and MT 13:2 is singular again — logged here as live evidence, weighed against, and outweighed by, the petuchah and the doubled closing frame. Confidence moves from low to medium on the strength of this corrected and better-corroborated ground.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The chapter division itself, and MT's own placement of 13:1 as the first verse of ch.13, invite reading the canon formula as the false-prophet law's own opening line rather than the centralization law's close. Checked directly, that reading requires the article on הַדָּבָר to point backward to the legislative complex just given; the identical construction at 4:2 shows the same definite-by-relative-clause pattern pointing forward instead, which removes that reading's main textual support. The Numeruswechsel is the one piece of evidence still favoring a fresh opening at MT 13:1 or 13:2, and it is disclosed rather than dismissed, but it stands alone against a petuchah and a repeated closing formula.

boundary_rationale: A bare general prohibition, 'You shall not eat any abominable thing' (לֹ֥א תֹאכַ֖ל כָּל תּוֹעֵבָֽה), functions as the heading for the dietary register that follows, distinct in scope from the specific land-animal criteria that open their own clause in v.4. It follows directly on a setumah that closes v.2 — the identity-and-holiness rationale ('for you are a holy people to Yahweh your God') — disclosed here as corroboration for treating v.3 as its own unit rather than folding backward into the holiness preamble.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The stronger-looking alternative merges vv.1-3 as one holiness-grounded preamble sharing a single theological ground; tested directly against the Masoretic apparatus, that reading has to explain away a setumah that falls after v.2, not after v.3 — the manuscript's own division sits at the seam this decision already uses, not at the one the backward merge would need. v.3 also lacks any grammatically marked heading of its own (no אֵלֶּה-colophon comparable to 12:1, contra the earlier record's precedent claim), so it reads better as a bare, general transitional prohibition than as the third clause of a three-verse preamble.

boundary_rationale: The bird register opens and closes on a variational inclusio, not a verbatim one: 'Of all clean birds you may eat' (כָּל צִפּ֥וֹר טְהֹרָ֖ה תֹּאכֵֽלוּ, v.11) is echoed rather than repeated at the close, 'Of all clean fowl you may eat' (כָּל ע֥וֹף טָה֖וֹר תֹּאכֵֽלוּ, v.20) — a different noun (צִפּוֹר, feminine, versus עוֹף, masculine) and a different adjective, sharing only the frame's syntax (כָּל + adjective + תֹּאכֵלוּ) and its permission-formula sense. That framing device still brackets the named unclean-bird catalogue and the winged-insect rider between two structurally matching openers, a real literary unit even though the wording is not identical. The petuchah nearest this stretch falls after v.21, one verse past this span's close, so it corroborates the following decision's opening rather than this one's; the close at v.20 rests on the frame alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer might split the unclean-bird list (vv.12-18) from its winged-insect rider (v.19) as two decisions; v.19 remains bound to the same variational frame the whole register shares, and its own vocabulary (שֶׁרֶץ הָעוֹף) plausibly feeds v.20's עוֹף more directly than v.11's צִפּוֹר does, so it stays inside the one closed register rather than becoming a separate case.

boundary_rationale: Verse 21 closes the dietary code with two prohibitions that share no vocabulary: the carrion clause, governing a self-dead animal (נְבֵלָה) that may be given to the foreigner within one's gates or sold to a foreigner, and the kid-in-milk clause, which opens its own fresh לֹא + verb with no term in common with the first -- לֹֽא תְבַשֵּׁ֥ל גְּדִ֖י בַּחֲלֵ֥ב אִמּֽוֹ, 'you shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk.' That lexical break is real, but it falls within a single verse with no intervening verse number, so it does not itself force a split, and it is not evidence for either edge of this decision. The closing edge is well made: a petuchah -- the strongest divider the two-witness apparatus carries -- stands after 14:21 itself, closing the whole clean-food code before v.22 opens the tithe law on its own topic (עַשֵּׂ֣ר תְּעַשֵּׂ֔ר, 'you shall surely tithe'). The opening edge at 14:20|21 needs its own ground, since no pe or samekh site exists at Deut.14.20 in the two-witness file and a mark at the far edge cannot supply evidence for the near one under mesh-r2, where markers corroborate rather than drive. That ground is a polarity flip on the same root: 14:20 grants permission with a positive verb, כָּל ע֥וֹף טָה֖וֹר תֹּאכֵֽלוּ ('every clean bird you may eat'), and 14:21 reverses polarity on the same root, לֹ֣א תֹאכְל֣וּ כָל נְ֠בֵלָה ('you shall not eat any carrion'), while also leaving the winged-creature taxonomy of vv.11-20 for carrion of any kind. With the opening edge carrying a genuine text signal but no marker at all, and the closing edge carrying both marker and topic-turn, confidence is capped at medium rather than high.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A reviewer could split the carrion clause from the kid-in-milk clause as two decisions since they address unrelated practices, but both remain within the single verse 21 with no intervening verse number, so I keep them as one minimal unit while flagging the internal seam.
