boundary_rationale: The notice 'The word of Samuel came to all Israel' (4:1a) is read here as a hinge before the narrative pivots hard to a fresh military scene at Ebenezer and Aphek, closing on the first defeat's casualty count -- that rear edge (4:2's casualty count against 4:3's elders-in-camp deliberation) remains solid and uncontested. But the front edge is genuinely unsettled: 4:1a shares the devar root with 3:19 and 3:21 in close range, and WEB's own paragraph metadata splits 4:1 internally, grouping the devar-clause with the chapter-3 summary rather than with the battle report that follows in 4:1b -- yet 4:1a is joined to 4:1b by a plain wayyiqtol chain (vayehi...vayetze) with no disjunctive marker, which pulls the other way. This decision discloses the alternative (4:1a closing M8-1Sam-018's summary rather than opening this battle unit) as live and unresolved rather than settled, and confidence is lowered accordingly.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching this pair to the following council scene was considered since both concern the same battle, but the elders' deliberation in vv.3-4 is a distinct scene located 'in the camp' after the army has already regrouped from the field defeat just narrated. Separately, and not fully resolved: reading 4:1a as the capstone of the prophetic-establishment summary (3:19-4:1a) rather than as this unit's opening hinge, on the strength of the shared devar root and WEB's mid-verse paragraph break, remains a live, undecided alternative -- see M8-1Sam-018.

boundary_rationale: The elders' rhetorical question and resulting decision to fetch the ark from Shiloh (4:3) forms a short deliberation scene that closes with the ark's dispatch and removal from Shiloh, and the notice that Eli's two sons were there with it (4:4: vayishlach ha'am Shiloh vayis'u misham et aron...vesham shenei venei Eli). The unit closes on this removal-from-Shiloh notice, not on an arrival at the camp -- the ark's arrival at the camp is narrated only in the next verse (4:5, vayehi kevo aron...el hammachaneh), which belongs to a separate unit. The real closing signal is the shift in narrative vantage from the dispatching party (Shiloh) to the camp about to receive the ark. WEB opens a paragraph at 4:4, grouping 4:3 with the preceding battle report rather than with this unit -- an untested alternative front edge worth noting even though the elders' single deliberation (question-and-decision) still reads most naturally as one unit with its own dispatch.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this through the ark's arrival shout (v.5) was considered, but the elders' speech-and-decision unit is complete once the ark is dispatched from Shiloh, and v.5 opens a new beat with a change of vantage to the camp's reception of the ark, distinct from the dispatch decision itself. Splitting at 4:3|4:4 to follow WEB's paragraph start at 4:4 is a live untested alternative, but the elders' single continuous deliberation (question in 4:3, decision-and-dispatch in 4:4) argues against fragmenting it.

boundary_rationale: The ark's arrival triggers Israel's shout, the Philistines' fearful recognition speech, and their mutual rallying cry ('Be strong and behave like men'), a self-contained speech-then-battle unit that ends just before the fighting itself resumes.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the rallying speech into the battle report that follows was rejected because the exhortation is explicitly a preparatory speech act, distinct from the report of engagement and casualties that opens v.10.

boundary_rationale: Following the rallying speech, the battle report proper begins ('The Philistines fought, and Israel was defeated') and closes on the capture of the ark and the death of Hophni and Phinehas, the two facts the rest of the chapter unpacks through the messenger scene.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Including the messenger's arrival at Shiloh in this same span was considered, but a new participant (the Benjamite runner) and a new location (Shiloh) open at v.12, marking a clean scene change.

boundary_rationale: A new participant enters ('A man of Benjamin ran out of the army') and a new location (Shiloh, Eli seated by the road) opens a self-contained messenger type-scene that builds through Eli's repeated questioning to the report itself and closes on Eli's death from his seat - a complete arc with independently marked entry and exit points.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the messenger's arrival (vv.12-14) from his actual report and Eli's death (vv.15-18) was considered, but the questioning and the answer are one sustained suspense-building exchange between the same two participants without a scene break.

boundary_rationale: A new participant (Phinehas's pregnant wife) and a new focus - her labor and death, and the naming of Ichabod - close the chapter on an etiological naming formula repeated twice ('The glory has departed from Israel'), a doubled closural device marking the unit's end clearly.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating v.22's repetition of the naming explanation as a separate coda span was considered, but it is a narratorial doubling of the same etiology already given in v.21, not a fresh unit with its own participants or setting.

boundary_rationale: The ark's arrival at Ashdod opens a new location and set of participants (the Philistines, Dagon), moving through the idol's double collapse and the etiological note about priests not stepping on the threshold 'to this day,' then closing on the plague notice that motivates the city's next move.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the two Dagon-falling episodes (vv.3-4) from the etiology and plague (vv.5-6) was considered, but the second collapse and the threshold custom are presented as one continuous cause-and-effect report before the affliction proper begins.

boundary_rationale: Ashdod's men convene and decide to relocate the ark to Gath, and the unit tracks the plague recurring there - a second stop in what functions as a register of city-by-city affliction rather than one static description, closing before Ekron's turn begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the council decision (v.7-8a) as its own unit apart from the Gath outcome (v.8b-9) was considered, but the decision and its immediate consequence at the new city are reported in one unbroken sentence-chain with no scene reset in between.

boundary_rationale: The ark's move to Ekron completes the three-city tour with the same relocate-then-afflict pattern as Ashdod and Gath, but here the Ekronites' own outcry opens the unit before the lords' assembly and the panic that closes the chapter, forming a register of episodes with cumulative narrative escalation rather than a bare list.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the span into chapter 6's opening deliberation was considered on the grounds that both concern what to do with the ark, but 6:1's 'seven months' notice is an explicit temporal jump that closes off the immediate three-city sequence.

boundary_rationale: A summary time-marker ('Yahweh's ark was in the country of the Philistines seven months.') is a self-contained duration notice, off the narrative action chain, opening a new phase distinct from the city-by-city plague episodes of chapter 5. It stands alone rather than running through the Philistines' consultation of their priests and diviners: 6:2's question (mah naaseh la'aron YHWH) is answered immediately and without any intervening pause by 6:3 (vayomeru im meshallechim), so 6:2 cannot be severed from 6:3 under the turn-marker principle and belongs with the consultation unit rather than with this duration notice. WEB opens a paragraph at 6:1.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this notice together with the Philistines' consultation (through 6:2 or further) was considered, since both concern the ark's disposition, but 6:2's question is answered without pause by 6:3 in the same breath, so keeping 6:2 attached to this one-verse durative notice would either orphan the question from its answer or manufacture a seam ('scene-internal pause') that the Hebrew does not contain.

boundary_rationale: The Philistines summon their priests and diviners and ask what to do with Yahweh's ark (6:2); the priests answer without any intervening pause (6:3, im meshallechim), opening one continuous consultation exchange with internal turn-taking that runs through the trespass-offering instruction, the Egypt/Pharaoh warning, and the diagnostic experimental design (new cart, unyoked cows, calves shut away), closing on 'it was a chance that happened to us' (6:9). This merges the formerly separate M8-1Sam-029 (6:3-6:6) and M8-1Sam-030 (6:7-6:9), and additionally draws 6:2 in from the old M8-1Sam-028: 6:2's question and 6:3's answer are one dialogue turn under the turn-marker principle and cannot be split. A second such turn occurs at 6:4, which itself contains two vayyomru frames - the Philistines' own question, mah ha'asham asher nashiv lo ('What should the trespass offering be which we shall return to him?'), answered by the priests' reply, mispar sarnei Pelishtim ('Five golden tumors and five golden mice, for the number of the lords of the Philistines...') - a genuine speaker exchange, but under the same turn-marker principle it is an internal Q&A turn inside one uninterrupted consultation scene, not a unit boundary: the same two parties remain in view, no relocation occurs, and the priests' answer at 6:4 continues directly into the same instruction that runs through 6:9. Likewise 6:7's ve'attah ('and now') is a discourse-internal pivot inside the still-running speech begun at 6:4b, not a new utterance - WEB's re-opened quotation mark at 6:7 is a typographic convention for continued direct speech, not evidence of a fresh speech act. The unit's front edge is the durative-to-action shift from the preceding 6:1 notice; its rear edge is genuinely strong - 6:10 turns to vaya'asu ha'anashim ken, a wayyiqtol with an explicit subject supplying both a compliance formula and a participant refocus.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the trespass-offering instruction from the Egypt warning, or the theological warning from the concrete cart-and-cows procedure, was considered, but all of it is one uninterrupted consultation by the same speakers answering the same question. Internal turn-taking occurs at 6:4, where the Philistines' question and the priests' answer form a genuine Q&A exchange, but this turn does not reset the scene or relocate either party, and is not itself promoted to a unit boundary under the turn-marker principle; the only genuine reset in the neighborhood is 6:10's compliance formula. The remaining internal markers (WEB paragraph starts at 6:3 and 6:7) are likewise turn-markers and pivot particles, not scene seams, and cannot be promoted to boundaries on their own.

boundary_rationale: The instructions are executed exactly as given, and the unit narrates the test's result - the cows going straight to Beth Shemesh without turning - which functions as the procedure's verdict before the human reception scene begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Including the Beth Shemesh reapers' sighting of the ark (v.13) in this span was considered, but that verse introduces a wholly new set of participants and a new location's vantage point rather than continuing the cart's own journey.

boundary_rationale: The Beth Shemesh reapers see the ark, the cart stops at the great stone, and the Levites offer sacrifice - a self-contained reception scene that closes before the narrative's attention shifts specifically to the watching Philistine lords in v.16.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Combining this with the lords' departure notice (v.16) was rejected because that verse changes the observing subject from the townspeople to 'the five lords of the Philistines,' a participant-focus shift worth its own short unit.

boundary_rationale: This single verse (vachamishah sarnei Pelishtim ra'u vayashuvu Eqron bayom hahu) is a disjunctive waw-plus-subject-plus-qatal construction that steps aside from the Beth Shemesh townspeople's action to close out the Philistine side of the ark's return, shifting vantage from the townspeople to the departing observers. The lords have in fact been on stage continuously through the cart sequence (named at 6:4 in the counsel, and again as the explicit subject of a disjunctive clause at 6:12 following the cart to the border of Beth Shemesh), so this is not a reappearance after an absence but the resolution of a role they have held since 6:12; the isolation rests on the verse's own clause type and on the enumerative formula that opens 6:17 (an itemized list of golden objects), not on any participant gap. A samekh sited after 6:16 gives weak corroboration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this verse into the reception scene before it was considered, but the lords' return to Ekron is marked by its own disjunctive construction distinct from the wayyiqtol narration of the Beth Shemesh townspeople's reaction, and the shift of vantage to the departing observers -- not any gap in their appearance, since they have been on stage since 6:12 -- is what sets this verse apart.

boundary_rationale: The narrator breaks into an explicit tally formula ('These are the golden tumors which the Philistines returned... for Ashdod one, for Gaza one...') that is grammatically and functionally a register rather than narrated action, opening and closing on its own enumerative form before the narrative resumes with the Beth Shemesh judgment.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the list to include the closing note about the great stone remaining 'to this day' was considered part of the same sentence, but that clause is retained here as the list's own etiological tag rather than split off, since it names the stone the list itself points to.

boundary_rationale: This span deliberately crosses the chapter line. The front edge is marked by the shift from the narrator's own to-this-day deictic close (6:18) to the resuming wayyiqtol vayach at 6:19 ('Yahweh struck the men of Beth Shemesh'), opening a new and darker beat. The rear edge is not, as previously claimed, an absence of any intervening scene break between the Kiriath Jearim invitation (6:21) and its fulfillment (7:1) -- WEB in fact opens paragraphs at both 6:21 and 7:1, and 7:1 introduces new participants (anshei Qiryat Ye'arim) at a new location (beit Avinadav bagiv'ah). The genuine rear-edge signal is instead the twenty-year jump at 7:2 (vayirbu hayamim vayihyu esrim shanah), corroborated by the pe sited after 7:1; the request-and-fulfillment continuity between 6:21 and 7:1 (the messengers' invitation answered directly by the men of Kiriath Jearim's action, with no renewed deliberation) is a real but secondary consideration for keeping the chapter-crossing span whole, not the absence of any marked break.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Bracketing 1Sam.6.21-1Sam.7.1 as its own unit (corroborated by the samekh sited after 6:20 and the pe sited after 7:1) was not previously tested and is recorded here as the live rejected alternative: it is textually available, since both verses carry participant/location signals of their own, but the request-and-fulfillment link between the messengers' invitation and its narrated completion, plus the shared 7:2 rear boundary, favor keeping 6:19-7:1 as one span over fragmenting the ark's-return material further.

boundary_rationale: A durative time-marker ('the time was long -- for it was twenty years') opens a new phase of national mourning, Samuel's reform call to abandon foreign gods, and the Mizpah water-pouring repentance ritual, closing with the summary note that Samuel judged Israel there. 7:2's opening clause is itself backward-referencing (vayehi miyom shevet ha'aron beQiryat Ye'arim, tying it to the ark's resting place just narrated at 7:1) before pivoting to the durative, all-Israel-scope 'twenty years... lamented' language that actually opens the reform movement -- this Janus-faced quality is disclosed here as a live alternative affiliation (7:2 could in principle close the preceding ark unit) rather than treated as settled. The span is nonetheless kept whole because 7:5 (Samuel's 'gather all Israel to Mizpah') is the same speech-act that convenes the assembly narrated at 7:6, binding the duration notice to the repentance ritual it introduces. A samekh sited after 7:2 gives weak corroboration and does not by itself decide the question.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating Samuel's reform speech (vv.3-4) from the Mizpah assembly (vv.5-6) was considered, but the speech directly sets up the assembly it calls for, and both belong to a single continuous movement toward national repentance. Also disclosed as live rather than settled: reading 7:2 as the closing verse of the preceding ark-at-Kiriath-Jearim unit (M8-1Sam-035) rather than as this unit's own opening, on the strength of its backward-referencing clause -- not adopted, since the assembly-convening link from 7:5 to 7:6 argues for keeping 7:2 with the reform movement it introduces.

boundary_rationale: The Philistines' approach in response to the Mizpah gathering opens a battle-under-threat scene, moving through the people's plea, Samuel's sacrifice and prayer, Yahweh's thunder, and the resulting rout, closing on Israel's pursuit to Beth Kar.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the sacrifice-and-prayer (vv.9-10a) from the battle's resolution (vv.10b-11) was considered, but the thunder that routs the Philistines is presented as the direct and immediate answer to Samuel's cry, with no scene gap between prayer and its effect.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's stone-setting and its Ebenezer etiology open a summarizing coda to the battle, broadening out to a generalized report of Philistine subjugation and restored borders that closes the war narrative before the office-summary notice begins. This span is deliberately kept as narrative_prose rather than regnal_summary_notice: although its durative, all-the-days-of-Samuel closing content resembles the register-shift pattern also present at 3:19-21 and 14:52, none of these three are true regnal accession formulas (contrast 13:1's bem shanah Shaul bemalcho...ushtei shanim malach, a closed age-plus-reign-length form). regnal_summary_notice is reserved in this half for 13:1 alone; 3:19-21 (M8-1Sam-018) has been correspondingly corrected to narrative_prose for the same reason, resolving the inconsistency this decision's own comparison exposed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping the etiology (v.12) attached to the battle report before it was considered, but the shift from a single dated victory to durative claims ('all the days of Samuel') marks a register step outward comparable to (but not formally identical with) the true accession formula at 13:1; retagging to regnal_summary_notice to match 3:19-21 was also considered and rejected, since 3:19-21 itself is corrected in this response set to narrative_prose on the same reserved-label grounds.

boundary_rationale: This closing notice generalizes entirely outside scene-time - 'Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life,' his circuit among Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah, his home base at Ramah and altar there - a durative office-summary that both opens on its own formula and closes the chapter before the sons-as-judges notice that opens chapter 8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this with the preceding Ebenezer summary was considered since both are summarizing in register, but this unit specifically catalogs an ongoing judicial office and itinerary, a distinct content-type from the war-and-borders summary before it.

boundary_rationale: A new temporal marker ('When Samuel was old') opens the notice that he appointed his sons as judges, naming them and stating their corruption - exposition that sets up the elders' demand without yet narrating any scene of confrontation.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this into the elders' arrival (v.4) was considered, but the elders' gathering and journey to Ramah is a distinct narrated action introduced by its own new-subject clause, not a continuation of the sons' corrupt-judging description.

boundary_rationale: The elders convene and voice the kingship demand, Samuel's displeasure leads to prayer, and Yahweh's response reframes the demand as a rejection of divine kingship while instructing Samuel to warn the people (8:9, vehiggadta lahem mishpat hammelekh) - a complete request-and-divine-response cycle. The unit's own close is 8:10, the report-frame verse in which the instruction of v.9 is actually discharged: vayomer Shemuel et kol divrei YHWH el ha'am hasho'alim me'ito melekh ('Samuel told all Yahweh’s words to the people who asked him for a king'), summarizing Samuel's compliance rather than narrating the warning's content. The seam falls at 8:10|8:11: v.11 opens the warning's actual content with its own fronted demonstrative declaration, vayomer zeh yihyeh mishpat hammelekh ('This will be the way of the king who shall reign over you'), a fronted-predicate construction distinct from v.10's report-frame vayomer and paralleling the fronted-object-plus-yiqqach morphology M8-1Sam-042 uses to argue its own opening at this same edge. The unit accordingly runs 8:4-8:10, closing on the discharge of Yahweh's instruction rather than on the instruction itself, before the catalogue of the king's practices begins at 8:11.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the elders' demand (vv.4-6) from Yahweh's answer (vv.7-9) was considered, but the prayer in v.6 is the direct hinge between them and both halves belong to one uninterrupted deliberation before Samuel acts.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's 'manner of the king' speech opens on its own introductory formula, zeh yihyeh mishpat hammelech ('This will be the way of the king,' 8:11) -- not 8:10, which is narratorial attribution ('Samuel told all Yahweh's words to the people') containing no enumeration. The catalog is a two-verb alternation, not uniform anaphora as previously claimed: a fronted-object-plus-yiqqach pattern at 8:11, 8:13, 8:14, and 8:16 (military conscription, land seizure, produce), alternating with the distinct verb ya'sor ('he will tithe') at 8:15 and 8:17; 8:12 has no finite taking verb at all (velasum lo sarei alafim); and 8:18 breaks the pattern completely with a second-person consequence clause (uze'aqtem bayom hahu, 'you will cry out in that day'). WEB's rendering of ya'sor as 'he will take one tenth of' had manufactured a false uniformity. The catalog closes at 8:18 and 8:19 resumes narrative (vayemaanu ha'am, 'the people refused'). A samekh sited after both 8:9 and 8:10 weakly corroborates 8:10 standing apart from the catalog it precedes; 8:10 itself needs separate attachment (to the preceding deliberation-cycle unit or as a standalone hinge), which lies outside this half's assigned decisions.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the catalog into thematic sub-lists (military conscription, land, tithes) was considered, but the two-verb alternation (yiqqach/ya'sor) runs across all the thematic groupings without any accompanying formula reset, so splitting by theme would manufacture seams the text does not itself mark. Including 8:10 in the span was also considered and rejected, since 8:10 is narratorial report with no enumeration, one verse before the catalog's own introductory formula.

boundary_rationale: The people's refusal to heed the warning and their repeated demand reopen dialogue after the catalog closes, moving through Yahweh's final instruction to grant the request and Samuel's dismissal of the assembly, which ends the chapter and the whole kingship-demand sequence.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the dismissal (v.22b) as its own coda was considered, but it is the direct and immediate action following Yahweh's instruction in the same verse, with no scene gap separating command from compliance.

boundary_rationale: A five-generation genealogy introducing Kish and then Saul, with the note of his height and handsomeness, opens the anointing type-scene proper before the donkey-search plot begins; the register form (a chain of 'the son of' clauses) is a distinct unit from the action that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this into the donkey-search narrative was considered, but the genealogical chain has its own closed form independent of any narrated event, unlike the search itself which begins only at v.3.

boundary_rationale: The donkeys go missing and Kish sends Saul out; the search widens through several districts (9:3-9:4) into the land of Zuph (9:5, hemmah bau be'eretz Tsuf), where Saul proposes turning back - and the servant's counter-proposal to consult the man of God (9:6), Saul's objection about the missing gift (9:7), and the servant's silver offer (9:8) are three turns of one continuous negotiation between the same two participants, with no relocation and no participant change anywhere in the stretch. This merges the formerly separate M8-1Sam-045 (9:3-9:5) and M8-1Sam-046 (9:6-9:8): the 9:5|9:6 seam previously drawn between them was a bare speaker-change turn, justified only by the servant's idea 'redirecting the plot' - a content judgment, not a text signal, and inconsistent with how this same unit correctly declines to split its own three internal turns: 9:6 and 9:7 open on a bare vayomer, while 9:8 opens instead on a yasaph-plus-infinitive continuation frame, vayyosef hanna'ar la'anot et Sha'ul vayomer ('the young man continued answering Saul, and said'), a stronger, different formula that intensifies rather than merely repeats the pattern - all three nonetheless carry WEB paragraph starts. The unit closes cleanly at 9:9, a register break of the first order (the narrator's aside on the seer/prophet terminology, set off by parentheses in translation).
strongest_rejected_alternative: 9:4|9:5 was tested as an internal candidate seam: 9:5's fronted-pronoun-plus-qatal circumstantial construction (hemmah bau) paired with relocation into Zuph and a shift into direct speech is a stronger formal signal than the 9:5|9:6 speaker-change turn this unit used to be cut at, but it falls within one continuous search-and-negotiation movement (the donkeys are still the subject at hand through 9:5's own proposal to turn back) and is not promoted to a boundary.

boundary_rationale: This verse is explicitly parenthetical in form and function - a narrator's aside explaining that 'seer' was the older term for what is now called 'prophet' - interrupting the dialogue rather than advancing it, with the text itself marking the insertion by parenthesis.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating it as scene-setting for the coming ascent to the city was considered, but the verse contains no narrated action or dialogue at all and reads as a lexical footnote the narrator felt necessary before Saul actually reaches the seer.

boundary_rationale: Saul assents and the journey resumes, the pair ascending to the city and meeting the maidens who direct them, closing just as Samuel himself comes into view - a build-up unit ending on the sighting that triggers the encounter proper.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this through the actual meeting with Samuel (v.15 onward) was considered, but v.15 pulls back into a flashback disclosing Yahweh's prior word to Samuel, a change of narrative vantage distinct from the approach sequence.

boundary_rationale: The narrator steps outside chronological sequence to disclose Yahweh's revelation to Samuel 'a day before Saul came' - a flashback opening on vaYHWH galah (waw+divine-subject+qatal, off the wayyiqtol chain), corroborated by a samekh after 9:14. The closing edge is weaker than the opening: 9:17 itself opens with the identical off-chain construction (uShemuel ra'ah, waw+named-subject+qatal) that marks the flashback's own opening, so this is the strongest formal signal in the neighborhood and it falls span-internally, one verse before the drafted close; 9:18 (vayigash Shaul) is a plain wayyiqtol, the chapter's default transition. Verse 17 is therefore better described as the flashback's resumption into present narrated time (Samuel actually seeing Saul, Yahweh's confirming word) than as still part of the flashback itself - consistent with the observation that v.17 completes the clause v.14 left hanging and hands the narrative forward into the encounter that follows, rather than closing a retrospective panel.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 9:16 and letting v.17 open the encounter narrative that follows (since 9:17's off-chain construction matches 9:15's and 9:18's plain wayyiqtol does not) is a live, well-evidenced alternative; it is not adopted outright because v.17 still functions as the flashback's confirming payoff (Yahweh's own 'behold, the man...') before the narrated encounter proper begins at 9:18's approach.

boundary_rationale: Saul approaches Samuel directly and the hospitality type-scene unfolds -- invitation to the high place, seating among the guests, the reserved portion set before Saul -- closing on the note that Saul ate with Samuel that day, before the pair withdraw to the housetop at 9:25 (vayeredu mehabamah ha'ir), a genuine relocation. The strongest internal competitor to atomizing this scene is the 9:21/9:22 mode change (four verses of quoted speech ending at Saul's self-deprecating question, 9:21, giving way to bare narrated action at 9:22, vayiqqach Shemuel...vayeviem, with a samekh after both 9:20 and 9:21) -- a dialogue-to-narration shift of the kind this campaign treats as a legitimate internal signal, though not strong enough on its own to divide one continuous hospitality scene that Samuel's invitation (9:19) already commits to completing at the table.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating 9:18-9:21 (the gateway exchange and quoted turns) from 9:22-9:24 (the meal itself) at the genuine mode-change seam (quoted speech to narrated action, corroborated by the samekh after 9:20 and 9:21) was tested and declined: Samuel's invitation in v.19 directly promises the meal that follows, and the four-turn exchange culminating in 9:21 reads as the same continuous hospitality encounter that the meal completes, not a separate scene.

boundary_rationale: The pair withdraw from the public meal to the housetop for a private conversation, then descend and part ways with the servant sent ahead, closing on Samuel's request that Saul stand still to hear a private word - a deliberate narrowing from public feast to private disclosure that sets up chapter 10's anointing.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this into the feast scene before it was considered, but the shift from the crowded guest hall to a private rooftop conversation, and later to the two men alone at the city's edge, marks a location and participant-count change worth its own unit.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's anointing act opens with the vial of oil and a kiss, then moves into a three-part list of confirmatory signs Saul will encounter on his way home, closing on the instruction to wait seven days at Gilgal - the anointing and its attached sign-speech form one bounded unit with a clear act-then-explanation shape.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the three signs into separate spans was considered given their list-like 'then you will' repetition, but they are presented as stages of a single itinerary rather than discrete self-standing episodes, so keeping them together respects the register better than atomizing it.

boundary_rationale: The narrator reports the signs' fulfillment - God gives Saul 'another heart,' the prophetic band meets him, the Spirit comes on him - closing on v.13's own notice, 'When he had finished prophesying, he came to the high place.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the uncle's interrogation (vv.14-16) to this unit was considered since it follows immediately, but a new participant (Saul's uncle) and a fresh question-and-answer scene open at v.14 with no continuity of setting from the high place.

boundary_rationale: Saul's uncle questions him about where he went, and Saul answers about the donkeys while deliberately withholding the kingship word Samuel spoke - a short private scene that closes on the narrator's explicit note of what Saul left unsaid, setting up dramatic irony for the public lottery to come.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this with the Mizpah assembly that follows was considered, but the private, domestic setting of the uncle's questioning is entirely different from the national convocation Samuel calls in v.17.

boundary_rationale: Samuel calls a national assembly at Mizpah, opening with a rebuking oracle-speech before the lot is cast by tribe, family, and man; the sequence climaxes in Saul's discovery among the baggage and the crowd's acclamation 'Long live the king!' - a bounded public type-scene with clearly marked convocation and acclamation edges.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the rebuke speech (vv.17-19) from the lottery procedure (vv.20-24) was considered, but the speech functions as the assembly's opening address before the same gathering proceeds directly to the lot it has been convened for.

boundary_rationale: Samuel records the regulations of the kingdom and dismisses the assembly, and the chapter closes on Saul's return home accompanied by loyal men and the scorn of a dissenting minority -- a closing notice that plants the seed of the Ammonite crisis without yet narrating it. Both edges carry a pe attested in both witnesses (after 10:24 and after 10:27). Disclosure note: the juncture between this unit's close (10:27, vayehi kemachrish, 'he held his peace') and 11:1's cold introduction of Nahash is the kind of seam where other textual traditions are sometimes said to preserve additional material; this campaign's assigned sources (MT-only OSHB, a WEB clean text with no footnote at either verse, and a parashah-mark witness file that records petuchah/setumah sites rather than variant readings) cannot confirm or deny any such plus, and that evidentiary limit -- not a specific claim about what any other tradition contains -- is what is recorded here, marked insufficient_evidence for the specific claim of versional expansion.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the dismissal (v.25) from the report of Saul's homecoming and the dissenters (vv.26-27) was considered, but both belong to a single winding-down movement after the acclamation, with no scene break between them.

boundary_rationale: A new location and threat opens the chapter -- Nahash's siege of Jabesh Gilead and his demand of mutilation -- and the elders negotiate a seven-day reprieve and propose dispatching messengers 'in all the borders of Israel' (11:3). This unit now extends through the messengers' dispatch itself: 11:4 (vayavou hamalachim Giv'at Shaul) discharges the elders' proposal with a bare wayyiqtol whose subject (hamalachim) is anaphoric to the 'messengers' just named, not an independent scene-opener. The genuine off-chain construction that re-introduces an absent participant -- vehinneh Shaul ba, waw-presentative plus named subject plus participle, the only such construction in the chapter -- falls one verse later, at 11:5, walking Saul back onto the page after his absence since chapter 10 closed. The boundary is therefore moved to 11:4|11:5, keeping the elders' decision to dispatch messengers together with its immediate discharge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at 11:3, with 'the messengers came' (11:4) opening the next scene, was the drafted position and is now rejected: 11:4's wayyiqtol has no independent subject of its own and simply completes the plan proposed one clause earlier, so cutting there splits a plan from its discharge at the weakest marker available, while the chapter's only waw-presentative construction sits untested one verse further on. Note for the boss: this revision consequently narrows the neighboring M8-1Sam-058 (currently 11:4-11:7 or similar) to begin at 11:5 rather than 11:4; that decision is outside Half A's assigned manifest and is flagged here rather than altered.

boundary_rationale: Saul is reintroduced by the chapter's only waw-presentative-plus-participle construction - wehinneh Sha'ul ba acharei habbaqar min hassadeh, 'Behold, Saul came following the oxen out of the field' (11:5) - an ordinary-life detail pointedly unlike a royal entrance; he then hears the news, and the Spirit's empowerment drives his oxen-summons, closing on the dread that brings 'all Israel' out as one man. The front edge falls at 11:4|11:5: 11:4 (the messengers reaching Gibeah and the people weeping) belongs to the preceding scene of Jabesh's appeal, while 11:5's own vehinneh-plus-participle construction reopens the narrative on Saul specifically, the chapter's only occurrence of this construction (per M8-1Sam-057's finding), marking a genuine front-edge signal rather than a bare continuation of v.4's crowd scene.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Saul's Spirit-empowerment (v.6) from the oxen-summons act (v.7) was considered, but the anger and the act are presented as one immediate cause-and-effect movement without any narrated pause between them.

boundary_rationale: The muster at Bezek, the reassurance sent back to Jabesh, and the three-company night attack form one battle unit, closing on the total rout of the Ammonites and the notice that no two of them remained together.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the troop count (v.8) from the battle itself (vv.9-11) was considered, but the count exists only to set up the battle that follows in the same breath, with no scene gap between mustering and marching.

boundary_rationale: In the flush of victory the people demand the execution of Saul's earlier detractors, Saul's clemency speech deflects the demand, and the whole assembly relocates to Gilgal to renew the kingship with sacrifice - a coda that both resolves the succession question raised in chapter 10 and closes the chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Saul's clemency speech (v.13) as its own unit apart from the Gilgal renewal was considered, but the speech's function is precisely to clear the way for the unified celebration that follows, and the two halves share the same assembled crowd without a scene break.

boundary_rationale: Samuel opens a formal farewell address with a self-presentation and an offer to be cross-examined for wrongdoing ('Here I am. Witness against me before Yahweh,' 12:1-3), and the people's exoneration (12:4), Samuel's witness-formula invoking Yahweh and the king (12:5a), and the closing exchange (12:5b) are the solicited response that same challenge explicitly calls for, not an independently initiated speech-act. This merges the formerly separate M8-1Sam-061 (12:1-12:3) and M8-1Sam-062 (12:4-12:5): the 12:3|12:4 seam previously drawn between them was a bare vayomeru turn marker, morphologically identical to the vayomer/vayomeru turns at 12:5 (twice) and 12:6, two of which the draft itself correctly treats as internal to a unit - an inconsistent application of the turn-marker principle. Chapter 12 as a whole is further textured by a near-verbatim inclusio bracketing the larger address: 12:2's ve'attah hinneh hammelekh mithhallekh lifneikhem is answered almost word for word at 12:13's ve'attah hinneh hammelekh asher becharttem. This inclusio is context for the chapter's overall rhetorical shape, not a boundary warrant for this unit's own span, since taken as a bracket it would run past this decision's own rear edge at 12:5; the case for closing here rests instead on the pe (two-witness) sited after 12:5 and the oath-of-clearance's own formal closure, with 12:6 opening a fresh topic marker (the historical recital) that begins the next unit. Note on 12:5's own closing clause: MT prints vayomer ed, third-masculine-singular with no expressed plural subject - 'he said, Witness' - while WEB renders the clause with a plural subject, 'They said, He is witness,' not present in MT; the seal is Samuel's own single-voice formula, not a chorused assembly response.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 12:1-3 (the challenge) and 12:4-5 (the exoneration) as two independently-bounded speech-acts, on the grounds that they are spoken by different parties, was the drafted position and is now rejected: this is exactly the situation the turn-marker principle (illustrated at 1:9-18) says should be resisted absent an independent scene or topic change, and the campaign's own recalibration already declined an identical rhetorical-function-only warrant. Splitting off 12:6 onward (the historical recital) remains correctly rejected, since 12:6 supplies its own fresh topic marker and content shift distinct from the oath-of-clearance ritual.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's address opens on a nominal predication about Yahweh (12:6, 'It is Yahweh who appointed Moses and Aaron') that introduces, but is not itself, the historical recital: the recital's own content begins only at 12:8 (ka'asher ba Ya'akov Mitzrayim), with 12:7 functioning as a distinct lawsuit-form element, the summons (ve'attah hityatzevu ve'ishaftah, reflexive imperative plus cohortative of judgment) - confirmed as a separable element by its own partial verbal echo at 12:16 (gam attah hityatzevu ur'u): only 'attah hityatzevu' recurs from 12:7's ve'attah hityatzevu, with a different opening particle (gam vs. ve-) and a different second verb (ur'u vs. ve'ishaftah). The unit's far edge is weaker than previously rated: 12:12 opens with vatiru, a second-plural wayyiqtol continuing the same address to the same audience; the pivot from the era of the judges to the recent Ammonite crisis is a topic change inside one continuous speech, not an independently text-evidenced seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the recital through the present-day indictment (vv.12-15) was considered and remains rejected, since v.12 pivots from past history to the present crisis, a recognizable topic shift even though it carries no independent text signal of its own. Separating the summons (12:6-7) from the recital proper (12:8-11) into two decisions was also considered; it is not adopted, since both remain part of one continuous covenant-lawsuit address bounded by the same speaker and audience, but the summons is noted as its own form-element within the span rather than folded silently into 'the recital's own introduction.'

boundary_rationale: The recital pivots to the present indictment - the Ammonite threat and the demand for a king despite Yahweh's own kingship - and closes on the conditional blessing-and-curse formula that frames obedience and rebellion as two starkly different futures.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this with the sign of thunder (vv.16-19) was considered as one 'consequences' unit, but v.16's imperative 'Now therefore stand still and see this great thing' opens a demonstrative act distinct from the conditional teaching just given.

boundary_rationale: Samuel calls down thunder and rain as a demonstrative sign confirming the wickedness of the request, and the people's terrified plea for intercession closes the unit, a sign-and-reaction pair distinct from both the preceding conditional teaching and the reassurance speech that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the people's plea to Samuel's reassuring answer (vv.20ff) as one exchange was considered, but Samuel's answer opens with its own address formula ('Don't be afraid') that reframes rather than merely continues the preceding fear.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's closing exhortation reassures the people, commits himself to continued intercession, and issues a final conditional warning, closing the whole farewell address and the chapter on the ominous 'you will be consumed, both you and your king' - a recognizable lawsuit-speech peroration bounded by the address formula that opens it and the book's next scene-change into chapter 13's regnal formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Samuel's self-commitment to prayer (vv.20-23) from the final warning (vv.24-25) was considered, but both are part of one uninterrupted closing speech with no renewed address formula in between.

boundary_rationale: This verse is the book's own accession formula, closed in form (subject plus accession-infinitive clause, ben shanah Shaul bemalcho, followed by a reign-length clause, ushtei shanim malach al Yisrael), sharing nothing with Samuel's peroration that ends chapter 12 or with the wayyiqtol muster that begins at 13:2. As printed, MT is not blank or damaged at the accession-age slot -- it reads ben shanah ('a son of one year'), an anomalous but present value. WEB's own footnote discloses that the traditional Hebrew text omits both 'thirty' (the tens digit of Saul's age) and 'forty-' (the tens digit of the forty-two-year reign length), with both numerals supplied from a few Septuagint manuscripts; this is a doubly reconstructed verse, not a single damaged figure. Both edges are form-marked, and a pe after 12:25 corroborates the near one.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this into the muster account (vv.2-7) as its introductory date-notice was considered, but the formula's closed regnal shape ('became king... reigned... years') matches the accession-notice pattern used elsewhere in the history and is anomalous (not merely a narrative lead-in) in a way that marks it as its own unit.

boundary_rationale: Saul's troop division, Jonathan's strike on the Geba garrison, and the Philistine mobilization it provokes form one escalating unit, closing on the Israelites' terrified scattering into caves and pits before Saul's seven-day wait at Gilgal is narrated.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating Jonathan's raid (v.3) from the Philistine response (vv.4-5) was considered, but the raid is presented as the direct trigger for the mobilization, with the trumpet call in the same verse announcing what Jonathan has just done.

boundary_rationale: Saul's seven-day wait, his unauthorized offering just as Samuel arrives, and Samuel's confrontation form the first rejection oracle of the book, closing on the announcement that Yahweh has sought 'a man after his own heart.' The rear edge is genuinely strong: a completed verdict at 13:14, answered at 13:15 by a two-verb exit (vayaqam Shemuel vaya'al min hagilgal), with a pe sited after 13:14 in both witnesses. The front edge is weaker than previously stated: 13:8 opens with vayochel (ketiv/qere), a wayyiqtol with no expressed subject, retrievable only from 13:7's medial clause naming Saul (veshaul odenu bagilgal), with the verse's own final clause naming kol ha'am instead (vechol ha'am charedu acharav); in the immediately preceding stretch (13:5, 13:6, 13:7), this narrator marks every change of focus with waw plus a fronted subject, and the withholding of that construction exactly at this seam counts against a boundary here rather than for one. The unit's own claimed opening marker ('the shift from waiting to arrival') is span-internal - Saul waits at 13:8, Samuel arrives at 13:10 - and describes the scene's development, not its edge. Disclosure note: 13:15's departure clause sits at a juncture sometimes discussed as a point of versional divergence; the sources assigned to this campaign (MT-only OSHB, a WEB clean text with no footnote at 13:15, and a chapter-level verse-count crosswalk that is silent about intra-verse pluses) cannot confirm or deny this, so the specific claim of versional divergence is marked insufficient_evidence here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Saul's self-justification (vv.11-12) from Samuel's verdict (vv.13-14) was considered, but the two form one uninterrupted exchange in which Samuel's rebuke directly answers Saul's excuse without any scene gap. Extending the span backward to include 13:7b (so the unit begins with the disjunctive clause that supplies vayochel's subject) is a live alternative not adopted here, since 13:7 belongs to the preceding, out-of-half decision; downgrading confidence and naming the true (silent) front-edge juncture is preferred instead.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's departure and the troop count at Gibeah shift attention back to the military situation, and the unit closes with the three-company deployment of Philistine raiders, a register-like listing of the three roads they take that prepares for the arms-shortage notice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the raiders' deployment to the arms-shortage notice that follows (vv.19-23) was considered, but the raiders' movement is reported before the narrator pauses to explain why Israel lacked weapons, a distinct explanatory register.

boundary_rationale: The narrator interrupts the battle build-up with an explanatory notice about the absence of blacksmiths in Israel and the Philistine monopoly on ironworking, before returning to report the garrison's advance to the pass. This is discursive explanation, not a list-register: a negated durative statement (13:19) with an embedded motive clause of direct speech, a purpose infinitive (13:20), a price notice built on a reconstructive rendering of pim (13:21, footnoted by WEB as a weight conversion), a temporal frame (13:22, vehayah beyom milchemet), and a wayyiqtol resuming the storyline (13:23) -- no enumerated series with a repeated frame appears, unlike the genuine three-member catalog at 13:17-18 in the preceding decision. A samekh sited after both 13:18 and 13:23 corroborates the edges, which are otherwise unaffected by this retagging.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the pricing detail (v.21) as a separate list-span apart from the surrounding explanation was considered, but the price is embedded in one continuous explanatory sentence about the disarmament policy, not set off as an independent catalog -- the very reasoning that argues against the list_register tag the decision was previously given.

boundary_rationale: Jonathan's secret plan to his armor-bearer opens the chapter, with the narrator's aside about Saul's location and the priest Ahijah's genealogy running back to Eli, closing on the pointed note that 'the people didn't know that Jonathan was gone' - dramatic-irony scene-setting before the topography and the armor-bearer's pledge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Including the crag description (vv.4-5) in this unit was considered, but the topography functions as scene-setting for the coming ascent and is introduced by its own descriptive clause rather than continuing Jonathan's private proposal.

boundary_rationale: A detailed topographical notice names the two crags, Bozez and Seneh, before Jonathan restates his plan directly to his armor-bearer and receives an unconditional pledge of loyalty. The closing edge is weaker than previously rated: 14:6, 14:7, and 14:8 are three turns of one uninterrupted two-party exchange, each introduced by an identical speech formula (vayomer Yehonatan / vayomer lo nose kelav / vayomer Yehonatan), with no narrated action, no participant change, and no relocation anywhere in the stretch -- the same defect this campaign's own recalibration already declined to accept as an edge at 12:3/12:4. A samekh sited after 14:7 gives weak corroboration under the Prophets-weighting rule, but cannot by itself install a boundary the text does not otherwise mark; the true marker at this edge is a bare speaker change, named honestly rather than dressed as a pledge-to-plan register shift.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this decision with M8-1Sam-074 into a single 1Sam.14.4-10 unit, which would keep the topography, the proposal, the pledge, and the sign-plan together and let the mood change at 14:10/14:11 carry the far edge, is a live and well-evidenced alternative; it is not adopted here because M8-1Sam-074 is outside this half's assigned manifest, and altering its span is not within this decision's authority. Flagging for the boss: a merge of 073 and 074 (or an equivalent boundary move) should be considered together with whoever holds 074.

boundary_rationale: Jonathan proposes a binary sign - if the garrison says 'wait,' retreat; if it says 'come up,' advance - a self-contained test-speech structurally similar to other sign-seeking scenes in the history, opening on his own formula 'we will reveal ourselves to them' and closing on the sign's stated meaning before its fulfillment is narrated.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the sign-speech into its fulfillment (vv.11-15) as one unit was considered, but the speech is entirely anticipatory and conditional in mood, distinct from the indicative, event-narrating register of what follows.

boundary_rationale: The garrison's taunt fulfills the sign, and the two climb, strike about twenty men, and trigger a trembling that spreads through the whole Philistine camp and field - closing on the note of an 'exceedingly great trembling' that becomes visible to the watchmen in the next unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this to the watchmen's sighting (v.16) was considered, but v.16 relocates the vantage point to Saul's lookout in Gibeah, a new participant-and-location pairing distinct from Jonathan and his armor-bearer's own action at the garrison.

boundary_rationale: The watchmen at Gibeah see the melting multitude, Saul orders a headcount that reveals Jonathan's absence, and he initiates a consultation involving the ark or its attendant -- only to cut the ritual short mid-request as the tumult grows, closing on the interrupted 'Withdraw your hand!' before the muster proper begins. Disclosure note: the content of what Saul calls for is genuinely uncertain in MT. 14:18b's explanatory clause (ki hayah aron ha'Elohim bayom hahu uvenei Yisrael) joins 'the ark of God' and 'the sons of Israel' with a bare conjunction and no predicate, so WEB must supply a preposition ('was with') to yield sense; the immediate context also sits oddly with a physically-summoned ark, since 14:3 has already stationed the priest as nose efod ('bearer of an ephod') and Saul's 14:19 command, esof yadecha ('withdraw your hand'), addresses a gesture rather than a transported object. This crux is disclosed rather than resolved; it does not affect the span or its edges (a new vantage and new participants open at 14:16, a pe closes both 14:19 and this unit in both witnesses).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the headcount (v.17) from the ark-or-ephod request (vv.18-19) was considered, but both are part of Saul's single improvised response to the news of a rising panic he does not yet understand.

boundary_rationale: Saul's forces join the battle already underway, and the unit tracks the cascading defections back to Israel - Hebrew mercenaries, then hidden men from the hill country - closing on v.23's full verdict, 'So Yahweh saved Israel that day; and the battle passed over by Beth Aven.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the two defecting groups (vv.21 and 22) as separate spans was considered, but they are presented as parallel instances of the same phenomenon - reinforcements swelling Israel's side as the rout becomes evident - within one continuous battle report.

boundary_rationale: Saul's rash food-oath opens a new complication distinct from the battle just resolved, and the unit follows the honey in the forest, Jonathan's unwitting violation, and his own rebuttal speech once he learns of the oath, closing on v.30's counterfactual, 'How much more, if perhaps the people had eaten freely today of the plunder of their enemies which they found? For now there has been no great slaughter among the Philistines.”'
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the oath's announcement (v.24) from its narrated violation (vv.25-27) was considered, but the oath exists in the text specifically to set up the violation that follows in the same breath, forming one cause-and-effect unit.

boundary_rationale: The pursuit continues until the famished troops fall on plunder and eat meat with the blood, a sin Saul moves quickly to correct by building an altar - the chapter's first, a notice the narrator flags explicitly - closing before the night-pursuit debate begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the altar-building to the following oracular inquiry (vv.36-37) was considered, but Saul's proposal to pursue the Philistines by night opens a fresh decision point with its own address to the people, distinct from the blood-eating correction just completed.

boundary_rationale: Saul's proposal to pursue by night meets the priest's counsel to inquire of God first, and God's silence triggers a lot-casting narrowing step by step from all Israel to Saul-and-Jonathan to Jonathan alone. The rear edge is weaker than previously rated: the seam at 14:42|14:43 is the sixth occurrence of the vayomer (Shaul) formula in eight verses (14:36, 14:38, 14:40 subjectless, 14:41, 14:42, 14:43), with nothing distinguishing the sixth from the fifth that the draft treats as internal; the span's final clause (vayilached Yonatan, 14:42) nearly repeats the outcome already given one verse earlier (vayilached Yonatan veShaul, 14:41), the profile of a resumption rather than a division. Disclosure note: the oracle request at 14:41, havah tamim ('give the perfect/complete one'), is two words naming one term, while the result clause immediately distinguishes two parties (Jonathan-and-Saul versus the people); WEB renders it 'Show the right' with no footnote, and the campaign's assigned sources cannot settle the fuller form of the request. The unit's internal narrowing sequence (all Israel to the royal pair to Jonathan) itself, rather than the procedure's 'formality,' is what argues for treating 14:36-14:42 as one unit; the front edge remains solid (the altar notice, a pe after 14:35, and a new proposal at 14:36).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the divine silence and diagnostic question (vv.37-38) from the lot-casting itself (vv.39-42) was considered, but they form one uninterrupted judicial procedure moving from failed inquiry to formal lot without any scene break. Closing instead at 14:40|14:41 or 14:45|14:46, where the witnesses actually place marks, is a live untested alternative not adopted here since the drafted span's own front edge and internal narrowing sequence remain the stronger overall account.

boundary_rationale: Jonathan confesses to tasting the honey, Saul pronounces a death sentence, and the people intervene with their own counter-oath invoking Yahweh's name to save him - closing the oath-crisis with Jonathan's rescue and Saul calling off the pursuit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the people's rescue speech (v.45) into a separate span from Saul's sentence (v.44) was considered, but the two speeches are presented as an immediate confrontation, sentence answered at once by counter-oath, without any narrated gap.

boundary_rationale: A war-catalog register opens with 'Now when Saul had taken the kingdom' and lists his enemies by name in a genuine five-member enumerated series, each introduced by the same preposition (bemoav uvivnei ammon uve'edom uvemalchei tzovah uvaplishtim, 14:47) -- a form distinct from both the oath-crisis narrative before it and the family register that follows. The list_register tag describes 14:47 cleanly but only half the span: 14:48 is three plain wayyiqtol clauses (vaya'as chayil vayach et Amalek vayatzel et Yisrael miyad shosehu) with no enumeration, formally indistinguishable from ordinary narrative summary; the two verses are held together by a samekh sited after 14:48 rather than by a shared register. The unit's actual closing clause is 14:48's vayatzel et Yisrael miyad shosehu ('he delivered Israel from the hand of him who plundered them'), not 14:47's uvechol asher yifneh yarshia -- a hiphil of r-sh-'a with no expressed object, whose base sense ('he condemned/acted wickedly') is rendered contextually by WEB as 'he defeated them,' an object supplied by the translation. A lexical hinge worth preserving: 14:47's vesha'ul lachad hamelucha ('Saul seized the kingship') reuses the root lachad just applied three times, passively, to Jonathan's capture by lot at 14:41-42 -- Saul seizes a kingship in the same verb by which his son was caught.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Combining the wars catalog with the family register into one closing-summary span was considered, but the two lists differ in kind -- military opponents versus kinship names -- and the text itself marks a fresh start at v.49 with 'Now the sons of Saul were.' Splitting 14:47 (catalogue) from 14:48 (narrative coda) into two decisions was also considered and declined, since a samekh after 14:48 corroborates keeping them together even though only one verse carries the list-register form.

boundary_rationale: A family register names Saul's sons and daughters, his wife Ahinoam, his army commander, and a note on the commander's father, a closed genealogical form opening on 'Now the sons of Saul were' and closing before the chapter's final generalizing refrain. As MT prints it, 14:51 (veqish avi Shaul veNer avi Avner ben Aviel) predicates Abiel's paternity of Ner alone, with ben grammatically singular; it does not itself state that Kish and Ner share a father. The genuine shared-grandfather relationship (Kish is elsewhere named ben Aviel at 9:1) is a cross-chapter inference, not the content of 14:51 taken alone, and is now stated as such. A smaller orthographic note preserved from the source check: MT spells the commander's name Avinner at 14:50 and Avner at 14:51, two forms one verse apart.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this list through the closing war-refrain (v.52) was considered, but v.52 shifts from naming individuals to a durative, unnamed-scope statement about lifelong warfare, a register change from genealogy to summary.

boundary_rationale: This closing verse generalizes outside any single episode - 'severe war against the Philistines all the days of Saul' - and notes his practice of conscripting any valiant man he saw, a durative refrain echoing the office-summary register of 7:12-14, rather than a regnal accession formula: it opens with a wayyiqtol of hayah, states a durative military condition, and closes on a habitual practice (vaya'asfehu elav), none of which shares 13:1's closed shape (age-at-accession clause plus reign-length clause). regnal_summary_notice is reserved in this half for 13:1 (M8-1Sam-067) alone, the book's one true accession formula; this decision and M8-1Sam-018 (3:19-3:21) are both retagged to narrative_prose accordingly, since neither carries an accession age, reign length, synchronism, or formulaic reign statement. Both edges remain well-marked: a samekh sited after both 14:51 and 14:52, the register plainly changing from named individuals to an unbounded statement, and 15:1 beginning a fresh commissioning speech.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this into the family register just before it was considered, but the shift from named individuals to an unbounded, ongoing military policy statement marks a distinct summary register worth isolating as the chapter's closing cadence. Retaining the regnal_summary_notice tag to match 13:1 was also considered and rejected, since 14:52 shares none of that formula's accession/reign-length shape.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's commission speech opens with a reminder of his own anointing role and moves into Yahweh's herem command against Amalek, a self-contained directive bounded by its own introductory 'Yahweh sent me to anoint you' and closing on v.3's full command, 'Now go and strike Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and don’t spare them; but kill both man and woman, infant and nursing baby, ox and sheep, camel and donkey.’”'
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the commission through the muster (v.4) was considered, but the counting of troops at Telaim is a narrated action responding to the command, distinct in register from the command's direct-speech form.

boundary_rationale: The muster, the Kenite warning, and the battle itself run as one campaign narrative, closing on the report that Saul and the people spared Agag and the best of the flocks while destroying only what was 'vile and refuse' - the partial compliance that becomes the chapter's central problem.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the Kenite exemption (v.6) from the battle account (vv.7-9) was considered, but the warning to the Kenites is issued as Saul is already positioned for battle and is best read as part of the same campaign movement.

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's word comes to Samuel using the root that will bracket the whole chapter - 'It grieves me [nichamti] that I have set up Saul' (15:11) - opening the chapter's inclusio (matched by 15:35's vaYHWH nicham), and the unit closes with Samuel's all-night cry and the morning report of his setting out to meet Saul. Genre-wise this span is majority narration framing a single clause of oracle: 15:10 is a bare word-event formula (vayehi devar YHWH el Shemuel lemor) with no speech content of its own; only 15:11a (nichamti...lo hekim) is first-person divine speech; and 15:11b-15:12 return to pure third-person narration - v.12 alone contains five wayyiqtols (vayashkem, vayuggad, vayissov, vaya'avor, vayered) reporting Samuel's grief, his cry, and his search for Saul. Tagged accordingly as narrative_and_prophetic_oracle rather than prophetic_oracle_speech, paralleling M8-1Sam-177's compound tag for a span with the opposite proportion (majority oracle there; majority narration here). The near edge is the strongest in this cluster: 15:10 opens the dedicated word-event formula vayehi devar YHWH el Shemuel lemor, corroborated by a pe after 15:9. The far edge is weaker than previously rated: 15:12 states Samuel's purpose (liqrat Shaul, 'to meet Saul') and 15:13 executes it (vayavo Shemuel el Shaul) with the same subject and no intervening narration, joined by a bare wayyiqtol - a journey-to-arrival split, the weakest kind of seam. Citation correction: 15:11's nacham anchor is content evidence for the chapter's inclusio, not edge evidence for this span's own boundary, and is cited here accordingly rather than among the boundary markers.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding Samuel's night-long cry into the confrontation scene that follows was considered, but the cry and the search for Saul the next morning belong to Samuel's private response before any dialogue with Saul begins. A stronger high-confidence unit in this neighborhood, if wanted, belongs to the decision covering 15:13 onward (outside this half's manifest), whose two edges are both independently marked; that observation does not change this decision's own span.

boundary_rationale: Saul greets Samuel with a claim of full obedience, and Samuel's pointed question about the bleating sheep punctures the claim, closing on Saul's admission that the people spared the best animals for sacrifice - a confrontation opening unit before the formal indictment speech.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this with the indictment that follows (vv.17-21) was considered, but v.17 opens with a fresh, extended speech-formula ('Though you were little in your own sight') that shifts from short question-and-answer into a sustained prophetic rebuke.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's formal indictment recalls Saul's anointing and the specific command disobeyed, closing with Saul's counter-defense that the plunder was intended for sacrifice - an accusation-and-defense pair distinct from the terser bleating-sheep exchange before it and from the summary verdict that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this through the 'to obey is better than sacrifice' oracle (vv.22-23) was considered, but that couplet has a distinct proverbial, near-poetic cadence that functions as the confrontation's climactic verdict rather than a continuation of the indictment's prose argument.

boundary_rationale: This couplet has a proverbial, balanced-clause cadence ('to obey is better than sacrifice... rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft') distinct from the surrounding prose argument, opening on the rhetorical question 'Has Yahweh as great delight' and closing on the formal rejection verdict 'he has also rejected you from being king,' the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating this as the closing two verses of the preceding indictment span was considered, but the shift into balanced, memorable proverbial form marks it as the rhetorical peak of the speech, worth isolating as its own unit.

boundary_rationale: Saul's confession and plea for pardon are met by Samuel's refusal and departure, the torn-robe sign-act, and the declaration 'Yahweh has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today.' The near edge is genuinely strong, corroborated by the samekh after 15:23 at the exit from the poetic couplet. The far edge is weaker than previously rated: 15:24 opens with vayomer Shaul el Shemuel chatati ('Saul said to Samuel, I have sinned') and 15:30, immediately past this span, opens vayomer chatati - the identical verb and confession word, with the speaker recoverable only from inside the closing span - a resumption signal rather than a division; the nearest samekh, after 15:26, sits span-internal. The closing counter-statement, 'the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent' (15:29, lo yeshaqer velo yinachem), is correctly read as ironic, but the irony runs through the nacham root's own three appearances - Yahweh's first-person grief at 15:11 (nichamti), its emphatic denial here at 15:29, and the narrator's reassertion at 15:35 (vaYHWH nicham) - not through Samuel's night-long response at 15:11, which is built on the unrelated roots ch-r-h ('was angry') and z-'-q ('cried out').
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the torn-robe sign-act (v.27) from its accompanying declaration (v.28) was considered, but the physical tearing and the verbal 'Yahweh has torn' pronouncement are presented as one symbolic gesture-plus-word event. Closing this unit earlier, at 15:26 (where a samekh does sit) rather than at 15:29, is a live alternative not adopted, since the torn-robe sign-act and its declaration (vv.27-29) form one continuous symbolic sequence with the refusal that precedes it.
