boundary_rationale: Saul renews his plea, this time asking only for public honor before the elders rather than reversal of the verdict, and Samuel's concession to return with him closes the confrontation proper before the ritual conclusion at Gilgal.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this into the preceding declaration was considered, but Saul's shift from requesting pardon to requesting honor is a distinct second appeal, and Samuel's changed response (returning, though the verdict stands) marks a real turn in the scene.

boundary_rationale: Samuel himself now enacts the herem Saul failed to complete, summoning Agag and pronouncing a poetic sentence over him ('as your sword has made women childless, so your mother will be childless…') before cutting him in pieces before Yahweh - an execution scene distinct from the preceding dialogue and from the closing departure notice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging Agag's brief, ironic greeting speech ('Surely the bitterness of death is past') into a separate span was considered, but it is answered immediately by Samuel's sentence within the same short scene, with no narrated gap.

boundary_rationale: The chapter closes with departures to Ramah and Gibeah and a double notice of grief - Samuel mourns for Saul, and Yahweh 'grieved' [niham] that he had made Saul king - closing the chapter's inclusio opened at v.11 with the same Hebrew root, an edge independently marked by both the vocabulary echo and the finality of 'Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death…'
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating v.34 (the departures) separately from v.35 (the mourning notice and inclusio) was considered, but both verses form one unbroken closing cadence with no scene change between the parting and the narrator's summarizing reflection on it.

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's commission to Samuel to anoint a successor among Jesse's sons opens the chapter, addressing Samuel's fear of Saul with a sacrificial ruse, and the unit closes on the trembling elders' welcome at Bethlehem and the invitation to the sacrifice - scene-setting before the sons are actually paraded.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this through Eliab's appearance (v.6) was considered, but v.6 begins the actual parade-and-rejection sequence with a new narrated action ('he looked at Eliab'), distinct from the commission and arrival just completed.

boundary_rationale: A type-scene of successive rejection unfolds as Eliab, then each of six more sons, is paraded and refused, opening on Samuel's mistaken assumption about Eliab and closing on the seventh rejection, with the theological aside about outward appearance versus the heart supplying the scene's own interpretive key mid-unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off the 'man looks at the outward appearance' saying (v.7) as its own reflective unit was considered, but it is delivered as Yahweh's direct answer to Samuel's specific misjudgment of Eliab, not a free-standing maxim, and belongs inside the rejection sequence it explains.

boundary_rationale: David is sent for as the overlooked youngest son, described with the same appearance-vocabulary just relativized in the preceding unit, and the anointing act itself closes the type-scene with the Spirit coming 'mightily on David from that day forward' - a climax independently marked by the send-for formula opening it and Samuel's departure to Ramah closing it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the anointing into the rejection sequence as its final beat was considered, but the shift from repeated refusal to an unqualified 'Arise! Anoint him, for this is he' is a decisive tonal and structural break marking the type-scene's resolution.

boundary_rationale: The Spirit's departure from Saul and the onset of the evil spirit open a second, distinct type-scene, moving through the servants' proposal and a courtier's unprompted commendation of David - already skilled, valiant, and favored by Yahweh - closing just before Saul actually sends for him.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the servants' diagnosis (v.15-16) apart from the courtier's commendation (v.18) was considered, but both speeches serve the same function of proposing and then supplying the specific candidate for the plan Saul is about to adopt.

boundary_rationale: Saul's messengers fetch David from the sheep, Jesse sends him with gifts, and the chapter closes on the resolution of the lyre-service problem set up two units earlier - David's music relieving Saul whenever the evil spirit comes on him - an edge marked by the problem's explicit narrated solution.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the summons and gift-giving (vv.19-20) from David's actual service (vv.21-23) was considered, but they form one uninterrupted sequence from Saul's request to its lasting result, with the notice that Saul 'loved him greatly' bridging them without a scene gap.

boundary_rationale: The armies of the Philistines and Israel take up positions on opposing mountains at the valley of Elah, a scene-setting notice that closes on the geography before the champion is introduced by name.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this to include Goliath's introduction (v.4) was considered, but v.4 opens with 'A champion out of the camp of the Philistines named Goliath,' a new-participant formula distinct from the general troop-positioning just described.

boundary_rationale: Goliath's introduction gives way to an itemized armor description running vv.5-7 as an unbroken chain of waw-plus-noun clauses -- wekhova' nechosheth, weshiryon qasqassim, umitschath nechosheth, wekhidon nechosheth, we'ets chanito (qere; ketiv vechets), welahevet chanito, wenose' hatsinnah -- with consecutive narration resuming only at v.8 (wayya'amod). That register break, not the translation's footnote apparatus, is the text signal marking this as a list_register unit distinct from the direct-speech challenge that follows. Only two of the five itemized pieces (the coat at 5,000 shekels, the spear's head at 600 shekels) carry an actual weight; the helmet, greaves, and kidon carry none, and the 'weaver's beam' line is a simile, not a measure -- the earlier claim that each piece 'is given its own weight or measure' overstated the text and is withdrawn. The unit is bounded by the champion's-name opening it and the shield-bearer notice closing it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the armor catalog into Goliath's challenge speech (vv.8-10) was considered, but the catalog is entirely descriptive third-person narration with no direct speech, while the challenge that follows shifts sharply into Goliath's own first-person taunt -- the waw-plus-noun chain of vv.5-7 gives way to consecutive narration (wayya'amod wayyiqra') at v.8, a genuine register change independent of any translator apparatus.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:1Sam.17.4 A champion out of the camp of the Philistines named Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span went out.
web:1Sam.17.7 The staff of his spear was like a weaver's beam; and his spear's head weighed six hundred shekels of iron. His shield bearer went before him.
oshb:1Sam.17.5 וְכ֤וֹבַע נְחֹ֨שֶׁת֙ עַל רֹאשׁ֔וֹ וְשִׁרְי֥וֹן קַשְׂקַשִּׂ֖ים ה֣וּא לָב֑וּשׁ וּמִשְׁקַל֙ הַשִּׁרְי֔וֹן חֲמֵשֶׁת אֲלָפִ֥ים שְׁקָלִ֖ים נְחֹֽשֶֽׁת (only the coat carries a weight in v.5)
oshb:1Sam.17.6 וּמִצְחַ֥ת נְחֹ֖שֶׁת עַל רַגְלָ֑יו וְכִיד֥וֹן נְחֹ֖שֶׁת בֵּ֥ין כְּתֵפָֽיו (greaves and kidon: no weight or measure given)
oshb:1Sam.17.7 וְלַהֶ֣בֶת חֲנִית֔וֹ שֵׁשׁ מֵא֥וֹת שְׁקָלִ֖ים בַּרְזֶ֑ל (the only other weighed item: the spear-head, 600 shekels)

boundary_rationale: Goliath's direct-speech challenge to single combat opens with 'Why have you come out' and closes with Israel's collective dismay and fear, a speech-and-reaction unit distinct from both the preceding armor description and David's family background that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the fear notice (v.11) to David's introduction (v.12ff) as one 'meanwhile' unit was considered, but Israel's fear is the direct narrated response to Goliath's own words in the same scene, not a separate narratorial aside.

boundary_rationale: The narrative pulls back to introduce David's family -- Jesse, his eight sons, and David's own back-and-forth between Saul's court and his father's sheep. This unit opens on a disjunctive waw-plus-noun clause, wedawid ben 'ish 'efrati hazzeh (v.12), and closes on a durative participle pair, wedawid holekh washav (v.15), rounding off the genealogical/background block before Jesse's specific errand instructions begin at v.16. (The earlier claim that this passage is 'regularly noted as absent' from a shorter Septuagint text is withdrawn: no Greek or Septuagint witness is present anywhere in this campaign's supplied source set, so the claim cannot be checked from anything available and is marked insufficient_evidence rather than narrated as an established textual fact. The span rests entirely on the disjunctive-clause evidence, which is sufficient on its own.)
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this background notice with the forty-day standoff (vv.16-19) was considered, but the family introduction is genealogical/expository in focus (a verbless-to-durative register) while vv.16-19 shift to Jesse's specific errand instructions to David, a distinct scene governed by the temporal frame of the standoff.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:1Sam.17.12 Now David was the son of that Ephrathite of Bethlehem Judah, whose name was Jesse; and he had eight sons.
web:1Sam.17.15 Now David went back and forth from Saul to feed his father's sheep at Bethlehem.
oshb:1Sam.17.12 וְדָוִד֩ בֶּן אִ֨ישׁ אֶפְרָתִ֜י הַזֶּ֗ה מִבֵּ֥ית לֶ֨חֶם֙ יְהוּדָ֔ה (disjunctive waw+noun opening the background block)
oshb:1Sam.17.15 וְדָוִ֛ד הֹלֵ֥ךְ וָשָׁ֖ב מֵעַ֣ל שָׁא֑וּל (durative participle pair closing it)

boundary_rationale: The forty-day standoff notice frames Jesse's errand -- provisions for the brothers and cheeses for their captain -- closing on the geographic note locating Saul and the army in the valley of Elah, setting up David's arrival at the camp. A two-witness pe falls after 17:16 (weak Prophets-grade corroboration only, disclosed here for completeness): v.16 is itself a formally self-standing frequentative sentence (wayyiggash happelishti hashkem weha'arev wayyityatstsev 'arba'im yom) sharing no participant with v.15 or v.17, so the rejected alternative below is disclosed as having weak concurring evidence even though it does not change the drawn boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the standoff notice (v.16) into the preceding family background was considered; a two-witness pe falls after 17:16, exactly at that seam, and v.16 is formally independent (a frequentative sentence sharing no participant with v.15). This is disclosed as weak, non-lifting corroboration for the alternative rather than treated as a driver. The span is retained because v.16 functions here specifically as the temporal frame for Jesse's errand (vv.17-19) rather than as part of the genealogical introduction (vv.12-15).
boundary_evidence_refs: web:1Sam.17.16 The Philistine came near morning and evening, and presented himself forty days.
web:1Sam.17.19 Now Saul, and they, and all the men of Israel were in the valley of Elah, fighting with the Philistines.

oshb:1Sam.17.19 וְשָׁא֤וּל וְהֵ֨מָּה֙ וְכָל אִ֣ישׁ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בְּעֵ֖מֶק הָֽאֵלָ֑ה נִלְחָמִ֖ים עִם פְּלִשְׁתִּֽים
parashah:pe after 1Sam.17.16 (two-witness; weak, non-lifting; disclosed per binding rules)

boundary_rationale: David's early rising and journey to the camp form a travel unit that closes precisely on his overhearing Goliath's renewed challenge - the same speech-content as vv.8-10, now heard by the story's actual protagonist for the first time.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the journey (v.20) from the arrival-and-overhearing (vv.21-23) was considered, but they form one continuous movement from departure to the moment of overhearing without any scene break.

boundary_rationale: The men of Israel flee in terror and voice the king's reward proclamation, and David's inquiry among the bystanders draws a confirming answer, closing the unit just before Eliab's angry intervention changes the scene's tone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Including Eliab's rebuke (vv.28-30) in this span was considered since it follows the same conversation, but Eliab's entrance as a new speaking participant with a hostile register marks a distinct beat within the crowd scene.

boundary_rationale: Eliab's angry accusation against his younger brother and David's deflecting reply form a family-conflict subplot, opening with a kinship-epithet participant introduction (wayyishma' 'eliav 'achiw haggadol) and closing when David simply turns to ask the same question of someone else, marked by wayyissov me'etslo 'el mul 'acher and the resumptive 'the people answered him again the same way' (kaddavar hari'shon). (The earlier claim that this exchange is 'regularly identified as absent from the shorter Septuagint text' is withdrawn: no Greek witness exists anywhere in this packet's supplied sources, so the claim has no evidence_ref and is marked insufficient_evidence; the span rests on the turn-away clause at v.30, which is sufficient on its own.)
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this exchange into the surrounding crowd scene was considered, but Eliab's is a distinctly hostile, personal register -- questioning David's motives and character -- introduced by a fresh kinship-epithet participant formula (v.28), unlike the bystanders' neutral confirmation just before it.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:1Sam.17.28 Eliab his oldest brother heard when he spoke to the men; and Eliab's anger burned against David,
web:1Sam.17.30 He turned away from him toward another, and spoke like that again; and the people answered him again the same way.
oshb:1Sam.17.28 וַיִּשְׁמַ֤ע אֱלִיאָב֙ אָחִ֣יו הַגָּד֔וֹל בְּדַבְּר֖וֹ אֶל הָאֲנָשִׁ֑ים וַיִּֽחַר אַף֩ אֱלִיאָ֨ב בְּדָוִ֜ד (kinship-epithet participant introduction; hostile register opens)
oshb:1Sam.17.30 וַיִּסֹּ֤ב מֵֽאֶצְלוֹ֙ אֶל מ֣וּל אַחֵ֔ר וַיֹּ֖אמֶר כַּדָּבָ֣ר הַזֶּ֑ה וַיְשִׁבֻ֤הוּ הָעָם֙ דָּבָ֔ר כַּדָּבָ֖ר הָרִאשֽׁוֹן (David turns away; the people answer as before)

boundary_rationale: David's words reach Saul, and a formal audience follows in which David offers his lion-and-bear résumé as evidence of Yahweh's protection, closing on Saul's assent - 'Go! Yahweh will be with you' - a complete persuasion scene bounded by the summons that opens it and the king's approval that closes it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Saul's initial refusal (v.33) from David's résumé speech (vv.34-37) was considered, but the refusal exists specifically to draw out the résumé that answers it, forming one continuous audience.

boundary_rationale: Saul dresses David in royal armor, David tests it and rejects it as untried, and he chooses instead his staff, sling, and five stones - a bounded equipping scene with a clear before-and-after shape, opening on the armor's imposition and closing on David's approach toward the Philistine with his own chosen gear.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this into the approach and mutual sizing-up (vv.41-44) was considered, but the equipping scene is complete once David's choice of weapons is settled, and v.41 opens a new movement as the Philistine himself begins walking toward David.

boundary_rationale: The two combatants approach and size each other up, and Goliath's contemptuous curse by his gods closes the unit just before David's own extended theological counter-speech begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging Goliath's taunt with David's reply into one exchange-span was considered, but David's answer is long enough and different enough in content - invoking Yahweh of Armies rather than trading insults - to warrant its own unit.

boundary_rationale: David's reply reframes the whole contest theologically -- 'the battle is Yahweh's' -- a self-contained speech opening on 'You come to me with a sword' (v.45) and bound together internally by an anaphoric weyed'u kol ('that...may know') pair spanning vv.46-47: v.46 closes 'that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel,' and v.47 answers with its own parallel clause, 'that all this assembly may know that Yahweh doesn't save with sword and spear; for the battle is Yahweh's, and he will give you into our hand.' The unit's actual closing-edge content is v.47's surrender formula, not v.46's clause (the earlier citation mis-described the close by quoting from the verse before the cited edge); independently bounded against Goliath's taunt before it and the narrated action that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this speech into the approach unit before it was considered, but its shift from physical description to sustained theological argument marks a clear register change worth its own boundary; the speech's internal cohesion is now grounded in the matched weyed'u kol anaphora across vv.46-47 rather than in a single, misattributed clause.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:1Sam.17.45 Then David said to the Philistine, 'You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies...'
web:1Sam.17.47 and that all this assembly may know that Yahweh doesn't save with sword and spear; for the battle is Yahweh's, and he will give you into our hand.
oshb:1Sam.17.46 וְיֵֽדְעוּ֙ כָּל הָאָ֔רֶץ כִּ֛י יֵ֥שׁ אֱלֹהִ֖ים לְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל (the anaphora's first member, actually in v.46)

oshb:1Sam.17.47 וְיֵֽדְעוּ֙ כָּל הַקָּהָ֣ל הַזֶּ֔ה כִּֽי לֹ֛א בְּחֶ֥רֶב וּבַחֲנִ֖ית יְהוֹשִׁ֣יעַ יְהוָ֑ה כִּ֤י לַֽיהוָה֙ הַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה וְנָתַ֥ן אֶתְכֶ֖ם בְּיָדֵֽנוּ (the anaphora's second member and the actual clause at the cited closing edge)

boundary_rationale: The combat itself -- the run, the sling, the fatal strike, the beheading with Goliath's own sword -- forms the story's physical climax, opening on 'the Philistine arose' (wehayah ki qam happelishti) and closing on the Philistines' flight once they see their champion is dead. The unit contains its own internal doublet, disclosed here rather than smoothed over: v.50 narrates the kill with the sling and stone and explicitly notes 'there was no sword in David's hand' (wayemitehu, wecherev 'en beyad dawid), while v.51 has David draw Goliath's own sword and kill him a second time with it (wayemotetehu, using a different causative form of the same root). This is the same kind of doublet pattern the campaign discloses at 18:10-12 versus 19:9-10, here internal to a single span; it does not move the unit's edges, since both verses belong to the same uninterrupted combat scene, but the tension is real and should not be described as an unqualified 'unmistakable turning point' without naming it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this through the pursuit and plunder (vv.52-54) was considered, but the flight notice at the end of v.51 is the direct trigger for the pursuit that follows, and the shift from single combat to a mass battle scene marks a real change of scale. Treating vv.50 and 51 as two separate decisions was not considered necessary, since both are part of one continuous combat scene; the internal weapon-detail doublet is disclosed above rather than used to argue for a respan.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:1Sam.17.48 When the Philistine arose, and walked and came near to meet David, David hurried and ran toward the army to meet the Philistine.
web:1Sam.17.50 So David prevailed over the Philistine with a sling and with a stone, and struck the Philistine and killed him; but there was no sword in David's hand.

web:1Sam.17.51 Then David ran, stood over the Philistine, took his sword, drew it out of its sheath, killed him, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.
oshb:1Sam.17.50 וַיַּ֥ךְ אֶת הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֖י וַיְמִיתֵ֑הוּ וְחֶ֖רֶב אֵ֥ין בְּיַד דָּוִֽד (he struck and killed him; no sword in David's hand)
oshb:1Sam.17.51 וַיִּקַּ֣ח אֶת חַ֠רְבּוֹ וַֽיִּשְׁלְפָ֤הּ מִתַּעְרָהּ֙ וַיְמֹ֣תְתֵ֔הוּ וַיִּכְרָת בָּ֖הּ אֶת רֹאשׁ֑וֹ (he takes the sword and kills him again with it)

boundary_rationale: Israel's pursuit and plunder of the Philistine camp widen the scene from single combat to mass battle, closing on the disposition of Goliath's head and armor - a resolution notice before the narrative turns back to David's identity, which Saul still does not know.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the identity question (vv.55-58) to this unit was considered, but Saul's inquiry to Abner is a distinct scene at Saul's own vantage point, separated from the battlefield plunder just narrated.

boundary_rationale: Saul's question to Abner about David's identity closes the chapter on a note that sits awkwardly beside chapter 16's introduction of David to Saul's own household staff. Two live readings of that tension should both be named rather than only one: a source-critical reading (this material's relationship to other textual traditions, which this packet's supplied sources -- WEB, OSHB, the verse crosswalk, and the two-witness apparatus -- cannot adjudicate, since no Greek witness is present anywhere in this packet) and a purely literary reading, in which Saul's failure to recognize a servant he supposedly already loves is coherent characterization given his affliction already established at 16:14 ('Yahweh's Spirit departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from Yahweh troubled him'), rather than only a seam from an unharmonized source layer. The unit itself opens on a vantage-shift disjunctive, wekhir'oth sha'ul (v.55), and closes on the chapter-final question-and-answer exchange (v.58) naming David's father.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv.55-58 as continuous with the pursuit-and-plunder unit before it was considered, but the shift in vantage from the battlefield to Saul watching David from a distance, and the reopening of a question chapter 16 seemed to have already settled, marks a distinct closing unit. The earlier ground for that reopened-question tension (an asserted Septuagint minus) is withdrawn as unsourced; the psychological reading (Saul's affliction from 16:14 already accounts for an unstable memory) is now named alongside it as an unresolved, live alternative rather than treated as settled by the text-critical claim.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:1Sam.17.55 When Saul saw David go out against the Philistine, he said to Abner, the captain of the army, 'Abner, whose son is this youth?'
web:1Sam.17.58 Saul said to him, 'Whose son are you, you young man?' David answered, 'I am the son of your servant Jesse the Bethlehemite.'
web:1Sam.16.14 Now Yahweh's Spirit departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from Yahweh troubled him.
oshb:1Sam.17.55 וְכִרְא֨וֹת שָׁא֜וּל אֶת דָּוִ֗ד יֹצֵא֙ לִקְרַ֣את הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י (vantage-shift disjunctive opening the unit)
oshb:1Sam.17.58 וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֵלָיו֙ שָׁא֔וּל בֶּן מִ֥י אַתָּ֖ה הַנָּ֑עַר וַיֹּ֣אמֶר דָּוִ֔ד בֶּֽן עַבְדְּךָ֥ יִשַׁ֖י בֵּ֥ית הַלַּחְמִֽי (question and answer closing the chapter)

boundary_rationale: The first Jonathan-David covenant scene opens immediately after David finishes speaking to Saul, with the soul-knitting notice, the covenant itself, and the transfer of robe and weapons, closing on the summary that David's promotion pleased both the people and Saul's own servants - a bounded relational unit before Saul's jealousy is introduced.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this through the women's victory song (vv.6-9) was considered, but that song is triggered by David's homecoming from battle, a new scene with a new set of participants (the women of the cities) rather than a continuation of the covenant-making just narrated.

boundary_rationale: The unit opens on wayehi bevo'am beshuv dawid mehakkoth 'eth happelishti (v.6), a temporal-anchor construction introducing a new participant group -- the women of the cities -- and runs through their antiphonal couplet in v.7 ('Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands') to Saul's angry monologue (v.8) and the durative notice that Saul watched David from that day forward (v.9, wayehi sha'ul 'oyen 'eth dawid). The couplet itself, embedded within this narrative unit, is set off in the WEB source by its own q1/q2 line markers, but that formatting cannot itself drive the unit's type or boundary: the actual poetic signal is the Hebrew bicolon's own parallel constituents and numerical escalation (hikkah sha'ul ba'alafaw, wedawid berivvothaw). Retagged accordingly as narrative_prose containing an embedded bicolon, since three of the span's four verses (6, 8, 9) are ordinary narration and only v.7 is verse.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the song couplet alone as a one-verse span apart from Saul's reaction was considered, but the song has no independent narrative weight apart from the jealousy it provokes in the same breath, so keeping cause (v.7) and immediate effect (vv.8-9) together, opened by the new-participant temporal anchor at v.6, better reflects the unit's function than isolating the couplet.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:1Sam.18.6 As they came, when David returned from the slaughter of the Philistine, the women came out of all the cities of Israel, singing and dancing...
web:1Sam.18.9 Saul watched David from that day and forward.

oshb:1Sam.18.6 וַיְהִ֣י בְּבוֹאָ֗ם בְּשׁ֤וּב דָּוִד֙ מֵהַכּ֣וֹת אֶת הַפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔י וַתֵּצֶ֨אנָה הַנָּשִׁ֜ים מִכָּל עָרֵ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ (temporal anchor + new participant group; the previously uncited opening edge)
oshb:1Sam.18.7 הִכָּ֤ה שָׁאוּל֙ באלפו בַּאֲלָפָ֔יו וְדָוִ֖ד בְּרִבְבֹתָֽיו (the bicolon itself -- the genuine poetic signal, not the WEB q-line markup)
oshb:1Sam.18.9 וַיְהִ֥י שָׁא֖וּל עון עוֹיֵ֣ן אֶת דָּוִ֑ד מֵהַיּ֥וֹם הַה֖וּא וָהָֽלְאָה (durative participle closing the unit)

boundary_rationale: The first of two javelin episodes -- an evil spirit comes on Saul, he prophesies in his house while David plays, and Saul hurls his spear (a single cast, wayyatel sha'ul 'eth hachanith) while David escapes his presence twice (wayyissov dawid mippanaw pa'amayim) -- is a compact, self-contained scene closing on the narrator's explanation that Saul feared David because Yahweh had left him. This episode's near-verbatim counterpart recurs at 19:9-10 (cited below), and this campaign's doublet discipline treats each as its own genuine event rather than collapsing them; the javelin motif in fact recurs a third time, still more closely in wording, at 20:33 (wayyatel sha'ul 'eth hachanith 'alaw lehakotho -- the identical opening four words), making this a three-member motif set (18:10-12; 19:8-10; 20:30-34) rather than a simple pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this with Saul's subsequent demotion of David (vv.13-16) was considered, but the demotion is a distinct administrative response narrated with its own new opening ('Therefore Saul removed him'), not a continuation of the spear-throwing scene itself. Collapsing this scene with 19:9-10 into a single cross-chapter span was also considered and rejected, since the two are narrated as separate dated incidents with different immediate consequences (demotion here, permanent flight there); the near-verbatim characterization is corrected to note that this scene shares only a partial formula with 19:9-10 (the evil-spirit-comes clause and the melee-with-David clause) but shares its opening four words verbatim with the later, third instance at 20:33.

web:1Sam.18.11 and Saul threw the spear, for he said, 'I will pin David to the wall!' David escaped from his presence twice.
web:1Sam.18.12 Saul was afraid of David, because Yahweh was with him, and had departed from Saul.

boundary_rationale: Saul's demotion of David to field command is followed by a report of David's continuing wise conduct and growing popularity, closing on the notice that 'all Israel and Judah loved David' - a summary of shifting public standing distinct from the private spear incident before it and the marriage negotiations that follow.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the Merab offer (vv.17-19) into this span was considered since both concern Saul's ongoing scheming, but v.17 opens a new, specific proposal ('Behold, my elder daughter Merab') distinct from the general popularity notice just given.

boundary_rationale: Saul's offer of his elder daughter Merab as a snare, with its explicit stated motive of exposing David to the Philistines, closes on the offer's quiet failure - she is given instead to Adriel - a short, self-contained betrothal episode that ends before Michal's parallel story begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Combining the Merab and Michal episodes into one marriage-scheme span was considered, but they are two distinct proposals with different outcomes, and the narrator marks the transition explicitly with 'Michal, Saul's daughter, loved David' as a fresh opening.

boundary_rationale: Michal's love for David opens a second, successful marriage scheme built on the foreskin bride-price plot, running through the servants' relayed message, David's response, the raid, and the marriage itself, closing on Saul giving Michal to David as wife (v.27, wayyitten lo sha'ul 'eth mikhal bittho le'ishah) -- the notice that Michal loved David and Saul saw it belongs to the following unit (M8-1Sam-121, 18:28-30) and is not part of this span's content. The deadline language ('Before the deadline,' v.26) occurs once, at the hinge between the proposal (vv.20-25) and its execution (v.26-27); it marks that turn rather than framing both halves of the episode.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the foreskin proposal (vv.20-25) from its execution and the wedding (vv.26-27) was considered, but the whole episode is bound together by David's own decisive completion of the task Saul set, with the deadline notice at v.26 marking (not spanning) the turn from proposal to execution.

boundary_rationale: The chapter closes with a generalizing summary of Saul's deepening fear and enmity alongside David's continued success against the Philistine princes, a durative register distinct from the dated marriage episode just concluded and closing the chapter on David's highly esteemed name.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching this closing summary to the Michal marriage narrative before it was considered, but the shift from a single dated wedding to an ongoing, repeated pattern ('as often as they went out') marks the summary-notice register the binding rules treat as a driving signal.

boundary_rationale: Saul's explicit kill order to Jonathan and the servants opens a new and more dangerous phase, met by Jonathan's intercession speech and Saul's oath not to put David to death, closing on David's restoration to Saul's presence 'as before' - a complete crisis-and-resolution arc before war resumes.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Jonathan's warning to David (vv.2-3) from his intercession with Saul (vv.4-6) was considered, but both halves serve one coordinated plan Jonathan lays out and carries through without a scene break in his own initiative.

boundary_rationale: War resumes and David's renewed success is followed immediately by the second javelin episode, opening on the evil spirit's return (wattehi ruach YHWH ra'ah 'el sha'ul) and closing on David's flight into the night, the episode that precipitates his permanent break with the court. This shares a three-element core with 18:10-12 (the evil-spirit-comes-on-Saul clause; 'David playing music with his hand'; the bedawid uvaqqir strike-formula) but is not a near-verbatim copy: the divine name and verb differ (wattitslach...'elohim at 18:10 vs. wattehi...YHWH here), 18:10's 'he prophesied in the house' clause is absent here, and the casting verb differs (wayyatel...'akkeh at 18:11 vs. wayevaqqesh lehakkoth here). This campaign's doublet discipline treats each as its own genuine, dated event rather than collapsing them; the motif in fact forms a three-member set with 20:30-34 (wayyatel sha'ul 'eth hachanith 'alaw lehakotho, verbally the closest match to 18:11's opening four words), not merely this two-member pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Collapsing this with 18:10-12 into a single cross-chapter span on the grounds of their near-verbatim parallel was considered and rejected, since the two are narrated as separate dated incidents with different immediate consequences -- the first ends in demotion, this one in flight. The relation is now described as a shared three-element formula inside materially different frames, and the fuller motif set (including 20:33's closer verbal match) is disclosed rather than treated as a simple pair.

boundary_rationale: Saul's messengers surround David's house, and Michal's teraphim ruse buys time for his escape through the window; the unit closes on her confrontation with her father, a bounded rescue-and-deception scene opening on the night watch and closing on Michal's self-protective lie to Saul. The escape itself is completed by the end of v.12 (a three-verb sequence: wayyelekh wayyivrach wayyimmalet, 'he went, fled, and escaped'), and only then does Michal stage the teraphim in the bed (v.13) as a delaying cover for an escape already made, not as preparation enabling it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the physical escape (vv.11-12) from the teraphim deception and its discovery (vv.13-17) was considered; the earlier ground for rejecting that split (that the ruse was prepared before the escape was complete) is corrected, since the text has the opposite order. The split is nonetheless still rejected, on the accurate ground that the whole sequence -- the messengers' night watch, David's completed escape, and Michal's delaying cover story -- functions as one coordinated rescue with a single deceptive object (the teraphim) at its center, resolving in her confrontation with Saul.

boundary_rationale: David flees to Samuel at Naioth, and three successive waves of Saul's messengers are seized by the prophetic Spirit before they can seize David, a triple-repetition pattern closing on the third wave's failure just before Saul goes himself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the three-wave pattern to include Saul's own journey and prophesying (vv.22-24) was considered, but Saul's personal involvement is introduced by a distinct 'Then he also went' clause that marks a climactic escalation beyond the messenger pattern.

boundary_rationale: Saul himself goes to Naioth, is overcome by the same prophetic Spirit, strips his clothes, and lies prophesying all day and night, closing on a distant etiological reprise of the proverb first coined at 10:11-12, 'Is Saul also among the prophets?' This is a distant reprise rather than an inclusio (the two occurrences bracket nine intervening chapters, not this unit), so the genuinely independent support for this unit's own closing edge is the chapter-final position itself together with a two-witness pe after 19:24 -- not the recurrence's borrowed force. The closer formal partner for the proverb-formation is 10:12 ('al ken hayethah lemashal, 'therefore it became a proverb'), which matches this verse's own 'al ken yo'meru ('therefore they say') more precisely than 10:11 does; the wording is identical at the qere/translation level but is spelled three different ways across the three consonantal printings (10:11 plene; 10:12 and 19:24 each with their own distinct defective spelling).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this into the preceding messenger-wave unit was considered, but Saul's own prophesying is a distinct climactic escalation with its own opening formula (wayyelekh gam hu', 'he too went') and its own chapter-final proverb-reprise, marking it off as the episode's capstone; the reprise is now described as an etiological recurrence resting on the chapter boundary and the two-witness pe, not as an inclusio.

boundary_rationale: David flees from Naioth to Jonathan and opens with a protest of innocence, met by Jonathan's confident denial that his father hides anything from him, closing on Jonathan's open-ended pledge to do whatever David's soul desires - an opening exchange before the specific new-moon plan is proposed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this to include the new-moon plan itself (vv.5-10) was considered, but David's specific proposal in v.5 shifts from general protest and reassurance into a concrete, detailed plan, a distinct rhetorical move.

boundary_rationale: David lays out the new-moon feast plan and the cover story Jonathan should give, and the two work through contingencies together, closing on David's question about how Jonathan will relay Saul's mood - a planning unit before the field conference where the actual covenant oath is sworn.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this planning conversation with the covenant oath that follows (vv.11-13) was considered, but v.11's move out into the field ('Let's go out into the field') marks a location shift away from wherever this initial conversation takes place.

boundary_rationale: The pair move to the field, and Jonathan swears his first oath by Yahweh to disclose any danger and send David away in peace, closing on the wish that Yahweh be with David as he was with Saul -- a personal, immediate pledge distinct from the trans-generational covenant terms that follow.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv.11-17 as one undivided covenant scene was considered, but the shift at v.14 broadens the oath's scope to concern for 'my house' (beithi, v.15; beith dawid, v.16) forever -- worth marking as its own unit. ('My offspring,' zar'i, is not part of this broadening: that word occurs in this chapter only at v.42, in the later parting oath, not in vv.14-17, and the earlier description is corrected accordingly.)

boundary_rationale: The covenant's scope extends explicitly to future generations - 'not when Yahweh has cut off every one of the enemies of David' - and the unit closes on the notice that Jonathan made David swear again 'for the love that he had for him,' a doubled oath-confirmation distinct from the initial personal pledge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this into the arrow-signal instructions that follow was considered, but v.18 opens a wholly practical, logistical register ('Tomorrow is the new moon, and you will be missed') distinct from the oath's relational and covenantal language.

boundary_rationale: Jonathan lays out the arrow-signal code in specific, list-like detail - three days, the stone Ezel, which words mean safety and which mean danger - closing on the reminder that Yahweh is witness 'between you and me forever,' a practical-instruction unit bounded by its own procedural content.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the arrow mechanics (vv.20-22) from the covenant reminder that closes the speech (v.23) was considered, but the reminder is presented as the rhetorical close of the same instructional speech, not a separate address.

boundary_rationale: The plan is enacted at the feast: David hides, Saul notices his empty seat over two days, and Jonathan finally offers the prepared cover story, closing the unit on Jonathan's explanation that David went to Bethlehem for a family sacrifice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the first day's silence (v.26) from the second day's confrontation (vv.27-29) was considered, but both are part of one continuous feast scene tracking the same empty seat across its two-day span without any change of setting.

boundary_rationale: Saul's fury erupts into a shaming rebuke of Jonathan and a spear cast aimed at his own son, closing on Jonathan's grief-driven refusal to eat and his departure from the table 'in fierce anger' - a violent rupture distinct in tone from the feast scene before it and the arrow-signal enactment that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching Jonathan's angry fast (v.34) to the arrow scene that follows was considered, but the fast is presented as the direct emotional consequence of the confrontation just narrated, closing that scene rather than opening the next morning's action.

boundary_rationale: The next morning the arrow signal is enacted, the boy is dismissed, and David and Jonathan meet for a final embrace and renewed oath 'between me and you, and between my offspring and your offspring, forever' (v.42, ending 'ad 'olam), closing the whole covenant sequence. Two disclosures follow from fresh verification of the underlying texts. First, this span's closing edge crosses the Masoretic chapter division without a dual citation: MT 1Sam.20.42 ends at 'ad 'olam, and the clause WEB prints as the remainder of the same verse -- 'He arose and departed; and Jonathan went into the city' -- is a separate verse in the Hebrew, MT 1Sam.21.1. This is the literal mechanical origin of chapter 21's mt_extra_1 status (WEB 15 verses vs. MT 16) recorded in web_mt_crosswalk.json; the crosswalk's chapter-20 'identical' relation (42/42) is a count-level artifact that conceals this content-level seam at the chapter's last verse. The closing edge is accordingly dual-cited below as WEB 1Sam.20.42 = MT 1Sam.20.42 + MT 1Sam.21.1, and the span is kept as drawn (WEB's own numbering is this campaign's citation register), rather than redrawn. A two-witness pe follows MT 20:42 -- i.e., it falls between the oath content and the departure clause, inside WEB's merged verse, and corroborates the MT chapter break rather than this span's WEB-numbered edge; disclosed rather than treated as supporting the drafted boundary at face value. Second, the claim that the arrow signal was enacted 'exactly as planned' is corrected: the plan specifies three arrows and a plural danger call (v.20, v.22), while the actual shooting is narrated with a singular arrow throughout (v.36, v.37), a plan/enactment divergence in number that v.38's own ketiv/qere (singular written, plural read) preserves rather than resolves.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the mechanical signal (vv.35-38) from the emotional farewell (vv.39-42) was considered, but the boy's ignorance of the code's real meaning is explicitly contrasted with what David and Jonathan alone know, binding the signal and the private farewell into one scene the boy's departure clears the stage for. The span is retained across the MT 20:42/21:1 seam rather than truncated at 'ad 'olam, since WEB's own verse numbering is the citation register this campaign uses throughout; what changes is disclosure, not the boundary.

boundary_rationale: David's flight brings him to Ahimelech at Nob, where his deceptive cover story about a secret royal mission secures him the holy bread; per this chapter's dual-citation status, both edges of this unit now carry MT pairings: the opening at oshb:1Sam.21.2 (=WEB 1Sam.21.1) and the closing at oshb:1Sam.21.7 (=WEB 1Sam.21.6), covering the same request-and-provision unit and closing when the priest hands over the show bread.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit to include the weapon request (vv.8-9) was considered, but the bread and the weapon are two separate requests, and the narrator inserts the Doeg notice between them, marking a deliberate pause rather than a single continuous ask.

strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this notice into either the bread request before it or the weapon request after it was considered, but its existential-clause form and its introduction of a wholly new character mid-scene mark it as a deliberate narratorial insertion distinct from David's own transaction with Ahimelech.

boundary_rationale: David's second request -- for a weapon, since he claims to have left in haste -- is answered with Goliath's own sword, still kept behind the ephod, closing on David's terse acceptance 'There is none like that. Give it to me.' Per this chapter's dual-citation status, both edges now carry MT pairings: oshb:1Sam.21.9 (=WEB 1Sam.21.8) at the opening and oshb:1Sam.21.10 (=WEB 1Sam.21.9) at the closing. A two-witness samekh falls at MT 21:9 (=WEB 21:8), i.e. inside this two-verse span between the request and the answer; disclosed as a weak, non-lifting internal division rather than treated as bearing on either outer edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this with the Nob bread scene as one continuous Ahimelech transaction was considered, but the intervening Doeg notice functions as a deliberate narrative pause the text itself inserts between the two requests.

boundary_rationale: David's flight to Achish of Gath opens the first of the book's two Gath episodes, and the servants' recognition of him via the very victory-song refrain already heard at 18:7 forces him into feigned madness, closing on Achish's dismissive question about why a madman was brought to him at all. The refrain the servants quote (MT 21:12 = WEB 21:11) is not a paraphrase but the same couplet as 18:7, and it recurs a third time at 29:5 in the mouths of the Philistine commanders -- a genuine triple, not a pair -- with the printed ketiv/qere varying at each site (18:7: first colon only; here: both cola; 29:5: second colon only), identical at the level a reader hears but variably spelled in the transmitted consonantal text. Per this chapter's dual-citation status, oshb:1Sam.21.11-1Sam.21.16 (=WEB 1Sam.21.10-1Sam.21.15).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the flight and recognition (vv.10-12) from the feigned-madness performance (vv.13-15) was considered, but the recognition is the direct cause of the performance, and both are part of one continuous crisis-and-response scene with the same participants throughout.

boundary_rationale: David's escape to the cave of Adullam opens a new phase entirely apart from Gath, drawing his family and then a band of the distressed, indebted, and discontented, closing on the notice that he became their captain over about four hundred men - the formation of David's outlaw following.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this to include the Moab relocation of his parents (vv.3-4) was considered, but that is a distinct diplomatic errand to a foreign king, introduced by David's own direct speech to Moab's ruler, not a continuation of the band's formation at Adullam.

boundary_rationale: David secures his parents' safety with the king of Moab, and the prophet Gad's oracle then redirects him out of the stronghold into the land of Judah, closing on his arrival in the forest of Hereth -- two short scenes bound by David's own itinerant movement between them. A two-witness samekh falls after 22:4, exactly at the seam between these two beats; disclosed here as weak, non-lifting corroboration for the alternative that was nonetheless not adopted.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the Moab errand and Gad's oracle as two separate spans was considered -- a two-witness samekh falls at exactly that seam (after 22:4) -- but both remain brief transitional beats governing David's whereabouts before the Saul court scene, and no sustained action develops within either alone, so they are kept together.

boundary_rationale: The scene shifts to Saul's own court under the tamarisk tree, where his accusatory speech to the assembled Benjamite officials draws out Doeg's volunteered report about Ahimelech's aid to David -- closing on the specific charges Doeg lays before the king.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding Doeg's report into the formal interrogation of Ahimelech that follows (vv.11-16) was considered, but a new participant group (Ahimelech and his father's whole priestly house, summoned from Nob) is brought before Saul at v.11, without any change of Saul's own location: the priests come to the king (wayyavo'u khullam 'el hammelekh), who remains where v.6 placed him. That summons-and-arrival of a new group, not a relocation to Nob, is the real seam distinguishing this scene from the interrogation that follows.

boundary_rationale: Ahimelech and his father's whole priestly house are summoned before Saul, and the interrogation-and-defense exchange (vv.11-15, closing on Ahimelech's protest of total ignorance, 'your servant knew nothing of all this, less or more') is answered by Saul's own formal death sentence against Ahimelech and his father's house, pronounced at v.16 ('You shall surely die, Ahimelech, you and all your father's house') -- this sentence is the unit's actual closing beat, not a development that occurs after it. The span closes on that sentence rather than 'before' it, correcting the earlier description, which mistakenly placed the sentence one verse later.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging the interrogation with the execution order and massacre that follow (vv.17-19) was considered, but v.17 opens a distinct speech act -- the king's command to the guard to carry out the sentence already pronounced at v.16 -- and its own darker register (command and killing) marks a second unit rather than a continuation of the interrogation-and-sentence scene. (The earlier rejected alternative mislabeled vv.17-19 itself as 'Saul's death sentence'; that sentence is v.16, inside this span, and vv.17-19 are the execution order and its carrying-out, corrected at M8-1Sam-143.)

boundary_rationale: The king's execution order to the guard -- carrying out the death sentence already pronounced against Ahimelech and his father's house at v.16 (in the preceding unit, M8-1Sam-142) -- meets the guards' refusal to strike Yahweh's priests, and Doeg's willing execution of eighty-five priests and the whole city of Nob forms the chapter's darkest and most decisive turn, opening on the king's order to the runners (sovvu wehamithu kohanei YHWH) and closing on the total destruction of the city 'with the edge of the sword.' A two-witness samekh falls after 22:17, exactly at the seam between the guards' refusal and Doeg's compliance; disclosed as weak, non-lifting corroboration for the rejected split.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the guards' refusal (v.17) from Doeg's compliance (vv.18-19) was considered -- a two-witness samekh falls at exactly that seam -- but the refusal exists specifically to set up Doeg's contrasting willingness in the same breath, forming one cause-and-effect unit about who will and will not do this violence.

boundary_rationale: Abiathar's escape and report of the massacre to David close the chapter on David's own acknowledgment of guilt and his offer of protection - 'I am responsible for the death of all the persons of your father's house' - a reflective, relational unit distinct from the massacre's action-driven register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Abiathar's flight (v.20) separately from David's response (vv.21-23) was considered, but the report and reaction form one uninterrupted exchange between the sole survivor and the man he has fled to.

boundary_rationale: News of the Philistine raid on Keilah opens a new campaign, and David's double oracular inquiry through Yahweh - overriding his men's fear the second time - leads directly into the rescue battle, closing on the notice that David saved Keilah's inhabitants.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the two inquiries (vv.2 and 4) from the battle itself (v.5) was considered, but the second inquiry's answer is presented as the immediate authorization for the attack narrated in the same verse-group, with no scene gap.

boundary_rationale: This single verse is an explanatory aside noting that Abiathar arrived at Keilah with an ephod in hand, supplying the mechanism the narrative will need for the oracular inquiries that follow in vv.9-12. Its isolating signal is not, as previously argued, a resemblance to the reader-directed terminology gloss at 9:9 (a different construction: lefanim plus an explanatory frame) -- the verse's own opening, wayehi bivroach, is an ordinary wayehi-plus-infinitive construction that elsewhere in this book opens perfectly ordinary main-line episodes (e.g. 25:2, 30:1) and carries no backgrounding force by itself. The genuine signal is the verse's second half, a fronted-object-plus-qatal clause ('efod yarad beyado, 'an ephod came down in his hand'), which registers a standing prop rather than advancing the action -- a retrospective, flashback-style clause supplying material the coming inquiry scenes will need, told out of strict narrative sequence.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this note into the following siege-and-inquiry unit was considered, but its explanatory, background-supplying function -- now grounded in the fronted-object-plus-qatal construction rather than in a false analogy to 9:9's authorial-commentary register -- is closer in kind to a flashback clause supplying a prop for the coming scenes than to the narrated sequence of Saul's plan that follows.

boundary_rationale: Saul's plan to besiege David at Keilah, David's use of the newly available ephod for a double oracular inquiry about the town's loyalty, and the resulting escape before Saul arrives form one bounded unit, opening on Saul's confident 'God has delivered him into my hand' and closing on the notice that Saul gave up going to Keilah once David had already left.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Saul's siege plan (vv.7-8) from David's inquiry and escape (vv.9-13) was considered, but the plan's specific threat is what prompts David's inquiry in the same breath, and both halves resolve together in the departure that closes the unit.

boundary_rationale: David's move to the wilderness of Ziph opens a new phase of pursuit, and Jonathan's secret visit there provides a third covenant renewal - 'you will be king over Israel, and I will be next to you' - closing on their mutual covenant before Yahweh and Jonathan's return home. This unit is not textured uniformly throughout: vv.14-15a form a general summary of David's fugitive condition, closing on a verbless disjunctive ('וְדָוִ֥ד בְּמִדְבַּר זִ֖יף בַּחֹֽרְשָׁה,' 'David was in the wilderness of Ziph in the woods'), while vv.15b-18 stage the specific, located Jonathan-visit episode. Chorshah ('the woods') recurs at all three of v.15 (bachorshah, closing the summary), v.16 (chorshah, opening the located episode), and v.18 (bachorshah, closing the covenant); its recurrence is weak corroboration of the whole unit's continuity across all three verses, not proof that binds only the second beat. A WEB paragraph break (immediately before v.16) and a two-witness samekh (after MT 23:15) corroborate treating vv.14-15a and vv.15b-18 as two beats within this larger unit, rather than reading the whole span as textured uniformly. Citation disclosure: chapter 23 is a WEB/MT verse-count mismatch (web_mt_crosswalk.json: relation=web_extra_1, 29 WEB verses / 28 MT verses), requiring dual citation per that file's own rule; 23:14-18 itself carries identical WEB and MT numbering throughout, since the extra WEB verse falls at the chapter's very end - WEB 1Sam.23.29 ('David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of En Gedi.') corresponds to MT 1Sam.24.1 (וַיַּ֥עַל דָּוִ֖ד מִשָּׁ֑ם וַיֵּ֖שֶׁב בִּמְצָד֥וֹת עֵֽין גֶּֽדִי), outside this span.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this visit with the Ziphite betrayal that follows (vv.19-23) was considered, but Jonathan's private, supportive visit and the Ziphites' hostile report to Saul are two starkly opposed encounters with different participants and outcomes, not one continuous scene. A split isolating vv.14-15a (the general pursuit summary) from vv.15b-18 (the dated Jonathan encounter) was also considered, since a WEB paragraph break and a two-witness samekh after MT 23:15 both corroborate that seam; it is subordinated here because both beats belong to one continuous movement - David's time in the Ziph wilderness - that only completes with the covenant sworn at v.18, rather than treated as two separate units.

boundary_rationale: The Ziphites travel to Saul at Gibeah with a betrayal offer, and Saul's blessing of the informants together with his detailed tracking instructions closes the unit just before the pursuit itself is narrated. This is the first of two Ziphite betrayal reports; its recurrence at 26:1 shares a six-word core ('to Saul at Gibeah, saying, Does not David hide himself') plus the toponym Hachilah, but is a compressed restatement rather than a near-verbatim echo: 26:1 changes the main verb, adds the article to the subject, drops the entire 'with us, in the strongholds, in Horesh' locative sequence present here, and recasts the modifier on hayeshimon. (For comparison, the book's genuine near-verbatim recurrence is the oracular-inquiry formula at 23:2/30:8, four words identical: wayyish'al dawid baYHWH le'mor.)
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this to include the actual pursuit to Maon (vv.24-28) was considered, but v.24 shifts from Saul's instructions to the Ziphites' own departure and the narrated chase, a distinct action-phase following the planning just completed.

boundary_rationale: The chase to the wilderness of Maon brings Saul's and David's forces to opposite sides of the same mountain, and just as capture seems imminent, a messenger's report of a Philistine raid pulls Saul away - closing on the etiological naming of Sela Hammahlekoth, 'rock of parting.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through David's relocation to En Gedi (v.29) was considered, but that verse is, per this chapter's own dual-citation status, the Masoretic text's actual opening verse of the En Gedi narrative rather than a coda to the Maon chase, and is treated here as opening the next, chapter-crossing unit instead.

boundary_rationale: This span deliberately crosses the chapter line: what WEB numbers as 23:29 is, per the verified crosswalk, the Masoretic text's own opening verse of the En Gedi narrative - oshb:1Sam.24.1 (=WEB 1Sam.23.29) - so the relocation notice, the cave encounter, and David's secret cutting of Saul's robe belong to one continuous scene that only completes with his men's restraint in v.7; ending at the WEB chapter line would sever the episode from its own textually-marked beginning.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Respecting the WEB chapter boundary and starting the En Gedi unit at 24:1 was considered and rejected, since the crosswalk explicitly identifies WEB 23:29 as the Hebrew text's structural opening of this narrative, making the chapter-line-crossing span the more text-faithful choice.

boundary_rationale: David emerges from the cave and calls after Saul, opening an extended self-defense oration - displaying the cut robe-corner as proof, invoking the ancients' proverb about wickedness, and asking rhetorically whether the king pursues 'a dead dog, a flea' - closing on his appeal for Yahweh to judge between them; per this chapter's dual-citation status, oshb:1Sam.24.9-1Sam.24.16 (=WEB 1Sam.24.8-1Sam.24.15).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the physical evidence display (vv.8-11) from the rhetorical appeal (vv.12-15) was considered, but both are part of one sustained, uninterrupted speech David delivers to Saul across the ravine without any narrated pause.

boundary_rationale: Saul's weeping response and acknowledgment that David is more righteous close out the En Gedi encounter, moving through his admission that David will surely be king and his request for an oath protecting his descendants, closing on David's oath and the two men's departure: Saul returns home (wayyelekh sha'ul 'el beitho, 'Saul went to his house'), while David and his men go up to the stronghold (wedawid wa'anashaw 'alu 'al hammetsudah, singular and definite) -- not, as previously described, a mutual parting to separate strongholds. Per this chapter's dual-citation status, oshb:1Sam.24.16-1Sam.24.23 (=WEB 1Sam.24.16-1Sam.24.22).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Saul's confession (vv.16-19) from his oath request (vv.20-22) was considered, but both are part of Saul's single continuous speech turn, with no intervening action or renewed address formula between them.

boundary_rationale: Samuel's death and burial notice is a self-contained obituary formula recurring in content (though not in grammatical construction) with the later reminder at 28:3, standing apart from both the En Gedi narrative just concluded and the Nabal story David's relocation to Paran opens. This verse is a wayyiqtol chain of six coordinated verbs (wayyamoth Shemu'el, wayyiqqavtsu, wayyispedu, wayyiqberuhu bevaitho baramah, 'Samuel died...and buried him at his house at Ramah,' then wayyaqom David, wayyered el midbar Paran, 'David arose and went down to the wilderness of Paran,' the relocation clause folding David's departure into the same notice), not a regnal-type notice: it carries no accession formula, reign-length figure, or succession clause, and its construction is the opposite of 28:3's own double waw-plus-subject-plus-qatal disjunctive. Retyped as narrative_prose accordingly; the relation to 28:3 is one of shared content (death, mourning, burial) rather than shared grammatical form. Disclosure, as weak corroborating metadata rather than a driver of this decision: WEB places its own paragraph break mid-verse, between the burial notice and 'Then David arose,' and a two-witness samekh sits at this verse's own rear edge (1Sam.25.1); neither is load-bearing for the boundary, which rests on the verse's self-contained obituary-plus-relocation content.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the relocation clause to the following Nabal exposition (vv.2-3) was considered, but the obituary and the relocation are reported as one compact notice functioning as a hinge -- confirmed by v.2's own verbless disjunctive opening ('we'ish bema'on,' 'there was a man in Maon'), which begins the Nabal exposition proper only after this verse closes -- not as the start of the Nabal narrative's own character introductions.

boundary_rationale: Nabal and Abigail are introduced by name and by contrasting character - his surliness against her intelligence and beauty - a short exposition unit that closes before David's messengers are dispatched.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this introduction into the messenger scene that follows (vv.4-9) was considered, but the character sketch is complete in itself and precedes any narrated action involving David directly.

boundary_rationale: David hears of the shearing and sends ten young men with a formally worded peace greeting and provision request, closing on the messengers' delivery of David's exact words and their waiting for a reply - a self-contained envoy scene bounded by dispatch and delivery.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this through Nabal's refusal (v.10 onward) was considered, but Nabal's answer opens with its own address formula ('Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse?') marking a clear speaker change and rhetorical turn from request to rejection.

boundary_rationale: Nabal's insulting refusal, the messengers' report back to David, and David's arming of four hundred men for reprisal form one escalation unit, closing on the detail that two hundred stayed with the baggage - a foreshadowing element that becomes relevant again in chapter 30.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Nabal's refusal speech (v.10-11) from David's armed response (vv.12-13) was considered, but the report and the reaction are presented in one uninterrupted narrative movement with no scene gap between hearing the insult and arming for revenge.

boundary_rationale: A servant's warning report to Abigail opens a new vantage point on the crisis, praising David's men's earlier protection of the flocks and urging Abigail to act, closing on his verdict that Nabal is 'such a worthless fellow that one can't speak to him.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this report with Abigail's own provisioning response (vv.18-22) was considered, but her decisive action begins with a fresh 'Then Abigail hurried' clause marking her own initiative as a distinct beat from the servant's warning that prompts it.

boundary_rationale: Abigail's swift, itemized provisioning - bread, wine, dressed sheep, grain, raisins, fig cakes, loaded on donkeys - functions almost as a register within the narrative, and the unit closes on David's own oath of vengeance sworn as she rides to meet him, a scene David's own words bring to a head just before their encounter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the provisioning list (v.18) from David's oath (vv.21-22) was considered, but both are bound together by Abigail's journey toward the encounter that the oath anticipates, forming one build-up unit before they actually meet.

boundary_rationale: Abigail dismounts and prostrates herself, opening an extended intercession speech with self-abasement and the presentation of her gift, closing on her request that the provisions be given to David's young men - the diplomatic, gift-giving half of her appeal before its theological argument begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv.23-31 as one undivided speech was considered, but the shift at v.28 from apology and gift-presentation to forward-looking theological argument about David's 'sure house' and future kingship marks a distinct rhetorical movement worth its own unit.

boundary_rationale: Abigail's speech turns from apology to theological and political argument -- Yahweh will make David 'a sure house,' his life is 'bound in the bundle of life,' and he is destined to be 'prince over Israel' -- closing on her forward-looking plea that he remember her once Yahweh has dealt well with him. The turn itself does not fall cleanly at the 27/28 boundary: v.28 is a compound verse, opening with the apology petition itself ('please forgive the trespass of your servant') before turning, in its second half, to the sure-house promise. Since spans are drawn at verse granularity, v.28 is assigned to this forward-looking unit because its dominant and longer content is the dynastic argument that continues through v.31, not because a clean formal break falls at 27/28.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping this as the closing section of one long undivided speech-span was considered, but the argument's content does shift, over the course of v.28, from present request to future destiny -- a change in rhetorical aim the campaign's binding rules treat as a legitimate internal seam, even though that shift completes inside v.28 rather than exactly at its boundary.
boundary_evidence_refs: web:1Sam.25.27 Now this present which your servant has brought to my lord, let it be given to the young men who follow my lord.
web:1Sam.25.28 Please forgive the trespass of your servant. For Yahweh will certainly make my lord a sure house...

web:1Sam.25.30 It will come to pass, when Yahweh has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you prince over Israel,

web:1Sam.25.31 that this shall be no grief to you, nor offense of heart to my lord, either that you have shed blood without cause, or that my lord has avenged himself. When Yahweh has dealt well with my lord, then remember your servant."

boundary_rationale: David's grateful response blesses Yahweh for sending Abigail, praises her discretion, and accepts her gift, closing on his instruction for her to go home in peace - a reply unit distinct from her preceding speech and from the Nabal household scene that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this to Nabal's feast (vv.36-38) was considered, but a full location and participant change - Abigail returning home to a drunken Nabal unaware of any of this - opens a new scene at v.36.

boundary_rationale: Nabal's drunken feast, Abigail's delayed disclosure the next morning, and the onset of what reads as a stroke followed by his death ten days later at Yahweh's hand form a tightly sequenced three-beat unit closing the Nabal half of the story. Two wayehi-plus-temporal markers sit inside this three-verse span -- wayehi babboqer at v.37 and, separately, wayehi ka'asereth hayyamim at v.38, a larger displacement (ten days against one morning). Both are disposed of rather than only one: the emphatic double-scope negation at v.36 ('she told him not a word, small or great, until the morning light') is answered directly by the morning collapse in the very next verse, and the ten-day marker at v.38 is the narrated delayed outcome of that same stroke -- Yahweh's striking of Nabal and his death are one causal event reported across two verses (the onset in v.37, the fatal end ten days later in v.38), not an independent new scene requiring its own boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the feast and delayed telling (v.36) from the death itself (vv.37-38) was considered, but the delay is explicitly narrated as a deliberate choice whose payoff is the collapse in the very next verse. A further split isolating v.38's own ten-day marker was also considered, since that wayehi-plus-temporal frame is treated as seam evidence elsewhere in this range (30:1, 27:7, 31:8); it is subordinated here because the stroke (v.37) and the death (v.38) are one continuous causal sequence -- onset and fatal outcome of the same divinely-caused event -- not two separately triggered scenes.

oshb:1Sam.25.38 וַיְהִ֖י כַּעֲשֶׂ֣רֶת הַיָּמִ֑ים וַיִּגֹּ֧ף יְהוָ֛ה אֶת נָבָ֖ל וַיָּמֹֽת (second, larger wayehi+temporal marker, now disposed of explicitly)

boundary_rationale: David's response to Nabal's death - blessing Yahweh for vindicating him - opens a marriage proposal to Abigail, and the unit closes on her acceptance and departure to become his wife, resolving the Nabal story's romantic thread.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the closing genealogical notices (vv.43-44) into this unit was considered, but those verses shift into a register of bare notation about a second wife and Michal's reassignment, without any narrated scene or dialogue, marking a distinct closing-notice unit.

boundary_rationale: The chapter closes with two matched marital/annalistic notices, each built on a suspended clause -- v.43 fronts its object (we'eth 'achino'am laqach dawid, 'David also took Ahinoam') and v.44 fronts its subject (wesha'ul nathan, 'Saul had given...') -- a matched syntactic pair rather than a lineage chain or begetting formula, so 'genealogical_register' is retyped as an annalistic-notice class. V.43's own wording ('gam shteihen,' 'also, the two of them') explicitly reaches back to the Abigail marriage just narrated; this is acknowledged as a genuine semantic tie across the 42/43 seam, but it is retained as texture rather than treated as grounds to relocate v.43 into the preceding unit, since the matched fronted-clause syntax of vv.43-44 is what actually binds this pair together as its own closing unit -- and a two-witness samekh falls between the two verses, an alternative (a 43/44 split) the earlier rejected alternative never named.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging these notices into the Abigail marriage unit was considered -- v.43's own 'also, the two of them' explicitly backreferences that marriage -- but the matched fronted-clause syntax linking v.43 and v.44 argues for keeping them as their own paired unit rather than folding v.43 backward. A split between v.43 and v.44 was also considered, since a two-witness samekh falls precisely between them, but is subordinated to the syntactic pairing, which binds the two verses together as parallel suspended-clause notices closing the chapter.

boundary_rationale: A second Ziphite betrayal report reopens the pursuit, and Saul's descent to Hachilah is met by David's own reconnaissance of the camp, closing on his sighting of where Saul and Abner actually lie -- the opening moves of the book's second full sparing narrative, run parallel to but independent of chapter 24's En Gedi episode. The report shares a six-word core with 23:19 ('to Saul at Gibeah, saying, Does not David hide himself') plus the Hachilah toponym, but is a compressed restatement rather than a near-copy: the main verb changes (wayya'alu -> wayyavo'u), the subject gains the article, the entire 'with us, in the strongholds, in Horesh' locative sequence present at 23:19 is dropped, and the hayeshimon modifier is recast.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the Ziphite report here as continuous with the earlier one at 23:19 was considered, but the two are separated by the Maon chase (23:24-28), the En Gedi encounter (23:29-24:22), and the entire Nabal narrative (ch.25) -- Achish does not enter the story until 27:1, after this chapter, so the earlier description citing 'the entire Nabal and Achish material' as the intervening content is corrected to name only the material that actually intervenes. The two reports are narrated as distinct, re-triggered episodes, so this occurrence opens its own unit rather than extending the earlier one; the near-verbatim characterization of their relationship is corrected as above.

boundary_rationale: The night infiltration of Saul's camp is a self-contained scene -- Abishai's volunteering, David's restraint speech invoking Yahweh's anointed, and the taking of the spear and water jar as silent proof -- opening on David's question 'Who will go down with me' and closing on the notice that a deep sleep from Yahweh had fallen on the whole camp. The exchange is not, in fact, wholly uninterrupted: David's speech is introduced twice with wayyomer dawid (v.9, addressing Abishai directly; v.10, resuming without any intervening answer from Abishai), and a two-witness pe falls exactly at that join. This doubled introduction is read as rhetorical emphasis -- David silencing Abishai's proposal and restating his own reasoning at greater length -- rather than a compositional seam, since the whole exchange still resolves directly into the action David proposes without any change of scene, location, or participants.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Abishai's offer to kill Saul (vv.8-9) from the taking of the relics (vv.11-12) was considered; the earlier ground for rejecting that split (an uninterrupted exchange) is corrected, since v.9 and v.10 each reintroduce David with wayyomer dawid and no answering turn from Abishai stands between them, with a two-witness pe marking that seam. The split is nonetheless still rejected: the doubled introduction reads as David's own emphatic restatement rather than a change of scene, and the whole passage resolves directly into the action it proposes.

web:1Sam.26.12 So David took the spear and the jar of water from Saul's head, and they went away... because a deep sleep from Yahweh had fallen on them.
