A PE mark (single-witness) already stands one verse earlier, after the building programme's own success formula at web:2Chr.14.7 = oshb:2Chr.14.6 (MT); a SAMEKH mark (single-witness) then follows the muster verse itself, so both tier-3 witnesses sit inside this closing pair rather than only the one the row leaned on.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the muster (v8) forward as the Zerah unit's own cause-clause is possible, but Jehoshaphat's later muster at 17:14-19 closes an identical list-shape ("אֵ֖לֶּה הַמְשָׁרְתִ֣ים אֶת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ מִלְּבַ֞ד אֲשֶׁר נָתַ֥ן הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ בְּעָרֵ֥י הַמִּבְצָ֖ר בְּכָל יְהוּדָֽה", WEB "These were those who waited on the king, in addition to those whom the king put in the fortified cities throughout all Judah.") and is trailed by wholly unrelated material at 18:1 ("וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט עֹ֥שֶׁר וְכָב֖וֹד לָרֹ֑ב וַיִּתְחַתֵּ֖ן לְאַחְאָֽב"), not a battle -- showing a tallied muster caps a king's-strength report in this book's own convention rather than setting a scene for whatever follows, which is the discriminating reason the 'descriptive inventory' label alone was missing.

boundary_rationale: Zerah's entrance, web:2Chr.14.9 = oshb:2Chr.14.8 (MT), וַיֵּצֵ֨א אֲלֵיהֶ֜ם זֶ֣רַח הַכּוּשִׁ֗י ("Zerah the Ethiopian came out against them"), opens the war the prior row's muster anticipated. Inside it Asa's prayer is quoted, web:2Chr.14.11 = oshb:2Chr.14.10 (MT), וַיִּקְרָ֨א אָסָ֜א אֶל יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהָיו֮ וַיֹּאמַר֒ ("Asa cried to Yahweh his God, and said"); under the inset rule it stays inside this battle report rather than forming its own row, since nothing frames it off on the far side and the very next clause is Yahweh's answering strike. The unit runs through pursuit and plunder to its close, web:2Chr.14.15 = oshb:2Chr.14.14 (MT), וְגַם אָהֳלֵ֥י מִקְנֶ֖ה הִכּ֑וּ וַיִּשְׁבּ֨וּ צֹ֤אן לָרֹב֙ וּגְמַלִּ֔ים וַיָּשֻׁ֖בוּ יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם ("They also struck the tents of those who had livestock...then returned to Jerusalem"), which is also the last verse of the WEB/MT offset. A SAMEKH mark (single-witness) follows this verse, and the next unit opens with an unrelated prophetic frame, web:2Chr.15.1, וַעֲזַרְיָ֨הוּ֙ בֶּן עוֹדֵ֔ד הָיְתָ֥ה עָלָ֖יו ר֥וּחַ אֱלֹהִֽים ("The Spirit of God came on Azariah the son of Oded"), where WEB and MT numbering realign.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating the prayer (v11) as its own row finds tier-3 color in the SAMEKH (single-witness) standing right behind it, between the prayer and the strike -- but per the marker policy that mark is weak corroboration only, never a driver, and the immediate divine strike shows prayer and victory are one continuous clause-chain, not a bracketed insert, so the mark does not unseat that continuity.

boundary_rationale: A fresh prophet-notice frame opens the row, וַעֲזַרְיָ֨הוּ֙ בֶּן עוֹדֵ֔ד הָיְתָ֥ה עָלָ֖יו ר֥וּחַ אֱלֹהִֽים ("The Spirit of God came on Azariah the son of Oded"), and Azariah addresses Asa with the same vocative device Abijah used earlier in this part (13:4), here at v2, וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֔וֹ שְׁמָע֕וּנִי אָסָ֖א וְכָל יְהוּדָ֣ה וּבִנְיָמִ֑ן ("and said to him, 'Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin'"). The oracle runs through Israel's lawless past to an exhortation and closes before Asa's reaction, וְכִשְׁמֹ֨עַ אָסָ֜א הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה וְהַנְּבוּאָה֮ עֹדֵ֣ד הַנָּבִיא֒ הִתְחַזַּ֗ק ("When Asa heard these words...he took courage"), a response formula that shifts from direct address to third-person report. A SAMEKH mark (single-witness) follows v7, corroborating the seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through v8 to include Asa's response would merge two distinct forms, oracle and reform report, under one label, when the 'when X heard' formula is itself a recognized transition.

boundary_rationale: "וְכִשְׁמֹ֨עַ אָסָ֜א הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה וְהַנְּבוּאָה֮ עֹדֵ֣ד הַנָּבִיא֒ הִתְחַזַּ֗ק וַיַּעֲבֵ֤ר הַשִּׁקּוּצִים֙ מִכָּל אֶ֤רֶץ יְהוּדָה֙ וּבִנְיָמִ֔ן וּמִן הֶ֣עָרִ֔ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר לָכַ֖ד מֵהַ֣ר אֶפְרָ֑יִם וַיְחַדֵּשׁ֙ אֶת מִזְבַּ֣ח יְהוָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֕ר לִפְנֵ֖י אוּלָ֥ם יְהוָֽה" ("When Asa heard these words and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage, and put away the abominations out of all the land of Judah and Benjamin, and out of the cities which he had taken from the hill country of Ephraim; and he renewed Yahweh’s altar that was before Yahweh’s porch.") opens his reform response to the oracle just closed, moving from idol removal to an assembly summons; the qal "וַיִּקְבֹּ֗ץ" of v.9, with Asa himself as agent, gives way to the niphal "וַיִּקָּבְצ֥וּ יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם בַּחֹ֣דֶשׁ הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֑י לִשְׁנַ֥ת חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה לְמַלְכ֥וּת אָסָֽא" of v.10 ("So they gathered themselves together at Jerusalem in the third month, in the fifteenth year of Asa’s reign."), the people now the grammatical subject of their own dated compliance -- a PE mark (single-witness) stands between the two verses, but v.10's niphal carries no independent subject expression of its own; it reads as the executed result of v.9's qal summons, with the date attaching to the compliance rather than opening a fresh scene, so the shift is summons-then-compliance inside one assembly frame, not an unmarked participant-change seam. (Disclosure: the strategy's device matrix labels this class 'קהל-family openings,' but a consonantal sweep of the whole of ch.15 returns zero קהל-root hits; the forms actually instantiated at 15:9-10 are both קבץ-root, so the device-matrix citation named for this locus is the wrong root family, and the text-internal grammatical reading above, not the matrix entry, is what carries this row's boundary reading.) Sacrifice and covenant oath follow, and the unit closes on the rest notice, "וַיִּשְׂמְח֨וּ כָל יְהוּדָ֜ה עַל הַשְּׁבוּעָ֗ה כִּ֤י בְכָל לְבָבָם֙ נִשְׁבָּ֔עוּ וּבְכָל רְצוֹנָ֣ם בִּקְשֻׁ֔הוּ וַיִּמָּצֵ֖א לָהֶ֑ם וַיָּ֧נַח יְהוָ֛ה לָהֶ֖ם מִסָּבִֽיב" ("All Judah rejoiced at the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and sought him with their whole desire; and he was found by them. Then Yahweh gave them rest all around."), which is no bare topic-marker: the same rest-and-'all around' diction closes Asa's earlier building report three rows back, "וַיָּ֥נַֽח לָ֖נוּ מִסָּבִ֑יב" (14:6 MT, WEB 14:7, "he has given us rest on every side"), bracketing the whole reform-battle-covenant complex this cluster's rows traverse; only after that echoed close does the text pivot, "וְגַֽם מַעֲכָ֞ה אֵ֣ם אָסָ֣א הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ" ("Also Maacah, the mother of Asa the king"), to a personal notice no longer tied to the assembly. That right-edge pivot is a plain topic change rather than a marked formula, but it follows an inclusio-strengthened rest notice rather than a bare one, which is why confidence moves up here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the row through v19 to include the Maacah and treasury notices would treat the whole chapter's second half as one block, obscuring that the assembly-and-oath material has its own inclusio-marked rest-notice close.

boundary_rationale: וְגַֽם מַעֲכָ֞ה אֵ֣ם אָסָ֣א הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ ("Also Maacah, the mother of Asa the king") opens a dynastic notice unconnected to the assembly just closed, at once qualified by וְהַ֨בָּמ֔וֹת לֹא סָ֖רוּ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵ֑ל ("the high places were not taken away out of Israel"), a caveat on the reform's completeness. It closes on the chronological peace notice, וּמִלְחָמָ֖ה לֹ֣א הָיָ֑תָה עַ֛ד שְׁנַת שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וְחָמֵ֖שׁ לְמַלְכ֥וּת אָסָֽא ("There was no more war to the thirty-fifth year of Asa's reign"), answered almost word for word by the next chapter's crisis, בִּשְׁנַ֨ת שְׁלֹשִׁ֤ים וָשֵׁשׁ֙ לְמַלְכ֣וּת אָסָ֔א עָלָ֞ה בַּעְשָׁ֤א מֶֽלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ עַל יְהוּדָ֔ה ("In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, Baasha...went up"). That paired year-count is the row's firm right edge; its own left edge, the 'also' notice, is a weaker connective, so confidence is held at medium.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 15:16-18 as a coda separate from the v19 peace notice is possible, but v19 carries no formula strong enough to isolate it from the Maacah-and-fidelity material it summarizes.

boundary_rationale: The year-count crisis notice, בִּשְׁנַ֨ת שְׁלֹשִׁ֤ים וָשֵׁשׁ֙ לְמַלְכ֣וּת אָסָ֔א עָלָ֞ה בַּעְשָׁ֤א מֶֽלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ עַל יְהוּדָ֔ה ("In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah"), answers 15:19's peace notice directly and opens the row. Asa's message to Ben-hadad is sent via the ordinary messenger formula closing v.2, "וַיֹּצֵ֨א אָסָ֜א כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֗ב מֵאֹֽצְר֛וֹת בֵּ֥ית יְהוָ֖ה וּבֵ֣ית הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיִּשְׁלַ֗ח אֶל בֶּן הֲדַד֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ אֲרָ֔ם הַיּוֹשֵׁ֥ב בְּדַרְמֶ֖שֶׂק לֵאמֹֽר" ("Then Asa brought out silver and gold out of the treasures of Yahweh’s house and of the king’s house, and sent to Ben Hadad king of Syria, who lived at Damascus, saying,"), with the message itself quoted in full at v.3 alone, "בְּרִית֙ בֵּינִ֣י וּבֵינֶ֔ךָ וּבֵ֥ין אָבִ֖י וּבֵ֣ין אָבִ֑יךָ הִנֵּ֨ה שָׁלַ֤חְתִּֽי לְךָ֙ כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֔ב לֵ֞ךְ הָפֵ֣ר בְּרִֽיתְךָ֗ אֶת בַּעְשָׁא֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְיַעֲלֶ֖ה מֵעָלָֽי" ("“Let there be a treaty between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I have sent you silver and gold. Go, break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, that he may depart from me.”"); it is a messenger speech rather than a letter -- no מכתב or אגרות lexeme appears in either verse, unlike the book's actual letter insets (21:12's "מִכְתָּ֔ב", 30:1's "אִגְּרוֹת֙") -- and as one verse of quoted content framed by v.2's sending notice, it stays inside this diplomatic-and-military report under the inset rule rather than forming its own row. Ben-hadad's raid answers the message at once, striking Israelite cities (v.4), and Baasha responds by abandoning the Ramah works, וַיְהִי֙ כִּשְׁמֹ֣עַ בַּעְשָׁ֔א וַיֶּחְדַּ֕ל מִבְּנ֖וֹת אֶת הָרָמָ֑ה וַיַּשְׁבֵּ֖ת אֶת מְלַאכְתּֽוֹ (“when Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah, and let his work cease,” v.5); a SAMEKH (single-witness) follows this verse too. The unit closes on Asa's own building notice, וַיִּ֣בֶן בָּהֶ֔ם אֶת גֶּ֖בַע וְאֶת הַמִּצְפָּֽה ("he built Geba and Mizpah with them"), completing rather than merely following v.5's abandonment: Asa dismantles the very Ramah fortress named at v.1's opening and repurposes its stones and timber to build Geba and Mizpah, an inclusio on Ramah rather than two adjacent, unrelated building notices; the next verse introduces a new figure with a time-marker, וּבָעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא בָּ֚א חֲנָ֣נִי הָרֹאֶ֔ה אֶל אָסָ֖א מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ("At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said"), a prophet-entrance frame unrelated to the building report. A SAMEKH mark (single-witness) follows the building notice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Asa's message off as its own row overstates a one-verse quoted speech that never functions apart from the two-verse sending-and-message frame that carries it.

boundary_rationale: Hanani's arrival, וּבָעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא בָּ֚א חֲנָ֣נִי הָרֹאֶ֔ה אֶל אָסָ֖א מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֑ה וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ("At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah, and said"), opens the row and echoes Azariah's earlier arrival in this same part (15:1-2), though the message here rebukes rather than exhorts, turning on כִּ֣י יְהוָ֗ה עֵינָ֞יו מְשֹׁטְט֤וֹת בְּכָל הָאָ֨רֶץ֙ לְ֠הִתְחַזֵּק עִם לְבָבָ֥ם שָׁלֵ֛ם אֵלָ֖יו נִסְכַּ֣לְתָּ עַל זֹ֑את ("Yahweh's eyes run back and forth throughout the whole earth...You have done foolishly in this"). Unlike the Azariah scene, the reaction here is folded into the same row rather than answered by reform: וַיִּכְעַ֨ס אָסָ֜א אֶל הָרֹאֶ֗ה וַֽיִּתְּנֵ֨הוּ֙ בֵּ֣ית הַמַּהְפֶּ֔כֶת כִּֽי בְזַ֥עַף עִמּ֖וֹ עַל זֹ֑את וַיְרַצֵּ֥ץ אָסָ֛א מִן הָעָ֖ם בָּעֵ֥ת הַהִֽיא ("Then Asa was angry with the seer, and put him in the prison...Asa oppressed some of the people at the same time"), a single verse of hostile reaction too slight to carry its own row. The row ends there because v.11 opens the reign-closing source-citation class in its own presentative variant, וְהִנֵּה֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י אָסָ֔א הָרִאשׁוֹנִ֖ים וְהָאַחֲרוֹנִ֑ים הִנָּ֤ם כְּתוּבִים֙ ("Behold, the acts of Asa, first and last...are written") — that fronted וְהִנֵּה֙ opener is unique to 16:11 among the book's reign-closers, though its own closing verb (“they are written”) is not distinctive on its own: a consonantal sweep for henam ketuvim returns 11 hits book-wide (16:11, 20:34, 24:27, 25:26, 27:7, 28:26, 32:32, 33:19, 35:25, 35:27, 36:8), so it is the class's ordinary closing verb rather than a mark of 16:11's own individuality. The class's opener otherwise runs וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י ten times (13:22 among them), וּשְׁאָר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י once at 9:29, or a bare וְדִבְרֵ֣י at 12:15 -- and 24:27 is a further exception, opening on neither pattern, וּבָנָ֞יו ורב יִ֧רֶ֞ב הַמַּשָּׂ֣א עָלָ֗יו (“and his sons, and the greatness of the burden that was on him”), a second morphologically-deviant reign-closer beside 12:15's bare form. 16:11 shares the class's citation register (divre plus first-and-last plus 'written in the book') without repeating any of these other openers. Reinforcing this row's own close, the phrase וּבָעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא that opens Hanani's arrival in v.7 recurs to close v.10, בָּעֵ֥ת הַהִֽיא, a temporal bracket binding rebuke and reprisal into one span rather than resting on brevity alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the oracle (7-9) from Asa's one-verse reaction (10) would mirror the Azariah/response split in ch15, but the reaction here is too brief and too tightly bound to the rebuke's closing clause to stand alone.

boundary_rationale: וְהִנֵּה֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י אָסָ֔א הָרִאשׁוֹנִ֖ים וְהָאַחֲרוֹנִ֑ים הִנָּ֤ם כְּתוּבִים֙ עַל סֵ֣פֶר הַמְּלָכִ֔ים לִיהוּדָ֖ה וְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל ("Behold, the acts of Asa, first and last...are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel") opens the row on the reign-closing source-citation class, though in its own presentative variant — a hinneh-opening rather than the וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י-type opener that heads ten other reign-closers in the book, Abijah's own included at 13:22 — sharing the class's register (divre plus first-and-last plus 'written in the book') without repeating 13:22's incipit. What follows is disease, וַיֶּחֱלֶ֣א אָסָ֡א בִּשְׁנַת֩ שְׁלוֹשִׁ֨ים וָתֵ֤שַׁע לְמַלְכוּתוֹ֙ בְּרַגְלָ֔יו עַד לְמַ֖עְלָה חָלְי֑וֹ ("Asa was diseased in his feet...in the thirty-ninth year of his reign"), then the death notice proper, וַיִּשְׁכַּ֥ב אָסָ֖א עִם אֲבֹתָ֑יו וַיָּ֕מָת בִּשְׁנַ֛ת אַרְבָּעִ֥ים וְאַחַ֖ת לְמָלְכֽוֹ ("Asa slept with his fathers, and died in the forty-first year of his reign"), an instance of the book's own REGNAL DEATH-AND-SUCCESSION class (verified specimen at 21:1), then burial, וַיִּקְבְּרֻ֣הוּ בְקִבְרֹתָ֗יו אֲשֶׁ֣ר כָּֽרָה לוֹ֮ בְּעִ֣יר דָּוִיד֒ וַיַּשְׁכִּיבֻ֗הוּ בַּמִּשְׁכָּב֙...וַיִּשְׂרְפוּ ל֥וֹ שְׂרֵפָ֖ה גְּדוֹלָ֥ה עַד לִמְאֹֽד ("They buried him in his own tomb...and they made a very great fire for him"). The real asymmetry with Abijah's own close is not sequence — MT 13:23 (= WEB 14:1) likewise opens on death-and-burial, וַיִּשְׁכַּ֨ב אֲבִיָּ֜ה עִם אֲבֹתָ֗יו וַיִּקְבְּר֤וּ אֹתוֹ֙ בְּעִ֣יר דָּוִ֔יד, right after 13:22's citation formula, the identical order this row follows — but completeness: 13:23 fuses death, burial, and succession in one verse, וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אָסָ֥א בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּ֑יו, while Asa's own successor is not named until 17:1, so nothing inside 16:12-14 supplies a rival succession notice to cut against. Together these four verses form Asa's whole reign-closing complex, and the row ends exactly at this part's assigned last verse; a PE mark (single-witness) follows it, and the next reign begins beyond this part with the succession formula וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּ֑יו ("Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place").
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the disease-and-death notices (12-14) from the source formula (11) would separate a citation formula from the reign-summary material it introduces; unlike at 13:22/13:23, no succession clause sits inside 16:12-14 to supply a natural joint for such a cut.

boundary_rationale: The unit opens on the succession formula וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּ֑יו (“Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place,” WEB 17:1), the accession-type specimen the book strategy already flags for this verse. Vv.2-6 unpack that opening as one theological assessment: military consolidation (v.2), the fidelity antithesis וְלֹ֥א דָרַ֖שׁ לַבְּעָלִֽים (“didn’t seek the Baals,” v.3) against לֵֽאלֹהֵ֤י אָבִיו֙ דָּרָ֔שׁ (“sought the God of his father,” v.4), the causal “therefore” of v.5 (Yahweh established the kingdom, tribute, riches and honor), and the closing reform notice הֵסִ֛יר אֶת הַבָּמ֥וֹת וְאֶת הָאֲשֵׁרִ֖ים מִיהוּדָֽה (“he took away the high places and the Asherah poles out of Judah,” v.6). V.7 then opens with its own dating clause, וּבִשְׁנַ֨ת שָׁל֜וֹשׁ לְמָלְכ֗וֹ שָׁלַ֤ח, tying the next episode to a specific regnal year with no antecedent in vv.1-6, marking a fresh initiative; restricted to this clause-initial form, the construction opens an episode at all five loci where it stands clause-initially — 13:1, 16:1, 17:7, 34:8, and 36:22 — whereas the same dated phrase continues a clause already underway wherever it falls mid-clause, at 3:2, 16:12, and 16:13, including twice within Asa's own account this very part closes. The PE mark following 17:6 (single-witness, tier-3) weakly corroborates this seam but is not the driver; the dated clause at v.7 is.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through v.9 to fold the law-teaching mission into the same assessment block loses the force of the v.7 regnal-year dating clause: narrowed to its clause-initial form, the construction opens a fresh episode at all five loci carrying it clause-initially (13:1, 16:1, 17:7, 34:8, 36:22), never continuing one already underway the way the identical dated phrase does at 3:2, 16:12, and 16:13, where it falls mid-clause.

boundary_rationale: A fresh regnal-year formula launches this unit, וּבִשְׁנַ֨ת שָׁל֜וֹשׁ לְמָלְכ֗וֹ שָׁלַ֤ח (“also in the third year of his reign he sent...”), introducing a named roster of officials, joined by the Levites and priests named at וְעִמָּהֶ֣ם הַלְוִיִּ֗ם...וְעִמָּהֶ֛ם אֱלִישָׁמָ֥ע וִֽיהוֹרָ֖ם הַכֹּהֲנִֽים ("with them the Levites...and with them Elishama and Jehoram the priests," v.8), whose task is stated in a resumptive repetition of the piel root lamad across three occurrences: v.7's purpose infinitive ("to teach in the cities of Judah") running into v.9's doubled finite verbs, וַֽיְלַמְּדוּ֙ בִּֽיהוּדָ֔ה וְעִ֨מָּהֶ֔ם סֵ֖פֶר תּוֹרַ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה וַיָּסֹ֨בּוּ֙ בְּכָל עָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה וַֽיְלַמְּד֖וּ בָּעָֽם, opening and closing v.9 ("taught in Judah...and taught among the people"); the medial occurrence's own בִּֽיהוּדָ֔ה complement echoes v.7's closing בְּעָרֵי יְהוּדָה, binding purpose and fulfillment on the shared place-name. This three-fold teach/taught/taught pattern closes the circuit report cleanly, with the intervening note that they carried וְעִ֨מָּהֶ֔ם סֵ֖פֶר תּוֹרַ֣ת יְהוָ֑ה (“the book of Yahweh’s law,” v.9). That teach/taught pairing closes the circuit report cleanly. V.10 pivots to a different grammatical subject and topic — a shift to what neighboring kingdoms now do toward Judah — with no verbal link back to the teaching mission’s vocabulary, so the unit does not run on into v.10.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading vv.7-11 as one ‘Jehoshaphat’s influence abroad’ unit conflates a completed teaching circuit, bracketed by its own teach/taught verbs, with a separate consequence-notice that opens its own vayehi clause; the PE after 17:11 (single-witness, tier-3) offers weak mark-level corroboration for that wider reading, but v.10's new-subject clause (a shift to what neighboring kingdoms now do toward Judah) breaks the teaching circuit before v.11 is reached, so the tier-1 grammatical signal still prevails over the tier-3 mark.

boundary_rationale: This two-verse notice opens on its own subject, וַיְהִ֣י פַּ֣חַד יְהוָ֗ה עַ֚ל כָּל מַמְלְכ֣וֹת (“the fear of Yahweh fell on all the kingdoms...,” v.10), rather than continuing the teaching mission’s vocabulary, and reports a distinct consequence: regional non-aggression, then מְבִיאִ֧ים לִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט מִנְחָ֖ה (“brought Jehoshaphat...tribute,” v.11) from Philistines and Arabians. V.12 opens a clause built on the identical new-subject device, וַיְהִ֧י יְהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט הֹלֵ֥ךְ וְגָדֵ֖ל עַד לְמָ֑עְלָה ("Jehoshaphat grew great..."), so the seam here rests on a device this book does not treat as reliably boundary-driving -- the very next instance is absorbed without comment into an eight-verse catalog next door (M8-2Chr-069) rather than prompting a comparable split. Book-wide, the exact 'fear of Yahweh' string recurs at 14:13 (MT; dual-cited web:2Chr.14.14 = oshb:2Chr.14.13 (MT)) and 19:7, but the closer structural analogue is the clause-type וַיְהִי֙ פַּ֣חַד at 20:29, וַיְהִי֙ פַּ֣חַד אֱלֹהִ֔ים עַ֖ל כָּל מַמְלְכ֣וֹת הָאֲרָצ֑וֹת בְּשָׁמְעָ֕ם כִּ֚י נִלְחַ֣ם יְהוָ֔ה עִ֖ם אוֹיְבֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל, matching 17:10 across six of its first seven words; that instance functions as an aftermath clause closing out the battle just narrated (20:27-30) rather than opening independent material, which cuts against, not for, reading vv.10-11 as their own unit. The marks bracket 17:7-11 as one unbroken witness-stretch, with a PE after 17:6 (single-witness) and a PE after 17:11 (single-witness) but no mark falling anywhere at 17:7-10 between them; that stretch is exactly co-extensive with the union of this row and M8-2Chr-067 (17:7-9), while the next marked stretch runs 17:12-19, exactly co-extensive with M8-2Chr-069's own span. This tier-3 material leans weakly toward the rival reading that would fold vv.10-11 forward with vv.7-9 rather than treating them as their own unit, but remains non-driving corroboration only.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv.10-11 as the direct fruit of vv.7-9's teaching campaign, or as an unmarked continuation folding forward into v.12's building notice, both remain live: the nearest analogue in the book (20:29) attaches this device to what precedes rather than launching a stand-alone unit. What differentiates vv.10-11 from both neighbors is content, not device: the two verses report Judah's external relations — regional non-aggression (v.10) then Philistine silver-tribute and quantified Arabian livestock (v.11) — a subject matter shared with neither the teaching circuit before it (17:7-9, M8-2Chr-067) nor the building-and-muster catalog after it (17:12-19, M8-2Chr-069).

boundary_rationale: Opens on the new subject-first clause וַיְהִ֧י יְהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט הֹלֵ֥ךְ וְגָדֵ֖ל עַד לְמָ֑עְלָה ("Jehoshaphat grew great exceedingly; and he built fortresses and store cities in Judah," v.12), then moves into a register-style roster of Judah's and Benjamin's captains (vv.14-18). The roster is itself bracketed: it opens וְאֵ֥לֶּה פְקֻדָּתָ֖ם ("This was the numbering of them according to their fathers’ houses," v.14) and closes אֵ֖לֶּה הַמְשָׁרְתִ֣ים אֶת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ ("These were those who waited on the king," v.19), a 'these...these' frame marking the list as one self-contained catalog rather than a run of independent entries. This is a genuine tier-1 list-register seam -- וְאֵ֥לֶּה פְקֻדָּתָ֖ם is one of only four clause-initial vav-prefixed 'these' register-openers book-wide (3:3, 8:10, 17:14, 24:26); the roster's own bare-form closer at v.19 is a further clause-initial member of the wider 'these' class beyond that vav-prefixed set, reinforcing rather than weakening the bracket argument -- so the row concedes rather than dismisses that vv.12-13 sit two verses ahead of the catalog's own textually-marked start; the roster's own closing phrase, בְּעָרֵ֥י הַמִּבְצָ֖ר ("fortified cities," v.19), draws on 17:2's own עָרֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה הַבְּצֻר֑וֹת ("the fortified cities of Judah") rather than v.12's differently-rooted building notice, so the catalog's back-reference does not itself bind vv.12-13 into the list. What keeps them in one row is the occasion-and-catalog relationship: the strategy elsewhere licenses coarser treatment for register material of exactly this kind, not a shared vocabulary tie. The five SAMEKH marks after each named captain (17:14-18, single-witness) are per-entry list punctuation and, being that dense and regular, corroborate the catalog's internal formatting rather than any macro-seam; the PE mark keyed to 17:19 (single-witness) sits precisely at the roster's own closing formula. 18:1 then opens Jehoshaphat's marriage alliance with Ahab, a wholly new topic with its own vayehi clause.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at 17:14, where the genuine list-register frame opens (one of only four clause-initial vav-prefixed 'these' register-openers in the book: 3:3, 8:10, 17:14, 24:26), is the real rival to weigh -- stronger than fragmenting the roster at each captain's SAMEKH (e.g., isolating 17:14-16 Judah from 17:17-18 Benjamin), which the marks themselves do not license as macro-divisions. It is not adopted here because vv.12-13's growth-and-building notice supplies the register's own occasion, and the book strategy's instruction to keep catalog material coarse favors holding occasion and catalog in one row over splitting on the register frame alone.

boundary_rationale: V.1 reuses 17:5's own royal-prosperity notice: 17:5 closes וַֽיְהִי ל֥וֹ עֹֽשֶׁר וְכָב֖וֹד לָרֹֽב ("he had riches and honor in abundance"), 18:1 opens וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט עֹ֥שֶׁר וְכָב֖וֹד לָרֹ֑ב וַיִּתְחַתֵּ֖ן לְאַחְאָֽב ("Jehoshaphat had riches and honor in abundance...allied himself with Ahab"), the identical existential-plus-quantifier collocation with only the beneficiary changed from bound pronoun to proper name. This is a stock Chronistic royal-prosperity frame rather than a bespoke echo -- the same existential-plus-beneficiary shape recurs with a different quantifier at 32:27, וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיחִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ עֹ֥שֶׁר וְכָב֖וֹד הַרְבֵּ֣ה מְאֹ֑ד ("gloss: Hezekiah had riches and honor in great abundance") -- so the reuse functions as a resumptive relaunch of the narrative rather than a bracketing inclusio closing a unit that began at 17:5. The scene then runs continuously: descent to Samaria, Ahab's feast, and the enticement to Ramoth Gilead, וַיֵּרֶד֩ לְקֵ֨ץ שָׁנִ֤ים אֶל אַחְאָב֙ ("gloss: at the end of some years he went down to Ahab," v.2), then Jehoshaphat's assent, כָּמ֤וֹנִי כָמ֨וֹךָ֙ וּכְעַמְּךָ֣ עַמִּ֔י וְעִמְּךָ֖ בַּמִּלְחָמָֽה ("gloss: I am as you are...we will be with you in the war," v.3). The bare noun for 'end' stands in exactly three verses book-wide -- 8:1, 18:2, and 21:19 -- each in a different prefixed or bare form, and only 8:1 and 18:2 carry it in a temporal-transition construction, which is all the positional argument needs. Unlike 8:1's own clause-initial opener, which opens a full temporal frame, 18:2's phrase is an adjunct subordinate to the already-fronted motion verb וַיֵּרֶד֩, continuing the subject Jehoshaphat established in v.1 rather than launching an independent time-frame; that positional difference, not silence about the lexeme, is why no formula break falls at v.2. V.4, by contrast, opens with Jehoshaphat's own counter-initiative ('inquire first for Yahweh's word'), redirecting the whole episode toward the prophetic inquiry that follows; that is the real pivot, not v.3.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading the 17:5/18:1 phrase repetition as an inclusio bracketing all of 17:1-18:1 into one ‘Jehoshaphat’s greatness’ unit ignores the dated and topic-shifted sub-episodes at 17:7, 17:10, and 17:12 that intervene, erasing real seams the text itself marks.

boundary_rationale: Jehoshaphat’s request, דְּרָשׁ נָ֥א כַיּ֖וֹם אֶת דְּבַ֥ר יְהוָֽה (“inquire first for Yahweh’s word,” v.4), opens the whole Micaiah episode by redirecting the king of Israel’s war plan toward prophetic consultation. What follows is one continuous movement: the king of Israel puts the question to the four hundred prophets, הֲנֵלֵ֞ךְ אֶל רָמֹ֥ת גִּלְעָ֛ד לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה אִם אֶחְדָּ֑ל (“shall we go to Ramoth Gilead to battle, or shall I forbear,” v.5), gets their unanimous yes, is pressed by Jehoshaphat for a genuine prophet, names and disparages Micaiah, and sends a messenger to fetch him who tries to coach his answer; the unit closes on Micaiah’s oath, חַי יְהוָ֕ה כִּ֛י אֶת אֲשֶׁר יֹאמַ֥ר אֱלֹהַ֖י אֹת֥וֹ אֲדַבֵּֽר (“as Yahweh lives...I will say what my God says,” v.13). V.14 narrates Micaiah’s arrival and puts the identical question to him, הֲנֵלֵ֞ךְ אֶל רָמֹ֥ת גִּלְעָ֛ד לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה אִם אֶחְדָּ֑ל, word-for-word identical to v.5 (verified: this exact phrase recurs nowhere else in 2Chr) — a deliberate two-stage ‘ask the crowd, then ask the true prophet’ design that marks v.13/14 as the real seam within the inquiry scene, not any point inside vv.4-13.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The book strategy's own instruction to keep the inquiry scene 18:4-27 coherent (§5) might seem to bar any internal split, but the identical must-not-be-over-split language governs Solomon's dedication complex (§5, 5:2-7:22) while that complex is itself decomposed into its own named sub-parts (procession, prayer, theophany); read the same way here, the repeated question bracketing vv.5 and 14 marks a sub-division of one coherent scene into its two type-scene stages (ask the compliant crowd, then the true prophet), not a violation of the coherence instruction. Splitting instead at v.9 (the enthronement-and-audience notice) to separate the summons from the messenger's coaching would cut through the single unbroken 'send for Micaiah' action and has no formulaic marker of its own -- the weaker rival this row should not lean on.

boundary_rationale: The scene restarts with Micaiah’s arrival and the same question repeated verbatim from v.5, הֲנֵלֵ֞ךְ אֶל רָמֹ֥ת גִּלְעָ֛ד לַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה אִם אֶחְדָּ֑ל (v.14), then runs through the ironic false ‘go up’ (14b), the adjuration to speak truth (15), the true sheep-without-shepherd oracle (16), the king’s complaint to Jehoshaphat (17), Micaiah’s throne-vision speech, לָכֵ֖ן שִׁמְע֣וּ דְבַר יְהוָ֑ה (“hear Yahweh’s word,” vv.18-22), Zedekiah’s blow, וַיִּגַּשׁ֙ צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ בֶֽן כְּנַעֲנָ֔ה (“Zedekiah...came near,” v.23), and closes on Micaiah’s own oath and public address, שִׁמְע֖וּ עַמִּ֥ים כֻּלָּֽם (“listen, you people, all of you,” v.27). SAMEKH marks fall after 18:17 and 18:22 (both single-witness) and could tempt a finer three-way split (complaint / vision / confrontation), but that would sever the vision-speech from Zedekiah's blow in v.23, a direct physical reaction to what Micaiah has just said; the scene's dramatic logic depends on keeping speech and retaliation together, so the marks are disclosed only as non-driving tier-3 corroboration, not as the row's actual warrant. The PE mark after 18:27 (single-witness) falls exactly where the narrative genuinely turns outward to the march on Ramoth Gilead in v.28.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating 18:18-22 as a separate oracle-inset row is defensible in the abstract -- וַיֹּ֕אמֶר לָכֵ֖ן שִׁמְע֣וּ supplies a real opening frame, and its 'hear the word' collocation occurs nowhere else in 2Chr -- but the book strategy's own INSET RULE requires both an opening frame AND a resumption formula after to isolate an inset, and no resumption follows v.22 before Zedekiah's blow in v.23; failing that second half of the test, the vision-speech stays inside its host regardless of the SAMEKH marks at vv.17/22, and severing it here would in any case strand v.23's blow without its narrative trigger, fragmenting the single confrontation the source presents as one beat.

boundary_rationale: A new movement formula opens the unit, וַיַּ֧עַל מֶֽלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל וִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֖ה אֶל רָמֹ֥ת גִּלְעָֽד (“the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat...went up to Ramoth Gilead,” v.28), leaving the court scene for the battlefield. The unit is held together by a deliberate matched pair of clauses: וַיְהִ֡י כִּרְאוֹת֩ שָׂרֵ֨י הָרֶ֜כֶב אֶת יְהוֹשָׁפָ֗ט (“when the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat,” v.31, the mistaken-identity danger, resolved when God diverts them) against וַיְהִ֗י כִּרְאוֹת֙ שָׂרֵ֣י הָרֶ֔כֶב כִּ֥י לֹא הָיָ֖ה מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל (“when the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel,” v.32, the correction that clears the way for Ahab’s actual death). Splitting between these mirrored clauses would break a doublet the text itself constructs; the unit only closes with the death notice וַיָּ֕מָת לְעֵ֖ת בּ֥וֹא הַשָּֽׁמֶשׁ (“he died at sunset,” v.34), which ends not just this row but the whole Ramoth Gilead episode — the next material, outside this part, opens a fresh return notice at 19:1.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v.31/32 to separate Jehoshaphat’s near-miss from Ahab’s actual death looks tidy by content but cuts directly through the mirrored ‘when the captains saw...when the captains saw’ doublet that binds the two halves into one action.

boundary_rationale: The opening breaks hard from the battlefield scene that closed the previous part: 18:34 ends with the king of Israel's death at sunset (וַיָּ֕מָת לְעֵ֖ת בּ֥וֹא הַשָּֽׁמֶשׁ), a different subject in a different place, while 19:1 pivots to Jehoshaphat's own homecoming on the שוב root, “Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned to his house in peace to Jerusalem” (וַ֠יָּשָׁב יְהוֹשָׁפָ֨ט מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֧ה אֶל בֵּית֛וֹ בְּשָׁל֖וֹם לִֽירוּשָׁלִָֽם). Jehu ben Hanani's arrival supplies a genuine oracle-opening frame, וַיֵּצֵ֣א אֶל פָּנָ֗יו יֵה֣וּא בֶן חֲנָ֘נִי֮ הַחֹזֶה֒ וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אֶל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ יְהוֹשָׁפָ֔ט (“gloss: he went out to meet him, Jehu ben Hanani the seer, and said to King Jehoshaphat”), for the rebuke-and-mitigation oracle: “should you help the wicked, and love those who hate Yahweh?” (הֲלָרָשָׁ֣ע לַעְזֹ֔ר וּלְשֹׂנְאֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה תֶּאֱהָ֑ב) answered by “you have set your heart to seek God” (וַהֲכִינ֥וֹתָ לְבָבְךָ֖ לִדְרֹ֥שׁ הָֽאֱלֹהִֽים). Verse 4 answers the return notice not through its own opening verb but through its own internal returning-root pair: the king “went out again among the people…and brought them back to Yahweh” (וַיָּ֜שָׁב וַיֵּצֵ֣א בָעָ֗ם מִבְּאֵ֥ר שֶׁ֨בַע֙ עַד הַ֣ר אֶפְרַ֔יִם וַיְשִׁיבֵ֕ם אֶל יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י אֲבוֹתֵיהֶֽם), a finite-plus-hiphil pairing on the same returning root that opens 19:1's own וַ֠יָּשָׁב -- a textually-verifiable root-level inclusio bracketing the whole return-rebuke-response arc. (V.4 itself opens on the unrelated dwelling root, וַיֵּ֥שֶׁב יְהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם, gloss: “Jehoshaphat lived at Jerusalem” -- a homograph of the returning-root form once vowel-pointing is set aside, not a shared root.) This inclusio is corroborated but not driven by the SAMEKH after v.4 (single-witness). That bracket is a real but unlisted device, thinner than a book_strategy_draft.md §1 tier-1 opener -- no time-frame transition, relocation, or new named subject falls at v.5 -- so the register shift to institutional appointment, “he set judges in the land” (וַיַּעֲמֵ֨ד שֹֽׁפְטִ֜ים בָּאָ֗רֶץ), rests on this thinner warrant, which is why this row's confidence does not claim more than the evidence supports.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating vv.2-3 as a standalone prophetic-judgment inset is not defeated merely by asserting no closing frame separates it: v.2's own arrival notice is a genuine oracle-opening frame, and v.4a's re-naming and re-locating of Jehoshaphat arguably answers it. The stronger ground for keeping vv.1-4 whole is structural: isolating vv.2-3 would strand the one-verse return notice at 19:1 as its own orphan row, and the SAMEKH mark (single-witness) falls after v.4 rather than between v.3 and v.4, so the only available tier-3 corroboration sits on the row's side of that seam, not the rival's.

boundary_rationale: Verse 5 opens a fresh administrative register, “he set judges in the land throughout all the fortified cities” (וַיַּעֲמֵ֨ד שֹֽׁפְטִ֜ים בָּאָ֗רֶץ), followed by a charge speech grounding the judges' authority in Yahweh rather than in man, “for you don't judge for man, but for Yahweh” (כִּ֣י לֹ֧א לְאָדָ֛ם תִּשְׁפְּט֖וּ כִּ֣י לַיהוָ֑ה). Verse 8 extends the same reform to Jerusalem with the additive “moreover”, “Moreover in Jerusalem Jehoshaphat appointed…” (וְגַ֣ם בִּ֠ירוּשָׁלִַם הֶעֱמִ֨יד יְהוֹשָׁפָ֜ט), explicitly continuing rather than restarting the report, so the local judges and the central tribunal read as one installation, not two. The unit closes on the charge's own benediction, “Deal courageously…and may Yahweh be with the good” (חִזְק֣וּ וַעֲשׂ֔וּ וִיהִ֥י יְהוָ֖ה עִם הַטּֽוֹב), the last verse of ch.19, where a PE follows (single-witness); 20:1's own time-formula, “After this…” (וַיְהִ֣י אַֽחֲרֵי כֵ֡ן בָּ֣אוּ בְנֵי מוֹאָב֩ וּבְנֵ֨י עַמּ֜וֹן), then opens an unrelated military crisis with new subjects, Moab and Ammon, confirming the break.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the local judges (5-7) from the Jerusalem tribunal (8-11) into separate rows ignores that v.8's “moreover” explicitly continues, rather than restarts, the appointment report.

boundary_rationale: “It happened after this” (וַיְהִ֣י אַֽחֲרֵי כֵ֡ן בָּ֣אוּ בְנֵי מוֹאָב֩ וּבְנֵ֨י עַמּ֜וֹן) opens a new crisis unrelated to the judicial reform just closed, and WEB signals the same reset with "After this". The coalition report escalates across two notices: a bare arrival (“the children of Moab, the children of Ammon…came against Jehoshaphat to battle”) and then a detailed messenger report locating the threat, “a great multitude is coming against you from beyond the sea…from Syria” (בָּ֣א עָלֶ֜יךָ הָמ֥וֹן רָ֛ב מֵעֵ֥בֶר לַיָּ֖ם מֵאֲרָ֑ם). Verse 3 answers with Jehoshaphat's own decisive act, reintroducing his name as grammatical subject: “Jehoshaphat was alarmed, and set himself to seek Yahweh. He proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah” (וַיִּרָ֕א וַיִּתֵּ֧ן יְהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט אֶת פָּנָ֖יו לִדְר֣וֹשׁ לַיהוָ֑ה וַיִּקְרָא צ֖וֹם עַל כָּל יְהוּדָֽה), a royal decree that closes the threat-and-response movement before the next verse shifts to the nation's own collective compliance, “Judah gathered themselves together”, a change of grammatical subject from king to people.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping only the two threat-notices (1-2) as their own row and folding v.3 into the assembly scene is defensible, since v.3's fast-proclamation directly triggers v.4's gathering; this rival is not clearly weaker, hence the reduced confidence on this row's closing edge.

boundary_rationale: Where the prior unit ended on the king's own decree to fast (וַיִּרָ֕א וַיִּתֵּ֧ן יְהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט אֶת פָּנָ֖יו לִדְר֣וֹשׁ לַיהוָ֑ה וַיִּקְרָא צ֖וֹם עַל כָּל יְהוּדָֽה), this one opens with the nation's collective action, “Judah gathered themselves together to seek help from Yahweh” (וַיִּקָּבְצ֣וּ יְהוּדָ֔ה לְבַקֵּ֖שׁ מֵֽיְהוָ֑ה גַּ֚ם מִכָּל עָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה בָּ֖אוּ לְבַקֵּ֥שׁ אֶת יְהוָֽה), flowing directly into Jehoshaphat's standing address in the assembly, “Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in Yahweh's house” (וַיַּעֲמֹ֣ד יְהוֹשָׁפָ֗ט בִּקְהַ֧ל יְהוּדָ֛ה וִירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם בְּבֵ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה לִפְנֵ֖י הֶחָצֵ֥ר הַחֲדָשָֽׁה). The prayer builds to its own admission of helplessness, “we don't know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (וַאֲנַ֗חְנוּ לֹ֤א נֵדַע֙ מַֽה נַּעֲשֶׂ֔ה כִּ֥י עָלֶ֖יךָ עֵינֵֽינוּ), and the unit closes on the tableau of the whole community's posture, “all Judah stood before Yahweh, with their little ones, their wives, and their children” (וְכָ֨ל יְהוּדָ֔ה עֹמְדִ֖ים לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה גַּם טַפָּ֖ם נְשֵׁיהֶ֥ם וּבְנֵיהֶֽם); a single-witness PE sits at this close. Verse 14 then introduces an entirely new actor by full genealogy, and the Spirit's descent “in the middle of the assembly” answers rather than continues the human posture just described, marking the seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the prayer itself (5-12) away from its closing tableau (13) would isolate the oracle's answer from the very posture it responds to, since the assembly Jahaziel addresses in v.15 is the standing congregation just described in v.13.

boundary_rationale: This unit is framed by name: Jahaziel is introduced with a five-generation genealogy, “Jahaziel the son of Zechariah, the son of Benaiah, the son of Jeiel, the son of Mattaniah, the Levite, of the sons of Asaph” (וְיַחֲזִיאֵ֡ל בֶּן זְכַרְיָ֡הוּ בֶּן בְּ֠נָיָה בֶּן יְעִיאֵ֧ל בֶּן מַתַּנְיָ֛ה הַלֵּוִ֖י מִן בְּנֵ֣י אָסָ֑ף הָיְתָ֤ה עָלָיו֙ ר֣וּחַ יְהוָ֔ה בְּת֖וֹךְ הַקָּהָֽל), far fuller than the single patronymic given the seer who confronted Jehoshaphat at 19:2, “Jehu the son of Hanani the seer” (יֵה֣וּא בֶן חֲנָ֘נִי֮ הַחֹזֶה֒), marking this oracle as a set-piece. The oracle's core, “for the battle is not yours, but God's” and “you will not need to fight this battle” (אַ֠תֶּם אַל תִּֽירְא֤וּ וְאַל תֵּחַ֨תּוּ֙ מִפְּנֵ֨י הֶהָמ֤וֹן הָרָב֙ הַזֶּ֔ה כִּ֣י לֹ֥א לָכֶ֛ם הַמִּלְחָמָ֖ה כִּ֥י לֵאלֹהִֽים; לֹ֥א לָכֶ֖ם לְהִלָּחֵ֣ם בָּזֹ֑את), is answered immediately, without narrative gap, by Jehoshaphat's prostration, “he bowed his head with his face to the ground” (וַיִּקֹּ֧ד יְהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט אַפַּ֖יִם אָ֑רְצָה), and the Levites' praise “with an exceedingly loud voice” (לְהַלֵּ֗ל לַיהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל בְּק֥וֹל גָּד֖וֹל לְמָֽעְלָה); per the inset rule the response stays inside the oracle's own unit since nothing frames it as resumed narrative. The next verse resets with a new day and place, “they rose early in the morning and went out into the wilderness of Tekoa” (וַיַּשְׁכִּ֣ימוּ בַבֹּ֔קֶר וַיֵּצְא֖וּ לְמִדְבַּ֣ר תְּק֑וֹעַ), which is the seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting the oracle (14-17) from the worship response (18-19) into two rows would sever the response from the very deliverance it thanks God for in advance, contrary to the inset rule's both-sides-framed test.

boundary_rationale: The march begins with the new-day formula that closed the previous row's argument (וַיַּשְׁכִּ֣ימוּ בַבֹּ֔קֶר וַיֵּצְא֖וּ לְמִדְבַּ֣ר תְּק֑וֹעַ), and Jehoshaphat's second speech, “…Believe in Yahweh your God, so you will be established! Believe his prophets, so you will prosper” (הַאֲמִ֜ינוּ בַּיהוָ֤ה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם֙ וְתֵ֣אָמֵ֔נוּ הַאֲמִ֥ינוּ בִנְבִיאָ֖יו וְהַצְלִֽיחוּ), sets up the singers who go out crying “give thanks to Yahweh, for his loving kindness endures forever” (וְאֹֽמְרִים֙ הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֔ה כִּ֥י לְעוֹלָ֖ם חַסְדּֽוֹ), the hymn line that triggers Yahweh's ambush against the coalition, “Yahweh set ambushers against the children of Ammon” (נָתַ֣ן יְהוָ֣ה מְ֠אָֽרְבִים עַל בְּנֵ֨י עַמּ֜וֹן), and their mutual slaughter, “…everyone helped to destroy each other” (עָזְר֥וּ אִישׁ בְּרֵעֵ֖הוּ לְמַשְׁחִֽית). The causally connected discovery of corpses, “behold, they were dead bodies fallen to the earth, and there were none who escaped” (וְהִנָּ֧ם פְּגָרִ֛ים נֹפְלִ֥ים אַ֖רְצָה וְאֵ֥ין פְּלֵיטָֽה), belongs to the same chain as the plunderers of v.25, “Jehoshaphat and his people” (יְהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט וְעַמּוֹ֮), the Beracah etiology, “…the name of that place was called “Beracah Valley” to this day” (עַל כֵּ֡ן קָֽרְא֞וּ אֶת שֵׁ֨ם הַמָּק֥וֹם הַה֛וּא עֵ֥מֶק בְּרָכָ֖ה עַד הַיּֽוֹם), the doubled-return notice that follows it, “Then they returned, every man of Judah and Jerusalem, with Jehoshaphat in front of them, to go again to Jerusalem with joy; for Yahweh had made them to rejoice over their enemies” (וַ֠יָּשֻׁבוּ כָּל אִ֨ישׁ יְהוּדָ֤ה וִֽירוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ וִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט בְּרֹאשָׁ֔ם לָשׁ֥וּב אֶל יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם בְּשִׂמְחָ֑ה כִּֽי שִׂמְּחָ֥ם יְהוָ֖ה מֵֽאוֹיְבֵיהֶֽם, v.27) and their temple arrival with instruments (וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ יְר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם בִּנְבָלִ֥ים וּבְכִנֹּר֖וֹת וּבַחֲצֹצְר֑וֹת אֶל בֵּ֖ית יְהוָֽה, v.28) -- a figura etymologica on the returning root -- the bare infinitive, without conjunctive prefix, stands only here at 20:27; the vav-prefixed form recurs at 30:9, a different unpointed string, not an identical word-form repetition -- and this finite-plus-cognate-infinitive pairing is itself unique to 20:27 book-wide. It shares its device-class with 19:1's own return notice, but functions here as the still-unfolding aftermath of the very battle just narrated rather than 19:1's pivot to a wholly new scene and participant (Jehu, the rebuke): the fear-of-nations (v.29) and rest-formula (v.30) that follow are direct consequences of this war, not a fresh initiative, which is why the device does not drive a split here the way it does at 19:1 -- the surrounding nations' dread, “the fear of God was on all the kingdoms of the countries” (וַיְהִי֙ פַּ֣חַד אֱלֹהִ֔ים עַ֖ל כָּל מַמְלְכ֣וֹת הָאֲרָצ֑וֹת), and the closing rest-formula, “the realm of Jehoshaphat was quiet, for his God gave him rest all around” (וַתִּשְׁקֹ֖ט מַלְכ֣וּת יְהוֹשָׁפָ֑ט וַיָּ֧נַֽח ל֦וֹ אֱלֹהָ֖יו מִסָּבִֽיב) — a PE, single-witness, marks the close here. Verse 31 breaks decisively into the reign's age-and-length notice, “…בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁים֩ וְחָמֵ֨שׁ שָׁנָ֜ה…” (“thirty-five years old”), a formula with no place in the narrative just closed.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the battle proper (20-24) from the plunder-to-rest sequence (25-30) would cut the chain at its weakest visible joint; no formula or mark falls there, and although the grammatical subject NP does shift, from v.24's collective וִֽיהוּדָ֛ה בָּ֥א ("Judah came") to v.25's named-plus-collective וַיָּבֹ֨א יְהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט וְעַמּוֹ֮ ("Jehoshaphat and his people came"), the plunderers of v.25 are referentially the same body as v.24's Judah, so continuity here is a matter of reference, not grammar -- the row is kept whole despite its length, at correspondingly reduced confidence.

boundary_rationale: The rest-formula that just closed the war narrative yields to the reign's own accession notice, “Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah; he was thirty-five years old when he began to reign” (וַיִּמְלֹ֥ךְ יְהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט עַל יְהוּדָ֑ה בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁים֩ וְחָמֵ֨שׁ שָׁנָ֜ה בְּמָלְכ֗וֹ), followed by evaluation formulas, “he walked in the way of Asa his father, and didn't turn away from it” (וַיֵּ֗לֶךְ בְּדֶ֛רֶךְ אָבִ֥יו אָסָ֖א וְלֹא סָ֣ר מִמֶּ֑נָּה), qualified by the concessive “however the high places were not taken away” (אַ֥ךְ הַבָּמ֖וֹת לֹא סָ֑רוּ). The unit closes on the source-citation formula, “the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, first and last…are written in the history of Jehu the son of Hanani” (וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י יְהוֹשָׁפָ֔ט הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאַחֲרֹנִ֑ים הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים בְּדִבְרֵי֙ יֵה֣וּא בֶן חֲנָ֔נִי), a pattern attested at reign-closes elsewhere in the book (e.g. 13:22, 25:26, 26:22); notably, the historian named here is the same Jehu ben Hanani who confronted the king in person at the opening of this part (19:2), closing this reign's record with the prophetic voice that had opened it. Verse 35 reopens the narrative register with a fresh time-marker, “After this, Jehoshaphat…joined himself with Ahaziah…” (וְאַחֲרֵי כֵ֗ן אֶתְחַבַּר֙ יְהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה עִ֖ם אֲחַזְיָ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל ה֖וּא הִרְשִׁ֥יעַ לַעֲשֽׂוֹת), showing the source-citation closed only this evaluative block, not the reign's remaining material.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row through v.37 on the grounds that the reign is not formally over until 21:1 misreads the source-citation as all-inclusive; the formula closes a sub-unit of the reign's record here, not the reign itself, so further appended material can and does follow.

boundary_rationale: A second “after this” marker reopens narrative time, sharing the אחרי כן idiom that opened the Moabite crisis at 20:1 (וַיְהִ֣י אַֽחֲרֵי כֵ֡ן, a wayyiqtol-of-hayah frame) though in the lighter construction וְאַחֲרֵי כֵ֗ן (a bare conjunctive waw directly on the adverbial, no preposed וַיְהִי): “Jehoshaphat king of Judah joined himself with Ahaziah king of Israel. The same did very wickedly” (וְאַחֲרֵי כֵ֗ן אֶתְחַבַּר֙ יְהוֹשָׁפָ֣ט מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה עִ֖ם אֲחַזְיָ֣ה מֶֽלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל ה֖וּא הִרְשִׁ֥יעַ לַעֲשֽׂוֹת). A book-wide sweep of אחרי כן finds five instances -- the wayyiqtol-headed type at 20:1 and 24:4, this lighter bare-waw type at 20:35 and, inside Manasseh's own reign account rather than at any major-unit opening, 33:14, and the unrelated verse-final idiom (prepositioned form, 'from then on') at 32:23 -- so the reopened-narrative-time reading rests on the shared idiom and on 20:34's own source-citation closure and the moral-verdict register change into the Tarshish venture, not on formula identity with 20:1. The Tarshish-ships venture, “to make ships to go to Tarshish” (לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת אֳנִיּ֖וֹת לָלֶ֣כֶת תַּרְשִׁ֑ישׁ), draws Eliezer ben Dodavahu's judgment oracle, “Eliezer…prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying” (וַיִּתְנַבֵּ֞א אֱלִיעֶ֤זֶר בֶּן דֹּדָוָ֨הוּ֙ מִמָּ֣רֵשָׁ֔ה עַל יְהוֹשָׁפָ֖ט לֵאמֹ֑ר), whose immediate fulfillment closes this unit and this part, “the ships were wrecked, so that they were not able to go to Tarshish” (וַיִּשָּׁבְר֣וּ אֳנִיּ֔וֹת וְלֹ֥א עָצְר֖וּ לָלֶ֥כֶת אֶל תַּרְשִֽׁישׁ). The following verse breaks into an entirely different formula-class, the death-and-succession notice “Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers” (וַיִּשְׁכַּ֤ב יְהֽוֹשָׁפָט֙ עִם אֲבֹתָ֔יו), attested at reign-ends throughout the book as a two-member type completed by a proper succession clause -- 9:31's וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ רְחַבְעָ֥ם בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו, 12:16's וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אֲבִיָּ֥ה בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו, and 27:9's fuller three-clause form וַיִּשְׁכַּ֤ב יוֹתָם֙ עִם אֲבֹתָ֔יו וַיִּקְבְּר֥וּ אֹת֖וֹ בְּעִ֣יר דָּוִ֑יד וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אָחָ֥ז בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו -- which both closes Jehoshaphat's story properly and opens Jehoram's accession, a different subject taking the throne, outside this part's range.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 21:1 into this unit because both concern the aftermath of Jehoshaphat's reign ignores that the death formula is an independently recurring closer that itself begins Jehoram's accession, so the true reign-boundary falls after v.37, not after v.1 of ch.21.

boundary_rationale: The row opens on the paired death-and-enthronement notice: “וַיִּשְׁכַּ֤ב” (“slept,” i.e. died) answered by “וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהוֹרָ֥ם בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו” (“Jehoram his son reigned in his place”), matching WEB 21:1 “Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers...and Jehoram his son reigned in his place” - the standard death-plus-succession opener, and also the seam-out point for the prior part. Verses 2-3 (WEB: brothers given gifts and fortified cities, but the kingdom to the firstborn) supply the family background that the purge in v4 requires. The unit closes on Jehoram's own consolidation of power: “וַיָּ֨קָם יְהוֹרָ֜ם עַל מַמְלֶ֤כַת אָבִיו֙ וַיִּתְחַזַּ֔ק וַיַּהֲרֹ֥ג אֶת כָּל אֶחָ֖יו בֶּחָ֑רֶב וְגַ֖ם מִשָּׂרֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל” (“Jehoram had risen up over the kingdom of his father...and killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel,” WEB 21:4). Verse 5 immediately pivots to an unrelated formulaic type (age-plus-reign-length), so v4's own narrative resolution is the natural close before that restart.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through v7 to absorb the age-formula and covenant clause is the weaker reading: vv5-7 constitute a distinct, self-contained formulaic type (evaluation plus Davidic-covenant promise) rather than a continuation of the succession-and-purge narrative.

boundary_rationale: Opening edge: v5 restarts the reign account with the age formula בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וּשְׁתַּ֛יִם שָׁנָ֖ה יְהוֹרָ֣ם בְּמָלְכ֑וֹ וּשְׁמוֹנֶ֣ה שָׁנִ֔ים מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם ("Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem," WEB 21:5), a fixed type distinct from the narrative just closed at v4. This formula block runs through the evil-evaluation clause and the covenant-preservation promise (vv6-7), then into the accumulating 'in his days' indictment -- Edom's revolt, opening with the book's only verse-initial instance of that fronted temporal adverbial, בְּיָמָיו֙ פָּשַׁ֣ע אֱד֔וֹם ("in his days Edom revolted," v.8; the one other occurrence, MT 13:23 (= WEB 14:1)'s בְּיָמָ֛יו שָׁקְטָ֥ה הָאָ֖רֶץ, sits verse-medially), then Libnah's revolt (vv9-10). Closing edge: v11 pivots from geopolitical failure to cultic apostasy with גַּם ה֥וּא עָשָֽׂה בָמ֖וֹת בְּהָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֑ה וַיֶּ֨זֶן֙ אֶת יֹשְׁבֵ֣י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם וַיַּדַּ֖ח אֶת יְהוּדָֽה ("Moreover he made high places in the mountains of Judah, and made the inhabitants of Jerusalem play the prostitute, and led Judah astray," WEB 21:11); this is the very charge Elijah's letter indicts in vv12-13, so v11 functions as the letter's narrative antecedent and the row closes just before the letter opens. A PE (single-witness) does stand exactly at this close, at 21:11, weak and non-driving corroboration only; the nearby PE at 21:3 belongs to the preceding row's own span, not this one. The seam itself rests on the topic pivot and the letter's back-reference, with the mark as available but non-determinative support.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v.8 to separate the covenant clause (5-7) from the revolt notices (8-11) is a genuine rival, not a non-issue: v.8's fronted temporal adverbial introduces a new subject, Edom -- in fact the book's only verse-initial instance of that adverbial, and so a tier-1-eligible marker by the device matrix's own time-frame-transition class. Vv.5-7 carry no 'in his days' language of their own to bracket against it. What keeps vv.8-11 with vv.5-7 in one row is not a shared temporal frame but the evaluative verdict vv.6-7 pass on Jehoram -- that he walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as Ahab's house did, doing evil in Yahweh's sight -- under which the Edom and Libnah revolts (8-10) and the cultic apostasy (11) accumulate as the substantiating record, one continuous catalog of the evil the verdict names, rather than a catalog Elijah's letter itself recites as a totality: the letter (12-13) charges only failure to walk in Jehoshaphat and Asa's ways, prostituting Judah and Jerusalem like the house of Ahab, and killing brothers -- answering v.4's fratricide, outside this row's own span, not the Edom/Libnah revolts of vv.8-10 by name. Severing at v.8 would still divide the verdict from its own substantiating record; that the catalog's own opening marker is real and tier-1-eligible is conceded, and a split there remains a live, credible alternative this row does not claim to foreclose.

boundary_rationale: The letter inset opens with its own frame, “וַיָּבֹ֤א אֵלָיו֙ מִכְתָּ֔ב מֵֽאֵלִיָּ֥הוּ הַנָּבִ֖יא לֵאמֹ֑ר” (“A letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying,” WEB 21:12), and its curses name two targets: “הִנֵּ֣ה יְהוָ֗ה נֹגֵ֛ף מַגֵּפָ֥ה גְדוֹלָ֖ה בְּעַמֶּ֑ךָ” (“Yahweh will strike your people with a great plague,” WEB 21:14) continuing into “וּבְבָנֶ֥יךָ וּבְנָשֶׁ֖יךָ וּבְכָל רְכוּשֶֽׁךָ” (“including your children, your wives, and all your possessions,” WEB 21:14) and the bowel-disease curse of v15. Per the inset rule the letter cannot be isolated as its own row because no closing frame resumes ordinary narration afterward; instead v16 launches directly into the first fulfillment, “וַיַּעֲל֤וּ בִֽיהוּדָה֙ וַיִּבְקָע֔וּהָ וַיִּשְׁבּ֗וּ אֵ֤ת כָּל הָרְכוּשׁ֙ הַנִּמְצָ֣א לְבֵית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ” (“they came up against Judah, broke into it, and carried away all the possessions that were found in the king's house,” WEB 21:17), echoed almost verbally by “וְגַם בָּנָ֖יו וְנָשָׁ֑יו” (“including his sons and his wives,” WEB 21:17) against the curse's own “your children...your wives”. This lexical repetition binds letter and invasion into one unit. The row closes at v17 because v18's “after all this” opens the second, later stage of judgment as an explicitly separate time-frame.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 21:12-15 as an isolated inset row cannot stand: no bilateral frame closes it off, since v16's new-subject clause reads as direct fulfillment of the letter's own curses rather than a narrative resumption, so the host unit's integrity requires keeping letter and fulfillment together.

boundary_rationale: An explicit time-frame transition opens this row: וְאַחֲרֵ֖י כָּל זֹ֑את ("After all this," WEB 21:18), a construction distinct from 8:1's own וַיְהִ֞י מִקֵּ֣ץ עֶשְׂרִ֣ים שָׁנָ֗ה (a different, single-instance formula) and matched instead, near-identically, by 35:20's אַחֲרֵ֣י כָל זֹ֗את, which opens the Necho unit; the shared idiom marks both as time-frame transitions, here separating the second curse's fulfillment (incurable bowel disease) from the first (invasion, vv16-17). The row runs through the two-year decline and death (v19) and closes on the reign-closing double formula: the age-and-length notice repeated from v5's own בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וּשְׁתַּ֛יִם שָׁנָ֖ה יְהוֹרָ֣ם בְּמָלְכ֑וֹ, with both the year-noun and the king's name giving way to the auxiliary verb הָיָה, בֶּן שְׁלֹשִׁ֤ים וּשְׁתַּ֨יִם֙ הָיָ֣ה בְמָלְכ֔וֹ -- an auxiliary-verb-for-name substitution recurring nowhere else in the book except, in a narrower form, at Jotham's own matching closing formula, 27:8's בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֧ים וְחָמֵ֛שׁ שָׁנָ֖ה הָיָ֣ה בְמָלְכ֑וֹ where only the name gives way to the auxiliary verb while the year-noun is retained, against his named opening at 27:1 -- then וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ֙ בְּלֹ֣א חֶמְדָּ֔ה וַֽיִּקְבְּרֻ֨הוּ֙ בְּעִ֣יר דָּוִ֔יד וְלֹ֖א בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים ("he departed with no one's regret...they buried him in David's city, but not in the tombs of the kings," WEB 21:20) - a dishonorable-burial notice that also seams Jehoram's whole account out before Ahaziah's accession opens ch.22.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding vv16-17 into this row is unconvincing, since “after all this” at v18 explicitly marks a distinct, later stage of judgment rather than a continuation of the same invasion scene.

boundary_rationale: This reign account opens on an irregular installation formula rather than the usual father-to-son succession clause: וַיַּמְלִיכוּ֩ יוֹשְׁבֵ֨י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֜ם אֶת אֲחַזְיָ֨הוּ בְנ֤וֹ הַקָּטֹן֙ תַּחְתָּ֔יו כִּ֤י ("The inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah his youngest son king in his place...because," WEB 22:1), the causal clause explaining why the people, not custom, chose him (his older brothers slain by the raiders of v1), closed within the same verse by the ordinary qal formula וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אֲחַזְיָ֥הוּ בֶן יְהוֹרָ֖ם מֶ֥לֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה ("Ahaziah...reigned," v.1b) -- an accession notice complete in its own clause-type but irregular in substance, since it reports an installation by the people rather than a straightforward succession. The age formula proper, בֶּן אַרְבָּעִ֨ים וּשְׁתַּ֤יִם שָׁנָה֙ אֲחַזְיָ֣הוּ בְמָלְכ֔וֹ (v.2), is the same device-type that opens a fresh reign-account on its own at 21:5 within this very part, and pmarks keys a PE (single-witness) to the very 22:1/22:2 juncture; both are disclosed here rather than treated as absent. What keeps v.2 inside this row rather than launching its own is that v.1's own accession is already anomalous -- an installation explained by a causal clause about slain brothers, not the book's standard succession pattern -- so v.2's age notice completes the standard accession-and-evaluation report v.1 alone leaves irregular, rather than opening independent material the way the identical formula does at 21:5. The actual ground distinguishing the two loci is not narrative closure -- 21:20 closes Jehoram's account in full immediately before 22:1, exactly as 21:1 closes Jehoshaphat's before 21:2, and in both cases new-king narrative then intervenes before the age formula (three verses at 21:2-4 versus one at 22:1) -- but v.1's own installation clause, which names its agents (the inhabitants of Jerusalem) and supplies a causal clause explaining the irregular choice (his older brothers slain by raiders), with no counterpart at 21:1's own bare death-burial-succession formula. The row carries through the war at Ramoth Gilead, Jehu's purge, and Ahaziah's death, closing on the explicit dynasty-collapse clause וְאֵין֙ לְבֵ֣ית אֲחַזְיָ֔הוּ לַעְצֹ֥ר כֹּ֖חַ לְמַמְלָכָֽה ("The house of Ahaziah had no power to hold the kingdom," WEB 22:9) - a summary formula terminating this reign before Athaliah's countercoup opens at v10 with a fresh, fronted subject.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at 22:2, treating v.1 alone as the accession notice and vv.2-9 as the reign-and-collapse account, is the stronger rival -- not the v.6/v.7 seam this row previously leaned on, where v.7 merely interprets the immediately preceding wound as divine causation rather than opening independent material. The 22:1/22:2 split is nonetheless not adopted here because v.1's own installation clause remains anomalous until v.2's age notice completes it; the reader should weigh for themselves whether that completion-relationship outweighs the identical age-formula device opening a fresh unit seventeen verses earlier, at 21:5 (sixteen verses intervening, since chapter 21 runs the full twenty verses before 22:1 opens).

boundary_rationale: A fronted new subject opens the row: “וַעֲתַלְיָ֨הוּ֙ אֵ֣ם אֲחַזְיָ֔הוּ רָאֲתָ֖ה כִּ֣י מֵ֣ת בְּנָ֑הּ וַתָּ֗קָם” (“Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose,” WEB 22:10), pivoting away from Ahaziah's own reign account just closed by v9's dynasty-collapse formula. The rescue of Joash by Jehoshabeath (v11) is the direct counter-action, and the row closes on the interval-summary clause “וַיְהִ֤י אִתָּם֙ בְּבֵ֣ית הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים מִתְחַבֵּ֖א שֵׁ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֖ים וַעֲתַלְיָ֖ה מֹלֶ֥כֶת עַל הָאָֽרֶץ” (“he was with them hidden in God's house six years while Athaliah reigned over the land,” WEB 22:12), which compresses the whole six-year span into a single retrospective notice - a natural resting point before 23:1's fresh “in the seventh year” marker resumes the story. A pe stands after 22:12 in WLC's sole witness, offering its usual weak support. This close is nonetheless the more contested edge of the wider Athaliah arc (22:10-23:21): the six-year summary is a narrative pause, not necessarily a hard terminus, though it is the only edge in this three-verse stretch that names a completed span of time.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 22:10-23:21 as one undivided decision is a live alternative, since v.12's interval-summary supplies its own internal closure even though both halves remain bracketed by the larger usurpation-to-overthrow arc; that closure is a narrative pause, not necessarily a hard terminus, and the split here does not depend on any project pacing target to be justified.

boundary_rationale: Opening edge: וּבַשָּׁנָ֨ה הַשְּׁבִעִ֜ית הִתְחַזַּ֣ק יְהוֹיָדָ֗ע וַיִּקַּ֣ח ("In the seventh year, Jehoiada strengthened himself, and took," WEB 23:1) supplies a fresh temporal anchor, a tier-1 time-frame transition, and a new agent taking initiative. The hitpael-חזק verb itself is not a marked echo of Jehoram's own power-seizure at 21:4 (וַיִּתְחַזַּ֔ק): the stem recurs eleven times as a finite verb across the whole book plus two infinitives inside speeches, several of them mid-account rather than at any unit's opening (וַיִּתְחַזֵּ֣ק at 13:21, after Abijah's war; הִתְחַזַּ֔ק at 25:11, inside Amaziah's Edom campaign; וַיִּתְחַזַּ֡ק at 32:5, inside Hezekiah's defensive works) -- the Chronicler's ordinary consolidation idiom, not a bespoke signal tying this seam to 21:4's. The seam itself rests on the fronted temporal phrase alone. The row carries the covenant with the captains, the gathering of Levites, Jehoiada's deployment speech (vv3-7, kept inside this host unit since v8's “so the Levites and all Judah did according to all that Jehoiada...commanded” is a command-fulfillment pairing, not an isolating frame), and the execution of the plan through the acclamation “וַיֹּאמְר֖וּ יְחִ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ” (“they said, ‘Long live the king!’,” WEB 23:11), corroborated weakly by the samekh at 23:11 (single-witness, Writings). The seventh-year marker that opens this row is nonetheless the more debatable edge of the wider arc: WEB 22:12's six-year interval notice does not read as an unambiguous terminus, so 23:1's opening could equally be read as mere continuation within one unbroken Athaliah narrative rather than a fresh unit-opener.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this row with 22:10-12 into a single continuous Athaliah-arc decision is a live alternative, since the interval clause at 22:12 is not a hard narrative terminus and “in the seventh year” could function as pure continuation; the split is kept here because the fronted temporal transition alone -- not the hitpael-חזק verb, which is the book's ordinary consolidation idiom -- marks a new initiating moment, but the case is not decisive either way.

boundary_rationale: A clean subject shift opens the row, from the crowd's celebration to Athaliah's perception of it: “וַתִּשְׁמַ֣ע עֲתַלְיָ֗הוּ” (“Athaliah heard,” WEB 23:12), a pivot corroborated weakly by the SAMEKH mark keyed to 23:11 (single-witness), immediately behind this seam rather than inside it, leading into her cry וַתֹּ֖אמֶר קֶ֥שֶׁר קָֽשֶׁר ("Treason! treason!," WEB 23:13). A second SAMEKH keyed to 23:13 falls interior to this span, at the 13/14 seam between the cry and Jehoiada's counter-order, and is disclosed here as non-driving color rather than boundary evidence. Jehoiada's counter-order (v14) and her removal follow, and the scene closes flatly on “וַיְמִית֖וּהָ שָֽׁם” (“they killed her there,” WEB 23:15) - a terse notice, its sole-witness pe adding the same weak confirmation, that ends the episode before v16 opens an entirely different ceremonial register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the prior row through the coronation to include this scene undersells the seam, since “Athaliah heard” at v12 is a clear pivot to her perspective, distinct from the priestly execution of Jehoiada's plan that precedes it.

boundary_rationale: A fresh covenant ceremony opens the row, distinct in scope from the covenants that preceded it: “וַיִּכְרֹ֤ת יְהוֹיָדָע֙ בְּרִ֔ית בֵּינ֕וֹ” (“Jehoiada made a covenant between himself, all the people, and the king,” WEB 23:16), now binding the nation itself to be Yahweh's people, rather than the captains' covenant of v.1 and the assembly's dynastic pact of v.3. The distinction rests on 23:16's own purpose clause -- “to be a people to Yahweh” -- with no counterpart at v.1 or v.3, and on the change of covenanting agent: Jehoiada personally at v.16, rather than the whole assembly at v.3, whose party otherwise overlaps v.16's almost entirely. The Baal-house demolition and priestly restoration follow; v.20's procession then moves the young king bodily out of the temple and installs him on the throne, וַיּ֤וֹרֶד אֶת הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ מִבֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֔ה...וַיּוֹשִׁ֨יבוּ֙ אֶת הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ עַ֖ל כִּסֵּ֥א הַמַּמְלָכָֽה ("...brought the king down from Yahweh's house. They came...and set the king on the throne of the kingdom," v.20), a genuine location-and-participant change of the class this book elsewhere treats as boundary-driving, and the strongest internal rival in this span; it is kept inside this row because the enthronement is the covenant's own completion, not a separate topic -- the throne-installation is what makes the people's earlier acclamation of the king (v.11) institutionally real, continuous with the purge and restoration rather than a fresh initiative. The row closes on וַיִּשְׂמְח֥וּ כָל עַם הָאָ֖רֶץ וְהָעִ֣יר שָׁקָ֑טָה וְאֶת עֲתַלְיָ֖הוּ הֵמִ֥יתוּ בֶחָֽרֶב ("all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet. They had slain Athaliah with the sword," WEB 23:21); WLC's sole witness appends a samekh right here too, for whatever that weak testimony is worth. This recap clause also answers 22:10 as a motif of violence recoiling on its author, rather than a formal inclusio: Athaliah seized power over the royal line by violence, וַעֲתַלְיָ֨הוּ֙ אֵ֣ם אֲחַזְיָ֔הוּ רָאֲתָ֖ה כִּ֣י מֵ֣ת בְּנָ֑הּ וַתָּ֗קָם וַתְּדַבֵּ֛ר אֶת כָּל זֶ֥רַע הַמַּמְלָכָ֖ה לְבֵ֥ית יְהוּדָֽה ("Athaliah...saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal offspring of the house of Judah," WEB 22:10), and here falls to violence in turn; the two verses share only the מות root, not a repeated phrase, so the frame is thematic -- violence recoiling on its author -- rather than a true bracket, and this row itself is bounded on its own terms by the covenant-renewal formula that opens it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v.20 to separate the Baal-purge-and-restoration report (16-19) from the enthronement procession (20-21) is the stronger internal rival, since v.20 supplies a genuine change of location and cast; it is not adopted because the throne-installation completes rather than launches the same covenant-restoration movement begun at v.16, and 22:10-23:21 remains bracketed as one violence-answers-violence arc regardless of where the internal seam falls.

boundary_rationale: Opens on the standard age formula “בֶּן שֶׁ֤בַע שָׁנִים֙ יֹאָ֣שׁ בְּמָלְכ֔וֹ וְאַרְבָּעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּֽירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְשֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔וֹ צִבְיָ֖ה מִבְּאֵ֥ר שָֽׁבַע” (“Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem,” WEB 24.1), followed at once by the evaluative clause naming the mentorship frame: “כָּל יְמֵ֖י יְהוֹיָדָ֥ע הַכֹּהֵֽן” (“all the days of Jehoiada the priest,” WEB 24:2). The same phrase recurs to close the unit at v14, shorn of its appositional title and with an added adverb, תָּמִ֔יד כֹּ֖ל יְמֵ֥י יְהוֹיָדָֽע ("continually all the days of Jehoiada," WEB 24:14) -- v14 drops הַכֹּהֵֽן and adds תָּמִ֔יד, so the bracket is a lexical echo rather than a byte-identical repetition, forming a loose inclusio around the mentored era. Inside that bracket, וַיְהִ֖י אַחֲרֵי כֵ֑ן ("After this," WEB 24:4) opens the repair project's own narrative (intent, fundraising, the chest, the workmen, completion and vessels); this construction is tier-1-eligible in its own right -- the same vayehi-plus-acharei-ken collocation occurs exactly once more in the book, at 20:1, where it alone opens a fresh unit (M8-2Chr-076) rather than being absorbed into anything preceding it -- so the inclusio does not by itself neutralize v.4 as a candidate seam the way this row's whole case requires. What keeps this row unsplit, honestly, is weaker than the inclusio alone suggests: the repair sequence's register-like, procedural character ("thus they did day by day," v11) parallels the coarser treatment construction catalogs receive elsewhere in the book -- specifically the book strategy's own instruction to keep chapters 3-4's construction material coarse (book_strategy_draft.md §5) -- and the mentored-era bracket still supplies a real, if lexical rather than verbatim, frame around the whole. But v.4's own vayehi-acharei-ken construction ties it to the 20:1 parallel, a live, tier-1-class rival this argument does not defeat. The row closes precisely where the inclusio phrase closes; a pe stands there too in the sole surviving witness, weak and corroborative only.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v4 to separate the accession/evaluation notice from the repair-project narrative deserves real weight, not a quick dismissal: v.4's vayehi-acharei-ken construction is the same tier-1 time-frame-transition device that alone opens M8-2Chr-076 at 20:1, and an inclusio does not automatically outrank a tier-1 opener standing inside it. The row is kept whole here on the weaker ground that the mentored-era bracket (vv2/14) and the repair project's own coarse, catalog-like register still read as one accountable unit, but this defense does not defeat the 20:1 parallel, which remains a live rival.

boundary_rationale: A short, self-contained obituary opens this row the moment the repair-project inclusio closes: “וַיִּזְקַ֧ן יְהוֹיָדָ֛ע וַיִּשְׂבַּ֥ע יָמִ֖ים וַיָּמֹ֑ת בֶּן מֵאָ֧ה וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֛ים שָׁנָ֖ה בְּמוֹתֽוֹ” (“Jehoiada grew old and was full of days, and he died; he was one hundred thirty years old when he died,” WEB 24:15). It closes on the honorable-burial rationale, extending to the verse's own terminus, “...among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house,” WEB 24:16; the lone witness sets a SAMEKH after the verse's own final word, for what little that is worth. The contrast is with dishonor, not mere formula-repetition: Jehoram's burial closes “וְלֹ֖א בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים” (“not in the tombs of the kings,” 21:20), and Joash's own reign later closes “וְלֹ֥א קְבָרֻ֖הוּ בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים” (“they didn’t bury him in the tombs of the kings,” 24:25) — the same denial, expanded with a resumptive verb (קְבָרֻ֖הוּ) Jehoiada's own notice is spared. Brevity here reflects the notice's hinge function: it is the pivot between “all the days of Jehoiada” (v2/v14) and “after the death of Jehoiada” (v17), not a continuation of either surrounding unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this notice into the following apostasy account does not work, since v17's “after the death of Jehoiada” is itself an opening time-marker for the next unit, presupposing rather than continuing this obituary.

boundary_rationale: The row opens on the deliberate antithesis of the just-closed inclusio phrase: “וְאַֽחֲרֵ֥י מוֹת֙ יְה֣וֹיָדָ֔ע” (“Now after the death of Jehoiada,” WEB 24:17), signaling the reversal of everything held while he lived. Prophets are sent and rejected (vv18-19), then Zechariah's Spirit-empowered indictment opens with its own frame, “וַֽיַּעֲמֹ֖ד מֵעַ֣ל לָעָ֑ם וַיֹּ֨אמֶר לָהֶ֜ם כֹּ֣ה אָמַ֣ר הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים” (“he stood above the people, and said to them, ‘God says,’” WEB 24:20); per the inset rule this oracle stays inside the host apostasy account because v21's stoning is an immediate narrative reaction, not a resumption after a gap. The row closes on Zechariah's dying imprecation “וּכְמוֹת֣וֹ אָמַ֔ר יֵ֥רֶא יְהוָ֖ה וְיִדְרֹֽשׁ” (“he said, ‘May Yahweh look at it, and repay it,’” WEB 24:22) - the single witness appends a pe here too, weak as always - a curse that v23's time-marker answers directly in the next row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating Zechariah's oracle (24:20) as its own row overreaches: no resumption formula separates it from the stoning that immediately follows, so the speech must stay inside its host unit per the inset rule.

boundary_rationale: A PE (single-witness) stands at 24:22, weak corroboration for the opening edge. Opens on the time-marker that directly answers Zechariah's dying curse: “וַיְהִ֣י לִתְקוּפַ֣ת הַשָּׁנָ֗ה עָלָ֣ה עָלָיו֮ חֵ֣יל אֲרָם֒” (“At the end of the year, the army of the Syrians came up against him,” WEB 24:23), followed by the explicit theological framing of v24 (“a small company...because they had forsaken Yahweh”). The conspirators' motive is stated in kind: “הִתְקַשְּׁר֨וּ עָלָ֜יו עֲבָדָ֗יו בִּדְמֵי֙ בְּנֵי֙ יְהוֹיָדָ֣ע הַכֹּהֵ֔ן” (“his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest,” WEB 24:25). A SAMEKH (single-witness, weak) follows v.25, interior to this row's own span; it does not disturb the absorption of vv.26-27 into this unit. 24:25's dishonor-notice differs from 21:20's by exactly one inserted word: 21:20 simply denies burial “וְלֹ֖א בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים”, while 24:25 repeats that same denial with a resumptive verb wedged in, “וְלֹ֥א קְבָרֻ֖הוּ בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים”, a form (קְבָרֻ֖הוּ) attested nowhere else in this book. V26 then names the conspirators, “וְאֵ֖לֶּה הַמִּתְקַשְּׁרִ֣ים עָלָ֑יו זָבָ֗ד בֶּן שִׁמְעָת֙ הָֽעַמּוֹנִ֔ית וִיה֣וֹזָבָ֔ד בֶּן שִׁמְרִ֖ית הַמּוֹאָבִֽית”; this ve'eleh-plus-demonstrative opener does head a list-register elsewhere in the book (foundation measurements at 3:3, the chief-officer register at 8:10, the fathers'-house muster at 17:14), and its demonstrative here is cataphoric in exactly the same way -- pointing forward to the two names, Zabad and Jehozabad, that follow it, not backward to the assassination just narrated. What ties v.26 to v.25 instead is the pronominal suffix and the participle: the suffix takes Joash, killed in v.25, as its antecedent, and the participle echoes v.25's own finite verb of conspiring -- v.26 supplies the killers' identity for a death already reported through this suffix-and-participle echo, not through its own opening demonstrative, and nothing resumes or reopens the narrative after it before v27's citation. The row closes on the fixed pair that ends nearly every reign account in the book: the source-citation formula “הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֔ים עַל מִדְרַ֖שׁ סֵ֣פֶר הַמְּלָכִ֑ים” (“behold, they are written in the commentary of the book of the kings,” WEB 24:27) and the succession clause “וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אֲמַצְיָ֥הוּ בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו” (“Amaziah his son reigned in his place,” WEB 24:27); a final PE in the sole witness closes the paragraph here as well - the seam-out point into the next part's Amaziah accession.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off v26 alone as its own register-opening unit fails, not because its own demonstrative is anaphoric -- it is cataphoric, like the book's other list-openers -- but because v.26 depends on v.25 through the suffix-and-participle echo that ties the killers' identity to the assassination just narrated, so it does not stand free the way a genuine list-opener would; splitting vv26-27 together from the invasion/death narrative would still sever the fixed source-citation-and-succession pair from the reign it closes.

boundary_rationale: The reign opens on the fixed age-formula, “בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ מָלַ֣ךְ אֲמַצְיָ֔הוּ וְעֶשְׂרִ֣ים וָתֵ֨שַׁע֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְשֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔וֹ יְהוֹעַדָּ֖ן מִירוּשָׁלָֽיִם” (“Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign” WEB), pairing accession age, reign-length, and mother's name in the same formulaic slot the book fills again for his son and grandson later in this very part. It is immediately followed, still inside the same reporting frame, by the evaluation clause “וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הַיָּשָׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה רַ֕ק לֹ֖א בְּלֵבָ֥ב שָׁלֵֽם”, whose reservation (WEB: “but not with a perfect heart”) already signals a qualified reign. The unit closes because v3 pivots into a narrated circumstantial clause rather than continuing the formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through the purge of the assassins (to v4) would merge a closed formulaic report with a freshly-opened narrative episode that has its own grammatical opener.

boundary_rationale: A circumstantial clause launches this episode: “וַיְהִ֕י כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר חָזְקָ֥ה הַמַּמְלָכָ֖ה עָלָ֑יו וַֽיַּהֲרֹג֙ אֶת עֲבָדָ֔יו הַמַּכִּ֖ים אֶת הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אָבִֽיו” (“when the kingdom was established to him, he killed his servants who had killed his father the king”). Verse-initial wayehi opens 38 verses across 2Chr, a common general device for launching narrative material, but this exact collocation — וַיְהִ֕י כַּאֲשֶׁ֛ר plus חָזְקָ֥ה הַמַּמְלָכָ֖ה — occurs nowhere else in the book; the seam rests on a book-wide singleton use of a common opener-type, which if anything sharpens rather than weakens the edge, since the specific wording marks this precise juncture rather than reusing a stock formula. The episode narrates the killing of his father's assassins and then anchors its restraint in an explicit legal citation, “כִּ֣י כַכָּת֣וּב בַּתּוֹרָ֡ה בְּסֵ֣פֶר מֹשֶׁה֩ אֲשֶׁר צִוָּ֨ה יְהוָ֜ה לֵאמֹ֗ר” (“according to that which is written in the law, in the book of Moses”), closing on the quoted maxim. A PE space-mark follows v4 (single-witness, weak corroboration only); v5 then turns to military mobilization, a topic change from justice to muster, though the grammatical subject remains the same: Amaziah continues as the 3ms actor across vv.3-5, renominalised at v.5's own opening verb rather than introduced as a fresh subject. The row's own close accordingly rests on the closed legal-citation terminus at v.4's end and the topic shift itself, corroborated by the single-witness PE already cited after v.4, not on any change of grammatical subject.
