strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading vv3-4 as still part of the accession report (1-4 combined) would collapse the closed evaluation formula into an open narrative episode that only begins with its own circumstantial clause.

boundary_rationale: Amaziah's own mobilization opens the row: “וַיִּקְבֹּ֤ץ אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ אֶת יְהוּדָ֔ה” (“Amaziah gathered Judah together”) — an unmarked wayyiqtol carrying Amaziah forward as the same grammatical subject from the purge just closed, not the locational motion-verb device the book uses to mark a genuine scene change (“וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ רְחַבְעָ֖ם שְׁכֶ֑מָה”, 10:1) nor the subject-fronted disjunctive this same reign uses six verses later (“וַאֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ הִתְחַזַּ֔ק”, v11); the seam here rests on topic-shift (justice to muster) as its only tier-1 signal, a weaker warrant than the row's own neighbors supply, which the medium grade already registers; a PE (single-witness) follows 25:4 immediately before this seam, weak tier-3 corroboration only, not counted among the tier-1 signals just described. It runs through the mercenary hire in v6, “וַיִּשְׂכֹּ֣ר מִיִּשְׂרָאֵ֗ל מֵ֥אָה אֶ֛לֶף גִּבּ֥וֹר חָ֖יִל בְּמֵאָ֥ה כִכַּר כָּֽסֶף” (“he hired one hundred thousand mighty men of valor out of Israel for one hundred talents of silver”); that hundred-talent absolute (בְּמֵאָ֥ה כִכַּר) is the hook Amaziah himself, not the man of God, reopens at v9 — “וּמַֽה לַּעֲשׂוֹת֙ לִמְאַ֣ת הַכִּכָּ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָתַ֖תִּי לִגְד֣וּד יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל” (“what shall we do for the hundred talents which I have given to the army of Israel?”), with the construct לִמְאַ֣ת הַכִּכָּ֔ר answering back to v6's absolute; the man of God's own words in vv7-8 never mention money at all. The row closes because v7 introduces the man of God with the entry formula “וְאִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים בָּ֤א אֵלָיו֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר הַמֶּ֕לֶךְ אַל יָבֹ֥א עִמְּךָ֖ צְבָ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֣י אֵ֤ין יְהוָה֙ עִם יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כֹּ֖ל בְּנֵ֥י אֶפְרָֽיִם”.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging vv5-6 with the preceding purge narrative (3-6 as one unit) remains a live rival precisely because v5's seam is topic-shift alone, without the locational or disjunctive marking that isolates other scene-changes in this reign (10:1, 25:11); the medium grade reflects that the row is kept separate on topic alone, not on a stronger grammatical signal.

boundary_rationale: Framed by the entry formula “וְאִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֗ים בָּ֤א אֵלָיו֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר הַמֶּ֕לֶךְ אַל יָבֹ֥א עִמְּךָ֖ צְבָ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֣י אֵ֤ין יְהוָה֙ עִם יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל כֹּ֖ל בְּנֵ֥י אֶפְרָֽיִם” (“A man of God came to him, saying”), an unnamed prophet's warning against hiring Israelite troops opens as a clearly bounded speech unit. It runs through the exchange in v9, closing on his reply “וַיֹּ֤אמֶר אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ לְאִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים וּמַֽה לַּעֲשׂוֹת֙ לִמְאַ֣ת הַכִּכָּ֔ר אֲשֶׁ֥ר נָתַ֖תִּי לִגְד֣וּד יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיֹּ֨אמֶר֙ אִ֣ישׁ הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים יֵ֚שׁ לַֽיהוָ֔ה לָ֥תֶת לְךָ֖ הַרְבֵּ֥ה מִזֶּֽה” (“Yahweh is able to give you much more than this”). The host narrative resumes immediately after in v10 with Amaziah again as grammatical subject of a plain wayyiqtol, “וַיַּבְדִּילֵ֣ם אֲמַצְיָ֗הוּ” (“Then Amaziah separated them”), satisfying the inset rule's requirement of a tier-1 frame on both sides.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv7-10 as one continuous mobilization scene would erase the direct-speech frame that isolates the oracle and would leave the muster report (5-6) without any narrative close of its own.

boundary_rationale: This stretch gathers three closely-linked beats around a single grievance: the dismissal notice in v10, “וַיַּבְדִּילֵ֣ם אֲמַצְיָ֗הוּ לְהַגְּדוּד֙ אֲשֶׁר בָּ֤א אֵלָיו֙ מֵֽאֶפְרַ֔יִם לָלֶ֖כֶת לִמְקוֹמָ֑ם וַיִּ֨חַר אַפָּ֤ם מְאֹד֙ בִּֽיהוּדָ֔ה וַיָּשׁ֥וּבוּ לִמְקוֹמָ֖ם בָּחֳרִי אָֽף”, ends on the Ephraimites' anger; a disjunctive subject-first clause then pivots to Amaziah's own resolve, “וַאֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ הִתְחַזַּ֔ק” (“Amaziah took courage”), launching the Edom campaign; and v13 explicitly recalls the dismissed troop by name, “וּבְנֵ֣י הַגְּד֗וּד אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵשִׁ֤יב אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ מִלֶּ֤כֶת עִמּוֹ֙ לַמִּלְחָמָ֔ה” (“the men of the army whom Amaziah sent back”), showing the raid on Judah's cities is the direct payoff of v10's dismissal. The Masoretic tradition marks this stretch at three points: a PE follows v.10, a SAMEKH follows v.12 (both interior to the span), and a SAMEKH follows v.13 -- all single-witness, weak corroboration only. V14's temporal clause opens an unrelated topic.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The harder rival is not merely lifting v10 out, but stopping the unit there and letting vv11-13 stand as their own row on the strength of v11's disjunctive, “וַאֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ הִתְחַזַּ֔ק”, which does break the wayyiqtol chain v10 sustains; that disjunctive, though, marks a shift of narrative attention back onto Amaziah after the aside about the dismissed troops' anger, not a change of scene, time, or addressee, and v13's anaphoric recall of that same dismissed troop shows the dismissal, the campaign, and the raid are one grievance-driven sequence rather than two.

boundary_rationale: A fresh scene begins where the campaign notice left off: “וַיְהִ֗י אַחֲרֵ֨י ב֤וֹא אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ מֵֽהַכּ֣וֹת אֶת אֲדוֹמִ֔ים” (“after Amaziah had come from the slaughter of the Edomites”), the same class of temporal-transition device the book uses at other major scene changes. The row's own internal candidate is v15's anger-plus-dispatch formula, “וַיִּֽחַר אַ֥ף יְהוָ֖ה בַּאֲמַצְיָ֑הוּ וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח אֵלָיו֙ נָבִ֔יא וַיֹּ֣אמֶר ל֗וֹ” (“Yahweh's anger burned against Amaziah, and he sent to him a prophet who said to him”), which shares its messenger-plus-speech-introduction shape with the book's other prophet-notice frames (Hanani's “וּבָעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא בָּ֚א חֲנָ֣נִי הָרֹאֶ֔ה אֶל אָסָ֖א”, 16:7-9). Unlike Hanani's notice, which opens after an already-completed and separately-narrated war episode, v15's anger clause is the direct, grammatically-marked consequence of the idolatry just narrated in v14 (the gods of the children of Seir he had just set up) -- nothing but the anger clause itself stands between sin and rebuke, so splitting v14 from v15-16 would sever a single cause-and-response unit at its own hinge rather than at an independent scene-opening frame. Amaziah's adoption of Seir's gods draws that prophet's rebuke, which the king cuts off mid-speech (v16); the row closes on the prophet's own last word, “כִּֽי עָשִׂ֣יתָ זֹּ֔את וְלֹ֥א שָׁמַ֖עְתָּ לַעֲצָתִֽי” (“because you have done this and have not listened to my counsel”), a direct-speech terminus. A PE space-marker in the Masoretic tradition sits after v16 too (single-witness, corroborative weight only); v17 then opens an entirely new diplomatic scene.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The closer rival -- splitting v14's idolatry notice from vv15-16's prophetic rebuke at the anger-plus-dispatch formula -- fails because that formula is the marked, grammatically-signaled consequence of v14's sin, not an independent scene-opening frame, so the cut would sever one cause-and-response unit at its own hinge. Extending this row through vv17-19 instead would fail for a different reason: v.17 renominalizes the subject and turns to a new addressee, Joash of Israel, opening a distinct diplomatic scene.

boundary_rationale: Diplomatic correspondence opens the row with a messenger formula, “וַיִּוָּעַ֗ץ אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה וַ֠יִּשְׁלַח” (“Amaziah...consulted...and sent to Joash”), matching the class of scene/participant-change device the book uses to launch new episodes. Joash's reply is a taunting fable, opening “הַח֜וֹחַ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּלְּבָנ֗וֹן שָׁ֠לַח אֶל הָאֶ֜רֶז אֲשֶׁ֤ר בַּלְּבָנוֹן֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר תְּנָֽה” (“The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar”), and it closes on the fable's moral in direct speech, “וְנָ֣פַלְתָּ֔ אַתָּ֖ה וִיהוּדָ֥ה עִמָּֽךְ” (“you should fall, even you and Judah with you”). The row ends there because v20 shifts from quoted dialogue to the narrator's own theological verdict.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the exchange straight through the battle (17-24 as one unit) would flatten the clean pivot from quoted taunt-speech to narrated military outcome that v20 itself marks.

boundary_rationale: v20's own clause is retrospective comment rather than a fresh opener: “וְלֹא שָׁמַ֣ע אֲמַצְיָ֔הוּ כִּ֤י מֵהָֽאֱלֹהִים֙ הִ֔יא” (“Amaziah would not listen; for it was of God”) reaches backward, its causal clause “כִּ֣י דָֽרְשׁ֔וּ אֵ֖ת אֱלֹהֵ֥י אֱדֽוֹם” (“because they had sought after the gods of Edom”) answering the prophet's own charge at v15, “לָ֤מָּה דָרַ֨שְׁתָּ֙ אֶת אֱלֹהֵ֣י הָעָ֔ם” (“why have you sought after the gods of the people”), and its bare pronoun הִ֔יא finding no antecedent inside the verse itself. The same waw-negative-qatal-plus-divine-causation shape closes the Rehoboam standoff at 10:15, “וְלֹֽא שָׁמַ֥ע הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֶל הָעָ֑ם כִּֽי הָיְתָ֤ה נְסִבָּה֙ מֵעִ֣ם הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים” (“the king didn't listen to the people; for it was brought about by God”), which likewise looks back at the just-finished exchange rather than opening the section that follows at 10:16 — the parallel is instructive: in both places the clause functions as the narrator's own verdict-hinge that turns a quoted confrontation into narrated consequence, not as a formulaic unit-opener in its own right. What licenses grouping v.20 forward with vv.21-24 here, unlike 10:15's own backward-looking placement relative to 10:16, is what follows each verdict-hinge: 10:16's sequel is the people's own quoted response, a new speech-act rather than a narrated consequence, so 10:15 closes the exchange it comments on; 25:21's sequel instead narrates the very consequence 25:20's verdict predicts -- Joash's advance and the ensuing battle -- so 25:20 opens the sequence it explains rather than closing the one before it. That is why this row keeps vv20-24 together as the single divine-judgment sequence the verdict frames — defeat at Beth Shemesh, capture, the breach of Jerusalem's wall, and the plunder of the temple and palace — rather than opening at v21's own re-nominated “וַיַּ֨עַל יוֹאָ֤שׁ מֶֽלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל֙”, which is a genuine internal rival for a fresh start but would orphan the verdict from the events it explains. It closes on the return notice, “וַיָּ֖שָׁב שֹׁמְרֽוֹן” (gloss: “returned to Samaria”); the Masoretic tradition likewise inserts a PE right after v24 (single-witness, merely corroborative). V25 then opens with a verb-initial apocopated wayyiqtol carrying its subject after it, “וַיְחִ֨י אֲמַצְיָ֤הוּ” (“Amaziah…lived”), pivoting the topic to lifespan reckoning rather than fronting any subject.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The stronger rival is not the wider 17-24 merge but opening at v21's own re-nominated wayyiqtol instead of v20's causal verdict; keeping v20 with vv21-24 is preferred because it is the verse that supplies the divine rationale for the defeat that follows, and severing it would leave that rationale stranded with the taunt-exchange it does not belong to.

boundary_rationale: A verb-initial apocopated wayyiqtol, its subject postposed rather than fronted, opens the close of the reign, “וַיְחִ֨י אֲמַצְיָ֤הוּ בֶן יוֹאָשׁ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֔ה אַחֲרֵ֣י מ֔וֹת יוֹאָ֥שׁ בֶּן יְהוֹאָחָ֖ז מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל חֲמֵ֥שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה שָׁנָֽה”, followed by the standard chronicle formula “וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י אֲמַצְיָ֔הוּ הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאַחֲרוֹנִ֑ים הֲלֹא֙ הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֔ים עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵי יְהוּדָ֖ה וְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל” (“the rest of the acts of Amaziah...written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel”) — the book's regular formula-then-death order, not an exception to it: the identical citation-before-death sequence recurs at Solomon's own close (“וּשְׁאָר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאֲחֲרוֹנִ֑ים” at 9:29, followed by 9:30's reign total, “וַיִּמְלֹ֨ךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֧ה בִֽירוּשָׁלִַ֛ם עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה”, then death at 9:31) and at Abijah's (13:22, then web 14:1/MT 13:23); two loci reverse this order rather than one: Josiah's close (35:26), following a death already narrated, and Joash's own earlier close within this book (24:25-27), where death and burial are narrated first at 24:25, וְלֹ֥א קְבָרֻ֖הוּ בְּקִבְר֥וֹת הַמְּלָכִֽים (“they buried him in David's city, but they didn't bury him in the tombs of the kings,” WEB 24:25), with the citation-plus-succession formula following only at 24:27, וִיסוֹד֙ בֵּ֣ית הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֔ים עַל מִדְרַ֖שׁ סֵ֣פֶר הַמְּלָכִ֑ים וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אֲמַצְיָ֥הוּ בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו (“they are written in the commentary of the book of the kings...Amaziah his son reigned in his place,” WEB 24:27). A further non-conforming case, 36:8, gives the citation-and-succession formula together with no death or burial notice for Jehoiakim anywhere in the book, וְהַנִּמְצָ֣א עָלָ֔יו הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל סֵ֛פֶר מַלְכֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִֽיהוּדָ֑ה וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהוֹיָכִ֥ין בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו (“they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah...Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place,” WEB 36:8). The conspiracy notice then opens with its own temporal clause, “וּמֵעֵ֗ת אֲשֶׁר סָ֤ר אֲמַצְיָ֨הוּ֙ מֵאַחֲרֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה וַיִּקְשְׁר֨וּ עָלָ֥יו קֶ֛שֶׁר בִּירוּשָׁלִַ֖ם” (“from the time that Amaziah turned away from following Yahweh, they made a conspiracy”), and the unit closes the chapter with burial. 26:1's fresh accession notice, “all the people of Judah took Uzziah,” marks the seam-out.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the source-citation formula (v26) from the conspiracy-and-death notice (27-28) would isolate a single closing clause from the reign-summary complex it functions inside, against the formula's usual role elsewhere in the book as a unit-closer paired with what follows it.

boundary_rationale: Uzziah's enthronement is narrated by the people rather than by the standard age-formula: “וַיִּקְח֞וּ כָּל עַ֤ם יְהוּדָה֙ אֶת עֻזִּיָּ֔הוּ” (“All the people of Judah took Uzziah...and made him king”), a distinct accession-type from the age-formula used for his father and son (25:1's בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ מָלַ֣ךְ and 27:1's בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ יוֹתָ֣ם) -- and a genuine structural twin of its own kind recurs at 36:1, “וַיִּקְחוּ֙ עַם הָאָ֔רֶץ אֶת” (“the people of the land took Jehoahaz”), narrowed to the take-and-install verb pairing 26:1 itself uses, this is the only other place in the book where 'the people' take and then install a king -- two further installations by 'the people' exist without a preceding take-verb, at 22:1 (וַיַּמְלִיכוּ֩ יוֹשְׁבֵ֨י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֜ם, “the inhabitants of Jerusalem made...king”) and 33:25 (וַיַּמְלִ֧יכוּ עַם הָאָ֛רֶץ, “the people of the land made...king”), and 33:25's own phrase is verbally closer to 36:1's identical phrasing than to 26:1's own 'all the people of Judah'. V2 appends a building note and a retrospective death-notice for Amaziah, closing on “אַחֲרֵ֥י שְׁכַֽב הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ עִם אֲבֹתָֽיו” (“after that the king slept with his fathers”) — the king in question being Amaziah, not Uzziah, a clause that looks backward rather than forward. Masoretic spacing marks the same spot with a PE after v2 (single-witness only), and v3 then restarts with the standard age-formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging vv1-2 straight into the formal age-formula (1-5 as one unit) would paper over the fact that the book gives Uzziah two distinct accession notices in immediate succession, a doubling worth isolating rather than smoothing over.

boundary_rationale: Only after the popular acclamation does the book supply the standard accession formula, “בֶּן שֵׁ֨שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֤ה שָׁנָה֙ עֻזִּיָּ֣הוּ בְמָלְכ֔וֹ וַחֲמִשִּׁ֤ים וּשְׁתַּ֨יִם֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם” (“Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign”), restating the age datum already given at v1 (“וְה֕וּא בֶּן שֵׁ֥שׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֖ה שָׁנָ֑ה”, which carries no reign-length figure at all) — a genuine doublet for age alone, the fifty-two-year reign-length being new information here, whose cause the text does not explain. The evaluation clause “וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הַיָּשָׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה כְּכֹ֥ל אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂ֖ה אֲמַצְיָ֥הוּ אָבִֽיו” follows, and the unit extends through the added piety notice naming Zechariah, closing on “as long as he sought Yahweh, God made him prosper.” The Masoretic tradition places a SAMEKH after v5 too (single-witness, weak corroboration); v6 then opens the military campaign with a bare wayyiqtol chain, “וַיֵּצֵא֙ וַיִּלָּ֣חֶם”, carrying no expressed subject at all — Uzziah is retrieved across a subject switch from the divine name that closes v5, not handed a fresh nominal subject of his own, so the junction is carried by topic and participant focus rather than by any new subject-verb pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv3-5 as continuous with vv1-2 risks obscuring the tier-1 seam where the formulaic register restarts after the narrated popular-enthronement notice has already closed.

boundary_rationale: Military success dominates this stretch, opened by a fresh verb pair with no subject repeated from the pious notice just closed: “וַיֵּצֵא֙ וַיִּלָּ֣חֶם בַּפְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים” (“he went out and fought against the Philistines”). Campaigns against Philistia, the Arabians, and Ammonite tribute culminate in a fame-and-strength notice that does not stop at the fame clause alone: “וַיֵּ֤לֶךְ שְׁמוֹ֙ עַד לְב֣וֹא מִצְרַ֔יִם כִּ֥י הֶחֱזִ֖יק עַד לְמָֽעְלָה” (“his name spread abroad even to the entrance of Egypt, for he grew exceedingly strong”) — a hiphil of the same ḥ-z-q root that threads 26:8, 9, 15, and 16 into the hubris pivot two rows later. V9 then opens an unrelated building topic with its own subject-verb pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the building projects of vv9-10 into this row would blend a discrete military-and-fame report with the separate architectural and agricultural catalog that follows.

boundary_rationale: Building, agriculture, and army organization are gathered as one register-like catalog, opening “וַיִּ֨בֶן עֻזִּיָּ֤הוּ מִגְדָּלִים֙ בִּיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם” (“Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem”) and running through towers, cisterns, farmers, a numbered muster, equipment, and siege devices. A SAMEKH sits after v10 (single-witness, weak corroboration only), right at the seam between the building material (vv9-10) and v11's own muster-and-army notice, “וַיְהִ֣י לְעֻזִּיָּ֡הוּ חַיִל֩ עֹשֵׂ֨ה מִלְחָמָ֜ה” (“Uzziah had an army of fighting men”) — a wayehi-plus-lamed-plus-royal-name opener that recurs at 9:25 (“וַיְהִ֨י לִשְׁלֹמֹ֜ה”, Solomon's stalls), 14:7 MT/14:8 WEB (“וַיְהִ֣י לְאָסָ֗א”, Asa's army), 18:1 (“וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיהוֹשָׁפָ֛ט”, Jehoshaphat's wealth), and 32:27 (“וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיחִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ”, Hezekiah's treasuries), though none of these four opens a fresh reign-section on its own: 9:25 follows directly on the tribute register of 9:23-24; MT 14:5-7 itself runs the identical fortified-cities-then-walls-and-towers-then-army buildup sequence this row attributes to 26:9-11, so the device recurs mid-sequence there too; and 18:1 and 32:27 both follow other narrative material already underway (the marriage-alliance context and the illness-and-humbling notice of 32:24-26, respectively), not a reign's opening beat. Like its four comparanda, v.11 does not open a new section here either: it continues the same buildup-of-resources theme v9-10 already narrate (fortification capacity, then military capacity), with no temporal or locational marker of the kind that elsewhere marks this book's actual scene changes (the temporal-transition opener at 8:1, וַיְהִ֞י מִקֵּ֣ץ עֶשְׂרִ֣ים שָׁנָ֗ה אֲשֶׁ֨ר בָּנָ֧ה שְׁלֹמֹ֛ה אֶת בֵּ֥ית יְהוָ֖ה וְאֶת בֵּיתֽוֹ; the motion-verb-plus-place opener at 10:1, וַיֵּ֥לֶךְ רְחַבְעָ֖ם שְׁכֶ֑מָה כִּ֥י שְׁכֶ֛ם בָּ֥אוּ כָל יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לְהַמְלִ֥יךְ אֹתֽוֹ). The catalog is kept whole on that ground alone -- this book's own coarse treatment of register material -- not on any claim that the wayehi-lamed device itself marks reign-section openings; a finer split at 9-10 | 11-15 on the strength of v11's opener alone remains a live, defensible alternative the boss round may weigh differently. It closes on the hook “עַ֥ד כִּֽי חָזָֽק” (“until he was strong”), the same ḥ-z-q root picked up — as a catchword, not verbatim — at the start of v16's “וּכְחֶזְקָת֗וֹ” (“but when he was strong”), the adjacency (last word of v15, first word of v16) marking the catalog's own terminus despite the differing forms.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this catalog at the building/army seam (9-10 versus 11-15) is the genuine rival: a SAMEKH sits there and v11 opens with the book's own recurring wayehi-lamed-royal-name register-opener. Both are real, but neither carries the force of an actual scene-change device (no time or place shift, no new addressee), so the row keeps the coarse catalog whole rather than multiplying rows inside a single register-type unit -- a call the boss round may revisit.

boundary_rationale: A single root supplies the pivot: v15 just closed on “עַ֥ד כִּֽי חָזָֽק” (“until he was strong”), and v16 opens “וּכְחֶזְקָת֗וֹ גָּבַ֤הּ” (“but when he was strong, his heart was lifted up”), turning the same word into the hinge from success to hubris. The temple trespass, Azariah's confrontation, and the leprosy outbreak run through v21, closing on “וְיוֹתָ֤ם בְּנוֹ֙ עַל בֵּ֣ית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ שׁוֹפֵ֖ט אֶת עַ֥ם הָאָֽרֶץ” (“Jotham his son was over the king's house, judging the people of the land”). V22's source-citation formula picks up right where this narrative leaves off.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Absorbing the leprosy narrative into the preceding catalog (9-21 as one span) would erase the deliberate verbal echo the text sets up between v15's closing word and v16's opening word.

boundary_rationale: The identical closing device recurs from ch25, this time crediting the record to a named prophet: “וְיֶ֨תֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י עֻזִּיָּ֔הוּ הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאֲחֲרֹנִ֑ים כָּתַ֛ב יְשַֽׁעְיָ֥הוּ בֶן אָמ֖וֹץ הַנָּבִֽיא” (“Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, wrote”). The death-and-succession formula follows immediately, closing the chapter on “וַיִּשְׁכַּ֨ב עֻזִּיָּ֜הוּ עִם אֲבֹתָ֗יו וַיִּקְבְּר֨וּ אֹת֤וֹ עִם אֲבֹתָיו֙ בִּשְׂדֵ֤ה הַקְּבוּרָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַמְּלָכִ֔ים כִּ֥י אָמְר֖וּ מְצוֹרָ֣ע ה֑וּא וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יוֹתָ֥ם בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו” (“Jotham his son reigned in his place”), the Masoretic tradition's own PE sits after v23 (single-witness, corroborative weight only). 27:1's fresh age-formula for Jotham marks the seam-out.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the source-citation (v22) to the leprosy narrative that precedes it would still leave v22 doing the same work it does everywhere else in the book: opening, not continuing, a reign's closing report. The two-part citation-then-death shape is common but not universal -- 9:29-31 inserts a reign-length figure between them, 16:11-13 an illness notice, 20:34-21:1 an entire fleet episode, 24:25-27 even inverts the order, 33:18-20 wedges in a second source note, 35:26-27 has no death formula follow at all, 36:8 fuses citation and succession into one verse, and 27:7-9 in this very cluster is itself a counter-instance -- so the merge is rejected on the citation formula's own unit-opening force alone, not on a book-wide universal that does not hold.

boundary_rationale: Jotham's reign opens exactly where Uzziah's closed, with the standard age-formula “בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙ יוֹתָ֣ם בְּמָלְכ֔וֹ וְשֵׁשׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּֽירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְשֵׁ֣ם אִמּ֔וֹ יְרוּשָׁ֖ה בַּת צָדֽוֹק”, and the evaluation clause that follows measures him against his leprous father rather than against David, closing with the qualifying note “רַ֕ק לֹא בָ֖א אֶל הֵיכַ֣ל יְהוָ֑ה וְע֥וֹד הָעָ֖ם מַשְׁחִיתִֽים” (“however he didn't enter into Yahweh's temple; the people still acted corruptly”) — the temple-entry clause is the pointed echo of Uzziah's own trespass in the preceding chapter, sharing a 17-codepoint run with 26:16's “וַיָּבֹא֙ אֶל הֵיכַ֣ל יְהוָ֔ה לְהַקְטִ֖יר” (“he went into Yahweh's temple to burn incense”), broken only by the two verses' differing cantillation on the divine name; the echo is negated here (Jotham did not enter) against Uzziah's own transgressive entry. V3 then opens a fresh building topic with a bare subject pronoun.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running the formula straight through the building notices (1-4 combined) would blur the closed evaluation clause, which ends on a specific comparative judgment, against the separate catalog of construction that follows.

boundary_rationale: Three building/tribute notices share a fronted-constituent-plus-qatal achievement register: the gate and wall of Ophel open the row, fronting the independent pronoun, “ה֗וּא בָּנָ֛ה אֶת שַׁ֥עַר בֵּית יְהוָ֖ה הָעֶלְי֑וֹן וּבְחוֹמַ֥ת הָעֹ֛פֶל בָּנָ֖ה לָרֹֽב” (“he built the upper gate of Yahweh's house”); hill-country cities and fortresses follow in v4, fronting the object rather than a pronoun there, tied to v.3 lexically by the repeated building verb rather than by the pronoun pattern; and the Ammonite war-and-tribute notice occupies v5, itself opening with the fronted-pronoun pattern again, “וְ֠הוּא נִלְחַ֞ם” (“he also fought…”). A tier-3 SAMEKH follows v5, single-witness and non-driving, sitting precisely where the register shifts: v6, “וַיִּתְחַזֵּ֖ק יוֹתָ֑ם כִּ֚י הֵכִ֣ין דְּרָכָ֔יו לִפְנֵ֖י יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהָֽיו” (“So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before Yahweh his God”), is a verb-initial evaluative summary, not another achievement clause — closer in shape to the piety verdict closing 26:5, “הִצְלִיח֖וֹ הָאֱלֹהִֽים”, than to the building and tribute notices it is grouped with here. The row keeps v6 attached as this catalog's own summary terminus rather than splitting it off, since nothing resumes a narrative after it before the source-citation formula opens v7; but the register shift is real, and the 5/6 seam -- not the 4/5 seam -- is the stronger internal candidate for a split within this catalog.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The stronger rival is not separating v5 from vv3-4 -- both share the fronted-pronoun achievement pattern -- but separating v6's evaluative summary from vv3-5's catalog at the register shift the SAMEKH there corroborates; v6 is kept because it functions as this catalog's own closing verdict rather than opening anything new, but a finer split at 5/6 remains defensible and is left for the boss round.

boundary_rationale: The citation-before-statistic ordering here is not unusual: Solomon's own close runs the identical three-part sequence — citation at 9:29, “וּשְׁאָר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י שְׁלֹמֹ֔ה הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאֲחֲרוֹנִ֑ים”, then a reign-length figure new to the text at 9:30, “וַיִּמְלֹ֨ךְ שְׁלֹמֹ֧ה בִֽירוּשָׁלִַ֛ם עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה”, then death-and-succession at 9:31 — so the standard chronicle formula opening this row, “וְיֶתֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י יוֹתָ֔ם וְכָל מִלְחֲמֹתָ֖יו וּדְרָכָ֑יו הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֔ים עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִיהוּדָֽה” (“the rest of the acts of Jotham...written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah”), yet v8 then restates the same age and reign-length figures given in v1 almost verbatim, “בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֧ים וְחָמֵ֛שׁ שָׁנָ֖ה הָיָ֣ה בְמָלְכ֑וֹ וְשֵׁשׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם”, before the death-and-succession formula closes on “וַיִּשְׁכַּ֤ב יוֹתָם֙ עִם אֲבֹתָ֔יו וַיִּקְבְּר֥וּ אֹת֖וֹ בְּעִ֣יר דָּוִ֑יד וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אָחָ֥ז בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו” (“Ahaz his son reigned in his place”). What is genuinely distinctive is the repetition itself: v8's figures restate what v1 already gave, whereas Solomon's 9:30 reign-length is new information at that point in the text — Jotham's close doubles a statistic already on the record, which Solomon's does not, and unlike Uzziah's close (26:22-23), which states no regnal statistic at all alongside its citation.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Assigning v8's restated formula to a row of its own, apart from the citation (v7) and death notice (v9) that bracket it, would treat a three-verse closing complex as if its middle verse were an independent unit despite no scene-change marker separating it from either neighbor.

boundary_rationale: Ahaz receives the book's bluntest evaluation clause among this part's four kings: “בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים שָׁנָה֙ אָחָ֣ז בְּמָלְכ֔וֹ וְשֵׁשׁ עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם וְלֹא עָשָׂ֧ה הַיָּשָׁ֛ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י יְהוָ֖ה כְּדָוִ֥יד אָבִֽיו”, immediately followed by an elaborated apostasy catalog rather than the usual brief formula — Baal images, Hinnom-valley child sacrifice, and high-place worship close the row at v4, “וַיְזַבֵּ֧חַ וַיְקַטֵּ֛ר בַּבָּמ֖וֹת וְעַל הַגְּבָע֑וֹת וְתַ֖חַת כָּל עֵ֥ץ רַעֲנָֽן” (“he sacrificed and burned incense in the high places...under every green tree”). The catalog is not a smooth wayyiqtol run: it is broken twice by non-subject-changing disjunctives. V.2 itself closes with a fronted-object-plus-qatal disjunctive, interrupting the wayyiqtol chain v.2's own opening establishes; v.3 then opens with a second disjunctive of a different type, “וְה֥וּא הִקְטִ֖יר” (“Moreover he burned incense”), independent pronoun plus qatal breaking the chain v2's “וַיֵּ֕לֶךְ” sustains, before v3's own wayyiqtol and v4's wayyiqtol pick the chain back up. Neither disjunctive reopens the unit, since neither changes the grammatical subject (Ahaz remains the actor throughout v1-4) nor introduces a new topic, scene, or addressee — it foregrounds one particularly severe act (child sacrifice) within a single catalog of sins under one evaluative heading: throughout vv1-4 there is one actor (Ahaz), one evaluative heading (the negative regnal formula of v.1), and no new addressee or scene at either disjunctive. The row's actual close comes only at v5, which shifts agency from Ahaz as actor to Yahweh as the one who “delivered him” — a genuine change of agency at this particular seam, though not a criterion this row claims to share uniformly with its neighbors: comparable seams elsewhere in this part hold their own subject constant across the seam (M8-2Chr-116's 28:21/22 keeps Ahaz as subject throughout; M8-2Chr-120's 29:2/3, part 3, keeps Hezekiah as subject throughout), so the v.5 shift is argued on its own local terms, not as an instance of a general grammatical-subject-change rule.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this row into the fixed accession pair alone (vv1-2, matching the two-verse pattern at 25:1-2 and 27:1-2) and pushing the apostasy catalog (vv3-4) into its own row would miss that the evaluation clause of vv1-2 is grammatically continuous with, not separate from, the sins that follow: the wayyiqtol chain running through v2-4 (broken twice -- at v.2's own fronted-object disjunctive and at v.3's independent-pronoun disjunctive, both non-subject-changing) completes rather than closes the indictment, so v1-2 and v3-4 read as one unit rather than two.

boundary_rationale: Divine agency takes over as grammatical subject at the row's open, “וַֽיִּתְּנֵ֜הוּ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהָיו֮ בְּיַ֣ד מֶ֣לֶךְ אֲרָם֒” (“Yahweh his God delivered him into the hand of the king of Syria”), turning the preceding apostasy catalog into the ground for military disaster at the hands of Aram and Israel. Pekah's slaughter and Zichri's killings of royal officials lead to a captives-and-plunder notice, closing on “וַיָּבִ֥יאוּ אֶת הַשָּׁלָ֖ל לְשֹׁמְרֽוֹן” (“they brought the plunder to Samaria”); the Masoretic tradition marks this span densely — SAMEKH breaks fall after v5, v7, and v8 alike (all single-witness, weak corroboration only), so the v8 break cited as the row's close is one of three in this short stretch, not a solitary corroborating signal. V9's existential clause then introduces a new character at that same location.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this judgment report straight into the Oded episode (5-15 as one span) would erase v9's own scene-introducing force: a named participant is brought on, “נָבִ֥יא לַֽיהוָה֮ עֹדֵ֣ד שְׁמוֹ֒” (“a prophet of Yahweh...Oded”), followed by a motion verb directed at the army just brought to Samaria, “וַיֵּצֵ֗א.” The seam rests on v.9's own naming-plus-motion construction alone, not on any book-wide sham-hayah ('there was') opener pattern: the only other sham-hayah sequence in 2Chr is 1:3's “כִּי שָׁ֣ם הָיָ֗ה אֹ֤הֶל מוֹעֵד֙ הָֽאֱלֹהִ֔ים”, a subordinate causal clause supplying an inanimate object as background, not a main-clause participant introduction, so the two are not parallel instances of one device.

boundary_rationale: An existential clause introduces the prophet at the same city just named: “וְ֠שָׁם הָיָ֨ה נָבִ֥יא לַֽיהוָה֮ עֹדֵ֣ד שְׁמוֹ֒ וַיֵּצֵ֗א” (“but a prophet of Yahweh was there...Oded”), a self-contained scene combining his oracle, the Ephraimite leaders' answering speech (closing v13, “כִּֽי רַבָּ֤ה אַשְׁמָה֙ לָ֔נוּ וַחֲר֥וֹן אָ֖ף עַל יִשְׂרָאֵֽל”, “our guilt is great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel”), and the captives' release. It closes on the return notice “וַיָּשׁ֖וּבוּ שֹׁמְרֽוֹן” (“then they returned to Samaria”); the Masoretic tradition also marks two further interior seams — SAMEKH after v11 and after v13 (both single-witness, weak corroboration only) — alongside the boundary-adjacent PE after v15, so the closing mark is one of three in this stretch, not a lone signal. V16's own temporal frame opens an unrelated Assyria episode. The exact edges of this scene remain genuinely debatable, since “Samaria” itself brackets both v8's arrival and v15's return.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating just Oded's speech (9-11) from the leaders' response and the captives' relief (12-15) is not, in fact, a cut with no frame reopening the narrative: v12 opens with a genuine participant-change device, “וַיָּקֻ֨מוּ אֲנָשִׁ֜ים מֵרָאשֵׁ֣י בְנֵֽי אֶפְרַ֗יִם” (“some of the heads of the children of Ephraim...stood up”), naming four new leaders by name — the plural verb itself recurs six times book-wide (20:19, 28:12, 28:15, 29:12, 30:14, 30:27), but the sharper pattern this construction actually instances here -- the verb followed by newly-named persons -- stands only at 28:12 and 29:12: 20:19 and 30:27 name only a class of persons, not individuals; 28:15 anaphorically reuses 28:12's own names rather than introducing new ones; and 30:14 expresses no group at all. This narrower count sharpens rather than weakens the parallel this cluster's own decision M8-2Chr-120 draws, which treats the same verb-plus-newly-named-persons pattern as the device that closes a unit at 29:12. What keeps 9-15 together despite that device is the anaphoric envelope the same construction supplies at both ends: v15's identical verb closes the group v12 opens, “וַיָּקֻ֣מוּ הָאֲנָשִׁים֩ אֲשֶׁר נִקְּב֨וּ בְשֵׁמ֜וֹת” (“the men who have been mentioned by name rose up”), naming the same four leaders anaphorically rather than introducing a new party — so the construction here brackets one scene rather than opening a second one, unlike its stand-alone use at 29:12. The merge does not rest on the absence of any frame at v.12 -- a real, named-group-introducing frame exists there -- but on the fact that both of its occurrences, at v.12 and v.15, belong to the same captive-release action rather than opening two separate scenes.

boundary_rationale: A temporal frame opens this row, “בָּעֵ֣ת הַהִ֗יא שָׁלַ֞ח הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ אָחָ֛ז עַל מַלְכֵ֥י אַשּׁ֖וּר לַעְזֹ֥ר לֽוֹ” (“At that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria to help him”), distinct from the scene just closed. Edomite and Philistine invasions follow, and the appeal to Tiglath-Pileser fails, closing on “וַיָּבֹ֣א עָלָ֔יו תִּלְּגַ֥ת פִּלְנְאֶ֖סֶר מֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר וַיָּ֥צַר ל֖וֹ וְלֹ֥א חֲזָקֽוֹ” (“he gave him trouble, but didn't strengthen him”); v21 then reports Ahaz's own last resort, not a restatement of anything already stated in vv.16-20: כִּֽי חָלַ֤ק אָחָז֙ אֶת בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֔ה וְאֶת בֵּ֥ית הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ וְהַשָּׂרִ֑ים וַיִּתֵּן֙ לְמֶ֣לֶךְ אַשּׁ֔וּר וְלֹ֥א לְעֶזְרָ֖ה לֽוֹ (“For Ahaz took away a portion out of Yahweh’s house, and out of the house of the king and of the princes, and gave it to the king of Assyria; but it didn’t help him.”) -- Ahaz himself is the agent here, stripping the temple, palace, and officials' own treasuries to pay Assyria, not a report of plunder taken from him; the closing clause seals the failure v.20 already stated, rather than introducing a new defeat. The chapter's actual plunder notice belongs to a different row and a different party: it is the Israelite army's own plunder at 28:8, part of M8-2Chr-114's span, not this one. V22 does not open with a fresh echo of v16's own temporal frame — its distress-clause, “וּבְעֵת֙ הָצֵ֣ר ל֔וֹ” (“in the time of his distress”), shares only the bare noun 'time' with v16's opener, and instead reproduces v20's own verb root-for-root and suffix-for-suffix, “וַיָּ֥צַר ל֖וֹ” (“gave him trouble”) — an anaphor pulling v22 backward into the very Assyria-appeal span it needs to be distinguished from, not a matching frame at the seam; the same idiom recurs independently at 33:12's “וּכְהָצֵ֣ר ל֔וֹ”, so it is not even unique to this pairing. The real, uncited seam-signal is v22's own closing resumptive naming, “ה֖וּא הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אָחָֽז” (“this same King Ahaz”), a full-title reintroduction unattested anywhere else in 2Chr, marking a fresh narrative beat at v22 despite the backward-looking distress-clause that opens it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying this Assyria-appeal notice straight through v22-25's further apostasy would erase v22's own resumptive naming, which reintroduces Ahaz by full title in a way the book uses nowhere else -- a stronger, if quieter, seam-signal than the distress-clause it opens with, which is anaphoric to v20 rather than a fresh frame.

boundary_rationale: A matching echo of “time” frames this unit's open, “וּבְעֵת֙ הָצֵ֣ר ל֔וֹ וַיּ֖וֹסֶף לִמְע֣וֹל בַּיהוָ֑ה” (“in the time of his distress, he trespassed yet more”), pairing against v16's “at that time” to mark a fresh but parallel beat. Sacrifice to Damascus's gods, the cutting-up of temple vessels, and high places in every city of Judah run through the row, closing on “וּבְכָל עִ֨יר וָעִ֤יר לִֽיהוּדָה֙ עָשָׂ֣ה בָמ֔וֹת לְקַטֵּ֖ר לֵֽאלֹהִ֣ים אֲחֵרִ֑ים וַיַּכְעֵ֕ס אֶת יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י אֲבֹתָֽיו” (“he provoked Yahweh, the God of his fathers, to anger”). V26 supplies its own source-citation formula the very next verse.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the temple-vessel plunder (vv24-25) as a fresh row apart from the Damascus-sacrifice notice (22-23) would split one continuous escalation of trespass that the text narrates without any intervening scene-change marker.

boundary_rationale: The chronicle formula closes the block a fourth time in this part, “וְיֶ֤תֶר דְּבָרָיו֙ וְכָל דְּרָכָ֔יו הָרִאשֹׁנִ֖ים וְהָאַחֲרוֹנִ֑ים הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֔ים עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵֽי יְהוּדָ֖ה וְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל”, repeating the dual-kingdom register also used for Amaziah (25:26, the same Judah-then-Israel order) and Jotham (27:7, “עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִיהוּדָֽה”, inverting the order to Israel-then-Judah). This is a construct-phrase device (sefer malkhei X), not a dual-kingdom-content one: a book-wide sweep of the construct phrase finds exactly seven hits (20:34, 25:26, 27:7, 28:26, 32:32, 35:27, 36:8), and 20:34 alone among them names Israel only, mediated through Jehu's own record, WEB "Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, first and last, behold, they are written in the history of Jehu the son of Hanani, which is included in the book of the kings of Israel." -- not the dual-kingdom phrasing the register argument needs. The book's true dual-kingdom phrase is a different construction, Asa's own closing citation at 16:11, WEB "Behold, the acts of Asa, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.", a definite-article-plus-lamed construction excluded from this seven-hit construct-phrase count on form rather than content. Uzziah's own closing citation at 26:22, “כָּתַ֛ב יְשַֽׁעְיָ֥הוּ בֶן אָמ֖וֹץ הַנָּבִֽיא” (WEB “Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, wrote.”), is a different device, a prophetic-authorship citation naming no book of kings at all, and does not belong to this register: a book-wide sweep finds the register phrase at exactly seven verses (20:34, 25:26, 27:7, 28:26, 32:32, 35:27, 36:8), 26:22 not among them. The death-and-succession formula follows, closing this part's final verse on Ahaz's denial of the royal tombs proper, “וַיִּשְׁכַּ֨ב אָחָ֜ז עִם אֲבֹתָ֗יו וַֽיִּקְבְּרֻ֤הוּ בָעִיר֙ בִּיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם כִּ֚י לֹ֣א הֱבִיאֻ֔הוּ לְקִבְרֵ֖י מַלְכֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְחִזְקִיָּ֥הֽוּ בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו” (“because they didn't bring him into the tombs of the kings of Israel”), corroborated by a PE mark following v27 (single-witness). This is narrower than a unique exclusion: Uzziah too received a differentiated, causally-explained burial, “בִּשְׂדֵ֤ה הַקְּבוּרָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַמְּלָכִ֔ים כִּ֥י אָמְר֖וּ מְצוֹרָ֣ע ה֑וּא” (26:23, “in the field of burial which belonged to the kings, for they said, he is a leper”), against the plain notices for Amaziah (25:28) and Jotham (27:9); Ahaz alone is denied the royal tombs (לְקִבְרֵ֖י) specifically. 29:1's accession formula for Hezekiah lies beyond this part's range.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching the burial-exclusion clause from the death formula it is grammatically part of would isolate a single causal clause (“because...”) from the sentence it explains.

boundary_rationale: The regnal-opening pair 29:1-2 begins exactly where the prior reign's death-and-succession formula ends: 'וַיִּשְׁכַּ֨ב אָחָ֜ז עִם אֲבֹתָ֗יו ... וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְחִזְקִיָּ֥הֽוּ בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו' (28:27; WEB 'Ahaz slept with his fathers... Hezekiah his son reigned in his place') and a WLC single-witness PE break registers exactly at that handoff. The age-formula proper, 'בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֤ים וְחָמֵשׁ֙ שָׁנָ֔ה' and 'וְעֶשְׂרִ֤ים וָתֵ֨שַׁע֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם' (29:1; WEB 'Hezekiah began to reign when he was twenty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem'), pairs with the fixed evaluation clause 'וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הַיָּשָׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה' (29:2; WEB 'He did that which was right in Yahweh's eyes') to close a self-contained two-verse unit before the narrative pivots to a dated first-act notice at 29:3.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 29:1-2 into the following temple-reopening narrative as one 'Hezekiah's first acts' span loses because the age+evaluation formula is a self-contained regnal-notice form, distinct from the dated first-year action that only begins at 29:3.

boundary_rationale: A dated first-year notice, “ה֣וּא בַשָּׁנָה֩ הָרִאשׁוֹנָ֨ה לְמָלְכ֜וֹ בַּחֹ֣דֶשׁ הָרִאשׁ֗וֹן פָּתַ֛ח אֶת דַּלְת֥וֹת בֵּית יְהוָ֖ה וַֽיְחַזְּקֵֽם” (29:3; WEB “In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of Yahweh’s house and repaired them.”), launches this span right after the evaluation formula closes at 29:2. Its own syntax is fronted and off-line -- an independent pronoun plus two date phrases ahead of the qatal פָּתַ֛ח -- unlike the wayyiqtol chain proper, which only begins at v4's וַיָּבֵ֥א; but nothing separates the dated act from what it triggers, since the doors Hezekiah opens are precisely what he then staffs by summoning the priests and Levites in the very next clause, so the 3/4 join shares one continuous first-act notice rather than splitting a date-heading from its own consequence. The summons of priests and Levites, “וַיָּבֵ֥א אֶת הַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים וְאֶת הַלְוִיִּ֑ם וַיַּֽאַסְפֵ֖ם לִרְח֥וֹב הַמִּזְרָֽח” (29:4), runs straight into direct address with no intervening frame, “וַיֹּ֥אמֶר לָהֶ֖ם שְׁמָע֣וּנִי הַלְוִיִּ֑ם עַתָּ֣ה הִֽתְקַדְּשׁ֗וּ וְקַדְּשׁוּ֙ אֶת בֵּ֤ית יְהוָה֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י אֲבֹתֵיכֶ֔ם וְהוֹצִ֥יאוּ אֶת הַנִּדָּ֖ה מִן הַקֹּֽדֶשׁ” (29:5; WEB “and said to them, “Listen to me, you Levites! Now sanctify yourselves, and sanctify the house of Yahweh, the God of your fathers, and carry the filthiness out of the holy place.”), so the inset rule keeps the reform-charge speech (5-11) inside its introducing narrative rather than isolating it. The speech's final imperative, “בָּנַ֕י עַתָּ֖ה אַל תִּשָּׁל֑וּ כִּֽי בָכֶ֞ם בָּחַ֣ר יְהוָ֗ה לַעֲמֹ֤ד לְפָנָיו֙ לְשָׁ֣רְת֔וֹ וְלִהְי֥וֹת ל֖וֹ מְשָׁרְתִ֥ים וּמַקְטִרִֽים” (29:11; WEB “My sons, don’t be negligent now; for Yahweh has chosen you to stand before him, to minister to him, and that you should be his ministers and burn incense.””), carries a WLC single-witness SAMEKH, after which 29:12 turns to a new grammatical subject, the Levites' own action.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating v3 as its own dated-heading row is the closer rival this challenge raised, but v3's opening clause is a real, completed action -- Hezekiah opening and repairing the temple doors, WEB "In the first year of his reign, in the first month, he opened the doors of Yahweh’s house and repaired them." -- not an emptiness the merger argument can lean on; the case for merger rests instead on sequence: v3 is a complete dated first act whose immediate consequence is the v4 summons, so treating it as a self-standing unit would strand a finished act from the very reform it sets in motion.

boundary_rationale: Subject change marks the seam here: “וַיָּקֻ֣מוּ הַ֠לְוִיִּם” (29:12; WEB “Then the Levites arose:”) follows directly on the SAMEKH-marked close of the speech at 29:11. The clan-by-clan roll (12-14) gives way to the Levites' own self-sanctifying and entry, “וַיַּֽאַסְפ֤וּ אֶת אֲחֵיהֶם֙ וַיִּֽתְקַדְּשׁ֔וּ וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ כְמִצְוַת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בְּדִבְרֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה לְטַהֵ֖ר בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה” (29:15; WEB “They gathered their brothers, sanctified themselves, and went in, according to the commandment of the king by Yahweh’s words, to cleanse Yahweh’s house.”), but the purge of the sanctuary's inner part is priestly, not Levitical: “וַיָּבֹ֣אוּ הַ֠כֹּהֲנִים לִפְנִ֣ימָה בֵית יְהוָה֮ לְטַהֵר֒” (29:16; WEB “The priests went into the inner part of Yahweh’s house to cleanse it,”), with the Levites relaying the debris out to Kidron in the same verse. The dated completion note follows, “וַ֠יָּחֵלּוּ בְּאֶחָ֞ד לַחֹ֣דֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן֮ לְקַדֵּשׁ֒ וּבְי֧וֹם שְׁמוֹנָ֣ה לַחֹ֗דֶשׁ בָּ֚אוּ לְאוּלָ֣ם יְהוָ֔ה וַיְקַדְּשׁ֥וּ אֶת בֵּית יְהוָ֖ה לְיָמִ֣ים שְׁמוֹנָ֑ה וּבְי֨וֹם שִׁשָּׁ֥ה עָשָׂ֛ר לַחֹ֥דֶשׁ הָרִאשׁ֖וֹן כִּלּֽוּ” (29:17; WEB “Now they began on the first day of the first month to sanctify, and on the eighth day of the month they came to Yahweh’s porch. They sanctified Yahweh’s house in eight days, and on the sixteenth day of the first month they finished.”), and the report to the king stays with this execution rather than opening a fresh unit: “וַיָּב֤וֹאוּ פְנִ֨ימָה֙ אֶל חִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֹּ֣אמְר֔וּ” (29:18; WEB “Then they went in to Hezekiah the king”), where the same rare verb-root that named the priests' own entry to the inner house at 29:16 (an adverbial locative, פְּנִימָה, not a verb-root, attested in exactly three places in the book -- here, 29:16, and 3:4, where it names no entry at all, describing only the overlaid gold of the porch, WEB "The porch that was in front, its length, across the width of the house, was twenty cubits, and the height one hundred twenty; and he overlaid it within with pure gold.") now names their entry to report -- an adverbial-locative echo, not a shared verb-root, and a change of referent from the temple's inner house to the king's presence at that. The book's actual entry-verb, בוא 3mp wayyiqtol, occurs sixteen times in the book, including at 29:15 itself, which any exclusivity claim for the execution/report cohesion here has to set aside. It ends on the note about King Ahaz's discarded vessels, “הִזְנִיחַ֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ אָחָ֧ז בְּמַלְכוּת֛וֹ” (29:19; WEB “which King Ahaz threw away in his reign”), where a second WLC single-witness SAMEKH corroborates the shift to 29:20's new day and new royal subject.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off 29:18-19 as its own report-unit is the closer rival, since it opens with a location-and-addressee shift into Hezekiah's presence, but the same adverbial-locative פְּנִימָה naming the priests' inner-house entry at 29:16 recurs at 29:18's entry to report, tying report to execution rather than opening a fresh scene, notwithstanding the different referent each occurrence has.

boundary_rationale: Hezekiah's early rising reopens the action at 29:20, “וַיַּשְׁכֵּם֙ יְחִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַיֶּאֱסֹ֕ף אֵ֖ת שָׂרֵ֣י הָעִ֑יר וַיַּ֖עַל בֵּ֥ית יְהוָֽה” (WEB “Then Hezekiah the king arose early, gathered the princes of the city, and went up to Yahweh’s house.”), immediately after the SAMEKH-marked report closes at 29:19. The rite proceeds through the sevenfold sin-offering “פָרִים שִׁבְעָה֩ וְאֵילִ֨ים שִׁבְעָ֜ה וּכְבָשִׂ֣ים שִׁבְעָ֗ה וּצְפִירֵ֨י עִזִּ֤ים שִׁבְעָה֙ לְחַטָּ֔את עַל הַמַּמְלָכָ֥ה וְעַל הַמִּקְדָּ֖שׁ וְעַל יְהוּדָ֑ה” (29:21; WEB “seven bulls, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven male goats, for a sin offering for the kingdom, for the sanctuary, and for Judah.”) and the priestly slaughter, ending on the summary atonement clause “לְכַפֵּ֖ר עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל כִּ֤י לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ אָמַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ הָעוֹלָ֖ה וְהַחַטָּֽאת” (29:24; WEB “they made a sin offering with their blood on the altar, to make atonement for all Israel; for the king commanded that the burnt offering and the sin offering should be made for all Israel.”). The primary officiant and authority-citation shift at 29:25, from the Aaronide priests slaughtering under the king's command, “וַיֹּ֗אמֶר לִבְנֵ֤י אַהֲרֹן֙ הַכֹּ֣הֲנִ֔ים” (29:21; WEB “He commanded the priests the sons of Aaron”), to Levitical musicians installed under a newly cited authority, “וַיַּֽעֲמֵ֨ד אֶת הַלְוִיִּ֜ם בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֗ה בִּמְצִלְתַּ֨יִם֙ בִּנְבָלִ֣ים וּבְכִנֹּר֔וֹת בְּמִצְוַ֥ת דָּוִ֛יד וְגָ֥ד חֹזֵֽה הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ וְנָתָ֣ן הַנָּבִ֑יא כִּ֧י בְיַד יְהוָ֛ה הַמִּצְוָ֖ה בְּיַד נְבִיאָֽיו” (29:25; WEB “He set the Levites in Yahweh’s house with cymbals, with stringed instruments, and with harps, according to the commandment of David, of Gad the king’s seer, and Nathan the prophet; for the commandment was from Yahweh by his prophets.”); the priests do not disappear -- they resume with trumpets at 29:26, “וְהַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים בַּחֲצֹצְרֽוֹת” -- but the authority-citation formula, absent from the atonement rite of 20-24, is what marks this as a fresh unit -- the Hebrew quote and this WEB span now matched, running from the atonement clause through the verse's own royal-command כִּ֤-clause on both sides.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 29:20-36 as one continuous 'sacrifice liturgy' span loses because 29:25's shift to Levitical musicians under the cited authority of David, Gad, and Nathan introduces a new officiant-class and a new authority-citation formula absent from the atonement rite of 20-24.

boundary_rationale: A new authority-citation formula opens this span: “וַיַּֽעֲמֵ֨ד אֶת הַלְוִיִּ֜ם בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֗ה בִּמְצִלְתַּ֨יִם֙ בִּנְבָלִ֣ים וּבְכִנֹּר֔וֹת בְּמִצְוַ֥ת דָּוִ֛יד וְגָ֥ד חֹזֵֽה הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ וְנָתָ֣ן הַנָּבִ֑יא כִּ֧י בְיַד יְהוָ֛ה הַמִּצְוָ֖ה בְּיַד נְבִיאָֽיו” (29:25; WEB “He set the Levites in Yahweh’s house with cymbals, with stringed instruments, and with harps, according to the commandment of David, of Gad the king’s seer, and Nathan the prophet; for the commandment was from Yahweh by his prophets.”), distinct from the priestly rite just closed; a first single-witness SAMEKH follows 29:25 and a second follows 29:26, both disclosed here as tier-3 corroboration that never drives the call. The unit's real cohesion is a dependency, not a bracket: the burnt offering and song beginning together at 29:27, “וּבְעֵ֞ת הֵחֵ֣ל הָֽעוֹלָ֗ה הֵחֵ֤ל שִׁיר יְהוָה֙” (WEB “When the burnt offering began, Yahweh’s song also began,”), presupposes the personnel and instruments in place at 29:25-26, so the performance cannot be cut from its own setup: 29:25 is hiphil with Hezekiah as subject and the Levites alone as object, while 29:26 switches to qal with the Levites and priests together as subject and no royal agent -- a stem contrast the row preserves rather than attributing both classes' positioning to Hezekiah's hiphil act alone. It runs until “הַכֹּ֕ל עַ֖ד לִכְל֥וֹת הָעֹלָֽה” (29:28; WEB “until the burnt offering was finished.”) and closes on a terminal worship-gesture cluster rather than a true inclusio -- a book-wide sweep of שתחו-root forms finds exactly eleven occurrences in 2Chr, three of them consecutive here (29:28-30) with nothing of the kind at the span's 25-26 opening -- so the bowing at the offering's end, “כָּרְע֗וּ הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ וְכָֽל הַנִּמְצְאִ֥ים אִתּ֖וֹ וַיִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֽוּ” (29:29), and the second bowing, “וַֽיִּקְּד֖וּ וַיִּֽשְׁתַּחֲוֽוּ” (29:30, bearing a WLC single-witness PE), form a closing doublet, not a frame proving unity on their own; the 29:27 dependency does that work instead. Hezekiah's own declarative speech opens a new phase at 29:31. A book-wide sweep of the שתחו-root confirms exactly eleven occurrences in 2Chr (7:3, 7:19, 7:22, 20:18, 24:17, 25:14, 29:28, 29:29, 29:30, 32:12, 33:3), three of them the consecutive closing doublet reported here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the instrument-setting (25-26) from the performance (27-30) loses because 29:27's burnt-offering-and-song opening presupposes the personnel and instruments just stationed in 25-26, a real dependency the two internal SAMEKH marks (25, 26) only weakly corroborate and cannot themselves overcome.

boundary_rationale: Hezekiah's own answered-and-said formula launches a new phase at 29:31, 'וַיַּ֨עַן יְחִזְקִיָּ֜הוּ וַיֹּ֗אמֶר עַתָּ֨ה מִלֵּאתֶ֤ם יֶדְכֶם֙ לַיהוָ֔ה' (WEB 'Then Hezekiah answered, Now you have consecrated yourselves to Yahweh'), distinct from the fixed liturgy just closed. Freewill thank-offerings follow, and the Chronicler's own editorial aside on the priest shortage caps the sequence: 'רַ֤ק הַכֹּֽהֲנִים֙ הָי֣וּ לִמְעָ֔ט' (29:34) and 'כִּ֤י הַלְוִיִּם֙ יִשְׁרֵ֣י לֵבָ֔ב לְהִתְקַדֵּ֖שׁ מֵֽהַכֹּהֲנִֽים' (WEB '...the Levites were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests'). The episode ends on the summary-notice formula 'כִּ֥י בְּפִתְאֹ֖ם הָיָ֥ה הַדָּבָֽר' (29:36; WEB 'for the thing was done suddenly'), flagged by a WLC single-witness PE at the chapter's close, before chapter 30 opens on an entirely new royal initiative addressed to all Israel and Judah.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Absorbing 29:31-36 back into the preceding liturgy row (treating 25-36 as one span) loses because 29:31's answered-and-said formula marks a new speech-initiated movement that only follows after the fixed cultic liturgy has already closed.

boundary_rationale: Chapter 30 begins on a scope shift beyond the prior row's Jerusalem-only reform: “וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח יְחִזְקִיָּ֜הוּ עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל וִֽיהוּדָ֗ה וְגַֽם אִגְּרוֹת֙ כָּתַב֙ עַל אֶפְרַ֣יִם וּמְנַשֶּׁ֔ה לָב֥וֹא לְבֵית יְהוָ֖ה בִּֽירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת פֶּ֔סַח לַיהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל” (30:1; WEB “Hezekiah sent to all Israel and Judah, and wrote letters also to Ephraim and Manasseh, that they should come to Yahweh’s house at Jerusalem, to keep the Passover to Yahweh, the God of Israel.”), right after the PE-marked close of chapter 29. The king's counsel-taking, “וַיִּוָּעַ֨ץ הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ וְשָׂרָ֛יו וְכָל הַקָּהָ֖ל בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת הַפֶּ֖סַח בַּחֹ֥דֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִֽי” (30:2), leads to the decree's establishment, “וַיַּֽעֲמִ֣ידוּ דָבָ֗ר לְהַעֲבִ֨יר ק֤וֹל בְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ מִבְּאֵֽר שֶׁ֣בַע וְעַד דָּ֔ן לָב֞וֹא לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת פֶּ֛סַח לַיהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם כִּ֣י לֹ֥א לָרֹ֛ב עָשׂ֖וּ כַּכָּתֽוּב” (30:5; WEB “from Beersheba even to Dan,”). A courier-dispatch frame plus the speech-opening infinitive construct לֵאמֹ֑ר takes over at 30:6, ending the deliberation-report register. The near edge, however, is thinner than the far one: 30:1's opening verb is an ordinary narrative wayyiqtol, structurally identical to the wayyiqtol forms opening 30:5, 30:6 and 30:10 elsewhere in this same chapter, carrying no distinguishing grammatical form of its own; the near edge in fact rests on the topical scope-widening plus the tier-3 PE after 29:36, which corroborates but never drives. Only the far edge, 30:6's courier-dispatch frame plus the speech-opening infinitive construct, is tier-1 grounded in its own distinct form. book_strategy_draft.md §6 flags 30:1-12 broadly as a low-confidence letter-section-edges region; that flag is better honored than overridden here, since only one of this row's two edges carries its own grammatical warrant.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row through the letter itself (30:1-9 as one 'royal Passover initiative') loses because 30:6's courier-dispatch frame plus the speech-opening infinitive construct לֵאמֹ֑ר marks a formal shift from reported deliberation to direct-quoted letter content.

boundary_rationale: A messenger formula frames the letter on its near side: “וַיֵּלְכוּ֩ הָרָצִ֨ים בָּֽאִגְּר֜וֹת מִיַּ֧ד הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ וְשָׂרָ֗יו בְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ וִֽיהוּדָ֔ה וּכְמִצְוַ֥ת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ לֵאמֹ֑ר בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל שׁ֚וּבוּ אֶל יְהוָ֗ה” (30:6; WEB “saying, “You children of Israel, turn again to Yahweh,”). The exhortation runs through “וְאַל תִּֽהְי֗וּ כַּאֲבֽוֹתֵיכֶם֙ וְכַ֣אֲחֵיכֶ֔ם” (30:7; WEB “Don’t be like your fathers and like your brothers,”) and “עַתָּ֕ה אַל תַּקְשׁ֥וּ עָרְפְּכֶ֖ם כַּאֲבוֹתֵיכֶ֑ם” (30:8; WEB “Now don’t be stiff-necked, as your fathers were,”), ending on its own appeal, “כִּֽי חַנּ֤וּן וְרַחוּם֙ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵיכֶ֔ם וְלֹא יָסִ֤יר פָּנִים֙ מִכֶּ֔ם אִם תָּשׁ֖וּבוּ אֵלָֽיו” (30:9; WEB “because Yahweh your God is gracious and merciful, and will not turn away his face from you if you return to him.””), which carries a WLC single-witness PE. The frame closes on the far side too: 30:10's “וַיִּֽהְי֨וּ הָרָצִ֜ים עֹבְרִ֨ים” resumes the same runners-motif that opened the letter, satisfying the inset rule's requirement of isolation on both sides.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping the letter merged with its surrounding courier narrative (30:1-12 as one unit) loses because the resumptive repetition of the runners-motif at 30:10, mirroring 30:6, is itself a tier-1 frame closing the inset on both sides, so isolating the quoted letter better preserves the deliberation-report and response-notice around it.

boundary_rationale: The runners-motif resumes narration once the letter's frame closes: “וַיִּֽהְי֨וּ הָרָצִ֜ים עֹבְרִ֨ים” (30:10; WEB “So the couriers passed from city to city”). Mixed response follows, and the contrast particle introduces the humbled exception, “אַךְ אֲנָשִׁ֛ים מֵאָשֵׁ֥ר וּמְנַשֶּׁ֖ה וּמִזְּבֻל֑וּן נִֽכְנְע֔וּ וַיָּבֹ֖אוּ לִירוּשָׁלִָֽם” (30:11; WEB “Nevertheless some men of Asher, Manasseh, and Zebulun humbled themselves and came to Jerusalem.”). The row ends on its own summary clause, “גַּ֣ם בִּיהוּדָ֗ה הָֽיְתָה֙ יַ֣ד הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים לָתֵ֥ת לָהֶ֖ם לֵ֣ב אֶחָ֑ד לַעֲשׂ֞וֹת מִצְוַ֥ת הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ וְהַשָּׂרִ֖ים בִּדְבַ֥ר יְהוָֽה” (30:12; WEB “Also the hand of God came on Judah to give them one heart, to do the commandment of the king and of the princes by Yahweh’s word.”), before 30:13 opens an entirely new gathering formula at Jerusalem. Though 30:12's cause clause -- to do the king's commandment -- is what 30:13's assembly then carries out, its opening גַּ֣ם ('also') continues the region-by-region tally begun at 30:10-11 (Ephraim/Manasseh/Zebulun, then Asher/Manasseh/Zebulun, then Judah) rather than launching the gathering itself, so the mixed-reception report stays a closed short unit before 30:13's fresh formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 30:12 forward into the assembly-and-Passover unit (30:10-13) is the stronger rival, since 30:12's cause clause is what 30:13's assembly executes, but it is answered by reading 30:12's גַּ֣ם as continuing the response tally already running through 30:10-11, keeping the mixed-reception report its own closed unit.

boundary_rationale: A fresh gathering formula launches this span at 30:13, “וַיֵּֽאָסְפ֤וּ יְרוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ עַם רָ֔ב ... קָהָ֖ל לָרֹ֥ב מְאֹֽד” (WEB “Many people assembled at Jerusalem ... a very great assembly.”), distinct from the 'one heart' summary that just closed. The assembly purges idolatrous altars, “וַיָּקֻ֕מוּ וַיָּסִ֨ירוּ֙ אֶת הַֽמִּזְבְּח֔וֹת אֲשֶׁ֖ר בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם” (30:14), slaughters the Passover on schedule, “וַיִּשְׁחֲט֣וּ הַפֶּ֔סַח בְּאַרְבָּעָ֥ה עָשָׂ֖ר לַחֹ֣דֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִ֑י” (30:15; WEB “Then they killed the Passover on the fourteenth day of the second month.”), following כְּתוֹרַ֖ת מֹשֶׁ֣ה אִישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֑ים (30:16; WEB “according to the law of Moses the man of God.”), and reaches its far edge in the verse accounting for the Levites' expanded role, “כִּי רַבַּ֥ת בַּקָּהָ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹא הִתְקַדָּ֑שׁוּ וְהַלְוִיִּ֞ם עַל שְׁחִיטַ֣ת הַפְּסָחִ֗ים לְכֹל֙ לֹ֣א טָה֔וֹר לְהַקְדִּ֖ישׁ לַיהוָֽה” (30:17; WEB “For there were many in the assembly who had not sanctified themselves; therefore the Levites were in charge of killing the Passovers for everyone who was not clean, to sanctify them to Yahweh.”). 30:18 opens with its own כי-clause, “כִּ֣י מַרְבִּ֣ית הָעָ֡ם רַ֠בַּת מֵֽאֶפְרַ֨יִם וּמְנַשֶּׁ֜ה יִשָּׂשכָ֤ר וּזְבֻלוּן֙ לֹ֣א הִטֶּהָ֔רוּ” (WEB “For a multitude of the people, even many of Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves,”), so the seam is not procedural mechanics giving way to causal explanation -- both verses open causally -- but a shift in what the cause clause accounts for. 30:15's slaughter verb has no stated subject; the same verse separately names the priests and Levites as those who "were ashamed and sanctified themselves," and 30:16 puts the Levites at the blood-relay, not at the knife. The text nowhere establishes that 30:15's unnamed slaughterers are the Levites, so 30:17's own Levitical slaughter is new information -- not an explanation of an act already told -- formally parallel to 30:18's eating-violation clause: 30:17 introduces the Levitical accommodation for the unsanctified, and 30:18's own causal clause introduces the unresolved Passover-eating violation among northern pilgrims that only Hezekiah's prayer, opening later in the same verse, resolves.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying this span through to 30:18b's prayer frame is the more serious rival, since both 30:17 and 30:18a open with coordinate כי-clauses on the same purity problem, but 30:17's introduces the Levites' new accommodating role while 30:18's introduces the unresolved eating-violation that only the prayer resolves, so the sharper register shift is the prayer's own mid-verse introduction, not the clause boundary at 17/18.

boundary_rationale: This row groups the whole verses that carry the amnesty prayer, as book_strategy_draft.md §5 (Block map) anticipates ('amnesty prayer 30:18-20'); §1 (Genre and device matrix) locates only the sub-verse span '30:18b-19' for this same prayer, and it is that narrower citation the row's own near-edge warrant matches, since the unit's governing device sits mid-verse, not at 30:18's opening: “כִּ֣י מַרְבִּ֣ית הָעָ֡ם רַ֠בַּת מֵֽאֶפְרַ֨יִם וּמְנַשֶּׁ֜ה יִשָּׂשכָ֤ר וּזְבֻלוּן֙ לֹ֣א הִטֶּהָ֔רוּ” (30:18a; WEB “For a multitude of the people, even many of Ephraim, Manasseh, Issachar, and Zebulun, had not cleansed themselves,”) is a כי-clause matching 30:17's own opening, “כִּי רַבַּ֥ת בַּקָּהָ֖ל אֲשֶׁ֣ר לֹא הִתְקַדָּ֑שׁוּ”, in particle, quantifier, and a negated purity verb, so it continues the previous row's purity-problem language rather than opening a fresh unit on its own. The row's actual near-edge warrant is the prayer's own introduction, arriving later in the same verse, “כִּי֩ הִתְפַּלֵּ֨ל יְחִזְקִיָּ֤הוּ עֲלֵיהֶם֙ לֵאמֹ֔ר יְהוָ֥ה הַטּ֖וֹב יְכַפֵּ֥ר בְּעַֽד” (WEB “For Hezekiah had prayed for them, saying, “May the good Yahweh pardon everyone”), the middle causal clause of 30:18, WEB "yet they ate the Passover other than the way it is written," being the fresh cultic-offence clause that the petition's own verb actually pardons, so 30:18a is not wholly retrospective, which book_strategy_draft.md §1 itself locates at '30:18b-19.' The petition continues in 30:19, “וְלֹ֖א כְּטָהֳרַ֥ת הַקֹּֽדֶשׁ” (WEB “even if they aren’t clean according to the purification of the sanctuary.””), and the divine-response notice answers it directly, “וַיִּשְׁמַ֤ע יְהוָה֙ אֶל יְחִזְקִיָּ֔הוּ וַיִּרְפָּ֖א אֶת הָעָֽם” (30:20; WEB “Yahweh listened to Hezekiah, and healed the people.”), where a WLC single-witness SAMEKH corroborates. Subject and scope shift entirely at 30:21 to the people's own seven-day celebration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping the prayer merged with the surrounding Passover-practice report (13-20 as one span) loses because the mid-verse prayer-introduction formula at 30:18b and 30:20's divine-response notice frame the intercession as its own resolvable unit, distinct from the ritual mechanics reported in 13-17, even though 30:18a's own opening still belongs to that prior problem-language rather than to the prayer itself.

boundary_rationale: New grammatical subject and new time-frame mark the seam at 30:21, “וַיַּעֲשׂ֣וּ בְנֵֽי יִ֠שְׂרָאֵל הַנִּמְצְאִ֨ים בִּירוּשָׁלִַ֜ם אֶת חַ֧ג הַמַּצּ֛וֹת שִׁבְעַ֥ת יָמִ֖ים בְּשִׂמְחָ֣ה גְדוֹלָ֑ה” (WEB “kept the feast of unleavened bread seven days with great gladness.”), replacing the Hezekiah-and-Yahweh focus of the prayer unit; a WLC single-witness SAMEKH falls after this verse too, alongside the one disclosed at its far edge; a third mark, also SAMEKH, sits at 30:20, the join immediately preceding this row's own near edge -- the only one of the three nearby marks that corroborates an edge of this row rather than its interior. The tally here is three marks in total, none driving the call. Hezekiah's encouragement of the Levites follows, “וַיְדַבֵּ֣ר יְחִזְקִיָּ֗הוּ עַל לֵב֙ כָּל הַלְוִיִּ֔ם” (30:22; WEB “Hezekiah spoke encouragingly to all the Levites”), reaching its far edge in the confession notice “וּמִ֨תְוַדִּ֔ים לַיהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י אֲבוֹתֵיהֶֽם”, where a second WLC single-witness SAMEKH falls; both marks corroborate the surrounding two-verse span only weakly and do not drive the call. A fresh deliberation opens the next verse, “וַיִּוָּֽעֲצוּ֙ כָּל הַקָּהָ֔ל לַעֲשׂ֕וֹת שִׁבְעַ֥ת יָמִ֖ים אֲחֵרִ֑ים” (30:23; WEB “The whole assembly took counsel to keep another seven days,”), over a new deliberative object, seven more days beyond the feast just completed; the counsel-verb itself is not distinctive -- niphal wayyiqtol י-ע-ץ recurs seven times in the book, including 10:8 mid-episode with no accompanying break, and 30:2's form is third-singular against 30:23's third-plural -- so the new time-object, not a repeated verb-form, is what marks the fresh assembly decision.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging 30:21-27 as one continuous 'feast of unleavened bread' span loses because 30:23's new deliberative object, seven additional days beyond the feast just completed, marks a fresh assembly decision separate from the days just reported, though the short span involved makes this a genuine close call.

boundary_rationale: A fresh assembly decision opens this span at 30:23, over a new deliberative object beyond the feast just completed, “וַיִּוָּֽעֲצוּ֙ כָּל הַקָּהָ֔ל לַעֲשׂ֕וֹת שִׁבְעַ֥ת יָמִ֖ים אֲחֵרִ֑ים” (WEB “The whole assembly took counsel to keep another seven days,”); the counsel-taking verb itself recurs as thematic resonance with the Passover's original authorization at 30:2, “וַיִּוָּעַ֨ץ הַמֶּ֧לֶךְ וְשָׂרָ֛יו וְכָל הַקָּהָ֖ל בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת הַפֶּ֖סַח בַּחֹ֥דֶשׁ הַשֵּׁנִֽי” (WEB “For the king had taken counsel with his princes and all the assembly in Jerusalem to keep the Passover in the second month.”), but the two verbs differ in number (30:2's third-singular against 30:23's third-plural) and the same niphal form recurs elsewhere in the book without any accompanying break (10:8), so it is the new object, not a repeated form, that opens the span. Provisioning by king and princes follows, “כִּ֣י חִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ יְ֠הוּדָה” (30:24; WEB “For Hezekiah king of Judah”), and the joy notice recalling Solomon, “כִּ֠י מִימֵ֞י שְׁלֹמֹ֤ה בֶן דָּוִיד֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל לֹ֥א כָזֹ֖את בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם” (30:26; WEB “for since the time of Solomon the son of David king of Israel there was nothing like this in Jerusalem.”), gives way to the priestly benediction ascending to heaven, “וַיָּקֻ֜מוּ הַכֹּהֲנִ֤ים הַלְוִיִּם֙ וַיְבָרֲכ֣וּ אֶת הָעָ֔ם וַיִּשָּׁמַ֖ע בְּקוֹלָ֑ם וַתָּב֧וֹא תְפִלָּתָ֛ם לִמְע֥וֹן קָדְשׁ֖וֹ לַשָּׁמָֽיִם” (30:27; WEB “Then the Levitical priests arose and blessed the people. Their voice was heard, and their prayer came up to his holy habitation, even to heaven.”), where a WLC single-witness PE falls exactly at this close; marks recur throughout this stretch -- SAMEKH at 30:22, 30:24, 30:26 and 31:1 as well, with 30:24 and 30:26 lying inside this row's own span -- so the closing PE reads as one of several tier-3 marks corroborating this run rather than an isolated signal. The book's next unit opens on the completion-transition formula “וּכְכַלּ֣וֹת כָּל זֹ֗את” (31:1; WEB “Now when all this was finished,”), a fresh scene outside this part's range.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the extension-decision (23) from the provisioning-and-closing material (24-27) loses because the decree and its immediate provisioning, joy, and benediction form one continuous festival-extension report closed only once, by the ascension-to-heaven formula at 30:27.

boundary_rationale: Opens on the temporal-completion formula וּכְכַלּ֣וֹת כָּל זֹ֗את, WEB “Now when all this was finished,”, pivoting from the just-completed Passover feast (outside this part) to its physical aftermath: the assembled worshippers fan out through Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh to break the pillars, cut down the Asherim, and tear down the high places and altars “until they had destroyed them all.” The verse is a bounded sweep-and-return report, closing on the collective dispersal formula וַיָּשׁ֜וּבוּ כָּל בְּנֵ֧י יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל אִ֥ישׁ לַאֲחֻזָּת֖וֹ לְעָרֵיהֶֽם, WEB “Then all the children of Israel returned, every man to his possession, into their own cities.” Verse 2 reopens on an entirely different actor and register with a fresh wayyiqtol subject, Hezekiah organizing priestly and Levitical rotas inside the temple, not the nationwide crowd tearing down shrines. The SAMEKH following v1 (single-witness) gives only weak corroboration that a unit break falls here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Annexing v1 to the preceding Passover complex as its coda is possible since “all this” refers back to it, but the prior part's seam-out already lands at 31:1 and the verse's own self-contained return-and-dispersal shape gives it complete internal unity apart from what follows.

boundary_rationale: Two explicit royal ordinances bracket a verbless middle clause, and the unit's real cohesion is the null-subject continuity across it: “וַיַּעֲמֵ֣ד יְחִזְקִיָּ֡הוּ אֶת מַחְלְק֣וֹת הַכֹּהֲנִ֣ים וְ֠הַלְוִיִּם עַֽל מַחְלְקוֹתָ֞ם אִ֣ישׁ כְּפִ֣י עֲבֹדָת֗וֹ לַכֹּהֲנִים֙ וְלַלְוִיִּ֔ם לְעֹלָ֖ה וְלִשְׁלָמִ֑ים לְשָׁרֵת֙ וּלְהֹד֣וֹת וּלְהַלֵּ֔ל בְּשַׁעֲרֵ֖י מַחֲנ֥וֹת יְהוָֽה”, “Hezekiah appointed the divisions of the priests…” (v2), names Hezekiah explicitly, but v3, “וּמְנָת֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ מִן רְכוּשׁ֜וֹ לָעֹל֗וֹת לְעֹלוֹת֙ הַבֹּ֣קֶר וְהָעֶ֔רֶב וְהָ֣עֹל֔וֹת לַשַּׁבָּת֖וֹת וְלֶחֳדָשִׁ֣ים וְלַמֹּעֲדִ֑ים כַּכָּת֖וּב בְּתוֹרַ֥ת יְהוָֽה”, has no finite verb and no expressed royal subject -- only the genitive 'the king's portion' inside a nominal clause -- so v4's null-subject וַיֹּ֤אמֶר … לָתֵ֕ת מְנָ֥ת הַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים וְהַלְוִיִּ֑ם, “he commanded… to give the portion of the priests and the Levites”, recovers its referent back across the nominal v3 to v2's explicit יְחִזְקִיָּ֡הוּ. The chain closes on a rare clause-final formula shared by only one other verse in the book: בְּתוֹרַ֥ת יְהוָֽה, 'in Yahweh's law,' ends both v3 and v4, and recurs just once more, at 35:26. A book-wide sweep confirms תורת יהוה occurs six times in 2Chr (12:1, 17:9, 31:3, 31:4, 34:14, 35:26) against תורת משה only twice (23:18, 30:16); restricted to the bound ב-form the chain here actually uses, the tally is three (31:3, 31:4, 35:26) against one (23:18, since 30:16 uses כ- rather than ב-). The unit stops before the causal hinge of v5, וְכִפְרֹ֣ץ הַדָּבָ֗ר, “as soon as the commandment went out”, which shifts the narrative from command to the people's response.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding vv2-4 into the compliance narrative that follows (vv5-10) as one long provisioning unit is tempting since v4's command is the direct antecedent of v5's response, but it would blur the command/response hinge and merge pure legislation with reported popular action.

boundary_rationale: Opens on the causal hinge, rendered by WEB as “As soon as the commandment went out,” (וְכִפְרֹ֣ץ הַדָּבָ֗ר, more literally 'when the matter broke forth'), turning royal legislation (vv2-4) into narrated compliance: firstfruits and tithe of grain, wine, oil and honey (v5); Israel and Judah bringing the tithe of herd, flock, and dedicated things and heaping it, “וַֽיִּתְּנ֖וּ עֲרֵמ֥וֹת עֲרֵמֽוֹת” (v6; WEB “and laid them in heaps.” -- the doubled Hebrew noun underlying WEB's single 'heaps'), corroborated by a single-witness SAMEKH; a fixed third-to-seventh-month timeline for completing the heaps, “בַּחֹ֨דֶשׁ֙ הַשְּׁלִשִׁ֔י הֵחֵ֥לּוּ הָעֲרֵמ֖וֹת לְיִסּ֑וֹד וּבַחֹ֥דֶשׁ הַשְּׁבִיעִ֖י כִּלּֽוּ” (v7), corroborated by a second single-witness SAMEKH; Hezekiah and the princes coming to inspect and bless what has accumulated, “וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ יְחִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ וְהַשָּׂרִ֔ים וַיִּרְא֖וּ אֶת הָעֲרֵמ֑וֹת וַֽיְבָרֲכוּ֙” (v8), corroborated by a single-witness PE; Hezekiah's inquiry (v9); and Azariah the chief priest's answer, closing on the summary וְהַנּוֹתָ֖ר אֶת הֶהָמ֥וֹן הַזֶּֽה, WEB “that which is left is this great store.”” (v10). None of the four tier-3 marks drives the seam -- a fourth mark, SAMEKH, sits at the span's own closing verse, v10, corroborating the far edge rather than the interior: the time-frame at v7 and the arrival of Hezekiah and the princes at v8 are real internal transitions, but both belong to the single inspection movement the tithe-bringing of vv5-7 is building toward -- the heaps have to be completed and dated before there is anything for the king to come inspect, question, and receive Azariah's answer about -- so the report holds together as one compliance-and-inspection unit rather than splitting at either point. Verse 11's fresh command, וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְחִזְקִיָּ֗הוּ לְהָכִ֧ין לְשָׁכ֛וֹת בְּבֵ֥ית יְהוָ֖ה, 'Hezekiah commanded... to prepare rooms...', pivots from narrated abundance to the administrative apparatus built to store and distribute it, introducing a roster of previously unnamed officials.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the span at v7's time-frame notice or v8's arrival of Hezekiah and the princes is the closer internal rival, but both mark stages within one inspection movement -- dated heap-completion feeding directly into the king's arrival to inspect and question -- rather than two separable reports, so the tier-3 SAMEKH/PE marks at each stage corroborate without dividing it.

boundary_rationale: Hezekiah's command to prepare rooms, וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְחִזְקִיָּ֗הוּ לְהָכִ֧ין לְשָׁכ֛וֹת בְּבֵ֥ית יְהוָ֖ה, immediately shifts into list-register mode: named overseers Conaniah and Shimei (v12); ten further named officers (v13); the gatekeeper Kore over the freewill offerings (v14); six named men, stationed under Kore's hand in the cities of the priests, distributing by division “to the great as well as to the small” (v15); three successive genealogical-registration clauses, covering males from age three (v16), then the priests by their fathers' houses and the Levites specifically from twenty years old and upward (v17, “וְהַ֨לְוִיִּ֔ם מִבֶּ֛ן עֶשְׂרִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה וּלְמָ֑עְלָה” -- the age qualifier attaches to the Levites alone, not to both groups), then the whole household congregation (v18). V19 puts the sons of Aaron in the lamed phrase as recipients and introduces a distinct group of named men as the ones distributing portions to them (matching WEB: 'for the sons of Aaron the priests... there were men who were mentioned by name to give portions'), closing וּלְכָל הִתְיַחֵ֖שׂ בַּלְוִיִּֽם, “and to all who were listed by genealogy among the Levites” (v19). The book strategy flags this whole span as register-like and directs coarse handling rather than a verse-by-verse split of its names and categories. Verse 20 breaks the list format outright with an evaluative clause, וַיַּ֧עַשׂ כָּזֹ֛את יְחִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ בְּכָל יְהוּדָ֑ה, “Hezekiah did so…”, assessing the king's conduct rather than cataloging personnel.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at the seam between named-overseer material (12-15) and the purely genealogical clauses (16-19) has some content support, but the strategy's explicit coarse-treatment instruction for this register outweighs multiplying near-identical list-formula rows.

boundary_rationale: Pivots entirely out of list-format into a summarizing verdict: וַיַּ֧עַשׂ כָּזֹ֛את יְחִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ בְּכָל יְהוּדָ֑ה, “Hezekiah did so throughout all Judah”, followed by the evaluative triad “the good, the right, and וְהָ֣אֱמֶ֔ת” (the faithful/true) before Yahweh his God (v20). Verse 21 extends the same verdict across “every work he began… with all his heart”, closing on בְּכָל לְבָב֥וֹ עָשָׂ֖ה וְהִצְלִֽיחַ, “he did it… and prospered” — a stock Chronicles success-formula close, corroborated weakly by the PE mark (single-witness) that follows v21. This two-verse unit is the evaluative coda to the whole provisions complex (31:1-19), not fresh narrative content.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Appending vv20-21 to the register of vv11-19 as its concluding lines shares the same reform program, but it would merge a summarizing verdict with a list-format catalog across a clean pivot in verb and rhetorical mode.

boundary_rationale: Opens with the time-frame transition אַחֲרֵ֨י הַדְּבָרִ֤ים וְהָאֱמֶת֙ הָאֵ֔לֶּה בָּ֖א סַנְחֵרִ֣יב מֶֽלֶךְ אַשּׁ֑וּר, “after these things and this faithfulness… Sennacherib… came”, a formula the book strategy expects at exactly this seam; it even echoes the root of וְהָ֣אֱמֶ֔ת from 31:20 while launching a wholly new arc: Sennacherib's invasion. The unit spans Hezekiah's defensive water-stopping (vv2-4), fortification and armament (v5), appointment of war-captains (v6), and his direct address to the mobilized people, חִזְק֣וּ וְאִמְצ֔וּ…, “be strong and courageous”, ending וַיִּסָּמְכ֣וּ הָעָ֔ם עַל דִּבְרֵ֖י יְחִזְקִיָּ֥הוּ מֶֽלֶךְ יְהוּדָֽה, “the people rested themselves on the words of Hezekiah king of Judah” (v8). Per the inset rule this royal speech stays inside its host mobilization scene: nothing frames it as isolated on both sides, since v6 sets it up and v8b folds straight back into narration without a resumption formula that would justify carving it out. Verse 9's אַ֣חַר זֶ֗ה שָׁ֠לַח, “after this, Sennacherib sent…”, returns Sennacherib himself to the grammatical subject and opens a different mode of aggression, verbal rather than defensive.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating Hezekiah's speech (vv7-8) as its own row is the natural rival given the direct quotation, but the inset rule requires a tier-1 closing frame that resumes narration distinctly from the speech, and v8b's report of the people's response continues the same beat rather than reopening one.

boundary_rationale: Reopens with אַ֣חַר זֶ֗ה שָׁ֠לַח, restoring Sennacherib as subject and launching the messenger-taunt scene, corroborated by a single-witness PE just before it at 32:8: his royal speech is quoted at length (vv10-15), addressed second-person to the besieged.
