Verse 16, וְעוֹד֙ דִּבְּר֣וּ עֲבָדָ֔יו, a paraphrase, not a WEB quotation (WEB reads "His servants spoke yet more against Yahweh God and against his servant Hezekiah."), signals continuation but its own plural verb governs only that clause; v17 shifts to a third-singular qatal with Sennacherib alone as subject and the object fronted, וּסְפָרִ֣ים כָּתַ֔ב, a paraphrase, not a WEB quotation (WEB reads "He also wrote letters insulting Yahweh, the God of Israel, and speaking against him, saying, “As the gods of the nations of the lands, which have not delivered their people out of my hand, so shall the God of Hezekiah not deliver his people out of my hand.”"), and v18 shifts again to a plural, spoken, public proclamation aimed at the wall's defenders, וַיִּקְרְא֨וּ בְקוֹל גָּד֜וֹל יְהוּדִ֗ית. None of these three shifts is itself an episode-opener of the kind the Chronicler otherwise uses to break a scene in this chapter -- though the exclusion criterion "fronts an off-line temporal marker" is falsified inside chapter 32 itself: 32:32's fronted nominal closes Hezekiah's reign with no temporal element, and 33:1's nominal age formula likewise has none, yet the sibling row M8-2Chr-139 lists both as belonging to "every other seam in this run" alongside 32:1, 32:9, and 32:24 -- under that wider criterion v17's own fronted-object qatal is precisely such an opener too, and what keeps this block together is referential continuity rather than the temporal-marker test: 32:9's own אַ֣חַר זֶ֗ה שָׁ֠לַח and 32:24's בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם חָלָ֥ה plus qatal both front an off-line temporal marker that vv16-19 never supply -- and the same blasphemy runs through the whole block: v19's summary comparison, מַעֲשֵׂ֖ה יְדֵ֥י הָאָדָֽם, “the work of men's hands”, closes the insult the letters (17) and the proclamation (18) both carried forward. The whole complex therefore stays together under the inset rule as one continuous taunt rather than three separable reports; the single-witness SAMEKH at 32:19 closes it, again as weak, non-driving corroboration. It closes before v20 pivots to an entirely different subject and genre: Hezekiah and Isaiah's prayer.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating v17's letters as their own inset row is the closer rival the strategy names, and under the wider off-line-fronting criterion this cluster's own M8-2Chr-139 applies to 32:32 and 33:1, v17's fronted-object qatal is exactly such an opener; the row nonetheless keeps it here because no resumption formula marks a return to any prior scene after v17, and the same blasphemy referent that v16 signals and v18 proclaims aloud runs continuously through the letters themselves, closed only by v19's summary comparison.

boundary_rationale: A single terse notice, “וַיִּתְפַּלֵּ֞ל יְחִזְקִיָּ֣הוּ הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ וִֽישַֽׁעְיָ֧הוּ בֶן אָמ֛וֹץ הַנָּבִ֖יא עַל זֹ֑את וַֽיִּזְעֲק֖וּ הַשָּׁמָֽיִם”, reports in third person (not a quoted prayer) that “Hezekiah the king and Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, prayed because of this, and cried to heaven.” The near edge is solid tier-1: a fresh subject pair, the king and the prophet named together, breaks from the preceding blasphemous speech-complex, corroborated (not driven) by the single-witness SAMEKH already disclosed after 32:19. The far edge is thinner and is stated as such rather than propped up by the mark: v21's וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח יְהוָה֙ מַלְאָ֔ךְ, “Yahweh sent an angel”, does install Yahweh as sole acting subject for the first time in the chapter, but unlike every other seam in this run -- 32:1's אַחֲרֵ֨י הַדְּבָרִ֤ים וְהָאֱמֶת֙ הָאֵ֔לֶּה, 32:9's אַ֣חַר זֶ֗ה שָׁ֠לַח, 32:24's בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם חָלָ֥ה plus qatal, 32:32's fronted וְיֶ֛תֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י, 33:1's nominal age formula בֶּן שְׁתֵּ֥ים עֶשְׂרֵ֛ה שָׁנָ֖ה מְנַשֶּׁ֣ה בְמָלְכ֑וֹ -- v21 fronts nothing off-line; it is a bare wayyiqtol subject change from the human pair of v20. The single-witness PE following v20 is disclosed as tier-3 corroboration only and does not itself decide the seam; the case for keeping v20 as its own beat rests on the subject-and-genre shift alone, human petition giving way to divine action, acknowledged here as the softest boundary in this stretch of the chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this one-verse notice into the deliverance narrative that follows (vv21-23) as a single petition-and-answer unit is a live, closely balanced rival rather than a decisively rejected one; it is set aside only because the petition's own named subject pair and the following verse's shift to Yahweh as sole actor are real actor changes worth keeping as adjoining beats, not because any mark settles the question.

boundary_rationale: Opens with Yahweh as sole grammatical subject, וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח יְהוָה֙ מַלְאָ֔ךְ, sending the angel that annihilates the Assyrian camp's commanders, forcing Sennacherib's shameful retreat and assassination by his own sons in the house of his god (v21) -- an ironic reversal of v17's letter insulting “Yahweh, the God of Israel.” Verse 22 states the theological verdict, “Yahweh saved,” before v23 reports the consequence: gifts pouring in to Yahweh and to Hezekiah, and the king exalted “in the sight of all nations,” closing מֵאַֽחֲרֵי כֵֽן, where a single-witness SAMEKH also falls (tier-3, non-driving, disclosed here alongside the PE already cited at the row's near edge). This is not itself a temporal closure formula: it is the ordinary phrase אחרי כן carrying a prefixed preposition and standing clause-final, adverbial to וַיִּנַּשֵּׂ֛א ('he was exalted... from that point on'), reaching forward past the episode rather than sealing it -- a book-wide sweep finds the phrase family five times (20:1, 20:35, 24:4, 32:23, 33:14), and 32:23 is the only one both prefixed with מן and clause-final; the other four are clause-initial episode-openers. The literary reading of v23 as summarizing a lasting royal consequence still holds, but as inference from content, not from a closural grammatical device. The unit's actual close instead rests on v24's own off-line opener, בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם חָלָ֥ה, a fronted time-frame notice of the kind this chapter uses elsewhere for genuine scene breaks (32:1, 32:9). The row's opening edge, at 32:20/21, is comparatively thinner: as decision 139 discloses, it turns on a bare subject change (from the human petitioners of v20 to Yahweh alone) rather than a fronted off-line marker, so this row's confidence is graded to reflect a firm far edge paired with a softer near edge rather than uniform strength across both.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit back to include v20's prayer notice as one continuous petition-through-consequence arc is a live, closely balanced rival that the row does not deny; v21's pivot to Yahweh as sole actor is what keeps the human petition and the divine response as adjoining but distinct beats, without the PE at 32:20 deciding the question.

boundary_rationale: Opens on the Chronicler's vague compressed-notice marker, בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם חָלָ֥ה יְחִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ עַד לָמ֑וּת, “in those days Hezekiah was sick to the point of death…”, a fresh crisis in subject matter, though its opening demonstrative phrase requires an antecedent, which the text supplies only in the days just narrated at vv21-23; the illness is a different crisis, but the text expressly dates it inside the preceding frame -- an anaphoric time-frame anchoring a fresh subject, not a wholly unconnected one. The three verses trace a complete moral arc: failure to reciprocate God's benefit because “his heart was lifted up,” bringing wrath on him, Judah and Jerusalem (v25); then self-humbling that averts Yahweh's wrath, closing on the adjunct “in the days of Hezekiah” (v26). A book-wide sweep confirms the בִּימֵי+name construction occurs five times in 2Chr (9:20, 13:20, 26:5 twice, 32:26), and v26's is the only clause-final instance among them; one clause-final occurrence cannot constitute a device class, which is exactly the test this cluster's own M8-2Chr-140 applies when it refuses closural force to the unique clause-final adjunct at 32:23. Any retrospective, sealing force in v26's adjunct is content inference from the completed moral arc, not a formula, consistent with how M8-2Chr-140 now treats its own adjunct. Verse 27's fresh clause, וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיחִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ עֹ֥שֶׁר וְכָב֖וֹד הַרְבֵּ֣ה מְאֹ֑ד, “Hezekiah had exceedingly great riches and honor…”, opens a new topic in its own right, the wealth catalog, even though it is not wholly unconnected to what precedes: 32:31's later definite הַמּוֹפֵת֙, “the portent”, -- the only other occurrence of this noun in the book besides v24's own indefinite וּמוֹפֵ֖ת -- reaches back across the wealth material to name the very sign this row reports, so the illness notice's own vocabulary resurfaces after the catalog rather than being sealed off from it. The seam kept here at 26/27 rests instead on v27's own topic-opening formula and on the pride-and-humbling arc that closes complete in itself at v25-26, sealed by בִּימֵ֖י יְחִזְקִיָּֽהוּ.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Grouping vv24-31 as one undifferentiated closing-notices block is a real rival strengthened by v31's definite הַמּוֹפֵת֙ reaching back to v24's sign, but the moral-closure formula sealing v25-26 still marks the pride-and-humbling episode complete in itself before v27 opens the wealth catalog that v31's own envoys-notice reaches back to answer.

boundary_rationale: Opens the wealth catalog proper, וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיחִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ עֹ֥שֶׁר וְכָב֖וֹד הַרְבֵּ֣ה מְאֹ֑ד… (treasuries of silver, gold, precious stones, spices and shields, v27; storehouses and stalls, v28; cities and herds WEB “for God had given him abundant possessions.” (v29), then folds in the Gihon engineering feat under the resumptive tag וְה֣וּא יְחִזְקִיָּ֗הוּ, glossed “and this same Hezekiah…” (v30) rather than quoted, a free rendering of the Hebrew rather than WEB’s own wording. Verse 31, introduced by the continuative וְכֵ֞ן, glossed here “and so… with the envoys of… Babylon” (a gloss, not a WEB quotation), does not behave like one more catalog item: its main clause inverts the pattern of vv27-30, which predicate acquisitions and works TO Hezekiah (וַיְהִ֧י לִֽיחִזְקִיָּ֛הוּ, עָֽשָׂה ל֠וֹ), by making God the subject and Hezekiah the object, עֲזָב֖וֹ הָֽאֱלֹהִ֑ים לְנַ֨סּוֹת֔וֹ, “God left him, to test him”; its closing לָדַ֖עַת כָּל בִּלְבָבֽוֹ, “to know all that was in his heart,” continues the same לב root that marked Hezekiah's pride at v25 (כִּ֥י גָבַ֖הּ לִבּ֑וֹ) and his humbling at v26 (בְּגֹ֣בַהּ לִבּ֔וֹ), a moral arc rather than a possession; and its definite הַמּוֹפֵת֙, 'the portent,' is anaphoric to v24's own indefinite וּמוֹפֵ֖ת (the only two occurrences of this noun in the book), pointing back to the illness notice rather than sideways to the treasuries. The row keeps v31 here because its own connective, וְכֵ֞ן, still ties it forward from v30 rather than opening independently, and because 32:32's fresh source-citation formula, expected at exactly this seam per the book strategy, is what actually closes the wealth-and-works material off from the reign's remaining formulas -- but the verse's true content belongs to the pride/humbling/testing arc opened at 32:24, not to the catalog it is grouped with.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching v31 to 141's illness-and-humbling unit (32:24-26) is the stronger rival now on record -- the shared לב root, the God-as-subject/Hezekiah-as-object reversal, and the מופת anaphora to v24 all pull it that direction -- and is only kept here because its own connective ties it forward from v30 and 32:32's source-citation formula is what actually closes this row off, not because the catalog reading is textually stronger.

boundary_rationale: Opens on the recurring reign-closing device, וְיֶ֛תֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י יְחִזְקִיָּ֖הוּ וַחֲסָדָ֑יו הִנָּ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים בַּחֲז֞וֹן יְשַֽׁעְיָ֤הוּ בֶן אָמוֹץ֙ הַנָּבִ֔יא עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵי יְהוּדָ֖ה וְיִשְׂרָאֵֽל, “now the rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his good deeds…”, citing the vision of Isaiah and “the book of the kings of Judah and Israel”, exactly the source-citation formula the book strategy lists as expected at this verse. It is immediately followed by the standard death-and-succession sequence, וַיִּשְׁכַּ֨ב יְחִזְקִיָּ֜הוּ עִם אֲבֹתָ֗יו, “Hezekiah slept with his fathers”, burial “in the ascent to the tombs of the sons of David”, national mourning, and closing וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ מְנַשֶּׁ֥ה בְנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו, “Manasseh his son reigned in his place.” This תַּחְתָּֽיו succession construction recurs twelve times across the book, but it stands verse-initial and reign-opening only once, at 17:1's וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהוֹשָׁפָ֥ט בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּ֑יו; everywhere else, 32:33 included, it is clause-final, closing the predecessor's own report. Here it closes Hezekiah's, handing the throne to Manasseh, whose own reign narrative (33:1, beyond this part's range) opens instead on the differently-shaped nominal age formula, בֶּן שְׁתֵּ֥ים עֶשְׂרֵ֛ה שָׁנָ֖ה מְנַשֶּׁ֣ה בְמָלְכ֑וֹ. A PE mark (single-witness) sits directly after v33, weak corroboration that the reign ends exactly here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: No serious rival groups these two verses with the preceding wealth catalog (vv27-31), since the source-citation formula is a recognized, distinct unit-closing device throughout Chronicles' regnal reports, not a continuation of narrative content.

boundary_rationale: בֶּן שְׁתֵּ֥ים עֶשְׂרֵ֛ה שָׁנָ֖ה מְנַשֶּׁ֣ה בְמָלְכ֑וֹ וַחֲמִשִּׁ֤ים וְחָמֵשׁ֙ שָׁנָ֔ה מָלַ֖ךְ בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם, ‘Manasseh was twelve years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem.’ (v1), opens directly onto the evaluation וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הָרַ֖ע בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה כְּתֽוֹעֲבוֹת֙ הַגּוֹיִ֔ם אֲשֶׁר֙ הוֹרִ֣ישׁ יְהוָ֔ה מִפְּנֵ֖י בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל, ‘He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, after the abominations of the nations whom Yahweh cast out before the children of Israel’ (v2). From v3's plain narrative continuation, וַיָּ֗שָׁב וַיִּ֨בֶן֙, an unbroken wayyiqtol chain runs the length of the indictment (rebuilt high places, Baal altars, host-of-heaven worship, child sacrifice in Hinnom, the idol set in God's house against Yahweh's own conditional word to David and Solomon) with no off-line opener inside it -- though v3's own opening verb is a plain wayyiqtol continuation, so the chain in fact opens at v4's waw-plus-qatal altar notice, וּבָנָ֥ה מִזְבְּח֖וֹת בְּבֵ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה אֲשֶׁר֙ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה בִּירוּשָׁלִַ֥ם יִֽהְיֶה שְּׁמִ֖י לְעוֹלָֽם, not at v3, contrasting v5's true wayyiqtol of the same root, וַיִּ֥בֶן מִזְבְּח֖וֹת לְכָל צְבָ֣א הַשָּׁמָ֑יִם בִּשְׁתֵּ֖י חַצְר֥וֹת בֵּית יְהוָֽה; v6's וְהוּא֩ הֶעֱבִ֨יר is a second verse-initial off-line continuation, an emphatic-subject tag of the same kind used at 32:30. Neither 33:4's waw-qatal opener nor 33:6's fronted-pronoun-plus-qatal tag introduces a new participant, setting, or time-frame, so neither breaks the scene; the chain is carried mainly by wayyiqtol with these two off-line continuations, not by an unbroken wayyiqtol run. The chain closes on וַיֶּ֣תַע מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה אֶת יְהוּדָ֖ה וְיֹשְׁבֵ֣י יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת רָ֔ע מִן הַ֨גּוֹיִ֔ם אֲשֶׁר֙ הִשְׁמִ֣יד יְהוָ֔ה מִפְּנֵ֖י בְּנֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל, ‘Manasseh seduced Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that they did more evil than did the nations whom Yahweh destroyed before the children of Israel’ (v9), a shared six-word relative clause differing from v2 only in one verb — הוֹרִ֣ישׁ ('cast out') giving way to הִשְׁמִ֣יד ('destroyed') — restating v2's verb-object shape at national scale. That inclusio, not any editorial paragraphing, is what binds vv1-9 into one unit. A PE follows v9 (single-witness, tier-3 corroboration only), and the true closing edge is the actor shift at v10's וַיְדַבֵּ֧ר יְהוָ֛ה אֶל מְנַשֶּׁ֥ה, ‘Yahweh spoke to Manasseh,’ where the subject moves from Manasseh to Yahweh in direct speech.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A bare vv1-2 accession-and-evaluation row, cut off from its catalog, would misrepresent the text: v3's וַיָּ֗שָׁב וַיִּ֨בֶן֙ is a plain wayyiqtol continuation, not one of the book's dating-clause or new-formula boundary types, so it simply illustrates the evil just named in v2 rather than opening a fresh unit.

boundary_rationale: V10's own actor shift, Yahweh replacing Manasseh as grammatical subject in the rejected-word formula, is this row's tier-1 opening warrant. A single WEB paragraph break sits inside this row, before v12, and another falls at the row's own opening edge, before v10; that opening-edge break is tier-4 markup only, alongside the PE trailing v9 (single-witness, tier-3) that the preceding row already carries as its own closing corroboration, and neither is promoted here to an affirmative warrant. Both halves report a single sin-judgment-repentance sequence the Chronicler treats as one theological arc elsewhere in the book. V10 opens the rejected-word formula וַיְדַבֵּ֧ר יְהוָ֛ה אֶל מְנַשֶּׁ֥ה וְאֶל עַמּ֖וֹ וְלֹ֥א הִקְשִֽׁיבוּ, ‘Yahweh spoke to Manasseh and to his people, but they didn’t listen.’, and v11 executes the judgment it threatens. V12 pivots on the distress-clause וּכְהָצֵ֣ר ל֔וֹ חִלָּ֕ה אֶת פְּנֵ֖י יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהָ֑יו וַיִּכָּנַ֣ע מְאֹ֔ד מִלִּפְנֵ֖י אֱלֹהֵ֥י אֲבֹתָֽיו, ‘When he was in distress, he begged Yahweh his God, and humbled himself greatly before the God of his fathers.’, and the row closes on the recognition formula וַיֵּ֣דַע מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה כִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה ה֥וּא הָֽאֱלֹהִֽים, ‘Then Manasseh knew that Yahweh was God.’ (v13), a settled verdict with nothing further until v14's fresh temporal clause. Keeping vv10-13 together preserves the judgment and its reversal as one cause-and-effect unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting before v12 (10-11 vs 12-13) has genuine tier-1 support, not ¶ alone: v12 opens with its own kaph-prefixed infinitive-construct protasis, וּכְהָצֵ֣ר, a time-frame transition independent of WEB's formatting. But the split still isolates the judgment from the very repentance it exists to provoke, and Manasseh's humbling-and-prayer sequence here (וַיִּכָּנַ֣ע ... וַיִּתְפַּלֵּ֣ל, vv12-13) realizes the same verb pair as Yahweh's own 7:14 conditions for restoration, וְיִכָּנְע֨וּ עַמִּ֜י ... וְיִֽתְפַּֽלְלוּ֙ וִֽיבַקְשׁ֣וּ פָנַ֔י, lexeme for lexeme — a programmatic fulfillment that only reads as one movement if vv10-13 stay together.

boundary_rationale: וְאַחֲרֵי כֵ֡ן בָּנָ֣ה חוֹמָ֣ה חִֽיצוֹנָ֣ה לְעִיר דָּוִ֡יד, ‘Now after this, he built an outer wall to David’s city’ (v14), is an explicit temporal transition of the same class as the book's other 'after this'-type time-frame openers -- confirmed comparanda at 20:1, 20:35, and 24:4, all clause-initial -- following directly on v13's settled recognition formula, so the topic-change to building and cultic restoration is clearly signaled rather than implied; 32:23's adjunct falls outside this class on form, per M8-2Chr-140, so this row and 140 read the phrase family consistently. The unit runs through the altar-restoration and sacrifice notices of vv15-16 and closes on the caveat אֲבָל֙ ע֣וֹד הָעָ֔ם זֹבְחִ֖ים בַּבָּמ֑וֹת רַ֖ק לַיהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵיהֶֽם, ‘Nevertheless the people still sacrificed in the high places, but only to Yahweh their God.’ (v17), which has no further development before v18's source-citation formula, וְיֶ֨תֶר דִּבְרֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁה֮, opens in an entirely different archival register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding v17's high-places caveat into the following source-citation unit (18-20) loses because v17 is still narrating Manasseh's own reign, not yet the 'rest of the acts' regesta formula that begins v18.

boundary_rationale: The row is framed by the reign-closing source-citation formula: וְיֶ֨תֶר דִּבְרֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁה֮ וּתְפִלָּת֣וֹ אֶל אֱלֹהָיו֒, ‘Now the rest of the acts of Manasseh, and his prayer to his God’ (v18), shifts register from narrated reform (v17) into archival citation, and v19 restates the citation with an alternate source label ('the history of Hozai'), a doubling that reads as the formula's own expansion rather than a second unit's opening. V20 closes on the death-and-succession pair וַיִּשְׁכַּ֤ב מְנַשֶּׁה֙ עִם אֲבֹתָ֔יו וַֽיִּקְבְּרֻ֖הוּ בֵּית֑וֹ וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ אָמ֥וֹן בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו, ‘So Manasseh slept with his fathers, and they buried him in his own house; and Amon his son reigned in his place.’, a formula type that recurs closing reigns elsewhere in this book. A PE follows v20, and WEB's next paragraph begins only at v21 with Amon's own age-formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating v20 as the opening half of Amon's account rather than the close of Manasseh's loses because the death-notice's subject and verb (Manasseh slept, was buried) belong entirely to the outgoing king; Amon's reign begins only with the age-formula at v21.

boundary_rationale: The age-formula pattern shared with every other reign-unit in this run supplies its opening line, בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֧ים וּשְׁתַּ֛יִם שָׁנָ֖ה אָמ֣וֹן בְּמָלְכ֑וֹ וּשְׁתַּ֣יִם שָׁנִ֔ים מָלַ֖ךְ בִּֽירוּשָׁלִָֽם, ‘Amon was twenty-two years old when he began to reign; and he reigned two years in Jerusalem.’ (v21). A PE, single-witness, tier-3, non-driving, follows the preceding row's own close at 33:20. The evaluation in vv22-23 measures Amon explicitly against his father, וַיַּ֤עַשׂ הָרַע֙ בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה כַּאֲשֶׁ֥ר עָשָׂ֖ה מְנַשֶּׁ֣ה אָבִ֑יו, ‘He did that which was evil in Yahweh’s sight, as did Manasseh his father’ (v22), and וְלֹ֤א נִכְנַע֙ מִלִּפְנֵ֣י יְהוָ֔ה כְּהִכָּנַ֖ע מְנַשֶּׁ֣ה אָבִ֑יו, ‘He didn’t humble himself before Yahweh, as Manasseh his father had humbled himself’ (v23), before the conspiracy report וַיִּקְשְׁר֤וּ עָלָיו֙ עֲבָדָ֔יו וַיְמִיתֻ֖הוּ בְּבֵיתֽוֹ, ‘His servants conspired against him, and put him to death in his own house.’ (v24). Vv24-25 do carry their own formulas — the same conspiracy shape closing Joash's report (הִתְקַשְּׁר֨וּ עָלָ֜יו עֲבָדָ֗יו, 24:25) and Amaziah's (וַיִּקְשְׁר֨וּ עָלָ֥יו קֶ֛שֶׁר, 25:27), and the people-of-the-land enthronement notice recurring for Jehoahaz (וַיַּמְלִיכֻ֥הוּ תַֽחַת אָבִ֖יו, 36:1) — but both remain inside this reign-report rather than opening a new one, since neither the conspiracy notice (v24) nor the enthronement notice (v25) IS an age formula or dating clause in itself -- unlike 34:1's age formula, identical in form to 33:1 and 33:21, which opens the next unit -- and every reign-unit in this run (33:1, 33:21, 34:1) is headed by one, which is why the report closes at v25 and the next unit opens only at 34:1; the report simply narrates its own king's death and successor within one unusually compact unit, closing on Josiah's enthronement at v25, with a PE following (single-witness).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v24 to isolate the conspiracy-and-succession notice is a genuinely stronger rival than 'no formula marks it' would suggest: v24's conspiracy formula and v25's people-of-the-land enthronement formula are both real, independently attested devices (24:25, 25:27; 36:1), not silence. But neither is followed by the age-formula or dating clause that opens every other reign-unit in this run, so they still function as this report's own closing notices rather than the head of a new one; the five verses hold together as one unusually compact reign-report.

boundary_rationale: Manasseh, Amon, and now Josiah share one age-formula shape at the head of their reigns: בֶּן שְׁמוֹנֶ֥ה שָׁנִ֖ים יֹאשִׁיָּ֣הוּ בְמָלְכ֑וֹ, ‘Josiah was eight years old when he began to reign, and he reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem.’ (v1), paired with the positive evaluation וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הַיָּשָׁ֖ר בְּעֵינֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה, ‘He did that which was right in Yahweh’s eyes’ (v2) — one of five uses of this evaluative clause, at the consonantal level, for a favorably-judged king (25:2, 26:4, 27:2, 29:2, 34:2) — reinforced here by the Davidic-conformity clause וַיֵּ֗לֶךְ בְּדַרְכֵי֙ דָּוִ֣יד אָבִ֔יו and closing on וְלֹא סָ֖ר יָמִ֥ין וּשְׂמֹֽאול, ‘and didn’t turn away to the right hand or to the left,’ which, checked against a book-wide sweep, is unique to this verse as a royal evaluation -- 27:2 alone among the five carries different cantillation, since its own verse continues past the clause, while 25:2, 26:4, 29:2 and 34:2 all close the clause on an atnach; the five remain uninterrupted-string instances all the same, distinguishing them from 24:2's subject-interposed variant; the book's nearest evaluative departure-idiom for a favorably-judged king is the differently-worded וְלֹא סָ֣ר מִמֶּ֑נָּה of Jehoshaphat (20:32). V3 breaks from this with an explicit new dating clause ('in the eighth year... in the twelfth year'), so the row closes before the reform narrative's own chronology begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A vv1-7 row, on the model of Manasseh's undivided vv1-9, would flatten a real difference: Josiah's v3 supplies an explicit dated clause reintroducing the synchronism-style device, rather than simply continuing the evaluation in narrative apposition as Manasseh's v3 does.

boundary_rationale: A double-dated clause reintroduces the year-count device that v2's fixed idiom had just closed off: וּבִשְׁמוֹנֶ֨ה שָׁנִ֜ים לְמָלְכ֗וֹ וְהוּא֙ עוֹדֶ֣נּוּ נַ֔עַר הֵחֵ֕ל לִדְר֕וֹשׁ לֵאלֹהֵ֖י דָּוִ֣יד אָבִ֑יו, ‘in the eighth year of his reign, while he was yet young, he began to seek after the God of David his father’ (v3). Vv4-6 extend the purge geographically, from Judah/Jerusalem's Baal-altars to the northern cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali, and the campaign closes on the return notice וַיָּ֖שָׁב לִירוּשָׁלִָֽם, ‘then returned to Jerusalem.’ (v7), with a SAMEKH following — a going-out-and-coming-back bracket that closes royal campaigns elsewhere in the book: 19:1's return-to-Jerusalem-in-peace notice closes the Ramoth-gilead campaign, and 20:27's return-to-Jerusalem-with-joy notice closes the Moabite-war campaign. V8's fresh eighteenth-year dating clause opens an unrelated administrative matter, so the boundary out is unusually sharp.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading v7's return notice as transitional rather than terminal, folding it forward into v8's temple-repair commissioning, loses not because v8 is severed from the purge campaign — its own לְטַהֵ֥ר הָאָ֖רֶץ וְהַבָּ֑יִת repeats the identical infinitive opening the campaign at v3, הֵחֵל֙ לְטַהֵ֔ר, and the finite form appears again at v5, וַיְטַהֵ֥ר אֶת יְהוּדָ֖ה וְאֶת יְרוּשָׁלִָֽם, a purification-verb chain running 34:3, 34:5, 34:8 — but because v8's clause is a subordinate back-reference summarizing a now-finished campaign under its own fresh eighteenth-year dating formula, which is what actually opens the new administrative unit, not a fresh topic severed from the old.

boundary_rationale: Eighteen years into the reign, a fresh dating formula redirects the narrative toward temple funding: וּבִשְׁנַ֨ת שְׁמוֹנֶ֤ה עֶשְׂרֵה֙ לְמָלְכ֔וֹ לְטַהֵ֥ר הָאָ֖רֶץ וְהַבָּ֑יִת שָׁ֠לַח אֶת שָׁפָ֨ן, ‘Now in the eighteenth year of his reign, when he had purged the land and the house, he sent Shaphan’ (v8), following directly on v7's return notice. Vv9-12 form a single administrative chain — money gathered by the Levite gatekeepers, handed to the overseeing workmen, then to carpenters and builders for stone and timber, with named overseers directing skilled Levites — and the row closes on the personnel register itself, וּמֵֽהַלְוִיִּ֔ם סוֹפְרִ֥ים וְשֹׁטְרִ֖ים וְשׁוֹעֲרִֽים, ‘Of the Levites, there were scribes, officials, and gatekeepers.’ (v13), a list-closing formula with nowhere further to extend. WEB opens a fresh paragraph only at v14, where the register gives way to the pivotal discovery notice, וּבְהוֹצִיאָ֣ם אֶת הַכֶּ֔סֶף.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping the whole 'money' thread together through v14 loses because v14's clause pivots the narrative onto an entirely different axis — the law-book's discovery — which the register in vv8-13 gives no hint of.

boundary_rationale: Although WEB inserts a paragraph break before v16, vv14-18 form one causally chained event: Hilkiah's discovery, וּבְהוֹצִיאָ֣ם אֶת הַכֶּ֔סֶף הַמּוּבָ֖א בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֑ה מָצָא֙ חִלְקִיָּ֣הוּ הַכֹּהֵ֔ן אֶת סֵ֥פֶר תּֽוֹרַת יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַד מֹשֶֽׁה, ‘When they brought out the money that was brought into Yahweh’s house, Hilkiah the priest found the book of Yahweh’s law given by Moses.’ (v14), leads directly to his handing the book to Shaphan (v15), Shaphan's carrying it to the king with his own report (vv16-17), and the reading itself, וַיִּקְרָא ב֥וֹ שָׁפָ֖ן לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ, ‘Shaphan read from it to the king.’ (v18). The seam out sits at v18/v19, where the topic shifts from Shaphan's report-and-reading to the king's own emotional and administrative response; no new dating clause or archival formula interrupts vv14-18 itself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The WEB ¶ before v16 (14-15 vs 16-18) has a scene-change in its favor (priest's chamber to throne room), but honoring it here severs the book's single unbroken hand-off chain — found, told, carried, reported, read — into two halves that neither closes on its own.

boundary_rationale: Grief, not reading, is the first note struck here: וַיְהִי֙ כִּשְׁמֹ֣עַ הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֣י הַתּוֹרָ֑ה וַיִּקְרַ֖ע אֶת בְּגָדָֽיו, ‘When the king had heard the words of the law, he tore his clothes.’ (v19), distinct from the reading that closed v18. V20 names the five commissioned officials and opens direct command speech, continuing through v21's rationale for urgency, כִּֽי גְדוֹלָ֤ה חֲמַת יְהוָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר נִתְּכָ֣ה בָ֔נוּ, ‘for great is Yahweh’s wrath that is poured out on us’. A PE follows v21, and v22 shifts to a new grammatical subject and location — ‘So Hilkiah and those whom the king had commanded went to Huldah the prophetess’ — compliance rather than command.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching v22's compliance notice to this row as the command's natural completion loses because v22 introduces a new subject (the delegation, not the king) and a new location (Huldah's quarter), matching the book's usual command-then-separate-compliance pattern rather than one continuous clause.

boundary_rationale: The delegation's errand, not the king's own words, supplies this row's first clause: וַיֵּ֨לֶךְ חִלְקִיָּ֜הוּ וַאֲשֶׁ֣ר הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ אֶל חֻלְדָּ֨ה הַנְּבִיאָ֜ה, ‘So Hilkiah and those whom the king had commanded went to Huldah the prophetess’ (v22), and its summarized speech to her ('they spoke to her to that effect') is completed only by her reply, which opens with a first messenger formula relaying instructions to the delegation itself, כֹּה אָמַ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל אִמְר֣וּ לָאִ֔ישׁ אֲשֶׁר שָׁלַ֥ח אֶתְכֶ֖ם אֵלָֽי, ‘Yahweh, the God of Israel says: ‘Tell the man who sent you to me,’ (v23); v22 stays attached to what follows rather than standing alone, since its closing clause names no content of its own. The doom content proper opens only with v24's own independent messenger formula, כֹּ֚ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֔ה הִנְנִ֨י מֵבִ֥יא רָעָ֛ה, ‘Yahweh says, ‘Behold, I will bring evil on this place...’ — the book's sole consecutive-verse doubling of this messenger formula (eight total occurrences: 11:4, 12:5, 18:10, 20:15, 21:12, 34:23, 34:24, 34:26) — and runs through the finality clause וְתִתַּ֧ךְ חֲמָתִ֛י בַּמָּק֥וֹם הַזֶּ֖ה וְלֹ֥א תִכְבֶּֽה, ‘my wrath is poured out on this place, and it will not be quenched’ (v25), before v26's adversative וְאֶל מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֗ה, ‘But to the king of Judah,’ opens a second, contrasting address. WLC marks a SAMEKH after both v22 and v23 (single-witness, weak), sitting exactly at the relay-then-oracle doubling; neither drives the split, since the relay formula (v23) and the doom formula (v24) read as one messenger-speech complex — the first authorizing the second — rather than two separate oracles.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A 22-23/24-25 division at the relay-then-oracle doubling is the strongest rival, since v24 opens its own independent messenger formula heading the actual doom content — a real tier-1 seam, not mere silence — but it still fails: v23's relay formula is what authorizes v24's oracle to be delivered at all, so treating them as separate units would sever one commissioned speech act in two.

boundary_rationale: A sharp adversative pivot launches this row, וְאֶל מֶ֣לֶךְ יְהוּדָ֗ה הַשֹּׁלֵ֤חַ אֶתְכֶם֙ לִדְר֣וֹשׁ בַּֽיהוָ֔ה, ‘But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of Yahweh’ (v26), turning the oracle from the doom just pronounced on 'this place' to a personal word for Josiah grounded in his own tenderness of heart (v27). The unit closes on the compliance-and-return notice וַיָּשִׁ֥יבוּ אֶת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ דָּבָֽר, ‘They brought back this message to the king.’ (v28), after which WEB opens a fresh paragraph at v29 with the king's own summons of the elders — prophetic word giving way to royal initiative. A SAMEKH follows v26 (single-witness, weak), internal to this row rather than at either edge, so it neither drives nor undermines the boundaries argued here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this row back into 22-25 as one seven-verse Huldah unit loses the distinctiveness between the two addresses, though not on the ground of 'this place and its inhabitants' — that phrase (עַל הַמָּק֥וֹם הַזֶּ֖ה וְעַל יוֹשְׁבָ֑יו / עַל הַמָּק֤וֹם הַזֶּה֙ וְעַל יֹ֣שְׁבָ֔יו / עַל הַמָּק֥וֹם הַזֶּ֖ה וְעַל יֹשְׁבָ֑יו) recurs at 34:24, 27, AND 28 alike and so cannot discriminate the two halves. The real edge is morphological: the doom oracle of vv24-25 never addresses Josiah directly, while from the tail of v26's הַדְּבָרִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר שָׁמָֽעְתָּ, 'the words which you have heard,' through v27's second-person forms (לְבָ֨בְךָ֜ / בְּשָׁמְעֲךָ֤ / בְּגָדֶ֖יךָ) and v28's (אֹֽסִפְךָ֜ / אֲבֹתֶ֗יךָ / תִרְאֶ֣ינָה עֵינֶ֔יךָ), second-person forms run continuously — a genuine shift into direct royal address substantial enough to argue for two rows.

boundary_rationale: Royal initiative, not prophetic word, restarts the action here: וַיִּשְׁלַ֖ח הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וַיֶּאֱסֹ֕ף אֶת כָּל זִקְנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה וִירוּשָׁלִָֽם, ‘Then the king sent and gathered together all the elders of Judah and Jerusalem.’ (v29), an assembly-summons device distinct from the prophetic-word register that just closed at v28 with a PE marked. V30 has the king read the covenant book publicly; v31 shifts to the covenant-ratification idiom וַיַּעֲמֹ֨ד הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ עַל עָמְד֗וֹ וַיִּכְרֹ֣ת אֶֽת הַבְּרִית֮ לִפְנֵ֣י יְהוָה֒, ‘The king stood in his place and made a covenant before Yahweh’, kept joined to the summons-and-reading rather than isolated, since both belong to one ceremonial event; v32 extends the covenant to the wider populace and closes on וַֽיַּעֲשׂוּ֙ יֹשְׁבֵ֣י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֔ם כִּבְרִ֥ית אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֱלֹהֵ֥י אֲבוֹתֵיהֶֽם, ‘The inhabitants of Jerusalem did according to the covenant of God, the God of their fathers.’ V33 then shifts scope from Jerusalem/Benjamin to 'all the countries... of Israel' and from ceremony-report to a lifetime-fidelity formula, marking the row's close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the public reading (29-30) from the covenant-cutting act (31-32) is a real option — כרת ברית is a distinct legal-ritual idiom from the reading that precedes it — but the two remain one uninterrupted ceremony in the text, with no dating clause, ¶, or change of participants separating them.

boundary_rationale: This single verse pivots scope and register at once: וַיָּ֨סַר יֹֽאשִׁיָּ֜הוּ אֶת כָּל הַתּוֹעֵב֗וֹת מִֽכָּל הָאֲרָצוֹת֮ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לִבְנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵל֒, ‘Josiah took away all the abominations out of all the countries that belonged to the children of Israel’, widens v32's local Jerusalem-and-Benjamin frame to the whole territory of Israel, and the verse closes on the lifetime-fidelity idiom כָּל יָמָ֕יו לֹ֣א סָ֔רוּ מֵֽאַחֲרֵ֕י יְהוָ֖ה אֱלֹהֵ֥י אֲבוֹתֵיהֶֽם, ‘All his days they didn’t depart from following Yahweh, the God of their fathers.’ — a summary formula with no ceremonial content of its own, unlike the concrete assembly-and-covenant acts of vv29-32. A PE follows v33, matching this part's assigned close ahead of the distinct Passover cultic-action opening of the next unit (35:1, outside this part's range).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding v33 into the covenant-assembly row (29-33) as its natural conclusion loses because v33's own grammar and geography step outside the assembly just narrated — a nationwide summary rather than a further covenant act performed at Jerusalem.

boundary_rationale: The unit opens on a fresh royal-action heading rather than a continuation of the covenant-renewal material closing ch34: וַיַּ֨עַשׂ יֹאשִׁיָּ֧הוּ בִֽירוּשָׁלִַ֛ם פֶּ֖סַח לַיהוָ֑ה, ‘Josiah kept a Passover to Yahweh in Jerusalem’ (v1, quoted in full; nothing is elided), which WEB likewise renders as a flat topic-opening declarative. From there an unbroken wayyiqtol chain runs through the priestly stationing at v2 (וַיַּעֲמֵ֥ד הַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים עַל מִשְׁמְרוֹתָ֑ם וַֽיְחַזְּקֵ֔ם, ‘He set the priests in their offices and encouraged them’) into direct royal speech, opened by the tier-1 speech frame וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לַ֠לְוִיִּם, WEB's ‘He said to the Levites who taught all Israel’ (v3), instructing them to house the ark and organize by division; the speech itself closes on the Mosaic-authority tag לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת כִּדְבַר יְהוָ֖ה בְּיַד מֹשֶֽׁה, ‘according to Yahweh’s word by Moses’ (v6, WEB's own wording; ‘by the hand of’ is a literal gloss of בְּיַד not present in WEB), with a PE tucked in right after it (single-witness, tier-3 only). Verse 7 breaks the pattern with a new subject-verb pairing, וַיָּ֣רֶם יֹאשִׁיָּ֣הוּ, WEB's ‘Josiah gave to the children of the people’, shifting register from command to gift list, so the charge-unit closes at v6 rather than absorbing it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The genuine rival, under the INSET RULE's own two-part test, is a 35:1-2/35:3-6 split: v3's וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לַ֠לְוִיִּם supplies an opening speech frame and v7's וַיָּ֣רֶם יֹאשִׁיָּ֣הוּ supplies a resumption after, which is exactly what the rule requires to isolate an inset. It still fails on host-unit integrity: the charge itself (vv3-6) has no narrative resumption of its own inside the span — nothing reports the Levites acting on the instruction before v7 moves to the king's own gifts — and vv1-2 supply the very occasion (the Passover, the priestly stationing) that the imperatives of vv3-6 presuppose, so the two halves read as one continuous inception notice rather than a host narrative plus a detachable inset.

boundary_rationale: A new register begins where the king's own gift is tallied, וַיָּ֣רֶם יֹאשִׁיָּ֣הוּ, WEB's ‘Josiah gave to the children of the people’ (v7) — thirty thousand animals from the flock, three thousand cattle — followed by the identical tally shape applied to his officials, וְשָׂרָ֞יו לִנְדָבָ֥ה, WEB's ‘His princes gave a free will offering to the people’ (v8, naming Hilkiah, Zechariah, Jehiel), and again to the Levite chiefs at v9 — the consonantal line opens וכונניהו with qere וְ֠כָֽנַנְיָהוּ, followed by וּשְׁמַֽעְיָ֨הוּ and the rest of the named list; the ketiv/qere pair covers only the first name, and וּשְׁמַֽעְיָ֨הוּ is simply the next donor, Shemaiah, in the list with no ketiv counterpart of its own. Each tier repeats donor-then-livestock-count, so the three verses read as one triadic tally rather than three independent notices. A SAMEKH trails v7 (single-witness, tier-3) — squarely inside this list — but a mark of that weight cannot outrank the matching threefold form binding the king's gift to the two that follow it. The tally closes before v10 switches into a completion-formula register describing the priests and Levites taking their stations.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading the SAMEKH after v7 as a hard break would peel the king’s gift away from the two parallel donor tiers sharing its exact list-form — a tier-3 mark overruling a matched internal pattern is the weaker call.

boundary_rationale: An establishment-formula opens this execution report, וַתִּכּ֖וֹן הָעֲבוֹדָ֑ה ... כְּמִצְוַ֥ת הַמֶּֽלֶךְ, WEB's ‘So the service was prepared... according to the king’s commandment’ (v10), and its own scaled echo closes it, וַ֠תִּכּוֹן כָּל עֲבוֹדַ֨ת יְהוָ֜ה ... כְּמִצְוַ֖ת הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ יֹאשִׁיָּֽהוּ, WEB's ‘So all the service of Yahweh was prepared the same day... according to the commandment of King Josiah’ (v16) — the same root widened from ‘the service’ to ‘all the service of Yahweh’ and from the bare ‘king’ to ‘King Josiah’ by name. Between the two brackets the priests and Levites slaughter, sprinkle, portion, and roast the offerings (vv11-13, wayyiqtol-driven -- v11 in fact ends on a subject-plus-participle clause with no finite verb, and v13 has a fronted-object plain-qatal middle clause before the wayyiqtol resumes, so the report already tolerates a participial clause and a fronted-object qatal inside vv11-13, which strengthens rather than weakens the parenthesis reading of vv14-15's own qatal/verbless register against a 10-13/14-15 split), before the register shifts to qatal at v14's doubled הֵכִ֤ינוּ ... הֵכִ֣ינוּ and a verbless clause at v15 naming the singers' and gatekeepers' standing posts, וְהַמְשֹֽׁרֲרִ֨ים בְּנֵי אָסָ֜ף עַל מַעֲמָדָ֗ם — a parenthetical aside on staffing that v16's wayyiqtol resumes and completes, rather than a break in the report. Because v16 restates and completes v10's own verb rather than opening fresh material, it reads as the closing half of a matched inclusio, not the head of what follows; v17 shifts the acting subject away from the cultic staff to the wider populace, וַיַּעֲשׂ֨וּ בְנֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֧ל הַֽנִּמְצְאִ֛ים אֶת הַפֶּ֖סַח, WEB's ‘The children of Israel who were present kept the Passover’ — a scene change strong enough to open the next unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading v16 as the opening line of the following national-observance summary is plausible on WEB's own paragraph break, which falls before v16, but the repeated root and shared 'commandment of the king' phrasing tie it back to v10 more tightly than forward to v17's population-focused clause; and the qatal/verbless staffing note in vv14-15 is best read as a parenthesis within this same execution report, not as a rival internal seam, since v16's wayyiqtol picks the report's own chain back up.

boundary_rationale: This unit's opening edge is the same one M8-2Chr-160 closes on: that row's completion-formula inclusio (וַתִּכּ֖וֹן הָעֲבוֹדָ֑ה v10 / וַ֠תִּכּוֹן כָּל עֲבוֹדַ֨ת יְהוָ֜ה v16) ends the cultic-execution report, and v17's shift to a new subject, וַיַּעֲשׂ֨וּ בְנֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֧ל הַֽנִּמְצְאִ֛ים אֶת הַפֶּ֖סַח, opens this national-observance unit rather than continuing that report. From there the claim widens into a superlative: וְלֹֽא נַעֲשָׂ֨ה פֶ֤סַח כָּמֹ֨הוּ֙ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל, ‘there was not made a Passover like it in Israel’ (v18), reaching back to Samuel's day, and the unit closes on the regnal date anchoring that same claim, בִּשְׁמוֹנֶ֤ה עֶשְׂרֵה֙ שָׁנָ֔ה לְמַלְכ֖וּת יֹאשִׁיָּ֑הוּ נַעֲשָׂ֖ה הַפֶּ֥סַח הַזֶּֽה, ‘in the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign this Passover was kept’ (v19), whose demonstrative 'this Passover' reaches back to the whole celebration reported from v16's לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת הַפֶּ֔סַח and v17's אֶת הַפֶּ֖סַח onward, not narrowly to v18's comparison alone. A SAMEKH sits between v18 and v19 (single-witness, tier-3) at exactly the point where the superlative claim meets its own date-stamp, but the mark falls inside one continuing sentence-pair rather than at a seam. The next verse opens an unrelated time-frame formula for Necho's campaign, which gives this unit its outer edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at the SAMEKH between v18 and v19 would strand the date-stamp from the very celebration it dates, since v19's demonstrative 'this Passover' reaches back to the whole report from v16 onward and points nowhere else for its referent.

boundary_rationale: A time-frame formula opens the unit and pivots away from the Passover material entirely: אַחֲרֵ֣י כָל זֹ֗את אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֵכִ֤ין יֹֽאשִׁיָּ֨הוּ֙, ‘After all this, when Josiah had prepared the temple’ (v20), introducing Necho's march on Carchemish and Josiah's decision to intercept him. The relative clause quoted here points back to the temple-service preparation summarized at 35:16, the opposite of a total pivot; the edge holds because the new finite verb launching Necho's campaign follows, not because the formula severs every backward connection. The action runs unbroken through the wounding and return to Jerusalem into the paired death-and-burial notice, וַיָּ֕מָת וַיִּקָּבֵ֖ר, ‘and he died and was buried’, and the mourning that follows, מִֽתְאַבְּלִ֖ים עַל יֹאשִׁיָּֽהוּ, ‘mourning for Josiah’ (v24), before closing on the elaboration of that same mourning into a fixed custom — Jeremiah's dirge, the singers' laments — ending on a written-record notice, וְהִנָּ֥ם כְּתוּבִ֖ים עַל הַקִּינֽוֹת, ‘behold, they are written among the laments’ (v25). A PE trails v24 (single-witness), sitting right at the join between the burial/mourning notice and the lament report, and it is a genuinely stronger rival seam than most marks in this part offer — but rather than sharing v24's subject, v25 in fact introduces two fresh named subjects of its own, יִרְמְיָהוּ֮ and כָֽל הַשָּׁרִ֣ים וְ֠הַשָּׁרוֹת; what ties the two verses is the repeated grief-object עַל יֹאשִׁיָּֽהוּ, closing v24 and recurring twice more in v25 (בְּקִינ֨וֹתֵיהֶ֤ם עַל יֹאשִׁיָּ֨הוּ֙), so the tier-3 mark still falls inside one continuing grieving report rather than at a seam. The following verse pivots the register entirely to bibliographic citation, giving this unit its far edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The PE after v24 could be read as closing the death narrative proper (vv20-24) apart from the lament report (v25), but v24's own closing clause already explicitly names the whole populace, Judah and Jerusalem, as mourners, so v25 does not fill a gap v24 leaves open; it instead adds named mourners, Jeremiah and then the singers, and a durative extension of the custom on top of the populace-wide grief v24 already reports, so severing it at the mark still strands half of one continuous grieving notice held together by the repeated grief-object.

boundary_rationale: Josiah’s reign closes on the Chronicler’s bibliographic tag, opening וְיֶ֛תֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י יֹאשִׁיָּ֖הוּ, literally ‘and the remainder of the words of Josiah’ (v26), and running through the paired first-and-last citation, עַל סֵ֥פֶר מַלְכֵֽי יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל וִיהוּדָֽה, ‘[written] in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah’ (v27). The same ‘rest of the acts of X ... written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah’ shape recurs within this very part at 36:8 for Jehoiakim, so this is not a one-off flourish but a closing register this part repeats when a reign ends — distinct in form from the narrative report in vv20-25 (action and grief) and from v25’s own written-record notice, which names ‘the laments’ specifically rather than the royal chronicle generally. Two different citation traditions sit back to back in the text, and only the second is this unit’s own genre.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Absorbing this formula into the preceding death-and-lament report would blur a self-contained bibliographic genre into the narrative it closes, and 36:8’s matching formula shows this shape is a recurring unit-closer within this part, not an extension of v25’s lament notice.

boundary_rationale: Jehoahaz’s brief reign opens not with the age-formula alone but with a populace-installation clause first: וַיִּקְחוּ֙ עַם הָאָ֔רֶץ אֶת יְהוֹאָחָ֖ז, ‘the people of the land took Jehoahaz’ (v1), then the standard age-notice, בֶּן שָׁל֧וֹשׁ וְעֶשְׂרִ֛ים שָׁנָ֖ה, ‘twenty-three years old’ (v2) — a three-month reign, the shortest recorded here. The report tracks Egypt’s deposition of him, the fine levied on the land, and Necho’s installation of a replacement brother, closing on Jehoahaz’s own removal, וַיְבִיאֵ֖הוּ מִצְרָֽיְמָה, ‘and he brought him to Egypt’ (v4), with a PE sitting just after it (single-witness). The Joahaz/Jehoahaz spelling alternation between v1's יְהוֹאָחָ֖ז and vv2/4's יוֹאָחָ֣ז / יוֹאָחָ֤ז is a genuine MT orthographic feature, not merely a translator's footnote choice (WEB's note only reports it); it still carries no weight here, since name-spelling is not one of the tier-1 device classes and the shift itself falls between v1 and v2, inside the span rather than at either edge. What closes this unit is the same age-formula device opening again at v5 for Jehoiakim — and again at v9 and v11 for Jehoiachin and Zedekiah — so the seam-out at v5 is the first of three repeats of one identical accession marker within this same chapter.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Grouping vv1-4 with Jehoiakim’s notice (vv5-8) into one ‘two short kings’ unit would erase the age-formula seam at v5, which recurs unaltered twice more later in this chapter.

boundary_rationale: The age-formula reopens for a new reign, בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֨ים וְחָמֵ֤שׁ שָׁנָה֙, ‘twenty-five years old’ (v5), followed at once by the evil-notice and then Nebuchadnezzar’s binding of Jehoiakim and the removal of temple vessels to Babylon (vv6-7). The unit closes on a double formula, both parts present intact: the citation heading וְיֶתֶר֩ דִּבְרֵ֨י יְהֽוֹיָקִ֜ים, ‘now the rest of the acts of Jehoiakim’, running straight into the successor-installation clause וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהוֹיָכִ֥ין בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו, ‘and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place’ (v8), trailed by a PE (single-witness) — echoing the same tier-1-formula-plus-tier-3-mark convergence already seen closing v4. Of the four reigns compressed into this chapter, only Jehoiakim’s retains the citation-and-succession pairing in full; Jehoiachin’s notice just below drops the citation half entirely (its own close is a bare deportation-and-succession clause at v10), which sharpens rather than blurs this unit’s edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through v10 to absorb Jehoiachin’s installation would splice the citation formula closing Jehoiakim’s reign onto an unrelated age-formula opening a fresh one at v9.

boundary_rationale: A fresh age-formula opens Jehoiachin's own notice, בֶּן שְׁמוֹנֶ֤ה שָׁנִים֙ יְהוֹיָכִ֣ין, ‘eight years old, Jehoiachin’ (v9) — וּשְׁלֹשָׁ֤ה חֳדָשִׁים֙ וַעֲשֶׂ֣רֶת יָמִ֔ים, three months and ten days, a brief reign but not the chapter's shortest, since Jehoahaz's three months (36:2, argued in M8-2Chr-164) runs ten days shorter still — followed by the evil-notice and then his deportation with the temple's valuable vessels. The unit closes on a different installation device than v8's: not the succession formula וַיִּמְלֹ֛ךְ יְהוֹיָכִ֥ין בְּנ֖וֹ תַּחְתָּֽיו closing Jehoiakim's report, where the incoming king himself is subject, but the causative וַיַּמְלֵךְ֙ אֶת צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ אָחִ֔יו עַל יְהוּדָ֖ה וִֽירוּשָׁלִָֽם, ‘and he made Zedekiah his brother king’ (v10), where the appointee is an accusative object under an agent left unexpressed within its own clause -- although the verse has already named Nebuchadnezzar earlier in the same sentence, וְלִתְשׁוּבַ֣ת הַשָּׁנָ֗ה שָׁלַח֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ נְבֽוּכַדְנֶאצַּ֔ר… — the same construction, stem for stem, as v4's foreign king installing Eliakim, וַיַּמְלֵ֨ךְ מֶֽלֶךְ מִצְרַ֜יִם אֶת אֶלְיָקִ֣ים אָחִ֗יו עַל יְהוּדָה֙ וִיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם, with a PE marked at its heel (single-witness). This reign carries no 'rest of his acts' citation at all — the deportation notice stands in its place — but that omission is a feature of the compressed regnal-report form here, not a weakening of the boundary itself: a sweep of the chapter's first three reign-units falsifies the generalization that the age-formula opening and causative-installation closing pair marks all three: unit 2 (Jehoiakim, vv5-8) closes on v8's Qal succession formula, not a causative clause; unit 2's own causative appointment (v4) stands mid-verse, not at the close; and unit 1 (Jehoahaz) opens on the causative v1, with the age-formula arriving only at v2, not at the head. The pairing holds in full only for this reign, vv9-10 (Jehoiachin); Zedekiah's own report (v11 on) closes differently, on no installation formula at all. This reign opens on the recurring age-formula and closes on a causative appointment clause whose only true parallel in the chapter is v4.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading v10 as an appendix tacked onto Jehoiakim’s block (vv5-8) rather than the close of Jehoiachin’s own notice would ignore that v9 opens with the identical age-formula launching every other reign here.

boundary_rationale: Zedekiah's reign opens with the chapter's fourth and final age-formula, בֶּן עֶשְׂרִ֧ים וְאַחַ֛ת שָׁנָ֖ה צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ, ‘twenty-one years old, Zedekiah’ (v11), then narrates his refusal to humble himself before Jeremiah and his broken oath of loyalty to Nebuchadnezzar, the rebellion clause heading v13 in full, so the two additive particles stand at the head of consecutive verses, ‘he also rebelled against King Nebuchadnezzar’ (vv12-13). From there the indictment widens past the king to the priestly and popular leadership, entering for the first time under the matching particle, גַּ֠ם כָּל שָׂרֵ֨י הַכֹּהֲנִ֤ים וְהָעָם֙ הִרְבּ֣וּ, ‘moreover all the chiefs of the priests and the people trespassed’ (v14), and closing on their desecration of the temple, וַֽיְטַמְּאוּ֙ אֶת בֵּ֣ית יְהוָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר הִקְדִּ֖ישׁ בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם, ‘they polluted the house of Yahweh which he had made holy in Jerusalem’ (v14). Whether v14 belongs here or opens the divine-response material that follows is a genuine fork, not a manufactured one: what ties it to vv11-13 is not repeated actors — the priests and people are new to the scene at v14 — but the additive particle chain running from v13's own head into v14, a particle this chapter uses only one more time, at v22 (three hits total), while v15 turns the subject to Yahweh's own initiative, so the corporate-guilt clause is kept as this unit's low point rather than promoted to the head of the next.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating v14 as the opening line of a guilt-then-response arc (vv14-16) is defensible given the tight causal link, but v14's own additive particle ties it backward to v13's matching particle rather than forward — the same subject-change from human to divine that would open a v14-16 unit already happens one verse later, at v15, not at v14 itself.

boundary_rationale: The acting subject turns from the corporate guilt just narrated to Yahweh's own repeated initiative, וַיִּשְׁלַ֡ח יְהוָה֩ אֱלֹהֵ֨י אֲבוֹתֵיהֶ֧ם עֲלֵיהֶ֛ם בְּיַ֥ד מַלְאָכָ֖יו הַשְׁכֵּ֣ם וְשָׁל֑וֹחַ כִּֽי חָמַ֥ל עַל עַמּ֖וֹ וְעַל מְעוֹנֽוֹ, ‘Yahweh, the God of their fathers, sent to them by the hand of his messengers, rising up early and sending, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place’ (v15) — the doubled infinitive-absolute pairing (הַשְׁכֵּ֣ם וְשָׁל֑וֹחַ) casting the sending as a repeated, iterative act — met with mockery in a cumulative summary building to the point of no return, עַ֠ד עֲל֧וֹת חֲמַת יְהוָ֛ה בְּעַמּ֖וֹ עַד לְאֵ֥ין מַרְפֵּֽא, ‘until Yahweh's wrath arose against his people, until there was no remedy’ (v16, paralleled in 2Chr only at 21:18's לָחֳלִ֖י לְאֵ֥ין מַרְפֵּֽא, both marking a point of irreversible ruin). This two-verse hinge both explains everything narrated since v11 and licenses the invasion that follows; its far edge rests not on a change of grammatical subject — Yahweh remains the operative subject into v17, where וַיַּ֨עַל עֲלֵיהֶ֜ם אֶת מֶ֣לֶךְ כשדיים כַּשְׂדִּ֗ים brings the Chaldean king on stage only as the accusative object of Yahweh's own action, and הַכֹּ֖ל נָתַ֥ן בְּיָדֽוֹ still needs Yahweh as its giver — but on the shift from vv15-16's iterative, summarizing register (repeated sending, cumulative mockery) to v17's punctual narrative action (a single punctual invasion, executed and complete). That shift is real but is not one of the book's named tier-1 formula types, and it sits inside the exile-compression stretch already flagged as thin ground for confident calls; graded down accordingly.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding vv15-16 forward into the Chaldean-invasion report (v17 on) as one cause-and-effect sweep has real appeal, and it is reinforced by the book's only other use of the compassion verb: כִּֽי חָמַ֥ל עַל עַמּ֖וֹ (v15) is answered by וְלֹ֥א חָמַ֛ל עַל בָּח֥וּר וּבְתוּלָ֖ה (v17), a positive-then-negative pair found nowhere else in 2Chr, straddling this exact seam — read as one deliberate antithesis, it would argue against splitting here at all. That pairing can also be composed across a genuine boundary, though, so it is weighed rather than decisive; what is judged the stronger case for keeping the split is the register shift itself, iterative divine patience versus a punctual invasion narrative, since no new grammatical agent actually enters at v17 to carry the break on its own.

boundary_rationale: The wrath just declared at v16's terminal עַד לְאֵ֥ין מַרְפֵּֽא, 'until there was no remedy' (its only other occurrence in the book, 21:18's לָחֳלִ֖י לְאֵ֥ין מַרְפֵּֽא, likewise seals off a moment past hope), is now executed: Yahweh — still the operative subject continuing from v15's וַיִּשְׁלַ֡ח יְהוָה֩ — וַיַּ֨עַל עֲלֵיהֶ֜ם אֶת מֶ֣לֶךְ כשדיים כַּשְׂדִּ֗ים, 'brought up against them the king of' the Chaldeans (v17), the gentilic itself the only genuinely new element here (ketiv כשדיים, qere כַּשְׂדִּ֗ים), since Nebuchadnezzar is already named four times earlier in this chapter (נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּ֖ר 36:6, נְבוּכַדְנֶאצַּ֖ר 36:7, נְבֽוּכַדְנֶאצַּ֔ר 36:10, נְבֽוּכַדְנֶאצַּר֙ 36:13); the opening pivot is not a new agent entering but the shift from prophetic-messenger action (vv15-16) to military execution, sparing no age group. The report moves through the seizure of every treasury (v18) into the burning of the temple, city wall, and palaces, וַֽיִּשְׂרְפוּ֙ אֶת בֵּ֣ית הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים, 'they burned the house of God', and וַֽיְנַתְּצ֔וּ אֵ֖ת חוֹמַ֣ת יְרוּשָׁלִָ֑ם, '[they] broke down the wall of Jerusalem' (v19, plural verbs throughout, trailing a SAMEKH, single-witness), then a pivot to a singular subject at v20's וַיֶּ֛גֶל הַשְּׁאֵרִ֥ית, 'he carried away the remnant' -- וַֽיִּהְיוּ ל֤וֹ וּלְבָנָיו֙ לַעֲבָדִ֔ים, 'they were servants to him and his sons' is 3mp ('and they were'), referring to the deported remnant collectively, not singular: an independent sweep (5:8, 13:13, 20:25, 24:12, 24:14) confirms this verb form is plural throughout the book, and a plural verb cannot itself confirm the number of the earlier, grammatically unrelated 3ms verb of exile; the element that actually continues a singular referent into the clause is instead the singular pronominal suffix in the following word, 'to him', running עַד מְלֹ֖ךְ מַלְכ֥וּת פָּרָֽס, 'until the reign of the kingdom of Persia' (v20). V21's purpose infinitive, לְמַלֹּ֖אות שִׁבְעִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה, 'to fulfill... seventy years', depends grammatically on v20's own finite וַיֶּ֛גֶל rather than standing free, so it cannot be detached from it; that dependency, not agent continuity, is what actually holds vv20-21 to what precedes. V21 is the strongest formal closer still available at this point in the stretch — not, as an unqualified superlative would claim, the strongest anywhere in it, since the source-citation series (וְיֶתֶר֩ דִּבְרֵ֨י יְהֽוֹיָקִ֜ים, its tenth and final member) already closed the same 36:1-21 material at v8 — and a fresh dating formula opens the Cyrus material immediately after v21, which is why the unit is capped here, even though it sits on ground the book strategy already flags as thin.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the destruction notices (vv17-19) from the exile-and-fulfillment notices (vv20-21) at the SAMEKH after v19 has a real tier-1 signal behind it that 'the same agent governs both halves' does not capture: v19's destruction verbs are all 3mp (וַֽיִּשְׂרְפוּ֙, וַֽיְנַתְּצ֔וּ, שָׂרְפ֣וּ) while v20 opens 3ms. It still fails: 36:21 contains two occurrences of the purpose infinitive. The verse-final one immediately follows and completes a finite qal perfect governed by 'all the days of its desolation' within v21 itself, an independent clause the row concedes elsewhere; the infinitive that actually rides grammatically on v20's finite verb is the verse-initial one, opening v21. A verse opening on a bare purpose infinitive cannot head a unit on its own, which defeats the 19/20 split without denying that v21 supplies its own independent clause.

boundary_rationale: A new regnal dating formula opens the book's final unit, וּבִשְׁנַ֣ת אַחַ֗ת לְכ֨וֹרֶשׁ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ פָּרַ֔ס, ‘in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia’ (v22), explicitly framed as the fulfillment of Jeremiah's word, לִכְל֥וֹת דְּבַר יְהוָ֖ה בְּפִ֣י יִרְמְיָ֑הוּ, ‘that Yahweh's word by the mouth of Jeremiah might be accomplished’ — a near-verbatim echo of v21's own purpose clause, לְמַלֹּ֤אות דְּבַר יְהוָה֙ בְּפִ֣י יִרְמְיָ֔הוּ, ‘to fulfill Yahweh's word by Jeremiah's mouth’. The echo is deliberate bracketing, not grounds for folding v22 backward into v21: each purpose-infinitive rides its own independent finite verb — v21's on v20's וַיֶּ֛גֶל, v22's own on הֵעִ֣יר יְהוָ֗ה, ‘Yahweh stirred up’ — so the two verses supply parallel but syntactically distinct fulfillment-frames bracketing the exile's start and the return's start respectively. The notice pivots from third-person narration of Cyrus's proclamation into Cyrus's own first-person edict, closing on the protasis-apodosis מִֽי בָכֶ֣ם מִכָּל עַמּ֗וֹ יְהוָ֧ה אֱלֹהָ֛יו עִמּ֖וֹ וְיָֽעַל, ‘whoever is among you of all his people, Yahweh his God be with him, and let him go up’ (v23) — a third-person apocopated jussive, וְיָֽעַל, not an imperative, distinguished from the wayyiqtol doubling pattern of v17's וַיַּ֨עַל by its simple conjunctive waw. A SAMEKH trails v22 (single-witness) between the narrated notice and Cyrus's quoted speech, span-internal rather than corroborating either outer edge; the PE keyed to v21 (single-witness), already carried in the refs, is what corroborates this unit's opening edge. The Ezra 1:1-3 overlap in this material is cross-book metadata under the book strategy's synoptic-discipline rule and plays no role in setting this boundary; the pair stands as its own closing unit regardless.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading v22 as the tail of the preceding exile-and-fulfillment report (folding it into vv17-21) rather than the head of the Cyrus unit would strip the dating formula from the edict it introduces. It is not, as it might seem, blocked merely because v21 stands complete without v22: v21's own purpose clause, לְמַלֹּ֤אות דְּבַר יְהוָה֙ בְּפִ֣י יִרְמְיָ֔הוּ, is a bare infinitive construct with no finite verb of its own — riding on v20's וַיֶּ֛גֶל — and the verse's one truly independent clause, כָּל יְמֵ֤י הָשַּׁמָּה֙ שָׁבָ֔תָה, is not the fulfillment clause at all. What actually blocks the fold is v22's own new finite verb and new dating formula launching a fresh, independent notice rather than continuing v21's dependent purpose clause.

boundary_rationale: The unit opens with a regnal-year time-frame, וּבִשְׁנַ֣ת אַחַ֗ת לְכ֨וֹרֶשׁ֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ פָּרַ֔ס (“in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia” web:Ezra.1.1), immediately fused to a fulfillment clause, לִכְל֥וֹת דְּבַר יְהוָ֖ה מִפִּ֣י יִרְמְיָ֑ה (“that Yahweh's word by Jeremiah's mouth might be accomplished” web:Ezra.1.1, oshb:Ezra.1.1). Narration then supplies a proclamation frame, וַיַּֽעֲבֶר קוֹל֙ בְּכָל מַלְכוּת֔וֹ וְגַם בְּמִכְתָּ֖ב לֵאמֹֽר (“he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and put it also in writing, saying” web:Ezra.1.1, oshb:Ezra.1.1), which hands directly into the king's own quoted words opening Ezra.1.2, כֹּ֣ה אָמַ֗ר כֹּ֚רֶשׁ מֶ֣לֶךְ פָּרַ֔ס (“Cyrus king of Persia says” web:Ezra.1.2, oshb:Ezra.1.2). The quotation runs as one continuous edict carried by its own volitive chain, יְהִ֤י ... וְיַ֕עַל ... וְיִ֗בֶן (Ezra.1.3, oshb:Ezra.1.3), which the directive יְנַשְּׂא֨וּהוּ֙ אַנְשֵׁ֣י מְקֹמ֔וֹ (“let the men of his place help him” web:Ezra.1.4, oshb:Ezra.1.4) carries forward through the closing clause of Ezra.1.4, עִם הַ֨נְּדָבָ֔ה לְבֵ֥ית הָאֱלֹהִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר בִּירוּשָׁלִָֽם (“the free will offering for God's house which is in Jerusalem” web:Ezra.1.4, oshb:Ezra.1.4). That directive modality is cut off precisely at Ezra.1.5's wayyiqtol, וַיָּק֜וּמוּ (“Then ... rose up” web:Ezra.1.5, oshb:Ezra.1.5), under a wholly fresh subject (the returning heads of households) -- the edict's own volitive-chain opening and its termination by that wayyiqtol, not chapter or verse numbering or WEB's punctuation, set both edges.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Ezra.1.1 through Ezra.1.11 as one undivided decree-to-vessels row loses the edict's own volitive-chain closure at Ezra.1.4 and the subject pivot to the community's own response marked by Ezra.1.5's wayyiqtol וַיָּק֜וּמוּ.

boundary_rationale: Narration resumes with a wayyiqtol opener naming the responders, וַיָּק֜וּמוּ רָאשֵׁ֣י הָאָב֗וֹת לִֽיהוּדָה֙ וּבִנְיָמִ֔ן וְהַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים וְהַלְוִיִּ֑ם (“Then the heads of fathers' households of Judah and Benjamin, the priests and the Levites” web:Ezra.1.5, oshb:Ezra.1.5), whose subject the asyndetic relative clause לְכֹ֨ל הֵעִ֤יר הָאֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת רוּח֔וֹ (“all whose spirit God had stirred” web:Ezra.1.5, oshb:Ezra.1.5) extends, echoing the king's own stirring in Ezra.1.1, הֵעִ֣יר יְהוָ֗ה אֶת ר֨וּחַ֙ (“Yahweh stirred up the spirit” web:Ezra.1.1, oshb:Ezra.1.1) -- the same stirring-of-spirit collocation binding king's response and people's response as one movement (purpose itself is carried separately, by the infinitive pair לַעֲל֣וֹת לִבְנ֔וֹת later in the verse). Ezra.1.6 continues that same donative movement under a widened subject, וְכָל סְבִיבֹֽתֵיהֶם֙ חִזְּק֣וּ בִֽידֵיהֶ֔ם (“All those who were around them strengthened their hands” web:Ezra.1.6, oshb:Ezra.1.6), 1:6 and Ezra.1.7's own opener, וְהַמֶּ֣לֶךְ כּ֔וֹרֶשׁ הוֹצִ֖יא (“Cyrus the king brought out” web:Ezra.1.7, oshb:Ezra.1.7), sharing that disjunctive waw-fronted-subject-qatal clause type -- but Ezra.1.5 itself opens with a wayyiqtol, וַיָּק֜וּמוּ, not that pattern, so clause form alone would put a seam at 1:5|1:6, not at 1:6|1:7, and cannot be the differentiator this row needs. What does differentiate them is content: Ezra.1.5-Ezra.1.6 share one donor-action class (gift-giving) with a widening beneficiary field, while Ezra.1.7 introduces a new agent (the king) and a new object class (temple vessels restored from the royal treasury, not a free-will gift) -- that actor/action-class break, not clause form, closes the unit before Ezra.1.7.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Ezra.1.5 (the rising) from Ezra.1.6 (the neighbors' gifts) into two rows overstates a minor actor-shift within one continuous donor-action-class mobilization wave; clause form does not decide the question either way, since 1:5 opens with a wayyiqtol while 1:6 and Ezra.1.7's accepted seam alone share the disjunctive waw-subject-qatal pattern; the content-level break at Ezra.1.7 (new agent, new object class) is what actually closes the unit, not any clause-type contrast internal to 1:5-1:6.

boundary_rationale: A fresh subject opens the unit, וְהַמֶּ֣לֶךְ כּ֔וֹרֶשׁ הוֹצִ֖יא (“Also Cyrus the king brought out” web:Ezra.1.7, oshb:Ezra.1.7), naming the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had earlier removed; the action runs through a chain of narrative verbs ending וַֽיִּסְפְּרֵם֙ לְשֵׁשְׁבַּצַּ֔ר הַנָּשִׂ֖יא (“and counted them out to Sheshbazzar the prince” web:Ezra.1.8, oshb:Ezra.1.8). Ezra.1.9 opens its own list with a demonstrative-fronted presentative clause, וְאֵ֖לֶּה מִסְפָּרָ֑ם (“This is the number of them” web:Ezra.1.9, oshb:Ezra.1.9) -- a bare demonstrative subject over a suffixed-noun predicate, formally paralleling Ezra.2.1's own register opener -- switching from finite-verb transfer narration to bare itemized enumeration. That syntactic-class switch, not the demonstrative alone, is the operative warrant: the same demonstrative pronoun also does sub-unit-level work elsewhere in the book (it opens a sub-register within the larger chapter-2 list at Ezra.2.59, and at Ezra.8.13, וּמִבְּנֵ֣י אֲדֹנִיקָם֮ אַחֲרֹנִים֒, it is not even clause-initial), so the incipit by itself cannot carry this seam. The item lines run through Ezra.1.10, and the unit closes on a colophon totaling the class and naming the carrier, כָּל כֵּלִים֙ לַזָּהָ֣ב וְלַכֶּ֔סֶף חֲמֵ֥שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֖ים וְאַרְבַּ֣ע מֵא֑וֹת הַכֹּ֞ל הֶעֱלָ֣ה שֵׁשְׁבַּצַּ֗ר (“All the vessels of gold and of silver were five thousand four hundred. Sheshbazzar brought all these up” web:Ezra.1.11, oshb:Ezra.1.11).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading Ezra.1.7 through Ezra.1.11 as one undivided transfer unit, hosting the inventory as an inset, is the stronger rival: Ezra.1.11's colophon closes עִ֚ם הֵעָל֣וֹת הַגּוֹלָ֔ה מִבָּבֶ֖ל לִירוּשָׁלִָֽם (“when the captives were brought up from Babylon to Jerusalem” web:Ezra.1.11, oshb:Ezra.1.11), resuming the very participant and transaction narrated at Ezra.1.8's וַֽיִּסְפְּרֵם֙ לְשֵׁשְׁבַּצַּ֔ר, and the demonstrative opener at Ezra.1.9 is not exclusive to full-unit openings elsewhere in the book. This row holds the finer Ezra.1.7-Ezra.1.8 | Ezra.1.9-Ezra.1.11 cut on the syntactic-class switch from narrated-transfer finite verbs to headless numeral enumeration at Ezra.1.9, against the coarser inset reading's own resumption of 1:8's transaction at 1:11.

boundary_rationale: The list opens on its own incipit, a demonstrative-fronted presentative (verbless-clause) opener, וְאֵ֖לֶּה מִסְפָּרָ֑ם (“This is the number of them” web:Ezra.1.9, oshb:Ezra.1.9) -- a bare demonstrative subject over a suffixed-noun predicate, no construct chain -- formally paralleling Ezra.2.1's own register opener, וְאֵ֣לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י הַמְּדִינָ֗ה (“Now these are the children of the province” web:Ezra.2.1, oshb:Ezra.2.1), whose predicate בְּנֵ֣י הַמְּדִינָ֗ה is a genuine construct chain with the demonstrative standing outside it as subject: the shared device is the demonstrative-fronted presentative pattern, not a shared construct state. The item lines (platters, knives, bowls) run through Ezra.1.10, and the unit closes on a colophon totaling the class and naming the carrier, כָּל כֵּלִים֙ לַזָּהָ֣ב וְלַכֶּ֔סֶף חֲמֵ֥שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֖ים וְאַרְבַּ֣ע מֵא֑וֹת הַכֹּ֞ל הֶעֱלָ֣ה שֵׁשְׁבַּצַּ֗ר (“All the vessels of gold and of silver were five thousand four hundred. Sheshbazzar brought all these up” web:Ezra.1.11, oshb:Ezra.1.11), closing with עִ֚ם הֵעָל֣וֹת הַגּוֹלָ֔ה מִבָּבֶ֖ל לִירוּשָׁלִָֽם (“when the captives were brought up from Babylon to Jerusalem” web:Ezra.1.11, oshb:Ezra.1.11) -- language sharing ordinary book-wide diction with Ezra.2.1's own captivity vocabulary (the golah lexeme recurs 12 times across 7 chapters, no seam-discriminating force on its own) and so hands forward to the golah register without merging into it, since the colophon still closes with its own total rather than opening a new one.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading the colophon's captivity language at Ezra.1.11 as already opening the Ezra.2.1 register would erase the colophon's own close of the vessel unit and the topic change from precious metal to returning persons.

boundary_rationale: A new register opens on וְאֵ֣לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י הַמְּדִינָ֗ה (“Now these are the children of the province” web:Ezra.2.1, oshb:Ezra.2.1), specifying its members as הָֽעֹלִים֙ מִשְּׁבִ֣י הַגּוֹלָ֔ה (“who went up out of the captivity of those who had been carried away” web:Ezra.2.1, oshb:Ezra.2.1) -- picking up the הַגּוֹלָ֔ה vocabulary Ezra.1.11's colophon had just used for the vessel-carrying. Ezra.2.2 names the caravan's leaders through the verse's atnach on בַּעֲנָ֑ה, then pivots -- in the verse's second half -- to its own transition phrase, מִסְפַּ֕ר אַנְשֵׁ֖י עַ֥ם יִשְׂרָאֵֽל (“The number of the men of the people of Israel” web:Ezra.2.2, oshb:Ezra.2.2), which syntactically heads the clan-by-clan enumeration beginning at Ezra.2.3 rather than closing the leader-roster frame that precedes the atnach; this row keeps it inside Ezra.2.1-Ezra.2.2 because whole-verse granularity governs this part's grain (no sub-verse rows), not because the heading itself belongs to the frame. The unit closes at the end of Ezra.2.2 because Ezra.2.3 is where a name-plus-figure line actually begins, בְּנֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔שׁ אַלְפַּ֕יִם מֵאָ֖ה שִׁבְעִ֥ים וּשְׁנָֽיִם (“The children of Parosh, two thousand one hundred seventy-two” web:Ezra.2.3, oshb:Ezra.2.3) -- nothing in Ezra.2.1-Ezra.2.2 itself is a counted entry. Ezra.1.11 closes the preceding vessel colophon immediately before this incipit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Two closer rivals were weighed and set aside at whole-verse grain: ending the frame at Ezra.2.2's own atnach (on בַּעֲנָ֑ה), which would treat מִסְפַּ֕ר אַנְשֵׁ֖י עַ֥ם יִשְׂרָאֵֽל as opening the following count rather than closing this row -- rejected because this part's grain does not split within a verse; and extending this row through Ezra.2.3 to give the incipit a worked counted example, which would blur the formal line between the register's own frame (name + transition phrase, no figures) and its entries (name + figure, repeated).

boundary_rationale: This is one uninterrupted run of name-plus-figure entries opening בְּנֵ֣י פַרְעֹ֔שׁ אַלְפַּ֕יִם מֵאָ֖ה שִׁבְעִ֥ים וּשְׁנָֽיִם (“The children of Parosh, two thousand one hundred seventy-two” web:Ezra.2.3, oshb:Ezra.2.3) and closing בְּנֵ֣י סְנָאָ֔ה שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת אֲלָפִ֔ים וְשֵׁ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת וּשְׁלֹשִֽׁים (“The children of Senaah, three thousand six hundred thirty” web:Ezra.2.35, oshb:Ezra.2.35). No entry in this stretch carries a determined-state class caption of its own; the variation that does occur is formulaic: the construct-chain form בְּנֵ֣י ('sons/children of') spans the whole run (Ezra.2.3-Ezra.2.21, Ezra.2.24-Ezra.2.26, Ezra.2.29-Ezra.2.35), while the alternate, place-linked form אַנְשֵׁ֥י ('men of') is confined to two interleaved pairs, Ezra.2.22-Ezra.2.23 and Ezra.2.27-Ezra.2.28, never attested before Ezra.2.22 (sweep.py --web 'The men of' returns 7 hits book-wide; sweep.py --skel confirms 10 Hebrew-skeleton hits, only 4 of which fall inside Ezra.2.3-Ezra.2.35). Interleaving after Ezra.2.23, not symmetric recurrence around it, is what shows the alternation tracks no content boundary. The row closes because Ezra.2.36 opens with an absolute-state caption standing outside the count formula, הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים (“The priests” web:Ezra.2.36, oshb:Ezra.2.36), a different grammatical class of opener from anything inside this row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this run at any of the sons-of/men-of alternations (Ezra.2.21|Ezra.2.22, Ezra.2.23|Ezra.2.24, Ezra.2.26|Ezra.2.27) would treat ordinary lexical variation -- not a class boundary -- as equivalent to Ezra.2.36's genuine caption break, which it is not.

boundary_rationale: An absolute-state caption opens the unit, הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים בְּנֵ֤י יְדַֽעְיָה֙ לְבֵ֣ית יֵשׁ֔וּעַ (“The priests: the children of Jedaiah, of the house of Jeshua” web:Ezra.2.36, oshb:Ezra.2.36), a class header standing grammatically apart from the construct-chain entries of the laity roll it follows. Three more priestly clans are counted, closing בְּנֵ֣י חָרִ֔ם אֶ֖לֶף וְשִׁבְעָ֥ה עָשָֽׂר (“The children of Harim, one thousand seventeen” web:Ezra.2.39, oshb:Ezra.2.39). The row ends there because Ezra.2.40 opens a parallel absolute-state caption for a different personnel class, הַלְוִיִּ֑ם (“The Levites” web:Ezra.2.40, oshb:Ezra.2.40) -- the same captioning device marking a fresh boundary rather than continuing the priestly count.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the priestly roll forward into Ezra.2.40 through Ezra.2.42 as one 'cultic personnel' row would erase two independent class captions (Ezra.2.36's and Ezra.2.40's) that the text itself supplies.

boundary_rationale: Three short cultic-support rolls share this unit, but they are not uniform in shape. Ezra.2.40 and Ezra.2.41 each open a bare absolute-state class caption, standing alone before its entry: הַלְוִיִּ֑ם (“The Levites” web:Ezra.2.40, oshb:Ezra.2.40) and הַֽמְשֹׁרְרִ֑ים (“The singers” web:Ezra.2.41, oshb:Ezra.2.41), each followed by one named sub-family and its own total (seventy-four; one hundred twenty-eight). Ezra.2.42's opener, בְּנֵ֣י הַשֹּֽׁעֲרִ֗ים (“The children of the gatekeepers” web:Ezra.2.42, oshb:Ezra.2.42), is a construct chain -- the shape of an ordinary entry line, formally identical to בְּנֵ֣י חָרִ֔ם at Ezra.2.39 -- not a third bare caption; the verse goes on to name six sub-families and closes on its own colophon total, הַכֹּ֕ל מֵאָ֖ה שְׁלֹשִׁ֥ים וְתִשְׁעָֽה (“in all one hundred thirty-nine” web:Ezra.2.42, oshb:Ezra.2.42) -- the same הַכֹּ֕ל totaling device that closes the vessel inventory at Ezra.1.11 and recurs seven times book-wide (sweep, skeleton tier: 2 in these two lists -- Ezra.1.11, Ezra.2.42 -- and 5 more in the chapter 8 treasure register -- Ezra.8.25, Ezra.8.28, Ezra.8.30, Ezra.8.33, Ezra.8.35). All three classes are nonetheless minor cultic-support personnel, each far smaller in scale and textual weight than the priestly roll immediately before them (Ezra.2.36-Ezra.2.39; its opening entry, Ezra.2.36, already counts nine hundred seventy-three), and none opens a stretch long enough to carry its own multi-verse row at this part's grain; that shared minor scale, not a shared caption shape, is what keeps Levites, singers, and gatekeepers in one row. The row closes because Ezra.2.43 opens a caption for an unrelated, non-cultic personnel class, הַנְּתִינִ֑ים (“The temple servants” web:Ezra.2.43, oshb:Ezra.2.43), beginning the next, longer bloc.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Levites (Ezra.2.40), singers (Ezra.2.41), and gatekeepers (Ezra.2.42) into three separate rows is defensible on caption grounds -- each does open its own class name, and Ezra.2.42 in particular is a compact sub-register with six internal entries and its own colophon, not a bare one-line caption matching Ezra.2.40-Ezra.2.41's shape -- and it would bring this stretch into line with the caption-driven boundaries this part uses elsewhere (Ezra.2.36's and Ezra.2.40's own captions each open a fresh row). This row instead groups the three on minor shared scale relative to the priesthood, a real but coarser-grained call than the caption rule alone would produce.

boundary_rationale: The unit opens הַנְּתִינִ֑ים (“The temple servants” web:Ezra.2.43, oshb:Ezra.2.43) and runs a name list through Ezra.2.54; a second caption at Ezra.2.55, בְּנֵ֖י עַבְדֵ֣י שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה (“The children of Solomon's servants” web:Ezra.2.55, oshb:Ezra.2.55), opens a further name list through Ezra.2.57. Both lists are gathered into a single joint colophon, כָּ֨ל הַנְּתִינִ֔ים וּבְנֵ֖י עַבְדֵ֣י שְׁלֹמֹ֑ה (“All the temple servants, and the children of Solomon's servants, were three hundred ninety-two” web:Ezra.2.58, oshb:Ezra.2.58); neither sub-list is totaled on its own, so the colophon itself argues against splitting them. Ezra.2.42 closes the preceding cultic-personnel bloc right before this unit's opening caption. The row ends there because Ezra.2.59 opens a fresh incipit, וְאֵ֗לֶּה הָֽעֹלִים֙ (“These were those who went up” web:Ezra.2.59, oshb:Ezra.2.59), for a differently defined group.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the nethinim (Ezra.2.43 through Ezra.2.54) from Solomon's servants (Ezra.2.55 through Ezra.2.57) at their separate captions ignores that Ezra.2.58's colophon totals both classes jointly without supplying either sub-list with its own figure.
