strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 11:1-2 forward to the WEB 11:3 superscription as one continuous register-opening remains a genuine, conceded overlap in theme — 11:1 already narrates princes dwelling in Jerusalem in terms close to what 11:3 restates — but it is answered by form rather than left merely open: 11:3 opens with its own demonstrative-plus-class-title incipit, “וְאֵ֨לֶּה֙ רָאשֵׁ֣י הַמְּדִינָ֔ה” ("and these are the heads of the province"), the same construction as the golah register header “אֵ֣לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י הַמְּדִינָ֗ה” ("these are the children of the province") at 7:6 (the class noun hamedinah: 2 verses book-wide; the full incipit collocation at 11:3 itself: a singleton, sweep: 1), marking 11:3 as a fresh register head rather than a continuation of 11:1's narrative report. The split is still argued at medium_low, since the thematic overlap remains real even where the form-based answer resolves the segmentation question.

boundary_rationale: WEB "Now these are the chiefs of the province who lived in Jerusalem; but in the cities of Judah, everyone lived in his possession in their cities-Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the children of Solomon's servants." opens with וְאֵ֨לֶּה֙ רָאשֵׁ֣י הַמְּדִינָ֔ה ("and these [are] heads of the province"), a formula that echoes 11:1's report but is not identical: 11:1 uses sarei ha'am ("princes of the people"); this verse uses rashei ha-medinah ("heads of the province"). The clause that follows, וּבְעָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֗ה יָֽשְׁב֞וּ אִ֤ישׁ בַּאֲחֻזָּתוֹ֙ בְּעָ֣רֵיהֶ֔ם ("and in the cities of Judah they dwelt, each in his holding, in their cities"), takes as its delayed subject -- no intervening verb -- the five-class inventory יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל הַכֹּהֲנִים֙ וְהַלְוִיִּ֣ם וְהַנְּתִינִ֔ים וּבְנֵ֖י עַבְדֵ֥י שְׁלֹמֹֽה ("Israel, the priests, the Levites, the nethinim, and the sons of Solomon's servants"): a population enumeration, not a table of contents for the register that follows. That register both adds classes the inventory omits (gatekeepers at 11:19, singers at 11:22-23) and never again names one it includes (sons of Solomon's servants, sweep: 3 book-wide, none after this verse). The same cities-of-Judah topic is what 11:20 resumes (sweep: arei Yehudah, 2 book-wide, only 11:3 and 11:20), so this verse opens the frame that 11:20 closes. A petuchah (single-witness) precedes it (oshb:Neh.11.2), closing the lot-casting report before this superscription begins, and the province-header formula itself parallels, well beyond this immediate seam, the header function a comparable formula serves for the golah list many chapters earlier at oshb:Neh.7.6.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 11:3 as merely resuming 11:1's report (so the two rows should be one) loses because the vocabulary shift (rashei ha-medinah, not sarei ha'am) marks a fresh formula opening the settlers account; reading its five-class inventory as a table of contents for the register that follows also loses, since the register both adds classes the inventory omits (gatekeepers, singers) and drops one it names (sons of Solomon's servants) -- the inventory belongs instead to the cities-of-Judah frame this verse opens and 11:20 closes.

boundary_rationale: WEB "Some of the children of Judah and of the children of Benjamin lived in Jerusalem. Of the children of Judah: Athaiah..." opens with וּבִֽירוּשָׁלִַ֨ם֙ יָֽשְׁב֔וּ ("and in Jerusalem dwelt") then names the class, מִבְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה וּמִבְּנֵ֣י בִנְיָמִ֑ן מִבְּנֵ֣י יְ֠הוּדָה ("of the sons of Judah and of the sons of Benjamin, of the sons of Judah"). The Judah genealogy runs through v.6, which supplies its own closing count, WEB "were four hundred sixty-eight valiant men," Hebrew אַרְבַּ֥ע מֵא֛וֹת שִׁשִּׁ֥ים וּשְׁמֹנָ֖ה אַנְשֵׁי חָֽיִל ("four hundred sixty-eight men of valor") after naming the whole clan, כָּל בְּנֵי פֶ֕רֶץ הַיֹּשְׁבִ֖ים בִּירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם ("all sons of Perez who dwelt in Jerusalem"). A setumah (single-witness) follows this verse (oshb:Neh.11.6), closing the Judah class before the Benjamin class opens fresh in v.7.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping Judah and Benjamin as one lay-settlers row loses the closing-total pattern (each clan gets its own head-count) and the corroborating mark that separates them, the same class-by-count structure seen in the priestly and Levitical sub-lists later in this chapter.

boundary_rationale: WEB "These are the sons of Benjamin: Sallu..." opens with וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י בִנְיָמִ֑ן סַלֻּ֡א ("and these [are] sons of Benjamin: Sallu"), the same ve'elleh ("and these") header-formula as the superscription at 11:3, now scoped to one clan. A setumah (single-witness) immediately precedes this verse (oshb:Neh.11.6, closing Judah). The unit runs through v.9's overseer notice, WEB "Joel the son of Zichri was their overseer; and Judah the son of Hassenuah was second over the city," Hebrew וְיוֹאֵ֥ל בֶּן זִכְרִ֖י פָּקִ֣יד עֲלֵיהֶ֑ם ("and Joel son of Zichri, overseer over them") and וִיהוּדָ֧ה בֶן הַסְּנוּאָ֛ה עַל הָעִ֖יר מִשְׁנֶֽה ("and Judah son of Hassenuah, over the city, second"), closed by a petuchah (single-witness) at oshb:Neh.11.9.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the overseer notice (v.9) into its own row loses because it names no new resident class -- it is an administrative coda to the Benjamin count, paralleled by the paqid-aleihem overseer note closing the priestly sub-list alone (11:14, Zabdiel; sweep: paqid, 4 book-wide -- 11:9, 11:14, 11:22, 12:42). The Levitical sub-list closes instead with a bare grand total (11:18); its own overseer notice, וּפְקִ֤יד הַלְוִיִּם֙ בִּיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם עֻזִּ֤י ("and overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem, Uzzi"), sits inside the temple-personnel appendix (11:22), three verses past the Levites' own close, and uses a construct chain (u-fqid ha-Leviyyim), not this verse's paqid-aleihem collocation.

boundary_rationale: WEB "Of the priests: Jedaiah the son of Joiarib, Jachin," opens with מִן הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים ("from/of the priests"), a min-partitive header sharing its family with Judah's own opener (11:4, מִבְּנֵ֥י יְהוּדָ֖ה) and the Levites' (11:15, וּמִֽן הַלְוִיִּ֑ם); the same partitive also opens the Levite closing note at 11:36 (וּמִן הַלְוִיִּ֔ם). Of the settlers-and-clergy register's four opener families -- ve'elleh (sweep: 4 book-wide), min-partitive (sweep: 5 book-wide), vav+definite-class-noun (11:19 וְהַשּֽׁוֹעֲרִים֙, 11:21, 12:8), and kol+class-noun (11:18 כָּל הַלְוִיִּם֙) -- only Benjamin's own incipit (11:7, וְאֵ֖לֶּה בְּנֵ֣י בִנְיָמִ֑ן) uses ve'elleh; this verse's partitive is not distinct from a uniform lay-clan formula, since Judah, the register's earliest-listed lay clan, is itself partitive-headed. A petuchah (single-witness) that closes the Benjamin section (oshb:Neh.11.9) precedes it. Three named sub-groups follow with running totals (822, 242, 128), and the unit closes with its own overseer notice, WEB "and their overseer was Zabdiel, the son of Haggedolim," Hebrew וּפָקִ֣יד עֲלֵיהֶ֔ם זַבְדִּיאֵ֖ל בֶּן הַגְּדוֹלִֽים ("and overseer over them, Zabdiel son of Haggedolim"), the same paqid-aleihem collocation used for Benjamin's overseers at 11:9. A setumah (single-witness) follows this verse (oshb:Neh.11.14).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Rowing the three priestly sub-totals (822/242/128) separately loses because none of the three carries its own header or mark; they run as one partitive-headed class bounded by petuchah (single-witness) before and setumah (single-witness) after. Treating this partitive as a marker distinguishing the priests from a uniform lay-clan ve'elleh also loses: the register runs a ve'elleh/min-partitive alternation (ve'elleh at 11:3, 11:7 only; sweep: 4 book-wide), not a lay-vs-clergy split.

boundary_rationale: WEB "Of the Levites: Shemaiah the son of Hasshub..." opens with וּמִֽן הַלְוִיִּ֑ם ("and of the Levites"), the same partitive header pattern as the priests' class at 11:10, following a setumah (single-witness) that closes it (oshb:Neh.11.14). The unit closes with its own grand total, unlike the priests' running sub-counts: WEB "All the Levites in the holy city were two hundred eighty-four," Hebrew כָּל הַלְוִיִּם֙ בְּעִ֣יר הַקֹּ֔דֶשׁ מָאתַ֖יִם שְׁמֹנִ֥ים וְאַרְבָּעָֽה ("all the Levites in the holy city: two hundred eighty-four"), followed by a petuchah (single-witness) at oshb:Neh.11.18.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row to include the gatekeepers (WEB 11:19) loses because the Levites already close with their own summary total and a petuchah (single-witness), and the gatekeepers open with a distinct class-name of their own.

boundary_rationale: WEB "Moreover the gatekeepers, Akkub, Talmon, and their brothers, who kept watch at the gates, were one hundred seventy-two." opens וְהַשּֽׁוֹעֲרִים֙ עַקּ֣וּב טַלְמ֔וֹן ("and the gatekeepers: Akkub, Talmon"), a fourth named class following a petuchah (single-witness) that closed the Levites (oshb:Neh.11.18), and supplies its own count in the same verse, מֵאָ֖ה שִׁבְעִ֥ים וּשְׁנָֽיִם ("one hundred seventy-two"). No mark follows this verse, which is not counterevidence here; the row stands on the class-name-plus-count pattern shared with every other sub-list in this register (the priests' at 11:14, the Levites' at 11:18), here compressed into a single verse -- a textual fact about this entry's length, not a claim about the gatekeeper class's actual size relative to the others.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding the gatekeepers into the Levite row loses their distinct class-name (hashsho'arim, applied to a separate group from the Levites in this list) and their own separately-counted total.

boundary_rationale: WEB "The residue of Israel, of the priests, and the Levites were in all the cities of Judah, everyone in his inheritance." opens וּשְׁאָ֨ר יִשְׂרָאֵ֜ל הַכֹּהֲנִ֤ים הַלְוִיִּם֙ בְּכָל עָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה אִ֖ישׁ בְּנַחֲלָתֽוֹ ("and the rest of Israel, the priests, the Levites, in all the cities of Judah, each in his inheritance"), a generic distributive statement with no named individual and no head-count, unlike every class-entry from 11:4 through 11:19. Grammatically it summarizes the whole preceding census (those not resident in Jerusalem specifically). The verse closes an inclusio with the register's own opening at 11:3: both share the Israel/priests/Levites class-sequence and an ish-be-X-o distributive clause, in chiastically inverted order -- 11:3 states the cities-clause then the class-list (וּבְעָרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֗ה יָֽשְׁב֞וּ אִ֤ישׁ בַּאֲחֻזָּתוֹ֙ בְּעָ֣רֵיהֶ֔ם יִשְׂרָאֵ֤ל הַכֹּהֲנִים֙ וְהַלְוִיִּ֣ם וְהַנְּתִינִ֔ים וּבְנֵ֖י עַבְדֵ֥י שְׁלֹמֹֽה), 11:20 states the class-list then the cities-clause -- and the phrase arei Yehudah is otherwise unique to these two verses (sweep: 2 book-wide). The opening וּשְׁאָ֨ר ("the rest") additionally ties this verse to the same root construction used at 11:1's report and at 10:28 (sweep: 3 book-wide). A forward reading is available -- 11:20's cities-of-Judah topic anticipates the one 11:25 opens with its own header, וְאֶל הַחֲצֵרִ֖ים בִּשְׂדֹתָ֑ם מִבְּנֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֗ה ("and as for the villages in their fields, some of the sons of Judah"), matching 11:4's own partitive-plus-dwelling opener -- but it is not adopted: 11:25 is independently self-headed and needs no assist from 11:20, while 11:20's inverted-order echo of 11:3 is a closing-bracket signature a forward heading for 11:25 would not carry. This verse functions as a colophon rather than another named entry; it is followed immediately by fresh, specifically-named notices (temple servants, a Levite overseer, singers, a royal deputy) that resume individual naming.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching this verse to the gatekeepers' entry (11:19) loses because it names no individual and gives no count -- its "everyone in his inheritance" is a summary formula closing the census, not a fifth counted class. Reading it instead as heading the Judah-village material that follows (11:20's cities-of-Judah clause anticipating 11:25's own header) also loses: 11:25 carries its own independent opener matching 11:4's, needing no assist from 11:20, while 11:20's inverted-order echo of 11:3 (class-list + distributive clause, chiastically reversed) is a closing-bracket signature a forward heading would not carry.

boundary_rationale: WEB "But the temple servants lived in Ophel; and Ziha and Gishpa were over the temple servants." opens וְהַנְּתִינִ֖ים יֹשְׁבִ֣ים בָּעֹ֑פֶל וְצִיחָ֥א וְגִשְׁפָּ֖א עַל הַנְּתִינִֽים ("and the temple-servants dwelt in Ophel, and Ziha and Gishpa over the temple-servants") after the colophon at 11:20; its first clause (class-noun + participle + place) continues the register's own dwelling-verb thread (11:1, 11:3, 11:4, 11:25; sweep: 8 book-wide), while its second clause opens the appointment-naming that structures the rest of the unit. Two more named appointments follow: the Levite overseer — web:Neh.11.22 “The overseer also of the Levites at Jerusalem was Uzzi the son of Bani…” — Hebrew וּפְקִ֤יד הַלְוִיִּם֙ בִּיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם עֻזִּ֤י ("and overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem, Uzzi"), grounded by the ki-clause at v23, כִּֽי מִצְוַ֥ת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ עֲלֵיהֶ֑ם וַאֲמָנָ֥ה עַל הַמְשֹׁרְרִ֖ים ("for the king's command was upon them, and a provision for the singers") -- a subordinate ground, not a further appointee -- and the royal deputy, WEB "Pethahiah the son of Meshezabel...was at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people," Hebrew וּפְתַֽחְיָ֨ה בֶּן מְשֵֽׁיזַבְאֵ֜ל ("and Pethahiah son of Meshezabel") and לְיַ֣ד הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לְכָל דָּבָ֖ר לָעָֽם ("at the king's hand for every matter concerning the people"). These three named appointments (Ziha/Gishpa, Uzzi, Pethahiah) share a "named person(s) over/responsible-for X" pattern distinct from both the counted classes above and the village list that follows at WEB 11:25; grouping them keeps that shared administrative-notice function together rather than imposing a count-based class boundary the text does not supply for any of the three.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the Nethinim notice (11:21) from the Levite-overseer/singers/royal-deputy notices (11:22-24) at the petuchah (single-witness) that follows oshb:Neh.11.21 is a live option, since that mark does fall inside this row, and 11:21 is itself formally split (a residence clause continuing the register's dwelling thread, then a separate appointment clause); the absence of a head-count or fresh class-name at that point is not by itself decisive -- 11:20 was accepted as its own unit under the same absence -- but no literary-type shift separates the residence/appointment seam the way one separates 071 from its neighbors, so the four verses are kept together as one administrative appendix rather than pressed into a further split the content does not clearly demand.

boundary_rationale: WEB "As for the villages with their fields, some of the children of Judah lived in Kiriath Arba and its towns..." opens וְאֶל הַחֲצֵרִ֖ים בִּשְׂדֹתָ֑ם מִבְּנֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֗ה יָֽשְׁב֞וּ ("and as for the villages with their fields, some of the sons of Judah dwelt"), a fresh discourse unit (villages-with-fields, not Jerusalem residency) following the temple-personnel appointment notices at 11:21 through 11:24. It closes with its own summary, WEB "So they encamped from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom," Hebrew וַיַּחֲנ֥וּ מִבְּאֵֽר שֶׁ֖בַע עַד גֵּֽיא הִנֹּֽם ("and they encamped from Beersheba to the valley of Hinnom"), before the Benjamin village list opens fresh with its own named subject at 11:31.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running the Judah and Benjamin village lists together as one row loses the closing geographic summary that marks off Judah's villages specifically, and the fresh subject-headed opening ("the children of Benjamin also...") that begins the next tribe's list.

boundary_rationale: WEB "The children of Benjamin also lived from Geba onward, at Michmash and Aija..." opens וּבְנֵ֥י בִנְיָמִ֖ן מִגָּ֑בַע ("and sons of Benjamin from Geba"), naming a fresh tribal subject after Judah's closing summary at 11:25 through 11:30. The village-name chain runs through v.35, and the part closes with a short Levite note, WEB "Of the Levites, certain divisions in Judah settled in Benjamin's territory," Hebrew וּמִן הַלְוִיִּ֔ם מַחְלְק֥וֹת יְהוּדָ֖ה לְבִנְיָמִֽין ("and of the Levites, divisions of Judah [attached] to Benjamin"), marked by a petuchah (single-witness) at oshb:Neh.11.36. This closing note opens with the same u-min partitive used at the priests' (11:10, מִן הַֽכֹּהֲנִ֑ים) and Levites' (11:15, וּמִֽן הַלְוִיִּ֑ם) own class-headers -- one of this register's four opener families (ve'elleh, sweep: 4 book-wide; min-partitive, sweep: 5 book-wide; vav+definite-class-noun, 11:19/11:21/12:8; kol+class-noun, 11:18) -- so it is not device-bare. What keeps it with the Benjamin village list rather than as its own register is topical, not formulaic: unlike 11:10 and 11:15, where the identical partitive introduces a named roster, 11:36 is a single verbless clause naming no individual -- a one-verse appendix to the just-completed geography, not a new register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Giving the Levite note (11:36) its own row is a live alternative worth taking seriously, since 11:36 does carry a genuine class-header partitive, not a bare fragment; it is not adopted because the note names no individual and supplies no verb of dwelling, unlike every roster the same partitive elsewhere introduces (11:10, 11:15) -- it is one verse of trailing information, not a register in its own right.

boundary_rationale: Opens with the joint roll-call header וְאֵ֨לֶּה֙ הַכֹּהֲנִ֣ים וְהַלְוִיִּ֔ם (web:Neh.12.1; WEB “Now these are the priests and the Levites who went up with Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua”), which names both clergy classes but the roll that actually follows (1b-7a) names priests, not Levites. The unit is its own bracket: "elleh" opens v1 and returns at the close, אֵ֣לֶּה רָאשֵׁ֧י הַכֹּהֲנִ֛ים וַאֲחֵיהֶ֖ם בִּימֵ֥י יֵשֽׁוּעַ (web:Neh.12.7; WEB “These were the chiefs of the priests and of their brothers in the days of Jeshua.”). The Levites proper get their own header at v8 ("Moreover the Levites were"), so the priestly roll's elleh...elleh inclusio is the tighter edge, not the coarser "returnee clergy vv1-9" grouping.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 12.1-9 as one row conflates the priestly roll's own elleh...elleh inclusio with the Levites' separate class header at v8.

boundary_rationale: Verse 8 opens its own class header, וְהַלְוִיִּ֗ם יֵשׁ֧וּעַ בִּנּ֛וּי קַדְמִיאֵ֥ל (web:Neh.12.8; WEB "Moreover the Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel"), distinct from the priestly roll's own anaphoric closer at v7b, אֵ֣לֶּה רָאשֵׁ֧י הַכֹּהֲנִ֛ים ("these are the chiefs of the priests"), which restricts the preceding roll to priests. The two-verse entry closes at v9 with the antiphonal-arrangement term לְנֶגְדָּ֖ם (web:Neh.12.9; WEB "were close to them according to their offices"); the same watch-arrangement term recurs at 12:24 describing the Levite chiefs' arrangement (sweep: 2 book-wide: 12:9, 12:24), tying this entry forward to that later verse. MT 12:9 carries a ketiv/qere pair on the name Unni (וענו וְעֻנִּ֧י; WEB follows the ketiv, "Unno") -- disclosed here as the verse is quoted/spanned. A petuchah (PE, single-witness) falls at oshb:Neh.12.7, exactly the v7/v8 seam this entry opens on; per this book's Writings tier-3 policy it corroborates only weakly and never drives the boundary, but it is present, not absent as a prior description had it -- the seam rests primarily on the v7b closer and v8's fresh class-noun, with the mark as tier-3 corroboration for it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding vv8-9 back into a single 12.1-9 "returnee clergy" row erases the vehalevi'im class-header shift and the shared watch-arrangement vocabulary that ties this entry forward to 12:24.

boundary_rationale: A new genre marker opens the unit: the patronymic chain formula וְיֵשׁ֖וּעַ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת יֽוֹיָקִ֑ים (web:Neh.12.10; WEB “Jeshua became the father of Joiakim”) repeats holid et three more times across the two verses (four occurrences total: twice in v10, twice in v11), a begetting-chain syntax distinct from the roll-call apposition the surrounding rows use instead (vv1-9, 12-26 name officeholders without tracing descent). The third link, Elyashiv to Yoiada, elides the verb entirely (וְאֶלְיָשִׁ֖יב אֶת יוֹיָדָֽע, the bare object-marker standing for it) -- a gap that is itself part of the chain's formal texture, not a defect in the text. The chain runs exactly five links to its terminus, וְיוֹנָתָ֖ן הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת יַדּֽוּעַ (web:Neh.12.11; WEB “and Jonathan became the father of Jaddua”), after which v12 opens a fresh "in the days of PN" list format, supplying the closing edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging the succession chain into the surrounding rosters would blur a distinct genealogical form with the roll-call forms bracketing it on both sides.

boundary_rationale: Opens with וּבִימֵי֙ יֽוֹיָקִ֔ים הָי֥וּ כֹהֲנִ֖ים רָאשֵׁ֣י הָאָב֑וֹת (web:Neh.12.12; WEB “In the days of Joiakim were priests, heads of fathers' households”), a generation-marker header that answers v7's closing "bimey...Yeshua" with the next reign. The list restates the Jeshua-era roll of 12:1b-7a (22 names once v1b's three -- שְׂרָיָ֥ה יִרְמְיָ֖ה עֶזְרָֽא (Seraiah, Jeremiah, Ezra) -- are counted; vv2-7 alone hold 19) as 21 lamed-headed courses here (counting each ketiv/qere doublet once -- 12:14 למלוכי לִמְלִ֨יכוּ֙, 12:16 לעדיא לְעִדּ֥וֹא -- the token count is 23, the course count 21), matching the earlier roll name-for-name in sequence with eight orthographic variants (e.g. 12:2's מַלּ֖וּךְ answered by 12:14's לִמְלִ֨יכוּ֙) and חַטּֽוּשׁ (Hattush) at 12:2 alone unmatched under that standard, now paired with each course's head under Joiakim (a lamed-prefixed correlation, e.g. 13 "of Ezra, Meshullam"; though לְמִ֨נְיָמִ֔ין לְמוֹעַדְיָ֖ה פִּלְטָֽי at v17 leaves Miniamin with no head paired to it, Piltai pairing instead with the following Moadiah), a format distinct from both the plain roll of 1-7 and the begetting-chain of 10-11. It runs through v21, since v22 opens a THIRD generation-marker header ("the Levites, in the days of Eliashib..."), which supplies the closing edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 12.1-26 as one long clergy-list row would erase the three-generation bimey-PN header sequence (Jeshua / Joiakim / Eliashib) that actually structures the section.

boundary_rationale: Opens the third generation-marker, הַלְוִיִּם֩ בִּימֵ֨י אֶלְיָשִׁ֜יב (web:Neh.12.22; WEB “As for the Levites, in the days of Eliashib”) -- naming, across the verse, four names -- Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, Jaddua -- that continue the succession chain at 12:10-11 through its generations three to six on the identification of v22's יוֹחָנָן֙ (Johanan) with the chain's fifth link, 12:11's יוֹנָתָ֔ן (Jonathan) -- and immediately shifts register voice from roster-listing to archival citation: v23 names its own written source, כְּתוּבִ֕ים עַל סֵ֖פֶר דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֑ים (web:Neh.12.23; WEB “were written in the book of the chronicles”), a source-citation formula absent from 1-21. The same verse's own interior terminus, וְעַד יְמֵ֖י יֽוֹחָנָ֥ן בֶּן אֶלְיָשִֽׁיב (WEB “even until the days of Johanan the son of Eliashib”), dates the archive one generation short of v22's own list (which continues through Jaddua) -- an interior marker, not itself a bracket edge, that fixes the citation's own historical horizon distinct from either v22's opening or v26's closing colophon. The note closes not with an inclusio answering v22 but with a colophon reaching back across the whole clergy-lists section: אֵ֕לֶּה בִּימֵ֛י יוֹיָקִ֥ים בֶּן יֵשׁ֖וּעַ בֶּן יוֹצָדָ֑ק וּבִימֵי֙ נְחֶמְיָ֣ה הַפֶּחָ֔ה וְעֶזְרָ֥א הַכֹּהֵ֖ן הַסּוֹפֵֽר (web:Neh.12.26; WEB “These were in the days of Joiakim the son of Jeshua, the son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor, and of Ezra the priest and scribe”) names Joiakim, generation two -- the same Joiakim heading the courses header at 12:12 -- an earlier generation than v22's own opening, anchoring the whole clergy-lists section running from 12:1 forward -- not just this unit -- to the book's two protagonists just before the dedication opens. The pe (single-witness) keyed to 12:22 (a mark follows the verse it keys) falls between v22 and v23, interior to this span, not at its opening edge; the pe (single-witness) at v26 alone marks the section's actual close -- weak corroboration, not a driver.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 22-26 as a mere coda to 12.12-21 misses the archival source-citation shift at v23, which changes register voice rather than simply continuing the priestly-courses list.

boundary_rationale: Opens with the dedication frame וּבַחֲנֻכַּ֞ת חוֹמַ֣ת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֗ם בִּקְשׁ֤וּ אֶת הַלְוִיִּם֙ (web:Neh.12.27; WEB “At the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, they sought the Levites”), third person throughout the summons (27-29) and purification (30). It closes at וַיִּֽטַּהֲר֔וּ הַכֹּהֲנִ֖ים וְהַלְוִיִּ֑ם וַֽיְטַהֲרוּ֙ אֶת הָעָ֔ם וְאֶת הַשְּׁעָרִ֖ים וְאֶֽת הַחוֹמָֽה (web:Neh.12.30; WEB “The priests and the Levites purified themselves; and they purified the people, the gates, and the wall”), the closing third-person clause of the summons before the memoir "I" resumes at v31. The edge is a person-shift, not a topic change: v31 continues the very same dedication event but switches into Nehemiah's own voice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running 27-30 straight into the procession as one 12.27-43 row obscures the third-person-to-memoir-voice seam that the text itself marks at v31.

boundary_rationale: Opens on a 3mp-to-1cs person shift against an unbroken wayyiqtol chain: 12:30's וַיִּֽטַּהֲר֔וּ and 12:31's וָאַעֲלֶה֙ אֶת שָׂרֵ֣י יְהוּדָ֔ה מֵעַ֖ל לַחוֹמָ֑ה וָאַעֲמִ֡ידָה שְׁתֵּ֣י תוֹדֹת֩ גְּדוֹלֹ֨ת (web:Neh.12.31; WEB “Then I brought the princes of Judah up on the wall, and appointed two great companies”) carry straight through with no disjunctive waw, no date frame, and no new location -- the person shift alone marks the change here, setting Nehemiah's own action apart from the communal purification notice just closed. The memoir "I" recedes again through 12:32-37 (Hoshaiah's company roster given entirely in third person, no 1cs form) and resumes at 12:38's וַאֲנִ֣י אַחֲרֶ֑יהָ; that inset functions as a named-roster register, parallel to the ch.3/ch.7 conventions, traveling inside the single procession list v31 opens and v40 closes, so its own internal recession of "I" does not itself divide the scene. The two-company procession is bracketed by its own inclusio: "two great companies" here is answered at וַֽתַּעֲמֹ֛דְנָה שְׁתֵּ֥י הַתּוֹדֹ֖ת בְּבֵ֣ית הָאֱלֹהִ֑ים (web:Neh.12.40; WEB “So the two companies of those who gave thanks in God's house stood”), which reunites both processions under the same numeral phrase named at the outset; the trumpeting priests and singers of 41-42 belong to that same convergence scene, and the unit closes on the celebration's own cadence, וַתִּשָּׁמַ֛ע שִׂמְחַ֥ת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֖ם מֵרָחֽוֹק (web:Neh.12.43; WEB “so that the joy of Jerusalem was heard even far away”). No mark falls at this edge; a samekh (single-witness) keyed to 12:34 falls interior to the roster inset (32-37), a roster-internal mark of the ch.3/ch.7 class, not a boundary signal.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Two rivals press against this edge. The stronger is upward attachment to the dedication complex opened at 12:27's וּבַחֲנֻכַּ֞ת חוֹמַ֣ת יְרוּשָׁלִַ֗ם: 12:27-30 runs unbroken third person, so the shift to "I" really is new at 12:31, and neither the wayyiqtol chain nor the dedication frame breaks there; but a topical header naming an occasion is not a lexically closed bracket the way a repeated numeral phrase is, so it does not bind across an interior person shift -- here it is the person shift alone that marks the change, without any accompanying date, disjunctive, or locative change. The weaker rival, splitting at 12:38, targets the wrong signal: v38 reads וְהַתּוֹדָ֧ה הַשֵּׁנִ֛ית, an ordinal-singular "the second [company]," not a fresh two-choir reference, and a split there would still cut through the very "two companies...two companies" bracket binding v31 to v40 -- though v38 is where that inclusio argument is tested hardest, since a genuine person-shift return (va'ani achareha) sits there too, after the third-person roster inset of 32-37; there it is the lexically closed bracket, not the person-shift return, that keeps 31-43 one scene, because that closed bracket -- unlike the dedication header at 12:27 -- is the kind of signal that binds across an interior change.

boundary_rationale: Opens וַיִּפָּקְד֣וּ בַיּוֹם֩ הַה֨וּא אֲנָשִׁ֜ים עַל הַנְּשָׁכ֗וֹת לָא֨וֹצָר֥וֹת (web:Neh.12.44; WEB “On that day, men were appointed over the rooms for the treasures”), the second of three bayom hahu frames in the book (12:43, 12:44, 13:1; sweep: 3 book-wide). 12:43 and 12:44 stand adjacent, but the third, at 13:1, is separated from 12:44 by the intervening 12:45-47 notice, so the three span six verse positions, not three consecutive verses. The topic change does not rest on that adjacency or on word order -- 12:43's וַיִּזְבְּח֣וּ בַיּוֹם הַ֠הוּא and 12:44's וַיִּפָּקְד֣וּ בַיּוֹם֩ הַה֨וּא both place the verb before the frame -- but on verb class and subject: 12:44's niphal וַיִּפָּקְד֣וּ introduces an indefinite new participant set, אֲנָשִׁ֜ים, where 12:43 continues the sacrificial wayyiqtol chain of the same celebrants already in view, a genuine shift from dedication-day sacrifice to treasury-room administration, and a different scene again from 13:1's later Torah-reading notice. The unit runs to v47's Zerubbabel-to-Nehemiah summary of singer and gatekeeper portions, closing before 13:1 reopens its own bayom hahu for a different scene. A pe follows Neh.12.47 (single-witness).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging 44-47 into the dedication on the strength of the shared bayom hahu wording would treat a recurring temporal frame as if it necessarily signals continuation, when here the verb class and subject shift -- niphal plus indefinite אֲנָשִׁ֜ים -- mark a change to cultic administration regardless of the frame's adjacency to 12:43.

boundary_rationale: Opens with בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא נִקְרָ֛א בְּסֵ֥פֶר מֹשֶׁ֖ה בְּאָזְנֵ֣י הָעָ֑ם (web:Neh.13.1; WEB “On that day they read in the book of Moses in the hearing of the people”), the third of three bayom hahu tokens in the book (12:43, 12:44, 13:1; sweep: 3 book-wide). 12:44 and 13:1 are not in tight succession -- the 12:45-47 notice intervenes -- so the topic-change reading rests on the register shift itself, not on adjacency: 13:1's impersonal niphal נִקְרָ֛א opening a public Torah-reading scene is a different scene type from 12:44-47's appointment notice. It closes with the vayehi kishmoa hinge וַיְהִ֖י כְּשָׁמְעָ֣ם אֶת הַתּוֹרָ֑ה וַיַּבְדִּ֥ילוּ כָל עֵ֖רֶב מִיִּשְׂרָאֵֽל (web:Neh.13.3; WEB “It came to pass, when they had heard the law, that they separated all the mixed multitude from Israel”), the same hearing-response frame that opens the book at 1:4 (sweep: 2 book-wide for vayehi+keshom-), here closing rather than opening a unit. Verse 13:4 then shifts register to a "before this" flashback (lifney mizzeh), a retrospective clause distinct from the bayom hahu frame just used.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Grouping 13.1-3 with 13.4-9 under one "Eliashib reforms" heading would merge a completed Torah-reading episode, closed by vayehi kishmoa, with a new "before this" flashback that explicitly reaches back in time.

boundary_rationale: Opens with a backward-looking frame, וְלִפְנֵ֣י מִזֶּ֔ה אֶלְיָשִׁיב֙ הַכֹּהֵ֔ן נָת֖וּן בְּלִשְׁכַּ֣ת בֵּית אֱלֹהֵ֑ינוּ (web:Neh.13.4; WEB “Now before this, Eliashib the priest, who was appointed over the rooms of the house of our God”), told in third person about Eliashib's misdeed (4-5). The memoir "I" does not resume until v6, to explain why Nehemiah had not known, וּבְכָל זֶ֕ה לֹ֥א הָיִ֖יתִי בִּֽירוּשָׁלִָ֑ם כִּ֡י בִּשְׁנַת֩ שְׁלֹשִׁ֨ים וּשְׁתַּ֜יִם לְאַרְתַּחְשַׁ֤סְתְּא מֶֽלֶךְ בָּבֶל֙ (web:Neh.13.6; WEB “But in all this, I was not at Jerusalem; for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon”), a dated parenthesis that explains rather than interrupts the "before this... I threw out... I commanded" action chain -- v8's grief-driven expulsion, וַיֵּ֥רַֽע לִ֖י מְאֹ֑ד וָֽאַשְׁלִ֜יכָה אֶֽת כָּל כְּלֵ֧י בֵית טוֹבִיָּ֛ה הַח֖וּץ מִן הַלִּשְׁכָּֽה (web:Neh.13.8; WEB “It grieved me severely. Therefore I threw all Tobiah's household stuff out of the room”) -- running to its close at וָאֹ֣מְרָ֔ה וַֽיְטַהֲר֖וּ הַלְּשָׁכ֑וֹת (web:Neh.13.9; WEB “Then I commanded, and they cleansed the rooms”). A pe follows Neh.13.9 (single-witness), coinciding with this close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating the thirty-second-year note (6-7a) as its own row would sever the "I was absent, therefore I did not know, so when I returned I acted" causal chain the episode depends on.

boundary_rationale: Opens on a new perception-verb hinge, וָאֵ֣דְעָ֔ה כִּֽי מְנָי֥וֹת הַלְוִיִּ֖ם לֹ֣א נִתָּ֑נָה (web:Neh.13.10; WEB “I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them”), moving from the finished chamber-cleansing to a fresh grievance. The treasurer appointment at v13, וְעַל יָדָ֔ם חָנָ֥ן (web:Neh.13.13; WEB “and next to them was Hanan”), uses "ve-al yadam" of Hanan's subordinate rank among the treasurers, not the chapter-3 wall-register connective of the same wording -- disambiguated here so the phrase is not mistaken for that device. The unit closes with זָכְרָה לִּ֥י אֱלֹהַ֖י עַל זֹ֑את (web:Neh.13.14; WEB “Remember me, my God, concerning this”), the second of four zokrah-li elohai closers in the book (sweep: 4 book-wide for zokrah-li; 6 book-wide for the refrain overall), echoing the first instance at 5:19.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through 13:22 as one long "Levite reforms" row would merge two structurally distinct episodes that each open on their own hinge and close on their own zokrah.

boundary_rationale: Opens with בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֡מָּה רָאִ֣יתִי בִֽיהוּדָ֣ה דֹּֽרְכִֽים גִּתּ֣וֹת בַּשַּׁבָּ֡ת (web:Neh.13.15; WEB “In those days I saw some men treading wine presses on the Sabbath in Judah”), the book's only bayamim hahemmah form (sweep: 1 book-wide, distinct from the two bayamim hahem instances at 6:17 and 13:23). The internal vayehi ka'asher beat at v19 (gate-closing enforcement) is one of eight book-wide members of that frame family (WEB 4:1, 4:7, 4:12, 4:15, 6:1, 6:16, 7:1, 13:19): members of this frame family do different work -- three open opposition-hearing episodes (WEB 4:1, 4:7, 6:1), two resolve an episode already opened (WEB 4:15, 6:16), WEB 4:12 is argued locally from its own text, and WEB 7:1 opens its own episode. This member, 13:19, is argued the same way, from its own clause: its apodosis continues the same 1cs subject unbroken from v15, and its protasis subject is inanimate, כַּאֲשֶׁ֣ר צָֽלֲלוּ֩ שַׁעֲרֵ֨י יְרוּשָׁלִַ֜ם, patterning with 7:1's own נִבְנְתָה֙ הַחוֹמָ֔ה rather than with the six members whose protases report an outside party hearing or arriving -- so here the frame escalates a reform already running rather than opening a fresh row-level unit. A pe (single-witness) keyed to 13:18 falls at the v18/v19 seam this row's rejected alternative litigates -- weak corroboration for a split there that the unbroken 1cs subject across the seam outweighs. A samekh (single-witness) keyed to 13:21 sits interior to the unit; a pe (single-witness) keyed to 13:22 falls at this unit's own closing edge -- weak, tier-3 corroboration for the boundary already established on other grounds. The unit closes on גַּם זֹאת֙ זָכְרָה לִּ֣י אֱלֹהַ֔י וְח֥וּסָה עָלַ֖י כְּרֹ֥ב חַסְדֶּֽךָ (web:Neh.13.22; WEB “Remember me for this also, my God, and spare me according to the greatness of your loving kindness”), the third zokrah-li closer.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at v19 would rest on its shared family membership with the other vayehi-ka'asher clauses, but membership in that frame family does not by itself decide function here: v19's apodosis keeps the same 1cs subject running from v15 and its protasis subject is inanimate, so a split would sever that continuity to credit a family label the clause's own grammar does not support.

boundary_rationale: Opens גַּ֣ם בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֗ם רָאִ֤יתִי אֶת הַיְּהוּדִים֙ הֹשִׁ֗יבוּ נָשִׁים֙ אשדודיות אַשְׁדֳּדִיּ֔וֹת עמוניות עַמֳּנִיּ֖וֹת מוֹאֲבִיּֽוֹת (web:Neh.13.23; WEB “In those days I also saw the Jews who had married women of Ashdod, of Ammon, and of Moab”), the second of two bayamim hahem instances (the earlier one is the Tobiah-letters notice at 6:17); the quote above carries both of this verse's ketiv/qere pairs (the unpointed ketiv spellings immediately followed by their pointed qere for the Ashdodite and Ammonite ethnonyms), disclosed here since the quoted span includes them. The unit closes on זָכְרָ֥ה לָהֶ֖ם אֱלֹהָ֑י עַ֚ל גָּאֳלֵ֣י הַכְּהֻנָּ֔ה וּבְרִ֥ית הַכְּהֻנָּ֖ה וְהַלְוִיִּֽם (web:Neh.13.29; WEB “Remember them, my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and of the Levites”), a hostile zokrah-lahem form (sweep: 1 book-wide) -- the book's only other hostile zokrah besides 6:14's zokrah-elohai-le- form -- a different sub-form from the favorable zokrah-li closers at 13:14, 13:22, and 13:31.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running 13:23-31 together as one unit would blur the hostile zokrah-lahem closer that ends the marriages episode with the favorable zokrah-li that ends the closing summary in 30-31.

boundary_rationale: Opens with a summary-register shift back to administrative action, וְטִֽהַרְתִּ֖ים מִכָּל נֵכָ֑ר וָאַעֲמִ֧ידָה מִשְׁמָר֛וֹת לַכֹּהֲנִ֥ים וְלַלְוִיִּ֖ם אִ֥ישׁ בִּמְלַאכְתּֽוֹ (web:Neh.13.30; WEB “Thus I cleansed them from all foreigners and appointed duties for the priests and for the Levites, everyone in his work”), which recaps rather than continues the preceding episode's specific quarrel (cursing, hair-plucking, oaths). It closes the whole book on זָכְרָה לִּ֥י אֱלֹהַ֖י לְטוֹבָֽה (web:Neh.13.31; WEB “Remember me, my God, for good.”), the last of six zokrah instances (sweep: 6 book-wide). This exact clause, zokhrah-li-elohai-le-tovah, stands twice in the book (sweep: 2 book-wide for the full refrain clause; a third le-tovah hit at 2:18 takes the unrelated preposition la-tovah outside the refrain): at 5:19 it opens the verse that closes the governor's-allowance aside, זָכְרָה לִּ֥י אֱלֹהַ֖י לְטוֹבָ֑ה כֹּ֥ל אֲשֶׁר עָשִׂ֖יתִי עַל הָעָ֥ם הַזֶּֽה, and at 13:31 it closes the book's own final verse -- the shared clause, not a shared verse-position, brackets the whole back half of the memoir from the economic-reform aside to the book's own final verse. That verbatim reprise, not a new coinage, gives 13:31 the memoir's final word.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 30-31 to the marriages episode as its tail would merge the hostile zokrah-lahem close of that reform with the book's own distinct final-word zokrah, missing the summary-register shift at v30.

boundary_rationale: The book opens with the verse-initial formula וַיְהִ֖י בִּימֵ֣י אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ “Now in the days of Ahasuerus” web:Esth.1.1, an opening formula occurring nowhere else in the book (sweep: 1 book-wide as a verse-initial opener), paired with the merism מֵהֹ֣דּוּ וְעַד כּ֔וּשׁ “from India even to Ethiopia” web:Esth.1.1 that sets the empire’s scope (sweep: 2 book-wide; the same merism recurs once more, at 8:9, framing the edict and its counter-edict). After the throne-and-Susa setting in 1:2, a fresh regnal-year clause בִּשְׁנַ֤ת שָׁלוֹשׁ֙ לְמָלְכ֔וֹ “in the third year of his reign” web:Esth.1.3 launches the nobles’ banquet, which the unit closes out with its own duration notice יָמִ֣ים רַבִּ֔ים שְׁמוֹנִ֥ים וּמְאַ֖ת יֽוֹם “many days, even one hundred eighty days” web:Esth.1.4, before a second transition formula opens the next unit at 1:5.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 1:1-2 as a self-contained unit would strand the royal formula from the very banquet it exists to introduce.

boundary_rationale: A new temporal-transition clause וּבִמְל֣וֹאת הַיָּמִ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה “When these days were fulfilled” web:Esth.1.5 marks a distinct banquet from the one just closed, this one for all the people of Susa, carrying its own wine-protocol note through 1:8. The particle in גַּ֚ם וַשְׁתִּ֣י הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה עָשְׂתָ֖ה מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה נָשִׁ֑ים “Also Vashti the queen made a feast for the women” web:Esth.1.9 signals a parallel banquet rather than a subordinate clause and opens no direct-speech frame of its own, so under the banquet-unit default this verse stays inside the span rather than splitting off; the SAMEKH mark follows 1:9 (oshb:Esth.1.9 (setumah, single-witness)), corroborating the close of the unit at exactly this point.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Peeling 1:9 into its own decision would fragment a banquet pairing that no speech frame interrupts.
literature_type_guess: banquet-scene (paired feast and parallel women's feast)

boundary_rationale: A new day-marker בַּיּוֹם֙ הַשְּׁבִיעִ֔י כְּט֥וֹב לֵב הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ בַּיָּ֑יִן “On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine” web:Esth.1.10 opens the crisis: the summons, then the refusal וַתְּמָאֵ֞ן הַמַּלְכָּ֣ה וַשְׁתִּ֗י לָבוֹא֙ “But the queen Vashti refused to come” web:Esth.1.12, closing on the king's wrath in an offline terminal clause, וַחֲמָת֖וֹ בָּעֲרָ֥ה בֽוֹ “and his anger burned in him” web:Esth.1.12; a fresh wayyiqtol then opens 1:13 with a new addressee, וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ לַחֲכָמִ֖ים יֹדְעֵ֣י הָֽעִתִּ֑ים “Then the king said to the wise men, who knew the times” web:Esth.1.13, but the king's actual question to them is deferred rather than posed at once: 1:13 goes on to name their standing before all יֹדְעֵ֖י דָּ֥ת וָדִֽין “who knew law and judgment” web:Esth.1.13, and 1:14 lists the seven Persian-and-Median princes, before the quoted question כְּדָת֙ מַֽה לַּעֲשׂ֔וֹת בַּמַּלְכָּ֖ה וַשְׁתִּ֑י “What shall we do to Queen Vashti according to law” web:Esth.1.15 finally closes the consultation, before Memucan's answer opens a new speech frame at 1:16. This deferred-question arc — addressee named at 1:13, expertise and personnel specified through 1:14, question posed only at 1:15 — runs as one continuous consultation scene across the 1:12|1:13 clause-type shift rather than splitting there.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting a seam at 1:12|1:13 would divide the deferred-question arc at the point where the addressee is first named but before the king's actual question is posed, three verses later at 1:15.

boundary_rationale: A new speech-formula וַיֹּ֣אמֶר מומכן מְמוּכָ֗ן לִפְנֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְהַשָּׂרִ֔ים “Memucan answered before the king and the princes” web:Esth.1.16 opens Memucan’s direct speech, which runs uninterrupted through the petition-formula recommendation אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֗וֹב יֵצֵ֤א דְבַר מַלְכוּת֙ מִלְּפָנָ֔יו “If it pleases the king, let a royal commandment go from him” web:Esth.1.19 (petition formula, sweep: 7 book-wide: 1:19, 3:9, 5:4, 5:8, 7:3, 8:5, 9:13) to the closing rationale about husbands’ honor in 1:20; the return to third-person narration at 1:21 marks the end of the quoted speech and the start of the next unit. Ketiv/qere note: the ketiv מומכן and qere מְמוּכָ֗ן share the same five consonants (mem, mem, vav, kaf, final-nun) with the vav transposed — second position in the ketiv, third in the qere — not a defective/plene difference; disclosed here because 1:16 is quoted.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 1:16-20 into the implementation notice at 1:21-22 would blur the seam between quoted speech and the narration that closes it.

boundary_rationale: Narration resumes with וַיִּיטַב֙ הַדָּבָ֔ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ וְהַשָּׂרִ֑ים “This advice pleased the king and the princes” web:Esth.1.21, a decision-approval formula that closes the quoted-speech unit and opens the implementation, culminating in the dispatch formula וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח סְפָרִים֙ אֶל כָּל מְדִינ֣וֹת הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ “for he sent letters into all the king’s provinces” web:Esth.1.22, each province and people addressed מְדִינָ֤ה וּמְדִינָה֙ כִּכְתָבָ֔הּ וְאֶל עַ֥ם וָעָ֖ם כִּלְשׁוֹנ֑וֹ “every province according to its writing, and to every people in their language” web:Esth.1.22, the same distributive formula core כִּכְתָבָ֔הּ (sweep: 3 verses book-wide: 1:22, 3:12, 8:9) that reappears at the edict (3:12) and the counter-edict (8:9) — not at the edict's own dispatch notice in 3:13, which carries no distributive element at all — together with the doubled distributive מְדִינָ֤ה וּמְדִינָה֙ (sweep: 8 verses book-wide: 1:22, 3:12, 3:14, 4:3, 8:9, 8:13, 8:17, 9:28), also present at both 3:12 and 8:9. The PE mark follows 1:22 (oshb:Esth.1.22 (petuchah, single-witness)), corroborating the chapter-close here.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit back into Memucan's speech would erase the narration-versus-quoted-speech seam at 1:20|1:21.

boundary_rationale: אַחַר֙ הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה כְּשֹׁ֕ךְ חֲמַ֖ת הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ “After these things, when the wrath of King Ahasuerus was pacified” web:Esth.2.1 opens a new temporal frame with the king’s private reflection on Vashti (byte sweep: 1 book-wide for this exact pointed clause; skeleton sweep: 2 book-wide — 2:1 and 3:1 differ only in accentuation on this opener, and 3:1 alone opens Haman’s rise — an intentional parallel opening both major escalations of the book), which the king’s own servants answer with a proposal-speech וַיֹּאמְר֥וּ נַעֲרֵֽי הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ מְשָׁרְתָ֑יו “Then the king’s servants who served him said” web:Esth.2.2, running through royal approval וַיִּיטַ֧ב הַדָּבָ֛ר בְּעֵינֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ וַיַּ֥עַשׂ כֵּֽן “The thing pleased the king, and he did so” web:Esth.2.4. The SAMEKH mark follows 2:4 (oshb:Esth.2.4 (setumah, single-witness)), closing this unit at the royal-approval formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 2:1 to the end of chapter 1 would ignore the fresh temporal formula that restarts the narrative clock.

boundary_rationale: The character-introduction formula אִ֣ישׁ יְהוּדִ֔י הָיָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֑ה “There was a certain Jew in the citadel of Susa” web:Esth.2.5 (sweep: 1 book-wide, occurring nowhere else) opens named-participant background for Mordecai and, by extension, וַיְהִ֨י אֹמֵ֜ן אֶת הֲדַסָּ֗ה הִ֤יא אֶסְתֵּר֙ “He brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther” web:Esth.2.7, his adopted cousin — a shift from the preceding unit's unnamed royal officials and general proposal-and-execution sequence (2:1-4) to the two individuals the rest of the book follows. This is a participant-introduction seam rather than a clause-type one: 2:1 itself opens with a fronted adjunct before its own qatal main verb, אַחַר֙ הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֔לֶּה כְּשֹׁ֕ךְ חֲמַ֖ת הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ זָכַ֤ר “After these things, when the wrath of King Ahasuerus was pacified, he remembered” web:Esth.2.1, and 2:3's proposal is a volitive weyiqtol inside quoted speech, וְיַפְקֵ֨ד הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ “Let the king appoint” web:Esth.2.3, not narrative wayyiqtol — while 2:7 itself opens with its own wayyiqtol, so grammatical mood alone does not separate 2:1-4 from 2:5-7. The background note on Mordecai and Esther ends before the plot resumes with a fresh participant return in 2:8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 2:5-7 as a continuation of the courtiers' proposal would merge a stative background note into the wayyiqtol action sequence it does not belong to.

boundary_rationale: 2:8 reopens the scene of 2:3 through a cluster of verbal and locational echoes rather than a decree-language echo: the Susa-citadel setting אֶל שׁוּשַׁ֤ן web:Esth.2.3 recurs at אֶל שׁוּשַׁ֥ן web:Esth.2.8 (sweep: 2 book-wide: 2:3, 2:8), the custody construction אֶל יַ֥ד web:Esth.2.3 recurs at אֶל יַ֣ד web:Esth.2.8 (sweep: 3 book-wide: 2:3, 2:8, 2:14), the gathering root recurs in causative form (swept per attested spelling: וְיִקְבְּצ֣וּ “gather together” web:Esth.2.3, sweep: 1 book-wide, 2:3; וּֽבְהִקָּבֵ֞ץ “gathered together” web:Esth.2.8, sweep: 2 book-wide: 2:8, 2:19), and the custodian's name recurs alef-final הֵגֶ֛א at 2:3 and yod-final הֵגָ֑י at 2:8 — together marking the return to plot action after the character background of 2:5-7. The resumptive formula itself, וַיְהִ֗י בְּהִשָּׁמַ֤ע דְּבַר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ וְדָת֔וֹ “So, when the king's commandment and his decree was heard” web:Esth.2.8, carries the chapter's first dat (“decree”) token at form level (form-level dat sweep restricted to chapter 2 — optional prefix plus dat plus optional suffix: 2 verses, 2:8 and 2:12 — none earlier; a bare consonantal-string sweep over the same range reaches 4 by admitting the substring trap at 2:10 (מֽוֹלַדְתָּ֑הּ, already quoted above) and web:Esth.2.20 (מַגֶּ֤דֶת מֽוֹלַדְתָּהּ֙), both unrelated roots, not the dat noun); the noun is absent from 2:3, which uses the unrelated root paqad (“appoint”) instead. It opens the account of Esther's favor with Hegai, the concealment notice לֹא הִגִּ֣ידָה אֶסְתֵּ֔ר אֶת עַמָּ֖הּ וְאֶת מֽוֹלַדְתָּ֑הּ “Esther had not made known her people nor her relatives” web:Esth.2.10, and Mordecai's daily-vigil notice וּבְכָל י֣וֹם וָי֔וֹם מָרְדֳּכַי֙ מִתְהַלֵּ֔ךְ “Mordecai walked every day” web:Esth.2.11, which closes before the general ritual-procedure description opens at 2:12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this span with the character introduction in 2:5-7 would collapse the stative-to-wayyiqtol seam marking the plot's resumption.

boundary_rationale: וּבְהַגִּ֡יעַ תֹּר֩ נַעֲרָ֨ה וְנַעֲרָ֜ה “Each young woman’s turn came” web:Esth.2.12 (turn-formula; the full four-word clause sweeps 1 book-wide at byte tier, occurring nowhere else pointed identically; its two-word opener וּבְהַגִּ֡יעַ תֹּר֩ sweeps 2 book-wide at the skeleton/consonantal tier, recurring only at 2:15 with different accentuation) opens a generalized, iterative description of the maidens’ purification cycle and nightly protocol, unattached to any named individual, running through the general rule לֹא תָב֥וֹא עוֹד֙ אֶל הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ כִּ֣י אִם חָפֵ֥ץ בָּ֛הּ הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ “She came in to the king no more, unless the king delighted in her” web:Esth.2.14; the same two-word opener recurs at the consonantal tier in 2:15 but there attached to Esther by name, marking the seam between the general rule and its specific application to her.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this general description into Esther's specific turn at 2:15 would erase the formula-echo that distinguishes rule from instance.

boundary_rationale: וּבְהַגִּ֣יעַ תֹּר אֶסְתֵּ֣ר בַּת “Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter” web:Esth.2.15 reapplies the 2:12 turn-formula by name, opening Esther’s specific path to the crown, through the king’s love-notice וַיֶּאֱהַ֨ב הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֶת אֶסְתֵּר֙ מִכָּל הַנָּשִׁ֔ים “The king loved Esther more than all the women” web:Esth.2.17 and her coronation, to the double banquet notice מִשְׁתֶּ֣ה גָד֗וֹל לְכָל שָׂרָיו֙ וַעֲבָדָ֔יו אֵ֖ת מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה אֶסְתֵּ֑ר “a great feast for all his princes and his servants, even Esther’s feast” web:Esth.2.18, which alone among the mishteh-bearing verses carries two tokens of the mishteh string in one verse (form-level count, he-final, excluding the hishtaphel verb and the name Parmashta: sweep: 19 verses / 20 tokens book-wide; 2:18 is the sole verse with 2 tokens, all others carrying 1), before the seam to the obscure second-gathering notice at 2:19.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 2:15-16 and 2:17-18 as separate decisions would split one turn-to-coronation-to-feast sequence at no textual seam.

boundary_rationale: This span covers a genuinely low-confidence seam: the second-gathering notice וּבְהִקָּבֵ֥ץ בְּתוּל֖וֹת שֵׁנִ֑ית “When the virgins were gathered together the second time” web:Esth.2.19 has no clear antecedent once Esther's coronation already closed the gathering process in 2:16-18, and the 2:18|2:19 seam carries no tier-1 opener on its face. Two clauses report Mordecai at the gate — verse-final at 2:19, וּמָרְדֳּכַ֖י יֹשֵׁ֥ב בְּשַֽׁעַר הַמֶּֽלֶךְ “Mordecai was sitting in the king's gate” web:Esth.2.19, and verse-medial, immediately opening the resumed narration after the time formula at 2:21, וּמָרְדֳּכַ֖י יֹשֵׁ֣ב בְּשַֽׁעַר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ “while Mordecai was sitting in the king's gate” web:Esth.2.21 (the defective, vav-prefixed form of this clause sweeps 2 book-wide, at exactly 2:19 and 2:21; a plene-spelled participle predication of Mordecai at the gate recurs separately (sweep: 2 book-wide, 5:13 and 6:10) — יוֹשֵׁ֖ב בְּשַׁ֥עַר הַמֶּֽלֶךְ at 5:13 and הַיּוֹשֵׁ֖ב בְּשַׁ֣עַר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ at 6:10 — and is not part of this count). Read on its own, this resumptive repetition signals continuity — a frame clause interrupted by 2:20's concealment reminder אֵ֣ין אֶסְתֵּ֗ר מַגֶּ֤דֶת מֽוֹלַדְתָּהּ֙ “Esther had not yet made known her relatives” web:Esth.2.20 and then resumed — and by itself would argue for binding 2:19 through 2:21 into one continuous unit with 2:20 as a parenthetical aside, not for a boundary at the second occurrence. The seam at 2:20|2:21 instead rests on a different, genuinely tier-1 signal: the verse-initial time formula בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם “In those days” web:Esth.2.21 (sweep: 2 book-wide — 1:2, 2:21 — the only other instance being the exposition notice at 1:2), which marks 2:21 as opening fresh narrated material rather than merely resuming 2:19's frame. The SAMEKH mark follows 2:20 (oshb:Esth.2.20 (setumah, single-witness)), landing exactly at that seam as tier-3 corroboration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 2:19 backward to Esther's feast in 2:18 is equally arguable from the text alone and cannot be ruled out on tier-1 grounds.

boundary_rationale: The verse-initial time formula בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם “In those days” web:Esth.2.21 (sweep: 2 book-wide, the only other instance being the exposition notice at 1:2) opens fresh narrated material at 2:21, driving this span's opening boundary; the gate-clause report that follows it in the same verse, וּמָרְדֳּכַ֖י יֹשֵׁ֣ב בְּשַֽׁעַר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ “while Mordecai was sitting in the king's gate” web:Esth.2.21, is verse-medial here — an opener for the resumed narration, in contrast to its verse-final, closing position in 2:19 — and, read as a resumptive repetition with 2:19 alone, signals continuity across 2:20's parenthetical rather than driving a boundary at its own second occurrence; the boundary itself rests on the time formula, not on the repetition. Together they introduce the Bigthan-Teresh plot, which runs through the discovery-and-report chain to Mordecai, Esther, and the king (2:22) and closes with the chronicle-recording formula וַיִּכָּתֵ֗ב בְּסֵ֛פֶר דִּבְרֵ֥י הַיָּמִ֖ים לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ “it was written in the book of the chronicles in the king's presence” web:Esth.2.23 (this full clause sweeps 1 verse book-wide, 2:23 alone; the shorter, unprefixed phrase as it appears at 10:2, סֵ֨פֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֔ים, sweeps 2 verses book-wide — 2:23, 10:2 — and the wider chronicle-phrase object, admitting 6:1's expanded form, sweeps 3 verses book-wide: 2:23, 6:1, 10:2). The PE mark follows 2:23 (oshb:Esth.2.23 (petuchah, single-witness)).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this notice into the preceding concealment reminder would overlook the verse-initial bayamim hahem formula that itself opens fresh narrated material at 2:21, independent of the gate-clause repetition.

boundary_rationale: אַחַ֣ר הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה גִּדַּל֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֜וֹשׁ אֶת הָמָ֧ן בֶּֽן הַמְּדָ֛תָא הָאֲגָגִ֖י וַֽיְנַשְּׂאֵ֑הוּ “After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, and advanced him” web:Esth.3.1 (sweep: 2 book-wide for the "after these things" formula, the only other instance opening 2:1’s search-for-a-queen episode) opens a new temporal frame introducing Haman and the universal-homage decree, against which וּמָ֨רְדֳּכַ֔י לֹ֥א יִכְרַ֖ע וְלֹ֥א יִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶֽה “But Mordecai didn’t bow down or pay him homage” web:Esth.3.2 sets the refusal that the gate-servants’ daily interrogation directly answers (3:3-4), closing when Mordecai discloses כִּֽי הִגִּ֥יד לָהֶ֖ם אֲשֶׁר ה֥וּא יְהוּדִֽי “for he had told them that he was a Jew” web:Esth.3.4 — the disclosure the servants then report to Haman, opening the next escalation. Ketiv/qere note: 3:4 spells "when they spoke" as ketiv באמרם against qere כְּאָמְרָ֤ם, disclosed because the verse is quoted here. 3:4's report of Mordecai's disclosure, וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לְהָמָ֗ן “that they told Haman” web:Esth.3.4, and 3:6's citation of that same report as Haman's stated motive, כִּֽי הִגִּ֥ידוּ ל֖וֹ “for they had made known to him” web:Esth.3.6, share the plene-hifil higid family (sweep: 8 verses book-wide: 2:10, 3:4, 3:6, 4:4, 4:8, 4:12, 6:2, 8:1; 3:4 itself carries two tokens, וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לְהָמָ֗ן and כִּֽי הִגִּ֥יד), and run as one unbroken report-to-motive chain across the 3:4|3:5 seam with no change of participant, place, or time. Three verses open with a temporal formula, each byte-verified verse-initial (1:3, 3:7, 9:1), explicitly not a single-string sweep: 3:7's verse-initial month-and-regnal-year formula בַּחֹ֤דֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן֙ הוּא חֹ֣דֶשׁ נִיסָ֔ן בִּשְׁנַת֙ שְׁתֵּ֣ים עֶשְׂרֵ֔ה לַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ “In the first month, which is the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus” web:Esth.3.7 stands among them as a materially tier-1 opener, corroborating the 3:6|3:7 seam over the 3:4|3:5 seam this span itself closes on.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the refusal in 3:1-2 from the interrogation that answers it in 3:3-4 would sever question from answer inside one continuous gate-scene.

boundary_rationale: The viewpoint shift וַיַּ֣רְא הָמָ֔ן כִּי אֵ֣ין מָרְדֳּכַ֔י כֹּרֵ֥עַ וּמִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֖ה “When Haman saw that Mordecai didn’t bow down nor pay him homage” web:Esth.3.5 opens Haman’s own perspective on the report just delivered, and his scorn at targeting Mordecai alone, וַיִּ֣בֶז בְּעֵינָ֗יו לִשְׁלֹ֤ח יָד֙ בְּמָרְדֳּכַ֣י לְבַדּ֔וֹ “But he scorned the thought of laying hands on Mordecai alone” web:Esth.3.6, directly motivates his own next act: the lot-casting date-formula הִפִּ֣יל פּוּר֩ ה֨וּא הַגּוֹרָ֜ל “they cast Pur, that is, the lot” web:Esth.3.7 (lot-gloss formula, sweep: 2 book-wide, recurring only at 9:24), all Haman’s own initiative before he turns to petition the king at 3:8. The SAMEKH mark follows 3:7 (oshb:Esth.3.7 (setumah, single-witness)). The 3:4|3:5 seam this span opens on carries a continuous report-to-motive chain rather than a change of scene: 3:5's viewpoint shift is the immediate wayyiqtol consequence of the report already stated inside 3:4 (וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לְהָמָ֗ן “that they told Haman” web:Esth.3.4), and 3:6 loops back to that same report as Haman's stated motive (כִּֽי הִגִּ֥ידוּ ל֖וֹ “for they had made known to him” web:Esth.3.6; shared plene-hifil higid family, sweep: 8 verses book-wide: 2:10, 3:4, 3:6, 4:4, 4:8, 4:12, 6:2, 8:1), with no participant, place, or time change separating 3:4 from 3:6. Three verses open with a temporal formula, each byte-verified verse-initial (1:3, 3:7, 9:1), explicitly not a single-string sweep: 3:7's own verse-initial month-and-regnal-year formula, בַּחֹ֤דֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן֙ הוּא חֹ֣דֶשׁ נִיסָ֔ן בִּשְׁנַת֙ שְׁתֵּ֣ים עֶשְׂרֵ֔ה לַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ “In the first month, which is the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus” web:Esth.3.7, sits among them as the stronger tier-1 opener, corroborating the 3:6|3:7 seam over the 3:4|3:5 seam this span itself opens on.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating the lot-casting verse alone from Haman's preceding wrath would strand it from the very motive that provokes it.

boundary_rationale: Haman’s petition-speech opens with וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָמָן֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ “Haman said to King Ahasuerus” web:Esth.3.8 and reaches the petition formula אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֔וֹב יִכָּתֵ֖ב לְאַבְּדָ֑ם “If it pleases the king, let it be written that they be destroyed” web:Esth.3.9 (petition formula, sweep: 7 book-wide, second of the book’s seven instances), to which the king’s authorization responds in the same continuous exchange, handing over the signet ring וַיָּ֧סַר הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶת טַבַּעְתּ֖וֹ מֵעַ֣ל יָד֑וֹ “The king took his ring from his hand” web:Esth.3.10 and the closing grant הַכֶּ֖סֶף נָת֣וּן לָ֑ךְ וְהָעָ֕ם לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת בּ֖וֹ כַּטּ֥וֹב בְּעֵינֶֽיךָ “The silver is given to you, the people also, to do with them as it seems good to you” web:Esth.3.11; no scene, participant, or day-marker separates request from response before the scribes-summons formula opens the edict inset at 3:12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Cutting a decision at 3:9|3:10 would separate a petition from its answer within one unbroken audience before the king.

boundary_rationale: The scribes-summons formula וַיִּקָּרְאוּ֩ סֹפְרֵ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ “Then the king’s scribes were called in” web:Esth.3.12 (sweep: 2 book-wide, the deliberate counter-edict parallel at 8:9) opens the inset, staying with its dispatch (3:13, addressed לְהַשְׁמִ֡יד לַהֲרֹ֣ג וּלְאַבֵּ֣ד אֶת כָּל הַ֠יְּהוּדִים “to destroy, to kill, and to cause to perish, all Jews” web:Esth.3.13) and publication (3:14) through its narrative-frame reaction verse: הָֽרָצִ֞ים יָצְא֤וּ דְחוּפִים֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֑ה “The couriers went out in haste by the king’s commandment, and the decree was given out in the citadel of Susa” web:Esth.3.15 opens the verse, its middle clause pivots to the king and Haman's ironic ease, וְהַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ יָשְׁב֣וּ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת “The king and Haman sat down to drink” web:Esth.3.15, and it closes on the city's alarm, וְהָעִ֥יר שׁוּשָׁ֖ן נָבֽוֹכָה “the city of Susa was perplexed” web:Esth.3.15 — three clauses inside one verse that cannot be split apart: the couriers' dispatch, the throne's complacency, and the streets' distress read as a single ironic beat, which 4:1's mourning directly answers. 4:1 opens a hard participant shift onto Mordecai alone, וּמָרְדֳּכַ֗י יָדַע֙ אֶת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֣ר נַעֲשָׂ֔ה “Now when Mordecai found out all that was done” web:Esth.4.1, moving outside the citadel into the city and into mourning ritual, וַיֵּצֵא֙ בְּת֣וֹךְ הָעִ֔יר וַיִּזְעַ֛ק זְעָקָ֥ה גְדֹלָ֖ה וּמָרָֽה “went out into the middle of the city, and wailed loudly and bitterly” web:Esth.4.1 — a scene, location, and participant break from the drinking king and the perplexed city that closes 3:15, with no narrative continuity carrying across the seam except Mordecai’s discovery of events, which itself opens a new information-relay unit rather than continuing this one. The PE mark follows 3:15 (oshb:Esth.3.15 (petuchah, single-witness)), landing exactly at this seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Severing 3:15's reaction clause from the edict that provokes it would split one verse's own three-clause sequence — dispatch, royal ease, civic alarm — apart from itself.

boundary_rationale: The preceding scene ends with the court at ease: “The king and Haman sat down to drink; but the city of Susa was perplexed” (web:Esth.3.15), a clause built on וְהַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ יָשְׁב֣וּ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת וְהָעִ֥יר שׁוּשָׁ֖ן נָבֽוֹכָה, the king and Haman as joint subject of a leisure verb. The new span opens on a fronted, contrastive subject — וּמָרְדֳּכַ֗י יָדַע֙ אֶת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֣ר נַעֲשָׂ֔ה, literally "and Mordecai knew all that was done" — reversing both the grammatical subject and the register: drinking gives way to grief, and the verse's own opening vav marks the pivot rather than a mere continuation. The WEB renders this “Now when Mordecai found out all that was done, Mordecai tore his clothes and put on sackcloth with ashes, and went out into the middle of the city, and wailed loudly and bitterly” (web:Esth.4.1). Esth.4.2 keeps the same subject and location (Mordecai at the gate) before Esth.4.3 opens a distributive formula, “In every province, wherever the king's commandment and his decree came, there was great mourning among the Jews, and fasting, and weeping, and wailing” (web:Esth.4.3), generalizing Mordecai's individual mourning into a province-wide notice — the same distributive shift from a single actor to an empire-wide report recurs at the joy notice that closes this part (Esth.8.17). The shared consonantal string underlying both the noun at Esth.4.3 and the imperative verb at Esth.4.16 is attested at exactly 2 verses book-wide, sweep: 2 (Esth.4.3 the noun, Esth.4.16 the imperative verb), so the mourning-fast pairing introduced here is picked up again within the same chapter. The fasting NOUN itself, tracked apart from that string, is a separate object at sweep: 2 (Esth.4.3; Esth.9.31 in the defective plural, unreachable by the string sweep since that spelling drops the vav) — so the same term that opens the mourning here is also the term the Purim institution later commemorates: “as they had imposed upon themselves and their descendants in the matter of the fastings and their mourning” (web:Esth.9.31). A petuchah closes the prior scene at Esth.3.15 (petuchah, single-witness); it is tier-3 corroboration for the seam, not its driver — the subject and register reversal is.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping 4:1-3 fused to the edict's closing scene ignores the change from the king and Haman's leisure at 3:15 to Mordecai's grief in the street.

boundary_rationale: The scene shifts from the city gate to the palace: וַ֠תָּבוֹאינָה נַעֲר֨וֹת אֶסְתֵּ֤ר וְסָרִיסֶ֨יהָ֙ וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לָ֔הּ, "Esther's maidens and her eunuchs came and told her" — a new participant set and location, WEB “Esther's maidens and her eunuchs came and told her this, and the queen was exceedingly grieved” (web:Esth.4.4). Esther's own failed gesture — clothing sent, “but he didn't receive it” (web:Esth.4.4) — triggers her dispatch of a named intermediary in Esth.4.5-6, who then carries Mordecai's report in Esth.4.7-8 and returns it to her in Esth.4.9, closing with וַיָּב֖וֹא הֲתָ֑ךְ וַיַּגֵּ֣ד לְאֶסְתֵּ֔ר אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֥י מָרְדֳּכָֽי, "Hathach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai" — WEB “Hathach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai” (web:Esth.4.9). The whole span is one bracketed fact-finding cycle: it opens with Esther learning secondhand and closes with her learning firsthand (via Hathach) exactly what Mordecai wants her to do, a closed messenger loop rather than a resting point mid-errand.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 4:4 as its own decision would sever the maidens' report from the very inquiry it triggers.

boundary_rationale: A second relay cycle opens with its own speech-formula: וַתֹּ֤אמֶר אֶסְתֵּר֙ לַהֲתָ֔ךְ וַתְּצַוֵּ֖הוּ אֶֽל מָרְדֳּכָֽי, "Then Esther spoke to Hathach, and commanded him to Mordecai" — WEB “Then Esther spoke to Hathach, and gave him a message to Mordecai” (web:Esth.4.10), introducing the content of Esth.4.11 (the law of unbidden entry, closing “I have not been called to come in to the king these thirty days.” web:Esth.4.11). The cycle closes with the delivery notice וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לְמָרְדֳּכָ֔י אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֥י אֶסְתֵּֽר in full, WEB “They told Esther's words to Mordecai” (web:Esth.4.12) — the same dispatch-then-delivery shape as the earlier Hathach cycle (Esth.4.5-Esth.4.9), now run in the opposite direction (Esther to Mordecai rather than Mordecai to Esther). A petuchah closes the verse, oshb:Esth.4.12 (petuchah, single-witness); tier-3 corroboration for a seam already driven by the completed delivery formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A backward merge into the preceding cycle is rejected because no mark falls at Esth.4.9 or Esth.4.10 and Esth.4.5-9 dispatches Esther's inquiry and returns with Mordecai's report while Esth.4.10-12 dispatches Esther's own reply-content to Mordecai, a fresh outgoing message rather than a continuation of the same errand, so the seam holds on content and direction alone.

boundary_rationale: Mordecai's reply opens with direct quoted content rather than a further third-person delivery notice: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר מָרְדֳּכַ֖י לְהָשִׁ֣יב אֶל אֶסְתֵּ֑ר, literally "Mordecai said, to cause word to be brought back to Esther" — WEB “Then Mordecai asked them to return this answer to Esther:” (web:Esth.4.13). The infinitive here (le-hashiv, "to cause to be brought back") is causative and names an unspecified relaying agency, exactly as the matched infinitive does two verses later at Esther's own reply (Esth.4.15) — so the relay itself is mediated in both directions, not unmediated at Esth.4.13 alone. What distinguishes this verse from the preceding delivery notice at Esth.4.12 (וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לְמָרְדֳּכָ֔י אֵ֖ת דִּבְרֵ֥י אֶסְתֵּֽר, WEB “They told Esther's words to Mordecai.” (web:Esth.4.12)) is that Esth.4.13 supplies quoted content — the "who knows" appeal of Esth.4.14 — rather than merely reporting that a message arrived. Esther's reply opens with the matched formula וַתֹּ֥אמֶר אֶסְתֵּ֖ר לְהָשִׁ֥יב אֶֽל מָרְדֳּכָֽי in full, WEB “Then Esther asked them to answer Mordecai” (web:Esth.4.15) — the same infinitive "to reply" (le-hashiv) used of Mordecai in Esth.4.13, now applied to Esther, a chiastic pairing of response-formulas that binds Esth.4.13-17 together as one challenge-and-resolution exchange, closing with her decision (“and if I perish, I perish.” web:Esth.4.16) and Mordecai's compliance (web:Esth.4.17). This span sits between two marks: a petuchah already closes the preceding relay at Esth.4.12 (petuchah, single-witness), and a setumah closes this one at Esth.4.17 (setumah, single-witness) — both tier-3 corroboration, framing but not driving a boundary set by the matched response-formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating 4:15-17 from Mordecai's preceding challenge would strand Esther's answer from the objection it answers.

boundary_rationale: A fresh temporal formula opens the chapter: וַיְהִ֣י בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֗י, "Now it happened on the third day" — WEB “Now on the third day, Esther put on her royal clothing...” (web:Esth.5.1), counting out the fast just vowed at “fast for me...three days, night or day” (web:Esth.4.16) and moving from private resolve to public act. The audience is granted in Esth.5.2 (scepter extended, favor found), the king's open-ended offer follows in Esth.5.3, and Esther's actual request — an invitation to a banquet — closes the unit in Esth.5.4-5, foreshadowing the invitation-formula echo at Esth.5.8. This span holds together as the approach-through-first-invitation movement, ending once king and Haman are seated (“So the king and Haman came to the banquet that Esther had prepared.” web:Esth.5.5). A setumah already closed the preceding dialogue at Esth.4.17 (setumah, single-witness); this scene carries its own setumah at Esth.5.2 (setumah, single-witness) marking the scepter-grant — both disclosed as corroboration, neither driving the seam set by the day-formula opener.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Halting this unit at 5:2 alone would cut the scepter-grant away from the royal offer it provokes.

boundary_rationale: At the banquet itself the king restates his open offer: מַה שְּׁאֵלָתֵ֖ךְ וְיִנָּ֣תֵֽן לָ֑ךְ וּמַה בַּקָּשָׁתֵ֛ךְ עַד חֲצִ֥י הַמַּלְכ֖וּת וְתֵעָֽשׂ — WEB “What is your petition? It shall be granted you. What is your request? Even to the half of the kingdom it shall be performed.” (web:Esth.5.6). Esth.5.3's own question is already two-part and already carries the identical half-kingdom clause (מַה לָּ֖ךְ אֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֑ה וּמַה בַּקָּשָׁתֵ֛ךְ עַד חֲצִ֥י הַמַּלְכ֖וּת וְיִנָּ֥תֵֽן לָֽךְ, 11 tokens across two members); Esth.5.6 restates it in 10 tokens, also two members, byte-identical in its second member (וּמַה בַּקָּשָׁתֵ֛ךְ עַד חֲצִ֥י הַמַּלְכ֖וּת), sweep: 3 book-wide for that exact clause (Esth.5.3, Esth.5.6, Esth.7.2) — a resequencing of the same two-part structure, not an expansion, and the half-kingdom offer is not new here. This banquet-of-wine refrain reopens the request rather than continuing the approach scene, and the same doubled formula recurs at Esth.7.2 when the second banquet reaches its own turning point. Esther defers again in Esth.5.7-8, closing on two petition formulas placed back to back: אִם מָצָ֨אתִי חֵ֜ן בְּעֵינֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ וְאִם עַל הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ ט֔וֹב לָתֵת֙ אֶת שְׁאֵ֣לָתִ֔י וְלַעֲשׂ֖וֹת אֶת בַּקָּשָׁתִ֑י יָב֧וֹא הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ וְהָמָ֗ן אֶל הַמִּשְׁתֶּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֣ה לָהֶ֔ם וּמָחָ֥ר אֶֽעֱשֶׂ֖ה כִּדְבַ֥ר הַמֶּֽלֶךְ, WEB “If I have found favor in the sight of the king, and if it pleases the king to grant my petition and to perform my request, let the king and Haman come to the banquet that I will prepare for them, and I will do tomorrow as the king has said.” (web:Esth.5.8) — the im-matzati-chen ("if I have found favor") formula, sweep: 3 book-wide (Esth.5.8, Esth.7.3, Esth.8.5), immediately followed by the im-al-hamelekh-tov ("if it pleases the king") formula, sweep: 7 book-wide (Esth.1.19, Esth.3.9, Esth.5.4, Esth.5.8, Esth.7.3, Esth.8.5, Esth.9.13) — two distinct formulas naming two different counts, not one.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Absorbing 5:6-8 into the preceding audience scene would erase the banquet-of-wine refrain that reopens the petition.

boundary_rationale: Scene and mood both turn: וַיֵּצֵ֤א הָמָן֙ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֔וּא שָׂמֵ֖חַ וְט֣וֹב לֵ֑ב, "Then Haman went out that day, joyful and glad of heart" — WEB “Then Haman went out that day joyful and glad of heart, but when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate...he was filled with wrath” (web:Esth.5.9), moving the setting from the banquet hall to the gate and then to Haman's own house, and the participants from the royal party to Haman's household. His boast to Zeresh and his friends (Esth.5.10-12) is immediately undercut in his own words, “Yet all this avails me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king's gate” (web:Esth.5.13), and Zeresh's counsel to build a gallows closes the unit: "and this thing pleased Haman, and he made the gallows" — WEB “This pleased Haman, so he had the gallows made” (web:Esth.5.14), וַיִּיטַ֧ב הַדָּבָ֛ר לִפְנֵ֥י הָמָ֖ן וַיַּ֥עַשׂ הָעֵֽץ. The fifty-cubit gallows built here becomes the very structure named again at Esth.7.9-10, so this scene, though short, is a self-contained cause set into motion rather than the tail of the banquet scene that precedes it. A petuchah closes the verse, oshb:Esth.5.14 (petuchah, single-witness); Writings marks are tier-3 at most and cannot themselves decide whether this venting-and-counsel scene stands alone or closes the banquet unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 5:9-14 into the first banquet's close would attach Haman's private humiliation to a scene he has already left.

boundary_rationale: A new night and a new cause open the pivot chapter: בַּלַּ֣יְלָה הַה֔וּא נָדְדָ֖ה שְׁנַ֣ת הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ, "On that night, the sleep of the king fled" — WEB “On that night, the king couldn't sleep. He commanded the book of records of the chronicles to be brought” (web:Esth.6.1), naming the chronicle-frame phrase סֵ֤פֶר הַזִּכְרֹנוֹת֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֔ים in its fullest form; the same source-notice recurs in shorter form at Esth.2.23 and Esth.10.2, sweep: 3 book-wide for the phrase "the book of the chronicles" in any of its three forms. The reading turns up Mordecai's unrewarded loyalty (Esth.6.2-3), and the king's follow-up question, “Who is in the court?” (web:Esth.6.4), is answered in the same verse by a disjunctive waw-fronted-subject clause naming Haman's arrival at a lexically marked location: וְהָמָ֣ן בָּ֗א לַחֲצַ֤ר בֵּית הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ הַחִ֣יצוֹנָ֔ה, “Haman had come into the outer court of the king’s house” (web:Esth.6.4) — the only occurrence of the qualified "outer" court in the book, sweep: 1 (Esth.6.4), against the qualified "inner" court at sweep: 2 (Esth.4.11, Esth.5.1), the only other qualified court term in the book. That locative clause is circumstantial background answering the king's own question, not a scene-opening device on the model of Esth.4.1: no register or topic shift accompanies it, and the interrogation about honoring Mordecai runs uninterrupted across the seam into the servants' answer at Esth.6.5. Haman's private assumption that the honor must be meant for him, “Who would the king delight to honor more than myself?” (web:Esth.6.6), closes the unit on the edge of dramatic irony rather than at a scene change. Chapter 6 itself carries no paragraph-division notation anywhere in its interior; the seams argued inside it rest on the wording alone, and that absence is not read as evidence against a boundary here — the span's own front edge is separately corroborated by the petuchah closing the preceding verse, Esth.5.14 (petuchah, single-witness).
strongest_rejected_alternative: A seam at 6:3|6:4 is rejected: Esth.6.4's lexically marked locative — the book's only "outer court," sweep: 1 — sits in a disjunctive clause that supplies circumstantial background to the king's own question rather than opening a new register, so the interrogation about honoring Mordecai runs unbroken from Esth.6.3 through the servants' answer at Esth.6.5, with no reversal of subject, tone, or topic of the kind that marks the genuine scene break at Esth.4.1.

boundary_rationale: Esth.6.6 opens the exchange with the king's spoken question, מַה לַעֲשׂ֕וֹת בָּאִ֕ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֥ר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ חָפֵ֣ץ בִּיקָר֑וֹ, “What shall be done to the man whom the king delights to honor?” (web:Esth.6.6), and then, unspoken, Haman's own aside, לְמִ֞י יַחְפֹּ֥ץ הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת יְקָ֖ר יוֹתֵ֥ר מִמֶּֽנִּי, “Who would the king delight to honor more than myself?” (web:Esth.6.6). This span opens with Haman voicing the answer to that already-posed question: וַיֹּ֥אמֶר הָמָ֖ן אֶל הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ אִ֕ישׁ אֲשֶׁ֥ר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ חָפֵ֥ץ בִּיקָרֽוֹ — WEB “Haman said to the king, “For the man whom the king delights to honor,” (web:Esth.6.7). The honor-formula recurs at the consonantal level across the whole pivot exchange, sweep: 4 verses, 5 tokens book-wide (Esth.6.6, Esth.6.7, Esth.6.9 x2, Esth.6.11) — a continuity device crossing this span's own front seam at Esth.6.6|Esth.6.7 into the preceding unit, disclosed here for that reason and not as the driver of this span's own cohesion. His script runs through Esth.6.9, and the king's reply reverses it in the same breath: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ לְהָמָ֗ן מַ֠הֵר קַ֣ח אֶת הַלְּב֤וּשׁ, "Then the king said to Haman, 'hurry, take the clothing'" — WEB “Then the king said to Haman, “Hurry and take the clothing and the horse, as you have said,” (web:Esth.6.10). Haman's forced execution of his own proposal on his rival closes the unit (web:Esth.6.11). This span's own cohesion rests on the proposal-reversal-compliance shape of Esth.6.7-11 alone, from Haman's answer through the king's reversal to Haman's compliance; no interior seam divides the honor either from the man who designed it or from the man forced to carry it out. Chapter 6 has no paragraph marks anywhere in the witness, so this internal shape is the span's sole warrant.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking 6:7-11 at the reversal command would divide a single irony into two decisions neither of which stands alone.

boundary_rationale: The two men part ways in the same verse: וַיָּ֥שָׁב מָרְדֳּכַ֖י אֶל שַׁ֣עַר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ נִדְחַ֣ף אֶל בֵּית֔וֹ אָבֵ֖ל וַחֲפ֥וּי רֹֽאשׁ in full, WEB “Mordecai came back to the king's gate, but Haman hurried to his house, mourning and having his head covered” (web:Esth.6.12) — Mordecai returns to his fixed post while Haman flees home in the posture of a mourner. The covering-root itself is a two-point book-wide device, sweep: 2 (Esth.6.12, Esth.7.8) — no third occurrence exists, and none falls at Esth.4.1, where Mordecai's own grief is marked instead by torn clothes and sackcloth and ashes (web:Esth.4.1), a related but textually distinct mourning register.
