The head covered here at Esth.6.12 is answered by Haman's own face covered later at Esth.7.8, when the king's word condemns him — the covering-root's two attested spellings in the book, וַחֲפ֥וּי (Esth.6.12) and חָפֽוּ (Esth.7.8), with no third occurrence. That echo crosses this span's own back seam at Esth.6.14|Esth.7.1 and reaches past it into the following unit; disclosed here as a forward-pointing continuity signal rather than a cohesion driver internal to Esth.6.12-Esth.6.14. Haman's execution itself falls later still, at Esth.7.10. Haman's household reprises its earlier counsel scene: Esth.6.13 opens by naming the same household first met at Esth.5.14 — “Haman recounted to Zeresh his wife and all his friends everything that had happened to him” (web:Esth.6.13) (וַיְסַפֵּ֨ר הָמָ֜ן לְזֶ֤רֶשׁ אִשְׁתּוֹ֙ וּלְכָל אֹ֣הֲבָ֔יו …), the identical household of “Then Zeresh his wife and all his friends said to him,” (web:Esth.5.14) (וַתֹּ֣אמֶר לוֹ֩ זֶ֨רֶשׁ אִשְׁתּ֜וֹ וְכָל אֹֽהֲבָ֗יו) — “Zeresh his wife” and “all his friends” each attested at the same 3 verses book-wide, sweep: 3 (Esth.5.10, Esth.5.14, Esth.6.13). Only the SPEAKING roster narrows: Esth.6.13's counsel is voiced by “Then his wise men and Zeresh his wife said to him,” (web:Esth.6.13) (וַיֹּ֩אמְרוּ֩ ל֨וֹ חֲכָמָ֜יו וְזֶ֣רֶשׁ אִשְׁתּ֗וֹ) — חֲכָמָ֜יו, "his wise men" attested nowhere else in the book, sweep: 1 (Esth.6.13) — replacing the collective “all his friends” as speakers while the wider household stays the same audience. It is that household's own prior counsel that reverses here: “If Mordecai, before whom you have begun to fall, is of Jewish descent, you will not prevail against him, but you will surely fall before him.” (web:Esth.6.13). The chapter's last verse then breaks off the fatalistic scene mid-conversation: עוֹדָם֙ מְדַבְּרִ֣ים עִמּ֔וֹ וְסָרִיסֵ֥י הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ הִגִּ֑יעוּ וַיַּבְהִ֨לוּ֙ לְהָבִ֣יא אֶת הָמָ֔ן אֶל הַמִּשְׁתֶּ֖ה אֲשֶׁר עָשְׂתָ֥ה אֶסְתֵּֽר — WEB “While they were yet talking with him, the king's eunuchs came, and hurried to bring Haman to the banquet that Esther had prepared.” (web:Esth.6.14). This closing clause is the low-confidence hinge into the next scene: the next material opens “So the king and Haman came to banquet with Esther the queen” (web:Esth.7.1) with no new time formula and no fresh introduction of the banquet, reading as the direct continuation of the "hurried" summons rather than a fresh scene-opener in its own right. No paragraph mark closes chapter 6 anywhere, including at its final verse; the hinge is argued from wording alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 6:12-14 as a coda to the parade scene overlooks the location and mood change once Mordecai and Haman part ways.

boundary_rationale: The banquet notice that closed the last chapter's hurried summons is realized in one line, “So the king and Haman came to banquet with Esther the queen” (web:Esth.7.1), and the king repeats the doubled petition-formula, also “on the second day at the banquet of wine, “What is your petition, queen Esther?” (web:Esth.7.2): גַּ֣ם בַּיּ֤וֹם הַשֵּׁנִי֙ בְּמִשְׁתֵּ֣ה הַיַּ֔יִן מַה שְּׁאֵלָתֵ֛ךְ אֶסְתֵּ֥ר הַמַּלְכָּ֖ה, the same doubled question-formula already met at Esth.5.6 — paired at the consonantal tier, skeleton sweep: 3 book-wide (Esth.5.6, Esth.7.2, Esth.9.12; the pairing unifies only at the skeleton tier, not byte-for-byte); this occurrence is the second of the three. Esther finally names her petitioner as her people and her opponent as Haman across Esth.7.3-6. The king's fury then drives him out and back within the same confrontation: וְהַמֶּ֜לֶךְ קָ֤ם בַּחֲמָתוֹ֙ מִמִּשְׁתֵּ֣ה הַיַּ֔יִן אֶל גִּנַּ֖ת הַבִּיתָ֑ן וְהָמָ֣ן עָמַ֗ד לְבַקֵּ֤שׁ עַל נַפְשׁוֹ֙ מֵֽאֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה כִּ֣י רָאָ֔ה כִּֽי כָלְתָ֥ה אֵלָ֛יו הָרָעָ֖ה מֵאֵ֥ת הַמֶּֽלֶךְ, “The king arose in his wrath from the banquet of wine and went into the palace garden. Haman stood up to make request for his life to Esther the queen, for he saw that there was evil determined against him by the king.” (web:Esth.7.7), then וְהַמֶּ֡לֶךְ שָׁב֩ מִגִּנַּ֨ת הַבִּיתָ֜ן אֶל בֵּ֣ית מִשְׁתֵּ֣ה הַיַּ֗יִן וְהָמָן֙ נֹפֵ֔ל עַל הַמִּטָּה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אֶסְתֵּ֣ר עָלֶ֔יהָ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ הֲ֠גַם לִכְבּ֧וֹשׁ אֶת הַמַּלְכָּ֛ה עִמִּ֖י בַּבָּ֑יִת הַדָּבָ֗ר יָצָא֙ מִפִּ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וּפְנֵ֥י הָמָ֖ן חָפֽוּ, “Then the king returned out of the palace garden into the place of the banquet of wine; and Haman had fallen on the couch where Esther was. Then the king said, “Will he even assault the queen in front of me in the house?” As the word went out of the king’s mouth, they covered Haman’s face.” (web:Esth.7.8) — an explicit exit and return between two named locations, the articled "garden of the pavilion" locative attested at exactly 2 verses book-wide at the consonantal tier, skeleton sweep: 2 (Esth.7.7, Esth.7.8), both interior to this span — the bare garden noun itself recurs a third time at Esth.1.5 in its unarticled construction, echoic of the book's opening banquet setting but outside this span — and the banquet-of-wine locative, skeleton sweep: 4 book-wide (Esth.5.6, Esth.7.2, Esth.7.7, Esth.7.8), three of them interior. The unit holds together not because no movement occurs but because the movement is contained within one ongoing confrontation: no new participant enters, no resolution is reached mid-transit, and the king returns to find Haman still fallen at the same couch, closing on וּפְנֵ֥י הָמָ֖ן חָפֽוּ, "and Haman's face was covered" — the covering-root's two attested spellings in the book, וַחֲפ֥וּי (Esth.6.12) and חָפֽוּ (Esth.7.8), with no third occurrence — now predicated of his face rather than his head as it was there. A setumah falls at Esth.7.4 (setumah, single-witness), interior to this span, and another at Esth.7.8 (setumah, single-witness), at the seam Esth.7.8|Esth.7.9 which is this span's own closing edge; neither is treated as the driver of any internal seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A finer split at Esth.7.4|Esth.7.5 carries this row's own strongest substrate corroboration — a setumah closes Esth.7.4 (setumah, single-witness) — but is rejected because Esther's accusation and its immediate fallout to Haman's terror read as one continuous confrontation, the mark corroborating only a rhetorical pause inside that single exchange rather than a unit break.

boundary_rationale: A background figure steps forward to speak: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר חַ֠רְבוֹנָה אֶחָ֨ד מִן הַסָּרִיסִ֜ים לִפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ גַּ֣ם הִנֵּה הָעֵ֣ץ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂ֪ה הָמָ֟ן לְֽמָרְדֳּכַ֞י אֲשֶׁ֧ר דִּבֶּר ט֣וֹב עַל הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ עֹמֵד֙ בְּבֵ֣ית הָמָ֔ן גָּבֹ֖הַּ חֲמִשִּׁ֣ים אַמָּ֑ה וַיֹּ֥אמֶר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ תְּלֻ֥הוּ עָלָֽיו — WEB “Then Harbonah, one of the eunuchs who were with the king, said, "Behold, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman has made for Mordecai, who spoke good for the king, is standing at Haman's house." The king said, "Hang him on it!"” (web:Esth.7.9). This is the same eunuch listed among the seven who attend the king: לִ֠מְהוּמָן בִּזְּתָ֨א חַרְבוֹנָ֜א בִּגְתָ֤א וַאֲבַגְתָא֙ זֵתַ֣ר וְכַרְכַּ֔ס שִׁבְעַת֙ הַסָּ֣רִיסִ֔ים הַמְשָׁ֣רְתִ֔ים אֶת פְּנֵ֖י הַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֽוֹשׁ, WEB “Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcass, the seven eunuchs who served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king,” (web:Esth.1.10) — one item in a seven-member list there, with no speaking part. His name is attested at exactly 2 verses book-wide across two consonantal spellings, sweep: 1 for the Esth.1.10 form and sweep: 1 for the Esth.7.9 form, and this is the only one of the two where he speaks; his reactivation as an actor here is the scene-internal signal, not a claim that the name is new to the book. He names the very gallows built at Esth.5.14. The king's one-line order and its execution close the confrontation: וַיִּתְלוּ֙ אֶת הָמָ֔ן עַל הָעֵ֖ץ אֲשֶׁר הֵכִ֣ין לְמָרְדֳּכָ֑י וַחֲמַ֥ת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ שָׁכָֽכָה in full, WEB “So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the king's wrath was pacified” (web:Esth.7.10) — a resolution notice ("the king's wrath was pacified") that answers the anger that opened the confrontation at Esth.7.7 and gives the unit its own closure distinct from the accusation scene that precedes it. A setumah already closed Esth.7.8 (setumah, single-witness) at the front seam of this span, and a petuchah closes Esth.7.10 (petuchah, single-witness) at its end; both disclosed together, with Harbonah's reactivation as speaker treated as the actual driver of the seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging 7:9-10 with the preceding confrontation would credit Harbonah's proposal, a reactivated voice, to a scene in which he has taken no active part.

boundary_rationale: A dated summary notice opens the new chapter in the third person: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא נָתַ֞ן הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ֙ לְאֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה, "On that day, King Ahasuerus gave to Esther the queen" — WEB “On that day, King Ahasuerus gave the house of Haman, the Jews' enemy, to Esther the queen” (web:Esth.8.1), reporting a property transfer as a completed act rather than staging a new appeal in direct speech. Esth.8.2 continues the same summary register — the ring transferred, Mordecai set over Haman's house — with no quoted speech anywhere in either verse. This closed, narrated notice is distinct in kind from the personal, tearful audience that opens immediately after it: “Esther spoke yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet and begged him with tears” (web:Esth.8.3). A petuchah already closed the previous scene at Esth.7.10 (petuchah, single-witness), and another closes this one at Esth.8.2 (petuchah, single-witness); both disclosed as corroboration for a boundary driven by the shift from narrated summary to direct, embodied appeal.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running 8:1-2 forward into Esther's plea would treat a completed property transfer as an unfinished appeal.

boundary_rationale: Esther returns to direct, embodied speech: וַתּ֣וֹסֶף אֶסְתֵּ֗ר וַתְּדַבֵּר֙ לִפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וַתִּפֹּ֖ל לִפְנֵ֣י רַגְלָ֑יו וַתֵּ֣בְךְּ וַתִּתְחַנֶּן ל֗וֹ, "Esther again spoke before the king, and fell before his feet, and wept, and begged him" — WEB “Esther spoke yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet and begged him with tears to put away the mischief of Haman the Agagite” (web:Esth.8.3), a bodily and emotional register (falling, weeping) absent from the narrated transfer notice that precedes it. Her formal request follows in Esth.8.4-5, and the unit closes on her own rhetorical question: כִּ֠י אֵיכָכָ֤ה אוּכַל֙ וְֽרָאִ֔יתִי בָּרָעָ֖ה אֲשֶׁר יִמְצָ֣א אֶת עַמִּ֑י, "For how can I endure, and see the evil that would find my people" — WEB “For how can I endure to see the evil that would come to my people? How can I endure to see the destruction of my relatives?” (web:Esth.8.6). A petuchah already closed the transfer notice at Esth.8.2 (petuchah, single-witness), and a setumah closes this appeal at Esth.8.6 (setumah, single-witness); both disclosed together as corroboration for a boundary driven by the change of register.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The royal audience and both petitioners are continuous across Esth.8.1-2|8.3 — no verse records the king dismissing or the petitioners departing and returning — so attaching Esther's renewed appeal to the transfer notice that precedes it is not ruled out by any break in audience; it is rejected instead because the two spans differ in speech-act register: Esth.8.1-2 narrates a completed grant in the third person with no quoted speech, while Esth.8.3 opens Esther's own embodied, tearful direct address — a register shift internal to one continuous audience rather than a change of scene.

boundary_rationale: A new speaker answers, and answers two people at once: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹשׁ֙ לְאֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֔ה וּֽלְמָרְדֳּכַ֖י הַיְּהוּדִ֑י, "Then King Ahasuerus said to Esther the queen and to Mordecai the Jew" — WEB “Then King Ahasuerus said to Esther the queen and to Mordecai the Jew, “See, I have given Esther the house of Haman,” (web:Esth.8.7). Mordecai has taken no speaking part since his reply relayed at Esth.4.13 — the string וַיֹּ֥אמֶר מָרְדֳּכַ֖י, "Mordecai said," his only speech-introducing occurrence book-wide, sweep: 1 (Esth.4.13) — and his reintroduction here as a direct addressee, alongside Esther, marks a participant shift distinct from Esther's solo appeal in the preceding verses. The king's reply authorizes rather than grants outright: “Write also to the Jews as it pleases you, in the king’s name, and seal it with the king’s ring” (web:Esth.8.8), closing on the irreversibility formula כִּֽי כְתָ֞ב אֲשֶׁר נִכְתָּ֣ב בְּשֵׁם הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ וְנַחְתּ֛וֹם בְּטַבַּ֥עַת הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֵ֥ין לְהָשִֽׁיב, "for a writing that is written in the king's name and sealed with the king's ring, there is no reversing" — the same writing-and-sealing-in-the-king's-name apparatus already used at the original edict's close, Esth.3.12 (בְּשֵׁ֨ם הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹשׁ֙ נִכְתָּ֔ב וְנֶחְתָּ֖ם בְּטַבַּ֥עַת הַמֶּֽלֶךְ), which shares the signet noun with this verse, sweep: 5 verses, 6 tokens book-wide (Esth.3.10, Esth.3.12, Esth.8.2, Esth.8.8, Esth.8.10; Esth.8.8 itself carries two); the decree noun itself is a separate object, absent from both this verse and Esth.3.12, and attested instead at Esth.1.19 among the wider decree-noun count, sweep: 20 tokens over 19 verses book-wide.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 8:7-8 as part of Esther's speech misassigns the king's own reply, addressed to Mordecai as much as to her.

boundary_rationale: The counter-edict opens with the same scribes-summons formula used of the original edict: וַיִּקָּרְא֣וּ סֹפְרֵֽי הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ בָּֽעֵת הַ֠הִיא, "Then the king's scribes were called at that time" — WEB “Then the king's scribes were called at that time, in the third month, which is the month Sivan” (web:Esth.8.9), matching וַיִּקָּרְאוּ֩ סֹפְרֵ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ at Esth.3.12 in substance though not letter for letter — the two pointed strings differ (byte sweep: 0, accent_stripped sweep: 0) and match only once points are stripped, skeleton sweep: 2 (Esth.3.12, Esth.8.9) — a deliberate edict/counter-edict pairing at the consonantal tier. The same verse repeats the merism, here מֵהֹ֣דּוּ וְעַד כּ֗וּשׁ, "from India to Cush" — in substance though not letter for letter against its Esth.1.1 form, מֵהֹ֣דּוּ וְעַד כּ֔וּשׁ: the two occurrences differ only in the cantillation of the final word (byte sweep: 0) — found at exactly 2 verses book-wide once cantillation is stripped, accent_stripped sweep: 2 (Esth.1.1, Esth.8.9), tying the counter-edict's geographic scope back to the book's opening frame. The inset runs through the date-setting (Esth.8.12) and publication (Esth.8.13) to its own dispatch notice, closing הָרָצִ֞ים רֹכְבֵ֤י הָרֶ֨כֶשׁ֙ הָֽאֲחַשְׁתְּרָנִ֔ים יָֽצְא֛וּ מְבֹהָלִ֥ים וּדְחוּפִ֖ים בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָֽה in full, WEB “So the couriers who rode on royal horses went out, hastened and pressed on by the king's commandment. The decree was given out in the citadel of Susa” (web:Esth.8.14), which echoes the closing clause of the first edict's dispatch notice at Esth.3.15 in substance though not letter for letter (the pointing differs where each clause sits differently inside its own sentence). This document inset stays with its narrative frame as a single unit, paralleling the edict block at Esth.3.12-15, and is not subdivided internally; a petuchah closes it at Esth.8.14 (petuchah, single-witness), disclosed as corroboration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the counter-edict at its date clause would sever 8:12 from the authorization it depends on.

boundary_rationale: The legal register of the edict gives way to a scene of public reception: וּמָרְדֳּכַ֞י יָצָ֣א מִלִּפְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ בִּלְב֤וּשׁ מַלְכוּת֙ תְּכֵ֣לֶת וָח֔וּר וַעֲטֶ֤רֶת זָהָב֙ גְּדוֹלָ֔ה וְתַכְרִ֥יךְ בּ֖וּץ וְאַרְגָּמָ֑ן וְהָעִ֣יר שׁוּשָׁ֔ן צָהֲלָ֖ה וְשָׂמֵֽחָה, "And Mordecai went out from before the king in royal clothing" — WEB “Mordecai went out of the presence of the king in royal clothing of blue and white...and the city of Susa shouted and was glad” (web:Esth.8.15), naming Susa specifically rather than the provinces generally. Esth.8.16 then summarizes the reaction for "the Jews" as a people rather than the city: לַיְּהוּדִ֕ים הָֽיְתָ֥ה אוֹרָ֖ה וְשִׂמְחָ֑ה וְשָׂשֹׂ֖ן וִיקָֽר in full, WEB “The Jews had light, gladness, joy, and honor” (web:Esth.8.16), carrying the simchah NOUN at chirik-sheva vocalization: sweep: 6 book-wide, 7 tokens (Esth.8.16, Esth.8.17, Esth.9.17, Esth.9.18, Esth.9.19, Esth.9.22 x2). The preceding verse's own וְשָׂמֵֽחָה, "was glad" (oshb:Esth.8.15), names a distinct object, the simchah ADJECTIVE at qamets-tsere vocalization — consonantally identical to the noun but pointed apart: sweep: 3 book-wide (Esth.5.9, Esth.5.14, Esth.8.15). Naming the wider ROOT that covers both forms together: sweep: 9 book-wide, 10 tokens. This local, Susa-and-the-Jews notice is bounded by the legal document that precedes it and by the empire-wide distributive report that follows it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying 8:15-16 forward into the province-wide notice would flatten the difference between Susa's local celebration and the empire-wide report that follows.

boundary_rationale: The verse opens its own distributive formula, doubling both terms of scope: וּבְכָל מְדִינָ֨ה וּמְדִינָ֜ה וּבְכָל עִ֣יר וָעִ֗יר, "and in every province and province, and in every city and city" — WEB “In every province and in every city, wherever the king's commandment and his decree came, the Jews had gladness, joy, a feast and a holiday” (web:Esth.8.17). That doubled medinah-umedinah shape occurs at 8 verses book-wide, sweep: 8 book-wide (Esth.1.22, Esth.3.12, Esth.3.14, Esth.4.3, Esth.8.9, Esth.8.13, Esth.8.17, Esth.9.28), the same formula that opened this part's own mourning notice at Esth.4.3, closing the circle it began. The verse ends on its own resolution clause, “for the fear of the Jews had fallen on them” (web:Esth.8.17), and adds a notice found nowhere else in the book: מִֽתְיַהֲדִ֔ים, "became Jews", sweep: 1 book-wide for that verb form (Esth.8.17 only). The next material opens on an entirely different formula, a specific calendar date rather than a summary report: “Now in the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the month” (web:Esth.9.1), וּבִשְׁנֵים֩ עָשָׂ֨ר חֹ֜דֶשׁ הוּא חֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֗ר בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֨ה עָשָׂ֥ר יוֹם֙ — a fresh day-by-day narrative beginning rather than a continuation of the present-tense, empire-wide summary that Esth.8.17 completes. No paragraph mark falls at either edge of this verse to corroborate or contest the seam; it is argued from the formula shift alone.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading past 8:17 into the next day's date formula would merge a summary notice with the narrative it summarizes.

boundary_rationale: This part opens where the joy notice closes: web:Esth.8.17 reports “In every province and in every city, wherever the king’s commandment and his decree came, the Jews had gladness, joy, a feast and a holiday” (web:Esth.8.17), an iterative summary of the edict’s spread. Esth.9.1 instead opens with a fronted double-date superscription, וּבִשְׁנֵים֩ עָשָׂ֨ר חֹ֜דֶשׁ הוּא חֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֗ר (oshb:Esth.9.1), “Now in the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the month” (web:Esth.9.1). This verse-opening month-then-day order is not shared by the book's other appositional month-naming verses: the recurring formula '[ordinal month], that is the month [name]' — sweep: 6 book-wide (Esth.2.16, Esth.3.7, Esth.3.13, Esth.8.9, Esth.8.12, Esth.9.1) — stands verse-initial at only two of those six (Esth.3.7, Esth.9.1), and of those two, Esth.9.1 alone orders month-then-day at its own opening. Esth.3.7 instead opens month-then-YEAR, בִּשְׁנַת֙ שְׁתֵּ֣ים עֶשְׂרֵ֔ה לַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ, "in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus" (oshb:Esth.3.7), with no day element anywhere in its opening clause; Esth.8.12’s own date clause instead falls clause-medial, six words into the verse, inverting there to day-then-month, בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֥ה עָשָׂ֛ר לְחֹ֥דֶשׁ שְׁנֵים עָשָׂ֖ר, "on the thirteenth day of the twelfth [month]" (oshb:Esth.8.12). The book's two edict-drafting verses front no date at all: both open on the scribes-summons wayyiqtol itself, וַיִּקָּרְאוּ֩ סֹפְרֵ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ (oshb:Esth.3.12) and וַיִּקָּרְא֣וּ סֹפְרֵֽי הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ (oshb:Esth.8.9), with their own date phrases medial to the verse. Esth.9.1 then pivots on the reversal-axis clause וְנַהֲפ֣וֹךְ ה֔וּא (oshb:Esth.9.1; sweep: 1 book-wide for this exact spelling), “but it turned out that the opposite happened” (web:Esth.9.1), stated as the chapter’s own thesis before any narrative wayyiqtol resumes at web:Esth.9.2. The fear motif that closes 8:17 — “for the fear of the Jews had fallen on them” (web:Esth.8.17) — recurs at web:Esth.9.2 and web:Esth.9.3 (sweep: 3 book-wide for the fear-fell formula), a thematic bridge across the seam that does not supply 9:1’s own date-anchored superscription or its reversal clause, so the formal boundary is not erased by the shared motif.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 9:1 into the joy-notice paragraph was rejected: the fronted month-day formula and the reversal clause open a discrete legal/temporal frame that 8:17’s iterative summary does not supply.

boundary_rationale: The mainline narrative resumes with a paragraph-opening Niphal perfect — no vav-consecutive prefix — נִקְהֲל֨וּ הַיְּהוּדִ֜ים בְּעָרֵיהֶ֗ם בְּכָל מְדִינוֹת֙ הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֳחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ לִשְׁלֹ֣חַ יָ֔ד בִּמְבַקְשֵׁ֖י רָֽעָתָ֑ם וְאִישׁ֙ לֹא עָמַ֣ד לִפְנֵיהֶ֔ם כִּֽי נָפַ֥ל פַּחְדָּ֖ם עַל כָּל הָעַמִּֽים (oshb:Esth.9.2), “the Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces of the King Ahasuerus, to lay hands on those who wanted to harm them. No one could withstand them, because the fear of them had fallen on all the people” (web:Esth.9.2), reporting the engagement in general terms and its universal reception. An independent waw-fronted clause with a compound four-member subject and a participial predicate then names who helped and why: וְכָל שָׂרֵ֨י הַמְּדִינ֜וֹת וְהָאֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנִ֣ים וְהַפַּח֗וֹת וְעֹשֵׂ֤י הַמְּלָאכָה֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר לַמֶּ֔לֶךְ מְנַשְּׂאִ֖ים אֶת הַיְּהוּדִ֑ים כִּֽי נָפַ֥ל פַּֽחַד מָרְדֳּכַ֖י עֲלֵיהֶֽם (oshb:Esth.9.3), “All the princes of the provinces, the local governors, the governors, and those who did the king's business helped the Jews, because the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them” (web:Esth.9.3) — only this verse's own final clause is causal; the clause naming the helpers is itself an independent statement, not a subordinate aside. A second, wholly causal clause follows: כִּֽי גָ֤דוֹל מָרְדֳּכַי֙ בְּבֵ֣ית הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ (oshb:Esth.9.4), “For Mordecai was great in the king’s house” (web:Esth.9.4) — a biographical aside on Mordecai’s rising fame. A single-witness mark falls one verse further in, interior to this span rather than at either of its edges: oshb:Esth.9.4 (petuchah, single-witness) is keyed to Esth.9.4 and so sits at Esth.9.4|9.5, between the biographical aside and the resumed mainline, not before either the aside or this span's own opening; disclosed here as tier-3 corroboration only, and, read in its actual direction, it would if anything weakly favor treating 9:2-9:4 apart from 9:5 rather than corroborating the grouping this row uses it for. The mainline resumes with the span's one true wayyiqtol, וַיַּכּ֤וּ הַיְּהוּדִים֙ בְּכָל אֹ֣יְבֵיהֶ֔ם מַכַּת חֶ֥רֶב וְהֶ֖רֶג וְאַבְדָ֑ן וַיַּֽעֲשׂ֥וּ בְשֹׂנְאֵיהֶ֖ם כִּרְצוֹנָֽם (oshb:Esth.9.5), “The Jews struck all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and with slaughter and destruction, and did what they wanted to those who hated them” (web:Esth.9.5), closing the unit with a general summary of the day’s violence before the locative-fronted shift to the named citadel, וּבְשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֗ה הָרְג֤וּ הַיְּהוּדִים֙ וְאַבֵּ֔ד חֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת אִֽישׁ (oshb:Esth.9.6), that opens the next unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off 9:3-4 as their own decision was set aside: neither carries a mainline wayyiqtol, and even though 9:3 opens as an independent clause naming the officials who helped, its own final clause and the whole of 9:4 both stay causal-explanatory to the surrounding battle report.

boundary_rationale: A locative-fronted clause opens a new, specific scene: וּבְשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֗ה הָרְג֤וּ הַיְּהוּדִים֙ וְאַבֵּ֔ד חֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת אִֽישׁ (oshb:Esth.9.6), “In the citadel of Susa, the Jews killed and destroyed five hundred men” (web:Esth.9.6), narrowing from the general provincial summary of web:Esth.9.5 to the named royal citadel. The register that follows, וְאֵ֧ת פַּרְשַׁנְדָּ֛תָא וְאֵ֥ת (oshb:Esth.9.7), continuing through web:Esth.9.8 and web:Esth.9.9, names Haman’s ten sons; the OSHB encoding carries ten x-paseq segs across these three verses (three at 9:7, three at 9:8, four at 9:9), each seg falling between the object marker and the following name (oshb:Esth.9.7 (paseq, single-witness), oshb:Esth.9.8 (paseq, single-witness), oshb:Esth.9.9 (paseq, single-witness)); this digital text carries no lb or milestone elements, so the traditional manuscript column layout and letter-size variants of the list are not represented here, and paseq itself is not unique to this register — it falls in twenty-seven verses book-wide (sweep: 27 book-wide). The register’s object and total are supplied by the summary verse that follows, עֲ֠שֶׂרֶת בְּנֵ֨י הָמָ֧ן בֶּֽן הַמְּדָ֛תָא צֹרֵ֥ר הַיְּהוּדִ֖ים הָרָ֑גוּ וּבַ֨בִּזָּ֔ה לֹ֥א שָׁלְח֖וּ אֶת יָדָֽם (oshb:Esth.9.10), “the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Jews’ enemy, but they didn't lay their hand on the plunder” (web:Esth.9.10) — the ten-sons phrase recurs at web:Esth.9.12, web:Esth.9.13, and web:Esth.9.14 (sweep: 4 book-wide) — closing with the plunder-refusal refrain, a refrain repeated at web:Esth.9.15 and web:Esth.9.16 (sweep: 3 book-wide), before the temporal-resumptive formula בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא בָּ֣א מִסְפַּ֧ר הַֽהֲרוּגִ֛ים בְּשׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ (oshb:Esth.9.11) opens the next scene at the king’s court.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Detaching the register (9:7-9) from its summary count at 9:10 was rejected, since the list supplies names alone, with no total or object apart from the verse that follows.

boundary_rationale: A temporal-resumptive formula opens a new court scene: בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא בָּ֣א מִסְפַּ֧ר הַֽהֲרוּגִ֛ים בְּשׁוּשַׁ֥ן הַבִּירָ֖ה לִפְנֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ (oshb:Esth.9.11), “On that day, the number of those who were slain in the citadel of Susa was brought before the king” (web:Esth.9.11). This 'on that day' string recurs at two other verses book-wide, sweep: 3 book-wide (Esth.5.9, Esth.8.1, Esth.9.11): at Esth.8.1 it likewise stands verse-initial and opens a genuine court scene, but at Esth.5.9 the same string sits clause-medial, behind an exit wayyiqtol and its subject (Haman leaving the banquet); of that 3-book-wide sweep, only one of the other two members shares this verse's own opening-formula function; named that way, the device is real but narrower than a blanket 'opens court scenes' claim. A single-witness mark keyed to this verse, oshb:Esth.9.11 (setumah, single-witness), falls interior to this span, one verse in at Esth.9.11|9.12, between the count-report clause and the direct speech that follows; disclosed here as weak corroboration for that internal sub-transition, not for Esth.9.11's own status as an opener. Direct speech then carries the unit: the king's report-and-offer, וַיֹּ֨אמֶר הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ לְאֶסְתֵּ֣ר הַמַּלְכָּ֗ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן (oshb:Esth.9.12), “The king said to Esther the queen … Now what is your petition? It shall be granted you” (web:Esth.9.12); Esther's reply, וַתֹּ֤אמֶר אֶסְתֵּר֙ אִם עַל הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֔וֹב (oshb:Esth.9.13), “If it pleases the king” (web:Esth.9.13) — the full seventh and last member of the petition formula that recurs across the book (sweep: 7 book-wide: 1:19, 3:9, 5:4, 5:8, 7:3, 8:5, 9:13), here also naming the gallows-tree, which recurs at 8 verses book-wide, 9 tokens (sweep: 8 book-wide, 9 tokens: Esth.2.23, Esth.5.14 carrying two, Esth.6.4, Esth.7.9, Esth.7.10, Esth.8.7, Esth.9.13, Esth.9.25); and the king's decree, וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לְהֵֽעָשׂ֣וֹת כֵּ֔ן וַתִּנָּתֵ֥ן דָּ֖ת בְּשׁוּשָׁ֑ן וְאֵ֛ת עֲשֶׂ֥רֶת בְּנֵֽי הָמָ֖ן תָּלֽוּ (oshb:Esth.9.14), “The king commanded this to be done. A decree was given out in Susa” (web:Esth.9.14). The exchange closes on the execution notice; the following verse opens a new temporal marker, וַיִּֽקָּהֲל֞וּ היהודיים הַיְּהוּדִ֣ים אֲשֶׁר בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן גַּ֠ם בְּי֣וֹם אַרְבָּעָ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ לְחֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֔ר (oshb:Esth.9.15), “on the fourteenth day also of the month Adar” (web:Esth.9.15), for the extended killing the decree just authorized. The quoted span pairs OSHB's ketiv form with its adjacent qere at this verse, a variant noted here because the text is quoted.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at 9:13 instead of 9:14 was set aside because the exchange has no formal close until the king's command is actually carried out and the decree is issued in Susa.

boundary_rationale: A new temporal marker opens the extended killing the king’s decree authorized: וַיִּֽקָּהֲל֞וּ היהודיים הַיְּהוּדִ֣ים אֲשֶׁר בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן גַּ֠ם בְּי֣וֹם אַרְבָּעָ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ לְחֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֔ר (oshb:Esth.9.15), “on the fourteenth day also of the month Adar” (web:Esth.9.15); the quoted span pairs OSHB’s ketiv immediately against its qere at this verse, disclosed because the text is quoted. A contrastive subject shift then turns to the provinces, וּשְׁאָ֣ר הַיְּהוּדִ֡ים אֲשֶׁר֩ בִּמְדִינ֨וֹת הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ נִקְהֲל֣וּ וְעָמֹ֣ד עַל נַפְשָׁ֗ם וְנ֨וֹחַ֙ מֵאֹ֣יְבֵיהֶ֔ם (oshb:Esth.9.16), “The other Jews who were in the king's provinces gathered themselves together, defended their lives, had rest from their enemies” (web:Esth.9.16), reporting rest from enemies with the infinitive-spelling form that recurs at web:Esth.9.17 and web:Esth.9.18 (sweep: 3 book-wide for that spelling: 9:16, 9:17, 9:18); naming the wider root that also reaches the finite form at web:Esth.9.22 (root sweep: 4 book-wide). A summary verse then states the thirteen/fourteen pattern for the provinces, בְּיוֹם שְׁלֹשָׁ֥ה עָשָׂ֖ר לְחֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֑ר וְנ֗וֹחַ (oshb:Esth.9.17), before a second contrastive shift back to Susa’s own thirteen/fourteen/fifteen pattern, והיהודיים וְהַיְּהוּדִ֣ים אֲשֶׁר בְּשׁוּשָׁ֗ן נִקְהֲלוּ֙ בִּשְׁלֹשָׁ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ בּ֔וֹ וּבְאַרְבָּעָ֥ה עָשָׂ֖ר בּ֑וֹ וְנ֗וֹחַ בַּחֲמִשָּׁ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ בּ֔וֹ (oshb:Esth.9.18), “But the Jews who were in Susa assembled together on the thirteenth and on the fourteenth days of the month; and on the fifteenth day of that month, they rested” (web:Esth.9.18) — a quotation that likewise carries its own ketiv reading immediately beside its qere, disclosed as quoted. An 'al ken' etiological clause then opens the closing notice, naming the villagers directly: עַל כֵּ֞ן הַיְּהוּדִ֣ים הפרוזים הַפְּרָזִ֗ים (oshb:Esth.9.19), “Therefore the Jews of the villages” (web:Esth.9.19). The verse’s remainder grounds the villages’ one-day custom in the two-city pattern just narrated: הַיֹּשְׁבִים֮ בְּעָרֵ֣י הַפְּרָזוֹת֒ עֹשִׂ֗ים אֵ֠ת י֣וֹם אַרְבָּעָ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ לְחֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֔ר שִׂמְחָ֥ה וּמִשְׁתֶּ֖ה וְי֣וֹם ט֑וֹב וּמִשְׁל֥וֹחַ מָנ֖וֹת אִ֥ישׁ לְרֵעֵֽהוּ (oshb:Esth.9.19), “who live in the unwalled towns, make the fourteenth day of the month Adar a day of gladness and feasting, a holiday, and a day of sending presents of food to one another” (web:Esth.9.19), which the following mark, oshb:Esth.9.19 (petuchah, single-witness), lends weak single-witness support without driving the reading. This etiology closes the day-itself material; Mordecai’s own writing project opens the next unit at web:Esth.9.20 with a change of subject and verb of composition rather than celebration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking this span at 9:16|9:17, so the provincial notice and the day-count summary would fall in separate decisions, was set aside because 9:17 states the very pattern 9:15-16 just narrated, without any new subject or scene change.

boundary_rationale: A single-witness petuchah mark, oshb:Esth.9.19 (petuchah, single-witness), keyed to Esth.9.19 falls at this span's own opening edge — weak corroboration for the same seam this row argues from the composition-verb shift below, disclosed here and never treated as the driver. A new subject and a verb of composition open this unit: וַיִּכְתֹּ֣ב מָרְדֳּכַ֔י אֶת הַדְּבָרִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח סְפָרִ֜ים (oshb:Esth.9.20), “Mordecai wrote these things, and sent letters to all the Jews” (web:Esth.9.20); the documents-plural noun sefarim, quoted above as the object of the sending verb, belongs to a small set of letter-dispatch notices across the book naming this same noun at the consonantal-skeleton tier (skeleton sweep: 6 book-wide: Esth.1.22, Esth.3.13, Esth.8.5, Esth.8.10, Esth.9.20, Esth.9.30; byte-tier sweep: 3, reaching only Esth.3.13, Esth.9.20, Esth.9.30), marking this as a fresh document inset rather than a continuation of the villages' etiology that closes the day-count material at web:Esth.9.19. Both purpose infinitives that follow stand inside a single verse: לְקַיֵּם֮ עֲלֵיהֶם֒ לִהְי֣וֹת עֹשִׂ֗ים אֵ֠ת י֣וֹם אַרְבָּעָ֤ה עָשָׂר֙ לְחֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֔ר וְאֵ֛ת יוֹם חֲמִשָּׁ֥ה עָשָׂ֖ר בּ֑וֹ בְּכָל שָׁנָ֖ה וְשָׁנָֽה (oshb:Esth.9.21), “to enjoin them that they should keep the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month Adar yearly” (web:Esth.9.21). The next verse opens instead on a comparative clause that grounds the observance in the day just narrated, then names the month's own reversal before a third purpose infinitive closes the inset: כַּיָּמִ֗ים אֲשֶׁר נָ֨חוּ בָהֶ֤ם הַיְּהוּדִים֙ מֵא֣וֹיְבֵיהֶ֔ם וְהַחֹ֗דֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר֩ נֶהְפַּ֨ךְ לָהֶ֤ם מִיָּגוֹן֙ לְשִׂמְחָ֔ה וּמֵאֵ֖בֶל לְי֣וֹם ט֑וֹב לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת אוֹתָ֗ם יְמֵי֙ מִשְׁתֶּ֣ה וְשִׂמְחָ֔ה וּמִשְׁל֤וֹחַ מָנוֹת֙ אִ֣ישׁ לְרֵעֵ֔הוּ וּמַתָּנ֖וֹת לָֽאֶבְיוֹנִֽים (oshb:Esth.9.22), “as the days in which the Jews had rest from their enemies, and the month which was turned to them from sorrow to gladness, and from mourning into a holiday; that they should make them days of feasting and gladness, and of sending presents of food to one another, and gifts to the needy” (web:Esth.9.22). The reversal-nifal clause at the verse's center, וְהַחֹ֗דֶשׁ אֲשֶׁר֩ נֶהְפַּ֨ךְ לָהֶ֤ם מִיָּגוֹן֙ לְשִׂמְחָ֔ה וּמֵאֵ֖בֶל לְי֣וֹם ט֑וֹב (oshb:Esth.9.22), carries a spelling distinct from 9:1's own thesis clause: sweep: 1 book-wide for this exact nifal form, counted separately from the nifal reversal clause at 9:1; both forms are nifal, with no stem contrast between them. This inset stays with its own frame through the instruction it issues; וְקִבֵּל֙ הַיְּהוּדִ֔ים אֵ֥ת אֲשֶׁר הֵחֵ֖לּוּ לַעֲשׂ֑וֹת וְאֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁר כָּתַ֥ב מָרְדֳּכַ֖י אֲלֵיהֶֽם (oshb:Esth.9.23), a change of grammatical subject and verb that opens the confirmation material rather than continuing Mordecai’s own instruction.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through 9:23 to include the Jews' acceptance was set aside, since 9:23 changes both the grammatical subject and the verb from writing to receiving.

boundary_rationale: The subject and verb change from Mordecai’s writing to the Jews’ reception: וְקִבֵּל֙ הַיְּהוּדִ֔ים אֵ֥ת אֲשֶׁר הֵחֵ֖לּוּ לַעֲשׂ֑וֹת וְאֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁר כָּתַ֥ב מָרְדֳּכַ֖י אֲלֵיהֶֽם (oshb:Esth.9.23), “The Jews accepted the custom that they had begun, as Mordecai had written to them” (web:Esth.9.23), opening the confirmation material rather than continuing the letter’s own instructions at web:Esth.9.22. A backgrounded causal clause then recounts Haman’s plot in full, כִּי֩ הָמָ֨ן בֶּֽן הַמְּדָ֜תָא הָֽאֲגָגִ֗י צֹרֵר֙ כָּל הַיְּהוּדִ֔ים חָשַׁ֥ב עַל הַיְּהוּדִ֖ים לְאַבְּדָ֑ם וְהִפִּ֥יל פּוּר֙ ה֣וּא הַגּוֹרָ֔ל לְהֻמָּ֖ם וּֽלְאַבְּדָֽם (oshb:Esth.9.24), “because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast “Pur”, that is the lot, to consume them and to destroy them” (web:Esth.9.24) — naming the pur-casting formula that also recurs at web:Esth.3.7 (sweep: 2 book-wide) — and the gallows-tree that closes the flashback at web:Esth.9.25. A qatal 'al ken' clause then opens the naming of the festival; no wayyiqtol falls anywhere in this span (checked verse-by-verse against 9:21-9:28's own bytes: every vav-initial form there is conjunctive-waw plus qatal or participle rather than the wayyiqtol shape), and the narrative mainline does not resume until Esther's own writing at web:Esth.9.29: עַל כֵּ֡ן קָֽרְאוּ֩ לַיָּמִ֨ים הָאֵ֤לֶּה פוּרִים֙ עַל שֵׁ֣ם הַפּ֔וּר (oshb:Esth.9.26), “Therefore they called these days “Purim”, from the word “Pur.”” (web:Esth.9.26). The plene spelling recurs at web:Esth.9.28 and web:Esth.9.29 (sweep: 3 book-wide: 9:26, 9:28, 9:29); the articled defective spelling at 9:31-9:32 is not reached by a contiguous skeleton sweep of the plene spelling, though the two share every consonant but the article prefix (sweep: 2 book-wide for the articled form, Esth.9.31 and Esth.9.32; the bare defective spelling without the article is itself a substring of sefarim and sweeps 8, the same six verses the neighboring letter-dispatch count reaches plus 9:31 and 9:32); WEB renders both spellings as the single term 'Purim' a reader sees (term sweep: 5 book-wide). A ratification formula then closes the block, קִיְּמ֣וּ וקבל וְקִבְּל֣וּ הַיְּהוּדִים֩ עֲלֵיהֶ֨ם (oshb:Esth.9.27), a quotation that carries OSHB’s ketiv reading immediately beside its qere for this verse, disclosed as quoted, and a remembrance clause, וְהַיָּמִ֣ים הָ֠אֵלֶּה נִזְכָּרִ֨ים וְנַעֲשִׂ֜ים בְּכָל דּ֣וֹר וָד֗וֹר (oshb:Esth.9.28), “these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation” (web:Esth.9.28), where weak single-witness corroboration follows in the mark oshb:Esth.9.28 (setumah, single-witness). Esther’s own composition then opens the next document inset at web:Esth.9.29 with a new subject, verb of writing, and explicit self-designation as 'this second letter.'
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the Haman flashback (9:24-25) into its own decision was rejected, because the 'al ken' clause that opens 9:26 continues, in the same qatal register, what the causal clause of 9:24 sets up, so the two verses function as one causal-resultative unit rather than two independent scenes.

boundary_rationale: A new subject and verb of composition open this unit, now with Esther named first: וַ֠תִּכְתֹּב אֶסְתֵּ֨ר הַמַּלְכָּ֧ה בַת אֲבִיחַ֛יִל וּמָרְדֳּכַ֥י הַיְּהוּדִ֖י אֶת כָּל תֹּ֑קֶף לְקַיֵּ֗ם אֵ֣ת אִגֶּ֧רֶת הַפּוּרִ֛ים הַזֹּ֖את הַשֵּׁנִֽית (oshb:Esth.9.29), “Then Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew wrote with all authority to confirm this second letter of Purim” (web:Esth.9.29) — the verse's own final word, הַשֵּׁנִֽית, 'the second' (oshb:Esth.9.29), is the explicit self-designation that marks this as a distinct document from the confirmation material closing at web:Esth.9.28. The setumah keyed to Esth.9.28, oshb:Esth.9.28 (setumah, single-witness), sits at this unit's own front edge as well — the same single-witness mark the neighboring confirmation block discloses at its own rear edge — offering tier-3 corroboration on both sides of the seam without settling it. The letter-dispatch noun recurs, וַיִּשְׁלַ֨ח סְפָרִ֜ים אֶל כָּל הַיְּהוּדִ֗ים אֶל שֶׁ֨בַע וְעֶשְׂרִ֤ים וּמֵאָה֙ מְדִינָ֔ה מַלְכ֖וּת אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ דִּבְרֵ֥י שָׁל֖וֹם וֶאֱמֶֽת (oshb:Esth.9.30), “He sent letters to all the Jews in the hundred twenty-seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus with words of peace and truth” (web:Esth.9.30); the hundred-twenty-seven-province numeral, אֶל שֶׁ֨בַע וְעֶשְׂרִ֤ים וּמֵאָה֙ מְדִינָ֔ה (oshb:Esth.9.30) — its three numeral words alone echo the same formula opening the book and naming the counter-edict above the byte tier (accent_stripped and skeleton sweep: 3 book-wide: 1:1, 8:9, 9:30; the full quoted phrase including 'province' is unique to this verse at every tier, byte sweep: 1 book-wide) — an empire-wide-scope echo spanning the whole book. A purpose clause follows (web:Esth.9.31), closing with a fasting notice, דִּבְרֵ֥י הַצֹּמ֖וֹת וְזַעֲקָתָֽם (oshb:Esth.9.31), “in the matter of the fastings and their mourning” (web:Esth.9.31) — the definite plural of the same fasting noun attested at 4:3 (sweep: 2 book-wide for that noun: 4:3, and 9:31 in its defective plural); the finite verb forms of that root stand only at 4:16 (sweep: 1 book-wide, two tokens: an imperative and a first-person yiqtol) — 4:3 itself carries the noun inside a coordinated mourning series, not a finite form. A closing ratification notice ends the unit and the whole institution sequence, וּמַאֲמַ֣ר אֶסְתֵּ֔ר קִיַּ֕ם דִּבְרֵ֥י הַפֻּרִ֖ים הָאֵ֑לֶּה וְנִכְתָּ֖ב בַּסֵּֽפֶר (oshb:Esth.9.32), “The commandment of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim; and it was written in the book” (web:Esth.9.32), where a single-witness mark follows, oshb:Esth.9.32 (petuchah, single-witness), offering weak corroboration at the level Writings marks allow. A new subject and topic then open the epilogue at web:Esth.10.1, turning from Purim to royal tribute.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 9:29 as a continuation of the confirmation block instead of a new document was set aside, because the verse explicitly labels itself a second, distinct letter rather than an extension of the first.

boundary_rationale: A new subject and topic open this final unit: וַיָּשֶׂם֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ אחשרש אֲחַשְׁוֵר֧וֹשׁ מַ֛ס עַל הָאָ֖רֶץ וְאִיֵּ֥י הַיָּֽם (oshb:Esth.10.1), a quotation that carries OSHB’s ketiv reading immediately beside its qere for the king’s name in this verse, disclosed as quoted, “King Ahasuerus laid a tribute on the land and on the islands of the sea” (web:Esth.10.1), turning from the Purim institution that closes at web:Esth.9.32 to a royal-administration notice naming the king in full title. Immediately before this span begins, Esth.9.32 carries its own petuchah, oshb:Esth.9.32 (petuchah, single-witness); named here as front-edge corroboration, tier-3 and non-driving. The chronicle-citation formula follows, וְכָל מַעֲשֵׂ֤ה תָקְפּוֹ֙ וּגְב֣וּרָת֔וֹ וּפָרָשַׁת֙ גְּדֻלַּ֣ת מָרְדֳּכַ֔י אֲשֶׁ֥ר גִּדְּל֖וֹ הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ הֲלוֹא הֵ֣ם כְּתוּבִ֗ים עַל סֵ֨פֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֔ים לְמַלְכֵ֖י מָדַ֥י וּפָרָֽס (oshb:Esth.10.2), “Aren't all the acts of his power and of his might, and the full account of the greatness of Mordecai, to which the king advanced him, written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia” (web:Esth.10.2). The closing clause of that formula, עַל סֵ֨פֶר֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י הַיָּמִ֔ים לְמַלְכֵ֖י מָדַ֥י וּפָרָֽס (oshb:Esth.10.2), is unique to this verse at every tier — byte sweep: 1 book-wide, skeleton sweep: 1 book-wide — since it opens with the separate-word preposition al; the exposition's Bigthan-and-Teresh notice instead closes on a prefixed-bet form of the shorter core phrase, sefer divrei hayamim, matching this verse's own core phrase already at the accent_stripped tier (accent_stripped sweep: 2 book-wide: Esth.2.23, Esth.10.2; at byte tier each verse's pointed form is unique to itself, sweep: 1 book-wide for each, since the two verses' cantillation accents differ even though the underlying consonants and vowel points agree). A closing tribute to Mordecai ends the book, כִּ֣י מָרְדֳּכַ֣י הַיְּהוּדִ֗י מִשְׁנֶה֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ וְגָדוֹל֙ לַיְּהוּדִ֔ים וְרָצ֖וּי לְרֹ֣ב אֶחָ֑יו דֹּרֵ֥שׁ טוֹב֙ לְעַמּ֔וֹ וְדֹבֵ֥ר שָׁל֖וֹם לְכָל זַרְעֽוֹ (oshb:Esth.10.3), “For Mordecai the Jew was next to King Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews … seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his descendants” (web:Esth.10.3), a benediction-style summary that supplies its own closing rather than opening onto further narration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this epilogue into Esther's second letter as one continuous closing unit was set aside, since 10:1 changes both subject and topic entirely, from Purim's ratification to an unrelated tribute notice.

boundary_rationale: The narrator opens with Job's name and place, then states his character in a fourfold formula: “That man was blameless and upright, and one who feared God, and turned away from evil” (web:Job.1.1), Hebrew תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר וִירֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְסָ֥ר מֵרָֽע (oshb:Job.1.1) -- the same four-word chain-- a six-word clause carrying the conjunctive waw on the yare-word that is this verse's own; Yahweh echoes the same character portrait twice more with the waw dropped (oshb:Job.1.8, oshb:Job.2.3). The two-word head תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר is the object that actually recurs byte-identically all three times -- sweep: 3 book-wide, byte tier (Job.1.1, Job.1.8, Job.2.3) -- anchoring the narrator's portrait to Yahweh's own repeated commendation. The row continues without any participant or scene change through the census of sons, daughters, and livestock and into the sons' recurring feast cycle, closed by Job's own precautionary sacrifices and the narrator's habitual summary “Job did so continually” (web:Job.1.5). A petuchah follows oshb:Job.1.5 (single-witness), marking a paragraph close immediately before the heavenly-court scene opens.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the wealth catalog from the sacrificial habit was considered, but nothing in the Hebrew marks an internal break inside this unified portrait of Job's piety.
literature_type_guess: prose frame: Job's character portrait and wealth catalog

boundary_rationale: A fresh scene opens with the verse-initial formula וַיְהִ֣י הַיּ֔וֹם (oshb:Job.1.6; skeleton-tier sweep: 3 book-wide (byte tier 2: 1:6 and 2:1 are byte-identical; 1:13 differs in accents), recurring at the next two court/disaster scenes), as the sons of God present themselves before Yahweh and “Satan also came among them” (web:Job.1.6); the satan is introduced with the article, הַשָּׂטָ֖ן (oshb:Job.1.6), a definite description carried through the whole frame rather than a proper name. Yahweh's opening question “Where have you come from?” (web:Job.1.7) and his commendation “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil” (web:Job.1.8) are both verse-initial vayomer frames naming Yahweh as speaker; the satan's own answer to Yahweh's opening question sits interior to Job.1.7, before his separate verse-initial vaya'an formula opens the sharper challenge at Job.1.9.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row through the wager and Job's commendation was considered, but the satan's own vaya'an formula marks where his sharper challenge properly begins.
literature_type_guess: heavenly audience: God's sons and satan present together

boundary_rationale: The satan's verse-initial vaya'an formula וַיַּ֧עַן הַשָּׂטָ֛ן אֶת יְהוָ֖ה (oshb:Job.1.9) opens his challenge, “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (web:Job.1.9), moving through his accusation to the wager formula שְֽׁלַֽח נָ֣א יָֽדְךָ֔ (oshb:Job.1.11), “But stretch out your hand now, and touch all that he has, and he will renounce you to your face” (web:Job.1.11; sweep: 2 book-wide, recurring in the second court scene). Yahweh's grant of permission, “Behold, all that he has is in your power. Only on himself don't stretch out your hand” (web:Job.1.12), is followed in the same verse by the satan's departure, וַיֵּצֵא֙ הַשָּׂטָ֔ן מֵעִ֖ם פְּנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה (oshb:Job.1.12), which closes the scene; no fresh scene-opening formula intervenes before this clause, so the row keeps challenge, wager, and exit together as one exchange.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the wager and the permission as two separate rows was weighed, but both belong to the one continuous exchange the satan's challenge formula opens.
literature_type_guess: satan's first challenge: wager to test Job's devotion

boundary_rationale: A second ויהי היום scene-opening formula, וַיְהִ֖י הַיּ֑וֹם (oshb:Job.1.13; skeleton-tier sweep: 3 book-wide (byte tier 2: 1:6 and 2:1 are byte-identical; 1:13 differs in accents)), turns the narrative from the court to the sons' and daughters' feast at their oldest brother's house. Four messengers arrive in sequence, the middle two introduced by the matching relay formula ע֣וֹד זֶ֣ה מְדַבֵּ֗ר (oshb:Job.1.16) and (oshb:Job.1.17) -- sweep: 2 book-wide for this spelling -- and the fourth by the variant spelling עַ֚ד זֶ֣ה מְדַבֵּ֔ר (oshb:Job.1.18; sweep: 1 book-wide, a distinct spelling from the other two and not a ketiv/qere note). Every one of the four reports, including the first, closes on the identical refrain וָֽאִמָּ֨לְטָ֧ה רַק אֲנִ֛י לְבַדִּ֖י לְהַגִּ֥יד לָֽךְ (oshb:Job.1.15), “I alone have escaped to tell you” (web:Job.1.15) At consonantal/skeleton tier the refrain sweeps 4 book-wide (oshb:Job.1.15, oshb:Job.1.16, oshb:Job.1.17, oshb:Job.1.19); at pointed/byte tier it sweeps 1 (oshb:Job.1.15 alone carries a meteg on its opening word that the other three lack). Naming the tier, the skeleton-level identity still binds all four blows into a single escalating relay rather than four independent reports.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating the earliest messenger's report from the three that follow was an option, but the shared escape-refrain binds all four into one relay.
literature_type_guess: disaster relay: four successive messengers and calamities

boundary_rationale: With the final messenger's report finished, the subject shifts to Job himself: “Then Job arose, and tore his robe, and shaved his head, and fell down on the ground, and worshiped” (web:Job.1.20). His own speech follows, “Yahweh gave, and Yahweh has taken away. Blessed be Yahweh's name” (web:Job.1.21), and the scene closes on the narrator's integrity verdict בְּכָל זֹ֖את (oshb:Job.1.22), “In all this, Job didn't sin, nor charge God with wrongdoing” (web:Job.1.22; sweep: 2 book-wide, recurring after the second affliction). A petuchah follows oshb:Job.1.22 (single-witness), corroborating the close of this opening movement before the second court scene reopens.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding Job's mourning posture into the messenger-relay row was possible, but the shift from the messengers' speech to Job's own action marks a new narrative beat.
literature_type_guess: Job's response: mourning posture and integrity maintained

boundary_rationale: The scene-opening formula recurs a third time, וַיְהִ֣י הַיּ֔וֹם (oshb:Job.2.1; skeleton-tier sweep: 3 book-wide (byte tier 2: 1:6 and 2:1 are byte-identical; 1:13 differs in accents), its final member), reopening the heavenly court: “Again, on the day when God's sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan came also among them to present himself before Yahweh” (web:Job.2.1). Yahweh's opening question itself changes wording from the first court scene -- אֵ֥י מִזֶּ֖ה תָּבֹ֑א (oshb:Job.2.2) against מֵאַ֣יִן תָּבֹ֑א (oshb:Job.1.7), two distinct interrogative constructions that WEB renders identically (“Where have you come from?”, web:Job.1.7 and web:Job.2.2) -- before his commendation is extended: “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil. He still maintains his integrity, although you incited me against him, to ruin him without cause” (web:Job.2.3). The clause itself, spliced fresh from Job.2.3's own bytes, reads אִ֣ישׁ תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר יְרֵ֥א אֱלֹהִ֖ים וְסָ֣ר מֵרָ֑ע (oshb:Job.2.3); its two-word head תָּ֧ם וְיָשָׁ֛ר is the character formula's third and byte-identical attestation -- skeleton-tier sweep: 3 book-wide (byte tier 2: 1:6 and 2:1 are byte-identical; 1:13 differs in accents) (Job.1.1, Job.1.8, Job.2.3) -- inside a commendation that now opens אֶל עַבְדִּ֣י אִיּוֹב֒ (oshb:Job.2.3), the preposition shifted from עַל עַבְדִּ֣י אִיּ֑וֹב (oshb:Job.1.8), and carrying the added clause about the satan's own incitement that the first court scene did not have.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this row through the satan's second challenge was considered, but his own vaya'an formula opens a distinct speech-turn at Job.2.4.
literature_type_guess: heavenly court reconvened: God's commendation renewed

boundary_rationale: The satan's second vaya'an formula, וַיַּ֧עַן הַשָּׂטָ֛ן אֶת יְהוָ֖ה (oshb:Job.2.4), opens his reply, “Skin for skin. Yes, all that a man has he will give for his life” (web:Job.2.4), and the wager formula recurs, שְֽׁלַֽח נָ֣א יָֽדְךָ֔ (oshb:Job.2.5), “But stretch out your hand now, and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will renounce you to your face” (web:Job.2.5; sweep: 2 book-wide). Yahweh's second grant of permission, “Behold, he is in your hand. Only spare his life” (web:Job.2.6), is followed in the same verse-initial chain by the satan's departure and, without any intervening scene-opening formula, by the blow itself: וַיֵּצֵא֙ הַשָּׂטָ֔ן מֵאֵ֖ת פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה וַיַּ֤ךְ אֶת אִיּוֹב֙ בִּשְׁחִ֣ין רָ֔ע מִכַּ֥ף רַגְל֖וֹ עד וְעַ֥ד קָדְקֳדֽוֹ (oshb:Job.2.7; the phrase after the departure carries a ketiv/qere pair עד / ועד, 'to' / 'and to', single-witness). Unlike the earlier court scene, where ויהי היום reopens a fresh scene at Job.1.13 after the satan's exit, no such formula separates the departure from the strike here; the row is drawn through the whole verse rather than cut at Job.2.6|Job.2.7, though that earlier-cutting alternative -- matching the earlier court scene's own shape -- is a live rival and is disclosed rather than resolved.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Placing the seam at Job.2.6|Job.2.7 instead, matching the earlier court scene's own pattern, remains a live alternative and is disclosed here rather than resolved.
literature_type_guess: satan's second wager: bodily affliction strike permitted

boundary_rationale: After the strike recorded at the end of Job.2.7, Job himself becomes the acting subject in his own right, apart from the divine court: “He took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, and he sat among the ashes” (web:Job.2.8). This shift in subject and setting -- from the divine court to Job alone on the ash heap -- is the clearest participant-based break available at whole-verse grain, since the striking itself is fused to the satan's departure inside Job.2.7 with no scene-opening formula of its own; the rival cut at Job.2.6|Job.2.7 remains disclosed from the row before this one. His wife's provocation follows, “Do you still maintain your integrity? Renounce God, and die” (web:Job.2.9), and Job's rebuttal closes the scene with the verdict formula's second and final attestation, בְּכָל זֹ֛את (oshb:Job.2.10), “In all this Job didn't sin with his lips” (web:Job.2.10; sweep: 2 book-wide). A petuchah follows oshb:Job.2.10 (single-witness), corroborating the close before the friends arrive.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Two distinct rivals were weighed for this row's near edge, each on its own ground. Opening at whole-verse Job.2.7 -- matching the earlier court scene's own shape, where Yahweh's permission and the satan's exit close at 1:12 before ויהי היום reopens a fresh scene at 1:13 -- remains a live alternative; it is not excluded because no formula supports it, but because Job.2.7's strike clause is bound to its own exit clause inside one unbroken verse with no mark keyed to either Job.2.6 or Job.2.7 separating them. A narrower rival, splitting Job.2.7 itself between its exit clause וַיֵּצֵא֙ הַשָּׂטָ֔ן מֵאֵ֖ת פְּנֵ֣י יְהוָ֑ה and its strike clause וַיַּ֤ךְ אֶת אִיּוֹב֙ בִּשְׁחִ֣ין רָ֔ע, is rejected because no fresh formula supports cutting a single verse in half.
literature_type_guess: affliction and wife: Job on ash heap with taunt

boundary_rationale: Job's three friends enter by name, אֱלִיפַ֤ז הַתֵּימָנִי֙ וּבִלְדַּ֣ד הַשּׁוּחִ֔י וְצוֹפַ֖ר הַנַּֽעֲמָתִ֑י (oshb:Job.2.11): Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite, “and they made an appointment together to come to sympathize with him and to comfort him” (web:Job.2.11). Their approach and grief are narrated at web:Job.2.12, “they raised their voices, and wept” before the row closes on the seven-day silent vigil, “So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great” (web:Job.2.13). This unit's closing edge rests on the wordlessness Job.2.13 states outright -- “no one spoke a word to him” -- which is broken precisely at the seam with web:Job.3.1, where the temporal marker אַחֲרֵי כֵ֗ן ('after this') reopens Job's own voice, ending the vigil's silence with his extended lament.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading through into Job's lament was considered, but the seven-day silence this row records is broken specifically by the temporal marker that reopens his voice after the vigil.
literature_type_guess: three friends arrive: gathering and seven-day silence

boundary_rationale: The narrator's report that “After this Job opened his mouth, and cursed the day of his birth.” (web:Job.3.1) is followed at once by the dialogue-formula “Job answered:” (web:Job.3.2; Hebrew וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר), a doubled introduction to the same speech-act: a mouth-opening idiom (פָּתַ֤ח אִיּוֹב֙ אֶת פִּ֔יהוּ) paired with the vaya'an-formula proper. Both verses stand apart in register from the wholly poetic curse that opens at 3:3, and together they mark the turn from the silence that closes 2:13 (“So they sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his grief was very great.” web:Job.2.13) to Job's own voice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Split the pair at the Masoretic paragraph break following 3:1 into two one-verse rows, Job.3.1-Job.3.1 and Job.3.2-Job.3.2, honoring that (single-witness) division over the shared introductory function argued here.
literature_type_guess: discourse frame: narrative mouth-opening and dialogue formula

boundary_rationale: The curse proper opens with the jussive incipit “Let the day perish in which I was born, the night which said, ‘There is a boy conceived.” (web:Job.3.3; Hebrew יֹ֣אבַד י֭וֹם, ‘let the day perish’), a form independently swept at 1 occurrence book-wide (sweep: 1 book-wide, byte tier), and runs a chain of day/night imprecations through “because it didn’t shut up the doors of my mother’s womb, nor did it hide trouble from my eyes.” (web:Job.3.10), which closes the chain by giving its motive (the day did not shut the womb). The next verse turns from cursing the day to interrogating Job's own birth, a distinct topic marked at its own opening (the seam at 3:10|3:11).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Break the curse chain at 3:6|3:7 was weighed differently from 3:8|3:9: 3:7 does open with a verse-initial presentative, הִנֵּ֤ה הַלַּ֣יְלָה הַ֭הוּא יְהִ֣י גַלְמ֑וּד אַל תָּבֹ֖א רְנָנָ֣ה בֽוֹ (oshb:Job.3.7), a tier-1 signal class in its own right, but it governs the same subject 3:6 has already introduced -- both verses open on 'that night' (הַלַּ֥יְלָה הַהוּא֮ יִקָּחֵ֪ה֫וּ אֹ֥פֶל אַל יִ֭חַדְּ בִּימֵ֣י שָׁנָ֑ה בְּמִסְפַּ֥ר יְ֝רָחִ֗ים אַל יָבֹֽא, oshb:Job.3.6) -- so the presentative resumes the day/night imprecation rather than turning to a new topic, and the chain is kept whole through it. No interrogative, vocative, or formula marks 3:8|3:9.
literature_type_guess: curse strophe: day perish and night imprecation opening

boundary_rationale: “Why didn’t I die from the womb? Why didn’t I give up the spirit when my mother bore me?” (web:Job.3.11; Hebrew לָ֤מָּה לֹּ֣א מֵרֶ֣חֶם אָמ֑וּת) opens a why-not-death interrogative -- the four-word clause itself is a singleton, sweep: 1 book-wide at byte tier. Its opening word לָ֤מָּה recurs pointed and accented identically at only one other verse, oshb:Job.3.20 -- sweep: 2 book-wide, byte tier (Job.3.11, Job.3.20) -- giving this strophe a matching bookend at its far edge, though 3:20's question shares only the opening particle with 3:11's, not the same interrogative content. The unit develops the death-wish through the rest-among-kings and rest-among-prisoners imagery down to “The small and the great are there. The servant is free from his master.” (web:Job.3.19), which closes on the small-and-great leveling motif before the topic turns again at 3:20.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treat 3:13-3:15 (rest among kings) and 3:16-3:19 (rest among the unborn and the leveled dead) as two separate rows, but neither sub-block opens on a fresh interrogative, vocative, or formula.
literature_type_guess: interrogative strophe: why birth and death's relief sought

boundary_rationale: “Why is light given to him who is in misery, life to the bitter in soul,” (web:Job.3.20; Hebrew לָ֤מָּה יִתֵּ֣ן לְעָמֵ֣ל א֑וֹר) reopens the interrogative with the same pointed form as 3:11 (sweep: 2 book-wide, byte tier), now turned from the wish for death to the question of light and life for the sufferer. The strophe, and Job's whole opening speech, closes at “I am not at ease, neither am I quiet, neither do I have rest; but trouble comes.” (web:Job.3.26), whose confession of unrest is corroborated (tier-3, single-witness) by the petuchah following that verse; the verse also carries a paseq, but paseq is an intra-verse disjunctive with no encoded position, so it is disclosed as a bare inventory fact rather than treated as edge corroboration. Eliphaz's formula opens fresh at Job.4.1, closing the lament this verse ends.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extend this row through 4:1 on the ground that the vaya'an formula is itself part of the lament's close, but the formula's speaker token (Eliphaz, not Job) marks a new speech, not a continuation of it.
literature_type_guess: why-light strophe: darkness preferred to light of being

boundary_rationale: “Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered,” (web:Job.4.1; Hebrew וַ֭יַּעַן אֱלִיפַ֥ז הַֽתֵּימָנִ֗י וַיֹּאמַֽר) is one member of the book's vaya'an inventory (sweep: 27 book-wide) and, with the spelling הַֽתֵּימָנִ֗י, one of three Eliphaz-token vaya'an members (sweep: 3 book-wide), spelling-distinct from the defective הַֽתֵּמָנִ֗י opening oshb:Job.22.1 -- the same WEB rendering at web:Job.22.1 ('Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered') erases the distinction, so the orthographic claim is anchored to the Hebrew bytes, not the English witness. The courteous but pointed opening address runs from “If someone ventures to talk with you, will you be grieved? But who can withhold himself from speaking?” (web:Job.4.2) through the rhetorical question closing “Isn’t your piety your confidence? Isn’t the integrity of your ways your hope?” (web:Job.4.6), after which the imperative zkhor na opens a fresh appeal.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolate 4:1 as its own one-verse frame row to mirror the treatment given the doubled introduction at 3:1-3:2, but 4:1 carries one formula, not a paired one, and does not warrant the same isolation.
literature_type_guess: Eliphaz opens: formula plus address to Job's former counsel

boundary_rationale: “Remember, now, who ever perished, being innocent? Or where were the upright cut off?” (web:Job.4.7; Hebrew זְכָר נָ֗א, ‘remember, now’) opens with an imperative topic-turn appealing to observed precedent, a pattern of retribution the strophe illustrates through the lion imagery running to “The old lion perishes for lack of prey. The cubs of the lioness are scattered abroad.” (web:Job.4.11). The following verse drops the generic proverb register for Eliphaz's own personal account (“Now a thing was secretly brought to me. My ear received a whisper of it.” web:Job.4.12), a participant shift that marks the far edge of this row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Divide the lion imagery of 4:10-4:11 from the retribution proverb of 4:7-4:9 as its own row, but the lions illustrate rather than reopen the argument, and no fresh interrogative or vocative marks 4:10.
literature_type_guess: retribution proverb strophe: lion figure illustrating doom

boundary_rationale: “Now a thing was secretly brought to me. My ear received a whisper of it.” (web:Job.4.12; Hebrew וְ֭אֵלַי דָּבָ֣ר יְגֻנָּ֑ב) turns to Eliphaz's own night-vision testimony, a personal-voice register distinct from the preceding proverb. The strophe narrates the experience of the vision through its close, “It stood still, but I couldn’t discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes. Silence, then I heard a voice, saying,” (web:Job.4.16), whose final clause (דְּמָמָ֖ה וָק֣וֹל אֶשְׁמָֽע, ‘silence, then a voice I heard’) is a discourse frame introducing direct speech -- a perception clause with no verb of speaking, not a member of the book's verse-initial vayomer formula family; the quoted content itself begins at 4:17, not before.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Fold 4:17-4:21 into this row on the ground that the vision is one continuous unit through 4:21, but the shift from narrated experience to quoted oracle is itself marked by the discourse frame closing 4:16b -- a perception clause, not a member of the book's verse-initial vayomer formula family -- and deserves its own row.
literature_type_guess: night-vision narrative: Eliphaz's oracle frame strophe

boundary_rationale: The quoted voice's oracle opens “Shall mortal man be more just than God? Shall a man be more pure than his Maker?” (web:Job.4.17; Hebrew הַֽ֭אֱנוֹשׁ מֵאֱל֣וֹהַ יִצְדָּ֑ק, a byte-true interrogative-he construction -- the row's own near-edge driver, since 4:16's closing clause דְּמָמָ֖ה וָק֣וֹל אֶשְׁמָֽע (oshb:Job.4.16) carries no verb of speaking and belongs to no formula family; WEB's trailing 'saying,' bridges the two verses in translation only. The oracle runs to “Isn’t their tent cord plucked up within them? They die, and that without wisdom.” (web:Job.4.21), which closes the embedded speech. Eliphaz's own voice resumes with a fresh imperative topic-turn at 5:1 (qra na), the seam bounding this row's far edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carry the oracle through 5:1 as one continuous unit, since both open with rhetorical questions, but 5:1's qra na addresses Job directly in Eliphaz's own voice, not the vision's.
literature_type_guess: night-voice oracle: mortal frailty against divine judgment

boundary_rationale: “Call now; is there any who will answer you? To which of the holy ones will you turn?” (web:Job.5.1; Hebrew קְֽרָא נָ֭א, ‘call now’) opens an imperative challenge paralleling the zkhor na of 4:7 (both topic-turn imperatives addressed to Job), and the strophe illustrates the fool's perishing down to “but man is born to trouble, as the sparks fly upward.” (web:Job.5.7), a proverbial close on man's trouble-bound birth. The following verse turns to Eliphaz's own stance with an adversative-plus-pronoun opening, marking the far edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Split the fool's-fate illustration of 5:2-5:7 from the opening challenge of 5:1 as its own row, but the challenge and its illustration share one interrogative frame with no internal topic-turn.
literature_type_guess: fool's-fate strophe: uncontained wrath leads to ruin

boundary_rationale: “But as for me, I would seek God. I would commit my cause to God,” (web:Job.5.8; Hebrew אוּלָ֗ם אֲ֭נִי, ‘but as for me’) marks a stance shift: Eliphaz sets his own counsel (seeking God) against the fool just described, and the strophe catalogs divine providence through “So the poor has hope, and injustice shuts her mouth.” (web:Job.5.16), which closes on the poor's hope and injustice's silenced mouth. The presentative hinneh reopens the address at 5:17, marking the far edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Break this providence catalog at 5:12|5:13, where the crafty-versus-wise contrast sharpens, but no vocative, interrogative, or formula marks that internal point.
literature_type_guess: providence catalog: God's counsel against the fool's way

boundary_rationale: “Behold, happy is the man whom God corrects. Therefore do not despise the chastening of the Almighty.” (web:Job.5.17; Hebrew הִנֵּ֤ה אַשְׁרֵ֣י) opens the discipline-and-blessing strophe with the presentative hinneh, and the speech closes on a second presentative at “Behold, we have researched it. It is so. Hear it, and know it for your good.” (web:Job.5.27; Hebrew הִנֵּה זֹ֭את), Eliphaz's own appeal to what he and his tradition have researched — verse-initial hinneh framing both edges of this row. The speech ends there: Job.6.1 opens “Then Job answered,” (web:Job.6.1) with the vaya'an formula under a new speaker token (Iyov); the formula closes Eliphaz's speech and opens Job's reply, corroborated (tier-3, single-witness) by the petuchah following oshb:Job.5.27.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Read the exhortation of 5:26-5:27 as a short coda separate from the discipline strophe of 5:17-5:25, but no interrogative, vocative, or formula opens 5:26, and both edges of the 5:17-5:27 span share the same hinneh framing.
literature_type_guess: discipline and blessing strophe: Eliphaz's closing hinneh frame

boundary_rationale: The seam at 5:27|6:1 is a speaker change: Eliphaz's admonition closes “Behold, we have researched it. It is so. Hear it, and know it for your good.” web:Job.5.27, and the verse-initial formula וַיַּ֥עַן אִיּ֗וֹב וַיֹּאמַֽר (oshb:Job.6.1) hands the floor to Job -- the tier-1 dialogue-formula spine's marker for a new voice, one of Job's eleven vaya'an-family tokens book-wide (sweep: 11 book-wide, per the formula inventory; Job also carries two vayosef-family tokens elsewhere in the dialogue, a distinct verb-family from vaya'an). Job opens by asking that his anguish be weighed, “Oh that my anguish were weighed, and all my calamity laid in the balances!” web:Job.6.2, a weight he then declares “heavier than the sand of the seas” web:Job.6.3, names the Almighty's arrows and God's terrors as the cause of his rash words web:Job.6.4, then defends the outburst with a pair of settled-nature analogies, “Does the wild donkey bray when he has grass? Or does the ox low over his fodder?” web:Job.6.5, extended by the tasteless-food pair web:Job.6.6, web:Job.6.7. The row keeps the formula and its immediate self-justification together as one opening movement of the reply.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Job.6.1 into its own row would isolate the bare formula from the self-justification it introduces, with no competing tier-1 signal before the wish-formula turn that follows.
literature_type_guess: Job's reply opens: affliction weight outweighs sand's measure

boundary_rationale: A topic-turn interrogative-wish opens the row: מִֽי יִ֭תֵּן תָּב֣וֹא שֶֽׁאֱלָתִ֑י וְ֝תִקְוָתִ֗י יִתֵּ֥ן אֱלֽוֹהַּ (oshb:Job.6.8), an instance of the dialogue-wide mi-yitten wish formula (sweep: 9 verses book-wide, 10 tokens, one verse carrying two, independently re-swept at skeleton tier). Job spells the wish out as a plea to be let go and cut off web:Job.6.9, holds his one consolation to be that he has “not denied the words of the Holy One” web:Job.6.10, then turns to a run of rhetorical questions about his exhausted capacity, “What is my strength, that I should wait? What is my end, that I should be patient?” web:Job.6.11, “Is my strength the strength of stones? Or is my flesh of bronze?” web:Job.6.12, closing on the admission that “wisdom is driven away from me” web:Job.6.13. The row ends before the next strophe's turn from Job's own exhausted capacity to a third-person accusation of the friends, opening at Job.6.14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through Job.6.14 would merge the wish-formula lament with the brook-metaphor rebuke of the friends that follows it.
literature_type_guess: death wish strophe: Job seeks release from torment

boundary_rationale: A third-person topic shift opens the row: “To him who is ready to faint, kindness should be shown from his friend; even to him who forsakes the fear of the Almighty.” web:Job.6.14 (Hebrew לַמָּ֣ס מֵרֵעֵ֣הוּ חָ֑סֶד וְיִרְאַ֖ת שַׁדַּ֣י יַעֲזֽוֹב, oshb:Job.6.14, grammatically third-person throughout -- the friend-word carries a 3ms suffix and the verb is 3ms imperfect, with no vocative particle), pivoting the subject-matter from Job's own exhaustion to a gnomic charge against companions in general. He extends the charge with the brook-caravan metaphor, “My brothers have dealt deceitfully as a brook, as the channel of brooks that pass away;” web:Job.6.15, traces the image through the melting ice and vanishing caravans of web:Job.6.16-Job.6.20, then the address itself turns second-person for the first time in the unit, “For now you are nothing. You see a terror, and are afraid.” web:Job.6.21 (Hebrew כִּֽי עַ֭תָּה הֱיִ֣יתֶם לא ל֑וֹ תִּֽרְא֥וּ חֲ֝תַ֗ת וַתִּירָֽאוּ, oshb:Job.6.21, all second-person plural), before closing on a pair of denials that he ever asked the friends for a gift or ransom, web:Job.6.22-Job.6.23. This second-person address shift at 6:21 is a genuine tier-1 signal, not mere texture; it runs unbroken to the end of the chapter, and it is disclosed here as a live internal candidate for this unit's own seam rather than dismissed. It is not adopted as the row's own edge because the third-person charge and its direct application are held together as one movement of the friend-rebuke closing on Job's self-examination through 6:23; the alternative seam at 6:20|6:21 is disclosed here as a live, comparably warranted rival rather than resolved.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the row at Job.6.20|Job.6.21 for the second-person turn there is a live rival, not a texture-only consideration: 6:21 opens the unit's first 2mp forms and second-person address runs unbroken through 6:29 (nine verses, Job.6.21-Job.6.29), a comparably or better-warranted internal seam than the 6:23|6:24 edge kept here. It is disclosed rather than adopted because the row is held as one continuous rebuke of the friends across the third-person charge and its direct application; the question is left open rather than resolved, in the same spirit as the frame's own disclosed 2:6|2:7 crux.
literature_type_guess: friends rebuke: why abandon one brought low and helpless

boundary_rationale: An imperative shift opens the row: ה֭וֹרוּנִי וַאֲנִ֣י אַחֲרִ֑ישׁ וּמַה שָּׁ֝גִ֗יתִי הָבִ֥ינוּ לִֽי (oshb:Job.6.24), Job's invitation to be corrected rather than the denial he had just voiced. He weighs “words of uprightness” against the friends' empty reproof web:Job.6.25, protests that their reproof treats the speeches of one who is desperate as mere wind while they would gamble away the fatherless web:Job.6.26-Job.6.27, then appeals directly, “Now therefore be pleased to look at me, for surely I will not lie to your face.” web:Job.6.28, repeats the appeal, “Please return. Let there be no injustice. Yes, return again. My cause is righteous.” web:Job.6.29, and closes on a self-examining question, “Is there injustice on my tongue? Can’t my taste discern mischievous things?” web:Job.6.30. The row runs from the imperative petition to the end of the chapter, closing Job's rebuke of the friends before the reply turns, in the next chapter, to a meditation on human toil in general.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying the row back to include the brook-metaphor rebuke above it would stretch one strophe well past a comfortable length without an intervening tier-1 seam to justify the span. A second rival was weighed at this row's own near edge: 6:28 opens with the ve'attah turn, וְ֭עַתָּה הוֹאִ֣ילוּ פְנוּ בִ֑י וְעַל פְּ֝נֵיכֶ֗ם אִם אֲכַזֵּֽב (oshb:Job.6.28) -- a device that sweeps 8 book-wide (Job.6.28, Job.30.1, Job.30.9, Job.30.16, Job.35.15, Job.37.21, Job.42.5, Job.42.8) and keys strophe structure elsewhere in the book -- followed at 6:29 by an imperative-plus-na, שֻֽׁבוּ נָ֭א אַל תְּהִ֣י עַוְלָ֑ה ושבי וְשׁ֥וּבוּ ע֝וֹד צִדְקִי בָֽהּ (oshb:Job.6.29), the same form-class opening 5:1 (קְֽרָא נָ֭א) and 4:7 (זְכָר נָ֗א). Splitting at 6:27|6:28 was rejected because 6:28's appeal ('look at me... I will not lie to your face') and 6:29's renewed imperative ('return... my cause is righteous') both continue rather than reopen the direct appeal Job begins at 6:24 -- one imperative-headed appeal running from ה֭וֹרוּנִי at 6:24 through the self-examining close at 6:30 -- so the row is kept whole through both internal signals rather than split at either.
literature_type_guess: Job appeals: teach me what error caused this punishment

boundary_rationale: The speech turns from direct address of the friends to a general reflection on human toil, opening with a rhetorical question about shared hardship rather than a second-person accusation: “Isn’t a man forced to labor on earth? Aren’t his days like the days of a hired hand?” web:Job.7.1. Job compares himself to “a servant who earnestly desires the shadow” web:Job.7.2, applies the image to his own “months of misery” and wearisome nights web:Job.7.3, describes lying awake until dawn web:Job.7.4, and catalogs his bodily affliction, “My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust. My skin closes up, and breaks out afresh.” web:Job.7.5, closing on “My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle, and are spent without hope.” web:Job.7.6. The row ends before the imperative that turns the complaint toward God directly.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading Job.7.1 as a continuation of chapter six's direct rebuke would erase the shift from second-person accusation to a general reflection on human labor.
literature_type_guess: hardship complaint strophe: hired servant and restless nights

boundary_rationale: An imperative addressed to God opens the row: זְ֭כֹר כִּי ר֣וּחַ חַיָּ֑י לֹא תָשׁ֥וּב עֵ֝ינִ֗י לִרְא֥וֹת טֽוֹב (oshb:Job.7.7), “Oh remember that my life is a breath. My eye will no more see good.” web:Job.7.7. The row stays with mortality across four verses: the eye that will see him no more web:Job.7.8, the cloud that vanishes and the one who goes down to Sheol web:Job.7.9, and the house and place that will no longer know him web:Job.7.10. The unit is short, but it is bounded on both sides by a change of mode -- the imperative petition opening it and the self-assertive resolve of the next strophe closing it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Job.7.7-10 as a continuation of the toil meditation above it would erase the imperative address-shift that opens it and turns the complaint to address God directly rather than the human audience.
literature_type_guess: remembrance complaint: God will not relent or acknowledge

boundary_rationale: An emphatic self-reference opens a new resolve: גַּם אֲנִי֮ לֹ֤א אֶחֱשָׂ֫ךְ פִּ֥י אֲֽ֭דַבְּרָה בְּצַ֣ר רוּחִ֑י אָ֝שִׂ֗יחָה בְּמַ֣ר נַפְשִֽׁי (oshb:Job.7.11), “Therefore I will not keep silent. I will speak in the anguish of my spirit. I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.” web:Job.7.11. Job asks “Am I a sea, or a sea monster, that you put a guard over me?” web:Job.7.12, describes a bed that fails to comfort him because God frightens him with dreams web:Job.7.13-Job.7.14, and concludes that his soul “chooses strangling, death rather than my bones” web:Job.7.15, then states outright, “I loathe my life. I don’t want to live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath.” web:Job.7.16. The row runs from the fronted-pronoun resolve to the loathing-of-life statement it produces, ending before the next topic-turn interrogative.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at Job.7.10 would cut the fronted-pronoun resolve of Job.7.11 away from the dream-terror and life-loathing material it introduces.
literature_type_guess: mortality complaint: days flee like fleeting wind patterns
