This row's own edge instead rests on the participant/focus shift at web:Job.41.30, where the grammatical subject changes from external agents (weapons) acting on Leviathan to Leviathan's own action on the world.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this weapons catalog through the verses that follow was rejected because the next verse shifts the grammatical focus from external agents (weapons) acting on him to his own locomotion and effect on the sea, a participant shift the weapons catalog does not share.
literature_type_guess: Leviathan impenetrable flesh: every weapon and assault fails

boundary_rationale: The focus shifts again, from weapons failing against him to his own destructive passage through the world, web:Job.41.30 = oshb:Job.41.22 “תַּ֭חְתָּיו חַדּ֣וּדֵי חָ֑רֶשׂ יִרְפַּ֖ד חָר֣וּץ עֲלֵי טִֽיט”, web:Job.41.30 “His undersides are like sharp potsherds, leaving a trail in the mud like a threshing sledge.”, churning the deep like a boiling pot and leaving a shining wake — web:Job.41.32 = oshb:Job.41.24 “אַ֭חֲרָיו יָאִ֣יר נָתִ֑יב יַחְשֹׁ֖ב תְּה֣וֹם לְשֵׂיבָֽה”, web:Job.41.32 “He makes a path shine after him. One would think the deep had white hair.”, carries the חשב root again (יַחְשֹׁ֖ב, accent_stripped-identical to 41:27's יַחְשֹׁ֣ב -- byte-distinct in cantillation alone, tipcha here vs munah there) that brackets the weapons catalog at 41:27 and 41:29, a continuity signal crossing the 41:29|41:30 seam rather than a device of this row's own, disclosed from this row's side to match the disclosure on the other — before the poem, and the second whirlwind speech's creature catalog, close on a double superlative: web:Job.41.33 = oshb:Job.41.25 “אֵֽין עַל עָפָ֥ר מָשְׁל֑וֹ הֶ֝עָשׂ֗וּ לִבְלִי חָֽת”, web:Job.41.33 “On earth there is not his equal, that is made without fear.”, and web:Job.41.34 = oshb:Job.41.26 “אֵֽת כָּל גָּבֹ֥הַּ יִרְאֶ֑ה ה֝֗וּא מֶ֣לֶךְ עַל כָּל בְּנֵי שָֽׁחַץ”, web:Job.41.34 “He sees everything that is high. He is king over all the sons of pride.”. A samekh follows the poem's actual end in the WLC (single-witness), corroborating (tier-3) the formula- and content-driven close of the poem at this point; Job's own retraction opens fresh with a vaya'an formula at 42:1.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the samekh (single-witness) as the driver for this poem's close was rejected because the mark is at most tier-3 corroboration in Writings; the actual driver is the closing double superlative at 41:33-34 (no equal on earth, king over all the sons of pride) together with the fresh vaya'an formula opening 42:1.
literature_type_guess: Leviathan churns deep waters and claims dominion over all

boundary_rationale: The vaya'an formula's Iyov-token member opens Job's retraction, oshb:Job.42.1 “וַיַּ֖עַן אִיּ֥וֹב אֶת יְהוָ֗ה וַיֹּאמַֽר”, web:Job.42.1 “Then Job answered Yahweh:”, followed by a general acknowledgment of divine power, web:Job.42.2 “I know that you can do all things, and that no purpose of yours can be restrained.”. The strophe closes on a direct quotation frame, oshb:Job.42.3 “מִ֤י זֶ֨ה מַעְלִ֥ים עֵצָ֗ה בְּֽלִ֫י דָ֥עַת לָכֵ֣ן הִ֭גַּדְתִּי וְלֹ֣א אָבִ֑ין נִפְלָא֥וֹת מִ֝מֶּ֗נִּי וְלֹ֣א אֵדָֽע”, web:Job.42.3 “You asked, 'Who is this who hides counsel without knowledge?' therefore I have uttered that which I didn't understand, things too wonderful for me, which I didn't know.”, in which Job quotes YHWH's own opening challenge back to him: the phrase מי זה recurs verbatim (sweep: 2 book-wide, byte tier, oshb:Job.38.2 and oshb:Job.42.3 only), though the verb and object differ (38:2 מחשיך עצה במלין בלי דעת against 42:3 מעלים עצה בלי דעת) — a deliberate but not verbatim inclusio bracketing the whole whirlwind exchange. oshb:Job.42.3 carries a paseq (single-witness), disclosed rather than used to corroborate either edge. This row's far edge instead turns on the commissioning-clause echo closing the next verse, web:Job.42.4 “You said, 'Listen, now, and I will speak; I will question you, and you will answer me.'”: the Hebrew of 42:4 carries no quotative verb of saying that attributes the words to a speaker — its own verb of speech, אֲדַבֵּ֑ר ('and I will speak'), is Job's own 1cs statement, not an amar-form — and the formula-spine inventory has no member at 42:3 or 42:4, so the 'You said' framing is a WEB translational supplement (tier-4) rather than a second Hebrew quotation-frame formula; the genuine near-edge driver at 42:4 is the commissioning clause closing the verse, אֶ֝שְׁאָלְךָ֗ וְהוֹדִיעֵֽנִי, byte-identical to the same clause closing oshb:Job.40.7 (sweep: 2 book-wide at that exact pointed clause) and matching the clause closing oshb:Job.38.3 only as a prefix-stripped substring at the accent_stripped/skeleton tiers, since 38:3's form carries a prefixed conjunctive vav (וְ֝אֶשְׁאָלְךָ֗) that the 40:7 and 42:4 forms both lack — two objects, not one — argued fully in the row that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating this whole retraction as one undivided row was rejected because two devices divide it into two rhetorically separate acts of recollection: the mi-zeh inclusio bracketing the whole whirlwind exchange (38:2/42:3), and the commissioning-clause echo closing 42:4 (אֶ֝שְׁאָלְךָ֗ וְהוֹדִיעֵֽנִי, shared with 38:3 and 40:7, not a Hebrew 'you-said' formula). A rival seam at 42:4|42:5 (the וְ֝עַתָּ֗ה turn, sweep: 8 book-wide) is disclosed rather than adopted here: it does not overturn this row's own span, which stands independently on the mi-zeh inclusio.
literature_type_guess: Job acknowledges Yahweh knowledge, quotes who darkens clause

boundary_rationale: An imperative opens this strophe at 42:4, oshb:Job.42.4 “שְֽׁמַֽע נָ֭א וְאָנֹכִ֣י אֲדַבֵּ֑ר אֶ֝שְׁאָלְךָ֗ וְהוֹדִיעֵֽנִי”, web:Job.42.4 “You said, 'Listen, now, and I will speak; I will question you, and you will answer me.'”, echoing not YHWH's opening challenge (quoted in the row before this one) but the question-and-answer commissioning clause shared with both whirlwind speeches: אֶ֝שְׁאָלְךָ֗ וְהוֹדִיעֵֽנִי is byte-identical to the same clause closing oshb:Job.40.7 (sweep: 2 book-wide at that exact pointed clause), and matches the clause closing oshb:Job.38.3 only as a prefix-stripped substring at the accent_stripped/skeleton tiers, since 38:3's form carries a prefixed conjunctive vav (וְ֝אֶשְׁאָלְךָ֗) that the 40:7 and 42:4 forms both lack — two objects, not one, disclosed here rather than claimed as a three-way exact match (a bare-spelling skeleton count of 3 is a substring artifact of the prefixed 38:3 form, not a third independent byte-identical member). The 'You said' attribution at web:Job.42.4 is a WEB translational supplement: the Hebrew carries no quotative verb of saying that attributes the words to a speaker — its own verb of speech, אֲדַבֵּ֑ר, is Job's 1cs 'and I will speak', not an amar-form — and the formula-spine inventory has no member at 42:3 or 42:4. The retraction turns from recollection to transformed perception, web:Job.42.5 “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.”, and closes on the confession of repentance, oshb:Job.42.6 “עַל כֵּ֭ן אֶמְאַ֣ס וְנִחַ֑מְתִּי עַל עָפָ֥ר וָאֵֽפֶר”, web:Job.42.6 “Therefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.”. A rival seam is disclosed rather than adopted: the ve'attah turn stands mid-verse at 42:5 (word 4 of 6, opening the second colon, וְ֝עַתָּ֗ה), the sole verse-medial member of an eight-member book-wide skeleton sweep (6:28, 30:1, 30:9, 30:16, 35:15, 37:21, 42:5, 42:8) whose other seven members are verse-initial; six of those seven elsewhere mark poetic strophe turns, and the seventh, 42:8, sits in the prose epilogue; the two-strophe grain of 42:1-6 (this row and the one before it) stays defensible on the mi-zeh inclusio (38:2/42:3, bracketing the whole whirlwind exchange, not only this row's material) and the commissioning-clause echo closing this row's own opening verse, without relying on a WEB-supplied quotation-frame warrant. A petuchah follows this verse (single-witness), corroborating this row's far edge, where the discourse shifts to the prose narrator's voice.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating the hearing/seeing verse as its own row was rejected because no intervening formula, vocative, or interrogative opens 42:5: the imperative-plus-commissioning-clause quotation that opens this row closes at the end of 42:4, and the transformed-perception statement of 42:5 follows immediately within the same strophe rather than opening a fresh one.
literature_type_guess: Job echoes gird-up commissioning then retracts prior words

boundary_rationale: The narrator's voice opens the prose epilogue with an explicit temporal-causal transition, oshb:Job.42.7 “וַיְהִ֗י אַחַ֨ר דִּבֶּ֧ר יְהוָ֛ה אֶת הַדְּבָרִ֥ים הָאֵ֖לֶּה אֶל אִיּ֑וֹב וַיֹּ֨אמֶר יְהוָ֜ה אֶל אֱלִיפַ֣ז הַתֵּֽימָנִ֗י חָרָ֨ה אַפִּ֤י בְךָ֙ וּבִשְׁנֵ֣י רֵעֶ֔יךָ כִּ֠י לֹ֣א דִבַּרְתֶּ֥ם אֵלַ֛י נְכוֹנָ֖ה כְּעַבְדִּ֥י אִיּֽוֹב”, web:Job.42.7 “It was so, that after Yahweh had spoken these words to Job, Yahweh said to Eliphaz the Temanite, "My wrath is kindled against you, and against your two friends; for you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has.”, immediately after the petuchah (single-witness) following the poetry's close. YHWH's verdict speech to Eliphaz names all three friends' failure and closes with a refrain, repeated verbatim at the end of the following verse, “for you have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job has” (web:Job.42.7, web:Job.42.8), a doubled formula binding the two verses of direct speech into one unit. The scene closes with the narrator's report of compliance and acceptance, web:Job.42.9 “So Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite went and did what Yahweh commanded them, and Yahweh accepted Job.”, before the topic shifts from the friends' obedience to Job's own restored fortune in the next row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting YHWH's direct speech from the friends' compliance report into two rows was rejected because the doubled refrain closing both verses of that speech binds the verdict scene into one unit, and the compliance report completes that same scene rather than opening a new one.
literature_type_guess: Verdict scene: Yahweh rebukes friends, demands sacrifice and intercession

boundary_rationale: The topic turns from the friends' compliance to Job's own restoration, oshb:Job.42.10 “וַֽיהוָ֗ה שָׁ֚ב אֶת שבית שְׁב֣וּת אִיּ֔וֹב בְּהִֽתְפַּֽלְל֖וֹ בְּעַ֣ד רֵעֵ֑הוּ וַ֧יֹּסֶף יְהוָ֛ה אֶת כָּל אֲשֶׁ֥ר לְאִיּ֖וֹב לְמִשְׁנֶֽה”, web:Job.42.10 “Yahweh restored Job's prosperity when he prayed for his friends. Yahweh gave Job twice as much as he had before.” (the OSHB extract carries a ketiv/qere pair here, שבית against שבות, disclosed rather than glossed over: the ketiv's medial yod and the qere's medial vav disagree on precisely which root the noun belongs to — shin-bet-he or shin-vav-bet — so the pair leaves the noun's root open rather than confirming a doubled root; what the verse does show is a consonantal echo, texture-tier, between the perfect שָׁ֚ב and the noun itself, marking the scene's opening). The scene continues with the family and acquaintance reunion, comfort, and gift-giving through web:Job.42.11 “Then all his brothers, all his sisters, and all those who had been of his acquaintance before, came to him and ate bread with him in his house. They comforted him, and consoled him concerning all the evil that Yahweh had brought on him. Everyone also gave him a piece of money, and everyone a ring of gold.”. A samekh follows this verse (single-witness); the next verse turns from social restoration to a formal, itemized count of possessions, marking this row's far edge.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating the restoration statement from the family reunion into two rows was rejected because both develop the same social/relational restoration before the itemized possessions count begins in the next row.
literature_type_guess: Restoration scene: fortune restored and family returns to Job

boundary_rationale: The register shifts from social comfort to a formal, itemized blessing-count, oshb:Job.42.12 “וַֽיהוָ֗ה בֵּרַ֛ךְ אֶת אַחֲרִ֥ית אִיּ֖וֹב מֵרֵאשִׁת֑וֹ וַֽיְהִי ל֡וֹ אַרְבָּעָה֩ עָשָׂ֨ר אֶ֜לֶף צֹ֗אן וְשֵׁ֤שֶׁת אֲלָפִים֙ גְּמַלִּ֔ים וְאֶֽלֶף צֶ֥מֶד בָּקָ֖ר וְאֶ֥לֶף אֲתוֹנֽוֹת”, web:Job.42.12 “So Yahweh blessed the latter end of Job more than his beginning. He had fourteen thousand sheep, six thousand camels, one thousand yoke of oxen, and a thousand female donkeys.”, naming sheep, camels, oxen, and donkeys in round numbers, then children, web:Job.42.13 “He had also seven sons and three daughters.”. The next verse narrows from this general count to naming the daughters specifically, marking this row's far edge as a participant-focus narrowing rather than a continuation of the general enumeration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the livestock count from the children count into separate rows was rejected because both continue one itemized enumeration of restored blessing with no discourse marker dividing them.
literature_type_guess: Restored livestock inventory: animals doubled in possession counts

boundary_rationale: The narrator narrows from the general children-count to naming the daughters specifically, oshb:Job.42.14 “וַיִּקְרָ֤א שֵׁם הָֽאַחַת֙ יְמִימָ֔ה וְשֵׁ֥ם הַשֵּׁנִ֖ית קְצִיעָ֑ה וְשֵׁ֥ם הַשְּׁלִישִׁ֖ית קֶ֥רֶן הַפּֽוּךְ”, web:Job.42.14 “He called the name of the first, Jemimah; and the name of the second, Keziah; and the name of the third, Keren Happuch.”, closing on their beauty and their unusual inheritance right alongside their brothers, oshb:Job.42.15 “וְלֹ֨א נִמְצָ֜א נָשִׁ֥ים יָפ֛וֹת כִּבְנ֥וֹת אִיּ֖וֹב בְּכָל הָאָ֑רֶץ וַיִּתֵּ֨ן לָהֶ֧ם אֲבִיהֶ֛ם נַחֲלָ֖ה בְּת֥וֹךְ אֲחֵיהֶֽם”, web:Job.42.15 “In all the land were no women found so beautiful as the daughters of Job. Their father gave them an inheritance among their brothers.”. A samekh follows this verse (single-witness); the next verse turns from the daughters to Job's own remaining lifespan, marking this row's far edge.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 3's title places it after the historical note “when he fled from Absalom his son” (web:Ps.3.0 = oshb:Ps.3.1), and the eight verses that follow move as one lament-to-confidence arc addressed to Yahweh: the complaint of web:Ps.3.1-web:Ps.3.2 (“Yahweh, how my adversaries have increased!”), the confidence of web:Ps.3.3-web:Ps.3.4, the untroubled sleep of web:Ps.3.5-web:Ps.3.6, and the imperative plea and blessing of web:Ps.3.7-web:Ps.3.8 turn on repeated address to Yahweh rather than a change of addressee. Selah closes three of these verses — web:Ps.3.2 (oshb:Ps.3.3), web:Ps.3.4 (oshb:Ps.3.5), and web:Ps.3.8 (oshb:Ps.3.9) — corroborating the internal pauses without independently dividing the psalm into separate rows.

device_notes: The rows here belong together under Psalm 9. Psalms 9 and 10 carry one irregular acrostic sequence running across both compositions, opening on a paired aleph at verses 1-2 (tier-1 surface letter data) before the letter pattern breaks — a typed cross-psalm relation; the pair stays two independent rows, not one merged row. The Greek Psalter numbers the pair as one composition (LXX 9 = MT 9-10 combined), a numbering-only crosswalk, not boundary evidence.

boundary_rationale: Continuing straight from the enemies’ defeat, the address turns to Yahweh’s universal acts of judgment: “You have rebuked the nations…You have destroyed the wicked” (web:Ps.9.5) gives way at verse 7 to third-person description — “Yahweh reigns forever” (web:Ps.9.7) — of his eternal throne, righteous judgment of “the world” (web:Ps.9.8), and refuge for “the oppressed” (web:Ps.9.9), closing on those who trust in Yahweh, “for you, Yahweh, have not forsaken those who seek you” (web:Ps.9.10). The strophe ends before the following imperative summons to communal praise.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the strophe at the second-to-third-person shift between verses 6 and 7 was rejected because both halves elaborate the one theme of Yahweh’s judgment of the nations and refuge for the oppressed without an accompanying imperative or vocative marker to justify a break.
observed_substrate_signals: second-person address to Yahweh (“You have rebuked… You have destroyed… You have blotted out” web:Ps.9.5) gives way to third-person description of Yahweh’s reign at “Yahweh reigns forever” (web:Ps.9.7; sweep: 1 verse book-wide carries this exact phrase) — an interior person-shift, not a strophe boundary here

boundary_rationale: An imperative onset — “Sing praises to Yahweh, who dwells in Zion” (web:Ps.9.11) — opens a call to communal praise grounded in Yahweh’s remembering “the cry of the afflicted” (web:Ps.9.12), then turns to the psalmist’s own petition, “Have mercy on me, Yahweh” (web:Ps.9.13), continuing through the vow to “rejoice in your salvation in the gates of the daughter of Zion” (web:Ps.9.14). The strophe closes on the nations “sunk down in the pit that they made” (web:Ps.9.15) and the declaration “Yahweh has made himself known… The wicked is snared by the work of his own hands” — which the verse’s own Selah closes (web:Ps.9.16 = oshb:Ps.9.17), a tier-3 corroboration of the strophe’s end.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating verse 16 alone as a Selah-marked coda was rejected because the verse's declaration “He has executed judgment.” (web:Ps.9.16) completes the nations' downfall reported in verse 15 rather than opening a new unit.
observed_substrate_signals: an imperative verb opens the strophe: “Sing praises” (web:Ps.9.11), a tier-1 formal signal distinct from the cohortative vows of verses 1-2
the psalmist’s own petition returns at “Have mercy on me, Yahweh” (web:Ps.9.13), addressed directly to Yahweh as in the opening strophe
Selah closes verse 16 (web:Ps.9.16 = oshb:Ps.9.17) — 1 of 2 Selah occurrences in Psalm 9 (sweep: Ps.9.16, Ps.9.20); tier-3 corroboration, not the boundary’s driver by itself
device_notes: The imperative-opened call to praise (verse 11) and the personal plea (verses 13-14) share this one strophe with the nations’ downfall (verses 15-16), bounded by the imperative onset and the Selah close.

boundary_rationale: The wicked’s reversal — “turned back to Sheol” (web:Ps.9.17) — sets against the needy who “shall not always be forgotten” (web:Ps.9.18), preparing the closing imperative plea: “Arise, Yahweh! Don’t let man prevail” (web:Ps.9.19), continuing “Put them in fear, Yahweh” (web:Ps.9.20). The psalm’s second Selah closes the verse and the composition (web:Ps.9.20 = oshb:Ps.9.21), a tier-3 corroboration matching the close that ended the previous strophe at Ps.9.16 (oshb:Ps.9.17), where the earlier Selah falls.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding verses 17-18 into the preceding strophe was rejected because the wicked/needy antithesis they declare supplies the ground the closing imperative plea (web:Ps.9.19-web:Ps.9.20) answers, tying 17-18 forward to this strophe's imperative return rather than back to the Selah-closed unit before it.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative verbs reopen direct address to Yahweh: “Arise, Yahweh!” (web:Ps.9.19) and “Put them in fear, Yahweh” (web:Ps.9.20), a tier-1 formal signal echoing the imperative onset at verse 11

Selah closes the psalm at verse 20 (web:Ps.9.20 = oshb:Ps.9.21) — 2 of 2 Selah occurrences in Psalm 9 (sweep: Ps.9.16, Ps.9.20), the front-seam instance falling at verse 16 (web:Ps.9.16 = oshb:Ps.9.17)

device_notes: Psalm 9 closes with 2 Selah-marked verses total (sweep: Ps.9.16, Ps.9.20); both end an imperative-framed unit, a consistent structural pattern within this one psalm (not tested against the book’s other 69 Selah verses here).

boundary_rationale: Untitled, Psalm 10 opens directly on a vocative lament question — “Why do you stand far off, Yahweh?” (web:Ps.10.1) — addressed to Yahweh in the second person, then turns in the third person to the portrait of “the wicked” that dominates the rest of the psalm: hunting “the weak” (web:Ps.10.2), boasting and condemning Yahweh (web:Ps.10.3), and having “no room in his thoughts for God” (web:Ps.10.4). The strophe closes before the extended description of the wicked’s methods that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Limiting the opening unit to verse 1 alone was rejected because the third-person portrait of the wicked beginning at verse 2 continues without an intervening imperative or vocative through verse 4.
observed_substrate_signals: a vocative second-person question opens the psalm (“Why do you stand far off, Yahweh?”, web:Ps.10.1) with no superscription preceding it — 1 of 8 psalms in this span carrying no title
third-person description of “the wicked” (web:Ps.10.2) begins at verse 2 and continues without a fresh imperative or vocative through verse 4
the acrostic’s surface letters (tier-1 data) open lamed, bet, kaph, resh across verses 1-4 — an irregular sequence, texture rather than a boundary driver here
device_notes: Psalm 10's rows converge on one parent grouping. Psalm 10 continues the irregular acrostic begun in Psalm 9 (typed cross-psalm relation; Psalm 10 keeps its own parent and is not merged with Psalm 9). Psalm 10 carries no superscription — 1 of 8 psalms in this span (Psalms 9-16) without a title. The second-person address to Yahweh that opens the psalm at web:Ps.10.1 recurs once more, embedded in the suffix of מִ֭שְׁפָּטֶיךָ (oshb:Ps.10.5, which carries an unrelated ketiv/qere pair earlier in the same verse), rendered “your laws” in the WEB (web:Ps.10.5), immediately past this row's own close, before the third-person wicked-catalog device proper begins at web:Ps.10.6. This opening strophe begins immediately after Psalm 9's closing selah (web:Ps.9.20 = oshb:Ps.9.21), a separate parent composition whose front-seam mark is corroborative texture, not a driver of this row's own boundary.

boundary_rationale: Framed by two matching inner-speech formulas — “He says in his heart” opening its report of self-deceived confidence (web:Ps.10.6) and reopening its report of denial (web:Ps.10.11) — the device-bounded catalog of the wicked one's methods proper runs web:Ps.10.6-web:Ps.10.10: a cursing and deceitful mouth (web:Ps.10.7), ambush and murder of the innocent (web:Ps.10.8), lion-like predation on the helpless (web:Ps.10.9), and the helpless crushed under his strength (web:Ps.10.10). The strophe's opening verse (web:Ps.10.5 = oshb:Ps.10.5, which also carries an unrelated ketiv/qere pair) still carries second-person address to Yahweh through the embedded suffix in מִ֭שְׁפָּטֶיךָ (oshb:Ps.10.5), rendered “your laws” in the WEB, tying it to the vocative unit opened at web:Ps.10.1 rather than to the third-person catalog. The “He says in his heart” formula recurs a third time, cantillation-variant, at web:Ps.10.13, closing the catalog's own inclusio at web:Ps.10.6/web:Ps.10.11.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the strophe at verse 8 (villages/ambush) was rejected because no vocative, imperative, or inner-speech formula interrupts the predatory portrait between the two ‘says in his heart’ verses; the catalog reads as one continuous unit bounded by that repeated formula.
observed_substrate_signals: the “He says in his heart” formula opens verse 6 and reopens verse 11 (web:Ps.10.6, web:Ps.10.11), recurring a third time (cantillation-variant) at web:Ps.10.13 (sweep: 3 verses book-wide, Ps.10.6/10.11/10.13), forming this strophe's own inclusio boundary at its first two instances
predatory-hunting vocabulary clusters at “lurks in secret as a lion…catches the helpless” (web:Ps.10.9)

no free vocative or imperative interrupts verses 6-10, the catalog device's own bound; verse 5 embeds a 2ms suffix (מִ֭שְׁפָּטֶיךָ, oshb:Ps.10.5, which also carries an unrelated ketiv/qere pair), “your laws” in the WEB (web:Ps.10.5), address without a free vocative, tying that verse to the preceding unit rather than the third-person catalog
device_notes: Paseq marks fall at verses 5, 8, and 9 within this strophe (seg-layer, single-witness, not quotable as verse bytes).

boundary_rationale: A fresh imperative onset — “Arise, Yahweh! God, lift up your hand!” (web:Ps.10.12) — opens the psalm's closing plea, echoing the same imperative that opens Psalm 9's closing strophe (web:Ps.9.19; sweep: 6 verses book-wide open with this imperative). The wicked's rhetorical question, “God won't call me into account” (web:Ps.10.13), carries the same “says in his heart” inner-speech formula (אָמַ֥ר בְּ֝לִבּ֗וֹ, oshb:Ps.10.13) that frames the preceding strophe's catalog at web:Ps.10.6 and web:Ps.10.11 — its third, cantillation-variant occurrence — and is answered by the counter-claim “you do see trouble and grief” (web:Ps.10.14); the strophe closes on the imperative “Break the arm of the wicked” (web:Ps.10.15).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the previous strophe through verse 12 was rejected because the imperative ‘Arise, Yahweh!’ marks the same kind of fresh address-shift used to open the closing strophe of Psalm 9.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative verbs open the strophe: “Arise” and “lift up your hand” (web:Ps.10.12), a tier-1 formal signal

a rhetorical question attributed to the wicked (“God won’t call me into account” web:Ps.10.13) is answered in the following verse (“But you do see trouble and grief” web:Ps.10.14), a question-answer pairing internal to the strophe

device_notes: Paseq marks total 5 within this strophe (2 at verse 13, 3 at verse 14; seg-layer, single-witness, not quotable as verse bytes).

boundary_rationale: The psalm closes on a declarative confession — “Yahweh is King forever and ever!” (web:Ps.10.16) — echoing the same kingship theme that opens the earlier portrait of Yahweh’s reign in Psalm 9 (web:Ps.9.7). Direct address returns at “Yahweh, you have heard the desire of the humble” (web:Ps.10.17), and the psalm ends on the purpose clause “to judge the fatherless and the oppressed” (web:Ps.10.18), closing the lament’s opening question about Yahweh standing far off with a declaration of his heard and answered attention.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching verse 16 to the preceding imperative strophe was rejected because it opens a declarative confession in a new grammatical mood, not a continuation of the imperative plea.
observed_substrate_signals: a declarative “Yahweh is King forever and ever” (web:Ps.10.16) shifts mood from the preceding imperatives to confession
second-person address to Yahweh returns at “you have heard the desire of the humble” (web:Ps.10.17), closing out the psalm’s direct address to Yahweh

device_notes: The acrostic’s surface letters bracket the psalm with lamed at verse 1 and again at verse 18, with tav — the alphabet’s twenty-second and closing letter — immediately preceding it at verse 17 (tier-1 surface letter data); texture, not the row’s driver.

boundary_rationale: The lamnatseach/le-David superscription (web:Ps.11.0 = oshb:Ps.11.1) opens one 7-verse movement: refuge declared in the psalmist's own voice (“In Yahweh, I take refuge” web:Ps.11.1) against a quoted taunt to flee — the taunt's verb carries a ketiv/qere pair inline in the MT (נודו/נ֝֗וּדִי, oshb:Ps.11.1) — answered by a rhetorical question about the foundations (web:Ps.11.3), then Yahweh's heavenly examination of the righteous and the wicked (web:Ps.11.4-5), the wicked's judgment (web:Ps.11.6), and a closing confession of Yahweh's own righteousness (web:Ps.11.7). At 7 verses the psalm stays under the whole-psalm threshold, and no imperative or vocative shift interrupts its one sustained argument from refuge through vindication.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the psalm at the shift from the psalmist's own refuge language (verses 1-3) to third-person description of Yahweh (verses 4-7) was rejected because no imperative or vocative marks the seam and the opening half (verses 1-3, 3 verses) falls under the 4-verse strophe norm, though the closing half (verses 4-7, 4 verses) meets it.
observed_substrate_signals: a self-referential refuge declaration opens the psalm (“In Yahweh, I take refuge” web:Ps.11.1) with a quoted taunt embedded inside the same verse
third-person description of Yahweh’s heavenly examination runs verses 4-6 without an intervening imperative or vocative
the psalm totals 7 verses, under the whole-psalm threshold (sweep: 7 verses)

boundary_rationale: The lamnatseach/al-hashsheminit/mizmor/le-David superscription (web:Ps.12.0 = oshb:Ps.12.1) opens a cry over failing faithfulness (“Help, Yahweh” web:Ps.12.1) and flattering deceit (web:Ps.12.2-4), pivots at its center to a quoted divine oracle — “I will now arise,” says Yahweh (web:Ps.12.5) — and closes with confession of Yahweh's flawless words (web:Ps.12.6) and their promised protection (web:Ps.12.7) against the pervasive wicked (web:Ps.12.8). At 8 verses the psalm sits at the whole-psalm threshold; the oracle at its center corroborates rather than divides it, since no imperative or vocative brackets a seam on either side.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the psalm before and after the quoted oracle at verse 5 was rejected because the opening lament (verses 1-4, 4 verses) meets the 4-verse strophe floor while the closing confession (verses 6-8, 3 verses) falls under it, with no independent imperative or vocative marker at either proposed seam.
observed_substrate_signals: a direct imperative cry opens the psalm (“Help, Yahweh” web:Ps.12.1)
a quoted divine oracle, introduced as Yahweh’s own words (“I will now arise,” says Yahweh, web:Ps.12.5), sits at the psalm’s center without an imperative or vocative marker introducing it
the psalm totals 8 verses, at the whole-psalm threshold (sweep: 8 verses)
device_notes: One parent spans Psalm 12’s rows.

boundary_rationale: The mizmor’s lamnatseach/le-David superscription (tier-1 opener evidence, web:Ps.13.0 = oshb:Ps.13.1) opens a fourfold “How long, Yahweh?” lament (web:Ps.13.1-2), turns to petition — “Behold, and answer me” (web:Ps.13.3) — against the enemy’s threatened triumph (web:Ps.13.4), and closes on trust and praise: “But I trust in your loving kindness” (web:Ps.13.5) and “I will sing to Yahweh, because he has been good to me” (web:Ps.13.6). WEB renders this closing confession as two verses; both draw on the one Hebrew verse MT 13:6 (web:Ps.13.5 = oshb:Ps.13.6; web:Ps.13.6 = oshb:Ps.13.6), so the split falls inside this whole-psalm span rather than at a boundary between two units. At 6 verses the psalm stays under the whole-psalm threshold, with no imperative or vocative shift marking an internal seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating verses 5 and 6 as two separate strophes was rejected because both halves render one Hebrew verse (MT 13:6) split by WEB alone; the split is a rendering seam, not an independent boundary in the source.
observed_substrate_signals: a fourfold ‘how long’ lament opens the psalm across verses 1-2 (web:Ps.13.1, web:Ps.13.2)
WEB verses 5 and 6 both translate the one Hebrew verse MT 13:6 (web:Ps.13.5 = oshb:Ps.13.6; web:Ps.13.6 = oshb:Ps.13.6) — a rendering split, not a Hebrew-verse boundary
the psalm totals 6 verses, under the whole-psalm threshold (sweep: 6 verses)
device_notes: This psalm’s row is drawn under one parent, Psalm 13. Psalm 13’s WEB verses 5-6 split one Hebrew verse (MT 13:6) between them — a rendering-level division internal to this psalm’s span, not a typed cross-psalm relation like the Psalm 9-10 pairing or the Psalm 14 doublet.

boundary_rationale: The lamnatseach/le-David superscription (web:Ps.14.0 = oshb:Ps.14.1) opens a diagnosis of universal corruption: “The fool has said in his heart” that “There is no God” (web:Ps.14.1), Yahweh's heavenly search from heaven (web:Ps.14.2) finding “no one who does good, no, not one” (web:Ps.14.3), and a rhetorical charge against the “workers of iniquity” who “don't call on Yahweh” (web:Ps.14.4). The psalm turns at verse 5 to the righteous under Yahweh's refuge (web:Ps.14.5-6) and closes on a wish for Israel's restoration from Zion (web:Ps.14.7). At 7 verses it stays under the whole-psalm threshold, with no imperative or vocative shift marking an internal seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the psalm between the diagnosis (verses 1-4) and the refuge/restoration close (verses 5-7) was rejected because doing so would leave a 3-verse closing unit under the 4-verse strophe floor, with no imperative or vocative marking that seam.
observed_substrate_signals: the fool's inner speech opens the psalm in direct quotation (“There is no God” web:Ps.14.1), echoed by the finding “no one who does good, no, not one” (web:Ps.14.3); the shorter clause “no one who does good” (web:Ps.14.1, web:Ps.14.3) recurs at 2 of 7 verses within this psalm (verses 1 and 3)
the doublet’s shared opening clause is book-wide unique to two psalms (sweep: 2 verses, Ps.14.1 and Ps.53.1)
the divine name Yahweh (not a generic term for God) is used at verse 4’s “don’t call on Yahweh” (web:Ps.14.4), part of Book I’s Yahweh-dominant texture
device_notes: Psalm 14's row answers to one parent composition. Psalm 14 opens with the same fool's-denial declaration that opens Psalm 53 (web:Ps.14.1; sweep: 2 verses book-wide share this opening, Ps.14.1 and Ps.53.1) and shares its “no one who does good” clause with Psalm 53 at 4 verses book-wide (Ps.14.1, Ps.14.3, Ps.53.1, Ps.53.3); the two stand as the book's doublet pair (typed relation, independent parents, kept as two separate rows here). The doublet's wording diverges at all 6 parallel verse pairs, with divine-name substitution accounting for 3 of them; one instance is Psalm 14's fourth verse, which names Yahweh as the object of its verb — “don't call on Yahweh” (web:Ps.14.4) — where the parallel verse in Psalm 53 uses a generic term for God instead.

boundary_rationale: The mizmor's le-David superscription (web:Ps.15.0 = oshb:Ps.15.1) opens a question addressed to Yahweh — “who shall dwell in your sanctuary? Who shall live on your holy hill?” (web:Ps.15.1) — answered by an unbroken catalog of the righteous person's qualities running verses 2-5: the MT carries 0 relative particles across web:Ps.15.2-web:Ps.15.5, instead alternating asyndetic participles — הוֹלֵ֣ךְ, 'walking' (oshb:Ps.15.2); נִבְזֶ֤ה and נִמְאָ֗ס, 'despised… rejected' (oshb:Ps.15.4) — with negated finite-verb clauses — לֹֽא רָגַ֨ל, 'has not slandered' (oshb:Ps.15.3); לֹא נָתַ֣ן and לֹ֥א לָ֫קָ֥ח, 'has not given… has not taken' (oshb:Ps.15.5) — bounded by the question at web:Ps.15.1 and the verdict clause “He who does these things shall never be shaken” (web:Ps.15.5). At 5 verses the psalm stays under the whole-psalm threshold as one question-and-answer unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the catalog of qualities in verses 2-5 into two shorter units was rejected because the asyndetic participial/negated-finite catalog runs continuously without any independent imperative or vocative marker to justify a break, and both halves would fall under the 4-verse strophe floor.
observed_substrate_signals: an opening question addressed to Yahweh (web:Ps.15.1) is answered by an asyndetic catalog spanning verses 2-5 that carries 0 relative particles, alternating participial and negated-finite clauses instead (sweep: 0 instances of the relative particle in oshb:Ps.15.2-oshb:Ps.15.5)
no imperative or vocative shift interrupts the catalog
the psalm totals 5 verses, under the whole-psalm threshold (sweep: 5 verses)
device_notes: One parent, Psalm 15, gathers this psalm’s row.

boundary_rationale: The miktam le-David superscription (tier-1 opener evidence, web:Ps.16.0 = oshb:Ps.16.1) opens a refuge declaration — “Preserve me, God, for I take refuge in you” (web:Ps.16.1) — and a confession naming Yahweh as the psalmist’s one good (“Apart from you I have no good thing” web:Ps.16.2), naming solidarity with “the saints who are in the earth” (web:Ps.16.3) against those who “give gifts to another god” (web:Ps.16.4). The strophe closes on Yahweh as the psalmist’s assigned “portion and my cup” (web:Ps.16.5) and “good inheritance” (web:Ps.16.6), before the counsel-and-confidence movement that follows turns from inheritance to guidance.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through the psalm’s counsel-and-confidence movement was rejected because a new note of guidance begins immediately after, distinct from the inheritance language that closes this strophe.
observed_substrate_signals: self-referential refuge and confession language opens the strophe (“Preserve me, God, for I take refuge in you” web:Ps.16.1)
the psalmist’s solidarity with “the saints who are in the earth” (web:Ps.16.3) stands against those loyal to “another god” (web:Ps.16.4)
portion/inheritance vocabulary closes the strophe (“my portion and my cup” web:Ps.16.5; “a good inheritance” web:Ps.16.6), giving way to counsel language in the verse that follows
device_notes: Psalm 16’s rows share one parent composition. The miktam label (tier-1 superscription genre, web:Ps.16.0 = oshb:Ps.16.1) marks 1 of 6 miktam-titled psalms in the book (Psalms 16 and 56-60).

boundary_rationale: Guidance language opens this strophe — “I will bless Yahweh, who has given me counsel” (web:Ps.16.7) — continuing through the confession “I have set Yahweh always before me” (web:Ps.16.8) and the resulting gladness (web:Ps.16.9). The strophe closes on resurrection confidence, “you will not leave my soul in Sheol” (web:Ps.16.10), and the psalm’s final vision of “the path of life” and “pleasures forever more” in Yahweh’s presence (web:Ps.16.11).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this strophe at the shift from counsel (verses 7-9) to the Sheol confession (verses 10-11) was rejected because the closing pair alone (verses 10-11, 2 verses) would fall under the 4-verse strophe floor; a genuine addressee shift does mark that seam (web:Ps.16.7-web:Ps.16.8 refer to Yahweh in the third person, “I will bless Yahweh, who has given me counsel”; web:Ps.16.10-web:Ps.16.11 address Yahweh directly in the second person, “For you will not leave my soul in Sheol”), but the floor count independently controls the outcome.
observed_substrate_signals: counsel and confidence language runs verses 7-9 without an intervening imperative or vocative
the psalm’s closing confession names Sheol directly (“you will not leave my soul in Sheol,” web:Ps.16.10), continuing without a break into the path-of-life close (web:Ps.16.11)
no Selah falls within this strophe’s span-relevant set (Psalm 16 has no Selah-marked verse)

boundary_rationale: The title “A Prayer by David.” (web:Ps.17.0 = oshb:Ps.17.1) opens with תְּפִלָּ֗ה לְדָ֫וִ֥ד, tefillah le-David, a superscription genre label (tier-1 opener class) echoed within the same MT verse by תְפִלָּתִ֑י, 'my prayer,' in “Give ear to my prayer that doesn't go out of deceitful lips” (web:Ps.17.1). The vocative-imperative cluster “Hear, Yahweh, my righteous plea. Give ear...” (web:Ps.17.1) and the jussive petition “Let my sentence come out of your presence” (web:Ps.17.2) open a plea for a verdict that the psalmist grounds in sworn self-testimony through “My steps have held fast to your paths. My feet have not slipped” (web:Ps.17.5), so the appeal and its supporting testimony read as one continuous unit addressed to Yahweh, with the next vocative-imperative cluster resuming at web:Ps.17.6.
