Three verses of synonym-paired praise for the law (law/covenant at web:Ps.19.7, precepts/commandment at web:Ps.19.8, fear/ordinances at web:Ps.19.9) run through “sweeter also than honey and the extract of the honeycomb” (web:Ps.19.10) before “Moreover your servant is warned by them” (web:Ps.19.11) turns from describing the law's qualities to the psalmist's own response, closing on the prayer formula “Let the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable in your sight, Yahweh, my rock, and my redeemer” (web:Ps.19.14), which readdresses Yahweh directly and closes the psalm.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this panel at web:Ps.19.10-Ps.19.11 into separate law-description and response strophes would divide one panel whose sevenfold Yahweh count marks it as one unit against the heavens panel, not evidence for a finer-grained seam within it.
observed_substrate_signals: יְהוָ֣ה (Yahweh) occurs twice each at oshb:Ps.19.8, oshb:Ps.19.9, oshb:Ps.19.10 and once at oshb:Ps.19.15 — seven token-occurrences across four verses (sweep: 7 occurrences across 4 verses)
no divine-name token (Yahweh or El) appears at web:Ps.19.11-Ps.19.13, the personal-response verses between the law's praise and the closing prayer formula
device_notes: No selah interrupts web:Ps.19.7-Ps.19.14; this torah panel and the heavens panel that precedes it remain one composition's two internal movements, not separate parents.

boundary_rationale: The opening strophe is second-person intercession addressed to Yahweh on the king’s behalf, opening “May Yahweh answer you in the day of trouble” (web:Ps.20.1) and running through a chain of jussive petitions (help, support, remembered offerings) that closes on the Selah-marked “remember all your offerings, and accept your burned sacrifice. Selah.” (web:Ps.20.3). The jussive register continues through web:Ps.20.4 (“May he grant you your heart's desire,” יִֽתֶּן, oshb:Ps.20.5), and the verb mood shifts from jussive petition to cohortative communal vow only at this row's own closing verse, “We will triumph in your salvation... we will set up our banners” (web:Ps.20.5, נְרַנְּנָ֤ה/נִדְגֹּ֑ל, oshb:Ps.20.6), which the strophe that follows carries forward as a confident declaration on the king's behalf.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One whole-psalm row was considered given the psalm’s 9-verse length, but the jussive-petition block (1-5) and the declarative confidence block (6-9, opening “Now I know”, web:Ps.20.6) are distinct enough in mood and person to warrant separate rows.
observed_substrate_signals: poetry_lines: 1 at Ps.20.1-Ps.20.2, 2 at Ps.20.5 (verse_map_web)
web_selah: true at Ps.20.3 (pmarks_Ps.json selah key Ps.20.4 MT)
title is a counted MT verse (oshb:Ps.20.1 is_counted_title=true; shift+1 psalm)
verb mood shift (jussive -> 1cp cohortative) falls at this row's own closing verse, web:Ps.20.5 (= oshb:Ps.20.6), not at web:Ps.20.4
device_notes: Psalm 20 holds together as one royal intercession, with its rows gathered under a shared parent. Psalm 20 and Psalm 21 form a royal pair — a pre-battle intercession for the king answered by a psalm of thanksgiving for his victory; two parents, no merged row.

boundary_rationale: The strophe opens on a declarative pivot, “Now I know that Yahweh saves his anointed” (web:Ps.20.6), moving from the congregation’s petition to a confident 1st-person assertion, then a contrastive couplet “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we trust in the name of Yahweh our God” (web:Ps.20.7) versus “They are bowed down and fallen, but we rise up, and stand upright” (web:Ps.20.8), closing on the renewed imperative cry “Save, Yahweh! Let the King answer us when we call!” (web:Ps.20.9).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping web:Ps.20.9 attached to the trust/fall couplet (6-9 as one block) was preferred over isolating it as its own coda, since its imperative “Save, Yahweh” (web:Ps.20.9) directly answers the “we trust” (web:Ps.20.7) and “we rise” (web:Ps.20.8) voice of the same strophe rather than opening new material.
observed_substrate_signals: no selah in this span (pmarks_Ps.json selah has no key for MT 20.7-20.10)
person shift 1cs (‘I know’) to 1cp (‘we trust’/‘we rise’) across web:Ps.20.6-Ps.20.8
device_notes: The confidence oracle and closing petition of Psalm 20 answer the intercession that opens the psalm.

boundary_rationale: The strophe is addressed to Yahweh in the second person throughout, opening “The king rejoices in your strength, Yahweh! How greatly he rejoices in your salvation!” (web:Ps.21.1), where the Hebrew opens on the divine name, יְֽהוָ֗ה (oshb:Ps.21.2 word 1), with the inflected noun-plus-suffix “your strength,” בְּעָזְּךָ֥ (oshb:Ps.21.2 word 2), following as its second word, and runs through the king’s granted requests (heart’s desire, crown, length of days, glory) to the summary line “For the king trusts in Yahweh” (web:Ps.21.7), which closes the direct-address block on a third-person hinge before the strophe that follows turns to assurance of victory.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A split after web:Ps.21.2 (isolating the Selah-marked couplet alone) was considered but rejected: the Selah at web:Ps.21.2 falls mid-thought, before the granted-blessings list (3-7) that the opening couplet introduces, so splitting there would sever one continuous address to Yahweh.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah: true at Ps.21.2 (pmarks_Ps.json selah key Ps.21.3 MT)
kq: 1 note at oshb:Ps.21.2 (ketiv/qere on the verb rendered ‘rejoices’, unrelated to the strength-root quoted)
second person address to Yahweh (‘your strength’, ‘your salvation’) runs web:Ps.21.1-Ps.21.6
device_notes: Psalm 21’s rows trace one royal thanksgiving and share a common parent grouping.

boundary_rationale: The strophe turns to second-person assurance of victory over the king’s enemies, “Your hand will find out all of your enemies. Your right hand will find out those who hate you” (web:Ps.21.8), through the furnace and dispersal imagery (9-12), and closes on a returned invocation to Yahweh, “Be exalted, Yahweh, in your strength, so we will sing and praise your power” (web:Ps.21.13), whose Hebrew, בְּעֻזֶּ֑ךָ (oshb:Ps.21.14), matches the opening verse's inflected noun-plus-suffix, בְּעָזְּךָ֥ (oshb:Ps.21.2), at the skeleton (consonant-only) tier — the pointed forms are byte-unequal — bracketing the whole psalm with the same 'your strength' collocation rather than a shared root in the technical sense.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.21.13 as its own one-verse coda row was considered, given its inclusio force, but folded back into this strophe since one verse falls well under the book’s strophe norm and the inclusio can be argued fully from within one row.
observed_substrate_signals: consonantal-skeleton sweep of the inflected 'your strength' string: 3 verses book-wide, 2 of which (oshb:Ps.21.2, oshb:Ps.21.14) bracket this psalm and one falls elsewhere in the book; the two in-psalm forms match at skeleton tier only, not byte-for-byte
the identity of the addressee across web:Ps.21.8-Ps.21.12 (the king assured of victory, versus continued address to Yahweh) is not settled by the bytes alone
device_notes: The closing strophe answers the opening strength-formula and completes Psalm 21’s shared parent grouping.

boundary_rationale: The opening strophe is the unanswered cry addressed to God, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, and from the words of my groaning?” (web:Ps.22.1), continuing “My God, I cry in the daytime, but you don’t answer” (web:Ps.22.2), then turning on a contrastive vocative, “But you are holy” (web:Ps.22.3), whose Hebrew opens “וְאַתָּ֥ה קָד֑וֹשׁ” (oshb:Ps.22.4), into the fathers’ trust (4-5); the whole span stays in direct second-person address to God.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A break after web:Ps.22.2 (isolating the bare complaint from the ‘but you are holy’ turn) was considered, but rejected because both halves stay addressed to God in the second person; the sharper addressee change comes at web:Ps.22.6, where address gives way to description.
observed_substrate_signals: poetry_lines: 3 at Ps.22.14 later in the psalm vs 1 at Ps.22.1-Ps.22.5 (verse_map_web)
no selah anywhere in Psalm 22 (pmarks_Ps.json selah carries no Ps.22.x key)
device_notes: Psalm 22 moves as one lament-to-praise composition, and its rows converge on a shared parent.

boundary_rationale: The strophe shifts out of direct address into third-person description of contempt, “But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people” (web:Ps.22.6), “All those who see me mock me” (web:Ps.22.7), and closes on the onlookers’ quoted taunt, “He trusts in Yahweh. Let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.” (web:Ps.22.8), a self-contained reported speech that seals the unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.22.11 (folding in the birth-trust return) was considered, but the direct second-person address to God that resumes at web:Ps.22.9 marks a clean addressee return distinct from this description-mode unit.
observed_substrate_signals: WEB sets off the taunt with quotation marks (web:Ps.22.8), a single-witness translation convention; the MT itself carries no speech-introducing verb at this seam (oshb:Ps.22.9 = web:Ps.22.8 opens asyndetically)
no 1st- or 2nd-person address to God within web:Ps.22.6-Ps.22.8
device_notes: The mockers’ taunt is set off by WEB’s quotation marks (a single-witness, tier-4 translation convention); the MT carries no speech-introducing verb or other formal marking device at this seam — oshb:Ps.22.9 (= web:Ps.22.8) opens asyndetically with the imperative גֹּ֣ל, confirmed clean of second-person address to God across web:Ps.22.6-Ps.22.8.

boundary_rationale: The strophe returns to second-person address to God with the birth-trust motif, “But you brought me out of the womb. You made me trust while at my mother’s breasts” (web:Ps.22.9), “I was thrown on you from my mother’s womb” (web:Ps.22.10), and closes the plea “Don’t be far from me, for trouble is near. For there is no one to help” (web:Ps.22.11), which hinges the psalm into the pure description that follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this strophe with the following enemy-imagery block (9-18) was considered; explicit you/your address recedes once the third-person bulls/lions imagery opens at web:Ps.22.12, though an embedded second-person verb-suffix recurs once more at web:Ps.22.15 (תִּשְׁפְּתֵֽנִי, 'you lay me,' oshb:Ps.22.16) before the catalog resumes uninterrupted third-person description; this row's own seam still marks the point where free-standing you/your address gives way to sustained third-person imagery.
observed_substrate_signals: second-person address to God (“you”, “your”) present in 2 of 3 verses across web:Ps.22.9-Ps.22.11 (web:Ps.22.9, web:Ps.22.10); web:Ps.22.11 carries no free-standing you/your token, though its verb (תִּרְחַ֣ק, oshb:Ps.22.12) continues address to God without an independent pronoun or suffix
device_notes: The birth-trust motif closes the psalm’s opening address cycle before its central affliction catalog opens.

boundary_rationale: The strophe is the extended affliction catalog in the third person, opening “Many bulls have surrounded me. Strong bulls of Bashan have encircled me” (web:Ps.22.12), through lions (13), the pouring-out and melting imagery (14-15), the encircling dogs and pierced hands and feet (16), the counted bones (17), and closing “They divide my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing” (web:Ps.22.18), with third-person description dominant throughout except a single embedded second-person verb-suffix at web:Ps.22.15 (תִּשְׁפְּתֵֽנִי, 'you lay me,' oshb:Ps.22.16), a brief address to God without a free pronoun before the catalog's third-person mode resumes.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the catalog at the animal-imagery/bodily-imagery seam (web:Ps.22.14) was considered, but the images run as one largely unbroken description — interrupted only by the embedded second-person verb-suffix at web:Ps.22.15 (תִּשְׁפְּתֵֽנִי, oshb:Ps.22.16) — with no other address shift or formal marker inside the span to argue a sub-boundary.
observed_substrate_signals: poetry_lines: 3 at Ps.22.14, 2 at Ps.22.15 and Ps.22.16 (verse_map_web), the psalm’s peak per-verse counts
WEB carries a footnote at web:Ps.22.16 on a Dead Sea Scrolls/Masoretic reading difference; the footnote is tier-4 and not used as boundary evidence
device_notes: The third-person affliction catalog forms Psalm 22's 7-verse strophe, sustained in one descriptive mode throughout except one embedded second-person verb-suffix (web:Ps.22.15 = oshb:Ps.22.16).

boundary_rationale: The strophe reopens direct address to God, “But don’t be far off, Yahweh. You are my help. Hurry to help me!” (web:Ps.22.19), whose Hebrew opens “וְאַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה” (oshb:Ps.22.20), echoing the same contrastive formula that opened the turn at web:Ps.22.3, then closes the plea “Save me from the lion’s mouth! Yes, you have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen” (web:Ps.22.21), where the verb shifts from imperative plea to a completed-action claim.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.22.22 (the vow-of-praise pivot) was considered, but web:Ps.22.22 opens a cohortative 1st-person vow (“I will declare”) distinct from the imperative plea register of 19-21.
observed_substrate_signals: consonantal-SKELETON SUBSTRING sweep of וְאַתָּ֥ה: 23 hits book-wide (22 as the free-standing pronoun+conjunction formula, plus 1 prefix-substring collision inside a longer word, e.g. oshb:Ps.119.45's בָרְחָבָ֑ה, sharing the same four-consonant run); exactly 2 of the free-standing occurrences fall inside Psalm 22 (oshb:Ps.22.4 and oshb:Ps.22.20), one at each renewed address
device_notes: The repeated contrastive-address formula corroborates two internal turns in Psalm 22 without driving either boundary alone.

boundary_rationale: This strophe opens on the celebrated lament-to-praise pivot, “I will declare your name to my brothers. Among the assembly, I will praise you.” (web:Ps.22.22), a cohortative vow answering the plea just closed, then moves into the call for the assembly’s praise (23), a reflection on God’s attention to the afflicted (24), and vows paid “in the great assembly” (25), closing “The humble shall eat and be satisfied… Let your hearts live forever” (web:Ps.22.26).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching web:Ps.22.22 to the preceding plea (19-22) as its resolution was the rival reading and cannot be excluded on the bytes alone; this row instead opens the vow-of-praise unit with it, since its opening cohortative, “I will declare” (אֲסַפְּרָ֣ה, oshb:Ps.22.23), together with the paired verb “I will praise” (אֲהַלְלֶֽךָּ, oshb:Ps.22.23, a 1cs form without the cohortative's paragogic he, its object suffix blocking the marker) match the register of the assembly-facing verses that follow rather than the imperative plea register before it.
observed_substrate_signals: verb mood shift: imperative (“Save me” web:Ps.22.21) to cohortative (“I will declare” web:Ps.22.22)
no selah anywhere in Psalm 22 (pmarks_Ps.json)
device_notes: The lament-to-praise pivot at web:Ps.22.22 is a contested seam in Psalm 22’s structure; this row registers the boundary at medium confidence rather than overstating it.

boundary_rationale: The closing strophe widens scope from the assembly to the whole earth, “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Yahweh. All the relatives of the nations shall worship before you.” (web:Ps.22.27), through universal worship (28-29) and posterity “that shall be born” (web:Ps.22.31), a scope expansion distinct from the Israel/assembly-facing vocabulary (‘my brothers’, ‘the great assembly’) of the preceding strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding these verses into the preceding vow-of-praise strophe (22-31 as one unit) was considered, but the shift from assembly-scoped vocabulary to “All the ends of the earth” (web:Ps.22.27) marks a real expansion of addressee scope.
observed_substrate_signals: lexical scope shift: “the great assembly” (web:Ps.22.25) to “All the ends of the earth” (web:Ps.22.27)
device_notes: Psalm 22 closes on a universal horizon that completes its shared parent arc from the opening cry.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 23 is one unbroken shepherd movement, opening “Yahweh is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing.” (web:Ps.23.1), through pastures and still waters (2), restored paths (3), the valley of the shadow of death (4), the table before enemies (5), and closing “I will dwell in Yahweh’s house forever” (web:Ps.23.6); at 6 verses it falls under the book’s short-psalm threshold for a single row, and the title sits inside MT verse 1 rather than as a separately counted verse.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A two-strophe split at web:Ps.23.3/Ps.23.4 (following the shift from third-person description of the shepherd to second-person address, “for you are with me”) was considered, but rejected as unnecessary fragmentation of a psalm short enough for one row: it carries no refrain, no vocative opener, and no selah to mark a formal internal seam.
observed_substrate_signals: person shift: third person (web:Ps.23.1-Ps.23.3) to second person (“you are with me” web:Ps.23.4) is texture, not a formal marker
psalm length 6 verses, within the owner-ruled whole_psalm threshold
device_notes: Psalm 23 is complete in itself as one composition, its parent grouping simply Psalm 23.

boundary_rationale: The opening strophe is a cosmic-ownership doxology, “The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it.” (web:Ps.24.1), grounded “For he has founded it on the seas, and established it on the floods.” (web:Ps.24.2); the psalm’s title sits inside MT verse 1 as an identity psalm. The unit ends where the mode shifts from declarative doxology to an interrogative gate-liturgy question at web:Ps.24.3.
strongest_rejected_alternative: One whole-psalm row spanning its ten verses was considered, but the declarative-to-interrogative mode shift at web:Ps.24.3 and the later antiphonal repetition (7-10) argue for the strophe-level question-answer structure the psalm is built on.
observed_substrate_signals: poetry_lines: 1 at both Ps.24.1 and Ps.24.2 (verse_map_web)
device_notes: The gate liturgy of Psalm 24 unfolds across rows that answer to one parent.

boundary_rationale: The strophe opens the entrance-liturgy question, “Who may ascend to Yahweh’s hill? Who may stand in his holy place?” (web:Ps.24.3), Hebrew opening “מִֽי יַעֲלֶ֥ה” (oshb:Ps.24.3), answered by the qualifications of clean hands, a pure heart, and truthful speech (4) and the blessing they receive (5), closing on the climactic identification “This is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek your face—even Jacob. Selah.” (web:Ps.24.6), Hebrew “זֶ֭ה דּ֣וֹר דרשו דֹּרְשָׁ֑יו מְבַקְשֵׁ֨י פָנֶ֖יךָ יַעֲקֹ֣ב סֶֽלָה” (oshb:Ps.24.6).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the qualifications (4-5) from the climactic identification (6) into separate rows was considered, but the two verses form one answer-and-identification unit to the one question opened at web:Ps.24.3, closed together by the Selah.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah: true at Ps.24.6 (pmarks_Ps.json selah key Ps.24.6 MT, identity psalm)
kq: 1 note at oshb:Ps.24.6 (ketiv “דרשו” / qere “דֹּרְשָׁ֑יו”, both quoted above as verse bytes)
device_notes: The entrance-liturgy question and its answer form the psalm’s middle movement, closed by the same Selah that opens the seam into the gate dialogue.

boundary_rationale: The closing strophe is the antiphonal gate dialogue, opening “Lift up your heads, you gates! Be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in.” (web:Ps.24.7), Hebrew “שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים רָֽאשֵׁיכֶ֗ם…” (oshb:Ps.24.7), answered “Who is the King of glory?” (8), whose opening 3-word formula repeats identically (sweep: 2 verses book-wide) at web:Ps.24.9, Hebrew “שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים רָֽאשֵׁיכֶ֗ם” (oshb:Ps.24.9) matching oshb:Ps.24.7’s own opening exactly, though the two full verses differ in 2 of 9 words elsewhere (niphal/qal at word 4, plene/defective spelling at word 7), and closes “Who is this King of glory? Yahweh of Armies is the King of glory! Selah.” (web:Ps.24.10). The strophe opens just after the Selah that marked the close of the preceding entrance-liturgy unit at Ps 24:6.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the two question-answer exchanges (7-8 and 9-10) into separate rows was considered, but the identical 3-word gate-command opening (sweep: 2 verses book-wide) that both exchanges share argues for one antiphonal unit rather than two, even though the two full verses differ in 2 of 9 words beyond that opening formula.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah: true at Ps.24.10 (pmarks_Ps.json selah key Ps.24.10 MT); the front-seam verse Ps.24.6 also carries selah (pmarks_Ps.json selah key Ps.24.6 MT)
consonantal sweep of the gate-command opening string: 2 verses book-wide, both inside this span (oshb:Ps.24.7, oshb:Ps.24.9)
consonantal sweep of ‘king of glory’: 4 verses / 5 occurrences book-wide, all inside this span (oshb:Ps.24.7-Ps.24.10)
device_notes: The gate liturgy’s antiphonal question-answer pattern is the psalm’s closing movement, gathered under its shared parent unit.

boundary_rationale: Ps.25.1 opens the psalm's address to Yahweh, “To you, Yahweh, I lift up my soul.” (web:Ps.25.1), and an imperative petition cluster carries through v. 7 — “Show me your ways, Yahweh. Teach me your paths.” (web:Ps.25.4), “Don't remember the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions. Remember me according to your loving kindness, for your goodness' sake, Yahweh.” (web:Ps.25.7). At v. 8 the register shifts to gnomic description of Yahweh's own character, “Good and upright is Yahweh, therefore he will instruct sinners in the way.” (web:Ps.25.8), continuing to the covenant-friendship saying of v. 14, “The friendship of Yahweh is with those who fear him. He will show them his covenant.” (web:Ps.25.14); a direct-address petition already recurs within this same span at v. 11, “For your name’s sake, Yahweh, pardon my iniquity, for it is great.” (web:Ps.25.11 = oshb:Ps.25.11, שִׁמְךָ֥ יְהוָ֑ה וְֽסָלַחְתָּ֥, ‘your name, Yahweh, and you have pardoned’), so the vv. 8-14 block is not pure third-person description but a gnomic frame interrupted once by direct petition, before petition resumes as the block’s sustained register at v. 15.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Ps 25 as one continuous row is also defensible, since the acrostic sequence (with its two documented irregularities — the buried bet at v. 2 and the skipped waw at v. 6) still runs across the whole psalm without a break in verse-per-letter sequencing at the seam this row proposes.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative petition-verb cluster (show/teach/guide/remember) runs vv. 4-7
verse-initial gnomic shift at v. 8 opens third-person description of Yahweh's dealings
the covenant-friendship saying at v. 14 closes the didactic unit before petition resumes
device_notes: Rows of Psalm 25 group to one parent unit. The acrostic is irregular (psalm_device_inventory.json): the aleph word is v. 1's second word, אֵלֶ֥יךָ (oshb:Ps.25.1), the title לְדָוִ֡ד occupying word 1; the expected second letter bet does not open v. 2 — its opening word is אֱֽלֹהַ֗י (aleph again), with בְּךָ֣ (bet) surfacing as the second word (oshb:Ps.25.2); the expected sixth letter waw is skipped — v. 6 opens with the seventh letter zayin in זְכֹר (oshb:Ps.25.6). This opening strophe begins immediately after Psalm 24's closing selah (web:Ps.24.10), a separate parent composition whose front-seam mark is corroborative texture, not a driver of this row's own boundary.

boundary_rationale: Personal petition resumes at v. 15, “My eyes are ever on Yahweh, for he will pluck my feet out of the net.” (web:Ps.25.15), and the imperative cluster of affliction and distress continues through v. 21 — “Turn to me, and have mercy on me, for I am desolate and afflicted.” (web:Ps.25.16), “Let integrity and uprightness preserve me, for I wait for you.” (web:Ps.25.21) — echoing the wait-for-Yahweh language that opened the psalm's earlier movement at v. 3 (web:Ps.25.3). V. 22 closes with a distinct address, shifting the petition's object from the psalmist to the nation, “God, redeem Israel out of all his troubles.” (web:Ps.25.22).
strongest_rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 16 rather than v. 15 is possible, since v. 15's eye-imagery could be read as transitional; the imperative petitions proper begin at v. 16.
observed_substrate_signals: wait-for-Yahweh language links v. 15's opening to v. 3's earlier profession, corroborating the return to personal petition register
v. 22's grammatical object shifts from the psalmist ("me"/"my") to the nation ("Israel")
device_notes: The doubled resh: v. 18 opens רְאֵ֣ה (oshb:Ps.25.18); v. 19 also opens רְאֵֽה (oshb:Ps.25.19) — the same word, "see," rather than progressing to a new letter, the acrostic's one repeated-word doubling. V. 21 completes the standard 22-letter sequence with tav (oshb:Ps.25.21); v. 22 opens פְּדֵ֣ה (oshb:Ps.25.22), a supernumerary close beyond the acrostic's own scheme.

boundary_rationale: V. 1 opens with a double petition for testing, “Judge me, Yahweh, for I have walked in my integrity. I have trusted also in Yahweh without wavering.” (web:Ps.26.1), “Examine me, Yahweh, and prove me. Try my heart and my mind.” (web:Ps.26.2), grounding the plea in a negative confession of avoiding the wicked — “I have not sat with deceitful men, neither will I go in with hypocrites.” (web:Ps.26.4), “I hate the assembly of evildoers, and will not sit with the wicked.” (web:Ps.26.5) — and a ritual-purity action, “I will wash my hands in innocence, so I will go about your altar, Yahweh,” (web:Ps.26.6), whose purpose clause continues directly into v. 7's thanksgiving. V. 8 opens a fresh declaration with a verse-initial vocative, “Yahweh, I love the habitation of your house, the place where your glory dwells.” (web:Ps.26.8), marking the next unit's start.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 6 rather than v. 7 is possible, since v. 7's purpose clause continues v. 6's ritual action rather than opening new content.
observed_substrate_signals: double petition-verb cluster (judge/examine/prove) opens vv. 1-2
the ritual-purity action of v. 6 closes with a purpose clause naming thanksgiving before the vocative pivot at v. 8
device_notes: Under one parent unit, Psalm 26 gathers the rows here. V. 1's integrity clause sits medial (words 6-7 of 11), בְּתֻמִּ֣י הָלַ֑כְתִּי (oshb:Ps.26.1), 'I have walked in my integrity.' V. 11's integrity clause is also medial (words 2-3 of 5, followed by פְּדֵ֣נִי וְחָנֵּֽנִי), בְּתֻמִּ֥י אֵלֵ֗ךְ (oshb:Ps.26.11), 'I will walk in my integrity' — only the noun בְּתֻמִּ֣י/בְּתֻמִּ֥י recurs (byte-unequal, matching from accent_stripped tier down); the verbs (qatal הָלַ֑כְתִּי vs yiqtol אֵלֵ֗ךְ) differ at every tier. A shared-word echo bracketing the psalm, not a repeated phrase at its edges.

boundary_rationale: V. 8's vocative declaration, “Yahweh, I love the habitation of your house, the place where your glory dwells.” (web:Ps.26.8), opens a love-and-devotion unit that turns to a negative petition echoing vv. 4-5's dissociation from evildoers — “Don't gather my soul with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men” (web:Ps.26.9) — before closing with the psalm's vow of integrity restated, “But as for me, I will walk in my integrity. Redeem me, and be merciful to me.” (web:Ps.26.11), resolving into the congregational blessing of v. 12.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 9 rather than v. 8 is possible, since v. 8's vocative could be read as concluding the ritual unit rather than opening a new one.
observed_substrate_signals: verse-initial vocative Yahweh opens v. 8 (oshb:Ps.26.8), a clean address-shift marker
vv. 4-5's dissociation from evildoers recurs as negative petition in v. 9, and the opening integrity-vow language recurs in v. 11, bracketing the whole psalm
device_notes: V. 12 closes in a congregational setting, בְמִישׁ֑וֹר בְּ֝מַקְהֵלִ֗ים אֲבָרֵ֥ךְ יְהוָֽה (oshb:Ps.26.12; 'in an even place, in the congregations, I will bless Yahweh', web:Ps.26.12), moving the integrity vow into public praise.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens in declarative confidence, “Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?” (web:Ps.27.1), reporting rather than directly petitioning Yahweh through v. 6's resolution, “Now my head will be lifted up above my enemies around me. I will offer sacrifices of joy in his tent. I will sing, yes, I will sing praises to Yahweh.” (web:Ps.27.6). The mode changes sharply at v. 7, where the psalm turns to direct imperative address, “Hear, Yahweh, when I cry with my voice. Have mercy also on me, and answer me.” (web:Ps.27.7).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading vv. 1-14 as one integrated composition is also arguable, since the salvation-root noun opening v. 1 (וְ֭יִשְׁעִי, oshb:Ps.27.1) recurs across the seam at v. 9 (יִשְׁעִֽי, oshb:Ps.27.9), a shared root the declarative and petitionary halves both carry.
observed_substrate_signals: declarative confidence mode (report about Yahweh) runs vv. 1-6 with no imperative petition verb
v. 7 opens with the imperative שְׁמַע (“hear”) plus vocative Yahweh, marking the mode shift (oshb:Ps.27.7)
device_notes: Psalm 27 supplies the parent for its strophes.

boundary_rationale: V. 7 turns from the declarative confidence of the preceding verses to direct imperative petition, “Hear, Yahweh, when I cry with my voice. Have mercy also on me, and answer me.” (web:Ps.27.7), continuing through appeals against abandonment, “Don't hide your face from me. Don't put your servant away in anger. You have been my help. Don't abandon me, neither forsake me, God of my salvation.” (web:Ps.27.9), and closing with a doubled exhortation, “Wait for Yahweh. Be strong, and let your heart take courage. Yes, wait for Yahweh.” (web:Ps.27.14), that brackets the unit as its own close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 8 rather than v. 7 is possible, since v. 7's imperative could be read as closing the confidence report rather than opening the petition.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative-plus-vocative opening at v. 7 (שְׁמַע יְהוָ֖ה, oshb:Ps.27.7) shifts the address mode from report to direct petition — WEB's “Hear, Yahweh” (web:Ps.27.7)
the doubled exhortation “wait for Yahweh” (web:Ps.27.14) brackets the unit's own close
device_notes: The closing doubled exhortation at v. 14 functions as this row's own resolution.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens with petition for a favorable divine answer, “To you, Yahweh, I call. My rock, don't be deaf to me, lest, if you are silent to me, I would become like those who go down into the pit.” (web:Ps.28.1), “Hear the voice of my petitions, when I cry to you, when I lift up my hands toward your Most Holy Place.” (web:Ps.28.2), then turns to an imprecation against the wicked, “Don't draw me away with the wicked, with the workers of iniquity who speak peace with their neighbors, but mischief is in their hearts.” (web:Ps.28.3), “Give them according to their work, and according to the wickedness of their doings. Give them according to the operation of their hands. Bring back on them what they deserve.” (web:Ps.28.4), closing with the reason for their judgment, “Because they don't respect the works of Yahweh, nor the operation of his hands, he will break them down and not build them up.” (web:Ps.28.5). V. 6 shifts abruptly to a declaration of answered prayer, “Blessed be Yahweh, because he has heard the voice of my petitions.” (web:Ps.28.6).
strongest_rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 4 rather than v. 5 is possible, since v. 5's stated reason for judgment could be grouped with the imprecation that precedes it rather than closing it.
observed_substrate_signals: petition-verb cluster (call/hear/draw away) frames vv. 1-3

the Qal imperative for “give” occurs twice in v. 4 as two differing pointed forms of the same lemma — תֶּן (word 1) and תֵּ֣ן (word 8), oshb:Ps.28.4 — before a third imperative, הָשֵׁ֖ב (“repay”), closes the verse (oshb:Ps.28.4)
device_notes: Psalm 28's rows share one parent, the psalm itself.

boundary_rationale: V. 6 pivots the psalm from petition to praise with a doxological formula, “Blessed be Yahweh, because he has heard the voice of my petitions.” (web:Ps.28.6), and the declaration of trust continues through v. 7, “Yahweh is my strength and my shield. My heart has trusted in him, and I am helped. Therefore my heart greatly rejoices. With my song I will thank him.” (web:Ps.28.7), in third-person report that widens to Yahweh's own anointed at v. 8, “Yahweh is their strength. He is a stronghold of salvation to his anointed.” (web:Ps.28.8 = oshb:Ps.28.8, the 3ms suffix on “his anointed” מְשִׁיח֣וֹ, taking Yahweh — not the king — as antecedent), before direct second-person address to Yahweh opens the closing petition, “Save your people, and bless your inheritance. Be their shepherd also, and bear them up forever.” (web:Ps.28.9).
strongest_rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 7 rather than v. 6 is possible, since v. 6's brief declaration could be read as closing the petition unit rather than opening the praise unit.
observed_substrate_signals: the doxological formula בָּר֥וּךְ יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.28.6) opens v. 6 as WEB's “Blessed be Yahweh” (web:Ps.28.6), marking the petition-to-praise pivot

third-person report runs through v. 8 (the anointed one's possessor is Yahweh, not the king: “his anointed” web:Ps.28.8 = oshb:Ps.28.8, 3ms suffix מְשִׁיח֣וֹ); direct second-person address to Yahweh begins only at v. 9, “your people... your inheritance” (web:Ps.28.9), a referent-widening scope shift, not an addressee shift, closing the psalm
device_notes: The בָּר֥וּךְ יְהוָ֑ה formula in v. 6 marks an internal petition-to-praise pivot, not one of the book's four boundary doxologies (oshb:Ps.28.6).

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens with a heavenly summons distinct from the storm theophany that follows: “Ascribe to Yahweh, you sons of the mighty, ascribe to Yahweh glory and strength.” (web:Ps.29.1), “Ascribe to Yahweh the glory due to his name. Worship Yahweh in holy array.” (web:Ps.29.2). The vocative addressee is “you sons of the mighty” (בְּנֵ֣י אֵלִ֑ים, oshb:Ps.29.1); Yahweh (לַֽ֭יהוָה) is the imperative's dative recipient, not its addressee. Vocative address stops after v. 2 rather than shifting to a different addressee — the storm's forces described from v. 3 onward (cedars, wilderness, deer) are third-person subjects, not addressees.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Grouping vv. 1-2 with the storm hymn as one unbroken invocation is also defensible, since both share the same imperative-vocative register; this candidate isolates the heavenly summons on its distinct addressee alone.
observed_substrate_signals: the imperative lemma “ascribe/give” (הבו) occurs 3 times across these 2 verses (oshb:Ps.29.1 words 3 and 7, oshb:Ps.29.2 word 1); the exact pointed spelling הָב֣וּ occurs 2 of those 3 times (oshb:Ps.29.1 word 3 and oshb:Ps.29.2 word 1), oshb:Ps.29.1 word 7 pointed differently as הָב֥וּ

the WEB phrase “sons of the mighty” (web:Ps.29.1) renders the vocative בְּנֵ֣י אֵלִ֑ים (oshb:Ps.29.1 words 5-6), this psalm's only named addressee; Yahweh, named as the imperative's dative recipient in vv. 1-2, is not himself addressed, and 0 vocative or second-person forms recur across oshb:Ps.29.3-Ps.29.9
device_notes: Psalm 29 forms one composition; its rows answer to one parent.

boundary_rationale: From v. 3 the storm theophany opens with the refrain that structures this unit, “Yahweh's voice is on the waters. The God of glory thunders, even Yahweh on many waters.” (web:Ps.29.3), and the phrase ק֥וֹל יְהוָ֗ה ("the voice of Yahweh"; oshb:Ps.29.3) recurs seven times across these six verses (vv. 3, 4 x2, 5, 7, 8, 9; sweep.py --skel, token tier) before the temple acclamation closes the refrain's reach at v. 9, “Yahweh's voice makes the deer calve, and strips the forests bare. In his temple everything says, "Glory!"” (web:Ps.29.9). The refrain is confined to this span, framed by the heavenly summons before it and the enthronement declaration after.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the refrain unit to include the surrounding summons or enthronement verses is possible, since the voice-of-Yahweh refrain's theophanic force colors the whole psalm; this candidate keeps the boundary at the refrain's own opening and closing occurrences.
observed_substrate_signals: the voice-of-Yahweh refrain (oshb:Ps.29.3) opens 6 of 7 verses in this span, doubled in v. 4, and is absent only from v. 6, which continues the storm's effects (Lebanon and Sirion skipping) rather than opening new content
device_notes: Yahweh is named 18 times across the psalm's 11 verses (device inventory), corroborating without driving this refrain-bounded reading.

boundary_rationale: The refrain drops after v. 9, and the psalm closes with an enthronement declaration, “Yahweh sat enthroned at the Flood. Yes, Yahweh sits as King forever.” (web:Ps.29.10), resolving into a blessing on Yahweh's people, “Yahweh will give strength to his people. Yahweh will bless his people with peace.” (web:Ps.29.11), a scope shift from the storm's cosmic reach to the covenant community.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping v. 10 inside the refrain unit is possible, since its enthronement language continues the theophany's storm imagery in form; this candidate isolates it with v. 11 on shared king/peace vocabulary that closes the psalm.
observed_substrate_signals: the refrain's final appearance is v. 9; v. 10 opens without the voice-of-Yahweh phrase, marking the drop (oshb:Ps.29.9, oshb:Ps.29.10)

the scope shifts from Yahweh's own cosmic enthronement (v. 10) to “his people” (the 3ms-suffixed noun עם, oshb:Ps.29.11 = web:Ps.29.11: dative לְעַמּ֣וֹ at word 3, direct object עַמּ֣וֹ at word 8 — related but byte-unequal forms), the psalm's first mention of a covenant community as object of blessing; the doubled-divine-name pattern itself recurs in 8 of the psalm's 11 verses and does not by itself distinguish this closing pair
device_notes: Yahweh appears twice in both v. 10 and v. 11, but the doubled-name pattern recurs in 8 of the psalm's 11 verses (device inventory) and is not unique to the closing pair; “his people” (לְעַמּ֣וֹ/עַמּ֣וֹ, oshb:Ps.29.11 = web:Ps.29.11) marks the psalm's scope-narrowing close instead.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens with testimony addressed to Yahweh, “I will extol you, Yahweh, for you have raised me up, and have not made my foes to rejoice over me.” (web:Ps.30.1), continuing through the report of healing and rescue from Sheol, “Yahweh, you have brought up my soul from Sheol. You have kept me alive, that I should not go down to the pit.” (web:Ps.30.3). V. 4 shifts from this testimony to a congregational summons, “Sing praise to Yahweh, you saints of his. Give thanks to his holy name.” (web:Ps.30.4).
strongest_rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 4 rather than v. 3 is also defensible, since v. 3's Sheol/pit language and v. 4's call to praise share the same rescue-and-response movement common to individual thanksgiving psalms.
observed_substrate_signals: testimony verbs (extol/raised up/cried/healed/brought up) address Yahweh directly through v. 3
v. 4 opens with the imperative זַמְּר֣וּ ("sing praise") plus a new addressee, "you saints of his", replacing direct address to Yahweh (web:Ps.30.4 = oshb:Ps.30.5)
device_notes: Psalm 30's rows converge on one parent, the psalm itself. The title verse carries its own genre labels (mizmor, shir) alongside the dedication note (web:Ps.30.0 = oshb:Ps.30.1).

boundary_rationale: V. 4 turns from personal testimony to a congregational summons, “Sing praise to Yahweh, you saints of his. Give thanks to his holy name.” (web:Ps.30.4), grounded in the maxim that follows, “For his anger is but for a moment. His favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the morning.” (web:Ps.30.5). V. 6 returns to the psalmist's own voice with a new temporal marker, “As for me, I said in my prosperity, "I shall never be moved."” (web:Ps.30.6).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping vv. 4-5 with the testimony that precedes them is also defensible, since the summons still addresses the congregation about Yahweh's saving acts already narrated; this candidate isolates the maxim on its own imperative-plus-vocative opening.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative זַמְּר֣וּ ("sing praise") plus vocative addressee "you saints of his" opens v. 4, shifting from Yahweh-directed address to a congregational summons (web:Ps.30.4 = oshb:Ps.30.5)
the moment/lifetime, night/morning antitheses of v. 5 state the maxim grounding the summons before the narrative resumes at v. 6
device_notes: The night-to-morning maxim of v. 5 anticipates the psalm's own mourning-to-dancing resolution at its close. A zamar-root inclusio also brackets the two strophes: the summons's opening imperative, זַמְּר֣וּ ("sing praise", web:Ps.30.4 = oshb:Ps.30.5), recurs in the psalm's closing verse, יְזַמֶּרְךָ֣ ("may sing praise to you", web:Ps.30.12 = oshb:Ps.30.13).

boundary_rationale: V. 6 returns to the psalmist's own voice with a temporal marker, “As for me, I said in my prosperity, "I shall never be moved."” (web:Ps.30.6), narrating the reversal that follows — Yahweh hiding his face (web:Ps.30.7) and the embedded cry quoted directly through v. 10, “Hear, Yahweh, and have mercy on me. Yahweh, be my helper."” (web:Ps.30.10) — before the psalm resolves in present-tense testimony, “You have turned my mourning into dancing for me. You have removed my sackcloth, and clothed me with gladness,” (web:Ps.30.11), closing with thanksgiving forever (web:Ps.30.12).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting vv. 6-7 (narrative setup), vv. 8-10 (the quoted cry), and vv. 11-12 (resolution) into three rows is also defensible on the same narrative movement; this candidate keeps the reversal-and-resolution arc as one row bounded by the congregational summons before it.
observed_substrate_signals: the psalmist's own voice (וַ֭אֲנִי אָמַ֣רְתִּי, "and I, I said") opens v. 6, marking the narrative's start (web:Ps.30.6 = oshb:Ps.30.7)
a direct quotation runs vv. 9-10 in the WEB's own punctuation, embedded inside the narrated cry of v. 8
the resolution verb הָפַ֣כְתָּ ("you have turned") opens v. 11, answering the reversal narrated from v. 6 (web:Ps.30.11 = oshb:Ps.30.12)
device_notes: A zamar-root inclusio brackets this strophe with the summons that precedes it: this closing verse's יְזַמֶּרְךָ֣ ("may sing praise to you", web:Ps.30.12 = oshb:Ps.30.13) answers the opening imperative זַמְּר֣וּ ("sing praise", web:Ps.30.4 = oshb:Ps.30.5); no shared root links this closing verse to the psalm's own opening verse (web:Ps.30.1), which instead uses the extolling verb rum.

boundary_rationale: The superscription “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David.” opens the psalm at web:Ps.31.0 (oshb:Ps.31.1). The strophe itself opens the refuge plea with בְּךָ֖ יְהוָ֣ה חָ֭סִיתִי (oshb:Ps.31.2) “In you, Yahweh, I take refuge” at web:Ps.31.1, vocative fused directly to the verb, then runs a cluster of second-person imperatives, הַטֵּ֤ה אֵלַ֨י אָזְנְךָ֮ מְהֵרָ֪ה הַצִּ֫ילֵ֥נִי הֱיֵ֤ה לִ֨י לְֽצוּר מָ֭עוֹז לְבֵ֥ית מְצוּד֗וֹת לְהוֹשִׁיעֵֽנִי (oshb:Ps.31.3) “Bow down your ear to me. Deliver me speedily. Be to me a strong rock, a house of defense to save me” (web:Ps.31.2). The mood pivots at web:Ps.31.5 with בְּיָדְךָ֮ אַפְקִ֪יד ר֫וּחִ֥י (oshb:Ps.31.6) “Into your hand I commend my spirit.” This self-consecration clause is followed by testimony that closes the strophe — “You have known my soul in adversities” (web:Ps.31.7) and “You have set my feet in a large place” (web:Ps.31.8) — reporting deliverance already granted rather than still being requested.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A break after web:Ps.31.4 was weighed and set aside: the imperative petitions run unbroken in verb mood and addressee from web:Ps.31.1 through the self-consecration clause at web:Ps.31.5, which itself renews the vocative address, פָּדִ֖יתָה אוֹתִ֥י יְהוָ֗ה אֵ֣ל אֱמֶֽת (oshb:Ps.31.6) “You redeem me, Yahweh, God of truth” (web:Ps.31.5); the strophe's next vocative renewal after that falls at web:Ps.31.9, already inside the imperative petition that opens the next strophe.
observed_substrate_signals: בְּךָ֖ יְהוָ֣ה חָ֭סִיתִי (oshb:Ps.31.2) fuses the vocative to the opening verb, matching the strophe's position immediately after the title

הַטֵּ֤ה אֵלַ֨י אָזְנְךָ֮ מְהֵרָ֪ה הַצִּ֫ילֵ֥נִי הֱיֵ֤ה לִ֨י לְֽצוּר מָ֭עוֹז לְבֵ֥ית מְצוּד֗וֹת לְהוֹשִׁיעֵֽנִי (oshb:Ps.31.3) runs consecutive second-person imperatives through the strophe's opening half
בְּיָדְךָ֮ אַפְקִ֪יד ר֫וּחִ֥י (oshb:Ps.31.6) shifts the verb mood from imperative petition to singular self-consecration, the strophe's hinge
device_notes: These rows resolve upward to Psalm 31 as parent. The title carries the mizmor, lamnatseach, and le-David genre labels (psalm_device_inventory.json), tier-1 opener evidence dual-cited at web:Ps.31.0 = oshb:Ps.31.1.

boundary_rationale: A fresh petition opens at web:Ps.31.9 with חָנֵּ֥נִי יְהוָה֮ (oshb:Ps.31.10) “Have mercy on me, Yahweh,” an imperative-plus-vocative pairing that reopens the address to God after the testimony register of web:Ps.31.7-Ps.31.8. The strophe stays in singular distress description — bones wasting, life spent with sorrow (web:Ps.31.10), contempt among neighbors (web:Ps.31.11) — and closes with נִ֭שְׁכַּחְתִּי כְּמֵ֣ת מִלֵּ֑ב (oshb:Ps.31.13) “I am forgotten from their hearts like a dead man” (web:Ps.31.12), completing the isolation image before the adversative pivot at web:Ps.31.14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding web:Ps.31.9-13 into the preceding strophe was rejected because חָנֵּ֥נִי יְהוָה֮ (oshb:Ps.31.10) restarts the imperative-plus-vocative petition form after the declarative testimony of web:Ps.31.7-8, marking a return to distress rather than a continuation of it.
observed_substrate_signals: חָנֵּ֥נִי יְהוָה֮ (oshb:Ps.31.10) repeats the imperative-plus-vocative petition form of the psalm's own opener
נִ֭שְׁכַּחְתִּי כְּמֵ֣ת מִלֵּ֑ב (oshb:Ps.31.13) closes the strophe on an isolation image before the adversative pivot that opens web:Ps.31.14
device_notes: The strophe's distress vocabulary (bones, contempt, oblivion) belongs to the same Davidic lament register named at the title; no further psalm-level device touches this span.

boundary_rationale: The pronoun-fronted וַאֲנִ֤י עָלֶ֣יךָ בָטַ֣חְתִּי יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.31.15) “But I trust in you, Yahweh” opens web:Ps.31.14 with the adversative pronoun fronting the clause, a contrastive pivot after the isolation close of web:Ps.31.13. Trust language carries through “My times are in your hand” (web:Ps.31.15) into a renewed petition for deliverance from enemies (web:Ps.31.15-16), then closes with an imprecation against שִׂפְתֵ֫י שָׁ֥קֶר (oshb:Ps.31.19) “the lying lips” that speak “against the righteous insolently” (web:Ps.31.18).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the prior strophe through web:Ps.31.14 was rejected: וַאֲנִ֤י (oshb:Ps.31.15) fronts the clause precisely where the isolation testimony of web:Ps.31.13 ends, and the trust declaration it introduces governs the petitions that follow rather than extending the lament catalogue.
observed_substrate_signals: וַאֲנִ֤י (oshb:Ps.31.15) fronts the independent pronoun against the preceding third-person image, marking the adversative turn; the same pronoun (וַאֲנִ֤י, oshb:Ps.31.23) recurs mid-strophe at web:Ps.31.22, inside the strophe that follows this one, without marking a seam there
שִׂפְתֵ֫י שָׁ֥קֶר (oshb:Ps.31.19) closes the strophe on an imprecation against slanderous speech, distinct from the petition-for-self register that opens it
device_notes: No selah, acrostic, or doxology device touches this strophe; the adversative-pronoun pivot is a syntactic, not a marks-layer, signal.

boundary_rationale: An exclamatory particle opens web:Ps.31.19: מָ֤ה רַֽב טוּבְךָ֮ (oshb:Ps.31.20) “Oh how great is your goodness,” shifting from second-person petition to a meditative admiration of goodness “laid up for those who fear you”. The strophe develops the shelter image (web:Ps.31.20) and closes with the berakhah formula בָּר֥וּךְ יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.31.22) “Praise be to Yahweh” (web:Ps.31.21) paired with a testimony recap — “you heard the voice of my petitions when I cried to you” (web:Ps.31.22) — before the psalm turns to address the community.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying this strophe through web:Ps.31.24 was rejected: the berakhah formula and its testimony recap remain addressed toward God (second- and third-person about Yahweh), while web:Ps.31.23 turns to address “all you his saints” directly — a distinct addressee.
observed_substrate_signals: מָ֤ה רַֽב (oshb:Ps.31.20) opens with an exclamatory particle absent from the surrounding petition verses, marking a register shift to praise
בָּר֥וּךְ יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.31.22) is the psalm's berakhah formula, closing the strophe on formal praise rather than petition
device_notes: The berakhah at web:Ps.31.21 belongs to Psalm 31's own praise turn; it is not one of the Psalter's book-boundary doxologies that close Books I through IV elsewhere in the Psalter, so no coda unit_type applies here.

boundary_rationale: The closing couplet turns from addressing Yahweh to addressing the congregation: אֶֽהֱב֥וּ אֶת יְהוָ֗ה כָּֽל חֲסִ֫ידָ֥יו (oshb:Ps.31.24) “Oh love Yahweh, all you his saints!” opens web:Ps.31.23 with a plural imperative and a third-person referent for God (“his saints”, not “you”), and חִ֭זְקוּ וְיַאֲמֵ֣ץ (oshb:Ps.31.25) “Be strong, and let your heart take courage” continues the same congregational address through the psalm's close at web:Ps.31.24.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading web:Ps.31.23-24 as a continuation of the praise strophe was rejected because the addressee changes from Yahweh — second person through most of web:Ps.31.19-22, but third person at the berakhah formula itself, בָּר֥וּךְ (oshb:Ps.31.22) “Praise be to Yahweh, for he has shown me his marvelous loving kindness” (web:Ps.31.21) — to “his saints” (web:Ps.31.23) and “you who hope in Yahweh” (web:Ps.31.24), a shift in who is spoken to rather than what is said about God.
observed_substrate_signals: אֶֽהֱב֥וּ אֶת יְהוָ֗ה כָּֽל חֲסִ֫ידָ֥יו (oshb:Ps.31.24) is a plural imperative addressed to “all you his saints” (web:Ps.31.23), not to Yahweh directly — the divine referent is embedded via the third-person possessive suffix (“his”) rather than a direct second-person address to God
חִ֭זְקוּ (oshb:Ps.31.25) sustains the plural-imperative congregational address through the psalm's final verse
device_notes: The psalm closes without a book-boundary doxology; the exhortation functions as this composition's own coda-like exit, kept here as strophe rather than coda since that unit_type is reserved for the four book-seam doxology closes.

boundary_rationale: The title “By David. A contemplative psalm.” sits inside MT v1 for this identity psalm, dual-cited web:Ps.32.0 = oshb:Ps.32.1 (maskil, le-David labels; psalm_device_inventory.json). The strophe opens with the paired beatitude אַשְׁרֵ֥י (oshb:Ps.32.1) “Blessed is he” and אַ֥שְֽׁרֵי אָדָ֗ם (oshb:Ps.32.2) “Blessed is the man” (web:Ps.32.1-2), pivots to singular confession at web:Ps.32.3 — כִּֽי הֶ֭חֱרַשְׁתִּי (oshb:Ps.32.3) “When I kept silence” — and moves through disclosure of sin (web:Ps.32.5) into instruction for “everyone who is godly” (web:Ps.32.6). Selah marks web:Ps.32.4, web:Ps.32.5, and closes the strophe at web:Ps.32.7, corroborating the pause before the divine speech that opens web:Ps.32.8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the beatitude (web:Ps.32.1-2) from the confession (web:Ps.32.3-7) into separate rows was rejected: the beatitude states the blessing the confession then narrates receiving, and no addressee or speaker shift separates them — no speaker change occurs before web:Ps.32.8.
observed_substrate_signals: אַשְׁרֵ֥י (oshb:Ps.32.1) opens the psalm's ashrei beatitude particle
אַ֥שְֽׁרֵי אָדָ֗ם (oshb:Ps.32.2) repeats the same ashrei beatitude particle one verse later
כִּֽי הֶ֭חֱרַשְׁתִּי (oshb:Ps.32.3) shifts from third-person maxim to singular confession without changing addressee
selah closes three verses of this seven-verse strophe (Ps.32.4, Ps.32.5, Ps.32.7 in pmarks_Ps.json), the three placed within this span
device_notes: The parent unit here is the full Psalm 32. Its eleven verses carry three of the book's 71 selah instances, together placed inside this psalm's span. Ps 32 also carries 5 paseq segs (a seg-layer, single-witness mark: MT 32:4, 32:6, 32:7, 32:8, and 32:9); the first three of these (MT 32:4, 32:6, 32:7) fall inside this row's own span.

boundary_rationale: A speaker change opens web:Ps.32.8: אַשְׂכִּֽילְךָ֨ וְֽאוֹרְךָ֗ (oshb:Ps.32.8) “I will instruct you and teach you” follows immediately after the selah close of web:Ps.32.7, read here as Yahweh's own answer rather than the psalmist's continued speech, addressed with a warning against the “horse” and “mule” (web:Ps.32.9). The strophe closes with a wisdom contrast between the wicked and וְהַבּוֹטֵ֥חַ בַּיהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.32.10) “him who trusts in Yahweh” (web:Ps.32.10) and an imperative call to “Be glad… rejoice… Shout for joy” (web:Ps.32.11).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping web:Ps.32.8-11 attached to the confession strophe was rejected: the instructing voice at web:Ps.32.8 addresses the psalmist rather than confessing, a role the confessing psalmist does not otherwise take in this psalm, and the selah at web:Ps.32.7 corroborates — without driving — the seam.
observed_substrate_signals: אַשְׂכִּֽילְךָ֨ (oshb:Ps.32.8) introduces an instructing voice distinct from the confessing “I” of web:Ps.32.3-5
וְהַבּוֹטֵ֥חַ בַּיהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.32.10) closes the wisdom contrast that the imperative call to rejoice (web:Ps.32.11) then answers
device_notes: This span opens immediately after the selah at web:Ps.32.7 (pmarks_Ps.json); selah is corroboration for the seam, not its driver — the speaker shift at web:Ps.32.8 is the independent driver.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 33 carries no WEB title and opens directly with an imperative cluster: רַנְּנ֣וּ צַ֭דִּיקִים בַּֽיהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.33.1) “Rejoice in Yahweh, you righteous!” (web:Ps.33.1), הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה (oshb:Ps.33.2) “Give thanks to Yahweh” (web:Ps.33.2), and שִֽׁירוּ ל֭וֹ (oshb:Ps.33.3) “Sing to him” (web:Ps.33.3), three consecutive plural imperatives addressed to the congregation. This is the psalm's opener evidence, functionally parallel to the superscriptions that open titled psalms even though Psalm 33 carries no title.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the imperative strophe through web:Ps.33.9 was rejected: the call-to-worship imperatives addressed to the congregation end at web:Ps.33.3, and web:Ps.33.4 opens a motive clause moving to third-person declaration about Yahweh. The nearest comparable volitive form after that is the jussive יִֽירְא֣וּ (web:Ps.33.8 = oshb:Ps.33.8) “Let all the earth fear Yahweh”, addressed to the whole earth rather than the congregation of “you righteous” (web:Ps.33.1); no further plural imperative addressed to a congregation recurs anywhere later in the psalm, including at its close (web:Ps.33.20-22, which is declarative throughout except for the 3ms jussive יְהִֽי (oshb:Ps.33.22, ‘let it be’), at web:Ps.33.22).
observed_substrate_signals: three verse-initial plural imperatives — רַנְּנ֣וּ (web:Ps.33.1 = oshb:Ps.33.1), הוֹד֣וּ (web:Ps.33.2 = oshb:Ps.33.2), שִֽׁירוּ (web:Ps.33.3 = oshb:Ps.33.3) — open the psalm, with two further plural imperatives closing v.2 (זַמְּרוּ) and inside v.3 (הֵיטִ֥יבוּ), five in all across the span; the addressee named is צַ֭דִּיקִים (web:Ps.33.1 = oshb:Ps.33.1) “you righteous”, not a divine vocative
web:Ps.33.4 opens with כִּֽי (oshb:Ps.33.4), a motive-clause particle shifting from imperative address to declarative predication
device_notes: Under Psalm 33 the rows form one family. The psalm's 22 verses match the Hebrew alphabet's count, but the acrostics table in psalm_device_inventory.json carries no entry for Psalm 33 (its keyed psalms are 9, 10, 25, 34, 37, 111, 112, 119, 145) — no acrostic scheme is claimed for this psalm; the imperative cluster of web:Ps.33.1-3 is the opener evidence instead.

boundary_rationale: כִּֽי יָשָׁ֥ר דְּבַר יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.33.4) “For Yahweh's word is right” opens web:Ps.33.4 with a motive clause explaining the preceding call to worship, moving into third-person declaration through creation-by-word imagery: בִּדְבַ֣ר יְ֭הוָה שָׁמַ֣יִם נַעֲשׂ֑וּ (oshb:Ps.33.6) “By Yahweh's word, the heavens were made” (web:Ps.33.6). The unit closes on the nations-versus-Yahweh antithesis: “Yahweh brings the counsel of the nations to nothing” (web:Ps.33.10) set against עֲצַ֣ת יְ֭הוָה לְעוֹלָ֣ם תַּעֲמֹ֑ד (oshb:Ps.33.11) “The counsel of Yahweh stands fast forever” (web:Ps.33.11), a resolved contrast that closes the unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the creation section (web:Ps.33.4-9) from the nations section (web:Ps.33.10-11) into separate rows was rejected: both develop the same point about the supremacy of Yahweh's spoken word, with the topic changing but no addressee, speaker, or imperative-mood signal marking a seam between web:Ps.33.9 and web:Ps.33.10.
observed_substrate_signals: כִּֽי (oshb:Ps.33.4) opens a motive clause immediately after the imperative cluster closes
עֲצַ֣ת יְ֭הוָה לְעוֹלָ֣ם תַּעֲמֹ֑ד (oshb:Ps.33.11) resolves the counsel/word antithesis opened at web:Ps.33.10, closing the unit
device_notes: This eight-verse span carries no selah or acrostic marker; its coherence is topical (Yahweh's word as creative and sovereign speech) rather than marks-layer.

boundary_rationale: A beatitude formula reopens the psalm's third movement: אַשְׁרֵ֣י הַ֭גּוֹי (oshb:Ps.33.12) “Blessed is the nation” at web:Ps.33.12, the same ashrei particle that opens Psalm 32 (web:Ps.32.1-2). From the elect nation the unit widens to Yahweh's oversight of humankind (web:Ps.33.13-15), the futility of military strength (web:Ps.33.16-17), and closes on הִנֵּ֤ה עֵ֣ין יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.33.18) “Behold, Yahweh's eye is on those who fear him” (web:Ps.33.18), extending through deliverance “from death” and “famine” at web:Ps.33.19.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging this span with the preceding word/creation unit was rejected: אַשְׁרֵ֣י (oshb:Ps.33.12) reopens the beatitude form used once already in this psalm's companion at web:Ps.32.1-2, a formulaic opener the intervening counsel-versus-counsel antithesis of web:Ps.33.10-11 does not carry.
observed_substrate_signals: אַשְׁרֵ֣י (oshb:Ps.33.12) reopens the beatitude particle after the resolved antithesis of web:Ps.33.11
הִנֵּ֤ה עֵ֣ין יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.33.18) opens the strophe's closing unit with a presentative particle shifting the focus to those who fear Yahweh, closing on deliverance from death and famine
device_notes: The ashrei opener at web:Ps.33.12 reuses, in its own wording, the same beatitude particle already seen at web:Ps.32.1-2 in the preceding psalm of this part; the two uses are treated as texture, not as a cross-psalm boundary relation.

boundary_rationale: A person shift closes the psalm: נַ֭פְשֵׁנוּ חִכְּתָ֣ה (oshb:Ps.33.20) “Our soul has waited for Yahweh” opens web:Ps.33.20 with נַ֭פְשֵׁנוּ, a noun (“soul”) bearing the first-person-plural possessive suffix (“our”), governing the third-person-feminine-singular verb חִכְּתָ֣ה (“has waited”, agreeing with the feminine noun nefesh); this plural self-reference is not used earlier in the psalm, replacing the third-person “he/his” language of web:Ps.33.13-19 with a congregational “we/our” voice that continues through the closing petition יְהִֽי חַסְדְּךָ֣ יְהוָ֣ה עָלֵ֑ינוּ (oshb:Ps.33.22) “Let your loving kindness be on us, Yahweh” (web:Ps.33.22).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.33.20-22 as a continuation of the providence unit was rejected: the pronoun shifts from third-person “him/his” description of Yahweh's oversight to a plural “our/we” congregational address, a change in speaker voice the preceding eight verses do not share.
observed_substrate_signals: נַ֭פְשֵׁנוּ (oshb:Ps.33.20) is a noun (‘soul’) with a first-person-plural possessive suffix (‘our’), taking the third-person-feminine-singular finite verb חִכְּתָ֣ה (‘has waited’, web:Ps.33.20); this plural self-reference is not used earlier in the psalm, against “he/his” forms in the immediately preceding span
יְהִֽי חַסְדְּךָ֣ (oshb:Ps.33.22) closes the psalm on a jussive petition in the same congregational voice
device_notes: This closing strophe carries no selah, doxology, or acrostic marker; Psalm 33's parent grouping (stated at web:Ps.33.1-3) covers this row as it does the rest of the psalm's rows.

boundary_rationale: The title “By David; when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech, who drove him away, and he departed” opens the psalm at web:Ps.34.0 (oshb:Ps.34.1) — title material naming the Abimelech episode, not a narrative row. Psalm 34 is acrostic (psalm_device_inventory.json: waw absent from the letter sequence) beginning אֲבָרֲכָ֣ה אֶת יְהוָ֣ה בְּכָל עֵ֑ת (oshb:Ps.34.2) “I will bless Yahweh at all times” (web:Ps.34.1), alef; בַּ֭יהוָה תִּתְהַלֵּ֣ל נַפְשִׁ֑י (oshb:Ps.34.3) “My soul shall boast in Yahweh” (web:Ps.34.2), bet; גַּדְּל֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה אִתִּ֑י (oshb:Ps.34.4) “Oh magnify Yahweh with me” (web:Ps.34.3), gimel — a communal invitation opening the strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Merging web:Ps.34.1-3 with web:Ps.34.4-7 was rejected: the communal invitation register (‘with me’, ‘let's exalt’ together) closes at web:Ps.34.3 — the psalm's one cohortative verb, וּנְרוֹמְמָ֖ה (oshb:Ps.34.4), occurs inside this row's own span (it occurs exactly once in the psalm) and does not recur later — and web:Ps.34.4 turns instead to individual singular testimony, “I sought Yahweh, and he answered me”
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe's three verses open the acrostic's first three letters alef, bet, gimel (byte-checked against web:Ps.34.1-3; sweep: 22 verses, waw the acrostic's only gap per psalm_device_inventory.json)

וּנְרוֹמְמָ֖ה שְׁמ֣וֹ יַחְדָּֽו (oshb:Ps.34.4) closes the strophe on the cohortative “Let's exalt his name together” (web:Ps.34.3), the final plural-cohortative verb before individual testimony resumes
device_notes: Psalm 34's rows answer to one shared parent grouping across this part. The historical title names Abimelech (1 Sam 21 material, kept as title text and not quoted as narrative); the acrostic surface is byte-confirmed alef through gimel here and continues waw-less through this psalm's remaining rows.

boundary_rationale: Individual testimony opens web:Ps.34.4, dalet: דָּרַ֣שְׁתִּי אֶת יְהוָ֣ה וְעָנָ֑נִי (oshb:Ps.34.5) “I sought Yahweh, and he answered me”. The acrostic's waw gap falls inside this strophe: web:Ps.34.5 opens with he, הִבִּ֣יטוּ אֵלָ֣יו (oshb:Ps.34.6) “They looked to him,” and web:Ps.34.6 opens with zayin, זֶ֤ה עָנִ֣י קָ֭רָא (oshb:Ps.34.7) “This poor man cried,” with no verse beginning waw between them (sweep: 22 verses byte-checked, one letter absent). The strophe closes at web:Ps.34.7, het, generalizing to “Yahweh's angel encamps around those who fear him”.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading a verse-length gap at the missing waw as a textual defect was rejected: the letters he and zayin at web:Ps.34.5-6 sit on consecutive, undamaged verses in the byte text, so the absence is a surface irregularity of the acrostic scheme, not a lost verse.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.34.5 opens he (הִבִּ֣יטוּ (oshb:Ps.34.6)) and web:Ps.34.6 opens zayin (זֶ֤ה (oshb:Ps.34.7)) with no intervening verse opening waw — the acrostic's one gap, byte-checked (sweep: 22 verses)
דָּרַ֣שְׁתִּי (oshb:Ps.34.5) opens singular testimony that generalizes by web:Ps.34.7 to “those who fear him” in the third person
device_notes: This is the strophe carrying the acrostic's missing waw; the gap is disclosed here as surface data (psalm_device_inventory.json), not harmonized or treated as damage.

boundary_rationale: An imperative pair addressed to Yahweh's own worshippers reopens web:Ps.34.8, tet: טַעֲמ֣וּ וּ֭רְאוּ כִּי ט֣וֹב יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.34.9) “Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good”. This is followed by יְר֣אוּ אֶת יְהוָ֣ה קְדֹשָׁ֑יו (oshb:Ps.34.10) “Oh fear Yahweh, you his saints” (web:Ps.34.9), yod. The strophe closes on the young-lions wisdom contrast at web:Ps.34.10, kaf: כְּ֭פִירִים רָשׁ֣וּ (oshb:Ps.34.11) “The young lions do lack, and suffer hunger”.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding web:Ps.34.8-10 into the following “children” address (web:Ps.34.11-14) was rejected: the taste-and-see and fear-Yahweh imperatives here address Yahweh's own worshippers, embedded as קְדֹשָׁ֑יו “his saints” (oshb:Ps.34.10, web:Ps.34.9), while web:Ps.34.11 opens with a different named vocative, “children” — a change in addressed party, not a shift from unaddressed to addressed, a distinction the wisdom-lion contrast at web:Ps.34.10 does not share with either.
observed_substrate_signals: טַעֲמ֣וּ וּ֭רְאוּ (oshb:Ps.34.9) and יְר֣אוּ אֶת יְהוָ֣ה קְדֹשָׁ֑יו (oshb:Ps.34.10) form a two-verse imperative cluster addressed to Yahweh's worshippers, קְדֹשָׁ֑יו “his saints” (web:Ps.34.9), an addressee embedded via a third-person possessive suffix rather than a separately named vocative
כְּ֭פִירִים רָשׁ֣וּ (oshb:Ps.34.11) closes the strophe on a wisdom antithesis (lions lack, seekers of Yahweh do not) preceding the vocative shift at web:Ps.34.11
device_notes: These letters (tet, yod, kaf) continue the byte-confirmed acrostic sequence past the waw gap disclosed in the preceding strophe; no further irregularity falls in this span.

boundary_rationale: A named addressee opens web:Ps.34.11, lamed: לְֽכוּ בָ֭נִים שִׁמְעוּ לִ֑י (oshb:Ps.34.12) “Come, you children, listen to me”, shifting from the general imperatives of the preceding span to direct address of בָ֭נִים (oshb:Ps.34.12) “children.” Wisdom instruction continues through mem, nun, and ס (web:Ps.34.12-14): “desires life… Keep your tongue from evil … Depart from evil, and do good.”
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.34.15 was rejected: the second-person imperative address to “children” closes with web:Ps.34.14, and web:Ps.34.15 returns to third-person declaration about Yahweh's eyes and ears — no second-person imperative addressed to a human hearer recurs afterward.
observed_substrate_signals: לְֽכוּ בָ֭נִים שִׁמְעוּ לִ֑י (oshb:Ps.34.12) is the one verse-opening vocative in this psalm addressed to a human party rather than to or about Yahweh
the strophe's four verses carry the acrostic letters lamed, mem, nun, ס in sequence (byte-checked against web:Ps.34.11-14; sweep: 22 verses)
device_notes: Wisdom-instruction address to “children” is this strophe's own device; the acrostic continues unbroken here (no further letter gap after waw).

boundary_rationale: Third-person declaration about Yahweh's governance closes the psalm, opening web:Ps.34.15, ayin: עֵינֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה אֶל צַדִּיקִ֑ים (oshb:Ps.34.16) “Yahweh's eyes are toward the righteous”, with no vocative or imperative until the acrostic runs פ through tav (web:Ps.34.16-21) and closes on the extra-alphabetic פ verse at web:Ps.34.22: פּוֹדֶ֣ה יְ֭הוָה נֶ֣פֶשׁ עֲבָדָ֑יו (oshb:Ps.34.23) “Yahweh redeems the soul of his servants”, a closing פ beyond the standard 22-letter sequence (psalm_device_inventory.json).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting off web:Ps.34.22 as its own row was rejected: the extra פ verse continues the same third-person declaration about Yahweh's redemption begun at web:Ps.34.15, with no addressee or speaker change setting it apart from the seven verses before it.
observed_substrate_signals: the span runs ayin through tav (web:Ps.34.15-21) in unbroken acrostic sequence, then closes on a פ verse one position beyond the standard 22-letter/22-verse acrostic run
פּוֹדֶ֣ה יְ֭הוָה נֶ֣פֶשׁ עֲבָדָ֑יו (oshb:Ps.34.23) opens with פ, the acrostic's trailing extra letter per psalm_device_inventory.json

boundary_rationale: The unit opens on direct imperative address to Yahweh, רִיבָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה אֶת יְרִיבַ֑י (oshb:Ps.35.1) “Contend, Yahweh, with those who contend with me.” (web:Ps.35.1), and runs an imprecation against the psalmist’s pursuers through web:Ps.35.8; it turns at web:Ps.35.9-Ps.35.10 into a vow spoken in the psalmist’s own voice, וְ֭נַפְשִׁי תָּגִ֣יל (oshb:Ps.35.9) “My soul shall be joyful in Yahweh.” (web:Ps.35.9), a petition-to-vow turn that recurs as the close of this psalm’s two later complaint cycles (web:Ps.35.18, web:Ps.35.27-Ps.35.28).

boundary_rationale: The unit opens with a transgression oracle that the psalmist locates in his own heart, נְאֻֽם פֶּ֣שַׁע לָ֭רָשָׁע בְּקֶ֣רֶב (web:Ps.36.1 = oshb:Ps.36.2) “A revelation is within my heart about the disobedience of the wicked” — בְּקֶ֣רֶב (“within my heart”) carries a first-person-singular suffix, the psalmist's own heart, not the wicked man's; the verse's own second half turns to the wicked man's eyes in the third person, “There is no fear of God before his eyes.” (web:Ps.36.1). He has ceased to be wise and to do good.” (web:Ps.36.3) and אָ֤וֶן יַחְשֹׁ֗ב עַֽל (oshb:Ps.36.5) “He plots iniquity on his bed” (web:Ps.36.4); the address then turns to second-person praise of Yahweh at web:Ps.36.5 = oshb:Ps.36.6 — a discourse-frame change from oracle-about-the-wicked to hymn.
strongest_rejected_alternative: web:Ps.36.4 = oshb:Ps.36.5 could be read as transitional rather than part of the oracle unit, but it keeps the same third-person subject as web:Ps.36.1-Ps.36.3 = oshb:Ps.36.2-Ps.36.4, with no addressee change.

boundary_rationale: Second-person address to Yahweh opens the unit, “Your loving kindness, Yahweh, is in the heavens.” (web:Ps.36.5 = oshb:Ps.36.6), replacing the third-person “he” of the oracle unit; loving-kindness (חַסְדֶּ֑ךָ, oshb:Ps.36.6) and righteousness (צִדְקָֽתְךָ֨, oshb:Ps.36.7) recur toward web:Ps.36.10 = oshb:Ps.36.11, while faithfulness (אֱ֝מֽוּנָתְךָ֗, oshb:Ps.36.6, ‘your faithfulness’) occurs in exactly 1 verse of the span, web:Ps.36.5 = oshb:Ps.36.6, and does not recur; the closing petition, “Don't let the foot of pride come against me.” (web:Ps.36.11 = oshb:Ps.36.12), and the psalm's final report, “There the workers of iniquity are fallen… and shall not be able to rise” (web:Ps.36.12 = oshb:Ps.36.13), drop the second-person suffix altogether but remain this same unit, since nothing in the psalm reopens a fresh discourse frame after web:Ps.36.5 = oshb:Ps.36.6 before its close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A split at web:Ps.36.9|Ps.36.10 was also weighed: the imperative מְשֹׁ֣ךְ (oshb:Ps.36.11) “Oh continue” that opens web:Ps.36.10 turns the unit from declarative hymn to petition one verse before the loving-kindness/righteousness vocabulary closes; the psalm's own petition-then-report close still runs to a single point without a fresh addressee or speech-act frame reopening after web:Ps.36.5 = oshb:Ps.36.6, so the whole span from the hymn's second-person open through the psalm's end stays one unit.

boundary_rationale: נ opens web:Ps.37.25, נַ֤עַר (oshb:Ps.37.25) “I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken”; ס opens web:Ps.37.27, ס֣וּר (oshb:Ps.37.27) “Depart from evil, and do good.” The acrostic's structural sequence then continues regularly through this span's close: פ opens web:Ps.37.30, פִּֽי צַ֭דִּיק (oshb:Ps.37.30) “The mouth of the righteous talks of wisdom”, with ayin absent between the samekh and pe positions (matching the acrostic's own missing-letter table), and צ opens web:Ps.37.32, צוֹפֶ֣ה רָ֭שָׁע לַצַּדִּ֑יק (oshb:Ps.37.32) “The wicked watch the righteous” — pe before tsade, the regular alphabetic order. The surface tsade content word at web:Ps.37.29, צַדִּיקִ֥ים (oshb:Ps.37.29) “The righteous shall inherit the land”, is a premature occurrence, surface noise ahead of the letter's structural turn, of the same kind already disclosed for other incidental letters in this psalm's acrostic (e.g. the aleph noise at MT 37:13). Content runs continuously from the psalmist's life-long testimony (web:Ps.37.25-Ps.37.26) through the righteous's inheritance, speech, and law (web:Ps.37.29-Ps.37.31) to the wicked watching to kill (web:Ps.37.32).

boundary_rationale: This row opens mid-way through the acrostic's tsade span: tsade's full structural span runs two verses, MT 37:32-33, straddling the seam with the row before it, and this row's own opening pronouns, “him” / “he” (oshb:Ps.37.33), grammatically depend on ‘the righteous’ (tsaddiq) named at MT 37:32, one verse outside this row's own span. ק opens web:Ps.37.34, “Wait for Yahweh, and keep his way”; ר opens web:Ps.37.35, “I have seen the wicked in great power”; ש opens web:Ps.37.37, “Mark the perfect man, and see the upright”; tav never occupies a structural position in this acrostic — consistent with 5 of the book's 9 acrostic psalms, where tav likewise never reaches a structural position — though tav does occur once as a surface (non-structural) letter, at MT 37:31. The content closes the psalm on one continuous movement — Yahweh will not abandon the righteous (web:Ps.37.33), the call to wait and watch the wicked's end (web:Ps.37.34-Ps.37.36), and the righteous's future against the wicked's cutting-off (web:Ps.37.37-Ps.37.40) — giving the psalm's closing row one continuous content arc.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens on direct address, “Yahweh, don’t rebuke me in your wrath, neither chasten me in your hot displeasure” (web:Ps.38.1), and that vocative launches an unbroken self-voiced complaint of bodily affliction under divine wrath — arrows, sickness, and the weight of sin — running through “I am faint and severely bruised. I have groaned by reason of the anguish of my heart” (web:Ps.38.8); the next vocative, “Lord” (web:Ps.38.9), opens a new address and closes this span.
