the same second-person address still governs the description of the queen at the strophe’s close, נִצְּבָ֥ה שֵׁגַ֥ל לִֽ֝ימִינְךָ֗, "the queen stands at your right hand" (oshb:Ps.45.10); no vocative or imperative addressed to a second party interrupts this span, and the bride enters as a new addressee at the strophe that follows
device_notes: Each row here traces to the one Psalm-45 parent. Its title carries the maskil, shir, bene-Qorach, and al-shoshannim genre labels (psalm_device_inventory.json); this strophe’s address to the king runs unbroken across its 8 verses (web:Ps.45.1-Ps.45.9).

boundary_rationale: The feminine-singular imperative vocative “Listen, daughter, consider, and turn your ear. Forget your own people, and also your father’s house” (web:Ps.45.10) opens direct address to the bride, sustained through her procession, “With gladness and rejoicing they shall be led. They shall enter into the king’s palace” (web:Ps.45.15), immediately before address returns to the king.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.45.17 was rejected because the second-person forms revert from feminine-singular (addressed to the bride) to masculine-singular (addressed to the king) at web:Ps.45.16.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the feminine-singular imperative pair שִׁמְעִי בַ֣ת, "listen, daughter" (oshb:Ps.45.11), the psalm’s vocative address shift from king to bride

the strophe’s close describes the bridal procession, תְּ֝בֹאֶ֗ינָה בְּהֵ֣יכַל מֶֽלֶךְ, "they shall enter into the king’s palace" (oshb:Ps.45.16), still narrated in feminine-plural forms about the bride’s companions
device_notes: This strophe carries the address-shift the wedding maskil is built around; it carries no selah, but a paseq seg falls at oshb:Ps.45.13 (=web:Ps.45.12), inside its span (pmarks_Ps.json; single-witness, seg-layer disclosure).

boundary_rationale: Masculine-singular address returns at “Your sons will take the place of your fathers. You shall make them princes in all the earth” (web:Ps.45.16), redirecting the poem from the bride back to the king for the closing promise, “I will make your name to be remembered in all generations” (web:Ps.45.17), which ends the psalm.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating these two verses as a coda closing the wedding maskil was rejected because the psalm carries no doxology formula here — the closing promise is addressed praise, not one of the book’s baruch/amen seams.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on masculine-singular suffixes, תַּ֣חַת אֲ֭בֹתֶיךָ יִהְי֣וּ בָנֶ֑יךָ, "in place of your fathers will be your sons" (oshb:Ps.45.17), resuming the king-directed address of the psalm’s opening strophe
the closing verse shifts to the poet’s own voiced promise, a pattern that also opened the psalm at web:Ps.45.1
device_notes: The address-return to the king closes the wedding maskil’s three-part movement (king, bride, king); this two-verse strophe carries no selah or other disclosure-object device.

boundary_rationale: The refrain psalm opens on confession, “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” (web:Ps.46.1), grounding the cosmic-upheaval imagery that closes the strophe, “though the mountains tremble with their swelling. Selah” (web:Ps.46.3); no refrain sentence follows this Selah, unlike the repeated formula that later closes web:Ps.46.7 and web:Ps.46.11.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the missing refrain after web:Ps.46.3 as a textual gap to be repaired by supplying the refrain sentence was rejected; the row is chunked on the bytes as attested, and whether an opening refrain instance is lost here is held open rather than resolved.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on אֱלֹהִ֣ים לָ֭נוּ מַחֲסֶ֣ה וָעֹ֑ז, "God is for us a refuge and strength" (oshb:Ps.46.2), the confession the rest of the psalm elaborates

the strophe closes with Selah (web:Ps.46.3 = oshb:Ps.46.4) but without the refrain sentence that closes the two strophes following it (web:Ps.46.7 = oshb:Ps.46.8; web:Ps.46.11 = oshb:Ps.46.12), a recognized gap in the refrain pattern that this row discloses rather than fills

the true driver of this strophe's close is the topic shift at web:Ps.46.4, where the river-and-city-of-God image opens the next strophe; Selah and the refrain's absence here corroborate but do not themselves drive the boundary
device_notes: One parent spans Psalm 46’s rows. Its title carries the shir, bene-Qorach, and al-alamot genre labels (psalm_device_inventory.json); this psalm frames a debated three-part refrain structure that the rows following it carry forward.

boundary_rationale: The city-of-God strophe opens “There is a river, the streams of which make the city of God glad, the holy place of the tents of the Most High” (web:Ps.46.4), and after the nations-rage report, closes on the psalm’s refrain, “Yahweh of Armies is with us. The God of Jacob is our refuge. Selah” (web:Ps.46.7), the refrain’s initial full statement.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the opening strophe through this refrain as one seven-verse unit (web:Ps.46.1-7) was rejected because web:Ps.46.4 introduces a new image (the river and city of God) unrelated to the cosmic-upheaval imagery the opening strophe closed on.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on נָהָ֗ר פְּלָגָ֗יו יְשַׂמְּח֥וּ עִיר אֱלֹהִ֑ים, "a river, its streams, make glad the city of God" (oshb:Ps.46.5), pivoting the psalm’s imagery from cosmic upheaval to the city of God

the strophe begins immediately after the front-seam Selah of the preceding strophe (web:Ps.46.3 = oshb:Ps.46.4) and closes on its own Selah paired with the refrain יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֣וֹת עִמָּ֑נוּ מִשְׂגָּֽב לָ֝נוּ אֱלֹהֵ֖י יַעֲקֹ֣ב (oshb:Ps.46.8), which repeats at web:Ps.46.11 = oshb:Ps.46.12 in wording that collates byte-identical across its 2 verse occurrences
device_notes: This row’s unit_type is refrain_unit because its close carries the refrain’s initial full statement rather than a plain strophe break; the refrain corroborates the close, and the topic shift at its opening verse drives the boundary.

boundary_rationale: The imperative “Come, see Yahweh’s works, what desolations he has made in the earth” (web:Ps.46.8) opens the closing movement, moving through the divine speech “Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations. I will be exalted in the earth” (web:Ps.46.10) to the refrain’s return, “Yahweh of Armies is with us. The God of Jacob is our refuge. Selah” (web:Ps.46.11), closing the psalm.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this strophe into the preceding one as one eight-verse unit was rejected because the imperative “Come, see” at web:Ps.46.8 opens a new address to an audience, distinct from the report-and-refrain movement the prior strophe closed on.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the imperative pair לְֽכוּ חֲ֭זוּ מִפְעֲל֣וֹת יְהוָ֑ה, "come, see the works of Yahweh" (oshb:Ps.46.9), addressing a second party directly again after the psalm’s opening confession

the strophe begins immediately after the front-seam Selah of the preceding strophe (web:Ps.46.7 = oshb:Ps.46.8) and closes on the refrain’s second occurrence, יְהוָ֣ה צְבָא֣וֹת עִמָּ֑נוּ מִשְׂגָּֽב לָ֝נוּ אֱלֹהֵ֖י יַעֲקֹ֣ב (oshb:Ps.46.12), paired again with Selah
device_notes: This row’s unit_type is refrain_unit for the same reason as the strophe before it: the boundary is driven by the imperative address shift at its opening verse, and the refrain corroborates the close.

boundary_rationale: The enthronement hymn opens on the imperative summons “Oh clap your hands, all you nations. Shout to God with the voice of triumph!” (web:Ps.47.1), grounded in the reason clause “For Yahweh Most High is awesome. He is a great King over all the earth” (web:Ps.47.2), closing “He chooses our inheritance for us, the glory of Jacob whom he loved. Selah” (web:Ps.47.4) before the psalm shifts from summons to narrative report.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A split after web:Ps.47.2 (the reason clause) was rejected because the second-person-plural imperative summons opened at web:Ps.47.1 continues to govern the psalm’s stance through the Selah at web:Ps.47.4 without a new address.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the imperative summons כָּֽל הָ֭עַמִּים תִּקְעוּ, "all peoples, clap" (oshb:Ps.47.2), addressed to the nations in second-person-plural imperative

this psalm’s opening strophe begins immediately after Psalm 46’s closing Selah and refrain (web:Ps.46.11 = oshb:Ps.46.12), a separate parent composition and not evidence for this psalm’s own boundary; this strophe closes on its own Selah (web:Ps.47.4 = oshb:Ps.47.5)
device_notes: Psalm 47’s rows answer to one parent composition. Its title carries the mizmor and bene-Qorach genre labels (psalm_device_inventory.json); this opening strophe’s imperative-to-the-nations summons frames the psalm’s clap-your-hands enthronement scene.

boundary_rationale: The narrative report “God has gone up with a shout, Yahweh with the sound of a trumpet” (web:Ps.47.5) turns the psalm from imperative summons to third-person account of the ascent, then returns to imperative in the fourfold “Sing praises to God! Sing praises! Sing praises to our King! Sing praises!” (web:Ps.47.6), closing on the enthronement declaration “God reigns over the nations. God sits on his holy throne” (web:Ps.47.8) and the assembly of the princes at web:Ps.47.9.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A split before the imperative cluster at web:Ps.47.6 was rejected because the report of God’s ascent and the ensuing call to sing praises share the same enthronement scene without a topic break between them.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the narrative report עָלָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים בִּתְרוּעָ֑ה, "God has gone up with a shout" (oshb:Ps.47.6), the psalm’s turn from address-to-nations to third-person account

the imperative זַמְּר֣וּ אֱלֹהִ֣ים זַמֵּ֑רוּ, "sing praises, God, sing praises" (oshb:Ps.47.7), opens the verse; the bare imperative token זַמְּר֣וּ/זַמֵּ֑רוּ recurs four times within the same verse (web:Ps.47.6), a different, word-level count from the 3-word phrase quoted here
device_notes: This strophe’s close, “God reigns over the nations. God sits on his holy throne” (web:Ps.47.8), forms the psalm’s structural climax rather than a book-boundary doxology. The strophe opens immediately after the psalm's selah, which closes the preceding unit at web:Ps.47.4 = oshb:Ps.47.5; the front-seam mark is corroborative texture, not a driver of this row's own boundary.

boundary_rationale: The Zion hymn opens on praise, “Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised, in the city of our God, in his holy mountain” (web:Ps.48.1), describing the city’s beauty through “Beautiful in elevation, the joy of the whole earth, is Mount Zion” (web:Ps.48.2) to the declaration “God has shown himself in her citadels as a refuge” (web:Ps.48.3), immediately before the narrative report of the kings’ assault opens the next strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A split after web:Ps.48.1 was rejected because the description of Zion’s beauty and defense continues one descriptive movement through web:Ps.48.3 without a narrative marker like the “For, behold” that opens the next strophe.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on גָּ֘ד֤וֹל יְהוָ֣ה וּמְהֻלָּ֣ל מְאֹ֑ד, "great is Yahweh, and greatly praised" (oshb:Ps.48.2), a declarative formula distinct from the narrative report that follows

the strophe closes on אֱלֹהִ֥ים בְּאַרְמְנוֹתֶ֗יהָ נוֹדַ֥ע לְמִשְׂגָּֽב, "God has made himself known in her citadels as a refuge" (oshb:Ps.48.4), summarizing the description before the kings’ assault narrative begins
device_notes: Psalm 48 forms one liturgical unit; one parent gathers its rows. Its title carries the shir, mizmor, and bene-Qorach genre labels (psalm_device_inventory.json); this opening strophe frames Zion as the city of the great King before the historical narrative that follows.

boundary_rationale: The explanatory “For, behold, the kings assembled themselves, they passed by together” (web:Ps.48.4) opens a narrative report of the kings’ failed assault, moving through their panic, “Trembling took hold of them there, pain, as of a woman in travail” (web:Ps.48.6), to the closing confirmation, “As we have heard, so we have seen, in the city of Yahweh of Armies, in the city of our God. God will establish it forever. Selah” (web:Ps.48.8), immediately before the psalm turns to meditation.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A split after web:Ps.48.6 (the kings’ terror) was rejected because the ships-of-Tarshish image and the closing confirmation both continue the same third-person report of the assault’s outcome without a new address.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the explanatory particle pair כִּֽי הִנֵּ֣ה הַ֭מְּלָכִים, "for behold, the kings" (oshb:Ps.48.5), marking the shift from description to narrative report

the strophe closes with Selah (web:Ps.48.8 = oshb:Ps.48.9), paired with the confirmation formula כַּאֲשֶׁ֤ר שָׁמַ֨עְנוּ כֵּ֤ן רָאִ֗ינוּ, "as we have heard, so we have seen," echoing the hearing-motif that opens Psalm 44 at web:Ps.44.1 in a separate parent composition
device_notes: This strophe’s Selah (web:Ps.48.8 = oshb:Ps.48.9) closes the narrative report; it corroborates the shift to meditation that opens the following strophe, though the mode change from report to direct address drives that boundary.

boundary_rationale: The meditative “We have thought about your loving kindness, God, in the middle of your temple” (web:Ps.48.9) turns the psalm from narrative report to direct second-person address, continuing “As is your name, God, so is your praise to the ends of the earth. Your right hand is full of righteousness” (web:Ps.48.10) to the closing wish, “Let Mount Zion be glad! Let the daughters of Judah rejoice because of your judgments” (web:Ps.48.11), immediately before the imperative cluster that opens the final strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.48.14 was rejected because the concrete imperative at web:Ps.48.12, “Walk about Zion, and go around her. Number its towers.”, opens a new address to the community distinct from this strophe’s direct address to God.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the meditative verb דִּמִּ֣ינוּ אֱלֹהִ֣ים חַסְדֶּ֑ךָ, "we have thought about your loving kindness, God" (oshb:Ps.48.10), shifting the psalm’s address from third-person report to direct second-person speech to God
the strophe’s wish, יִשְׂמַ֤ח הַר צִיּ֗וֹן, "let Mount Zion be glad" (oshb:Ps.48.12), still addresses God in the same verse even as it names Zion in the third person
device_notes: This strophe’s close pivots from wish to the imperative address that follows without a new disclosure-object marker between them; the preceding strophe’s Selah (web:Ps.48.8 = oshb:Ps.48.9) closes the narrative report that this meditation follows.

boundary_rationale: The imperative cluster “Walk about Zion, and go around her. Number its towers.” (web:Ps.48.12) opens direct address to the community, continuing “Notice her bulwarks. Consider her palaces, that you may tell it to the next generation.” (web:Ps.48.13), and closes the psalm on confession, “For this God is our God forever and ever. He will be our guide even to death.” (web:Ps.48.14).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.48.14 as a coda separate from the imperative cluster was rejected because the confession “For this God is our God” answers the imperative to observe Zion’s bulwarks as its stated purpose, “tell it to the next generation”, rather than closing a distinct doxology.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe opens on the imperative-plus-object phrase סֹ֣בּוּ צִ֭יּוֹן, "walk about Zion" (oshb:Ps.48.13), the first of the verse’s three imperatives (of which only סֹ֣בּוּ is quoted here), addressing the community directly for the psalm’s closing movement
the psalm’s final verse, כִּ֤י זֶ֨ה אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֱ֭לֹהֵינוּ עוֹלָ֣ם וָעֶ֑ד, "for this God is our God forever and ever" (oshb:Ps.48.15), closes on confession rather than a baruch/amen doxology formula
device_notes: This strophe is not one of the book’s four doxology seams (41|42, 72, 89|90, 106); its unit_type stays strophe, closing Psalm 48 on direct confession instead.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 49 opens with a universal-audience summons — “Hear this, all you peoples. Listen, all you inhabitants of the world,” (web:Ps.49.1) — paired with the wisdom-instruction performative “I will incline my ear to a proverb. I will solve my riddle on the harp.” (web:Ps.49.4), where the OSHB verse pairs לְמָשָׁ֣ל (proverb) with חִידָתִֽי (my riddle) (oshb:Ps.49.5), with בְּ֝כִנּ֗וֹר ('on the harp') naming the instrument between them. This vocative-plus-genre-performative opening is the tier-1 opener signature that starts the psalm's instructional frame, distinct from the title's own genre labels “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by the sons of Korah.” (web:Ps.49.0).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 1-2 alone as the opening unit and folding 3-4 into the opening meditation was considered, but the riddle/proverb performative of 49:4 belongs to the summons register, not the argument that begins at 49:5.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.49.1 pairs two imperative verbs of hearing, “Hear this, all you peoples”, addressed to “all you peoples” and “all you inhabitants of the world”
oshb:Ps.49.5 anchors the genre claim with לְמָשָׁ֣ל (proverb) and חִידָתִֽי (riddle) as the fixed word pair, with בְּ֝כִנּ֗וֹר ('harp') naming the instrument between them
device_notes: The strophes gather under Psalm 49 as one unit. Its title “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by the sons of Korah.” (web:Ps.49.0) carries the mizmor, lamnatseach, and bene-Qorach labels; the composition is a wisdom psalm whose two meditations converge on a shared closing line at 49:12 and 49:20.

boundary_rationale: The opening meditation begins with the rhetorical question “Why should I fear in the days of evil, when iniquity at my heels surrounds me?” (web:Ps.49.5) and argues that wealth cannot buy off death — “none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him.” (web:Ps.49.7), reasoning through the fact that “For he sees that wise men die; likewise the fool and the senseless perish, and leave their wealth to others.” (web:Ps.49.10) — and closes on the refrain “Their inward thought is that their houses will endure forever, and their dwelling places to all generations. They name their lands after themselves. But man, despite his riches, doesn't endure. He is like the animals that perish.” (web:Ps.49.11, web:Ps.49.12). The refrain line at 49:12 recurs at 49:20 with a three-word-slot delta rather than a single substitution: oshb:Ps.49.21 drops the vav-conjunctive that opens וְאָדָ֣ם at oshb:Ps.49.13, and swaps both the negator and the verb of the medial clause, בַּל יָלִ֑ין ('does not lodge') becoming וְלֹ֣א יָבִ֑ין ('does not understand') — a word-level comparison across the 2-verse refrain pair (sweep: 2 verses compared), so the pair reads as a near-repeated refrain rather than a byte-identical one, and it is this recurring line, not the intervening Selahs (which fall in the next span), that closes this movement.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting 5-12 at the death/wealth pivot around 49:10 was considered, but no vocative or speech-frame shift supports an internal break there — the refrain at 49:12 closes the unit.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.49.13 opens וְאָדָ֣ם בִּ֭יקָר and closes נִמְשַׁ֖ל כַּבְּהֵמ֣וֹת, with the medial verb בַּל יָלִ֑ין
oshb:Ps.49.21 shares the same closing but drops the opening vav-conjunctive and swaps both the negator and verb of the medial clause relative to oshb:Ps.49.13, ending on וְלֹ֣א יָבִ֑ין
device_notes: The refrain pair (web:Ps.49.12, web:Ps.49.20) is this psalm's structural spine, binding the two meditation panels to one parent grouping.

boundary_rationale: The second meditation restates the fate of the self-assured — “This is the destiny of those who are foolish, and of those who approve their sayings. Selah.” (web:Ps.49.13) — contrasts it with the psalmist's own hope — “But God will redeem my soul from the power of Sheol, for he will receive me. Selah.” (web:Ps.49.15) — and pivots to direct exhortation, “Don't be afraid when a man is made rich, when the glory of his house is increased;” (web:Ps.49.16), before closing on the refrain “he shall go to the generation of his fathers. They shall never see the light. A man who has riches without understanding, is like the animals that perish.” (web:Ps.49.19, web:Ps.49.20), which repeats 49:12's frame with a three-word-slot delta — the opening vav-conjunctive dropped and both the negator and verb of the medial clause swapped — rather than one substituted verb (see the seam at 49:12|49:13). Selah punctuates the span twice, after 49:13 and again after 49:15 (web:Ps.49.13, web:Ps.49.15); per book policy Selah corroborates but does not itself drive the boundary, which rests on the refrain.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this panel at the Selah-marked 49:13|49:15 seams (yielding a short 13-15 unit on Sheol and a 16-20 exhortation unit) was considered as the mandated rival reading; web:Ps.49.16 does open a genuine pivot to direct exhortation immediately after the second Selah, addressing a second party for the first time in the panel. It is set aside because the refrain at 49:12/49:20 gives the whole 13-20 stretch a matching close that outranks this mid-panel address shift, and Selah alone is not an independent driver in this book.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah is true at Ps.49.13 and Ps.49.15 per the verse map (two Selah instances inside this span)
oshb:Ps.49.16 opens with אַךְ אֱלֹהִ֗ים (‘But God’), pivoting the psalmist's voice against the fate just described
device_notes: Second refrain-closed panel; both Selahs of this span (49:13, 49:15) are disclosed together per book policy.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 50's title, “A Psalm by Asaph.” (web:Ps.50.0 = oshb:Ps.50.1), sits inside MT verse 1 as an identity psalm; the verse continues directly into the theophany's opening triple divine name, אֵ֤ל אֱֽלֹהִ֡ים יְֽהוָ֗ה (El, Elohim, YHWH) (oshb:Ps.50.1). The narrated theophany — “Our God comes, and does not keep silent. A fire devours before him. It is very stormy around him.” (web:Ps.50.3) — runs in third-person narration through the embedded summons “"Gather my saints together to me, those who have made a covenant with me by sacrifice."” (web:Ps.50.5) and closes with the narrator's own comment, “The heavens shall declare his righteousness, for God himself is judge. Selah.” (web:Ps.50.6), before direct divine speech to the people begins at the next seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row through 50:9 to include the opening lines of God's speech was considered, but the addressee changes from third-person narration about God to first-person divine self-address beginning at 50:7, which belongs to the next span.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.50.1 stacks three divine names (אֵ֤ל, אֱֽלֹהִ֡ים, יְֽהוָ֗ה) before any verb of speech
web_selah is true at Ps.50.6, the row's closing verse
device_notes: Psalm 50 functions as the single parent grouping. Its title “A Psalm by Asaph.” (web:Ps.50.0) carries the mizmor and le-Asaph labels; Ps 50 is Book II's sole le-Asaph psalm (1 of 12), with the other 11 le-Asaph psalms sitting in Book III (73-83); this is a divine-lawsuit psalm whose three speech frames (narration, address to the covenant people, address to the wicked) organize the rows below.

boundary_rationale: Direct divine speech to the covenant people opens with the self-identification formula “"Hear, my people, and I will speak. Israel, I will testify against you. I am God, your God.” (web:Ps.50.7), where OSHB stacks אֱלֹהִ֖ים אֱלֹהֶ֣יךָ אָנֹֽכִי (God, your God, I) as the speech-frame marker (oshb:Ps.50.7). This is the first of the psalm's 2 divine discourse blocks introduced by an explicit narrator speech formula (oshb:Ps.50.7, oshb:Ps.50.16), distinct from the embedded first-person summons at oshb:Ps.50.5, and runs through the sacrifice polemic — “I have no need for a bull from your stall, nor male goats from your pens.” (web:Ps.50.9) — to the positive instruction that closes it, “Offer to God the sacrifice of thanksgiving. Pay your vows to the Most High.” (web:Ps.50.14). Selah at the preceding verse (web:Ps.50.6) is this span's front-seam corroboration for the frame shift, not a driver in its own right.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this speech at the anaphoric ‘mine’ sequence of 50:10-12 (the animals of the forest, the wild animals, the world) was considered, but that repetition is rhetorical elaboration within one unbroken first-person speech, not a new speech-frame or addressee.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.50.7 opens with the imperative שִׁמְעָ֤ה (Hear) matching the psalm's own opening summons register
web_selah is true at Ps.50.6, immediately preceding this span's start
device_notes: The psalm's earlier divine speech, addressed to ‘my people’; its close at 50:14-15 anticipates the psalm's final line (50:23).

boundary_rationale: A new speech frame opens with an explicit narrator formula, “But to the wicked God says, "What right do you have to declare my statutes, that you have taken my covenant on your lips,” (web:Ps.50.16), where OSHB marks the addressee change directly: וְלָ֤רָשָׁ֨ע אָ֘מַ֤ר אֱלֹהִ֗ים — ‘but to the wicked, God said’ (oshb:Ps.50.16). This rebuke runs through the closing appeal, “"Now consider this, you who forget God, lest I tear you into pieces, and there be no one to deliver.” (web:Ps.50.22), and ends on “Whoever offers the sacrifice of thanksgiving glorifies me, and prepares his way so that I will show God's salvation to him."” (web:Ps.50.23), which repeats the phrase “the sacrifice of thanksgiving” from web:Ps.50.14, framing the whole psalm.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 50:22-23 as a separate closing unit was considered, since ‘Now consider this’ shifts from accusation to appeal, but the same addressee and speech-frame continue across that shift, unlike the explicit dixit formula opening at 50:16.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.50.16 opens with the explicit speech-frame formula וְלָ֤רָשָׁ֨ע אָ֘מַ֤ר אֱלֹהִ֗ים, reintroducing direct divine speech to a new addressee
device_notes: Second divine speech, addressed to ‘the wicked’; its close echoes the sacrifice-of-thanksgiving instruction of 50:14, an inclusio internal to the psalm.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 51's title carries the Nathan/Bathsheba historical note, “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” (web:Ps.51.0 = oshb:Ps.51.1, web:Ps.51.0 = oshb:Ps.51.2), and the psalm opens with the imperative petition “Have mercy on me, God, according to your loving kindness. According to the multitude of your tender mercies, blot out my transgressions.” (web:Ps.51.1), doubled by “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity. Cleanse me from my sin.” (web:Ps.51.2), where OSHB pairs the qere הֶ֭רֶב (a ketiv/qere pair at oshb:Ps.51.4; the rbh root, ‘greatly/thoroughly’) with the wash-root proper, כַּבְּסֵ֣נִי (‘wash me’, oshb:Ps.51.4), the same root recurring as תְּ֝כַבְּסֵ֗נִי at oshb:Ps.51.9. The petition grounds itself in confession — “Against you, and you only, I have sinned, and done that which is evil in your sight, so you may be proved right when you speak, and justified when you judge.” (web:Ps.51.4), whose Hebrew opens לְךָ֤ לְבַדְּךָ֨ חָטָאתִי֮ ‘against you, you alone’ (oshb:Ps.51.6) — through the admission “Behold, I was born in iniquity. My mother conceived me in sin.” (web:Ps.51.5) and closes on the wisdom claim “Behold, you desire truth in the inward parts. You teach me wisdom in the inmost place.” (web:Ps.51.6), before the volitive-petition register resumes at the next seam.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking after 51:2 (petition) from 51:3-6 (confession) was considered, since the register shifts from imperative to indicative there, but both halves address God without any vocative or speech-frame change, so they are kept as one petition-grounded-in-confession movement.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.51.6 opens לְךָ֤ לְבַדְּךָ֨ חָטָאתִי֮, fronting the second-person object before the verb of sinning

oshb:Ps.51.4's כַּבְּסֵ֣נִי (‘wash me’) anticipates the same wash-root's reuse as תְּ֝כַבְּסֵ֗נִי (oshb:Ps.51.9) at the next span's opening petition (51:7); oshb:Ps.51.4 also carries a ketiv/qere pair (ketiv הרבה, qere הֶ֭רֶב) undisclosed elsewhere in this row
device_notes: One composition, Psalm 51, parents this row set. Its title “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David, when Nathan the prophet came to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” (web:Ps.51.0) carries the mizmor, lamnatseach, and le-David labels plus the Nathan/Bathsheba historical note; this +2 psalm's rows dual-cite both MT title verses at this, the opening row; the psalm's other three rows (146-148) do not repeat the title dual-cite.

boundary_rationale: A cluster of renewal petitions opens “Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.” (web:Ps.51.7), where OSHB's תְּ֝כַבְּסֵ֗נִי (‘wash me’, a prefix-conjugation volitive, oshb:Ps.51.9) reuses the wash-root already voiced as the true imperative כַּבְּסֵ֣נִי at oshb:Ps.51.4 (see the seam at 51:6|51:7; that verse's הֶ֭רֶב is a separate ketiv/qere token, the rbh intensifier, not the wash-root), and continues through the imperative pair “Create in me a clean heart, O God. Renew a right spirit within me.” (web:Ps.51.10), where OSHB pairs לֵ֣ב טָ֭הוֹר בְּרָא לִ֣י — ‘a clean heart create for me’ (oshb:Ps.51.12) — to the closing petition “Restore to me the joy of your salvation. Uphold me with a willing spirit.” (web:Ps.51.12), where OSHB opens הָשִׁ֣יבָה (‘restore’, an imperative, oshb:Ps.51.14). The span is a dense cluster of renewal petitions, the strongest of the psalm's 3 internal seams by imperative density.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the span through 51:13 (‘Then I will teach transgressors’) was considered, since it continues the first-person address to God, but 51:13 shifts from imperative petition to a cohortative vow of future action, which belongs with the psalm's next movement.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.51.9's תְּ֝כַבְּסֵ֗נִי repeats the wash-root of oshb:Ps.51.4's כַּבְּסֵ֣נִי (not the ketiv/qere token הֶ֭רֶב at the same verse, which is the separate rbh intensifier)

oshb:Ps.51.12 opens with its fronted object לֵ֣ב טָ֭הוֹר (“a clean heart”, web:Ps.51.10), with the verb בְּרָא (‘create’) as the third token — the verse quoted as “Create in me a clean heart” at web:Ps.51.10
device_notes: Renewal-petition cluster; re-derived from source bytes: 5 true imperative-form tokens across 3 of this span's 6 verses — hide, blot out (web:Ps.51.9); create, renew (web:Ps.51.10); restore (web:Ps.51.12) — excluding the taw-preformative prefix forms that open web:Ps.51.7 (purify, wash), which read as volitive petitions rather than true imperatives. oshb:Ps.51.3-Ps.51.4 independently carry 5 imperative tokens across those 2 verses, so this span is not, by that count, the psalm's highest imperative concentration.

boundary_rationale: The psalmist's voice turns from petition to vow, “Then I will teach transgressors your ways. Sinners will be converted to you.” (web:Ps.51.13), where OSHB's אֲלַמְּדָ֣ה (“I will teach”, a 1cs cohortative with paragogic he, oshb:Ps.51.15) opens the verse, and moves through the plea “Deliver me from the guilt of bloodshed, O God, the God of my salvation. My tongue will sing aloud of your righteousness.” (web:Ps.51.14) and “Lord, open my lips. My mouth will declare your praise.” (web:Ps.51.15) into a theological claim about sacrifice, “For you don't delight in sacrifice, or else I would give it. You have no pleasure in burnt offering.” (web:Ps.51.16), closing “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit. O God, you will not despise a broken and contrite heart.” (web:Ps.51.17). This unit's cohortative-vow opening and its sacrifice-theology close both mark it off from the imperative cluster before it and the Zion petition after it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 51:16-17's sacrifice theology into the closing Zion petition (51:18-19) was considered, since both touch on sacrifice, but 51:16-17 argues against animal sacrifice in the first person while 51:18-19 shifts to imperative petition for the city.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.51.13 opens with a first-person cohortative (“I will teach”), a register shift from the imperative cluster of 51:7-12
device_notes: Vow-and-sacrifice-theology unit; its claim that God is not pleased with sacrifice sets up the debated petition that follows.

boundary_rationale: The psalm closes with an imperative petition for the city, “Do well in your good pleasure to Zion. Build the walls of Jerusalem.” (web:Ps.51.18), where OSHB names צִיּ֑וֹן תִּ֝בְנֶ֗ה — ‘Zion—you will build’ (oshb:Ps.51.20) — and resolves in “Then you will delight in the sacrifices of righteousness, in burnt offerings and in whole burnt offerings. Then they will offer bulls on your altar.” (web:Ps.51.19). The topographic naming of Zion and Jerusalem's walls, absent from the rest of the psalm, marks this as a distinct closing unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 51:18-19 as continuous with 51:13-17 rather than a separate unit is the mandated rival: commentators disagree on whether the Zion petition is integral to the psalm or a later liturgical addition responding to Jerusalem's walls being broken, since the verse names actual city walls rather than speaking figuratively of the individual penitent. The candidate holds it as its own unit given its topographic register shift (see observed_substrate_signals), but the seam is registered as uncertain.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.51.20 (web:Ps.51.18) is the sole occurrence in the psalm of צִיּ֑וֹן תִּ֝בְנֶ֗ה (‘Zion—you will build’; sweep: 1 verse); the standalone lexeme צִיּ֑וֹן (Zion) likewise occurs only here in the psalm (sweep: 1 verse)
device_notes: Closing Zion petition; a debated seam (see rejected_alternative) held here as its own low-confidence unit.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 52's title carries the Doeg historical note, “For the Chief Musician. A contemplation by David, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, "David has come to Ahimelech's house."” (web:Ps.52.0 = oshb:Ps.52.1, web:Ps.52.0 = oshb:Ps.52.2), and the psalm opens with direct second-person address to the wicked, “Why do you boast of mischief, mighty man? God's loving kindness endures continually.” (web:Ps.52.1), continuing “Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, working deceitfully.” (web:Ps.52.2) and “You love evil more than good, lying rather than speaking the truth. Selah.” (web:Ps.52.3), where OSHB's אָהַ֣בְתָּ רָּ֣ע (‘you love evil’, oshb:Ps.52.5) opens the same verb the next verse repeats — “You love all devouring words, you deceitful tongue.” (web:Ps.52.4) — before the address closes on the imprecation “God will likewise destroy you forever. He will take you up, and pluck you out of your tent, and root you out of the land of the living. Selah.” (web:Ps.52.5). Selah falls twice inside this span, after 52:3 and after 52:5 (web:Ps.52.3, web:Ps.52.5); the sustained second-person address to the ‘mighty man’ is the driver, with both Selahs as interior and end corroboration.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this span at the earlier Selah (after 52:3) into a 1-3 and a 4-5 unit was considered, but the second-person address to the ‘mighty man’ is unbroken across both Selahs, so no independent driver supports a break there.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah is true at Ps.52.3 and Ps.52.5, both inside this span
oshb:Ps.52.5 opens with the verb אָהַ֣בְתָּ (you love), a verb the next verse (oshb:Ps.52.6) repeats, an anaphoric repetition binding 52:3-4
device_notes: The parent relation points every row to Psalm 52. Its title “For the Chief Musician. A contemplation by David, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, "David has come to Ahimelech's house."” (web:Ps.52.0) carries the maskil, lamnatseach, and le-David labels plus the Doeg historical note; this +2 psalm's rows dual-cite both MT title verses throughout.

boundary_rationale: The address shifts from second-person accusation to third-person report, “The righteous also will see it, and fear, and laugh at him, saying,” (web:Ps.52.6), where OSHB opens with וְיִרְא֖וּ צַדִּיקִ֥ים (‘and-they-will-see the-righteous’, oshb:Ps.52.8), and quotes their verdict, “"Behold, this is the man who didn't make God his strength, but trusted in the abundance of his riches, and strengthened himself in his wickedness."” (web:Ps.52.7). The psalmist's own first-person voice then closes the psalm, “But as for me, I am like a green olive tree in God's house. I trust in God's loving kindness forever and ever.” (web:Ps.52.8) and “I will give you thanks forever, because you have done it. I will hope in your name, for it is good, in the presence of your saints.” (web:Ps.52.9). Selah at the preceding verse (web:Ps.52.5) is this span's front-seam corroboration for the addressee shift, not a driver in its own right.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting 52:6-7 (the righteous' reported speech) from 52:8-9 (the psalmist's own testimony) was considered: WEB does close the quoted speech at the end of web:Ps.52.7, and oshb:Ps.52.10 (=web:Ps.52.8) does open with the contrastive independent pronoun וַאֲנִ֤י, a genuine speech-frame terminus and pivot — a real seam, not an absence. The split was nonetheless rejected because both halves share the same third-person-then-first-person vantage against the wicked man of 52:1-5, which the row treats as the stronger, unifying warrant at this length.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah is true at Ps.52.5, immediately preceding this span's start
oshb:Ps.52.8 opens וְיִרְא֖וּ צַדִּיקִ֥ים, marking the addressee shift from second to third person
device_notes: Closing unit: the righteous' verdict on the wicked man, then the psalmist's contrasting self-testimony ‘like a green olive tree.’

boundary_rationale: Psalm 53 is a short, indivisible movement of six WEB verses and is chunked as one row per book policy. Its title, “For the Chief Musician. To the tune of "Mahalath." A contemplation by David.” (web:Ps.53.0 = oshb:Ps.53.1), opens directly into “The fool has said in his heart, "There is no God." They are corrupt, and have done abominable iniquity. There is no one who does good.” (web:Ps.53.1), where OSHB reads אָ֘מַ֤ר נָבָ֣ל בְּ֭לִבּוֹ אֵ֣ין — ‘said [the] fool in-his-heart, there-is-no God’ (oshb:Ps.53.2) — and the poem runs one unbroken argument through the divine survey, “God looks down from heaven on the children of men, to see if there are any who understood, who seek after God.” (web:Ps.53.2), the universal verdict, “Every one of them has gone back. They have become filthy together. There is no one who does good, no, not one.” (web:Ps.53.3), and the closing hope for Israel's restoration, “Oh that the salvation of Israel would come out of Zion! When God brings back his people from captivity, then Jacob shall rejoice, and Israel shall be glad.” (web:Ps.53.6), where OSHB's mi-yitten optative idiom מִ֥י יִתֵּ֣ן (‘oh that—will give’) opens the verse, naming מִצִּיּוֹן֮ (Zion) and יִשְׂרָ֫אֵ֥ל (Israel) around the construct-plural יְשֻׁע֪וֹת (‘salvation(s) of’) (oshb:Ps.53.7).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting 53:1-3 (the universal indictment) from 53:4-6 (address to the ‘workers of iniquity’ and closing hope) was considered given the six-verse length is at the edge of the book's whole-psalm threshold, but no vocative or speech-frame shift marks an internal seam, and the psalm reads as one movement.
observed_substrate_signals: skeleton sweep of this psalm's WEB span (53:1-6, MT 53:2-7) finds Elohim seven times across five of its six verses and YHWH zero times (sweep: 7 occurrences, 5 verses; oshb:Ps.53.3, oshb:Ps.53.6) — independently re-derived from the bytes, matching the book's Elohistic-Psalter inventory
device_notes: Grouped, the rows answer to Psalm 53 alone. Psalm 53 stands in a typed doublet relation with Psalm 14 (an Elohistic recension of the same composition, per the book's doublet inventory); this row addresses Psalm 53's own text and makes no byte claim about Psalm 14. The Elohim-for-YHWH substitution is this psalm's own Elohistic-Psalter texture, legitimate discussion but not a boundary driver, since the psalm is chunked whole.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 54 coheres as one liturgical composition, and this row reports to one parent. The historical-note title fixes the setting: the Ziphites' report to Saul, “Isn't David hiding himself among us?” (web:Ps.54.0 = oshb:Ps.54.1) — and the seven verses that follow run one continuous movement: an imperative plea (web:Ps.54.1), a grounding complaint closed by Selah (web:Ps.54.3), and a vow-and-report close (web:Ps.54.6-Ps.54.7), with no internal address shift strong enough at this length to warrant a split.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting at the Selah (web:Ps.54.3) into a plea half and a vow half was rejected: the psalm runs seven verses, under the short-psalm threshold, and Selah is capped at tier-3 corroboration by policy, not treated as a driver alone.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative doublet “Save me, God, by your name. Vindicate me in your might” opens the psalm (web:Ps.54.1)
a Selah closes the complaint before the vow (web:Ps.54.3)
the closing verse pairs deliverance with a report clause, “My eye has seen triumph over my enemies” (web:Ps.54.7)
device_notes: The title carries maskil, lamnatseach, and le-David labels (tier-1 opener evidence) alongside the Ziphite historical note; Book II runs Elohim-heavy here (unsuffixed Elohim in 4 verses, one token each, oshb:Ps.54.3-54.6 / unsuffixed YHWH in 1 verse, oshb:Ps.54.8), matching the Elohistic Psalter texture at this position in the book.

boundary_rationale: One parent gathers Psalm 55's rows: the composition itself. This strophe opens on direct address to God — “Listen to my prayer, God. Don't hide yourself from my supplication” (web:Ps.55.1) — and holds together as the psalmist's inner-turmoil report through the wish to flee, “Oh that I had wings like a dove! Then I would fly away, and be at rest” (web:Ps.55.6), continuing past an interior Selah into the shelter-wish of web:Ps.55.8 before the seam: the next verse turns to an imperative against the enemy's city rather than the self.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the strophe at web:Ps.55.7, where the Selah sits, was rejected: WEB punctuates web:Ps.55.6-Ps.55.7 and web:Ps.55.8 as two separate quotations, but MT carries no closing marker between them, and the flight-wish “I would hurry to a shelter” (web:Ps.55.8) reads as one continuous wish with the Selah falling interior to it rather than at its edge.
observed_substrate_signals: vocative-plus-imperative pair “Listen...Don't hide” opens the psalm (web:Ps.55.1)
a Selah sits mid-quote, before the wish resumes (web:Ps.55.7)
the quoted wish runs continuously from web:Ps.55.6 through web:Ps.55.8
device_notes: Psalm 55 carries a maskil, lamnatseach, le-David title with no historical note; its rows track a plea, betrayal, confidence, and verdict movement.

boundary_rationale: The strophe opens on a fresh imperative address, “Confuse them, Lord, and confound their language, for I have seen violence and strife in the city” (web:Ps.55.9), pivots at web:Ps.55.12's “For it was not an enemy who insulted me” into naming the betrayer as “a man like me, my companion, and my familiar friend” (web:Ps.55.13), and closes on an imprecation grounded in a ketiv/qere pair (oshb:Ps.55.16: ketiv ישימות, qere יַשִּׁ֤י מָ֨וֶת), “Let death come suddenly on them” (web:Ps.55.15).
strongest_rejected_alternative: A seam between web:Ps.55.11 and web:Ps.55.12, separating the city-violence description from the betrayer's naming, was rejected: web:Ps.55.12's “For” argues directly from the city description to the betrayer's identity within one continuous accusation.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative “Confuse them, Lord” opens the strophe (web:Ps.55.9)
the causal pivot “For it was not an enemy” marks the turn to the betrayer (web:Ps.55.12)
the strophe closes on an imprecation, “go down alive into Sheol” (web:Ps.55.15)

boundary_rationale: An explicit contrastive turn opens the strophe, “As for me, I will call on God. Yahweh will save me” (web:Ps.55.16), moving through confidence in being heard (web:Ps.55.17-Ps.55.18) to a verdict on the unrepentant at web:Ps.55.19, where the psalm's second Selah sits mid-verse (token 6 of 13 in oshb:Ps.55.20) as corroboration; the verdict clause following it, together with the referent's narrowing from the unrepentant “them” to a specific “he” at the seam with web:Ps.55.20, are what actually close this strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the strophe through web:Ps.55.20 was rejected: web:Ps.55.20 returns the subject to a specific “he” (the betrayer) rather than the “them” of web:Ps.55.19's verdict, marking a fresh referent shift.
observed_substrate_signals: contrastive self-reference “As for me” opens the strophe (web:Ps.55.16)

a Selah (oshb:Ps.55.20) sits mid-verse in the strophe's closing verse (token 6 of 13), corroborating rather than driving the boundary; the verdict clause and the referent-narrowing at the seam with web:Ps.55.20 are the actual drivers

boundary_rationale: The strophe's front seam carries the psalm's second Selah, sitting mid-verse in web:Ps.55.19 (token 6 of 13 in oshb:Ps.55.20) as corroboration for the prior verdict's close, before this unit resumes on a specific referent, “He raises his hands against his friends. He has violated his covenant” (web:Ps.55.20), and closes the psalm on a contrastive turn to trust, “But you, God, will bring them down into the pit of destruction...but I will trust in you” (web:Ps.55.23).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading web:Ps.55.20-Ps.55.23 as a continuation of the prior strophe, rather than its own unit, was rejected: the shift from “them” (the verdict's plural target) to “he” (a specific betrayer) reopens the friend-betrayal thread named at web:Ps.55.13.
observed_substrate_signals: the strophe's front-seam verse carries the psalm's second Selah (web:Ps.55.19)
the referent narrows from plural “them” to singular “he” at the seam (web:Ps.55.19-Ps.55.20)
the closing verse turns on a contrastive “But you, God...but I will trust in you” (web:Ps.55.23)

boundary_rationale: Both rows of Psalm 56 report to one parent grouping for the psalm. This strophe opens the historical-note title's setting — “when the Philistines seized him in Gath” (web:Ps.56.0 = oshb:Ps.56.1) — into a plea, “Be merciful to me, God, for man wants to swallow me up” (web:Ps.56.1), and holds the complaint through a trust declaration, “In God, I praise his word. In God, I put my trust. I will not be afraid. What can flesh do to me?” (web:Ps.56.4), before the seam returns to the enemies' conspiracy (web:Ps.56.5-Ps.56.7).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating web:Ps.56.4 as its own row was rejected: the trust declaration's return is split across web:Ps.56.10-Ps.56.11 later in the psalm rather than repeated whole here, so this occurrence functions as an interior turn within the strophe, not an edge.
observed_substrate_signals: the trust declaration “In God, I praise his word” (web:Ps.56.4) recurs, reworded, at web:Ps.56.10-Ps.56.11
the strophe closes back on the enemies' conspiracy, “They conspire and lurk, watching my steps” (web:Ps.56.6 = oshb:Ps.56.7; ketiv יצפינו, qere יִצְפּ֗וֹנוּ)
device_notes: The title carries miktam, lamnatseach, le-David labels plus the al-yonat-elem tune name (“Silent Dove in Distant Lands”, web:Ps.56.0) and a historical note — distinct from the al-tashcheth tune shared by Psalms 57, 58, 59, and 75.

boundary_rationale: The strophe opens on a shift to divine record-keeping, “You count my wanderings. You put my tears into your container. boundary_rationale: The title carries two counted MT verses — the tune note naming “The Lily of the Covenant” plus Joab’s Aram-Naharaim/Aram-Zobah/Valley-of-Salt historical note (web:Ps.60.0 = oshb:Ps.60.1, web:Ps.60.0 = oshb:Ps.60.2) — tier-1 opener evidence for the lament that follows. device_notes: Elohistic-Psalter texture (Book II, Ps 42-72): this psalm carries no Yahweh and 3 Elohim occurrences (psalm_device_inventory.json), consistent with the book's Book-II count of 32 Yahweh against 165 Elohim — corroborating discussion, not a boundary driver.

boundary_rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.62.0 = oshb:Ps.62.1), naming the Jeduthun setting (one of 3 Ps psalms so labeled, with Psalms 39 and 77). The unit is a ring: it opens on (oshb:Ps.62.2) אַ֣ךְ אֶל אֱ֭לֹהִים דּֽוּמִיָּ֣ה “My soul rests in God alone” (web:Ps.62.1), turns at web:Ps.62.3 to a complaint against attackers, “How long will you assault a man?”, and returns to the same confidence idiom at (oshb:Ps.62.6) אַ֣ךְ לֵ֭אלֹהִים דּ֣וֹמִּי נַפְשִׁ֑י “My soul, wait in silence for God alone, for my expectation is from him.” (web:Ps.62.5), completing the envelope. Collated against oshb:Ps.62.6, oshb:Ps.62.2 shares no tier — real lexical substitution: (oshb:Ps.62.2) אֶל אֱ֭לֹהִים against (oshb:Ps.62.6) לֵ֭אלֹהִים, and (oshb:Ps.62.2) יְשׁוּעָתִֽי against (oshb:Ps.62.6) תִּקְוָתִֽי — so the return is thematic anaphora (sweep: 6 verses open with אך in Ps 62, 34 book-wide), not a repeated line.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the ring at its individual אך-openings into separate one- or two-verse rows was rejected, since the confidence-complaint-confidence pattern needs the full envelope to complete, not one opening on its own.
observed_substrate_signals: אך opens (oshb:Ps.62.2) אַ֣ךְ, oshb:Ps.62.3, and (oshb:Ps.62.5) אַ֤ךְ inside this row, plus 2 more later in the psalm: 6 verse-initial occurrences of אך among Ps 62’s 12 MT body verses; a separate contiguous-consonantal-substring sweep finds 34 occurrences book-wide.

oshb:Ps.62.3 opens with אַךְ ה֣וּא צ֭וּרִי, echoed at this row’s own closing verse, oshb:Ps.62.7 (=web:Ps.62.6), which opens with the same 3 words at skeleton tier; oshb:Ps.62.3 carries a closing word oshb:Ps.62.7 lacks.
Selah closes web:Ps.62.4 (oshb:Ps.62.5), mid-ring rather than at the row’s own end — disclosed, not treated as the driver.
device_notes: This row family has Psalm 62 for its parent.

boundary_rationale: This unit opens still in first-person voice, continuing the rock vocabulary of the prior row's close: “My salvation and my honor is with God. The rock of my strength, and my refuge, is in God.” (web:Ps.62.7), where OSHB's צוּר עֻזִּ֥י (“rock of my strength”, oshb:Ps.62.8) echoes the prior row's own close. One verse in, register shifts to public exhortation: (oshb:Ps.62.9) בִּטְח֘וּ ב֤וֹ בְכָל עֵ֨ת עָ֗ם “Trust in him at all times, you people” (web:Ps.62.8), closing on the psalm’s second Selah. The unit moves through the wisdom reflection on human vanity, “men of low degree are just a breath” (web:Ps.62.9), and the warning against riches (web:Ps.62.10), closing on the revelatory formula (oshb:Ps.62.12) אַחַ֤ת דִּבֶּ֬ר אֱלֹהִ֗ים שְׁתַּֽיִם “God has spoken once; twice I have heard this” (web:Ps.62.11).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating Ps.62.7-62.8 as a continuation of the preceding confidence refrain rather than a fresh public-facing unit was rejected, given the shift from first-person soul-address to plural imperative address.
observed_substrate_signals: Plural imperative address (oshb:Ps.62.9) בִּטְח֘וּ opens the exhortation, marking the register shift from the preceding first-person ring.
Selah closes web:Ps.62.8 (oshb:Ps.62.9) — the psalm’s later of 2 Selah instances (sweep: 2 verses); no further Selah in web:Ps.62.9-web:Ps.62.12.
device_notes: The Hebrew word for "silence" opening (oshb:Ps.62.2) דּֽוּמִיָּ֣ה recurs, from the same root, at the opening of oshb:Ps.65.2 (web:Ps.65.1) — shared vocabulary texture, not a boundary signal.

boundary_rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.63.0 = oshb:Ps.63.1) naming the desert-of-Judah setting. The strophe opens on a vocative, (oshb:Ps.63.2) אֱלֹהִ֤ים אֵלִ֥י אַתָּ֗ה “God, you are my God” (web:Ps.63.1), with a נפשי (“My soul”) occurrence already in the same verse, (oshb:Ps.63.2) צָמְאָ֬ה לְךָ֨ נַפְשִׁ֗י “My soul thirsts for you”. It moves through the sanctuary vision “So I have seen you in the sanctuary” (web:Ps.63.2) and closes on the resolve to bless, “I will lift up my hands in your name” (web:Ps.63.4).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this opening unit through web:Ps.63.5 was rejected: the second כן inclusio-closer (oshb:Ps.63.5) falls inside this row's own span, at web:Ps.63.4, not beyond it; web:Ps.63.5 (oshb:Ps.63.6) opens instead with כמו (‘like/as’) and begins the psalm's sensory-satisfaction imagery that continues through Ps.63.8, not the sanctuary-vision material of Ps.63.2-63.4.
observed_substrate_signals: כן opens both oshb:Ps.63.3 and oshb:Ps.63.5 — an intra-row inclusio inside this row's own span (sweep: 2 verses in Ps 63); the next row's opening verse, oshb:Ps.63.6, opens instead with כמו (‘like/as’), a different word.
נפשי opens this row's own inclusio at (oshb:Ps.63.2) נַפְשִׁ֗י (sweep: 4 verses carry נפשי in Ps 63).
device_notes: The parent grouping for this row set is Psalm 63 whole.

boundary_rationale: The unit is bracketed by its own נפשי (“my soul”) pair: it opens (oshb:Ps.63.6) תִּשְׂבַּ֣ע נַפְשִׁ֑י “My soul shall be satisfied” (web:Ps.63.5) and closes (oshb:Ps.63.9) דָּבְקָ֣ה נַפְשִׁ֣י “My soul stays close to you” (web:Ps.63.8), moving through night-watch meditation (web:Ps.63.6) and the refuge image “the shadow of your wings” (web:Ps.63.7).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at Ps.63.7 instead of Ps.63.8 was rejected, since Ps.63.8's closing 'my soul' clause closes the same bracket that Ps.63.5's opening clause begins.
observed_substrate_signals: נפשי opens the span at (oshb:Ps.63.6) נַפְשִׁ֑י and closes it at (oshb:Ps.63.9) נַפְשִׁ֣י — an internal lexical inclusio, though not exclusive to this row's edges: the lexeme recurs once more just past this row's own close, at oshb:Ps.63.10 (web:Ps.63.9) — those who seek my soul.

boundary_rationale: An adversative pivot opens this unit away from the psalmist’s own voice: (oshb:Ps.63.10) וְהֵ֗מָּה “But those who seek my soul to destroy it” (web:Ps.63.9), continuing through “They shall be jackal food” (web:Ps.63.10) to a second adversative, (oshb:Ps.63.12) וְהַמֶּלֶךְ֮ “But the king shall rejoice in God” (web:Ps.63.11), the psalm’s closing verse.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the enemies' judgment (Ps.63.9-63.10) from the king's contrasting joy (Ps.63.11) into separate rows was rejected, since both share the adversative pivot away from the psalmist's own voice and no independent driver separates them.
observed_substrate_signals: (oshb:Ps.63.10) וְהֵ֗מָּה, glossed ‘but they’, opens the enemies’ judgment; (oshb:Ps.63.12) וְהַמֶּלֶךְ֮ (“But the king”, web:Ps.63.11) opens the closing verse — two adversative openings inside a 3-verse unit.
נפשי recurs once more at (oshb:Ps.63.10) יְבַקְשׁ֣וּ נַפְשִׁ֑י, this psalm's 4th instance in Ps 63, now naming the object the enemies seek — an ironic reversal of the row at Ps.63.5-63.8.

boundary_rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.64.0 = oshb:Ps.64.1). The unit opens on imperative petition, (oshb:Ps.64.2) שְׁמַע אֱלֹהִ֣ים “Hear my voice, God, in my complaint” (web:Ps.64.1), “Hide me from the conspiracy of the wicked” (web:Ps.64.2), then continues in an אשר relative clause describing the plotters, (oshb:Ps.64.4) אֲשֶׁ֤ר “who sharpen their tongue like a sword” (web:Ps.64.3), through their secrecy (web:Ps.64.4-web:Ps.64.5) to “Surely man’s mind and heart are cunning” (web:Ps.64.6).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating the opening plea (Ps.64.1-64.2) from the description of the plotters (Ps.64.3-64.6) as separate rows was rejected, since Ps.64.3's relative clause grammatically continues Ps.64.2's 'evildoers' rather than opening independent material.
observed_substrate_signals: אשר relative clause opens (oshb:Ps.64.4) אֲשֶׁ֤ר, tying the plotters’ description back to the “evildoers” of the preceding verse.

Third-person plural verbs for “they/their” run from oshb:Ps.64.4 through oshb:Ps.64.6, breaking at this span's closing verse (oshb:Ps.64.7), which opens with a 1cp verb (תַּ֭מְנוּ, glossed 'we have completed') and closes on a singular-subject verbless clause.
device_notes: Psalm 64 forms one parent composition; its rows answer to that one grouping.

boundary_rationale: A reversal opens this unit with God as subject in place of the plotters: (oshb:Ps.64.8) וַיֹּרֵ֗ם אֱלֹ֫הִ֥ים “But God will shoot at them” (web:Ps.64.7), “Their own tongues shall ruin them” (web:Ps.64.8), “All mankind shall be afraid” (web:Ps.64.9), closing on “The righteous shall be glad in Yahweh” (web:Ps.64.10) with (oshb:Ps.64.11) בַּ֭יהוָה — Psalm 64’s one Yahweh occurrence (psalm_device_inventory.json: Ps 64 yhwh=1, elohim=3; Ps 60-65 together carry 1 yhwh against 22 elohim, Elohistic-Psalter texture).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at Ps.64.9 instead of Ps.64.10 was rejected, since the universal fear of Ps.64.9 and the righteous celebration of Ps.64.10 both continue the aftermath introduced by the divine reversal at Ps.64.7.
observed_substrate_signals: Subject shift to God opens (oshb:Ps.64.8) וַיֹּרֵ֗ם אֱלֹ֫הִ֥ים, reversing the previous unit’s “they” subject.
(oshb:Ps.64.11) בַּ֭יהוָה (Yahweh) is this row’s and Psalm 64’s one Yahweh occurrence (device inventory count: 1).

boundary_rationale: The title is one counted MT verse (web:Ps.65.0 = oshb:Ps.65.1). This unit opens the Zion/temple material, (oshb:Ps.65.2) לְךָ֤ דֻֽמִיָּ֬ה תְהִלָּ֓ה אֱלֹ֘הִ֥ים בְּצִיּ֑וֹן “Praise waits for you, God, in Zion” (web:Ps.65.1), moves through “You who hear prayer” (web:Ps.65.2) and the atonement confession “you atoned for our transgressions” (web:Ps.65.3), closing on the temple-dweller beatitude “Blessed is the one whom you choose” (web:Ps.65.4).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this opening unit through Ps.65.5 was rejected, since that verse turns to God's awesome deeds and cosmic power rather than the Zion/temple material of Ps.65.1-65.4.
observed_substrate_signals: (oshb:Ps.65.2) לְךָ֤ דֻֽמִיָּ֬ה — literally 'silence to-you'; web:Ps.65.1 renders it “Praise waits for you, God, in Zion” — opens the psalm, from the same root quoted twice in Ps 62 (oshb:Ps.62.2, oshb:Ps.62.6) — shared vocabulary, not a boundary signal.
device_notes: Psalm 65 is one parent composition spanning its own rows.

boundary_rationale: Register turns from temple-address to cosmic praise: (oshb:Ps.65.6) נ֤וֹרָא֨וֹת בְּצֶ֣דֶק “By awesome deeds of righteousness, you answer us” (web:Ps.65.5), then a run of participial predicates for God’s acts, (oshb:Ps.65.7) מֵכִ֣ין הָרִ֣ים “you form the mountains” (web:Ps.65.6) and (oshb:Ps.65.8) מַשְׁבִּ֤יחַ “You still the roaring of the seas” (web:Ps.65.7), closing on the distant peoples’ awe, “They also who dwell in faraway places are afraid at your wonders” (web:Ps.65.8).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at Ps.65.7 instead of Ps.65.8 was rejected, since Ps.65.8's report of the distant peoples' awe still describes the effect of the cosmic acts introduced in Ps.65.6-65.7, before the harvest material begins at Ps.65.9.
observed_substrate_signals: A mountain-forming participle opens one verse, (oshb:Ps.65.7) מֵכִ֣ין, and a sea-stilling participle opens the next in the same grammatical form, (oshb:Ps.65.8) מַשְׁבִּ֤יחַ (2 verses).

2nd-person divine address continues past this unit's own close: web:Ps.65.9 (oshb:Ps.65.10), the following row's opening verb, keeps addressing God directly — a cross-seam continuity disclosed here, not counted against the closing boundary.

boundary_rationale: A tense/topic pivot opens the harvest hymn proper: (oshb:Ps.65.10) פָּקַ֥דְתָּ הָאָ֨רֶץ “You visit the earth, and water it” (web:Ps.65.9), moving through the furrows and showers (web:Ps.65.10-web:Ps.65.11) and the grasslands (web:Ps.65.12), closing the psalm — and the consecutive le-David run recorded in psalm_device_inventory.json across Ps 51-65 (15/15 psalms) — on personified nature: (oshb:Ps.65.14) יִ֝תְרוֹעֲע֗וּ אַף יָשִֽׁירוּ “They shout for joy! They also sing.” (web:Ps.65.13).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the closing harvest unit at the shift from divine action (Ps.65.9-65.11) to personified nature (Ps.65.12-65.13) was rejected, since no independent tier-1 driver marks that shift as a fresh strophe rather than the harvest hymn's closing crescendo.
observed_substrate_signals: Perfect-tense 2ms verb for God’s action opens the unit, (oshb:Ps.65.10) פָּקַ֥דְתָּ, before the closing verse turns to 3rd-person nature imagery at (oshb:Ps.65.14) לָבְשׁ֬וּ.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 66 opens on a two-line imperative summons, “Make a joyful shout to God, all the earth!” (web:Ps.66.1), continuing “Sing to the glory of his name! Offer glory and praise!” (web:Ps.66.2); the address then turns to quoted second-person speech to God through web:Ps.66.3-web:Ps.66.4, closing on the nations' submission and a Selah (web:Ps.66.4). The imperative opening plus the Selah close bound this strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.66.7 to gather both Selah-closed calls into one span was rejected: web:Ps.66.5 reopens with its own imperative, “Come, and see” (web:Ps.66.5), a fresh address distinct from the quoted speech of web:Ps.66.3-web:Ps.66.4.
observed_substrate_signals: “Make a joyful shout” (web:Ps.66.1), “Sing to the glory of his name!” and “Offer glory and praise!” (web:Ps.66.2) form a 3-token imperative chain, not a doublet, continuing into a 4th imperative at “Tell God…” (web:Ps.66.3).
The address to God shifts into quoted second-person speech through web:Ps.66.3-web:Ps.66.4.
A Selah closes the strophe at web:Ps.66.4.
device_notes: The whole-psalm parent for these rows is Psalm 66. The title carries mizmor, shir, and lamnatseach labels (tier-1 opener evidence) with no historical note or Davidic ascription; MT holds the title as the prefix of 66:1 rather than a counted verse (web:Ps.66.0 = oshb:Ps.66.1).

boundary_rationale: A fresh imperative reopens the address, “Come, and see God’s deeds— awesome work on behalf of the children of men.” (web:Ps.66.5), recalling the exodus in miniature, “He turned the sea into dry land.” (web:Ps.66.6), and closing on divine kingship, “He rules by his might forever.” (web:Ps.66.7). A Selah already closed the preceding summons at web:Ps.66.4; a second Selah closes this recollection at web:Ps.66.7, bracketing the two calls to worship that open the psalm.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing this strophe at web:Ps.66.6, before the kingship declaration, was rejected: web:Ps.66.7's declaration of divine rule continues the same recollection through to its own Selah rather than opening a new address.
observed_substrate_signals: Imperative “Come, and see” reopens the strophe after the Selah at web:Ps.66.4 (web:Ps.66.5).
Selah closes web:Ps.66.4 (front seam of this strophe) and again web:Ps.66.7 (this strophe's own close).
MT Ps.66.7 (web:Ps.66.7) carries a ketiv/qere note in the inventory, not engaged by the English-level warrant argued here.

boundary_rationale: The third of the psalm's four strophe-opening imperative pairs (66:1, 66:5, 66:8, 66:16) redirects the address to “you peoples” — “Praise our God, you peoples! Make the sound of his praise heard,” (web:Ps.66.8) — opening a national testing report that runs “For you, God, have tested us. You have refined us, as silver is refined.” (web:Ps.66.10) through captivity, fire, and water to “the place of abundance” (web:Ps.66.12). The plural first-person voice (us, our) running through web:Ps.66.8-web:Ps.66.12 stops at this strophe's close; web:Ps.66.13 turns to a singular first-person vow, the seam this row's boundary answers to.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing this strophe at web:Ps.66.9 and reopening at web:Ps.66.10 was rejected: no imperative, vocative, or addressee shift separates the “preserves our life” clause of web:Ps.66.9 from the testing report that follows it.
observed_substrate_signals: Imperative “Praise our God, you peoples!” reopens the address after web:Ps.66.7's Selah (web:Ps.66.8).
Plural pronouns (us, our) run through web:Ps.66.8-web:Ps.66.12: “tested us”, “You have refined us,” “our backs” (web:Ps.66.8, web:Ps.66.10-web:Ps.66.11).
The report moves from testing and refining (web:Ps.66.10) through captivity (web:Ps.66.11) to “the place of abundance” (web:Ps.66.12), this strophe's own close.

boundary_rationale: The pronoun shifts from plural to singular first person at this row's opening, “I will come into your temple with burnt offerings. I will pay my vows to you,” (web:Ps.66.13), continuing the individual vow through “which my lips promised, and my mouth spoke, when I was in distress.” (web:Ps.66.14) to a closing sacrificial description, “I will offer to you burnt offerings of fat animals, with the offering of rams, I will offer bulls with goats.” (web:Ps.66.15), marked by a Selah. The we-to-I pronoun turn at web:Ps.66.12-web:Ps.66.13 is the psalm's internal seam: the testing report speaks for a community (“us,” “our”) through web:Ps.66.12, and this row opens on an individual vow (“I,” “my”) that runs uninterrupted to this strophe's own close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Opening this row at web:Ps.66.12 rather than web:Ps.66.13 was rejected: web:Ps.66.12's pronoun set (us, our) belongs to the preceding community report; web:Ps.66.13 is where the vow's singular first-person voice begins.
observed_substrate_signals: The pronoun set turns from plural (us, our; web:Ps.66.8-web:Ps.66.12) to singular (I, my; web:Ps.66.13-web:Ps.66.15) exactly at this row's opening.
The vow register (“I will come”, “I will pay”, “I will offer”) runs web:Ps.66.13-web:Ps.66.15.
A Selah closes the vow at web:Ps.66.15.

boundary_rationale: A fresh imperative reopens the address to a human audience, “Come and hear, all you who fear God. I will declare what he has done for my soul.” (web:Ps.66.16), continuing the individual testimony through “If I cherished sin in my heart, the Lord wouldn’t have listened.” (web:Ps.66.18) to a closing benediction, “Blessed be God, who has not turned away my prayer, nor his loving kindness from me.” (web:Ps.66.20). The imperative “Come and hear” addressed to “you who fear God” reopens the vocative register carried earlier by web:Ps.66.5's “Come, and see”, marking a fresh unit after the vow's Selah close at web:Ps.66.15.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding web:Ps.66.16-web:Ps.66.20 into the preceding vow strophe was rejected: the vow's Selah at web:Ps.66.15 closes the sacrificial description, and web:Ps.66.16 opens a new imperative addressed outward to “all you who fear God” rather than continuing the vow's own first-person report to God.
observed_substrate_signals: Imperative “Come and hear” reopens direct address to a human audience after the Selah at web:Ps.66.15 (web:Ps.66.16).
The testimony report (heard prayer, unrejected loving kindness) runs web:Ps.66.17-web:Ps.66.20 in the first person, continuing the vow strophe's singular first-person voice into a benediction close.
The psalm closes on a benediction, “Blessed be God” (web:Ps.66.20), rather than a book-boundary doxology formula.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens on a blessing invocation, “May God be merciful to us, bless us, and cause his face to shine on us.” (web:Ps.67.1), closed by a Selah, then states its missionary purpose, “That your way may be known on earth, and your salvation among all nations,” (web:Ps.67.2), before the refrain enters, “let the peoples praise you, God. Let all the peoples praise you.” (web:Ps.67.3). The refrain's return at web:Ps.67.5 closes a parallel second call; this row runs the blessing-invocation-to-refrain movement that the strophe at web:Ps.67.4-web:Ps.67.5 repeats.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the blessing invocation (web:Ps.67.1) from its purpose clause (web:Ps.67.2) into separate rows was rejected: the Selah at web:Ps.67.1 falls interior to this opening unit, not at a seam candidate, and no imperative or addressee shift separates web:Ps.67.1 from web:Ps.67.2; the refrain's parallel return at web:Ps.67.5, not the interior Selah, is what closes the answering strophe at web:Ps.67.4-web:Ps.67.5.
observed_substrate_signals: A Selah closes the blessing invocation at web:Ps.67.1, interior to this row rather than at its edge.
The refrain “let the peoples praise you, God” opens at web:Ps.67.3 and returns at web:Ps.67.5, framing two parallel calls.
Second-person address to God (“your way”, “your salvation”) begins at web:Ps.67.2 (oshb:Ps.67.3); web:Ps.67.1 (oshb:Ps.67.2) uses 1cp object suffixes (“bless us”) rather than 2nd-person forms.
device_notes: Psalm 67 carries the parent grouping for the set. The title carries mizmor, shir, lamnatseach, and binginot labels (tier-1 opener evidence); MT counts the title as 67:1 (web:Ps.67.0 = oshb:Ps.67.1). Book II Elohistic texture at this position: 0 YHWH / 5 Elohim occurrences (inventory count) — texture, not a boundary driver.

boundary_rationale: A second strophe reopens with a plea for the nations, “Oh let the nations be glad and sing for joy, for you will judge the peoples with equity, and govern the nations on earth.” (web:Ps.67.4), closed by a Selah, then the refrain returns in English, “Let the peoples praise you, God. Let all the peoples praise you.” (web:Ps.67.5). Collation confirms the MT anchors byte-match (oshb:Ps.67.4 = oshb:Ps.67.6); the refrain's return is a tier-1 structural seam closing this second call.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.67.4-web:Ps.67.5 as a continuation of the opening strophe rather than its own refrain-closed unit was rejected: the refrain's byte-matching return (oshb:Ps.67.4 = oshb:Ps.67.6) marks a structural close matching the one at web:Ps.67.3, giving the psalm two parallel refrain-closed calls before its closing couplet.
observed_substrate_signals: MT יוֹד֖וּךָ עַמִּ֥ים אֱלֹהִ֑ים י֝וֹד֗וּךָ עַמִּ֥ים כֻּלָּֽם (oshb:Ps.67.4) recurs byte tier at oshb:Ps.67.6, grounding the refrain-identity claim.
A Selah closes the plea for the nations at web:Ps.67.4.
The refrain wording repeats in English at web:Ps.67.3 and web:Ps.67.5, with sentence-initial capitalization as the difference.

boundary_rationale: The closing couplet turns from the refrain's imperative mood to a declarative harvest report, “The earth has yielded its increase. God, even our own God, will bless us.” (web:Ps.67.6), repeating the blessing verb into a closing line, “God will bless us. All the ends of the earth shall fear him.” (web:Ps.67.7). The near-refrain repetition of “will bless us” (web:Ps.67.6-web:Ps.67.7) closes the psalm without returning to the peoples-praise refrain itself.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding web:Ps.67.6-web:Ps.67.7 into the second refrain-closed strophe (web:Ps.67.4-web:Ps.67.5) was rejected: the imperative-plus-refrain pattern of the two earlier calls gives way here to declarative harvest language with no repetition of the “let the peoples praise” line.

Never let me be disappointed.” The imperative cluster that follows — “Deliver me…rescue me…Turn your ear to me, and save me” (web:Ps.71.2) — closes with ‘כִּֽי סַלְעִ֖י וּמְצוּדָתִ֣י אָֽתָּה’ (oshb:Ps.71.3), “for you are my rock and my fortress” (web:Ps.71.3). web:Ps.71.5 shifts to a youth-and-birth retrospective register, closing this opening refuge-and-rescue cluster at web:Ps.71.4's plea to be rescued “from the hand of the wicked”. The refuge root that opens the psalm here, (oshb:Ps.71.1) חָסִ֑יתִי, recurs once more in Psalm 71, (oshb:Ps.71.7) מַֽחֲסִי, inside the following row's span — a bracket straddling this row's own closing seam (web:Ps.71.4|web:Ps.71.5), disclosed here rather than argued as a boundary driver.

The span continues “I have relied on you from the womb…I will always praise you” (web:Ps.71.6) — birth-trust language that parallels Psalm 22's own “you brought me out of the womb…I was thrown on you from my mother's womb” (web:Ps.22.9-web:Ps.22.10), a Psalter-internal parallel decided from this psalm's own text, not a boundary driver. The span closes “My mouth shall be filled with your praise, with your honor all day long” (web:Ps.71.8), before web:Ps.71.9 opens an explicit old-age plea.

My God, hurry to help me” (web:Ps.71.12), and closes with imprecation against the accusers (web:Ps.71.13). web:Ps.71.14 opens with an adversative pivot, closing this old-age-and-enemies span.

boundary_rationale: The li-Shlomo title sits inside MT verse 1 (web:Ps.72.0 = oshb:Ps.72.1) and opens straight into a petition: the imperative תֵּ֑ן (oshb:Ps.72.1), “give,” asks God to give the king God’s own justice — “God, give the king your justice; your righteousness to the royal son.” (web:Ps.72.1) The verb chain then runs third-person masculine singular about the king — יִשְׁפֹּ֤ט, ‘he will judge’ (oshb:Ps.72.4) — through the close of verse 4. All nations shall serve him.” (web:Ps.72.11) Verse 12 opens a new clause on the causal כִּֽי (oshb:Ps.72.12), which marks the boundary here.

boundary_rationale: The maskil le-Asaph title sits inside MT verse 1 (web:Ps.74.0 = oshb:Ps.74.1) and opens the lament on לָמָ֣ה, “why” (oshb:Ps.74.1): “God, why have you rejected us forever?” (web:Ps.74.1) Verses 2-3 answer with twin imperatives, זְכֹ֤ר, “remember” (oshb:Ps.74.2), and הָרִ֣ימָה, ‘lift up’ (oshb:Ps.74.3): “Lift up your feet to the perpetual ruins,” (web:Ps.74.3). Verse 4 shifts to a third-person account of the enemy's own acts, closing this strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading verse 1 alone as the opening row was rejected because verses 2-3 supply the imperative petition (remember / lift up) that verse 1's question calls for, forming one opening unit.

device_notes: Parent: the whole of Psalm 74. It carries the maskil and le-Asaph labels (13 and 12 psalms book-wide) and continues the Asaph collection opened at Psalm 73.

boundary_rationale: Verse 4 opens the enemy's own account on שָׁאֲג֣וּ, ‘they roared’ (oshb:Ps.74.4): “Your adversaries have roared in the middle of your assembly.” (web:Ps.74.4) The third-person-plural narrative of the sanctuary's destruction runs through “They have burned up all the places in the land where God was worshiped.” (web:Ps.74.8) Verse 9 shifts to a first-person-plural admission (oshb:Ps.74.9), closing this strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the strophe through verse 9 was rejected because verse 9 changes grammatical person (third-person-plural narrative to 1cp admission), a different voice from the enemy-focused narrative of 4-8.

device_notes: This block recounts the sanctuary's desecration in the third person, between the community's imperative petition (1-3) and its own first-person crisis statement (9-11); its own 'signs' language (plene אוֹתֹתָ֣ם and defective אֹתֽוֹת at oshb:Ps.74.4) recurs across the seam, opening oshb:Ps.74.9 (אֽוֹתֹתֵ֗ינוּ, 'our signs').

boundary_rationale: אֽוֹתֹתֵ֗ינוּ, ‘our signs’ (oshb:Ps.74.9), opens a first-person-plural admission that answers, negated, the same root already used twice at oshb:Ps.74.4 for the enemies' own standards (plene אוֹתֹתָ֣ם, defective אֹתֽוֹת): “We see no miraculous signs. There is no longer any prophet” (web:Ps.74.9). The unit continues on twin interrogatives, עַד מָתַ֣י, “how long” (oshb:Ps.74.10), and לָ֤מָּה, “why” (oshb:Ps.74.11, carries a ketiv/qere pair at חוקך/חֵֽיקְךָ֣, not quoted here) — the same interrogative that opened the psalm at verse 1. Verse 12 turns to a hymnic recital of God's own past acts, closing this strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying this crisis-question unit through verse 17 was rejected because verse 12 opens on an adversative pivot into praise (‘yet God’), distinct in mood from the interrogatives of 9-11.

boundary_rationale: וֵ֭אלֹהִים, ‘yet God’ (oshb:Ps.74.12), pivots away from complaint into a hymnic recital: “Yet God is my King of old, working salvation throughout the earth.” (web:Ps.74.12) The recital opens or reinforces the clause in 5 verses (74:13-17; verse-initial in 4 of the 5, all but 74:16) on the emphatic pronoun אַתָּ֤ה, “you” (oshb:Ps.74.13, repeated through verse 17: sweep: skeleton אתה, 5 verses — 74:13-17), running through “You have set all the boundaries of the earth. You have made summer and winter.” (web:Ps.74.17) Verse 18 returns to the imperative “remember,” closing this strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the creation recital (13-17) from its adversative opening (12) into two rows was rejected because verse 12's adversative opening introduces the very subject (“God”) that the emphatic “you” clauses of 13-17 continue to address.

boundary_rationale: זְכָר, “remember” (oshb:Ps.74.18), returns to the imperative that opened the petition at verse 2, now applied to the enemy's mockery: “Remember this, that the enemy has mocked you, Yahweh.” (web:Ps.74.18) The same imperative recurs at זְכֹ֥ר (oshb:Ps.74.22), alongside קוּמָ֣ה, “arise” (oshb:Ps.74.22): “Arise, God! Plead your own cause.” (web:Ps.74.22) The psalm closes on “The tumult of those who rise up against you ascends continually.” (web:Ps.74.23) Ps 74 has 23 verses in both witnesses; no further verse follows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating verse 22's “arise” imperative into its own row was rejected because it stands inside one continuous petition with the “remember” imperatives of 18 and 22, closing the psalm as one continuous unit.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 75 is a shift+1 psalm: the lamnatseach/al-tashcheth/mizmor/shir/le-Asaph title occupies MT verse 1 in full (web:Ps.75.0 = oshb:Ps.75.1), so WEB verse 1 dual-cites oshb:Ps.75.2. It opens on the first-person-plural ה֘וֹדִ֤ינוּ, ‘we give thanks’ (web:Ps.75.1 = oshb:Ps.75.2): “We give thanks to you, God. We give thanks, for your Name is near.” (web:Ps.75.1) Verse 2 switches to a first-person-singular voice (web:Ps.75.2 = oshb:Ps.75.3), which closes this strophe at the person shift.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this verse into the divine oracle that follows was rejected because its grammatical person (1cp “we”) differs from the 1cs “I” that opens verse 2.
