oshb:Ps.75.3 shifts to 1cs grammatical person
device_notes: The rows here belong together under Psalm 75. The psalm carries the mizmor, shir, lamnatseach, le-Asaph, and al-tashcheth labels and continues the Asaph collection (73-83) inside Book III; it is a shift+1 psalm (title = MT v1), unlike the three identity psalms preceding it in this part.

boundary_rationale: Verse 2 continues a first-person divine oracle: after the verse's own opening causal particle, it carries אֲ֝נִ֗י, “I” (web:Ps.75.2 = oshb:Ps.75.3, the pronoun stands mid-verse, word 4 of 6): “When I choose the appointed time, I will judge blamelessly.” (web:Ps.75.2) The same voice continues with אָנֹכִ֨י, “I” (web:Ps.75.3 = oshb:Ps.75.4): “The earth and all its inhabitants quake. I firmly hold its pillars. Selah.” (web:Ps.75.3) and is framed explicitly by the quotative אָמַ֣רְתִּי, ‘I said’ (web:Ps.75.4 = oshb:Ps.75.5), which introduces direct speech to the arrogant: “Don't boast!” (web:Ps.75.4) The quoted speech closes at verse 5's “Don't speak with a stiff neck.” (web:Ps.75.5) Verse 6 shifts to third-person reflection about God, closing this strophe at the oracle's own frame.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading verses 2-3 as the psalmist's own vow rather than a divine oracle was rejected: their own first-person singular content (setting the appointed time, holding the pillars firm) already marks them as oracle speech distinct from the congregation's plural thanksgiving in verse 1, and the quotative frame at verse 4 (“I said to the arrogant”, web:Ps.75.4) governs the speech that follows it, addressed to the arrogant and wicked, rather than retroactively marking what precedes it.

boundary_rationale: Verse 6 opens on כִּ֤י לֹ֣א, ‘for not’ (web:Ps.75.6 = oshb:Ps.75.7), returning to third-person reflection about God rather than God's own first-person voice: “For neither from the east, nor from the west, nor yet from the south, comes exaltation.” (web:Ps.75.6) The unit closes on כִּ֤י כ֪וֹס, ‘for a cup’ (web:Ps.75.8 = oshb:Ps.75.9): “For in Yahweh's hand there is a cup ... the wicked of the earth drink and drink it to its very dregs.” (web:Ps.75.8) Verse 9 returns to a first-person singular vow (web:Ps.75.9 = oshb:Ps.75.10), closing this strophe.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading this unit as a continuation of the divine oracle was rejected because its verbs describe God in the third person (“He puts down one, and lifts up another.” web:Ps.75.7) rather than voicing God's own first-person speech as verses 2-5 do.

device_notes: Psalm 76 forms a single liturgical unit; every row here shares that one parent. The title carries five byte-swept genre labels (mizmor, shir, lamnatseach, le-Asaph, binginot) placing it among the eleven le-Asaph superscriptions of Book III (73-83); twelve carry the label book-wide, the twelfth being Psalm 50 in Book II.

boundary_rationale: Second-person address to God opens the row at web:Ps.76.4 (“Glorious are you, and excellent…”) immediately after the Selah closing the prior unit (web:Ps.76.3 = oshb:Ps.76.4, “סֶֽלָה”), and the same address sustains through the vocative at web:Ps.76.6, “At your rebuke, God of Jacob…” (oshb:Ps.76.7 “אֱלֹהֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֑ב”), and the fear-vocabulary of web:Ps.76.7-8 (“You, even you, are to be feared… You pronounced judgment from heaven…”). The psalm's second Selah, web:Ps.76.9 (oshb:Ps.76.10 “לְהוֹשִׁ֖יעַ כָּל עַנְוֵי אֶ֣רֶץ סֶֽלָה”), sits inside the row rather than closing it: the God-directed address continues past it, without a person change across its 7 verses (web:Ps.76.4-Ps.76.10), through the row's own close at web:Ps.76.10, “Surely the wrath of man praises you. The survivors of your wrath are restrained.” The closing verb's own suffix, “תּוֹדֶ֑ךָּ” (oshb:Ps.76.11, final kaf + dagesh + qamats), is second-person-masculine-singular, 'it praises you', so the address opened at web:Ps.76.4 runs to this row's own close without an addressee change (7 of 7 verses, web:Ps.76.4-Ps.76.10). The seam falls right after it: web:Ps.76.11 (oshb:Ps.76.12) opens the plural imperative summons, “Make vows to Yahweh your God…”, addressed to the worshiping congregation rather than to God -- the addressee shift that closes this row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through web:Ps.76.11 (oshb:Ps.76.12) was rejected: its plural imperative, “Make vows to Yahweh your God, and fulfill them!”, addresses the worshiping congregation rather than God, so folding it into this row would erase the addressee change the seam is meant to mark; this row's own close instead sits one verse earlier, at web:Ps.76.10 (oshb:Ps.76.11), whose own verb, “תּוֹדֶ֑ךָּ”, still carries the second-person address to God that opened the row at web:Ps.76.4.

the vocative 'God of Jacob' at oshb:Ps.76.7 (web:Ps.76.6) marks mid-strophe address, not a strophe boundary

the closing verb of web:Ps.76.10, תּוֹדֶ֑ךָּ (oshb:Ps.76.11), carries a byte-legible final-kaf + dagesh + qamats 2ms suffix -- second-person address to God, not yet the 2mp congregational imperative that opens the next verse

device_notes: The 'אֱלֹהֵ֣י יַעֲקֹ֑ב' epithet at web:Ps.76.6 (oshb:Ps.76.7) belongs to a recurring divine title swept at 9 verses book-wide (skeleton tier), a psalm-external texture rather than a driver for this seam. The seam itself rests on a morphological device: the row's closing verb at web:Ps.76.10, תּוֹדֶ֑ךָּ (oshb:Ps.76.11), carries the second-person-masculine-singular pronominal suffix -- final kaf with dagesh and qamats -- so the row's own close is fixed by the final byte-legible 2ms form addressed to God, immediately before the 2mp imperative verbs open the next verse.

boundary_rationale: This row opens on the addressee shift that follows the psalm's God-directed second-person address: the plural imperative summons “Make vows to Yahweh your God, and fulfill them!” (web:Ps.76.11), matching “נִֽדֲר֣וּ וְשַׁלְּמוּ֮ לַיהוָ֪ה אֱֽלֹהֵ֫יכֶ֥ם” (oshb:Ps.76.12), turns from the petition register of the preceding row -- which closes at web:Ps.76.10 (oshb:Ps.76.11) still carrying a second-person-masculine-singular suffix, “תּוֹדֶ֑ךָּ”, 'it praises you' -- to a 2mp summons addressed to the worshiping congregation. Third-person report of divine power then resumes at web:Ps.76.12, “He will cut off the spirit of princes. He is feared by the kings of the earth.” This closes the psalm on the same report register that opened it (web:Ps.76.1 = oshb:Ps.76.2). Yahweh (skeleton tier) occurs in 1 verse of Psalm 76, prefixed as “לַיהוָ֪ה” at oshb:Ps.76.12 (web:Ps.76.11).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Opening this row at web:Ps.76.10 (oshb:Ps.76.11), as the corpus previously read it, is rejected: that verse's own closing verb, “תּוֹדֶ֑ךָּ”, is itself second-person-masculine-singular, 'it praises you', addressed to God rather than to the congregation, so it belongs with the preceding row's God-directed address block rather than opening this one; the addressee shift begins one verse later, at web:Ps.76.11 (oshb:Ps.76.12), where the imperative verbs “נִֽדֲר֣וּ” and “וְשַׁלְּמוּ֮” (oshb:Ps.76.12) turn to the plural congregation.

boundary_rationale: The opening row carries the title's dual-cite (web:Ps.77.0 = oshb:Ps.77.1); the title's ketiv/qere pair “ידיתון יְדוּת֗וּן” (oshb:Ps.77.1) renders the al-Yeduthun label (“To Jeduthun”, web:Ps.77.0), structurally matching Psalm 62's al-prefixed title (web:Ps.62.0 = oshb:Ps.62.1, 0 ketiv/qere notes there) rather than Psalm 39's lamed-prefixed one (web:Ps.39.0 = oshb:Ps.39.1) -- yet it is Psalm 39's title that carries the one ketiv/qere note sharing this psalm's own ketiv spelling. The psalm opens on a doubled cry, “My cry goes to God! Indeed, I cry to God for help…” (web:Ps.77.1), matching “קוֹלִ֣י אֶל אֱלֹהִ֣ים וְאֶצְעָ֑קָה קוֹלִ֥י אֶל אֱ֝לֹהִ֗ים וְהַאֲזִ֥ין אֵלָֽי” (oshb:Ps.77.2), where the phrase for 'my voice to God' repeats within the verse. The distress deepens through web:Ps.77.2 (“In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord… My soul refused to be comforted”) and closes on Selah: “I remember God, and I groan… Selah” (web:Ps.77.3; oshb:Ps.77.4 “אֶזְכְּרָ֣ה אֱלֹהִ֣ים וְאֶֽהֱמָיָ֑ה…סֶֽלָה”).
strongest_rejected_alternative: The title could be treated as a bare label carrying no boundary weight of its own, but it shares three genre labels with Psalm 76 (mizmor, lamnatseach, le-Asaph) and carries its own al-Yeduthun label besides, and the body's own addressee profile marks a real seam here: oshb:Ps.77.2-Ps.77.4 carry 0 second-person forms (first-person distress report alone) before the 2ms perfect address opens at oshb:Ps.77.5, so the title's dual-cite anchors this row's front seam rather than floating free of it.

device_notes: One parent, Psalm 77, spans all of this psalm's rows. Its title shares three genre labels with Psalm 76 (web:Ps.76.0 = oshb:Ps.76.1; mizmor, lamnatseach, le-Asaph) plus the al-Yeduthun label it does not share with 76.

boundary_rationale: The row opens just after the Selah at web:Ps.77.3 (oshb:Ps.77.4, “סֶֽלָה”), with direct address to God beginning at web:Ps.77.4, “You hold my eyelids open”, then turning reflective at web:Ps.77.5-6 (“I have considered the days of old… I remember my song in the night… my spirit diligently inquires”). That inquiry opens into quoted rhetorical questions at web:Ps.77.7, “Will the Lord reject us forever?”, continuing through web:Ps.77.8 and closing at web:Ps.77.9, “Has God forgotten to be gracious?” Selah closes the row, matching “הֲשָׁכַ֣ח חַנּ֣וֹת אֵ֑ל…סֶֽלָה” (oshb:Ps.77.10) for the closing pair.
strongest_rejected_alternative: The row could split at 77:6/77:7, separating the silent meditation from the quoted despair-questions it introduces, but web:Ps.77.6 ends by announcing the inquiry that web:Ps.77.7-9 then voices in quotation, so the two halves form one continuous movement from reflection to its own quoted content.

boundary_rationale: Just past the Selah that closes the quoted despair-questions (web:Ps.77.9 = oshb:Ps.77.10, “סֶֽלָה”), this row opens at the psalm's pivot: “I will appeal to this: the years of the right hand of the Most High” (web:Ps.77.10), matching “וָ֭אֹמַר חַלּ֣וֹתִי הִ֑יא שְׁ֝נ֗וֹת יְמִ֣ין עֶלְיֽוֹן” (oshb:Ps.77.11). The register-list formula “This one was born there.” — oshb:Ps.87.4's “זֶ֝֗ה יֻלַּד שָֽׁם”, recurs, matching at the skeleton (consonantal) tier, at oshb:Ps.87.6's “זֶ֖ה יֻלַּד שָׁ֣ם” (web:Ps.87.6, sweep: 2 verses in Psalm 87, skeleton zeh yulad sham) framing web:Ps.87.5's variant “This one and that one was born in her;” before the unit closes on the communal declaration of web:Ps.87.7. Confidence is held at medium_low: the register-list genre and the Rahab identification carry real interpretive uncertainty, and the internal shape of this four-verse unit is argued from one repeated formula rather than a full set of tier-1 markers.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the nations-register (web:Ps.87.4-Ps.87.6) from the closing communal declaration (web:Ps.87.7) into two rows is defensible given the Selah at web:Ps.87.6, but web:Ps.87.7's singers and dancers are naturally read as responding to the census just declared, not opening a new unit.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.87.4 and oshb:Ps.87.6 match at the skeleton (consonantal) tier on the closing formula zeh yulad sham (raw/nfd/accent_stripped tiers do not converge)
web_selah:true at Ps.87.3 (front seam) and Ps.87.6 (interior)
the WEB footnote at web:Ps.87.4 identifying Rahab with Egypt is translator commentary, not verse text

boundary_rationale: A single parent unit gathers every row of Psalm 88. The title (web:Ps.88.0 = oshb:Ps.88.1) carries eight genre/authorship labels — mizmor, shir, maskil, lamnatseach, livnei-Qorach, al-machalat, leannot, and oshb:Ps.88.1's closing “מַ֝שְׂכִּ֗יל לְהֵימָ֥ן הָאֶזְרָחִֽי” (“a contemplation by Heman, the Ezrahite”) — naming the psalm's only individually-named author within the Korah collection (le_heman: 1 of 116 titled psalms; psalm_device_inventory.json). The strophe opens on direct invocation, oshb:Ps.88.2's “יְ֭הוָה אֱלֹהֵ֣י יְשׁוּעָתִ֑י” (“Yahweh, the God of my salvation”, web:Ps.88.1), and holds a sustained second-person address describing the psalmist's descent toward Sheol and the pit (web:Ps.88.2-Ps.88.6) before closing on the wrath-affliction climax and Selah of web:Ps.88.7.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A shorter opening row of web:Ps.88.1-Ps.88.2 alone would separate the invocation from the descent-imagery it introduces without any address or speaker change between them.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.88.1 carries eight distinct genre/authorship labels (psalm_device_inventory.json)
web_selah:true at Ps.88.7 (verse_map_web.json)
web:Ps.88.1-Ps.88.7 hold one continuous 2nd-person address to Yahweh describing the psalmist's own plight
device_notes: A single parent unit gathers every row of Psalm 88.

boundary_rationale: The strophe opens immediately after the Selah at web:Ps.88.7 (oshb:Ps.88.8) on isolation from human companionship: “You have taken my friends from me” (web:Ps.88.8), “My eyes are dim from grief” (web:Ps.88.9). It moves into 3 verse-initial interrogative-he particles addressed to Yahweh about the dead (MT 88:11, 88:12, 88:13; 6 WEB question marks across web:Ps.88.10-Ps.88.12), opening oshb:Ps.88.11's “הֲלַמֵּתִ֥ים תַּעֲשֶׂה פֶּ֑לֶא” (“Do you show wonders to the dead?”, web:Ps.88.10, with Selah) and continuing web:Ps.88.11-Ps.88.12 (“Is your loving kindness declared in the grave?”, “Are your wonders made known in the dark?”) before the psalm returns to direct petition at web:Ps.88.13.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the isolation report (web:Ps.88.8-Ps.88.9) from the rhetorical-question triad (web:Ps.88.10-Ps.88.12) into two rows is possible, but nothing marks a hard grammatical seam between them beyond a shift from statement to question.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.88.10-Ps.88.12 carry 3 verse-initial interrogative-he particles (MT 88:11, 88:12, 88:13) about divine action toward the dead, rendered as 6 WEB question marks across the 3 verses (“Do/Is/Are…?”)
web_selah:true at Ps.88.7 (front seam) and Ps.88.10 (interior)

An undisclosed cross-seam envelope binds this row's own seam at web:Ps.88.12|Ps.88.13 to two verses outside it: web:Ps.88.8 = oshb:Ps.88.9 (הִרְחַ֥קְתָּ מְיֻדָּעַ֗י מִ֫מֶּ֥נִּי שַׁתַּ֣נִי תוֹעֵב֣וֹת לָ֑מוֹ כָּ֝לֻ֗א וְלֹ֣א אֵצֵֽא, ‘you have distanced my acquaintances from me’) and web:Ps.88.18 = oshb:Ps.88.19 (הִרְחַ֣קְתָּ מִ֭מֶּנִּי אֹהֵ֣ב וָרֵ֑עַ מְֽיֻדָּעַ֥י מַחְשָֽׁךְ, ‘you have distanced from me lover and friend, my acquaintances -- darkness’) share the same opening verb and the same noun, in reversed word order between the two verses

boundary_rationale: The closing strophe pivots on an adversative reopening of direct petition, oshb:Ps.88.14's “וַאֲנִ֤י אֵלֶ֣יךָ יְהוָ֣ה” (“But to you, Yahweh, I have cried”, web:Ps.88.13). It moves through renewed complaint (“why do you reject my soul?”, web:Ps.88.14) and terror imagery (web:Ps.88.15-Ps.88.17) to a final image of encirclement, closing on oshb:Ps.88.19's final word “מַחְשָֽׁךְ” (“darkness,” web:Ps.88.18): “You have put lover and friend far from me, and my friends into darkness.” No selah falls within this span, and the psalm ends on this word without any turn to praise or resolution within its own bytes.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading web:Ps.88.13-Ps.88.18 as a continuation of the question-triad span rather than its own unit would miss the shift from interrogative address back to first-person petition at web:Ps.88.13.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.88.14 opens with a fronted first-person pronoun (waani, an emphatic but-I opening) marking a return to direct address after the interrogatives of web:Ps.88.10-Ps.88.12
oshb:Ps.88.19's final word מַחְשָֽׁךְ (“darkness”) is the psalm's final byte, with no praise or resolution clause following it within the span

An undisclosed cross-seam envelope binds this row's own front seam at web:Ps.88.12|Ps.88.13 to a verse outside it: web:Ps.88.8 = oshb:Ps.88.9 (הִרְחַ֥קְתָּ מְיֻדָּעַ֗י מִ֫מֶּ֥נִּי שַׁתַּ֣נִי תוֹעֵב֣וֹת לָ֑מוֹ כָּ֝לֻ֗א וְלֹ֣א אֵצֵֽא, ‘you have distanced my acquaintances from me’), which web:Ps.88.18 = oshb:Ps.88.19 (הִרְחַ֣קְתָּ מִ֭מֶּנִּי אֹהֵ֣ב וָרֵ֑עַ מְֽיֻדָּעַ֥י מַחְשָֽׁךְ, ‘you have distanced from me lover and friend, my acquaintances -- darkness’, inside this row’s own span) answers in reversed word order -- same opening verb, same noun

boundary_rationale: The maskil-le-Ethan title heads the psalm (מַ֝שְׂכִּ֗יל לְאֵיתָ֥ן הָֽאֶזְרָחִֽי, web:Ps.89.0 = oshb:Ps.89.1) and the opening verse states the composition’s own double topic — “I will sing of the loving kindness of Yahweh forever” (web:Ps.89.1) — before the psalmist’s declaration turns, at 89:3, into a quoted first-person divine oath: “I have made a covenant with my chosen one, I have sworn to David, my servant” (web:Ps.89.3). The unit closes on that oath’s own guarantee, “I will establish your offspring forever, and build up your throne to all generations” (web:Ps.89.4), corroborated by Selah (web:Ps.89.4 = oshb:Ps.89.5).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 89:2 and moving the oath-citation into the next row was considered, but 89:3 opens without a distinct topic header of its own and the oath’s guarantee is what Selah corroborates at 89:4, binding the citation to the vow that introduces it.
observed_substrate_signals: superscription genre label maskil + attribution le-Ethan opens the psalm (tier-1)
first-person vow (89:1-2) shifts into quoted divine oath at 89:3 with no intervening topic marker
Selah closes the unit at web:Ps.89.4 = oshb:Ps.89.5 (tier-3 corroboration)
device_notes: Psalm 89 is a single composition; every row here shares one parent, Psalm 89, from title to closing doxology. Selah corroborates this unit’s close (web:Ps.89.4 = oshb:Ps.89.5).

boundary_rationale: The address shifts from the quoted oath back to direct praise of Yahweh: “The heavens will praise your wonders, Yahweh” (web:Ps.89.5) opens a doxological question — “who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh?” (web:Ps.89.6) — pursued through the council of the holy ones (web:Ps.89.7) to “Yahweh, God of Armies, who is a mighty one, like you?” (web:Ps.89.8). The preceding oath-citation closed under Selah at web:Ps.89.4 = oshb:Ps.89.5; this unit’s own content — the heavenly council’s incomparability question — is untouched by that closing mark and begins a new address.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this unit through web:Ps.89.9 = oshb:Ps.89.10’s dominion-over-the-sea material was considered, but that verse trades the incomparability question (‘who is like Yahweh’) for a declarative act (“You rule the pride of the sea”), a different predicate class.
observed_substrate_signals: 3 WEB question marks over web:Ps.89.6-Ps.89.8 (Yahweh’s incomparability among the bene elim)
the heavenly council (sod qedoshim) as addressee-class shifts to declarative acts at 89:9

boundary_rationale: The hymn turns from the incomparability question to declarative acts of cosmic dominion: “You rule the pride of the sea” and “You have broken Rahab in pieces” (web:Ps.89.9-Ps.89.10), then creation itself — heavens, earth, north, south, Tabor and Hermon (web:Ps.89.11-Ps.89.12) — before the strength imagery of “Your hand is strong, and your right hand is exalted” (web:Ps.89.13) grounds the throne’s own foundation: “Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne” (web:Ps.89.14).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the sea/Rahab pair (89:9-10) from the north-south creation list (89:11-12) as two rows was considered, but both develop the same declarative-act catalogue with no addressee or topic break between them.
observed_substrate_signals: declarative 2nd-person acts replace the interrogative mode of the preceding council question
the throne’s foundation clause (89:14) closes the catalogue of acts before the beatitude on “the people” (web:Ps.89.15) opens the next unit

boundary_rationale: The grammatical subject shifts at this row’s own seam: web:Ps.89.14 = oshb:Ps.89.15’s verbless clause, צֶ֣דֶק וּ֭מִשְׁפָּט מְכ֣וֹן כִּסְאֶ֑ךָ חֶ֥סֶד וֶ֝אֱמֶ֗ת יְֽקַדְּמ֥וּ פָנֶֽיךָ, is headed by the third-person nominal pair ‘righteousness and justice’ as its subject, with ‘your throne’ sitting inside the predicate’s construct chain as a possessive genitive rather than as the clause’s own subject; the beatitude that opens this unit, “Blessed are the people who learn to acclaim you” (אַשְׁרֵ֣י הָ֭עָם, web:Ps.89.15 = oshb:Ps.89.16), makes ‘the people’ the new nominal subject instead. Second-person address to Yahweh continues unbroken through the unit -- “They walk in the light of your presence, Yahweh” (web:Ps.89.15), “In your name they rejoice all day. In your righteousness, they are exalted” (web:Ps.89.16), and the unit’s own close “our shield belongs to Yahweh, our king to the Holy One of Israel” (web:Ps.89.18) -- so the seam is a subject-class shift (righteousness/justice to the people), not a break in addressee.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 89:15-18 into the preceding creation-hymn as one long unit was considered, but the grammatical subject moves from ‘righteousness and justice’ (the verbless clause’s own subject at the seam verse, web:Ps.89.14 = oshb:Ps.89.15) to ‘the people’, a fresh third-person nominal subject, a discourse-level shift; second-person address to Yahweh itself continues on both sides of the seam and does not mark it.
observed_substrate_signals: the beatitude’s own nominal subject, ‘the people’, replaces ‘righteousness and justice’ as the verse-initial grammatical subject at 89:15, while second-person address to Yahweh (‘your presence’, ‘your name’, ‘your righteousness’) continues unbroken through 89:15-89:17
the unit closes back on “Yahweh”/“the Holy One of Israel” (web:Ps.89.18) as the possessor of the people’s shield and king, returning to direct naming before the oracle opens

boundary_rationale: The divine oracle proper opens on its own discourse marker: “Then you spoke in vision to your saints” (אָ֤ז דִּבַּ֥רְתָּֽ בְחָ֡זוֹן לַֽחֲסִידֶ֗יךָ…, web:Ps.89.19 = oshb:Ps.89.20), introducing quoted first-person divine speech that names David — “I have found David, my servant. I have anointed him with my holy oil” (web:Ps.89.20) — and runs through his establishment (web:Ps.89.21), protection from enemies (web:Ps.89.22-Ps.89.24), to dominion extended over sea and rivers (web:Ps.89.25).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Starting the oracle’s own row at 89:20, the naming of David, rather than 89:19 was considered, but 89:19’s ‘then’ is the vision-formula’s own opening word and separating it would strand the introduction from the speech it introduces.
observed_substrate_signals: az (‘then’) opens the verse as a temporal discourse marker introducing reported divine speech, tier-1
the vision-formula’s own verb of address (‘and said’) marks the quotation’s start at 89:19

boundary_rationale: The oracle’s voicing shifts as David’s own cry is quoted within Yahweh’s speech: “He will call to me, ‘You are my Father, my God, and the rock of my salvation!’” (web:Ps.89.26), before Yahweh’s promise resumes with his appointment as heir above the kings of the earth (web:Ps.89.27) and the everlasting terms of the covenant and offspring (web:Ps.89.28-Ps.89.29).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping this unit attached to the preceding vision-and-establishment unit was considered, but 89:26 embeds a second, nested first-person voice, David’s own address to God, that the unconditional ‘I will’ promises before it do not carry.
observed_substrate_signals: nested quotation: David’s own voice (‘You are my Father’) is quoted inside Yahweh’s reported speech at 89:26
heir/covenant/offspring promises (89:27-29) form the oracle’s unconditional close before the conditional clause opens the next unit

boundary_rationale: A conditional clause opens the unit on its own particle: “If his children forsake my law” (אִם יַֽעַזְב֣וּ בָ֭נָיו תּוֹרָתִ֑י…, web:Ps.89.30 = oshb:Ps.89.31), threatening discipline “with the rod” (web:Ps.89.32) before the adversative “But I will not completely take my loving kindness from him” (web:Ps.89.33) reasserts the oath’s irrevocability through the holiness-oath of web:Ps.89.35 to the unit’s own close: “It will be established forever like the moon, the faithful witness in the sky” (web:Ps.89.37), corroborated by Selah (web:Ps.89.37 = oshb:Ps.89.38).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the conditional threat (89:30-32) from the reaffirmation (89:33-37) into two rows was considered, but the adversative at 89:33 answers the very threat the conditional clause raises, and the pair resolves together under one Selah at 89:37.
observed_substrate_signals: im (‘if’) opens a conditional protasis at 89:30, tier-1, distinct from the unconditional ‘I will’ series that precedes it
adversative ‘But I will not’ at 89:33 answers the conditional threat within the same unit
Selah closes the unit at web:Ps.89.37 = oshb:Ps.89.38 (tier-3 corroboration)

boundary_rationale: The psalm’s reversal opens on its own fronted, adversative pronoun: “But you have rejected and spurned. You have been angry with your anointed” (וְאַתָּ֣ה זָ֭נַחְתָּ וַתִּמְאָ֑ס הִ֝תְעַבַּ֗רְתָּ עִם מְשִׁיחֶֽךָ, web:Ps.89.38 = oshb:Ps.89.39). Direct second-person address to Yahweh, absent for the preceding 11 verses (oshb:Ps.89.28-Ps.89.38 = web:Ps.89.27-Ps.89.37, 0 second-person suffixes or independent pronouns across all 11), resumes at this unit’s own opening verse, but the mode inverts from oath-fulfillment to accusation: the covenant is renounced (web:Ps.89.39), the hedges broken (web:Ps.89.40), the adversaries exalted (web:Ps.89.42), and the anointed’s youth shortened “with shame” (web:Ps.89.45), corroborated by Selah at the unit’s own close (web:Ps.89.45 = oshb:Ps.89.46). The preceding oracle closed under Selah at web:Ps.89.37 = oshb:Ps.89.38, the front seam this unit inverts.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Starting the lament one verse later, at 89:39, so that “you have rejected and spurned” (web:Ps.89.38) and “You have been angry” (web:Ps.89.38) split across two rows was considered, but both clauses share one verse (web:Ps.89.38 = oshb:Ps.89.39) and one fronted pronoun, and dividing one verse defeats the tiling rule.
observed_substrate_signals: ve-attah (‘but/and you’), a fronted independent pronoun with vav, opens a strong adversative at 89:38, tier-1

second-person address to Yahweh does NOT run unbroken into this unit: oshb:Ps.89.28-Ps.89.38 (=web:89.27-89.37, the preceding 11 verses) carry 0 second-person suffixes or independent pronouns; direct address to Yahweh resumes exactly at this unit’s own opening verse, oshb:Ps.89.39 (=web:89.38), while the mode flips from promise-fulfillment to accusation
Selah brackets the unit at both seams: web:Ps.89.37 = oshb:Ps.89.38 (front) and web:Ps.89.45 = oshb:Ps.89.46 (end)

boundary_rationale: The lament shifts from a series of accusing declaratives (“You have…”) to direct interrogative address: “How long, Yahweh? Will you hide yourself forever?” (web:Ps.89.46), moving through a meditation on mortality — “What man is he who shall live and not see death” (web:Ps.89.48) — to a closing plea that names the taunts “with which they have mocked the footsteps of your anointed one” (web:Ps.89.51). The preceding unit closed under Selah at web:Ps.89.45 = oshb:Ps.89.46, the front seam of this row; a further Selah falls inside this unit at web:Ps.89.48 = oshb:Ps.89.49.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the whole lament as one long row was considered, but “How long, Yahweh?” (web:Ps.89.46) opens a question-and-address mode distinct from the accusing “You have…” declaratives that precede it, and Selah marks a break at the seam between them.
observed_substrate_signals: interrogative address, עַד מָ֣ה (‘how long’, oshb:Ps.89.47 = web:Ps.89.46), replaces the declarative accusation series as the unit’s opening mode
Selah recurs at the front seam (89:45=46 MT) and again inside this unit (89:48=49 MT)

boundary_rationale: The psalm closes on the fixed book-boundary doxology formula: “Blessed be Yahweh forever more. Amen, and Amen” (בָּר֖וּךְ יְהוָ֥ה לְ֝עוֹלָ֗ם אָ֘מֵ֥ן וְאָמֵֽן, web:Ps.89.52 = oshb:Ps.89.53), baruch followed by amen x2. The formula answers nothing in the immediately preceding lament by content; it is the same closing class attested at the ends of Books I, II, and IV, marking the end of Book III’s collection (Psalms 73-89) rather than resolving the anointed one’s complaint.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this verse into the lament as its final line was considered, but the baruch-plus-double-amen formula shares its closing class with the book’s other book-boundary doxologies rather than continuing the lament’s own address to Yahweh in the second person.
observed_substrate_signals: baruch (‘blessed’) + amen x2 formula, matching in class the book I, II, and IV closing doxologies
the doxology stands outside the lament’s own second-person complaint address

boundary_rationale: The tefillah-le-Moshe title opens the psalm (תְּפִלָּה֮ לְמֹשֶׁ֪ה אִֽישׁ הָאֱלֹ֫הִ֥ים…, web:Ps.90.0 = oshb:Ps.90.1; the title sits inside MT verse 1, which also carries the prayer’s own opening line) and the unit states Yahweh’s eternity in two movements: relational — “Lord, you have been our dwelling place for all generations” (web:Ps.90.1) — then absolute — “before the mountains were born… וּֽמֵעוֹלָ֥ם עַד ע֝וֹלָ֗ם אַתָּ֥ה אֵֽל” (oshb:Ps.90.2), rendered “even from everlasting to everlasting, you are God” (web:Ps.90.2).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through 90:3 was considered, but 90:3 turns from Yahweh’s own eternity to a direct statement about human mortality (“You turn man to destruction”, web:Ps.90.3), a new subject.
observed_substrate_signals: tefillah + le-Moshe title, the book’s only Moses-attributed superscription (sweep: 1 of 150 psalms; genre-label inventory), tier-1 opener
the unit’s content moves from relational dwelling-place language (90:1) to the fixed phrase ‘from everlasting to everlasting’ (90:2), both predicated of Yahweh/God
device_notes: One parent, Psalm 90, holds all of this prayer’s rows together as a single composition.

boundary_rationale: Human transience displaces divine eternity as the subject: “You turn man to destruction, saying, "Return, you children of men."” (web:Ps.90.3) sets the theme, developed through a timescale comparison — “a thousand years in your sight are just like yesterday… like a watch in the night” (web:Ps.90.4) — then the grass metaphor: swept away in sleep, sprouting in the morning, “By evening, it is withered and dry” (web:Ps.90.6).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the ‘return, you children of men’ saying (90:3) from the timescale and grass images (90:4-6) into two rows was considered, but both illustrate the same theme that 90:3 announces, with no addressee or mode break between them.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative-within-quotation ‘Return’ (shuvu) opens the transience theme at 90:3
two illustrations of the same theme (timescale, 90:4; grass, 90:5-6) run without a further mode shift

boundary_rationale: A causal connective binds mortality to divine wrath as its explanation: “For we are consumed in your anger. We are troubled in your wrath” (web:Ps.90.7) names sin as the cause (web:Ps.90.8) and totals the lifespan — “seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty years” (web:Ps.90.10) — before the unit closes on the wisdom petition its own meditation earns: “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (web:Ps.90.12).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying this unit through web:Ps.90.13 so that the wisdom petition and the plea to relent form one row was considered; both this unit’s own close and web:Ps.90.13 open on imperatives addressed to Yahweh (הוֹדַ֑ע, ‘make known!’, oshb:Ps.90.12; שׁוּבָ֣ה, ‘relent!’, oshb:Ps.90.13), so the seam is not reflection-to-imperative. The stronger warrant for keeping them apart is a root echo in reversed direction: וַ֝תֹּ֗אמֶר (‘return!’, oshb:Ps.90.3), Yahweh’s own imperative to ‘the children of men,’ is answered by שׁוּבָ֣ה (‘relent/return!’, oshb:Ps.90.13), the psalmist’s imperative back to Yahweh -- a role-reversal this unit’s own close (90:12) does not yet supply.
observed_substrate_signals: כִּֽי (‘for’, oshb:Ps.90.7) opens a causal connective tying the wrath-theme to the preceding transience images; standalone ki opens 3 verses in Psalm 90 (90:4, 90:7, 90:9), of which only 90:7 is this row’s own seam
the unit’s own close (90:12) is a request for wisdom, not yet the imperative petition series that follows

boundary_rationale: The psalm’s closing petition opens on a fresh imperative: “Relent, Yahweh! How long? Have compassion on your servants!” (שׁוּבָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה עַד מָתָ֑י…, web:Ps.90.13 = oshb:Ps.90.13), moving through the plea to be satisfied “in the morning with your loving kindness” (web:Ps.90.14) and for gladness proportioned to the years of affliction (web:Ps.90.15), to the psalm’s own final request, repeated for emphasis: “Establish the work of our hands for us. Yes, establish the work of our hands” (web:Ps.90.17).

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens in third-person description, “He who dwells…” (web:Ps.91.1), before the voice turns to first-person confession, “I will say of…” (web:Ps.91.2), whose object clause WEB itself closes inside quotation marks at the end of the verse. The second-person address that runs from web:Ps.91.3 onward has not yet opened, so the opening description and its confession stand together as one unit before the address begins.
strongest_rejected_alternative: web:Ps.91.3 shifts both grammatical person and addressee, opening the protective second-person address that governs the rest of the psalm rather than continuing the speaker's own confession, so folding it into this row was rejected.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.91.1's opening participle יֹ֭שֵׁב (oshb:Ps.91.1, 'dwells') names a generic figure, not an addressed 'you'
WEB's own quotation marks close the confession within web:Ps.91.2, one verse before the second-person address opens
device_notes: Rows of Psalm 91 group to one parent unit.

boundary_rationale: From web:Ps.91.3 the psalm addresses a singular 'you' directly, cataloguing dangers the addressee is protected from -- snare, pestilence, terror by night, the arrow by day -- through web:Ps.91.8, then restates the premise of that protection, “Because you have made Yahweh your…” (web:Ps.91.9), and its result, “no evil shall happen…” (web:Ps.91.10). This eight-verse span holds one continuous second-person address before a new governing image -- the angels of web:Ps.91.11 -- opens the next unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A break at web:Ps.91.9, where the refuge premise is restated, was rejected because vv.9-10 supply the reason and result for the preceding danger catalogue rather than opening a new topic; standalone ki opens 4 verses in Psalm 91 (91:3 כִּ֤י, 91:9 כִּֽי, 91:11 כִּ֣י, 91:14 כִּ֤י), 3 of which open this cluster’s own unit boundaries, but 91:9’s ki resumes the address already running since 91:3 rather than introducing a new grammatical subject or addressee the way the other three do.

web:Ps.91.10's closing clause answers web:Ps.91.9's premise within the same span
device_notes: No superscription or refrain marking touches this span, and no selah falls within it either; the danger catalogue forms one continuous address unit, distinct from the psalm's other spans.

boundary_rationale: web:Ps.91.11 introduces a new protective agent as the verb’s fronted object rather than the span’s grammatical subject: כִּ֣י מַ֭לְאָכָיו יְצַוֶּה לָּ֑ךְ לִ֝שְׁמָרְךָ֗ בְּכָל דְּרָכֶֽיךָ (oshb:Ps.91.11, 'for he will command his angels for you') keeps Yahweh, the 3ms referent already explicit at 91:3/91:9, as the verb’s subject, with מַ֭לְאָכָיו ('his angels', plural) as the fronted object/complement of the singular verb יְצַוֶּה; naming the specific agent of protection rather than the generic dangers of the preceding span; the angelic guardianship carries through web:Ps.91.13's triumph over the lion and serpent, before the voice shifts again to Yahweh's own first-person speech at web:Ps.91.14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: web:Ps.91.14 introduces a first-person divine speaker, a distinct voice from the third-person angels of vv.11-13, so carrying this span forward into it was rejected.
observed_substrate_signals: מַ֭לְאָכָיו (oshb:Ps.91.11, 'his angels') is plural while יְצַוֶּה (oshb:Ps.91.11, 3ms singular) is singular; number disagreement rules out the plural noun as the verb's subject, identifying it instead as the fronted object naming the protective agent, distinct from the implied dangers of the previous span
device_notes: The angelic-guardianship image is local to this span; it does not recur elsewhere in the psalm.

boundary_rationale: web:Ps.91.14 opens with the causal clause כִּ֤י בִ֣י חָ֭שַׁק וַאֲפַלְּטֵ֑הוּ (oshb:Ps.91.14, 'because he has clung to me and I will deliver him'), a first-person divine verb shifting the speaker from the address-voice of vv.3-13 to Yahweh's own voice; WEB marks the shift with its own quotation mark, opening “Because he has set his love on me,…” (web:Ps.91.14) and closing “…show him my salvation.” (web:Ps.91.16) at the psalm's end. This closing oracle, in which God speaks of the trusting individual in the third person ('him'), is a distinct unit from the second-person address that precedes it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.91.13 as the oracle's opening verse was rejected because it still addresses 'you' in the second person, while web:Ps.91.14 is where Yahweh's own first-person voice begins.
observed_substrate_signals: WEB brackets this span in its own quotation marks, opening at web:Ps.91.14 and closing at web:Ps.91.16, the psalm's final verse

the verb וַאֲפַלְּטֵ֑הוּ (oshb:Ps.91.14, 'and I will deliver him') is first-person, first-person divine speech -- Yahweh's own voice, distinct in speaker from the third-person and second-person address of the rest of the psalm, though not the psalm's only first-person verb -- 2 occurrences (אֹמַ֗ר/אֶבְטַח) recur at oshb:Ps.91.2, also 1cs
device_notes: The closing oracle carries the psalm's direct divine first-person speech, distinct in voice from its other three spans.

boundary_rationale: The title, מִזְמ֥וֹר שִׁ֗יר לְי֣וֹם הַשַּׁבָּֽת (oshb:Ps.92.1, 'a psalm, a song for the Sabbath day'), names this psalm for the Sabbath -- “A Psalm. A song for the Sabbath day.” (web:Ps.92.0) is the book's only WEB title to do so (sweep: 1 verse, book-wide 'Sabbath' search over WEB titles and text). Three infinitive clauses then open the body -- לְהֹד֥וֹת ('to give thanks', oshb:Ps.92.2) and וּלְזַמֵּ֖ר ('and to sing praise', oshb:Ps.92.2), both at web:Ps.92.1 = oshb:Ps.92.2, then לְהַגִּ֣יד ('to declare', oshb:Ps.92.3) at web:Ps.92.2 = oshb:Ps.92.3 -- with web:Ps.92.3 = oshb:Ps.92.4 as a verbless instrumental extension naming the instruments rather than a fourth infinitive clause, forming one syntactic unit that the causal 'For you, Yahweh' of web:Ps.92.4 breaks off from.
strongest_rejected_alternative: web:Ps.92.4 leaves the infinitive chain of thanksgiving-instructions for a direct second-person address to Yahweh, so extending this row through it was rejected.
observed_substrate_signals: the genre_label_membership inventory records this psalm under both mizmor and shir, matching the title's own two nouns

the psalm's 3 infinitives are לְהֹד֥וֹת/וּלְזַמֵּ֖ר (oshb:Ps.92.2) and לְהַגִּ֣יד (oshb:Ps.92.3); web:Ps.92.3 = oshb:Ps.92.4 (the ten-stringed lute, the harp, the lyre) is verbless, an instrumental extension of that chain rather than a third clause; all 3 verbal/instrumental elements are governed by 'It is a good thing' (web:Ps.92.1)
device_notes: Psalm 92 serves as parent for the rows it contains.

boundary_rationale: web:Ps.92.4 = oshb:Ps.92.5 opens with כִּ֤י שִׂמַּחְתַּ֣נִי יְהוָ֣ה ('for you have made me glad, Yahweh'), a direct second-person address that continues through “How great are your works, Yahweh!” (web:Ps.92.5 = oshb:Ps.92.6); the reflection on Yahweh's works then turns to what the senseless fail to grasp -- that the wicked, though they flourish, will be destroyed forever (web:Ps.92.6 = oshb:Ps.92.7; web:Ps.92.7 = oshb:Ps.92.8) -- before the adversative 'But you' of web:Ps.92.8 resumes direct address.

boundary_rationale: web:Ps.92.8 = oshb:Ps.92.9 opens with the adversative independent pronoun וְאַתָּ֥ה מָר֗וֹם ('but you, on high'), turning back to direct address after the wisdom reflection of vv.6-7; the enemies' perishing (web:Ps.92.9) and the psalmist's own exaltation and anointing (web:Ps.92.10) continue that address; the unit's own close, web:Ps.92.11, drops to first-person report ('my eyes...my ears') without renewing the second-person address, but stays inside the psalmist's own perspective; the fronted, unaddressed subject 'the righteous' at web:Ps.92.12 is what closes off the unit.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the enemies' perishing and exaltation (web:Ps.92.9-Ps.92.10) from the closing first-person report (web:Ps.92.11) was rejected because all 3 verses stay inside the psalmist's own perspective opened at web:Ps.92.8, without a fresh grammatical subject marking a seam until 'the righteous' at web:Ps.92.12.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens “Yahweh reigns!” (web:Ps.93.1), the verb clause יְהוָ֣ה מָלָךְ֮ (oshb:Ps.93.1, 'Yahweh has become king') -- sweep: the skeleton יהוה מלך returns 6 verses book-wide (web:Ps.10.16, web:Ps.29.10, web:Ps.93.1, web:Ps.96.10, web:Ps.97.1, web:Ps.99.1), but the pointed verb מָלָךְ֮ (oshb:Ps.93.1), distinct from the noun מֶ֭לֶךְ (oshb:Ps.10.16, 'king', in 'Yahweh is king forever and ever'), narrows the 6 to 4 verses carrying the verb (web:Ps.93.1, web:Ps.96.10, web:Ps.97.1, web:Ps.99.1: sweep, 4 verses); web:Ps.93.1 precedes the other 3, making this the book's first YHWH-malak proclamation of the 4 (sweep, 4 verses). Five verses carry one continuous enthronement acclamation, from the throne 'established from long ago' (web:Ps.93.2) through the flood's roar (web:Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4) to the closing statement that “Your statutes stand firm.” (web:Ps.93.5); the address pattern forms an envelope across the whole psalm (5 verses): third-person acclamation opens it (מָלָךְ֮, 93:1), second-person address brackets its near side (oshb:Ps.93.2, כִּסְאֲךָ֣/אָֽתָּה), the flood imagery of 93:3-93:4 (2 verses) returns to third-person/impersonal description with no address of its own, and second-person address closes it again (oshb:Ps.93.5, עֵֽדֹתֶ֨יךָ/לְבֵיתְךָ֥) -- one indivisible unit built from that envelope, not from an unbroken absence of address.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the psalm at web:Ps.93.2, separating the enthronement acclamation from the throne's antiquity, was rejected because the second-person address at oshb:Ps.93.2 (אָֽתָּה, an independent pronoun) is answered by the same address class again at the psalm's own close (93:5), an envelope bracketing the whole 5 verses rather than a seam opening a new unit; the flood imagery between them (93:3-93:4) carries no address of its own to mark a break.
observed_substrate_signals: מָלָךְ֮ (oshb:Ps.93.1) is a finite qal perfect verb, opening the psalm before any addressee is named

second-person address to Yahweh brackets the psalm as an envelope -- an independent pronoun at 93:2 (אָֽתָּה, oshb:Ps.93.2) and 2ms suffixes at 93:5 (עֵֽדֹתֶ֨יךָ/לְבֵיתְךָ֥, oshb:Ps.93.5) -- rather than running continuously or being wholly absent; no internal quotation marks a seam
device_notes: The psalm coheres as one composition -- parent grouping Psalm 93.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens with an imperative appeal to the avenging God, אֵל נְקָמ֥וֹת יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.94.1, 'God of vengeance, Yahweh'), continuing in direct address through web:Ps.94.5 (עַמְּךָ֣/וְֽנַחֲלָתְךָ֥, 'your people'/'your heritage', oshb:Ps.94.5); the complaint then turns to third-person description of the wicked's deeds -- oppressing the widow, the foreigner, and the fatherless, named at web:Ps.94.6 -- and closes on their own quoted boast, “Yah will not see, neither will Jacob’s God consider.” (web:Ps.94.7). This seven-verse complaint ends before the imperative rebuke of the 'senseless' opens a new addressee at web:Ps.94.8.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at web:Ps.94.4, where the wicked's arrogant words are named, was rejected because their specific acts (vv.5-6) and their quoted boast (v.7) continue the same complaint without a new addressee or speaker.

boundary_rationale: web:Ps.94.8 opens with the imperative בִּ֭ינוּ בֹּעֲרִ֣ים בָּעָ֑ם (oshb:Ps.94.8, 'consider, you dullards among the people'), addressing the senseless and the fools directly rather than Yahweh -- a wisdom-instruction register distinct from the preceding complaint. The rebuke's rhetorical questions (web:Ps.94.9-Ps.94.10) give way to a beatitude, “Blessed is the man” (web:Ps.94.12), on the man Yahweh disciplines, and the span closes on the promise that judgment 'will return to righteousness' (web:Ps.94.15); the rhetorical 'who' of web:Ps.94.16 then reopens the psalm in the first person, marking this eight-verse wisdom-instruction stretch as the psalm's internal seam between the opening complaint and the closing personal appeal.

boundary_rationale: web:Ps.94.16 reopens the psalm in the first person, “Who will rise up for…” (web:Ps.94.16), a personal testimony -- Yahweh as help (web:Ps.94.17), comfort amid anxious thoughts (web:Ps.94.19) -- that gives way to direct second-person address to Yahweh already running by oshb:Ps.94.18 (חַסְדְּךָ֥ 'your loving kindness') and oshb:Ps.94.19 (תַּ֝נְחוּמֶ֗יךָ 'your comforts') and continuing at web:Ps.94.20's 'throne of wickedness' question, then closes on the psalm's final declaration, “Yahweh, our God, will cut them off.” (web:Ps.94.23). This eight-verse span carries the psalm from personal testimony to its concluding confidence, with no further addressee change strong enough to mark an internal boundary.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this span at web:Ps.94.20, where the address turns back to Yahweh, was rejected because the surrounding first-person testimony (vv.16-19, 22) and the address to Yahweh (v.20) share the same complaint against 'the throne of wickedness' without a change of topic.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens with the imperative לְ֭כוּ נְרַנְּנָ֣ה (oshb:Ps.95.1, 'come, let us sing'), “Oh come, let’s sing to Yahweh.” (web:Ps.95.1), continuing in the same imperative-plural voice with נְקַדְּמָ֣ה (oshb:Ps.95.2, 'let us come before') through “Let’s come before his presence with thanksgiving.” (web:Ps.95.2); the causal 'For' opening web:Ps.95.3 shifts from imperative summons to the grounds for it, closing this two-verse call to worship as one unit.

observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.95.1 and oshb:Ps.95.2 both open with imperative or cohortative-plural forms (לְ֭כוּ, נְקַדְּמָ֣ה), a pairing distinct from web:Ps.95.3's causal opener

boundary_rationale: web:Ps.95.3 opens with the causal כִּ֤י אֵ֣ל גָּד֣וֹל יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.95.3, 'for Yahweh is a great God'), giving the grounds for the preceding summons in a hymn of creation that names the deep places of the earth, the mountain heights (web:Ps.95.4), and “The sea is his, and he made it. His hands formed the dry land.” (web:Ps.95.5); the second imperative 'Oh come, let's worship' at web:Ps.95.6 opens a fresh summons, closing this three-verse causal unit.

device_notes: The creation imagery (deep places, mountains, sea, dry land) is local to this span.

boundary_rationale: web:Ps.95.6 opens a second imperative summons, בֹּ֭אוּ נִשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֣ה (oshb:Ps.95.6, 'come, let us bow down'), “Oh come, let’s worship and bow down.” (web:Ps.95.6), grounded in the covenant self-identification “We are the people of his pasture” (web:Ps.95.7); the verse then pivots on its own closing clause, “Today, oh that you would hear his voice!” (web:Ps.95.7), into the oath-oracle that follows at web:Ps.95.8, closing this two-verse summons-and-pivot unit before Yahweh's own first-person voice opens.

observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.95.6 echoes web:Ps.95.1's opening imperative with a second, distinct verb of coming, pairing the two summonses that bracket the psalm's opening praise
