boundary_rationale: This span is bracketed by the same simile word: “My heart is blighted like grass, and withered, for I forget to eat my bread.” (web:Ps.102.4), whose second word is כָ֭עֵשֶׂב (oshb:Ps.102.5), and “My days are like a long shadow. I have withered like grass.” (web:Ps.102.11), whose second-to-last word is כָּעֵ֥שֶׂב (oshb:Ps.102.12) — the same lexeme עשב bracketing the complaint body, skeleton-matching across the 2 verses (oshb:Ps.102.5, oshb:Ps.102.12). Between the brackets the row moves from bodily affliction (“By reason of the voice of my groaning, my bones stick to my skin.”, web:Ps.102.5) through the paired bird similes (“I am like a pelican of the wilderness. I have become as an owl of the waste places.”, web:Ps.102.6, and “I watch, and have become like a sparrow that is alone on the housetop.”, web:Ps.102.7) to the enemies' reproach (“My enemies reproach me all day. Those who are mad at me use my name as a curse.”, web:Ps.102.8), the ashes-for-bread image (web:Ps.102.9), and the second-person address returning at “because of your indignation and your wrath; for you have taken me up and thrown me away.” (web:Ps.102.10) before the shadow-and-grass close at web:Ps.102.11.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting this span at the pelican/owl/sparrow simile pair (web:Ps.102.6-web:Ps.102.7) into two shorter rows was rejected because it would cut the grass-bracketed unit without any comparable seam signal inside it.
observed_substrate_signals: כָ֭עֵשֶׂב (web:Ps.102.4 = oshb:Ps.102.5) and כָּעֵ֥שֶׂב (web:Ps.102.11 = oshb:Ps.102.12) share the consonantal root עשב, bracketing the span
second-person address is absent across web:Ps.102.3-web:Ps.102.9 (seven verses) and returns at web:Ps.102.10, inside this row's own close
device_notes: This row is the individual-lament movement's body, framed by the grass inclusio (web:Ps.102.4, web:Ps.102.11) inside one row rather than split across the seam.

boundary_rationale: The row opens on the tier-1 adversative and addressee pivot, “But you, Yahweh, will remain forever; your renown endures to all generations.” (web:Ps.102.12), whose Hebrew opens וְאַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.102.13) — a conjunctive vav plus the independent second-person pronoun אתה that readdresses Yahweh directly in the second person after web:Ps.102.3-web:Ps.102.9 (seven verses) run without it, the address returning briefly at web:Ps.102.10 before this row's own return at web:Ps.102.12. The turn opens the Zion oracle: “You will arise and have mercy on Zion, for it is time to have pity on her. Yes, the set time has come.” (web:Ps.102.13), the servants' pleasure “For your servants take pleasure in her stones, and have pity on her dust.” (web:Ps.102.14), the nations' fear of Yahweh's name (web:Ps.102.15), and the report “For Yahweh has built up Zion. He has appeared in his glory.” (web:Ps.102.16; byte: כִּֽי בָנָ֣ה יְהוָ֣ה צִיּ֑וֹן נִ֝רְאָ֗ה בִּכְבוֹדֽוֹ, oshb:Ps.102.17), which opens an asyndetic completed-action chain that continues without a break through “He has responded to the prayer of the destitute, and has not despised their prayer.” (web:Ps.102.17; oshb:Ps.102.18); the genuine register break -- a new subject and the non-completed verb תִּכָּ֣תֶב (oshb:Ps.102.19) -- sits one verse later, at the seam 102:17|102:18, so this row closes on the rebuilding-and-response half of that chain.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through web:Ps.102.22 as one continuous Zion-oracle block was rejected: the asyndetic completed-action chain opened at web:Ps.102.16 runs on, without a causal-particle break, through web:Ps.102.17; the row is closed here on topical grounds -- the rebuilding-and-response report -- while the chain's own grammatical break falls one verse later, at 102:17|102:18.
observed_substrate_signals: וְאַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה (web:Ps.102.12 = oshb:Ps.102.13) pairs the conjunctive vav with the independent pronoun אתה, a stronger contrastive marking than a bare vav
device_notes: The Zion-restoration movement (web:Ps.102.12-web:Ps.102.22) begins here; this row covers its rebuilding half.

boundary_rationale: The row opens with the closing member of the rebuilding-and-response chain begun at the seam 102:16|102:17, “He has responded to the prayer of the destitute, and has not despised their prayer.” (web:Ps.102.17; byte: פָּ֭נָה אֶל תְּפִלַּ֣ת הָעַרְעָ֑ר וְלֹֽא בָ֝זָ֗ה אֶת תְּפִלָּתָֽם, oshb:Ps.102.18), an asyndetic continuation with no causal particle of its own; the genuine register break -- a new subject ('this'/'a people') and the non-completed verb תִּכָּ֣תֶב (oshb:Ps.102.19) -- sits at this row's own next seam, 102:17|102:18, opening the forward-looking purpose clause “This will be written for the generation to come. A people which will be created will praise Yah,” (web:Ps.102.18); the sanctuary vantage “for he has looked down from the height of his sanctuary. From heaven, Yahweh saw the earth,” (web:Ps.102.19) opens onto the prisoner's release (web:Ps.102.20) and the proclamation “that men may declare Yahweh’s name in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem,” (web:Ps.102.21), closing on “when the peoples are gathered together, the kingdoms, to serve Yahweh.” (web:Ps.102.22).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Grouping web:Ps.102.17 with the preceding rebuilding report (web:Ps.102.12-web:Ps.102.16) was rejected because the purpose clause at web:Ps.102.18 opens a distinct forward-looking movement that this row keeps intact through its close at web:Ps.102.22.
observed_substrate_signals: the purpose clause at web:Ps.102.18 ('this will be written for the generation to come') marks a future-oriented register shift from the completed-action report closing web:Ps.102.16
device_notes: This row completes the Zion-restoration movement opened at web:Ps.102.12, closing on the nations gathered to serve Yahweh before web:Ps.102.23 returns to the psalmist's own voice.

boundary_rationale: The row returns abruptly to the psalmist's own voice, “He weakened my strength along the course. He shortened my days.” (web:Ps.102.23), reopening the first-person complaint that closed at web:Ps.102.11 and that the intervening Zion oracle (web:Ps.102.12-web:Ps.102.22) had set aside; MT web:Ps.102.23 (oshb:Ps.102.24) carries a ketiv כחו against a qere כֹּחִ֗י (pmarks_Ps.json kq), disclosed here though this row's boundary does not depend on either reading. The direct petition “I said, “My God, don’t take me away in the middle of my days. Your years are throughout all generations.” (web:Ps.102.24) turns at web:Ps.102.25 to creation theology, “Of old, you laid the foundation of the earth. The heavens are the work of your hands.” (byte: לְ֭פָנִים הָאָ֣רֶץ יָסַ֑דְתָּ וּֽמַעֲשֵׂ֖ה יָדֶ֣יךָ שָׁמָֽיִם, oshb:Ps.102.26), and closes on the contrast between what perishes and what endures, “They will perish, but you will endure. Yes, all of them will wear out like a garment. You will change them like a cloak, and they will be changed.” (web:Ps.102.26), “But you are the same. Your years will have no end.” (web:Ps.102.27), and the hope “The children of your servants will continue. Their offspring will be established before you.”” (web:Ps.102.28).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading web:Ps.102.23-web:Ps.102.24 as a continuation of the Zion oracle was rejected because the first-person pronouns reopen the psalmist's own complaint voice that the Zion oracle (web:Ps.102.12-web:Ps.102.22) had set aside; that oracle is third-person-only only across its stretch web:Ps.102.16-web:Ps.102.22 (MT 102:17-102:23, 7 verses), since its own opening verses (web:Ps.102.12-web:Ps.102.15) carry direct second-person address to Yahweh (וְאַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה, oshb:Ps.102.13; אַתָּ֣ה, oshb:Ps.102.14; עֲ֭בָדֶיךָ, oshb:Ps.102.15; כְּבוֹדֶֽךָ, oshb:Ps.102.16).
observed_substrate_signals: MT oshb:Ps.102.24 carries a ketiv/qere pair כחו כֹּחִ֗י inside this row's span (web:Ps.102.23), matching pmarks_Ps.json's kq entry for this verse
device_notes: This row closes Psalm 102, moving from the psalmist's shortened days (web:Ps.102.23) through the earth's foundation (web:Ps.102.25) to the enduring servants' line (web:Ps.102.28).

boundary_rationale: The title “By David.” (web:Ps.103.0) sits as the prefix לְדָוִ֨ד of MT v.1 (oshb:Ps.103.1) rather than a separate counted verse — an identity-psalm title, still tier-1 opener evidence. The psalm opens on the self-summons “Praise Yahweh, my soul! All that is within me, praise his holy name!” (web:Ps.103.1), whose Hebrew clause בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי אֶת יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.103.1) the psalm's own close will echo; “Praise Yahweh, my soul, and don’t forget all his benefits,” (web:Ps.103.2) turns the summons into a catalog, itemized across “who forgives all your sins, who heals all your diseases,” (web:Ps.103.3), “who redeems your life from destruction, who crowns you with loving kindness and tender mercies,” (web:Ps.103.4), as well as “who satisfies your desire with good things, so that your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.” (web:Ps.103.5), continuing the second-person address to the summoned soul.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Starting the row at web:Ps.103.2 and treating web:Ps.103.1 as title-adjacent overflow was rejected because the barchi-nafshi clause already appears in web:Ps.103.1 itself, not merely in the title.
observed_substrate_signals: the title word לְדָוִ֨ד (oshb:Ps.103.1) sits inside MT v.1 with no separate title verse number, matching the identity-psalm numbering rule
device_notes: The parent unit here is the full Psalm 103. Its opening and closing clauses (web:Ps.103.1, web:Ps.103.22) form the barchi-nafshi inclusio that frames the whole psalm; this row carries the inclusio's opening half.

boundary_rationale: The row's grammatical subject shifts from the summoned soul to Yahweh himself: “Yahweh executes righteous acts, and justice for all who are oppressed.” (web:Ps.103.6) opens with the participle עֹשֵׂ֣ה צְדָק֣וֹת (oshb:Ps.103.6), moving from second-person imperative address (web:Ps.103.1-web:Ps.103.5) to third-person declaration; “He made known his ways to Moses, his deeds to the children of Israel.” (web:Ps.103.7) grounds the declaration historically before the row states Yahweh's own character, “Yahweh is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness.” (web:Ps.103.8), and closes on the negated-accusation pair “He will not always accuse; neither will he stay angry forever.” (web:Ps.103.9) and “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us for our iniquities.” (web:Ps.103.10).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Keeping web:Ps.103.6 with the preceding catalog (web:Ps.103.1-web:Ps.103.5) was rejected because the shift from second-person imperative address to third-person declaration about Yahweh marks a distinct discourse register.
observed_substrate_signals: עֹשֵׂ֣ה צְדָק֣וֹת (oshb:Ps.103.6) is a participial third-person predicate, unlike the second-person imperative clause בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי אֶת יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.103.1)
device_notes: This row opens the chesed catalog's declarative half, restating in the third person what the second-person summons of web:Ps.103.1-web:Ps.103.5 addressed to the soul.

boundary_rationale: A three-verse correlative tricolon opens the row's second movement: “For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is his loving kindness toward those who fear him.” (web:Ps.103.11) — Hebrew כִּ֤י כִגְבֹ֣הַּ שָׁ֭מַיִם (oshb:Ps.103.11), where כִּ֤י is a plain causal/asseverative particle and the comparison itself is carried by the kaf-prefix on כִגְבֹ֣הַּ — continues through “As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our transgressions from us.” (web:Ps.103.12) and “Like a father has compassion on his children, so Yahweh has compassion on those who fear him.” (web:Ps.103.13); the row then turns from simile to ground, “For he knows how we are made. He remembers that we are dust.” (web:Ps.103.14), whose own second כִּי (oshb:Ps.103.14, כִּי עָפָ֥ר אֲנָֽחְנוּ) is complementizing, governed by זָ֝כ֗וּר ('he remembers that'), not causal -- the dust motif that hinges into the transience movement of web:Ps.103.15-web:Ps.103.16.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Placing web:Ps.103.14 with the transience movement that follows (web:Ps.103.15-web:Ps.103.16) was rejected because its verb still has Yahweh as subject, matching the compassion-simile chain rather than the new grammatical subject, man, that opens web:Ps.103.15.
observed_substrate_signals: כִּ֤י כִגְבֹ֣הַּ שָׁ֭מַיִם (oshb:Ps.103.11) opens with a causal/asseverative כִּ֤י -- the comparison itself is carried by the kaf-prefix on כִגְבֹ֣הַּ, not by כִּ֤י -- and כִּי עָפָ֥ר אֲנָֽחְנוּ (oshb:Ps.103.14) repeats the particle in a complementizing use (governed by זָ֝כ֗וּר), neither instance a fresh simile marker
device_notes: The dust motif closing this row (web:Ps.103.14) hinges toward the grass-and-flower transience imagery of web:Ps.103.15-web:Ps.103.16 without changing grammatical subject.

boundary_rationale: The subject changes to man at the row's opening, “As for man, his days are like grass. As a flower of the field, so he flourishes.” (web:Ps.103.15), continued by the wind image “For the wind passes over it, and it is gone. Its place remembers it no more.” (web:Ps.103.16); the vav-initial clause “But Yahweh’s loving kindness is from everlasting to everlasting with those who fear him, his righteousness to children’s children,” (web:Ps.103.17), Hebrew וְחֶ֤סֶד יְהוָ֨ה (oshb:Ps.103.17, a construct chain in which Yahweh (יְהוָ֨ה) is the possessor / nomen rectum, and the vav-prefixed וְחֶ֤סֶד ('lovingkindness') is the grammatical subject) — a plainer conjunctive-vav contrast than the emphatic pronoun-plus-vav pivot at web:Ps.102.12, but still legible against the transience just described — turns from man's transience back to Yahweh's own loving kindness as subject and closes the row on the covenant-keepers of “to those who keep his covenant, to those who remember to obey his precepts.” (web:Ps.103.18).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.103.17's vav-clause as a return to the preceding compassion-simile row (web:Ps.103.11-web:Ps.103.14) was rejected because it answers the intervening transience description (web:Ps.103.15-web:Ps.103.16), not the simile chain three verses earlier.
observed_substrate_signals: וְחֶ֤סֶד יְהוָ֨ה (oshb:Ps.103.17) opens with a plain conjunctive vav on חסד, weaker than the vav-plus-pronoun construction וְאַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה at oshb:Ps.102.13
device_notes: This row's transience-to-chesed pivot (web:Ps.103.15-web:Ps.103.17) parallels in shape, though not in Hebrew grammatical force, the adversative turn at web:Ps.102.12.

boundary_rationale: The row opens on the enthronement declaration “Yahweh has established his throne in the heavens. His kingdom rules over all.” (web:Ps.103.19), Hebrew יְֽהוָ֗ה בַּ֭שָּׁמַיִם הֵכִ֣ין (oshb:Ps.103.19), then widens the imperative ‘praise Yahweh’ from the soul addressed at web:Ps.103.1-web:Ps.103.2 outward to the angels, “Praise Yahweh, you angels of his, who are mighty in strength, who fulfill his word, obeying the voice of his word.” (web:Ps.103.20), Hebrew בָּרֲכ֥וּ יְהוָ֗ה (oshb:Ps.103.20) — a plural imperative, unlike the singular בָּרֲכִ֣י (oshb:Ps.103.1) addressed to the soul — then to his armies and his works (web:Ps.103.21-web:Ps.103.22) before the row's own closing clause, “Praise Yahweh, all you works of his, in all places of his dominion. Praise Yahweh, my soul!” (web:Ps.103.22), returns to the singular imperative and to the clause the psalm opened with. That closing clause, Hebrew בָּרֲכִ֥י נַ֝פְשִׁ֗י אֶת יְהוָֽה (oshb:Ps.103.22), matches the opening clause בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי אֶת יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.103.1) only at the skeleton tier across the 2 verses (oshb:Ps.103.1, oshb:Ps.103.22): 3 of the clause's 4 words differ across 4 accent codepoints (word 1 munah/merkha; word 2 dehi/geresh-muqdam+revia; word 4 etnachta/meteg), so the match is claimed at the skeleton tier, not the byte tier.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading web:Ps.103.22 as belonging with the cosmic-praise catalog of web:Ps.103.20-web:Ps.103.21 without separately flagging its closing clause was rejected because that clause repeats the psalm's own opening words and closes the inclusio opened at web:Ps.103.1.
observed_substrate_signals: בָּרֲכ֥וּ יְהוָ֗ה (oshb:Ps.103.20) is a plural imperative addressed to the angels, contrasting with the singular בָּרֲכִ֣י (oshb:Ps.103.1, oshb:Ps.103.22) addressed to the soul

the closing clause (oshb:Ps.103.22) matches the opening clause (oshb:Ps.103.1) at the skeleton tier across the 2 verses; 3 of 4 words differ across 4 accent codepoints (word 1 munah/merkha; word 2 dehi/geresh-muqdam+revia; word 4 etnachta/meteg)
device_notes: This row closes the barchi-nafshi inclusio opened at web:Ps.103.1, completing Psalm 103's parent grouping; the angelic call-to-bless (web:Ps.103.20-web:Ps.103.21) widens the summons before the closing return to my soul.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens with the imperative inclusio that frames it, “Bless Yahweh, my soul” (web:Ps.104.1), with the Hebrew 'בָּרֲכִ֥י נַפְשִׁ֗י' at oshb:Ps.104.1; the address then turns to second-person praise of Yahweh’s robing in light before shifting to third-person description of the heavens stretched “like a curtain” (web:Ps.104.2), the waters-roofed chambers and cloud-chariot (web:Ps.104.3), and the wind/fire messengers (web:Ps.104.4). This four-verse unit covers the robing-in-light and sky-building movement before the earth itself becomes the subject at 104:5.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 104:5 (the earth’s foundation) was considered, but 104:5 introduces a new created object (the earth, not the heavens) under a new governing verb, marking a fresh movement rather than a continuation of the sky-building imagery.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative inclusio opener 'בָּרֲכִ֥י נַפְשִׁ֗י' (oshb:Ps.104.1, tier: byte)
movement covers robing/light, heavens-as-curtain, water-chambers, cloud-chariot, wind/fire messengers (104:2-4)
the governing subject shifts from the heavens (104:2-4) to the earth (104:5), tier-1 topic seam
device_notes: Psalm 104 stands as one liturgical composition, spanning web:Ps.104.1 through web:Ps.104.35. The opening 'בָּרֲכִ֥י נַפְשִׁ֗י' (oshb:Ps.104.1) recurs at the accent_stripped/skeleton tier at the psalm's own close (oshb:Ps.104.35) as its inclusio (byte tier differs: word 1 merkha at 104:1 vs munach at 104:35; word 2 revia at 104:1 vs dehi at 104:35); the identical phrase also frames the preceding psalm as its own opener and closer — sweep: 5 verses book-wide carry the skeleton 'ברכי נפשי', three of them outside this psalm — a typed cross-psalm relation (shared inclusio phrasing), never a merged row or shared authorship claim.

boundary_rationale: A new creative act opens the unit: “He laid the foundations of the earth” (web:Ps.104.5) — the Hebrew reads 'יָֽסַד אֶ֭רֶץ' (oshb:Ps.104.5) — governed by the verb 'יָֽסַד' (roughly 'founded') rather than the stretching/covering verbs of 104:2-4. The unit then narrates the primeval waters standing above the mountains (web:Ps.104.6), fleeing “At your rebuke” and “the voice of your thunder” (web:Ps.104.7), the mountains rising and valleys sinking (web:Ps.104.8), and closes on the fixed boundary set so the waters “may not pass over” and “don't turn again to cover the earth” (web:Ps.104.9).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 104:8 and folding the boundary clause (104:9) into the following springs unit was considered, but 104:9’s “that they may not pass over” (web:Ps.104.9) completes the waters-in-retreat action begun at 104:6-7, not the springs-in-the-valleys topic that opens fresh at 104:10.
observed_substrate_signals: governing verb shifts from participial sky-building (104:2-4) to perfect 'יָֽסַד' 'founded' (104:5, oshb:Ps.104.5), tier-1 topic seam

second-person address to Yahweh (2ms suffix/verb forms: 'your rebuke' at 104:7, 'you set' at 104:9) runs alongside the primeval waters' own 3rd-person plural action sequence (flee, retreat, boundary-set) across 104:6-9

boundary_rationale: The topic turns from the sea’s retreat to fresh water given: “He sends springs into the valleys” (web:Ps.104.10), matching 'הַֽמְשַׁלֵּ֣חַ מַ֭עְיָנִים' at oshb:Ps.104.10 -- opening a water-provision sequence that runs as one topic through animals drinking at these springs (web:Ps.104.11), birds nesting and singing by them (web:Ps.104.12), and closes with Yahweh watering the mountains “from his rooms” so “The earth is filled with the fruit of your works” (web:Ps.104.13).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running 104:10-13 together with the vegetation catalogue of 104:14-18 as one long unit was considered, but 104:14 opens with its own new participial verb ('מַצְמִ֤יחַ', roughly 'causing to sprout,' oshb:Ps.104.14) governing plant growth, a distinct topic from the springs/mountain-watering of 104:10-13.
observed_substrate_signals: the participial verb 'הַֽמְשַׁלֵּ֣חַ' opening the unit (104:10, oshb:Ps.104.10) shares its mem-preformative participial shape with 104:13 inside this row's own span, so it does not alone discriminate the seam
unit runs springs → animal drink → bird nesting → mountain-watering as one water-provision sequence

boundary_rationale: A second participial verb opens a new movement: “He causes the grass to grow” (web:Ps.104.14), whose Hebrew is 'מַצְמִ֤יחַ חָצִ֨יר' (oshb:Ps.104.14), governing vegetation rather than water. The catalogue runs through wine, oil, and bread “that strengthens man's heart” (web:Ps.104.15), the well-watered cedars of Lebanon “which he has planted” (web:Ps.104.16), nesting birds and the stork’s home in the cypress trees (web:Ps.104.17), and closes with the high mountains for wild goats and the rocks as “a refuge for the rock badgers” (web:Ps.104.18).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the human provisions (104:14-15) from the tree/animal habitat material (104:16-18) as two rows was considered, but neither stretch addresses anyone, and both develop the same unbroken habitat-and-provision topic opened by 'מַצְמִ֤יחַ' (oshb:Ps.104.14) -- even though 104:16 opens its own finite verb, יִ֭שְׂבְּעוּ (oshb:Ps.104.16), governing a new subject (the trees), rather than continuing 104:14's participle.
observed_substrate_signals: new participial verb 'מַצְמִ֤יחַ' opens the unit (104:14, oshb:Ps.104.14), tier-2 topic seam
catalogue moves from cultivated food (14-15) to wild trees and their animal residents (16-18) within one vegetation topic

boundary_rationale: The topic turns to the luminaries: “He appointed the moon for seasons” (web:Ps.104.19), rendering 'עָשָׂ֣ה יָ֭רֵחַ לְמוֹעֲדִ֑ים' (oshb:Ps.104.19), a perfect verb ('עָשָׂ֣ה', roughly 'he made') that opens the day/night movement. Darkness and the forest’s prowling animals follow (web:Ps.104.20), young lions roaring for prey “from God” (web:Ps.104.21), the sun’s rising and the lions’ retreat to their dens (web:Ps.104.22), and the unit closes on man going out “to his labor until the evening” (web:Ps.104.23), completing the diurnal cycle the moon and sun opened.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 104:22 (the lions’ retreat) and giving man’s labor its own one-verse row was considered, but 104:23 completes the same night-to-day handoff opened at 104:20 rather than starting an independent topic.
observed_substrate_signals: new perfect verb 'עָשָׂ֣ה' opens the luminaries topic (104:19, oshb:Ps.104.19), tier-2 topic seam
unit alternates night (20-21) and day (22-23) actors around the sun/moon appointment, one diurnal-cycle movement

boundary_rationale: A vocative-plus-exclamation in direct address opens the unit — a new rhetorical form, though not a new grammatical person, since second-person address to Yahweh is already continuous immediately before (104:20) and continues inside this row's own span (104:24, 104:26): “Yahweh, how many are your works!” (web:Ps.104.24), collated to 'מָֽה רַבּ֬וּ מַעֲשֶׂ֨יךָ יְֽהוָ֗ה' (oshb:Ps.104.24). “The earth is full of your riches” leads into the sea catalogue: “There is the sea, great and wide” (web:Ps.104.25), with ships and “leviathan, whom you formed to play there” (web:Ps.104.26), set against 'לִ֝וְיָתָ֗ן' (oshb:Ps.104.26).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running 104:24-30 together as one providence unit was considered, but 104:27 opens with the collective pronoun 'כֻּ֭לָּם' (roughly 'the whole of them,' oshb:Ps.104.27) turning the address from the sea’s specific inhabitants to creation’s general dependence, a distinct referential class from the sea catalogue of 104:24-26.
observed_substrate_signals: direct-address vocative-plus-exclamation opens the unit (104:24); the grammatical person itself is unbroken (2ms address to Yahweh continues from 104:20 through 104:24 and 104:26), so the new element is the rhetorical form, not a shift from third-person description
sea catalogue (104:25-26) is a self-contained topic bounded by the exclamation before it and the collective-pronoun pickup after it
device_notes: WEB renders the sea creature at 104:26 as lowercase “leviathan” (byte-tier reading of the clean WEB text, not a title or proper-name capitalization); sweep: 2 verses book-wide carry the skeleton 'לויתן' (oshb:Ps.104.26), one other occurrence sitting outside this psalm.

boundary_rationale: The collective pronoun כֻּ֭לָּם opens this unit's clause, “These all wait for you” (web:Ps.104.27; oshb:Ps.104.27, כֻּ֭לָּם אֵלֶ֣יךָ יְשַׂבֵּר֑וּן) -- the identical pointed form כֻּ֭לָּם already occurs at 104:24, inside the preceding row's own span, referring there to Yahweh's works broadly; the recurrence does not itself mark the seam, since the 2nd-person addressee (Yahweh) is unbroken from 104:24 through this row's own close at 104:30. What changes at 104:27 is the 3rd-person referent -- from the sea's named inhabitants to creation's general dependence -- run through a sustained second-person cluster: “You give… You open your hand” (web:Ps.104.28), “You hide your face… You take away their breath” (web:Ps.104.29), plus “You send out your Spirit… You renew the face of the ground” (web:Ps.104.30), which closes the providence movement before the doxological response opens at 104:31.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 104:31 was considered, but 104:31 shifts to jussive mode ('יְהִ֤י', roughly 'let there be,' oshb:Ps.104.31) petitioning on Yahweh’s behalf, a distinct grammatical mood from the second-person description of divine action in 104:27-30.
observed_substrate_signals: collective pronoun 'כֻּ֭לָּם' opens the unit (104:27, oshb:Ps.104.27) -- byte-identical to the same pointed form already used at 104:24, inside the preceding row's own span -- marking a third-person-referent shift (from named sea creatures to creation broadly), not an addressee-class shift, since the 2nd-person addressee (Yahweh) is unbroken from 104:24 through 104:30
sustained 2nd-person give/open/hide/take/send/renew verb cluster runs 104:28-30 as one providence-and-mortality sequence

boundary_rationale: The mode shifts to jussive petition: “Let Yahweh's glory endure forever” (web:Ps.104.31), the Hebrew 'יְהִ֤י כְב֣וֹד יְהוָ֣ה לְעוֹלָ֑ם' at oshb:Ps.104.31, a grammatical break from the second-person description preceding it. Third-person description of Yahweh’s power returns at 104:32, then the psalmist’s own first-person vow opens at “I will sing to Yahweh as long as I live” (web:Ps.104.33); the Hebrew 'אָשִׁ֣ירָה' underlies it at oshb:Ps.104.33, and continues through 104:34, before the unit closes with a wish against sinners, the psalm’s own inclusio — “Bless Yahweh, my soul” (web:Ps.104.35), in Hebrew 'בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי' (oshb:Ps.104.35) — and the hallelu-Yah that ends the psalm: 'הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ' (oshb:Ps.104.35).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the closing doxology (104:31-32) from the first-person vow and final wish (104:33-35) as two rows was considered, but no selah or addressee-class break separates them, and the inclusio at 104:35 answers the imperative that opened the whole psalm at 104:1, tying the closing movement together as one unit.
observed_substrate_signals: jussive mode 'יְהִ֤י' opens the doxological turn (104:31, oshb:Ps.104.31), grammatical mood shift from the preceding second-person providence cluster
first-person vow ('אָשִׁ֣ירָה', oshb:Ps.104.33) opens at 104:33, a further register shift within the same unit

inclusio 'בָּרֲכִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי' (oshb:Ps.104.35) closes the unit, matching the psalm's opening 'בָּרֲכִ֥י נַפְשִׁ֗י' (oshb:Ps.104.1) at accent_stripped/skeleton tier (byte tier differs: word 1 merkha at 104:1 vs munach at 104:35, word 2 revia at 104:1 vs dehi at 104:35), then hallelu-Yah closes the psalm verse-finally
device_notes: Psalm 104 closes with 'הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ' (oshb:Ps.104.35), the earliest by psalm order among the curated hallelu-Yah frame inventory’s 25 book-wide occurrences (psalm_device_inventory.json: sweep: 11 verse-initial + 13 verse-final + 1 interior = 25); a naive skeleton substring sweep for 'הללו יה' returns 26 hits because it also matches the imperfect verb 'yehalelu' ('they will praise') run directly into the start of the divine name at oshb:Ps.22.27 — a consonantal false positive, not a hallelu-Yah particle; the curated inventory, not the naive sweep, is the count of record. As texture: of the two psalms following in this cluster, Ps 105 opens with the hodu-le-YHWH formula (not hallelu-Yah) and closes with hallelu-Yah only (web:Ps.105.45); only Ps 106 genuinely both opens (web:Ps.106.1) and closes (web:Ps.106.48) with the hallelu-Yah frame — texture, not evidence bearing on this row's own close.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens with the verse-initial hodu-le-YHWH call: “Give thanks to Yahweh!” (web:Ps.105.1), with the Hebrew 'הוֹד֣וּ לַ֭יהוָה' at oshb:Ps.105.1, a tier-1 opener device (psalm_device_inventory.json hodu_openings). The imperative cluster continues: “Call on his name” (web:Ps.105.1), “Sing to him, sing praises to him” (web:Ps.105.2), “Glory in his holy name” (web:Ps.105.3), “Seek Yahweh and his strength” (web:Ps.105.4), and also “Remember his marvelous works” (web:Ps.105.5), before the unit closes addressing “you offspring of Abraham… you children of Jacob, his chosen ones” (web:Ps.105.6), naming the addressees the historical recital that follows will retell.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 105:5 (its final imperative) and giving the vocative “offspring of Abraham” (web:Ps.105.6) its own row was considered, but 105:6 is the vocative addressee of 105:5’s “remember,” not its grammatical object, so splitting it would sever the imperative from its addressee.
observed_substrate_signals: verse-initial hodu-le-YHWH opener ('הוֹד֣וּ לַ֭יהוָה', 105:1, oshb:Ps.105.1), tier-1 device per the frame inventory
sustained imperative-cluster mode runs 105:1-6 (give thanks, call, sing, glory, seek, remember), closing on the vocative addressee it governs
device_notes: Psalm 105 coheres as one composition — parent grouping Psalm 105; every row below shares that single parent. The historical recital moves covenant → Joseph → Egypt/plagues → exodus → settlement across the rows that follow.

boundary_rationale: A declarative statement opens the unit with its own independent pronoun: “He is Yahweh, our God” (web:Ps.105.7) — the Hebrew reads 'ה֭וּא יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵ֑ינוּ' (oshb:Ps.105.7) — turning from the imperative calls of 105:1-6 to covenant declaration. “He has remembered his covenant forever” (web:Ps.105.8) names “the covenant which he made with Abraham, his oath to Isaac” (web:Ps.105.9), matching 'לְיִשְׂחָֽק' at oshb:Ps.105.9, confirmed “to Jacob… to Israel” (web:Ps.105.10), and closes with the land grant quoted in direct speech: “To you I will give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance” (web:Ps.105.11).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 105:10 and giving the quoted land grant (105:11) its own row was considered, but 105:11’s “saying” clause is the direct object of 105:8-10’s covenant-remembering, not a new speech act beginning a fresh unit.
observed_substrate_signals: independent-pronoun declaration 'ה֭וּא' opens the unit (105:7, oshb:Ps.105.7), a subject-class shift from the imperative mode of 105:1-6
covenant chain runs patriarch-by-patriarch (Abraham 105:9, Jacob/Israel 105:10) to its quoted land-grant close (105:11)
device_notes: The oath “to Isaac” (web:Ps.105.9) at 105:9 is spelled 'לְיִשְׂחָֽק' (oshb:Ps.105.9) with sin rather than the standard tzade; a skeleton sweep of the lamed-prefixed spelling as quoted ('לישחק') returns 1 verse book-wide (105:9 only), while a skeleton sweep of the bare-root spelling (ישחק, lamed stripped) returns 4 verses book-wide (Ps.2.4, Ps.37.13, Ps.52.6, Ps.105.9) — the other three are the common verb 'he will laugh' (root s-h-q), a consonantal homograph found elsewhere in the Psalter; a skeleton sweep for the standard tzade spelling returns 0 verses book-wide, so 105:9 is the Psalter’s one occurrence of Isaac’s name, and it carries the alternate spelling.

boundary_rationale: A temporal clause opens the narrative proper: “when they were but a few men in number” (web:Ps.105.12), whose Hebrew is 'בִּֽ֭הְיוֹתָם מְתֵ֣י מִסְפָּ֑ר' (oshb:Ps.105.12), shifting from covenant declaration to the patriarchs’ own wandering. “They went about from nation to nation” (web:Ps.105.13) and Yahweh “reproved kings for their sakes” (web:Ps.105.14), closing on the quoted royal warning: “Don't touch my anointed ones! Do my prophets no harm!” (web:Ps.105.15), rendering 'אַֽל תִּגְּע֥וּ בִמְשִׁיחָ֑י' (oshb:Ps.105.15).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 105:16 was considered, but 105:16 opens with a wayyiqtol narrative verb ('וַיִּקְרָ֣א', roughly 'and he called,' oshb:Ps.105.16) beginning the famine that triggers the Joseph narrative, a new narrative-sequence link rather than a continuation of the royal-protection material.
observed_substrate_signals: temporal clause 'בִּֽ֭הְיוֹתָם' opens the unit (105:12, oshb:Ps.105.12), a narrative-time shift into the patriarchal period
unit closes on quoted divine speech protecting “my anointed ones” / “my prophets” (105:15, web:Ps.105.15)

boundary_rationale: A wayyiqtol narrative verb opens the Joseph story: “He called for a famine on the land” (web:Ps.105.16), collated to 'וַיִּקְרָ֣א רָ֭עָב' (oshb:Ps.105.16). “He sent a man before them. Joseph was sold for a slave” (web:Ps.105.17), set against 'יוֹסֵֽף' (oshb:Ps.105.17), his feet bruised “with shackles” (web:Ps.105.18) until “Yahweh's word proved him true” (web:Ps.105.19), the king’s release of him (web:Ps.105.20), his rule over the royal house (web:Ps.105.21), and the unit closes with Joseph’s authority “to discipline his princes… and to teach his elders wisdom” (web:Ps.105.22).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting Joseph’s imprisonment (105:17-19) from his exaltation (105:20-22) as two rows was considered, but both develop one reversal-of-fortune narrative arc, with no wayyiqtol restart marking a break before 105:23; the arc runs to its close at 105:22, and only the wayyiqtol at 105:23 opens the next unit, corporate Israel’s entry into Egypt.
observed_substrate_signals: wayyiqtol narrative verb 'וַיִּקְרָ֣א' opens the unit (105:16, oshb:Ps.105.16), narrative-sequence link distinct from the temporal clause of 105:12

the reversal-of-fortune arc (enslaved, tested, then exalted) runs unbroken from Joseph’s sale (105:17) through his rule (105:20-22), with no wayyiqtol restart marking a break until 105:23 opens the next unit
device_notes: A ketiv/qere note sits at oshb:Ps.105.18 (pmarks_Ps.json kq) on the word rendered “his feet” (web:Ps.105.18) / 'his foot'; not quoted here, disclosed because the span crosses it.

boundary_rationale: A new wayyiqtol verb introduces a new named subject: “Israel also came into Egypt” (web:Ps.105.23) — MT reads 'וַיָּבֹ֣א יִשְׂרָאֵ֣ל מִצְרָ֑יִם' (oshb:Ps.105.23) — turning from Joseph individually to Israel corporately. “He increased his people greatly” (web:Ps.105.24) and “turned their heart to hate his people” (web:Ps.105.25) set up the oppression that “He sent Moses, his servant, and Aaron” answers (web:Ps.105.26), the Hebrew 'שָׁ֭לַח מֹשֶׁ֣ה עַבְדּ֑וֹ' at oshb:Ps.105.26; the unit closes with Moses and Aaron performing “miracles among them, and wonders in the land of Ham” (web:Ps.105.27), the general statement the plague catalogue itemizes from 105:28.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through the whole nine-verse plague list was considered, but 105:28 opens the itemized catalogue proper with its own perfect verb ('שָׁ֣לַֽח', roughly 'he sent [darkness],' oshb:Ps.105.28 — a ketiv/qere note sits later in this verse per pmarks_Ps.json kq, not quoted here), where 105:27 still speaks in the general terms (“miracles… wonders”, web:Ps.105.27) that the catalogue then specifies.
observed_substrate_signals: new wayyiqtol verb with new named subject Israel opens the unit (105:23), narrative-subject shift from Joseph
unit runs population growth → oppression → the sending of Moses/Aaron → a general miracles/wonders statement that the following catalogue itemizes
device_notes: The plague sequence itemized from 105:28 (darkness, blood, frogs, insects, hail, locusts, and the death of the “firstborn”) covers 7 of the traditional plagues and omits the livestock-pestilence and boils material present in this psalm's own catalogue by their absence; a cross-book relation to Exodus’s narrative noted as texture, not boundary authority for these rows.

boundary_rationale: The plague catalogue opens: “He sent darkness, and made it dark” (web:Ps.105.28); the Hebrew 'שָׁ֣לַֽח חֹ֭שֶׁךְ' underlies it at oshb:Ps.105.28 (a ketiv/qere note sits later in this verse per pmarks_Ps.json kq, not quoted here), opening a plague disruption group: waters “turned… into blood” killing the fish (web:Ps.105.29), the land “swarmed with frogs, even in the rooms of their kings” (web:Ps.105.30), and “swarms of flies… and lice in all their borders” (web:Ps.105.31), which closes the group before the destruction-class plagues open at 105:32.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating the full plague list as one nine-verse unit was considered as the more conservative reading of one unbroken catalogue, but the darkness/blood/frogs/insects group (105:28-31) is closed by “all their borders” (web:Ps.105.31), while the hail/locusts/“firstborn” group that follows escalates toward the climactic strike — the split is a content grouping inside one catalogue, not a strong grammatical break, and is held at medium confidence for that reason.
observed_substrate_signals: disruption group opens with 'שָׁ֣לַֽח חֹ֭שֶׁךְ' (105:28, oshb:Ps.105.28; a ketiv/qere note sits later in this verse per pmarks_Ps.json kq, not quoted here), spanning 4 verses (105:28-31) but 5 plague nouns under 4 verbs, since 105:31 carries two nouns (arov, kinnim) under one verb (vayavo)

group closes on the summarizing phrase “all their borders” (105:31, web:Ps.105.31); the verb pattern is unbroken across five consecutive waw-less 3ms openers (105:28-32, oshb:Ps.105.28-Ps.105.32); the first waw-initial opener in the catalogue is 105:33 (oshb:Ps.105.33), making 105:32|33 the byte-true rival seam, so the 105:31|32 split stands only as a content grouping, not a grammatical break
the two-word opening formula 'אָ֭מַר וַיָּבֹ֣א' recurs byte-identically at 105:31 and 105:34 (oshb:Ps.105.31, oshb:Ps.105.34), a continuity signal straddling the 105:31|32 boundary

boundary_rationale: The destruction-class plagues open: “He gave them hail for rain, with lightning in their land” (web:Ps.105.32), in Hebrew 'נָתַ֣ן גִּשְׁמֵיהֶ֣ם' (oshb:Ps.105.32), striking “their vines and also their fig trees” (web:Ps.105.33). Locusts follow “without number” (web:Ps.105.34), eating “every plant in their land” (web:Ps.105.35), and the catalogue climaxes with the “firstborn” struck: “He struck also all the firstborn in their land” (web:Ps.105.36), with the Hebrew 'וַיַּ֣ךְ כָּל בְּכ֣וֹר' at oshb:Ps.105.36, closing the plague sequence before the exodus departure opens at 105:37.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at 105:35 and giving the “firstborn” strike its own one-verse row was considered, but 105:36 opens with its own wayyiqtol verb ('וַיַּ֣ךְ', 'and he struck,' oshb:Ps.105.36) continuing the same destruction sequence as its capstone rather than opening an independent unit.
observed_substrate_signals: hail/locust/“firstborn” destruction group opens with 'נָתַ֣ן גִּשְׁמֵיהֶ֣ם' (105:32, oshb:Ps.105.32); the verb pattern is unbroken across five consecutive waw-less 3ms openers (105:28-32, oshb:Ps.105.28-Ps.105.32); the first waw-initial opener in the catalogue is 105:33 (oshb:Ps.105.33), making 105:32|33 the byte-true rival seam, so the 105:31|32 split stands only as a content grouping, not a grammatical break
wayyiqtol 'וַיַּ֣ךְ' (oshb:Ps.105.36) at 105:36 continues the same sequence rather than marking a fresh start
the two-word opening formula 'אָ֭מַר וַיָּבֹ֣א' recurs byte-identically at 105:31 and 105:34 (oshb:Ps.105.31, oshb:Ps.105.34), a continuity signal straddling the 105:31|32 boundary

boundary_rationale: A new verb opens the exodus-departure movement: “He brought them out with silver and gold” (web:Ps.105.37), reading 'וַֽ֭יּוֹצִיאֵם בְּכֶ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֑ב' at oshb:Ps.105.37, shifting from Egypt-focused plague narrative to Israel-focused wilderness journey. “Egypt was glad when they departed” (web:Ps.105.38), the cloud “for a covering” and fire “in the night” (web:Ps.105.39), the quail and “bread of the sky” (web:Ps.105.40), and the unit closes with water from the rock: “He opened the rock, and waters gushed out” (web:Ps.105.41) — the Hebrew reads 'פָּ֣תַח צ֭וּר וַיָּז֣וּבוּ מָ֑יִם' (oshb:Ps.105.41).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the unit through 105:42 was considered, but 105:42 opens with a causal 'כִּֽי' (roughly 'for') clause returning explicitly to the covenant memory named at 105:8-9, a theological-summary register distinct from the wilderness-provision narrative of 105:37-41.
observed_substrate_signals: new wayyiqtol verb 'וַֽ֭יּוֹצִיאֵם' opens the unit (105:37, oshb:Ps.105.37), narrative-focus shift from Egypt to Israel in transit
unit runs departure → pillar of cloud/fire → quail and manna → water from the rock as one wilderness-provision sequence

boundary_rationale: A causal clause returns explicitly to the psalm’s own covenant theme: “For he remembered his holy word” (web:Ps.105.42), matching 'כִּֽי זָ֭כַר אֶת דְּבַ֣ר קָדְשׁ֑וֹ' at oshb:Ps.105.42, echoing the covenant-memory language of 105:8-9. “He brought his people out with joy” (web:Ps.105.43) and “gave them the lands of the nations” (web:Ps.105.44) lead to the closing purpose clause — “that they might keep his statutes, and observe his laws” (web:Ps.105.45) — and the psalm ends with hallelu-Yah, whose Hebrew is 'הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ' (oshb:Ps.105.45).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the covenant-memory clause (105:42) from the closing purpose statement (105:43-45) as two rows was considered, but 105:42’s 'כִּֽי' clause is the causal ground for the whole closing movement ('he remembered his holy word, he brought his people out with joy, that they might keep his statutes'), one argument chain.
observed_substrate_signals: causal 'כִּֽי' clause opens the unit (105:42), a theological-register return to the covenant language of 105:8-9
unit closes on a purpose clause (105:45) plus the psalm-final hallelu-Yah, tier-1 closer device
device_notes: Psalm 105 closes with 'הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ' (oshb:Ps.105.45), matching Psalm 104’s own hallelu-Yah close; both sit inside the curated frame inventory’s 24 imperative-frame occurrences (11 verse-initial + 13 verse-final), with two skeleton-tier collisions disclosed separately (web:Ps.115.17 = oshb:Ps.115.17, a verbal collocation; web:Ps.22.26 = oshb:Ps.22.27, a full-divine-name collision). As texture, not evidence bearing on this row's own close.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens with paired exclamations, הַֽלְלוּ יָ֨הּ הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה כִּי ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.106.1), rendered “Praise Yahweh! Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.” (web:Ps.106.1). Hallelu-Yah (הַֽלְלוּ יָ֨הּ (oshb:Ps.106.1)) is verse-initial, the tier-1 frame opener the device inventory records; hodu (הוֹד֣וּ (oshb:Ps.106.1)) is present in the same verse but stands as its third word rather than a verse-initial hodu-le-YHWH opening — the inventory's verse-initial hodu list runs to 6 openings book-wide, and Ps.106.1 is not one of them. A rhetorical question over Yahweh's praiseworthiness follows, “Who can utter the mighty acts of Yahweh, or fully declare all his praise?” (web:Ps.106.2), and a beatitude on those who keep justice closes the overture, “Blessed are those who keep justice. Blessed is one who does what is right at all times.” (web:Ps.106.3), before the address turns to a first-person singular petition.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the hodu clause from the hallelu-Yah exclamation into its own opening row was considered, but both stand in one verse and the tiling rule forbids dividing one verse across two rows.
observed_substrate_signals: hallelu-Yah opens the verse (v1), tier-1 frame opener per the device inventory
hodu is present at v1 but positioned as the verse's third word, not verse-initial (6 verse-initial hodu openings run book-wide; this verse is not among them)
a beatitude formula ('blessed are') opens v3, a distinct form from the imperative and question forms of vv1-2
device_notes: Psalm 106's confession, historical recital, and closing doxology all answer to one parent: Psalm 106.

boundary_rationale: The address shifts to a first-person singular petition: “Remember me, Yahweh, with the favor that you show to your people. Visit me with your salvation,” (web:Ps.106.4) opens on the imperative-plus-suffix זָכְרֵ֣נִי (oshb:Ps.106.4), 'remember me, Yahweh' — distinct in person from the plural hymn just closed. Three purpose clauses stack in the verse that follows, לִרְא֤וֹת … לִ֭שְׂמֹחַ … לְ֝הִתְהַלֵּ֗ל (oshb:Ps.106.5), “that I may see the prosperity of your chosen, that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation, that I may glory with your inheritance.” (web:Ps.106.5), before the voice returns to first-person plural at the confession that opens next.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Grouping 106:4-5 with the confession formula that follows as one row was considered, but the plea's singular voice gives way to the confession's plural voice at the verse boundary, a person-shift the tiling should respect.
observed_substrate_signals: a first-person singular imperative-suffix verb ('remember me') opens v4, a voice shift from the plural imperatives of v1
three infinitive-construct purpose clauses (le- prefix) stack across v5
the plural first-person voice returns at the next verse's confession formula

boundary_rationale: The confession formula that launches the historical recital stands alone: “We have sinned with our fathers. We have committed iniquity. We have done wickedly.” (web:Ps.106.6) stacks three plural perfect verbs, חָטָ֥אנוּ עִם אֲבוֹתֵ֗ינוּ הֶעֱוִ֥ינוּ הִרְשָֽׁעְנוּ (oshb:Ps.106.6), with no historical referent yet named — the recital's initial named episode, Egypt and the Red Sea, opens the verse immediately after.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 106:6 to the Egypt/Red Sea episode as its opening line was considered — the two verses share the byte-distinct but accent-stripped-identical catchword 'our fathers' (oshb:Ps.106.6, oshb:Ps.106.7) straddling this boundary — but the confession verbs of 106:6 name no place or event of their own, standing as a general formula the named recital then fills in rather than opening it.
observed_substrate_signals: three stacked plural perfect verbs ('we have sinned...committed iniquity...done wickedly') with no object or place-name, unlike the episodes that follow
the verse's voice shifts to first-person plural ('we') for the first time in the psalm — 106:4-5's petition is entirely first-person singular — a voice shift rather than a return
no proper name occurs in this verse, contrasting with the named settings that structure the recital from the next verse forward

boundary_rationale: The recital's initial episode narrates Egypt and the Red Sea: “Our fathers didn't understand your wonders in Egypt. They didn't remember the multitude of your loving kindnesses, but were rebellious at the sea, even at the Red Sea.” (web:Ps.106.7) names the setting, בְמִצְרַ֨יִם … עַל יָ֣ם בְּיַם סֽוּף (oshb:Ps.106.7), that the following verses develop — rescue for Yahweh's name's sake (web:Ps.106.8), the sea rebuked and dried, וַיִּגְעַ֣ר בְּיַם ס֭וּף וַֽיֶּחֱרָ֑ב (oshb:Ps.106.9), “He rebuked the Red Sea also, and it was dried up; so he led them through the depths, as through a desert.” (web:Ps.106.9), deliverance from the enemy's hand (web:Ps.106.10), the drowned adversaries (web:Ps.106.11), and the people's belief and song (web:Ps.106.12) — before the recital's next episode turns from the sea to the wilderness craving.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at 106:11 and giving 106:12's belief-and-song response its own row was considered, but the response completes the episode's own arc — rebellion at the sea, then rescue, then belief — rather than opening a new referent.
observed_substrate_signals: Egypt and the Red Sea are both named at v7, the recital's initial specific setting
the Red Sea name recurs at v9, a verbal echo of v7's naming within the same episode
the episode closes on a belief-and-song formula at v12, a different response-class from the 'forgot' formula that opens the next episode

the recital's opening word here ('our fathers', oshb:Ps.106.7) is accent_stripped/skeleton-identical to, but byte-distinct from, the 'our fathers' token closing the preceding verse (oshb:Ps.106.6), a catchword straddling this row's own opening seam

boundary_rationale: A new formula opens the next episode: “They soon forgot his works. They didn't wait for his counsel,” (web:Ps.106.13) turns from the sea episode's belief-and-song close to a fresh failure — וַיִּתְאַוּ֣וּ תַ֭אֲוָה בַּמִּדְבָּ֑ר (oshb:Ps.106.14), “but gave in to craving in the desert, and tested God in the wasteland.” (web:Ps.106.14). The episode closes with the request granted and leanness sent into their soul, “He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their soul.” (web:Ps.106.15), before the referent shifts to Moses and Aaron by name.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Carrying this unit through the naming of Moses, Aaron, Dathan, and Abiram that follows was considered, but those verses introduce specific persons the craving episode does not name, a referent-class shift.
observed_substrate_signals: a 'forgot' formula opens the episode at v13, answering the belief-and-song close of the sea episode without repeating its wording
the craving root is doubled as verb plus cognate noun at v14
no personal name occurs in this episode, unlike the Moses/Aaron naming that opens the next verse

boundary_rationale: Named persons enter the recital: “They envied Moses also in the camp, and Aaron, Yahweh's saint.” (web:Ps.106.16) opens with Moses and Aaron named, לְ֭מֹשֶׁה … לְ֝אַהֲרֹ֗ן (oshb:Ps.106.16), then Dathan and Abiram named as the ground opens and swallows them, וַתִּבְלַ֣ע דָּתָ֑ן וַ֝תְּכַ֗ס עַל עֲדַ֥ת אֲבִירָֽם (oshb:Ps.106.17), “The earth opened and swallowed up Dathan, and covered the company of Abiram.” (web:Ps.106.17). The fire that burns the company closes the episode, “A fire was kindled in their company. The flame burned up the wicked.” (web:Ps.106.18), before the calf narrative opens with its own place name, Horeb.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv16-18 as a continuation of the craving episode rather than its own row was considered, but the shift to naming specific persons marks a distinct narrative unit from the unnamed craving-in-the-desert failure.
observed_substrate_signals: personal names Moses, Aaron, Dathan, and Abiram cluster across vv16-17, a naming density the craving episode (vv13-15) lacks entirely
a fire-consumes-the-wicked formula closes the episode at v18
the following episode opens on a place name, Horeb, rather than a person

boundary_rationale: The golden-calf episode opens on its own place name: “They made a calf in Horeb, and worshiped a molten image.” (web:Ps.106.19) — עֵ֥גֶל בְּחֹרֵ֑ב (oshb:Ps.106.19). The exchanged glory (web:Ps.106.20), the forgotten Savior who had worked wonders in Egypt and at the Red Sea (web:Ps.106.21-Ps.106.22, עַל יַם סֽוּף (oshb:Ps.106.22)), and Moses' own intercession close the episode: “Therefore he said that he would destroy them, had Moses, his chosen, not stood before him in the breach, to turn away his wrath, so that he wouldn't destroy them.” (web:Ps.106.23) — עָמַ֣ד בַּפֶּ֣רֶץ (oshb:Ps.106.23) — before the recital turns to the spies' rejection of the land.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the calf-worship narration (106:19-20) from the forgetting-and-intercession unit (106:21-23) into two rows was considered, but both share Horeb's episode, and Moses' intercession answers the same forgetting the unit itself narrates, with no independent referent break between them.
observed_substrate_signals: the place name Horeb opens the episode at v19, distinct from the Dathan/Abiram naming that precedes it
the Red Sea name recurs at v22, echoing its earlier naming at vv7 and 9 without reopening that episode
Moses named as intercessor ('stood in the breach') closes the episode at v23

boundary_rationale: The recital turns from Horeb to the promised land: “Yes, they despised the pleasant land. They didn't believe his word,” (web:Ps.106.24) — בְּאֶ֣רֶץ חֶמְדָּ֑ה (oshb:Ps.106.24). Murmuring against Yahweh's voice follows (web:Ps.106.25), then the sworn oath of judgment, “Therefore he swore to them that he would overthrow them in the wilderness,” (web:Ps.106.26) — וַיִּשָּׂ֣א יָד֣וֹ (oshb:Ps.106.26) — extended to scattering their offspring among the nations (web:Ps.106.27), before the recital names a new place, Baal Peor.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 106:24-27 to the preceding calf episode as one long wilderness-rebellion unit was considered, but the referent shifts from Horeb and the calf to the land itself, and the oath at v26 answers this episode's own despising rather than the calf's.
observed_substrate_signals: a 'pleasant/desirable land' phrase names the promised-land referent at v24, distinct from Horeb's calf-and-image referent
an oath formula ('lifted his hand', i.e. swore) opens the judgment at v26
the episode's offspring-scattering close carries no personal name, unlike the Baal Peor episode's Phinehas that follows

boundary_rationale: A new named place opens the episode: “They joined themselves also to Baal Peor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead.” (web:Ps.106.28) — לְבַ֣עַל פְּע֑וֹר (oshb:Ps.106.28) — followed by the plague (web:Ps.106.29) and Phinehas's own intervention: “Then Phinehas stood up and executed judgment, so the plague was stopped.” (web:Ps.106.30) — פִּֽ֭ינְחָס (oshb:Ps.106.30) — credited to him for righteousness across generations (web:Ps.106.31), a second named intercessor after Moses' stand at Horeb's aftermath, before the recital names its next place, Meribah.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending this unit at 106:29 and giving Phinehas's intervention (106:30-31) its own row was considered, but the plague's stopping and Phinehas's act are the same event described from two angles, not two episodes.
observed_substrate_signals: the place name Baal Peor opens the episode at v28, distinct from the land-despising episode that precedes it
the personal name Phinehas enters at v30 as the episode's own intercessor, paralleling Moses' intercession at v23 without repeating its vocabulary
a credited-for-righteousness formula closes the episode at v31 on covenant-legal language absent from the surrounding narrative verses

boundary_rationale: A fourth named place closes the recital's cluster of wilderness-rebellion sites: “They angered him also at the waters of Meribah, so that Moses was troubled for their sakes;” (web:Ps.106.32) — עַל מֵ֥י מְרִיבָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.106.32) — and the cause is named directly: “because they were rebellious against his spirit, he spoke rashly with his lips.” (web:Ps.106.33) — וַ֝יְבַטֵּ֗א בִּשְׂפָתָֽיו (oshb:Ps.106.33). Moses himself now suffers the consequence, a reversal from his intercessor's role at Horeb's aftermath (עָמַ֣ד בַּפֶּ֣רֶץ (oshb:Ps.106.23)).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 106:32-33 into the Baal Peor unit as its closing pair was considered, but Meribah is a distinct named site with its own cause-and-effect clause, not a continuation of the Baal Peor plague and Phinehas's act.
observed_substrate_signals: the place name Meribah opens the episode at v32, the recital's fourth specific rebellion-site naming after Egypt/the Red Sea, Horeb, and Baal Peor
Moses is named as the one troubled, rather than as intercessor, a role reversal from v23's 'stood in the breach'
the episode's two verses form one cause-and-effect clause, unlike the multi-verse episodes surrounding it

boundary_rationale: The recital turns from named individual sites to the land's peoples collectively: “They didn't destroy the peoples, as Yahweh commanded them,” (web:Ps.106.34) opens with a negated command-formula, לֹֽא הִ֭שְׁמִידוּ (oshb:Ps.106.34), developed through intermarriage and idol-service (web:Ps.106.35-Ps.106.36) to child sacrifice, “Yes, they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.” (web:Ps.106.37), וַיִּזְבְּח֣וּ … בְּ֭נֵיהֶם … בְּנֽוֹתֵיהֶ֗ם (oshb:Ps.106.37), named by place: whom they sacrificed “to the idols of Canaan” (web:Ps.106.38) — לַעֲצַבֵּ֣י כְנָ֑עַן (oshb:Ps.106.38) — and the land's own defilement, וַתֶּחֱנַ֥ף הָ֝אָ֗רֶץ בַּדָּמִֽים (oshb:Ps.106.38), closing on a prostitution metaphor for their deeds (web:Ps.106.39) before the recital's mode shifts from narrated deeds to Yahweh's own anger.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the negated-command opening (106:34) from the idol-service and child-sacrifice narration (106:35-39) into two rows was considered, but v34 states the general failure the following verses specify, with no referent break between them.
observed_substrate_signals: a negated command-formula ('they did not destroy') opens the unit at v34, distinct from the named-place formulas of the three preceding episodes
Canaan names the land collectively at v38, after Egypt, Horeb, Baal Peor, and Meribah named specific sites earlier in the recital
child-sacrifice vocabulary intensifies across vv37-38 into the land's own defilement, a closing image distinct from the snare-and-service language that opens the unit

boundary_rationale: The recital shifts from narrated deeds to Yahweh's own response, summarizing a repeated cycle rather than one episode: “Therefore Yahweh burned with anger against his people. He abhorred his inheritance.” (web:Ps.106.40) opens the cycle — subjection to the nations (web:Ps.106.41-Ps.106.42), repeated rescue answered by repeated rebellion, “He rescued them many times, but they were rebellious in their counsel, and were brought low in their iniquity.” (web:Ps.106.43) — the Hebrew adversative וְ֭הֵמָּה ('but they', oshb:Ps.106.43) marks the cycle's actual contrastive pivot, not the English 'Nevertheless' introduced by WEB's rendering of the wayyiqtol that follows at “Nevertheless he regarded their distress, when he heard their cry.” (web:Ps.106.44), וַ֭יַּרְא (oshb:Ps.106.44), which opens with a bare waw-consecutive and carries no MT adversative of its own; covenant remembrance, וַיִּזְכֹּ֣ר לָהֶ֣ם בְּרִית֑וֹ (oshb:Ps.106.45) (the verse carries a ketiv/qere pair, חסדו (oshb:Ps.106.45) ketiv against חֲסָדָֽיו (oshb:Ps.106.45) qere, at the same ref), and compassion before captors (web:Ps.106.46), before the recital's own voice returns to direct petition.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the anger-and-subjection verses (106:40-43) from the mercy-and-remembrance verses (106:44-46) into two rows was considered, but the adversative at v44 answers the very cycle the anger-and-subjection verses narrate, within one summarizing movement rather than two separate episodes.
observed_substrate_signals: the Hebrew adversative וְ֭הֵמָּה ('but they', oshb:Ps.106.43) marks the cycle's actual contrastive pivot; the English 'Nevertheless' at 106:44 and 106:8 (oshb:Ps.106.8, oshb:Ps.106.44) is WEB's rendering of a bare waw-consecutive at each verse, not a shared MT particle
a ketiv (unpointed) stands against a qere (pointed, 'his loving kindnesses') at v45 — the psalm's ketiv/qere pair, per the inventory
the verb sequence at v43 compresses the whole preceding recital's rescue-then-rebellion pattern into one summary verse

boundary_rationale: The recital's voice returns to direct petition, echoing the individual plea that opened the psalm: “Save us, Yahweh, our God, gather us from among the nations, to give thanks to your holy name, to triumph in your praise!” (web:Ps.106.47) — הוֹשִׁיעֵ֨נוּ יְה֘וָ֤ה אֱלֹהֵ֗ינוּ וְקַבְּצֵנוּ֮ (oshb:Ps.106.47). The imperative here is singular with a first-person-plural object suffix (הוֹשִׁיעֵ֨נוּ (oshb:Ps.106.47), 'save us'), structurally matching the singular imperative-plus-suffix pattern of the plea at 106:4, the contrast lying in the suffix's number (1cs 'me' vs. 1cp 'us') rather than the imperative's own form (זָכְרֵ֣נִי (oshb:Ps.106.4), 'remember me'); לְ֭הֹדוֹת (oshb:Ps.106.47) ('to give thanks') echoes the psalm's own opening (הוֹד֣וּ (oshb:Ps.106.1), 'give thanks') at v1. The psalm's own closing doxology follows with a blessing formula rather than continuing this petition.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Grouping 106:47 with the doxology of 106:48 as one closing unit was considered, but the plea's imperative petition and the doxology's fixed baruch-formula belong to different discourse types — request versus benediction — and the coda class is reserved for the fixed formula alone.
observed_substrate_signals: a plural imperative-suffix verb ('save us') echoes the singular ('remember me') of v4 in form (imperative plus pronominal suffix) while inverting its number
'to give thanks' at v47 verbally echoes the psalm's own opening 'give thanks' at v1
the plea closes with no book-boundary formula of its own; the doxology proper occupies the following verse

boundary_rationale: The psalm — and Book IV (Psalms 90-106) — closes on the fixed book-boundary doxology: “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, from everlasting even to everlasting! Let all the people say, "Amen." Praise Yah!” (web:Ps.106.48) — בָּר֤וּךְ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֵ֪י יִשְׂרָאֵ֡ל מִן הָ֤עוֹלָ֨ם וְעַ֬ד הָעוֹלָ֗ם וְאָמַ֖ר כָּל הָעָ֥ם אָמֵ֗ן הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.106.48). The verse carries one baruch clause, one amen, and the hallelu-Yah exclamation, הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.106.48), that answers the psalm's own opening (הַֽלְלוּ יָ֨הּ (oshb:Ps.106.1)), closing the frame the psalm's own opening verse announced. The formula shares its class with the book's other book-boundary doxologies, but hallelu-Yah closes this one, and the amen count differs too: the book's other 3 book-boundary doxologies each carry 2 amens (41:13, 72:19, 89:52) and close without hallelu-Yah, against 1 amen here, per the inventory.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 106:48 into the preceding petition as its closing line was considered, but the baruch-plus-amen-plus-hallelu-Yah formula shares its closing class with the book's other book-boundary doxologies rather than continuing the petition's own second-person request.
observed_substrate_signals: a baruch + amen x1 + hallelu-Yah formula matches, in class, the book I, II, and III closing doxologies (each baruch + amen x2, without hallelu-Yah)
the closing hallelu-Yah echoes the hallelu-Yah that opens v1, completing the frame the psalm announced at its own start
the doxology stands outside the petition's own second-person request, matching the book-boundary class rather than resolving the plea's content

boundary_rationale: Untitled, Psalm 107 opens Book V with the imperative “הֹד֣וּ” (oshb:Ps.107.1), spelled defectively at byte tier -- the he takes no mater vav, against the verb's usual full spelling. Sweep of the verse-initial hodu-la-Yahweh formula (psalm_device_inventory.json hodu_openings, skeleton tier, both spellings checked) finds 6 such openings book-wide; this is the only one spelled defectively (1 of 6), the other 5 in full. The verse continues “Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever.” (web:Ps.107.1), then the summons turns outward: “Let the redeemed by Yahweh say so, whom he has redeemed from the hand of the adversary,” (web:Ps.107.2) and “and gathered out of the lands, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the south.” (web:Ps.107.3). These three verses name no particular company and carry neither the cry-refrain nor the yodu-refrain that structures the four rescue-vignettes beginning at 107:4; they form the psalm's general frame, addressed to the redeemed of Yahweh as a class before that class is broken into its particular companies.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending this row through 107:4 to fold in the wilderness company was considered, but 107:4 opens the psalm's own rescue-vignette sequence with a named plight, while 1-3 names no company and carries neither refrain that binds the vignettes to follow.
observed_substrate_signals: verse-initial hodu-la-Yahweh imperative, defective spelling (oshb:Ps.107.1, byte tier)
sweep: 6 verse-initial hodu-la-Yahweh occurrences book-wide (skeleton tier, both spellings), 1 defective against 5 full
no cry-refrain or yodu-refrain token present in 107:1-3 (absence relative to the refrain lattice pattern later in the psalm)
device_notes: Psalm 107 gathers all its rows under one parent, from the untitled hodu-opening through the closing wisdom maxim. The book's five-part architecture (I 1-41, II 42-72, III 73-89, IV 90-106, V 107-150) places this psalm's opening at the seam heading Book V.

boundary_rationale: The wilderness company: “They wandered in the wilderness in a desert way. They found no city to live in.” (web:Ps.107.4), “Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted in them.” (web:Ps.107.5). Their plight closes on the cry-refrain “וַיִּצְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם” (oshb:Ps.107.6) -- "they cried to Yahweh in their trouble" -- spelled with tsade; deliverance follows at “He led them also by a straight way, that they might go to a city to live in.” (web:Ps.107.7), and the vignette closes on the yodu-refrain “יוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה חַסְדּ֑וֹ וְ֝נִפְלְאוֹתָ֗יו לִבְנֵ֥י אָדָֽם” (oshb:Ps.107.8): "let them praise Yahweh for his loving kindness, for his wonderful deeds to the children of men," plus a motive clause at “For he satisfies the longing soul. He fills the hungry soul with good.” (web:Ps.107.9). This plight-cry-deliverance-praise sequence, bounded by the two refrains (oshb:Ps.107.6, oshb:Ps.107.8), forms one recurring vignette pattern; three further companies repeat it through web:Ps.107.32.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the plight (4-5) from the cry-deliverance-praise sequence (6-9) into two rows was considered, but no refrain or discourse marker separates them -- the cry-refrain itself is the seam the vignette lattice recognizes, not a break inside the vignette.
observed_substrate_signals: cry-refrain, tsade spelling: וַיִּצְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם (oshb:Ps.107.6)
yodu-refrain byte-quoted at oshb:Ps.107.8; recurs 4 times total across the vignette lattice, once per company closing it
device_notes: The four rescue-vignettes (107:4-9, 10-16, 17-22, 23-32) share a double refrain: a cry-to-Yahweh formula whose sibilant root changes by company, and a yodu-praise formula that returns byte-identical at each vignette's close (sweep: 4 of 4 returns byte tier).

boundary_rationale: A distinct company opens without transition: “Some sat in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron,” (web:Ps.107.10), with cause given at “because they rebelled against the words of God, and condemned the counsel of the Most High.” (web:Ps.107.11) and “Therefore he brought down their heart with labor. They fell down, and there was no one to help.” (web:Ps.107.12). The cry-refrain returns at “וַיִּזְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם” (oshb:Ps.107.13), now spelled with zayin rather than the tsade of the wilderness company's cry (oshb:Ps.107.6) -- the four cry-openers run tsade-zayin-zayin-tsade across the lattice (an ABBA frame, not a strict alternation) rather than repeating one fixed spelling. Deliverance follows at “He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke away their chains.” (web:Ps.107.14), and the yodu-refrain opens the close at “יוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה חַסְדּ֑וֹ” (oshb:Ps.107.15), continuing to match oshb:Ps.107.8 at byte tier, with a further motive clause at “For he has broken the gates of bronze, and cut through bars of iron.” (web:Ps.107.16).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 107:9 and 107:10 as one continuous unit was considered since neither carries an explicit conjunction, but 107:9 completes the wilderness company's own motive clause after its yodu-refrain, and 107:10 opens an unrelated company (those seated in darkness) with its own cry-and-yodu pair.
observed_substrate_signals: cry-refrain, zayin spelling: וַיִּזְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם (oshb:Ps.107.13), against tsade at oshb:Ps.107.6
yodu-refrain opening tokens יוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה חַסְדּ֑וֹ match oshb:Ps.107.8 at byte tier

boundary_rationale: A third company: “Fools are afflicted because of their disobedience, and because of their iniquities.” (web:Ps.107.17), “Their soul abhors all kinds of food. They draw near to the gates of death.” (web:Ps.107.18). The cry-refrain returns at “וַיִּזְעֲק֣וּ אֶל יְ֭הוָה בַּצַּ֣ר לָהֶ֑ם” (oshb:Ps.107.19), again zayin-spelled, matching the prisoners' company's cry (oshb:Ps.107.13) rather than the wilderness company's tsade (oshb:Ps.107.6). Deliverance follows at “He sends his word, and heals them, and delivers them from their graves.” (web:Ps.107.20); this row's span carries 3 of the book's 7 inverted-nun segs (reversednun inventory: oshb:Ps.107.20, oshb:Ps.107.21, oshb:Ps.107.22, single-witness, seg layer, not quotable as verse bytes). The yodu-refrain closes at “יוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה חַסְדּ֑וֹ” (oshb:Ps.107.21), matching its earlier instances at byte tier, and the company responds in its own key at “Let them offer the sacrifices of thanksgiving, and declare his deeds with singing.” (web:Ps.107.22) -- sacrifice and song rather than the plain motive clause of the two companies before it.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading 107:22 as the opening of a new unit (a sacrifice-vow row) was considered, but it carries no cry-refrain of its own and reads as this company's own response clause, parallel to 107:9 and 107:16.

All the wicked will shut their mouths.” (web:Ps.107.42). boundary_rationale: The mizmor-shir-le-David title heads the psalm (“שִׁ֖יר מִזְמ֣וֹר לְדָוִֽד”, web:Ps.108.0 = oshb:Ps.108.1). “My heart is steadfast, God. I will sing and I will make music with my soul.” (web:Ps.108.1 = oshb:Ps.108.2) opens a resolve to sing that continues through “Wake up, harp and lyre! I will wake up the dawn.” (web:Ps.108.2 = oshb:Ps.108.3), “I will give thanks to you, Yahweh, among the nations. I will sing praises to you among the peoples.” (web:Ps.108.3 = oshb:Ps.108.4), “For your loving kindness is great above the heavens. Your faithfulness reaches to the skies.” (web:Ps.108.4 = oshb:Ps.108.5), closing on “Be exalted, God, above the heavens! Let your glory be over all the earth.” (web:Ps.108.5 = oshb:Ps.108.6). This unit is this psalm's earlier source-panel: its Hebrew closely parallels, without running word for word throughout, the tail of Psalm 57 -- the closing line “ר֣וּמָה עַל שָׁמַ֣יִם אֱלֹהִ֑ים וְעַ֖ל כָּל הָאָ֣רֶץ כְּבוֹדֶֽךָ” (oshb:Ps.108.6) is a close paraphrase of Psalm 57's own doxology line, not a verbatim match (oshb:Ps.57.12 collates at tier none against it; the sole divergence is the conjunctive vav on "and upon"). The genuine byte-tier anchor sits two verses earlier: “ע֭וּרָֽה הַנֵּ֥בֶל וְכִנּ֗וֹר” (web:Ps.108.2 = oshb:Ps.108.3) collates byte-identical against the tail of oshb:Ps.57.9 (“ע֭וּרָֽה הַנֵּ֥בֶל וְכִנּ֗וֹר אָעִ֥ירָה שָּֽׁחַר”), the wake-the-dawn call Psalm 57 itself doubles from a longer opening. Two verses after that shared line, the divine name differs: oshb:Ps.57.10's parallel line names Adonai where oshb:Ps.108.4 names Yahweh in the same slot -- WEB keeps that distinction, rendering Psalm 57's word "Lord" (web:Ps.57.9) against Psalm 108's "Yahweh" (“I will give thanks to you, Yahweh, among the nations. I will sing praises to you among the peoples.”, web:Ps.108.3).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Running this row through 108:6 to keep the whole psalm's earlier half together was considered, but 108:6 (oshb:Ps.108.7) is the verse whose wording turns to match Psalm 60 rather than Psalm 57, so the panel seam sits at 108:5|108:6. boundary_rationale: The panel turns: “That your beloved may be delivered, save with your right hand, and answer us.” (web:Ps.108.6 = oshb:Ps.108.7) opens a petition whose Hebrew now aligns with Psalm 60's tail rather than Psalm 57's -- “לְ֭מַעַן יֵחָלְצ֣וּן יְדִידֶ֑יךָ הוֹשִׁ֖יעָה יְמִֽינְךָ֣ וַעֲנֵֽנִי” (oshb:Ps.108.7) is close to oshb:Ps.60.7's own wording -- byte-identical to it once MT 60:7's own inline ketiv (the unpointed הוֹשִׁ֖יעָה preceding the pointed qere יְמִֽינְךָ֣, both "and answer me") is set aside -- not to anything in Psalm 57. boundary_rationale: The row covers the whole psalm because its acrostic runs at the colon level across 10 verses (sweep: 10 of 10 verses carry the scheme, per the inventory): the verse-opening letters, read in sequence after V1_STRIP normalization (the inventory's own layer: the raw verse 1 opens with the hallelu-Yah heading's he; the acrostic's own aleph is word 3)—aleph, gimel, he, zayin, tet, kaf, mem, samekh, pe, resh—occupy alphabet positions 1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17, 20 of 22: 9 odd-position letters plus one even (resh, position 20), so a verse's opening colon takes one letter while the interlocking second colon (the full 12-letter missing set — bet, dalet, vav, het, yod, lamed, nun, ayin, tsade, qof, shin, tav, which includes the odd-position qof and shin, not only even positions) sits mid-verse; every one of the 9 internal boundaries inside web:Ps.111.1-Ps.111.10 (v1|v2 through v9|v10) opens a new acrostic letter, which is why the series privileges no one internal boundary as a tier-1-supported seam over any other. The psalm opens הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ אוֹדֶ֣ה יְ֭הוָה בְּכָל לֵבָ֑ב (web:Ps.111.1 = oshb:Ps.111.1, “Praise Yah! I will give thanks to Yahweh with my whole heart”) and closes רֵ֘אשִׁ֤ית חָכְמָ֨ה יִרְאַ֬ת יְהוָ֗ה (web:Ps.111.10 = oshb:Ps.111.10, “The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom”), an envelope from praise-invocation to reflective maxim.
