boundary_rationale: The psalm opens with a doubled self-effacing petition, “Not to us, Yahweh, not to us, but to your name give glory” (web:Ps.115.1), pivots to the nations' taunting question, “Where is their God, now?” (web:Ps.115.2), and answers it with a counter-affirmation of divine freedom, “But our God is in the heavens. He does whatever he pleases” (web:Ps.115.3). The three verses form one rhetorical unit -- petition, taunt, retort -- before the idol catalogue opens at web:Ps.115.4 with עֲֽ֭צַבֵּיהֶם (oshb:Ps.115.4) ('their idols'), a third-person description with no addressee, unlike v1's second-person address to Yahweh (2ms suffixes throughout); v3's own "our God is in the heavens, he does whatever he pleases" is itself first-person-plural-plus-third-person narration, not address, but still distinct in register from the idols' bare third-person description.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A row spanning web:Ps.115.1-Ps.115.8 could fold the retort into the idol polemic it provokes, but the address shifts from second person to Yahweh (vv1,3) to third-person idol description (v4ff), marking a seam at 3|4.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.115.1's doubled negation has no title pseudo-verse preceding it -- Ps 115 is untitled, and no WEB title pseudo-verse exists for it in the verse map
web:Ps.115.2's question אַיֵּה נָ֝֗א אֱלֹהֵיהֶֽם (oshb:Ps.115.2) is answered directly by web:Ps.115.3's assertion וֵֽאלֹהֵ֥ינוּ בַשָּׁמָ֑יִם (oshb:Ps.115.3) that God is in the heavens
device_notes: All of Psalm 115's rows meet in one parent. The psalm opens without a superscription, so this opening row is also the psalm's opening Hebrew content.

boundary_rationale: The idol polemic runs as one catalogue: idols are מַ֝עֲשֵׂ֗ה יְדֵ֣י אָדָֽם (oshb:Ps.115.4) ('the work of men's hands') with mouths that don't speak, eyes that don't see, ears that don't hear, noses that don't smell, hands that don't feel, and feet that don't walk (web:Ps.115.5-7), before the maker/trust indictment closes it, “Those who make them will be like them; yes, everyone who trusts in them” (web:Ps.115.8). The catalogue's cola (e.g. פֶּֽה לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יְדַבֵּ֑רוּ עֵינַ֥יִם לָ֝הֶ֗ם וְלֹ֣א יִרְאֽוּ (oshb:Ps.115.5)) share one noun-then-negated-verb syntax across web:Ps.115.5-7 through 115:7's first two cola ("their hands, they don't feel" / "their feet, they don't walk"); the pattern breaks at 115:7's own third colon ("nor do they speak through their throat," negative-verb-first with no leading body-part noun) -- the catalogue still runs as one unbroken unit through the seam at 8|9, just not on a fully uniform syntax; the closing verb כֹּ֭ל אֲשֶׁר בֹּטֵ֣חַ בָּהֶֽם (oshb:Ps.115.8) ('everyone who trusts in them') catches on the imperative יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל בְּטַ֣ח (oshb:Ps.115.9) ('Israel, trust!') that opens the next strophe, marking the seam at 8|9.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the sense-organ catalogue (vv5-7) from its opening (v4) and closing indictment (v8) would fragment one anaphoric list across three rows with no independent tier-1 seam between them.
observed_substrate_signals: the 3 sense-organ cola of web:Ps.115.5-7 pair a body-part noun with a negated verb apiece, e.g. אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יִשְׁמָ֑עוּ אַ֥ף לָ֝הֶ֗ם וְלֹ֣א יְרִיחֽוּן (oshb:Ps.115.6), in the same pattern (sweep: 3 verses)

web:Ps.115.8's closing root (כֹּ֭ל אֲשֶׁר בֹּטֵ֣חַ בָּהֶֽם (oshb:Ps.115.8), 'everyone who trusts in them') recurs as the imperative opening web:Ps.115.9 (יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל בְּטַ֣ח (oshb:Ps.115.9), 'Israel, trust!')
device_notes: The maker/trust catchword bridges idols and Yahweh across the row seam at 8|9: the psalm's argument turns on the same root used initially for misplaced trust, then for rightly placed trust.

boundary_rationale: Three vocatives receive a shared two-part formula (3 times) in turn -- an imperative to trust in Yahweh (singular at 115:9, plural at 115:10-11) followed by the closing clause “He is their help and their shield” -- which alone is byte-identical across all 3 verses -- addressed to Israel (יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל (oshb:Ps.115.9), web:Ps.115.9), the house of Aaron (בֵּ֣ית אַ֭הֲרֹן (oshb:Ps.115.10), web:Ps.115.10), and those who fear Yahweh (יִרְאֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.115.11), web:Ps.115.11); the closing refrain (עֶזְרָ֖ם וּמָגִנָּ֣ם הֽוּא (oshb:Ps.115.9)) is byte-identical (collate.py, byte tier) across all 3 verses. The same three-member roster recurs at web:Ps.118.2-Ps.118.4 with a jussive 'let…say' verb replacing the imperative; the fixed collocation בֵּ֣ית אַ֭הֲרֹן (oshb:Ps.115.10) sweeps to 4 verses book-wide and יִרְאֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.115.11) to 6 verses book-wide, both concentrated in this recurring triad (Ps 135:19-Ps 135:20, outside this span, inserts a fourth member, house of Levi, before repeating the fearers clause).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating vv9-11 as three separate one-verse rows would split one triadic (3-member) refrain unit whose members share one closing clause verbatim (byte tier, 3 verses).
observed_substrate_signals: the refrain עֶזְרָ֖ם וּמָגִנָּ֣ם הֽוּא (oshb:Ps.115.10) (sweep: 3 verses, web:Ps.115.9-11) closes each of the three vocatives identically at byte tier

בֵּ֣ית אַ֭הֲרֹן (oshb:Ps.115.10) sweeps to 4 verses book-wide (skeleton, sweep.py) and יִרְאֵ֣י יְ֭הוָה (oshb:Ps.115.11) to 6 verses book-wide, both fixed collocations concentrated in this triad and its recurrences
device_notes: The Israel / house of Aaron / fearers-of-Yahweh triad is the psalm's central structuring device, returning as a bless-declaration triad at web:Ps.115.12-13 and, differently worded, at web:Ps.118.2-4.

boundary_rationale: The verb יְבָ֫רֵ֥ךְ (oshb:Ps.115.12) ('he will bless') repeats across a second, narrated triad -- “He will bless the house of Israel. He will bless the house of Aaron” (web:Ps.115.12), “He will bless those who fear Yahweh, both small and great” (web:Ps.115.13) -- before the strophe widens into a direct blessing on the congregation, “May Yahweh increase you more and more” (web:Ps.115.14) and “Blessed are you by Yahweh, who made heaven and earth” (web:Ps.115.15). The root behind יְ֭בָרֵךְ (oshb:Ps.115.13) occurs 4 finite times across web:Ps.115.12-13 alone, mirroring the trust-triad's three-member roster in narrated rather than imperative form before the address widens at v14.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Breaking the narrated bless-triad (vv12-13) from the widened blessing that follows (vv14-15) is a genuine rival: 115:14 shifts to 2mp address ('increase you', x2) and 115:15 opens with the 2mp independent pronoun 'you' -- a real addressee-register change at 13|14, not the absence an earlier reading of this seam claimed. The row nonetheless keeps 12-15 together because the 'bless' root (oshb:Ps.115.12 x3, oshb:Ps.115.13 x1) that opens the narrated triad reappears at oshb:Ps.115.15's 'blessed are you,' framing the whole span as one blessing-movement from narration to direct declaration; the seam is live, and this reading is held at medium confidence.
observed_substrate_signals: יְהוָה֮ זְכָרָ֪נוּ יְבָ֫רֵ֥ךְ יְ֭בָרֵךְ אֶת בֵּ֣ית יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל יְ֝בָרֵ֗ךְ אֶת בֵּ֥ית אַהֲרֹֽן (oshb:Ps.115.12) carries the root ברך three times in one verse, and יְ֭בָרֵךְ (oshb:Ps.115.13) once more opening v13 -- 4 finite occurrences across the two verses

web:Ps.115.15's participle עֹ֝שֵׂ֗ה שָׁמַ֥יִם וָאָֽרֶץ (oshb:Ps.115.15) ('who made heaven and earth') supplies the heaven/earth vocabulary that web:Ps.115.16 picks up immediately after this row's close
device_notes: The bless-triad (vv12-13) answers the trust-triad (vv9-11) member for member, narrating what the imperative called for.

boundary_rationale: The heaven/earth antithesis (“The heavens are Yahweh's heavens, but he has given the earth to the children of men” web:Ps.115.16) sets up a second antithesis between the silent dead and the blessing living: לֹ֣א הַ֭מֵּתִים יְהַֽלְלוּ יָ֑הּ וְ֝לֹ֗א כָּל יֹרְדֵ֥י דוּמָֽה (oshb:Ps.115.17) (“The dead don't praise Yah,” web:Ps.115.17) against “but we will bless Yah, from this time forward and forever more. Praise Yah!” (web:Ps.115.18). The closing הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.115.18) is verse-final -- the psalm's sole hallelu-Yah occurrence among its 18 verses; it is byte-distinct from v17's יְהַֽלְלוּ יָ֑הּ (oshb:Ps.115.17) -- a different, imperfect verb form ('they will praise') rather than the imperative liturgical formula.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Grouping v16 with the preceding blessing strophe (ending v15) is possible since both touch heaven/earth language, but v16 restates the theme as an independent cosmological claim rather than a continuation of the second-person blessing of v14-15.
observed_substrate_signals: a skeleton sweep of the hallelu-Yah collocation returns 26 verses book-wide (sweep.py --skel); two of those are not the imperative liturgical formula -- web:Ps.115.17 is the imperfect verb יְהַֽלְלוּ (oshb:Ps.115.17) ('they will praise'), and oshb:Ps.22.27 is a skeleton-only collision (a 3mp-imperfect plus the full divine name, not the imperative-plus-Yah idiom) -- leaving 24 imperative-frame instances (11 verse-initial + 13 verse-final), the disclosure inventory's ratified count

web:Ps.115.18 carries 1 paseq per the marks inventory (single-witness; a bare count disclosure, not a positional claim -- the inventory records no offset/word-index for paseq occurrences); corroborating texture, not a boundary driver
device_notes: The living/dead antithesis of vv17-18 closes the psalm's argument begun at v1: those who bless Yah's name (not the silent dead) are the psalm's speaking community.

boundary_rationale: The thanksgiving opens with a love-declaration and its ground, “I love Yahweh, because he listens to my voice” (web:Ps.116.1) and “I will call on him as long as I live” (web:Ps.116.2), then narrates the crisis that provoked the calling -- “The cords of death surrounded me… I found trouble and sorrow” (web:Ps.116.3) -- closing on the quoted cry itself, אָנָּ֥ה יְ֝הוָ֗ה מַלְּטָ֥ה נַפְשִֽׁי (oshb:Ps.116.4) ('Yahweh, I beg you, deliver my soul,' web:Ps.116.4).
strongest_rejected_alternative: A shorter row ending at v2 (declaration alone) would separate the reason for loving Yahweh from the crisis-and-cry narrative that the declaration's 'therefore' (v2) sets up.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.116.1-2 gives the ground clause (כִּֽי יִשְׁמַ֥ע יְהוָ֑ה, oshb:Ps.116.1, 'because he listens') and the resulting resolve (therefore I will call) before the crisis is narrated at v3
web:Ps.116.4's cry, אָנָּ֥ה יְ֝הוָ֗ה מַלְּטָ֥ה נַפְשִֽׁי (oshb:Ps.116.4), is the psalm's opening quoted direct speech, closing the opening movement
device_notes: Psalm 116, taken whole, is this row set's parent. Psalm 116 moves from a love-declaration through a crisis-and-deliverance report into a doubled vow movement (vv13-14 mirrored at vv17-18).

boundary_rationale: Yahweh's character is stated generally -- “Yahweh is gracious and righteous… Yahweh preserves the simple” (web:Ps.116.5-6) -- before the speaker addresses their own soul, שׁוּבִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי (oshb:Ps.116.7) (“Return to your rest, my soul,” web:Ps.116.7), reports the deliverance in three parts, “my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling” (web:Ps.116.8), and resolves to “walk before Yahweh in the land of the living” (web:Ps.116.9).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at v7 (self-address alone) would separate the resolve 'return to your rest' from the report of deliverance it anticipates in v8.
observed_substrate_signals: נַפְשִֽׁי (oshb:Ps.116.4, 'my soul') occurs at 116:4 (word index 6), again in the self-address שׁוּבִ֣י נַ֭פְשִׁי (oshb:Ps.116.7) of v7, and again at oshb:Ps.116.8 (word index 2, נַפְשִׁ֗י) in the deliverance report -- 3 verse occurrences of the soul-noun (oshb:Ps.116.4, oshb:Ps.116.7, oshb:Ps.116.8) threading the crisis-to-report movement, the earliest at 116:4 (disclosed as cross-seam texture, not a driver here)

web:Ps.116.7's imperative self-address שׁוּבִ֣י (oshb:Ps.116.7) ('return') addresses the speaker's own soul, a distinct addressee from Yahweh; the psalm's next self-address is the servant self-naming at 116:16
device_notes: The soul-address device (v7) frames this row's report of deliverance, resolving into the resolve-to-walk clause of v9.

boundary_rationale: A reflective aside on the affliction just survived -- “I believed, therefore I said, "I was greatly afflicted."” (web:Ps.116.10) and “I said in my haste, "All people are liars."” (web:Ps.116.11) -- leads into the pivotal question that launches the vow movement, “What will I give to Yahweh for all his benefits toward me?” (web:Ps.116.12).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching v12's question to the following cup-of-salvation verse (v13) as its answer is defensible, but the question itself closes the reflective aside begun at v10 and is the strophe's rhetorical hinge rather than the start of the vow's content.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.116.10-11 (הֶ֭אֱמַנְתִּי כִּ֣י אֲדַבֵּ֑ר אֲ֝נִ֗י עָנִ֥יתִי מְאֹֽד (oshb:Ps.116.10) … אֲ֭נִי אָמַ֣רְתִּי בְחָפְזִ֑י כָּֽל הָאָדָ֥ם כֹּזֵֽב (oshb:Ps.116.11)) is a well-known crux in Hebrew syntax -- the exact logical relation between 'I believed' and the quoted self-report is debated among translations -- a content difficulty distinct from the row's boundary, which rests on the aside's self-contained question-and-answer shape

web:Ps.116.12's question מָֽה אָשִׁ֥יב (oshb:Ps.116.12) ('what will I give') has no grammatical antecedent in vv10-11, which themselves carry no divine-name token at all -- the same feature that makes v13's answer ('I will take the cup...') a live continuation; the row keeps v12 with the aside because its interrogative form, not its content, closes the self-contained question-and-answer shape of vv10-12 rather than opening the vow's declarative content
device_notes: The reflective aside (vv10-11) is the psalm's hinge between the deliverance report and the vow movement that the question of v12 opens.

boundary_rationale: The opening vow half-strophe begins, כּוֹס יְשׁוּע֥וֹת (oshb:Ps.116.13) (“I will take the cup of salvation,” web:Ps.116.13), closing on וּבְשֵׁ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה אֶקְרָֽא (oshb:Ps.116.13) ('and call on Yahweh's name') then the vow-payment formula (web:Ps.116.14); an interlude on death's value follows, “Precious in Yahweh's sight is the death of his saints” (web:Ps.116.15), and the speaker names themself “your servant, the son of your servant girl” (עַ֭בְדְּךָ בֶּן אֲמָתֶ֑ךָ, oshb:Ps.116.16, web:Ps.116.16), immediately followed by “You have freed me from my chains” (פִּ֝תַּ֗חְתָּ לְמוֹסֵרָֽי, oshb:Ps.116.16, web:Ps.116.16). The vow-payment clause closing v14 (נְ֭דָרַי לַיהוָ֣ה אֲשַׁלֵּ֑ם נֶגְדָה נָּ֝֗א לְכָל עַמּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.116.14)) matches the one closing v18 at byte tier (collate.py; 2 verses), marking vv13-14 as one half of a matched pair whose other half opens the next row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at v14 (cup and opening vow alone) would isolate the servant self-naming of v16, which the row keeps attached despite v15's intervening third-person nominal clause ("Precious in Yahweh's sight is the death of his saints") breaking any direct grammatical continuity; v13 itself names Yahweh in the third person rather than addressing him, so the connective thread through 13-16 is thematic (vow-and-service) rather than a single uninterrupted address.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.116.14's vow clause (נְ֭דָרַי לַיהוָ֣ה אֲשַׁלֵּ֑ם נֶגְדָה נָּ֝֗א לְכָל עַמּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.116.14)) is byte-identical (2 verses) to web:Ps.116.18's (נְ֭דָרַי לַיהוָ֣ה אֲשַׁלֵּ֑ם נֶגְדָה נָּ֝֗א לְכָל עַמּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.116.18))

web:Ps.116.13's closing clause (וּבְשֵׁ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה אֶקְרָֽא (oshb:Ps.116.13)) is byte-identical to web:Ps.116.17's closing clause, forming a second matched pair (2 verses) alongside the vow-payment refrain
device_notes: This row carries one half of the psalm's 2-part vow pairing (cup/call/vow); its other half recurs at 116:17-18.

boundary_rationale: The closing vow half-strophe mirrors the opening one: לְֽךָ אֶ֭זְבַּח זֶ֣בַח תּוֹדָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.116.17) (“I will offer to you the sacrifice of thanksgiving,” web:Ps.116.17) closes on the same call-on-the-name clause that closed v13, then repeats the vow-payment formula of v14 verbatim (2 verses) at web:Ps.116.18, before the psalm closes with its one location detail, “in the courts of Yahweh's house, in the middle of you, Jerusalem. Praise Yah!” (web:Ps.116.19).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the vow repetition (v17-18) from the closing location and hallelu-Yah (v19) is possible, but v19's courts-of-Yahweh's-house locates the very vow just repeated, completing rather than beginning a new movement.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.116.19's close (הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.116.19)) is the psalm's sole hallelu-Yah among its 19 verses, verse-final, matching web:Ps.115.18's and web:Ps.117.2's verse-final closes at byte tier

the compound noun-phrase זֶ֣בַח תּוֹדָ֑ה ('sacrifice of thanksgiving') in זֶ֣בַח תּוֹדָ֑ה וּבְשֵׁ֖ם יְהוָ֣ה אֶקְרָֽא (oshb:Ps.116.17) occurs once within this psalm (2 verses book-wide total), pairing with the one 'cup' noun of v13 as the two named offerings of the doubled vow movement
device_notes: This row completes the 2-part vow pairing opened at vv13-14 and closes the psalm on its sole hallelu-Yah (1 of 19 verses).

boundary_rationale: Psalm 117 is the shortest of the Psalter's 150 psalms -- 2 verses, the book's minimum (next-shortest 131, 133, and 134 at 3 verses each; verse counts from verse_map_web.json, is_title-filtered) -- and its two verses form one indivisible imperative-and-ground movement: “Praise Yahweh, all you nations! Extol him, all you peoples!” (web:Ps.117.1) grounded by “his loving kindness is great toward us. Yahweh's faithfulness endures forever” (web:Ps.117.2), closing on the psalm's sole hallelu-Yah (1 of its 2 verses).
strongest_rejected_alternative: No internal seam is available to split web:Ps.117.1 (the summons) from web:Ps.117.2 (its ground clause and close) -- the imperative has no content without the 'for' clause that grounds it.
observed_substrate_signals: verse_map_web.json's per-psalm verse counts confirm Ps 117 has the book's single minimum at 2 verses (sweep of all 150 psalms, is_title pseudo-verses excluded)
web:Ps.117.2's close (הַֽלְלוּ יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.117.2)) is byte-identical across 3 verses (115:18, 116:19, 117:2) to the hallelu-Yah closing web:Ps.115.18 and web:Ps.116.19
device_notes: The psalm coheres as one composition -- parent grouping Psalm 117. Its universal summons “all you nations! Extol him, all you peoples” (web:Ps.117.1) answers, at the level of the whole Hallel run, the nations' taunt quoted at web:Ps.115.2.

boundary_rationale: The psalm opens, הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה (oshb:Ps.118.1) (“Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good,” web:Ps.118.1), then repeats its own closing clause (כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.118.2), “for his loving kindness endures forever”) three more times as three groups are called to say it in turn -- Israel (web:Ps.118.2), the house of Aaron (web:Ps.118.3), those who fear Yahweh (web:Ps.118.4) -- the same three-member roster addressed by imperative at web:Ps.115.9-Ps.115.11. The refrain clause is byte-identical (collate.py, byte tier) across all 4 verses of this row.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading v1 as its own opening row separate from the triadic call of vv2-4 would sever the hodu declaration from the refrain clause it supplies verbatim (3 verses) to the following calls.
observed_substrate_signals: the closing clause (כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.118.2)) recurs byte-identical at web:Ps.118.1, 118.2, 118.3, and 118.4 -- 4 verses
the Israel / house of Aaron / fearers-of-Yahweh roster (3 members) corresponds to web:Ps.115.9-11's trust-triad member for member, with 'let…say' replacing 'trust'
device_notes: For grouping, Psalm 118 stands over its rows. The psalm frames itself with a byte-identical hodu declaration (collate: byte tier; sweep: 2 verse-initial hodu verses in this psalm, oshb:Ps.118.1 and oshb:Ps.118.29) at its opening (this row) and its close (web:Ps.118.29), a true verbal inclusio confirmed at byte tier.

boundary_rationale: A distress-and-answer report, מִֽן הַ֭מֵּצַ֥ר קָרָ֣אתִי יָּ֑הּ עָנָ֖נִי בַמֶּרְחָ֣ב יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.118.5) (“Out of my distress, I called on Yah. Yah answered me with freedom.” web:Ps.118.5 -- a wordplay between הַ֭מֵּצַ֥ר (oshb:Ps.118.5) 'distress/narrow-place' and בַמֶּרְחָ֣ב (oshb:Ps.118.5) 'spacious place'), grounds a confidence declaration, “Yahweh is on my side. I will not be afraid” (web:Ps.118.6-7), which closes on a doubled proverb: “It is better to take refuge in Yahweh, than to put confidence in man” (web:Ps.118.8) / “…than to put confidence in princes” (web:Ps.118.9), sharing an opening clause (ט֗וֹב לַחֲס֥וֹת בַּיהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.118.8)) byte-identical (collate.py, byte tier, 2 verses) before the pair diverges on its final word.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the confidence declaration (vv6-7) from the doubled proverb (vv8-9) is possible, but both develop the same 'trust Yahweh, not man' claim opened by the distress report at v5.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.118.8's opening (ט֗וֹב לַחֲס֥וֹת בַּיהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.118.8)) is byte-identical (2 verses) to web:Ps.118.9's opening, diverging solely at the final word -- בָּאָדָֽם (oshb:Ps.118.8) ('man') against בִּנְדִיבִֽים (oshb:Ps.118.9) ('princes')
web:Ps.118.5's הַ֭מֵּצַ֥ר (oshb:Ps.118.5) / בַמֶּרְחָ֣ב (oshb:Ps.118.5) pair is the row's single wordplay (1 verse), setting distress against the 'freedom' Yah answers with
device_notes: The distress/confidence movement (vv5-9) is this psalm's opening first-person testimony block, distinct from the triadic hodu call that opens the psalm.

boundary_rationale: A tripled battle report -- “All the nations surrounded me” (web:Ps.118.10), “They surrounded me, yes, they surrounded me” (web:Ps.118.11), “They surrounded me like bees” (web:Ps.118.12) -- closes all 3 verses on the identical 4-token clause (בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה כִּ֣י אֲמִילַֽם (oshb:Ps.118.10), “in Yahweh's name I cut them off”), before an adversative turn, “You pushed me back hard, to make me fall, but Yahweh helped me” (web:Ps.118.13), resolves into “Yah is my strength and song. He has become my salvation” (web:Ps.118.14).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Isolating the tripled surrounding refrain (vv10-12) from the adversative resolution (vv13-14) is defensible on refrain grounds alone, but v13's 'pushed back… but Yahweh helped' directly answers the threat just described, continuing one battle-report movement.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.118.10-12's closing clause (בְּשֵׁ֥ם יְ֝הוָ֗ה כִּ֣י אֲמִילַֽם (oshb:Ps.118.10)) is byte-identical (collate.py, byte tier) across all 3 verses

the surround-verb recurs 4 times across web:Ps.118.10-12 in two spelled forms, a long one (סְבָב֑וּנִי, oshb:Ps.118.10 word index 2, recurring at oshb:Ps.118.11 word index 2) shared by v10 and the latter half of v11, and a short one (סַבּ֤וּנִי (oshb:Ps.118.12)) shared by the earlier half of v11 and v12 -- the two v11/v12 short-form tokens equate at accent_stripped tier only (a cantillation difference), and the long and short spellings are not byte-identical to one another, so cited as a root repetition (4 occurrences) rather than a word-for-word refrain
device_notes: The tripled surrounding refrain (vv10-12) is this psalm's most concentrated battle-report device (3 verses), resolved by the adversative help-clause of v13.

boundary_rationale: A quoted acclamation, “The voice of rejoicing and salvation is in the tents of the righteous” (web:Ps.118.15), doubles its own closing clause (יְמִ֥ין יְ֝הוָה עֹ֣שָׂה חָֽיִל (oshb:Ps.118.15), “The right hand of Yahweh does valiantly”) at web:Ps.118.16, byte-identical (collate.py, byte tier, 2 verses); the strophe then turns to survival testimony, “I will not die, but live, and declare Yah's works” (web:Ps.118.17), and its cost, “Yah has punished me severely, but he has not given me over to death” (web:Ps.118.18).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at v16 (doubled right-hand refrain alone) would cut the acclamation off from the survival declaration it grounds -- v17's 'I will not die, but live' restates in the speaker's own voice what vv15-16 just quoted as communal acclamation.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.118.15's closing clause (יְמִ֥ין יְ֝הוָה עֹ֣שָׂה חָֽיִל (oshb:Ps.118.15)) is byte-identical (2 verses) to web:Ps.118.16's closing clause

web:Ps.118.15's second half opens an embedded quotation at "the right hand of Yahweh does valiantly" (יְמִ֥ין יְ֝הוָה עֹ֣שָׂה חָֽיִל, oshb:Ps.118.15) that WEB marks with an opening quotation mark carried through v16's doubled repetition -- a voiced acclamation distinct from the surrounding first-person testimony; "the voice of rejoicing" (v15a) itself carries no quotation mark
device_notes: The doubled right-hand-of-Yahweh acclamation (vv15-16) is quoted communal speech that the speaker's own survival testimony (vv17-18) answers in the first person.

boundary_rationale: An antiphonal gate scene: פִּתְחוּ לִ֥י שַׁעֲרֵי צֶ֑דֶק אָֽבֹא בָ֝ם אוֹדֶ֥ה יָֽהּ (oshb:Ps.118.19) (“Open to me the gates of righteousness. I will enter into them. I will give thanks to Yah.” web:Ps.118.19) is a plea addressed to unnamed gatekeepers, answered by זֶֽה הַשַּׁ֥עַר לַיהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.118.20) (“This is the gate of Yahweh; the righteous will enter into it.” web:Ps.118.20) -- a declarative reply in a different grammatical voice, third person rather than imperative-to-second-person -- before the speaker's own thanksgiving resumes at web:Ps.118.21.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading v19 alone as the close of the preceding testimony strophe is possible, but its imperative plea 'open to me' has no addressee across the preceding 5 verses (118:14-18) and instead opens a new liturgical scene answered by v20.
observed_substrate_signals: the gate scene shifts grammatical voice twice within 2 verses: second-person imperative plea (v19) to third-person declarative reply (v20) to first-person resumed testimony (v21); a comparable plea/reply/testimony movement recurs later in the psalm at 118:25-26/27/28, sharing the same 2ms thanksgiving-verb tie (the root shared by 118:21 and 118:28 sweeps to 14 verses book-wide at skeleton tier; 118:21's own pointed form recurs at only 3 verses book-wide at byte tier -- oshb:Ps.35.18, oshb:Ps.118.21, oshb:Ps.119.7), so this pattern is the psalm's clearest instance rather than its only one
שַׁעֲרֵי צֶ֑דֶק (oshb:Ps.118.19) ('gates of righteousness,' v19) and הַשַּׁ֥עַר לַיהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.118.20) ('the gate of Yahweh,' v20) are the psalm's 2 gate references, both inside this row
device_notes: This row is Psalm 118's sharpest antiphonal seam (2 verses), argued from the voice return: plea, then reply in a distinct grammatical voice.

boundary_rationale: Three interpretive declarations follow the preceding scene: אֶ֭בֶן מָאֲס֣וּ הַבּוֹנִ֑ים הָ֝יְתָ֗ה לְרֹ֣אשׁ פִּנָּֽה (oshb:Ps.118.22) (“The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” web:Ps.118.22), “This is Yahweh's doing. It is marvelous in our eyes” (web:Ps.118.23 = oshb:Ps.118.23, whose Hebrew demonstrative זֹּ֑את sits at word index 3, not the verse-initial position its English rendering suggests), together with “This is the day that Yahweh has made. We will rejoice and be glad in it!” (web:Ps.118.24 = oshb:Ps.118.24, the row's only genuinely verse-initial demonstrative, זֶה) -- a triad of interpretive sayings rather than the antiphonal request-and-reply shape of the gate scene at 118:19-21. The verse-initial demonstrative device itself is not what unites the triad -- a book-wide sweep finds it only at 118:20 and 118:24, so it actually straddles this row's own opening seam at 118:21|118:22 (118:20 sits in the preceding row) rather than running through all three of this row's verses. The triad's own unity rests on its shared interpretive-declaration shape and its position after the gate liturgy, not on a verse-initial demonstrative.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching the rejected-stone saying (v22) to the gate scene that precedes it is possible on liturgical-procession grounds, but v22 introduces a fresh image (building, not gate) interpreted by the This-is sayings of vv23-24 rather than continuing the gate dialogue.
observed_substrate_signals: of web:Ps.118.22-24, only v24 opens with a genuine demonstrative (זֶה הַ֭יּוֹם, oshb:Ps.118.24, naming the festal day); v23's demonstrative זֹּ֑את (oshb:Ps.118.23) names the stone's reversal but sits at word index 3, after the opening prepositional phrase מֵאֵ֣ת יְ֭הוָה ('from Yahweh'); v22 has no demonstrative at all

the rejected-stone saying's original setting (building metaphor, royal or communal) is not settled by the row's own bytes; the referent of 'the stone' is an open interpretive question this candidate holds rather than resolves
device_notes: The This-is triad (vv22-24) interprets the reversal just enacted, sitting between the gate liturgy (vv19-21) and the festal procession (vv25-27).

boundary_rationale: A hosanna plea, אָנָּ֣א יְ֭הוָה הוֹשִׁ֘יעָ֥ה נָּ֑א (oshb:Ps.118.25) (“Save us now, we beg you, Yahweh!” web:Ps.118.25), is met by a blessing acclamation, בָּר֣וּךְ הַ֭בָּא בְּשֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.118.26) (“Blessed is he who comes in Yahweh's name!” web:Ps.118.26) spoken in a different grammatical voice than the plea it answers, before the procession moves to the altar, “Bind the sacrifice with cords, even to the horns of the altar” (web:Ps.118.27).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the hosanna-and-blessing exchange (vv25-26) from the altar instruction (v27) is defensible since v27 shifts from acclamation to procedural imperative, but both belong to one festal-procession scene with no independent speaker change marking a seam inside it.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.118.25's אָנָּ֣א (oshb:Ps.118.25) ('we beg you') plea and web:Ps.118.26's בָּר֣וּךְ (oshb:Ps.118.26) ('blessed') acclamation are addressed to different grammatical objects -- Yahweh directly (v25), then a third party 'he who comes' (v26) -- a voice shift this candidate reads as antiphonal across the 2 lines without settling which party (priests, pilgrims) speaks which
web:Ps.118.27's אֵ֤ל יְהוָה֮ (oshb:Ps.118.27) ('Yahweh is God') is the row's single explicit el-Yahweh identification (1 of 3 verses) in this part
device_notes: The festal-procession scene (vv25-27) is the psalm's second antiphonal moment, moving from plea to acclamation to altar instruction.

boundary_rationale: A final personal declaration -- אֵלִ֣י אַתָּ֣ה וְאוֹדֶ֑ךָּ ("my God, you, and I will thank you") and אֱ֝לֹהַ֗י אֲרוֹמְמֶֽךָּ ("my God, I will exalt you") (oshb:Ps.118.28, web:Ps.118.28 “You are my God, and I will give thanks to you. You are my God, I will exalt you.”) -- names God with two distinct Hebrew words (אֵלִ֣י, אֱ֝לֹהַ֗י) that WEB renders identically as "You are my God," the doubling a rendering effect rather than a repeated Hebrew lexeme -- closes the psalm with its opening line repeated verbatim: הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה כִּי ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.118.29) is byte-identical (collate.py, byte tier) to הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה כִּי ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.118.1), a true hodu inclusio framing all 29 verses of the psalm.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Reading v29 as belonging with the altar procession at 118:25-27 would merge the closing inclusio into festal-procession texture; the word-for-word repetition of v1 (7 words) instead marks v29 as the psalm's deliberate frame-closing verse.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.118.29 (הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה כִּי ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.118.29)) is byte-identical (2 verses) to web:Ps.118.1 (הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה כִּי ט֑וֹב כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ (oshb:Ps.118.1)) across their shared 7-word formula

web:Ps.118.28 names God with two distinct 1cs-suffixed forms in one verse, אֵלִ֣י ('my God/El') and אֱ֝לֹהַ֗י ('my God/Elohim') (oshb:Ps.118.28) -- WEB's identical 'You are my God' rendering of both is a translation effect, not a repeated Hebrew word; the verb-plus-2ms-suffix thanksgiving formula this verse shares with oshb:Ps.118.21 (א֭וֹדְךָ, 'I will give thanks to you') is not unique to v28 -- a skeleton sweep of that form returns exactly 2 verses book-wide, Ps.118.21 and Ps.118.28
device_notes: This row closes the hodu inclusio opened at web:Ps.118.1-4, the psalm's outermost frame.

boundary_rationale: The community's own recollection follows David's oath: an unquoted report “Behold, we heard of it in Ephrathah. We found it in the field of Jaar.” (web:Ps.132.6) gives way to a quoted communal vow, “We will go into his dwelling place. We will worship at his footstool.” (web:Ps.132.7), then to unquoted imperative address to Yahweh: “קוּמָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה לִמְנוּחָתֶ֑ךָ” (oshb:Ps.132.8) -- “Arise, Yahweh, into your resting place,” (web:Ps.132.8) -- continuing through the petition “For your servant David's sake, don't turn away the face of your anointed one.” (web:Ps.132.10). The row groups the search-recollection, the processional vow, and the petition as one liturgical movement; grammatical address turns from third person at web:Ps.132.6-web:Ps.132.7 (oshb:Ps.132.7: נִ֝שְׁתַּחֲוֶ֗ה לַהֲדֹ֥ם רַגְלָֽיו, 'we will worship at his footstool') to second-person vocative address to Yahweh beginning at web:Ps.132.8 (קוּמָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה, 'arise, Yahweh'), but no fresh narrative report clause comparable to 132:6's own opening intervenes before the next report opens at web:Ps.132.11, so the movement holds as one row: it opens where the quoted vow of 132:3-132:5 closes and ends where that next report opens at web:Ps.132.11.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the vow (132:6-7) from the petition (132:8-10) was considered, since 132:8 drops the quotation marks that bound 132:7 and turns from third-person description to second-person address; rejected because no fresh narrative report clause comparable to 132:6's own opening intervenes before 132:11's own next report -- 132:8's imperative-plus-vocative continues the same movement's action rather than opening a fresh report.
observed_substrate_signals: quotation-marked communal vow at web:Ps.132.7, bounded by unquoted material on both sides (132:6, 132:8)
second-person imperative address to Yahweh begins at web:Ps.132.8 and continues without a fresh vocative through web:Ps.132.10
no selah occurs anywhere in this row's own span, web:Ps.132.6-web:Ps.132.10, per the pmarks_Ps.json inventory (the absence claim is scoped strictly to that span)

boundary_rationale: A reciprocal oath answers David's: “נִשְׁבַּֽע יְהוָ֨ה לְדָוִ֡ד אֱמֶת֮” (oshb:Ps.132.11) -- “Yahweh has sworn to David in truth. He will not turn from it:” (web:Ps.132.11) -- opens a quotation mid-verse, after this reporting clause, that runs through web:Ps.132.12's own final character (“…their children also will sit on your throne forever more.”), reusing at the skeleton tier the same swearing-verb root that opened the report at oshb:Ps.132.2 (נִ֭שְׁבַּע). web:Ps.132.13 then drops the quotation and reports, in the third person, “For Yahweh has chosen Zion. He has desired it for his habitation.” -- a motive clause that names the ground of the oath just sworn and supplies the only naming of Zion that the following oracle's web:Ps.132.15-web:Ps.132.17 (outside this row's own span) depend on grammatically, and sets up the first-person oracle quotation that opens immediately after it at web:Ps.132.14. The two-word phrase עֲדֵי עַ֑ד ('forever and ever') stands byte-identically (2 of 2 words match) at oshb:Ps.132.12 and oshb:Ps.132.14, straddling this row's own closing seam without moving it. The row closes at 132:13 rather than carrying the motive clause into the following quotation.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching 132:13 to the following oracle (132:14-18) instead was considered, since both concern Zion's election; rejected here because 132:13 stays in third-person report while 132:14 opens a first-person quotation of Yahweh's own voice -- the stronger, quotation-marked seam sits at 132:13|14, not 132:12|13.
observed_substrate_signals: the oath-verb forms at oshb:Ps.132.2 (נִ֭שְׁבַּע) and oshb:Ps.132.11 (נִשְׁבַּֽע) match at skeleton tier only (byte=False, accent_stripped=False since 132:11 retains a meteg absent from 132:2); not claimed to govern the whole row

the quotation opens mid-132:11, after the reporting clause, not at that verse's first character; it closes at web:Ps.132.12's own final character, not mid-verse; 132:13 is unquoted third-person report
no selah in Ps.132.11-Ps.132.13 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)

132:13 supplies the only naming of Zion that the following oracle's web:Ps.132.15-web:Ps.132.17 (outside this row's own span) depend on grammatically; the two-word phrase עֲדֵי עַ֑ד ('forever and ever') repeats byte-identically (2 of 2 words match) at oshb:Ps.132.12 and oshb:Ps.132.14, straddling this row's own 132:13|14 seam without moving it

boundary_rationale: A first-person divine oracle opens “זֹאת מְנוּחָתִ֥י עֲדֵי עַ֑ד” (oshb:Ps.132.14) -- “This is my resting place forever. I will live here, for I have desired it.” (web:Ps.132.14) -- and runs in Yahweh's own voice through the psalm's close, “I will clothe his enemies with shame, but on himself, his crown will shine.” (web:Ps.132.18), where the quotation mark shuts with the psalm. The oracle promises Zion's provision (132:15), her priests' salvation (132:16), David's horn and lamp (132:17), and his enemies' shame against his own shining crown (132:18). The oracle's Zion-provision promise (132:15-132:17) depends grammatically on the antecedent Zion named once, at web:Ps.132.13, one verse outside this row's own span. The two-word phrase עֲדֵי עַ֑ד that opens this row's own quotation at 132:14 also stands byte-identically (2 of 2 words match) at oshb:Ps.132.12, in the preceding oath quotation, straddling this row's opening seam without moving it: the third-person-to-first-person voice pivot at 132:13|14 remains the stronger driver. This is the Zion-election oracle proper, distinct from 132:13's third-person report of the same election.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Opening the row at 132:13, where Zion's election is initially named, was considered; rejected because 132:13 is third-person narration while 132:14 is the oracle's own first-person voice, marked by the WEB quotation boundary.
observed_substrate_signals: first-person divine quotation opens web:Ps.132.14 and closes at the psalm's own end, web:Ps.132.18 (WEB quotation marks)
no selah in Ps.132.14-Ps.132.18 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)
עֲדֵי עַ֑ד ('forever and ever') is byte-identical (2 of 2 words match) at oshb:Ps.132.12 and oshb:Ps.132.14 (this row's own opening word), straddling the 132:13|14 seam without moving it

boundary_rationale: Unlike 132, Psalm 133's title carries a name in title position: “שִׁ֥יר הַֽמַּעֲל֗וֹת לְדָ֫וִ֥ד” (oshb:Ps.133.1) (oshb:Ps.133.1) places the David-word directly after the genre label, a le-David attribution -- contrast 132:1 (web:Ps.132.0 = oshb:Ps.132.1), where the same word functions as the verb's indirect object, not a title element. Its three verses move as one indivisible image: “הִנֵּ֣ה מַה טּ֭וֹב וּמַה נָּעִ֑ים” (oshb:Ps.133.1) -- “See how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to live together in unity!” (web:Ps.133.1) -- develops through the anointing-oil simile (web:Ps.133.2) into the dew-of-Hermon simile and its closing blessing, “for there Yahweh gives the blessing, even life forever more.” (web:Ps.133.3). No vocative, quotation, or addressee shift divides the three verses; the whole is one wisdom-styled beatitude on communal unity.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the oil simile (133:2) from the dew simile (133:3) was considered, since the two develop distinct images; rejected as the two similes share one grammatical frame (comparison clauses elaborating 133:1's opening exclamation) with no independent seam marker between them.
observed_substrate_signals: title (oshb:Ps.133.1): “שִׁ֥יר הַֽמַּעֲל֗וֹת לְדָ֫וִ֥ד” -- the David-word sits in title position, immediately after the genre label (contrast 132:1)
psalm_device_inventory.json superscriptions entry for 133 lists le_david alongside shir/shir_hammaalot
no selah in Ps.133 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence, whole psalm)
device_notes: Psalm 133 anchors the parent grouping for these rows. -- Psalm 133 entire.

boundary_rationale: Psalm 134's title repeats 132's own wording, bare shir hamma'alot with no name attached (web:Ps.134.0 = oshb:Ps.134.1). Its three verses form one antiphonal exchange: an imperative call to the night-watch temple servants, “Look! Praise Yahweh, all you servants of Yahweh, who stand by night in Yahweh's house!” (web:Ps.134.1), continuing “Lift up your hands in the sanctuary. Praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.134.2), (בָּרֲכ֣וּ אֶת יְ֭הוָה, oshb:Ps.134.1, the imperative 'bless Yahweh', which WEB renders 'praise'; וּ֝בָרֲכוּ אֶת יְהוָֽה, oshb:Ps.134.2, the same 2mp imperative repeated), then a reply that reverses the direction of blessing: “יְבָרֶכְךָ֣ יְ֭הוָה מִצִּיּ֑וֹן” (oshb:Ps.134.3) -- “May Yahweh bless you from Zion, even he who made heaven and earth.” (web:Ps.134.3). The same root now stands 3ms with a 2ms object suffix ('he will bless you'). The call (134:1-2) addresses the servants in the imperative; the reply (134:3) turns the blessing back onto whoever has just spoken it, closing the short ascents collection's coda with this exchange rather than a further imperative.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 134:1-2 and 134:3 as two rows was considered, since the addressee reverses between them (servants addressed, then the worshipper blessed); rejected because three verses is too little to divide without padding, and no vocative, quotation, or report boundary marks an independent seam between the call and its answer.
observed_substrate_signals: title: shir hamma'alot, no name label (as 132, against 133's le-David; oshb:Ps.134.1)
second-person imperative addressee ("you" plural, the servants) in 134:1-2 reverses to second-person singular blessing-recipient in 134:3
no selah in Ps.134 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence, whole psalm)

the blessing root appears 3 times: 2mp imperative at oshb:Ps.134.1 (בָּרֲכ֣וּ) and oshb:Ps.134.2 (וּ֝בָרֲכוּ), then 3ms-with-2ms-suffix at oshb:Ps.134.3 (יְבָרֶכְךָ֣) -- the imperative call is answered in the same root, reversed in direction
device_notes: The psalm coheres as one composition: parent grouping Psalm 134, whole and undivided.

boundary_rationale: Untitled, Psalm 135 opens “הַ֥לְלוּ יָ֨הּ הַֽ֭לְלוּ אֶת שֵׁ֣ם יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.1) -- “Praise Yah! Praise Yahweh's name! Praise him, you servants of Yahweh,” (web:Ps.135.1) -- an imperative call to praise that continues through web:Ps.135.3's own hallelu-Yah (“Praise Yah, for Yahweh is good. Sing praises to his name, for that is pleasant.”), then supplies an opening motive for praise, “For Yah has chosen Jacob for himself, Israel for his own possession.” (web:Ps.135.4). The psalm's hallelu-Yah frame opens here in both its occurrences (verse-initial at 135:1 and 135:3, per psalm_device_inventory.json's halleluyah inventory) and, on that inventory, recurs verse-finally at the psalm's own close -- a frame this opening row does not itself carry evidence for past its own span.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Ending the row at 135:3, keeping just the imperative praise-calls together, was considered and is a serious rival reading. The particle "for" that opens both 135:4 and 135:5 stands on both sides of the 4|5 seam and is absent from 135:3's own opening, so it cannot itself be the reason a seam falls at 3|4 rather than 4|5 -- as a shared particle it argues for extending the rival span through 135:4, not against it. The stronger reason to keep 135:4 with this row instead is 135:5's own first-person-singular opening (oshb:Ps.135.5: כִּ֤י אֲנִ֣י, 'for I'), which launches an eight-verse third-person-dominant unit that 135:4's own motive clause does not share.
observed_substrate_signals: hallelu-Yah verse-initial at web:Ps.135.1 and web:Ps.135.3 (psalm_device_inventory.json halleluyah.verse_initial; 2 of the book's 11 verse-initial occurrences fall in this span)
motive-clause particle "for" opens both 135:4 and the following verse 135:5, a lexical bridge across this row's own closing seam
device_notes: One parent, Psalm 135, spans every row below it.

boundary_rationale: “כִּ֤י אֲנִ֣י יָ֭דַעְתִּי כִּי גָד֣וֹל יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.5) -- “For I know that Yahweh is great, that our Lord is above all gods.” (web:Ps.135.5) -- opens a declarative unit that runs through creation (“Whatever Yahweh pleased, that he has done, in heaven and in earth,” web:Ps.135.6; the clouds, lightning, and wind of web:Ps.135.7) into historical recital: “He struck the firstborn of Egypt, both of man and animal.” (web:Ps.135.8), signs and wonders sent on Pharaoh (web:Ps.135.9), many nations and mighty kings struck (web:Ps.135.10), “Sihon king of the Amorites, Og king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan-” (web:Ps.135.11), and their land given as a heritage to Israel (web:Ps.135.12). 135:5 itself is first-person (כִּ֤י אֲנִ֣י יָ֭דַעְתִּי, 'for I know', the row's own opening quote) and web:Ps.135.9 addresses Egypt directly in the second-person feminine singular (oshb:Ps.135.9: בְּתוֹכֵ֣כִי מִצְרָ֑יִם, 'in your midst, Egypt'); third-person description of Yahweh's own acts otherwise holds across 6 of 8 verses (135:6,7,8,10,11,12). The row closes where the psalm's address turns from Egypt (135:9) to Yahweh by name at web:Ps.135.13 (“Your name, Yahweh, endures forever”) -- an addressee-identity shift, not a person-number one, since 135:9 already carries second-person address inside this row's own span.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting creation (135:5-7) from the historical recital (135:8-12) was considered; rejected because no vocative, quotation, or addressee change marks that content transition -- Yahweh remains the third-person grammatical subject throughout, even where 135:9 addresses Egypt directly in the second person as the object of his acts.
observed_substrate_signals: third-person description of Yahweh's acts holds across 6 of 8 verses (135:6,7,8,10,11,12); 135:5 opens first-person (oshb:Ps.135.5: כִּ֤י אֲנִ֣י יָ֭דַעְתִּי) and 135:9 addresses Egypt in the second-person feminine singular (oshb:Ps.135.9: בְּתוֹכֵ֣כִי מִצְרָ֑יִם, 'in your midst, Egypt')

second-person address continues at web:Ps.135.13, now naming Yahweh rather than Egypt -- an addressee-identity shift, not a first appearance of second person, since 135:9 already addresses Egypt in second person within this row's own span

boundary_rationale: “יְ֭הוָה שִׁמְךָ֣ לְעוֹלָ֑ם” (oshb:Ps.135.13) -- “Your name, Yahweh, endures forever; your renown, Yahweh, throughout all generations.” (web:Ps.135.13) -- turns briefly to direct second-person address of Yahweh, naming him twice by vocative; web:Ps.135.14 then reverts to third person, “For Yahweh will judge his people and have compassion on his servants.” Both of 135:14's own verbs (oshb:Ps.135.14: יָדִ֣ין, יִתְנֶחָֽם) are prefix-conjugation forms, distinct from the suffix-conjugation forms that open the historical recital's own verses (135:8, 135:10). This two-verse span sits as a hinge between the historical recital closing at 135:12 and the idol polemic opening at 135:15: it neither continues the third-person recital's unbroken run nor opens the polemic's own topic.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Attaching this couplet to the preceding historical recital (135:5-12) was considered and rejected for the second-person vocative that opens 135:13; attaching it to the idol polemic that follows (135:15-18) was also considered and rejected because 135:14 names Yahweh's compassion on his own people, not yet the idols' impotence that 135:15 begins.
observed_substrate_signals: second-person vocative address to Yahweh ("Yahweh" named twice) opens web:Ps.135.13, unlike the third person on both sides of this span
no selah in Ps.135.13-Ps.135.14 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)

boundary_rationale: “עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם כֶּ֣סֶף וְזָהָ֑ב” (oshb:Ps.135.15) -- “The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.” (web:Ps.135.15) -- opens an idol polemic that runs through mouths that cannot speak and eyes that cannot see (web:Ps.135.16), ears that cannot hear (web:Ps.135.17), to the closing verdict, “Those who make them will be like them, yes, everyone who trusts in them.” (web:Ps.135.18). This four-verse unit shows cross-psalm texture with Ps 115's idol polemic (115:4-115:8): a word-by-word byte comparison of both psalms' own text (verse_map_oshb.json) finds oshb:Ps.135.16 matching oshb:Ps.115.5 and oshb:Ps.135.18 matching oshb:Ps.115.8 letter-for-letter, while 135:15's construct chain with the article (עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם) differs from 115:4's suffixed plural (oshb:Ps.115.4: עֲֽ֭צַבֵּיהֶם), and 135:17's own clause (oshb:Ps.135.17: אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ) is longer than 115:6 alone on all 3 measures taken (skeleton words, consonants, codepoints), running shorter only against 115:6-115:7 combined, and substitutes a different verb root (יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ for oshb:Ps.115.6's יִשְׁמָ֑עוּ) inside the clause the two verses share. It is discussed here as a recognizable, recurring cross-psalm texture, not merged with Ps 115's own rows.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Opening the row at 135:14 instead, to fold in Yahweh's compassion as a foil to the idols' impotence, was considered; kept separate because 135:14's two verbs (oshb:Ps.135.14: יָדִ֣ין, יִתְנֶחָֽם) are prefix-conjugation forms belonging with 135:13 in a distinct hinge couplet, not the suffix-conjugation forms of the historical recital (135:8, 135:10) -- and 135:14 does not yet reach the idols' inertness that 135:15 introduces as a fresh topic either way.
observed_substrate_signals: comparison against Ps 115's own idol polemic (115:4-115:8, verse_map_oshb.json): oshb:Ps.135.16 matches oshb:Ps.115.5 and oshb:Ps.135.18 matches oshb:Ps.115.8 letter-for-letter; 135:15's opening (oshb:Ps.135.15: עֲצַבֵּ֣י הַ֭גּוֹיִם) differs from 115:4's (oshb:Ps.115.4: עֲֽ֭צַבֵּיהֶם); 135:17 (oshb:Ps.135.17: אָזְנַ֣יִם לָ֭הֶם וְלֹ֣א יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ) is longer than 115:6 alone on all 3 measures (skeleton words, consonants, codepoints), shorter only against 115:6-115:7 combined, and substitutes a different verb root (יַאֲזִ֑ינוּ for oshb:Ps.115.6's יִשְׁמָ֑עוּ) -- cross-psalm texture, not a merged row
no selah in Ps.135.15-Ps.135.18 (pmarks_Ps.json; span-scoped absence)

boundary_rationale: A fourfold bless-call opens “בֵּ֣ית יִ֭שְׂרָאֵל בָּרֲכ֣וּ אֶת יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.19) -- “House of Israel, praise Yahweh! House of Aaron, praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.135.19) -- and continues “בֵּ֣ית הַ֭לֵּוִי בָּרֲכ֣וּ אֶת יְהוָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.135.20) -- “House of Levi, praise Yahweh! You who fear Yahweh, praise Yahweh!” (web:Ps.135.20). Four addressee groups are named across these two verses (house of Israel, house of Aaron, house of Levi, those who fear Yahweh); comparison against Ps 115's own trust-call (Israel, house of Aaron, those who fear Yahweh, named at 115:9-11) and Ps 118's own call-and-response (the same three) finds both naming three groups where this psalm's own bless-call names four, adding house of Levi as a fourth member; Ps 115's own bless-call (115:12-13,18) opens instead with 'house of Israel', not bare 'Israel'. The imperative vocative form returns after the idol polemic, bracketing the psalm with its opening call, and web:Ps.135.21's closing benediction carries this psalm's own verse-final hallelu-Yah, “Blessed be Yahweh from Zion, who dwells in Jerusalem. Praise Yah!”
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 135:19-20's fourfold call and 135:21's benediction as two rows was considered; kept together because 135:21 closes the same imperative sequence that 135:19-20 open, without introducing a fresh addressee.
observed_substrate_signals: bless-call names four addressee groups across web:Ps.135.19-Ps.135.20 (2 verses): house of Israel, house of Aaron, house of Levi, those who fear Yahweh

Ps 115's own trust-call (115:9-11) and Ps 118's own call-and-response name three groups (Israel, house of Aaron, those who fear Yahweh), without house of Levi; Ps 115's own bless-call (115:12-13,18) opens with 'house of Israel' rather than bare 'Israel'
hallelu-Yah verse-final at web:Ps.135.21, closing the frame opened at 135:1 and 135:3 (psalm_device_inventory.json halleluyah.verse_final)

boundary_rationale: Untitled, Psalm 136 opens “הוֹד֣וּ לַיהוָ֣ה כִּי ט֑וֹב” (oshb:Ps.136.1) -- “Give thanks to Yahweh, for he is good,” (web:Ps.136.1) -- the verse-initial hodu-le-YHWH formula listed in psalm_device_inventory.json's hodu_openings (one of six book-wide, alongside 33:2, 105:1, 107:1, 118:1, 118:29). A triadic escalation follows: “Give thanks to the God of gods” (web:Ps.136.2), “Give thanks to the Lord of lords” (web:Ps.136.3), each closed by this psalm's own refrain. A verse-by-verse comparison of the refrain's own tail across all 26 verses of this psalm finds “כִּ֖י לְעוֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ” (oshb:Ps.136.1) present in all 26, but not always in the same spelling: 136:3 spells the refrain's "forever" defectively, “לְעֹלָ֣ם חַסְדּֽוֹ” (oshb:Ps.136.3) (no vav in the second word), against the plene spelling in the other 25 -- an erratum-class spelling variant, not a break in the refrain's presence. web:Ps.136.4 then drops the imperative hodu-plus-object frame for a participial construction ("to him who…") that recurs through 136:4-25 but is interrupted by six finite-verb-headed verses (136:11,14,15,18,21,24), with the imperative hodu-plus-object frame itself returning at the psalm's own closing verse, 136:26 -- marking this row's own close at 136:3.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Extending the row through 136:4 was considered, since 136:4's own participle still names an attribute of Yahweh; rejected because 136:1-3 share one grammatical frame (imperative hodu + direct object) that 136:4 replaces with a participial construction recurring through 136:4-25 (interrupted by six finite-verb verses: 136:11,14,15,18,21,24) before the imperative frame itself returns at the psalm's own close, 136:26.
observed_substrate_signals: hodu-le-YHWH verse-initial at web:Ps.136.1 (psalm_device_inventory.json hodu_openings)

sweep: 26 of 26 verses in Ps 136 carry the closing refrain tail (direct verse-by-verse comparison of the final three words of each verse's own oshb text); 25 spelled plene, 1 (oshb:Ps.136.3) spelled defectively -- both attested spellings swept
grammatical frame shifts from imperative-plus-object (136:1-3) to participial construction beginning web:Ps.136.4
device_notes: Psalm 136's rows share a single parent composition throughout.

boundary_rationale: “לְעֹשֵׂ֣ה הַ֭שָּׁמַיִם בִּתְבוּנָ֑ה” (oshb:Ps.136.5) -- “to him who by understanding made the heavens, for his loving kindness endures forever;” (web:Ps.136.5) -- opens the creation recital, continuing through the great wonders of web:Ps.136.4, the earth spread above the waters (web:Ps.136.6), the great lights (web:Ps.136.7), and their assignment to rule day and night (web:Ps.136.8-9). 4 of 6 verses (136:4,5,6,7) keep the participial "to him who…" construction; 136:8 and 136:9 open instead with the object marker, naming the sun/moon/stars as objects rather than repeating the participle, though all 6 close with this psalm's refrain. The row's content turns from cosmic creation to Israel's history at its own close, where web:Ps.136.10 turns to Egypt.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A seam within 136:4-9, separating the general "great wonders" of 136:4 from the specific creation acts of 136:5-9, was considered; rejected as no grammatical marker distinguishes 136:4 from what follows -- the span still forms one syntactic chain (136:8-9 continue it with the object marker rather than a fresh participle) under the psalm's own refrain.
observed_substrate_signals: the participial "to him who…" construction opens 4 of 6 verses (136:4,5,6,7); 136:8 and 136:9 continue the same syntactic chain with the object marker introducing their objects (the sun, the moon and stars) rather than repeating the participle -- one continuous chain, not a self-standing sentence break, across this book-wide seam
content turns from cosmic creation (136:4-9) to Egypt/exodus beginning web:Ps.136.10, without a grammatical-form change

boundary_rationale: The recital turns to the exodus: “to him who struck down the Egyptian firstborn,” (web:Ps.136.10), Israel brought out (web:Ps.136.11), with a strong hand and outstretched arm (web:Ps.136.12), the Red Sea divided (“לְגֹזֵ֣ר יַם ס֭וּף לִגְזָרִ֑ים” (oshb:Ps.136.13)), Israel passed through (web:Ps.136.14), and Pharaoh's army overthrown in the sea (web:Ps.136.15). All 6 verses in this span (136:10-15) close with this psalm's refrain, as do all 26 verses of this psalm. The row's content turns from the sea crossing to the wilderness march at its own close, where web:Ps.136.16 turns to the wilderness.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding 136:10 into the preceding creation row (136:4-9) was considered, since both share the participial frame; rejected because 136:10 is the recital's opening Egypt-naming verse, opening the exodus content movement rather than closing the creation one.
observed_substrate_signals: content moves from Egypt's plague (136:10) through the Red Sea crossing (136:13-15); grammatical form (participle/finite-verb alternation) does not itself mark this row's edges -- content alone does
wilderness march named beginning at web:Ps.136.16, immediately after this row's own close

boundary_rationale: The recital moves from wilderness to conquest: Yahweh led his people through the wilderness (web:Ps.136.16), struck great kings (web:Ps.136.17) and killed mighty kings (web:Ps.136.18), naming them by name -- “לְ֭סִיחוֹן מֶ֣לֶךְ הָאֱמֹרִ֑י” (oshb:Ps.136.19) (web:Ps.136.19) and “וּ֭לְעוֹג מֶ֣לֶךְ הַבָּשָׁ֑ן” (oshb:Ps.136.20) (web:Ps.136.20) -- before their land is given as a heritage to Israel (web:Ps.136.21-22). This Sihon/Og notice shows cross-psalm texture with Ps 135's own Sihon/Og verses (135:11-135:12): the Sihon clause (136:19 against 135:11) matches at the skeleton/accent-stripped tier only (differing in cantillation), the Og clause (136:20 against 135:11) is byte-identical, and the land-grant clause that follows (136:21-22 against 135:12) varies from Ps 135's own wording in two words at the skeleton/accent-stripped tier (four words differ at the byte tier, since two more carry accent-only differences). web:Ps.136.23 then shifts from third-person "his people" to first-person-plural "us", marking this row's own close.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the wilderness march (136:16) from the conquest naming (136:17-22) was considered; rejected because no grammatical or addressee change divides them -- both stay third-person description of Yahweh's acts toward "his people"/"Israel" under the shared refrain.
observed_substrate_signals: comparison against Ps 135's own Sihon/Og verses (135:11-135:12, verse_map_oshb.json): the Sihon clause (136:19) matches 135:11 at skeleton/accent-stripped tier only (cantillation differs); the Og clause (136:20) is byte-identical to 135:11; the land-grant clause (136:21-22) differs from 135:12 in two words at skeleton/accent-stripped tier, four words at byte tier -- cross-psalm texture, not a merged row

boundary_rationale: “שֶׁ֭בְּשִׁפְלֵנוּ זָ֣כַר לָ֑נוּ” (oshb:Ps.136.23) -- “who remembered us in our low estate,” (web:Ps.136.23) -- turns from the historical third person to first-person-plural address, continuing “and has delivered us from our adversaries,” (web:Ps.136.24) before web:Ps.136.25 widens to a universal, impersonal close, “who gives food to every creature,” before the psalm's own final verse returns to its opening imperative, “ה֭וֹדוּ לְאֵ֣ל הַשָּׁמָ֑יִם” (oshb:Ps.136.26) -- “Oh give thanks to the God of heaven,” (web:Ps.136.26) -- an inclusio repeating web:Ps.136.1's own hodu-le-YHWH opening imperative at the skeleton/accent-stripped tier (byte-identical to 136:2 and 136:3's own opening word, though not 136:1's, which differs only in cantillation); the divine-name member itself changes from 'Yahweh' (136:1) to 'the God of heaven' (136:26). The row closes the psalm at its own closing verse.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Treating 136:26 as its own one-verse coda, separate from 136:23-25, was considered for its inclusio function; rejected as too short to divide from the closing movement it caps, and the psalm's own refrain still binds it to 136:23-25 without a fresh addressee change.

boundary_rationale: Untitled, Psalm 137 opens “עַ֥ל נַהֲר֨וֹת בָּבֶ֗ל שָׁ֣ם יָ֭שַׁבְנוּ” (oshb:Ps.137.1) -- “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down. Yes, we wept, when we remembered Zion.” (web:Ps.137.1) -- a first-person-plural scene of captivity, continuing “On the willows in that land, we hung up our harps.” (web:Ps.137.2), then reporting the captors' own demand in quotation, “Sing us one of the songs of Zion!” (web:Ps.137.3), before the exiles' own rhetorical refusal closes the row, “How can we sing Yahweh's song in a foreign land?” (web:Ps.137.4). All 4 verses of this span stay in the communal "we" voice; the row closes where that voice narrows to first-person-singular at web:Ps.137.5.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting the captivity scene (137:1-2) from the captors' demand and the refusal (137:3-4) was considered; rejected because both share the same first-person-plural "we" voice with no addressee shift between them, 0 of 4 verses (137:1-4) carry a second-person or first-person-singular form outside the captors' own quoted demand, and 137:4's question is the direct rhetorical answer to 137:3's own demand.

boundary_rationale: The voice narrows from communal "we" to first-person-singular self-imprecation: “אִֽם אֶשְׁכָּחֵ֥ךְ יְֽרוּשָׁלִָ֗ם” (oshb:Ps.137.5) -- “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand forget its skill.” (web:Ps.137.5) -- continuing “Let my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth if I don't remember you, if I don't prefer Jerusalem above my chief joy.” (web:Ps.137.6). Jerusalem is addressed directly by name in apostrophe across both verses, distinct from the preceding "we"-voiced captivity scene and the imprecation that follows: 137:7 opens a fresh second-person imperative addressed to Yahweh against Edom, while 137:8-9 turn to address Babylon directly in the second-person feminine singular.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Folding this couplet into the following imprecation (137:7-9) was considered, since both continue the psalm's private voice; rejected because 137:5-6 is self-imprecation addressed to Jerusalem by apostrophe, while 137:7 opens a fresh imperative addressed to Yahweh against a third party.

boundary_rationale: The imprecation turn opens “זְכֹ֤ר יְהוָ֨ה לִבְנֵ֬י אֱד֗וֹם” (oshb:Ps.137.7) -- “Remember, Yahweh, against the children of Edom in the day of Jerusalem,” (web:Ps.137.7) -- quoting Edom's own cry, “Raze it! Raze it even to its foundation!” The address then turns from Yahweh to Babylon directly, “Daughter of Babylon, doomed to destruction, he will be happy who repays you, as you have done to us.” (web:Ps.137.8), closing with the psalm's own harsh closing line, “Happy shall he be, who takes and dashes your little ones against the rock.” (web:Ps.137.9). The row groups the Edom imprecation and the Babylon imprecation as one closing movement, opened by the second-person imperative to Yahweh at 137:7 and sustained in second-person address (now to Babylon) through the psalm's end.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Separating the Edom imprecation (137:7) from the Babylon imprecation (137:8-9) into two rows was considered, since the addressee shifts from Yahweh to Babylon between them; rejected because both remain second-person imperative/vocative address sustained without a first-person or third-person report intervening, and the row is already short.

boundary_rationale: The composition opens with a thanksgiving vow, “I will give you thanks with my whole heart” (web:Ps.138.1), and closes with a confident petition, “Don’t forsake the works of your own hands” (web:Ps.138.8), an envelope from vow to petition that runs across only 8 verses -- within the short-psalm threshold for a whole-psalm row. The middle sets direct address aside for the kings’ report (web:Ps.138.4-5) and Yahweh’s care for the lowly (web:Ps.138.6), a third-person interval framed by direct address on both sides (web:Ps.138.4, web:Ps.138.7), before web:Ps.138.7 returns to address Yahweh directly through the close; the interval develops the opening vow rather than opening an independently marked strophe (no selah, no vocative reset, no genre-label shift inside the body).
strongest_rejected_alternative: Splitting after web:Ps.138.4’s shift from personal thanksgiving to the kings’ response was considered, but web:Ps.138.5 continues the same third-person report about Yahweh’s ways without a vocative reset strong enough to carry a strophe break in a psalm this short.

boundary_rationale: The meditation opens its known movement on the root pair “יְהוָ֥ה חֲ֝קַרְתַּ֗נִי וַתֵּדָֽע” (oshb:Ps.139.1) -- “Yahweh, you have searched me, and you know me” (web:Ps.139.1) -- which surveys Yahweh’s knowledge of the psalmist’s sitting/rising, path, and unspoken word (web:Ps.139.2-4) before closing on the psalmist’s own confession, “This knowledge is beyond me” (web:Ps.139.6). The root pair recurs at web:Ps.139.23 (“Search me, God, and know my heart”), so this opening row anchors one half of the psalm’s inclusio.
strongest_rejected_alternative: A break after web:Ps.139.3’s summary of “all my ways” was considered, but vv4-6 continue the same second-person survey of Yahweh’s knowledge without a discourse-marking shift until the rhetorical questions of web:Ps.139.7.

boundary_rationale: The movement turns from Yahweh’s knowledge to Yahweh’s presence, opening with the rhetorical double question “Where could I go from your Spirit? Or where could I flee from your presence?” (web:Ps.139.7), surveying heaven, Sheol, and the wings of the dawn (web:Ps.139.8-10) before closing on darkness and light (web:Ps.139.11-12). An anaphoric “gam” (גם, “even/also”) opens both web:Ps.139.10 and web:Ps.139.12 at the consonantal (skeleton) tier, tying the unit's middle to its own close rather than to the prior movement's close at web:Ps.139.6.
strongest_rejected_alternative: Closing the unit at web:Ps.139.10 (after “your right hand will hold me”) was considered, but vv11-12 continue the same spatial-evasion logic under the rhetorical-question frame opened at web:Ps.139.7, so the movement is kept whole through its own close.

boundary_rationale: The movement shifts to the psalmist’s formation, opening “For you formed my inmost being. You knit me together in my mother’s womb” (web:Ps.139.13), grounding the prior movements’ claims in a remembered event, and continuing through the “fearfully and wonderfully made” confession (web:Ps.139.14) and the divine book of ordained days (web:Ps.139.16) to close on “When I wake up, I am still with you” (web:Ps.139.18) -- a relational close distinct from the abrupt imprecation that opens web:Ps.139.19.

boundary_rationale: The petition opens “מֵאִ֖ישׁ חֲמָסִ֣ים תִּנְצְרֵֽנִי” (oshb:Ps.140.2) -- “Preserve me from violent men” (web:Ps.140.1) -- and the same phrase recurs at web:Ps.140.4, “מֵאִ֣ישׁ חֲמָסִ֣ים תִּנְצְרֵ֑נִי” (oshb:Ps.140.5); the two occurrences share their consonants (skeleton tier) but differ by one meteg mark on the final verb (accent_stripped tier), so the repetition is a reprise of the petition rather than a copied line.
